These are the notes I took in the middle of the night while wrapping up my first playthrough of this amazing game a few months ago:
- Combat feels like hitting a packets of crisps with a metal bat (unlike Kingdom Hearts, where combat feels like hitting a shallow pool with a fish).
- You know it's an an action game when you have to rebind your keys. You ever had to rebind your keys for a JRPG? I rest my case.
- Played [the last boss] all night, in a romantically obsessive sort of way. Then I see it getting light again outside, and it stops being romantic and starts being sad. But soon, at about 5:30am, I beat him.
- My heart hasn't been beating that hard in... [?]
- Maybe sleep deprivation is affecting my judgement here, but it seems like that was pretty much the most incredible boss fight I have ever played. I'm comparing it to Megaman Zero and ZX, Iga Castlevania, God of War... I guess Megaman ZX comes closes, but so much of the excitement in those games is beating the boss guantlet, committing all that time before you even get to the actual last boss. Oath's last boss is self contained. You die, you start again at the beginning of the fight — and after, what, 4 hours, it was still incredible fun.
I can't wait to play Origins.

I was very hesitant about buying this game at first because of all the Reviews complaining about artificial difficulty, which badly reminded me of Dark Souls II and it's horrible "LOL U DIED PRAISE THE SON XD SO HARD"-marketing campaign. Luckily I can say that this game is nothing like Dark Souls II (except for the marketing campaign which thinks that difficulty is a good selling point and a "consult and FAQ already XDDD" achievement are funny) and I really cannot understand all the reviews complaining about this game being unnecessarily hard. I played on normal, which I think is the intended difficulty and I never had a problem with artifical difficulty the only thing that I can think of that comes close, is that the hitbox of one of the 2nd boss' attacks is büllshit when he's in his last phase. The dungeons themselves are pretty easy, thanks to the carefully placed save points, but the Bosses are the real challenge. The Bossfights are hard but always fair. This game really forces you to learn all the patterns of every boss in and out. If you don't know how to deal with an attack of a boss, you're dead. That's it. You can't afford to not know how to deal with all of the enemies attacks, as this game has no healing during bossfights, meaning that if you take damage, you will have to continue with your reduced health for the rest of the fight. One thing that always annoyed me about Dark Souls (even though I really like Dark Souls, or at least the first half of it) is that you always had to make a "corpse run" from the last bonfire to a boss and while this mechanic is okay the first few times, after a while it gets really tedious and loses its point of making you learn the level. This game doesn't have that, you restart the fight instantly and can die as many times as you want without any penalty or downside. You can learn the boss' patterns as long as it takes you, even if it takes you 100 tries. This game doesn't really put an emphasis on this but you really, really need to carefully scan your environments for loot because having the best possible equipment at all times is key to victory. This also means that you should constantly keep your equipment upgraded to max. Regarding the story, it's about as cliche as it get's and while all the characters are likeable, they have about as much depth as a puddle. But still, the story does it's job and doesn't get in the way of the gameplay. The soundtrack however is an absolute masterpiece, it fits all the situations perfectly, gets you pumped up and just sounds great. As for the controls, I strongly encourage setting the magic button to one of the shoulder buttons as that way it's much easier to charge magic and use your sword at the same time. Otherwise they're perfectly fine, every button is rebindable and you can chose which connected controller you want to use. The graphics are dated but the pre-rendered sprites look great and allow for some detailed enemy designs, also this probably runs on a toaster.
Overall I would give this game a solid 8.5 out of 10

I gotta admit, this is a game I grew up playing on the SNES, although at the time I believe it was called Wanderer's of YS 3 and not Oath of Felghana. I always worry whenever a game gets switched to an isometric or 3d playstyle from a 2d side scroller but this one was perfectly executed. They captured the same challenges as the first game, the movement and combat are fluid even jumping around. I do admit that the ring system on the SNES version gave you a few more abilities you could use opposed to what we have now but I also understand their design decision because they were going for a more action packed, fast to play game style.
It all worked well. I mean I admit my first playthrough picking hard difficulty may not have been the best choice. I raged, oh boy did I rage LOL. But I won! That satisfying feeling of winning something really difficult can't be beat. That is what the developers did right with this remake. They captured that satisfying feeling of victory with fast, action packed gameplay that didn't depend on game design that punishes you for 'dying' by making you waste time backtracking. You die? Jump right back in and try again gives it that arcade feeling where you get addicted and just keep putting in those quarters until you finally win and shout YES! WOOHOO! I'M AWESOME!
I have absolutely no complaints about the gameplay at all. If you don't like your games to be difficult, this isn't the game for you. If you appreciate a challenge and feel the victory of overcoming such challenges is a sweet reward, you will love this.
As far as the story goes? Well I had to install some mod to get the voice acting from the PSP working here. I really liked the voice acting and the story overall is pretty good. It's really your stereotypical hero who conquors evil with some really nice twists. I can't call it the most riveting story ever told but it is absolutely enjoyable, at least to me.
Also the music... wow. The composer did a fantastic job with the music score in this game. It's so blood pumping and at times emotional and makes up some of the best music I've heard in the industry actually.
The Art style? Well it's an isometric 2d style, top down camera, pixel art and level design giving the illusion of 3d but I can really appreciate this style it's colorful and creative.
Lastly, the level design. Many of it feels maze-like with some hidden secrets. They did a pretty good job capturing that old school level design we appreciated on the SNES game. But it isn't so maze-like that you can find yourself lost and going around in circles constantly.
Ys: The Oath of Felghana is a masterful recreation of the SNES game Wanderer's of YS 3 and i've enjoyed every minute I spent in this game thoroughly and will continue to support Xseed's future YS projects.

Overfall is an RPG which uses tactical-turn-based combat, exploration and roguelike elements in it’s core. It has enormous potential in terms of story, innovative turn-based combat, replayability, unending possibilities and is a world full of different procedurally-generated floras of islands. Also, there is permanent death. Thus, once you fail you start again.
From my experience, as for closed-beta builds, there are no current game-breaking bugs and the devs are constantly updating the game.
You start the game by running away from some mysterious Viking-like horde called the Vorn which seeks to find an artifact you've been stolen from them. Literally, this is the main menu scenery. After you hit the start, you see the character creation. What I really like about character creation is that there are huge amount of combinations, but they must be unlocked by going through many playthroughs(as like many other roguelike games). In a regular playthrough, you’re almost guaranteed to unlock some stuff you can try at your next one.
Best part is, you choose two heroes instead of one to start the game. You get to choose their weapons(each weapon has 3 skills, but we’ll get to that later in combat), utility skills and trinkets(passive abilities). Apart from the starting gear, all of these include a lot of things to unlock within them.
Once you choose your combination and hop into the game, an old wizard-like man welcomes you at the entrance and says your arrival has been foretold in the prophecy, and that they’ve been waiting for you for ages. Gives you a little bit of introduction to the basic lore and sends you out to the ocean to reach your king. The main goal is; you must find your King who sent you through the Portal to steal the “artifact” and deliver it. But since it has been hundreds of years(probably because of some cosmic stuff done by the portal’s cosmic structure), nothing stayed the same as you left them. Your King is missing, there are conflicts all over the place and as if that’s not enough, you brought some nasty invaders with your arrival.
The game consists of “scenes” or whatever you call them all the way through. Every scene includes a beautifully painted and animated background image, your party members at the left side of the screen, thought bubbles as a reaction to the current situation, and responding situation at the other side the scene or NPCs to conversate. The bubbles are your clickable options and the way of choosing a response to what’s going on was implemented in such a cute way like I’ve never seen in a game before. There is also a narrative bar at the top of your screen that tells you about what’s happening in short sentences like a GM in D&D games. The scene with the old-guy who enlightens you about what’s the current situation is first of these scenes.
The “prophecy”’s advice to you is that you must activate 2 of the 6 beacons who are under control of the races of Dys.
What are beacons? Great question. The Beacons are magical wells who were given to the six main races, by raising your reputation and activating two of these magic beans, you break the invisibility spell of your king’s Citadel and reveal it on your map. This is the main progression of the game if your desire is to finish it.
Real conflict is, the Vorn somehow know about the beacons as well and are seeking to find them. Before you do… The progression of the reputations, beacon activities and the Vorn invasion are shown to you very clearly within the UI and it’s like a real time race-to-end combination of FTL and Risk of Rain, because the game gets harder as the invasion grows.
The Vorn constantly raze the islands they encounter to gather resources. They use these resources to establish a base, build officer ships, their King’s ship and by using all of that power, they start to invade homelands of main races to actually unlock the beacons you’re looking for.
After hopping to your ship, you start to visit the islands one-by-one. Encountering different adventures, gathering resources to upgrade your skills and weapons, adding new members to your party, raising/lowering reputations are few of the things you can expect in these islands.
At the moment, the game has limited amount of encounters but as I said, it’s an unending growth in terms of development.
As of encounters, the devs used a system where each character you include in your party might have a different opinion to what’s going on. Apart from that, there are multiple outcomes to each decision you make. This increases the chance to see different situations in an encounter every time you play.
So, the combat. Even though at first you may think that it looks like a regular turn-based RPG combat, the uniqueness of it is really convinced me that they like to innovate a lot. What’s the difference, you say? They didn’t use action points.(I personally hate that mechanic) instead, they added something called the “Phase” system at the bottom of the classic turn-round cycle. Each character goes through 3 phases. “Movement”, “Utility” and “Weapon”. And the other thing I really liked is “Conditions”.
Conditions include tons of buffs(good) or debuffs(bad) that you can apply to your foes, allies or even to yourself. Instead of getting used to each individual skill in the game, they compiled everything you can expect from an RPG game to these conditions. Once you get through the learning curve and master these conditions, It becomes an intense and evenly fun experience.
Back to the those “Phases”; Movement Phase consists of simply moving your character to an hex or a unique Movement Skill suited to the each character that alters the positioning of the characters in the battlefield. Which could be the Fighter leaping or the Cleric pulling an ally towards herself for protection.
Utility phase is where you “utilize” the battlefield in a larger scale with your 3 skills. Only thing is, you can do anything except dealing direct damage in this phase. It may include applying/removing/transferring conditions, healing, pulling/pushing etc.
Lastly, you get to use your mighty weapon within the “Weapon Phase”. Each unique weapon has 3 skills based on it’s capabilities and lore. All of these skills deal direct damage and are aimed to weaken your foe with conditions as a side-work. The thing to remember is these skills are not your character’s, but the weapon’s. Your character is just the wielder.
The skill effects are really cool, some sound effects are still missing though. Combat balance changes between patches, but is OK and kinda hard(which is good) in my opinion. Combats are always a part of the encounter you’re going through with a little story behind them, which makes it more memorable.
After each combat, your characters have a chance to earn “Personas” - a part of the character progression and can change character stats or act as a passive ability with a trigger that pops up during the combat. These could be both negative or positive ones. For example, your characters can become “Brain Damaged”, or “Avenger” during the combat depending on what happened. Apart from these, you can unlock new things, earn/lose loot or increase/reputations with a race after a combat.
Party size may increase up to 4 depending on your reputation level with a single race. But once you lose a companion in battle, you can’t hire him/her again in the same playthrough, so they’re gone for good. With their hardly earned Personas.
Conclusion : Overfall

Despite being a huge Warhammer fan, I have to strongly advise you to not buy this game.
- The Game is 5 Missions long, which I finished in 2 hours. So beware of that.
- Out of 4 Classes, 2 are virtually useless because being a melee class just ends up getting you killed extremely fast.

However, basically this would be a competent and fun twin-stick shooter but two things kill this game entirely. Glitches and the worst camera of gaming. Seriously, the camera is pure sin. I had to restart so many times because the camera decided it doesn't want to follow me anymore, and even when it works it tends to be in really bad spots.
And the most notable glitch I experienced was with moving platforms, aka elevators. I don't know what was wrong but my Marine and enemies would glitch through or get bounced off from it, falling to my death.
Tl;dr
---------
I had to start the third Mission like 14 times because I died in the cutscene to the elevator. I died in the cutscene. Don't buy this broken piece of Warhammer blasphemy. Go buy Space Marine instead.
EDIT: As a sidenote: I played alone, maybe the class balance issue is lessened if you play co-op. Still, my argument remains that you should not buy this.

Now, the veterans can defend this game all they like, but I started playing the game around the day that the infamous level 90 patch came out so let me release a review from the viewpoint of a new play who has reach level 75 and stopped playing due to immense boredom
Pros
>Combat System
-The combat system is the only thing that this game has going for it, you can pull intricate strings of combos and abilities
>Classes
-Each class is unique and awesome, I love how they all look
Cons
>EVERYTHING ELSE!
-Let me elaborate
>Any dungeons below level 90 are SUPER MEGA ULTRA..... easy
-Apparently, these dungeons USED to be difficult, but they decided to completely F***ING remove the hardest difficulties for all low level dungeons. The nests are easy when they used to require a party, (I MEAN FOR GOD'S SAKE, YOU'RE NOT EVEN ALLOWED TO PARTY FOR THE FIRST NEST) you take no damage while the enemies all die in one hit, and you can't even stumble over to higher level dungeons if you want a challenge because it's barred by a level cap, and by the time you reach the recommended level for the dungeon, it'll be too easy. I was waiting for the game to get difficult FOR 75 LEVELS. I WAS ONE SHOTTING EVERY ENEMY AND BOSS IN EVERY DUNGEON FOR 75 LEVELS! At that point, if the game can provide zero excitement for what was essentially 70% of the game, then it's not good game design. And I'm patient, oh I'm very patient, I'm always willing to give a game a chance, but this game could not impress me, it took too long.
>Story missions progress way too slowly
-I won't talk too much for this one. Basically, once you reach level 60, the dungeons that you have to traverse through for the story will have a recommended level of 45. Not to mention, really intimidating monsters appear in the story cutscenes a lot, and you end up getting excited at the fact that you'll be able to finally get a challenge, only to have your  character get stomped on in the cutscene and have the bad guy run off with the important McGuffin that you were sent to chase after and you instead have to fight some insignificant boss, that just basically ends up becoming a miniboss in later dungeons. But hey, at least there's occasional voice acting and almost every character has a unique personality why you can then elborate on through giving them gifts, but that's only fun if you're actually interested in this game's story.
>PvP is "Balanced"
-Unless you're playing with friends who are around the same level as you, you're essentially not allowed to PvP until you're level 90. Oh, don't worry though, there's and equalizer put into play so that your stats are basically increased to what they would be around level 90. The problem is that your skills still do garbage damage against players who have more points put into their skill trees, have better armor, and have learned their combos while you have nothing to protect yourself with.. The equalizer just makes killing you take like 30 more seconds than it should.
Don't play this game unless you have a time machine. I've heard countless good things about the game before the update, all things that I wish I could've been a part of, but from what I can guess, the developers wanted to make it easier to reach level 90 to appeal to players who want have level 90 characters for all the classes, and for some reason they decided to remove content that didn't need to be removed in the first place.

Okay, before I start my rant, I gotta let you know that I still love this game and I assure you that it's totally worth the $30. The mod support alone makes it well worth it. The combat mechanics are solid, the platforming is great, all that jazz. That said, the content we've been waiting on for so long is a big disappointment.
There's less story in here than there was in the Lugaru campaign. While it normally wouldn't be a problem, especially since it does offer some new experiences, everything happens on such a small scale and ends so abruptly. This was okay in Lugaru, since you're out in the middle of friggin' nowhere. But when you hear things about separate races and a slave trade conspiracy, you'd think that all those conversations and arena battles would build up to something a bit more than one-shotting a cat. What's even more insulting is climbing that huge tower of rock and the final boss is just a tough looking rabbit with two swords that ends up being easier to kill than some regular guard rabbits you encounter early in the game. I was so eager to find out what was in store just for the story to drop for little reason other than it wants to without any payoff whatsoever.
On top of this, Turner as a character has become a bland, Mary-Sue type badass whose only shtick is how easily he can kill people because he's taken down wolves so many times. It pretty much boils down to "I just wanted to live a quiet life, but you guys need help so I'll just kick everybody's♥♥♥♥♥to help you since I'm so awesome. Also, I almost never talk about my origins, just vaguely reference them in a way that would confuse even those that have played through the Lugaru campaign."
Though the Lugaru campaign isn't much less bland, it at least has some theming going on. Turner's wife and daughter were murdered and possibly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ along with the rest of his tribe. Those he cared about died horribly and he had nothing left to lose, and since he's an experienced warrior, then he might as well find and kill those responsible or die trying because there's nothing else to live for anymore. This has a lot more impact than "I don't want any trouble, OOPS I accidentally stepped in some trouble, now I guess I have to kill everybody." That's why I still enjoyed Lugaru even though it wasn't that much to write home about.
After the comic, all the new races, and the promising lore, there was so much opportunity for world building. That opportunity was squandered. If it wasn't for how good the game is outside the campaign, I wouldn't be recommending it as I am. Sorry Wolfire, but the Overgrowth campaign isn't that good.
So yes, DEFINITELY BUY THE GAME. But, as an addendum, go to the workshop and download Therium 2. It's a mod campaign with a much better story, more lore, and multiple endings. It's not the best written, but it's immersive and captivating enough to keep your attention. And the level design is fantastic.

I've been following Wolfire games for years now and am really excited to see this game finally leave it's alpha after 9 years. Honestly I had a great time playing this game. I read a lot of bad things about the gameplay and while I can't disagree it has its problems, I still had a lot of fun. The fighting feels unique and exciting. The biggest complaint I have is how little content there is in the game. I guess they are allowing the community to pick up slack what with their mod support, but the story to both lugaru prequel and the game itself felt short and left much to be desired. The story was just way to linear, then again I still enjoyed the game mechanics enough to beat them all.
The platforming feels floaty but I didn't find it that dificult like some others have said, and climbing to insane heights only to mispress a button and fall down huge cliff faces whats exciting and humourous all at the same time. There were definitely sometimes where I feel as though the character does not do what you're trying to get him to do. Luckily checkpoints are frequent and there are no loading screens so you're right back into it in seconds.
The game's arena mode is where I spent a lot of my time after beating the story, though it got repetitive fast and only has 4 levels.
Overall I recommend this game if you're just looking for a short and sweet experience that you can come back to from time to time. If you're looking for a vast playthough and gripping story, maybe skip it.
Although the developers released the game, I'm hoping they can maybe add more in the future. Otherwise, maybe I'll have to give a crack at mods.

TL;DR the fight mechanics are incredible.
After playing the hell out of this game's predecessor, Lugaru, I preordered Overgrowth back in 2011 and I've watched the development videos for years. I waited until release to actually play through it and man it's fun. The combat is so satisfying, and it's more rewarding the better you become at it. Once you're really comfortable it's incredibly satisfying to duke it out and trade blows in a proper fight. Of course you can cheese it with the bunny kick but it's way more fun to use counters, disarms, and trade blows.
The weapons are a lot of fun to use, and when you're facing a level with a bunch of enemies, it's fun to try different strategies. You can go in stealthily, choke the enemies, or use a weapon, maybe just run up and stab them or use the kick for a quick knockdown. The campaign is so much fun to play through, and pretty challenging! It took me about 4 hours to play through and I kind of wish there was more!
Plus my number one wish would be to have avian characters in the game. This is kind of possible with mods, although it's not quite properly implemented in the game.
The dev team went to great lengths to make the game moddable and there's entire campaigns to check out! Therium-2 is a cool one which I haven't finished yet.
I'm excited the devs will continue to support the game as it's clearly been a labour of love - nine years in the making. I can't wait to see what other mods the community comes out with and it would be cool to even be a part of that somehow.
So this game gets my recommendation!

Let me get a few things out of the way first.
Yes, this game is a grind. The grind is the acutal gameplay, to be precise. If you don't like grinding, this isn't your game.
Yes, this game takes a long time until you get the feeling of being "in the late game", whatever that might mean to you.
Yes, this game does a horrible job explaining things.
And if you don't have a lot of time to spare, you will probably feel disadvantaged, or that it seems to push you towards buying premium currency.
However - if you DO have time to spare, this game is a gem.
A huge selection of different weapons (that actually FEEL different) and Warframes (let's just call them characters for now), with different, MOBA-like abilities, short or endless mission types, a surprisingly relevant clan system, and since recently, the plains of eidolon, which feel like a seperate, additional game.
The community is incredibly helpful and kind, and recruiting chat is active for almost all possible activities.
The trade chat is confusing, but there are third-party sites which do a really good job of organizing the player-based market.
Once you got a bit into the game, the quests start following a surprisingly interesting story (which you wouldn't expect from a game about space ninjas, to be completely honest...)
About the free-to-play aspect:
I HAVE spent money on this, but I did it because I wanted to pay the developers. If i didn't want to, I would have no disadvantage.
The big, big step the developers took, is that the premium currency (platinum) is tradeable. Need more weapon slots? Do a few vault runs, sell the results on the market, and there you go. Don't want to grind for that one specific mod? Look for it on the market, and buy it for a couple plat, that you got from earlier trades.
The only few things that are not available with platinum are purely cosmetical, and only those which are part of the Tennogen project - skins developed by the community.
This game has come far. It is nowhere near the place it was on launch in 2013, it has evolved and grown and while it does have its flaws, the devs are always trying to improve and expand the game.
Thank you, DE, for this massive grindfest, which gave me so many hours of entertainment.

This is a very fun game, and I would reccomend it to any fans of the strategy genre. The game is fun, engaging, interesting and sometimes hilarious, with the occasional occurence that is just messed up. I was once playing as a lustful old guy with a couple lovers. My wife is away at a convent or something, and I decide to see my lover when the event pops up... Little did I know that I would proceed to.... ♥♥♥♥ myself.... And become pregnant.... With my own child....... I think that's definitely a bug, and you can rest assured that the child that was born was disowned and banished.
However, with that aside, I do have one major complaint about this game, namely the DLC. While I understand that Paradox needs to make money and pay its employees, it is utterly ridiculous that a hundred dollars worth of DLC is mostly features that should be in the vanilla game for no extra cost. The Ruler Designer DLC, for example. For five more dollars, you get the ability to customize your character! And that is literally it. For an eighth of the price of the entire game extra, you get the ability to customize the first character of a dynasty. And only the first character.
For the added bonus of being able to play a non-christian ruler, you have to pay more money. Want to have a couple more options for the character customization? Fork out a little extra cash and you can. Want an earlier starting date? Pay Paradox! Twice! Want Genghis Khan to actually look like a Mongol and NOT an Arab? PAY MORE MONEY!
While this is probably the best stategy game I have ever played, it is utterly ridiculous that you have to pay truckloads of money extra to use some features that should be in the CORE GAME. The ability to customize your ruler should NOT be something you pay an extra five dollars for, it should be in the core game for no extra cost. Too large a chunk of the available DLC are simply features that should be in the main game for no extra charge. So while I would recommend this game to fans of the genre, I would NEVER reccomend the DLC, at least not to people who are on a budget. Some of the DLC is worthy of extra cost, most of it is not.

I reviewed this game back in 2013. Now I'm forced to come back & change this review.
The move to F2P is a somewhat welcome change, allowing the playerbase to expand, which was one of the main issues with the game as of recently.
That, unfortunately, is currently the only good thing so far...
First of all: All offline functionality has been removed from the game. All of it. No initial sign-in then offline play, everything requires you to be connected to the game servers, even offline practice against bots. I live in the middle of nowhere with broadband only a couple of steps better than dial-up, so not being able to play the game, even against bots, is damning, especially for existing players.
EDIT: 4th May: As it turns out, you can play this offline, you must disconnect from the game servers after the online verification. There should be an offline game option regardless of wether or not you're connected to the servers though. They have stated that there will be an offline version of 4.0, but will not be updated. This does seem pointless though, since Steam apparently "installs" the characters according to the DLC window in the client. As of right now though, it's certainly not obvious that is the case & needs to be more obvious & worked on. Until then, the recommendation remains unchanged
Speaking of existing players: All existing players who bought the previous expansions (before they were removed & replaced with the All-Nauts pack) keep get all future Nauts for free, plus a medal for your profile...
That's it
There are no extra perks of being an existing long-time player, no extra AwesomePoints, nothing. It does come as a bit of a slap to the face to existing players. Couple that with the lack of offline functionallity & it comes off as downright insulting.
Oh, but you get to keep your expansion characters if you bought them, so I guess that makes it OK...riiiiiight
As of the last edit (4th May '17), this is currently in a Beta period, so I hope to high heaven these get resolved as soon as possible, because right now there is a large amount of backlash from veteran players

I didn't expect much from this. And while it's never going to top the Greatest Games Ever list, it turned out to be a pleasant surprise.
The voice acting and music are solid, both informative and thematically appropriate. The graphics are serviceable, and the physics interactivity is balanced just right to give weight to the combat without the bounciness Havok can occasionally lead to. It also allows for a bit of strategy, as heavy objects can be moved to provide cover. And the combat feels right, too - the Orks come at you in a tide that feels *almost* - but not quite - unstoppable, the weapon sounds are mostly sufficient, and set dressing crumbles and explodes all over the place.
Add to that well-placed checkpoints, nicely-balanced difficulty curves, a fairly wide range of skins and rather nice level design, and there's a fair amount of game here for a not terribly onerous price.
There are downsides - an anaemic options menu, a lack of mouse control in the menu and slightly sluggish controls in-game, and of course the occasionally infuriating automatic camera - but for this price it's a really fun game for a quick 40K topup in between dinner and bedtime.

And you also must finish it in less than 5 hours, for another achievement.. Plus, you must beat the whole bossh rush on different difficulties..
So, if you're an achievement hunter, expect this game to take many hours from your weeks.. :) Even because some puzzles are not frustrating, they're easy, but they're very long and six times is really something unbelievable..
But the game is great, graphics are awesome and even if the lovely bump battle system has been dropped since the first episodes this is a hack n' slash action jrpg that will not disappoint even those who like me love turn-based systems.
As any other Ys game, it's short (of course, there's an achievement that requires you beat it in less than 5 hours!! on very easy difficulty obviously).. but enjoyable like the rest of the series, even though Ys 1 and 2 are still better to me :)

The game is definitely a casual, third person platforming game.  However, the reason why I don't recommend this game is due to the horrible camera.  There were times when I fell off the edge that the camera would shift a full 180 degrees compared to what it should be. Overall your kids may like this game if they can past the frustrations.

The game itself is basically a form of board game where you have to complete tasks (normas) either by getting 'stars' (granted by either the end of a 'chapter' by defeating a CPU, Player, or Flash Enemy, or by landing on a bonus tile), or by getting wins (granted by defeating a CPU, Player, or Flash Enemy).
You're allowed to start of as four different characters (Sugure, QP, Kai, and Marc) and progress through their campaigns, which allows you to amass star points, which can then be used to unlock other characters which are unlocked for buying through the campaigns. Each character has a different specialty in terms of skills (Attack, Defense, and Evasion) and each have different hypers (Unique skills that attune to a specific character, an example being Marc's 16x Big Cannon, which damages a specific character in attunement with how many 'star levels' that Marc has.)
Overall, the game is filled with kawaii, board games, a little bit of friendly murderous rivalry, and a lot of fun.

The Shadows of Amn portion of this game is pretty good, giving you plenty of quests to pursue from inside the main city and the areas you subsequently travel to. I spent over 40 hours in this section (and there were plenty of quests I hadn't pursued) and party members got to around level 20. This feels like the sweet spot in D&D rules for character power; you've hit the peak of your thac0 and saving throws, have access to your highest level spells, and get your first  taste of the high level abilities at 3 million XP. The main villain in this part of the game is the best one in the entire series, with good voice acting to boot.
In contrast, the final Throne of Bhaal portion is a very linear march through the final bosses, adding 15 hours of gameplay. At these few extra levels, your progression is mainly adding high level abilities and upgrading gear. Bosses get tougher since they start using HLA's on you, and casters are deadly if you don't keep pressure on them. The final fight has satisfying difficulty, but the story is far less engaging than Shadows of Amn.

This is a great MOBA and combines it with a platformer very well. What's nice about this game, is that there are only 3 people per side. This makes every hero important, and doesn't allow much room for slackers. This also allows you to keep track of who is who and where they are much easier, as there are only three people. It's also much easier to find a group of people to play with, when you only need 2 other people.
Another great thing about this game is the fact that there are not tons of Awesomenauts in the game. Every MOBA has the learning curve part of it, but this game's learning curve isn't too steep. Each Awesomenaut only has 2 special attacks, and 1 regular punch(or shoot) attack, giving it a lot of similarities to Super Smash Bros. One thing that game did really well was its ease of adoption: it was easy to pick up and learn and play.
That's not to say there isn't depth. The game allows you to unlock new skills as you gain overall account experience, and this allows you to customize what skills each awesomenaut has, forcing you to choose to fit a play style. This allows for depth later on, but presents each skill one or two a time, allowing you to digest them and make sense of them.
Overall, a very fun and compelling experience. The online play isn't too tough at first, but ramps up as you advance in levels. Recommend to anyone wanting a MOBA with Super Smash Bros controls and aesthetic.

This is actually 2 kinds of games in 1: a hack-and-slash action game, and a quick-time-event-like game.  Make sure you enjoy both types of gameplay before jumping in.
The majority of the dungeons is the hack-and-slash RPG type.  You can kite enemies, make big long chain combos, with plenty of non-stop action until everything is dead.
Then the boss fights are more like quicktime events.  While it's not exactly the same a QTE, it might as well be.  There's no more continuous action, no chaining combos.  90% of boss fights are learning the timing of the boss's attacks and jumping dodge at the right time - i.e. press X to not die right now.
The difficulty is not an issue, as the game has multiple difficulty levels from very easy to ridiculously hard.  However, the sudden change in gameplay style remains regardless of difficulty level.
As for the story and characters, I didn't get through the whole thing obviously, but it seems to be a pretty generic JRPG style of story.  Not much to say there.
Me personally, I don't like the dodge-forever and wait for the chance to land 1 hit style of gameplay, which made the boss fights annoying and boring enough that I ended up putting the game down.
I'd only recommend if you can be patient or are somehow a millionaire, because that is the only way you are going to enjoy this game.

If you're into the whole 'Kawaii-Ness' of japanese chibi characters, then this game is already worth it.
Despite having gotten it during the summer 2014 steam sale, I would of easily bought this at its' full price, due to the fun and interest in the game.
The game itself is basically a form of board game where you have to complete tasks (normas) either by getting 'stars' (granted by either the end of a 'chapter' by defeating a CPU, Player, or Flash Enemy, or by landing on a bonus tile), or by getting wins (granted by defeating a CPU, Player, or Flash Enemy).
You're allowed to start of as four different characters (Sugure, QP, Kai, and Marc) and progress through their campaigns, which allows you to amass star points, which can then be used to unlock other characters which are unlocked for buying through the campaigns. Each character has a different specialty in terms of skills (Attack, Defense, and Evasion) and each have different hypers (Unique skills that attune to a specific character, an example being Marc's 16x Big Cannon, which damages a specific character in attunement with how many 'star levels' that Marc has.)
Overall, the game is filled with kawaii, board games, a little bit of friendly murderous rivalry, and a lot of fun.

My Personal Review from a Chivalry player with 450+ hours of experience
Pros:
- Average community of chiv players who host competitive tournaments occasionally
- Somewhat actively engaged developers
- Pretty realistic gameplay and medieval atmosphere (before rank 15)
- Horde servers where you battle several waves of AI and have the option to upgrade your class/weapons
- Star wars servers where you get to battle with♥♥♥♥♥♥♥lightsabers / badass maps
- Funny servers where you mess around and play 2d super mario on chiv
- Dank Moor server where you get to be play as:
Dankald Trump and his army of Deplorables
Hillary Crackton and her army of Democrats
Crunkie Sanders and his army of Socialists
Jeb Kush and his army of Republicans
and special guest Mexican Jesus and his army of Illegal Immigrants on a map that has several funny and badass things
- Black Knight Mode where you can run around a map with your limbs chopped off when attacked by enemies (funny af)
- Giant Slayers where you start off 60% of normal size then with every kill you increase in size to the point where you can almost take the size of the whole map and crush enemies below your feet.
- and other great mods /servers that Chivalry has to offer
Cons:
I have been a Chivalry player for quite a while now. First thing I would like to address is YES it's true after level 15 it sort of turns into a hellhole when you start to face the big boys who use every pixel of the enemy hitbox to induce damage. Now, this has been a huge reason why many people stop liking the game after rank 15. Although, this shouldn't be the entire reason to dislike this game as it has still a lot to offer in my opinion. The developers of this game truly care about their players and there is a probably a good reason they do not want to fix the ballerina simulator problem a lot of noobies have unfortunatelty come to face. Due to this, Chivalry loses it's immersive value as a medieval game later on because of the un-realistic movements/exploits. So now you may ask, why aren't the developers doing anything about this? In my opinion, this may be because of the current mass supporters / players who love the game for what it has become, a very competitive multiplayer environment. This creates a large gap between high level and new players which in turn brings the Chivalry player population to slowly die down. So what does this mean for new players? They have around 3 options:
1. Adapt to the competitive environment, look up on youtube strategies / different techniques to face these players.
2. Ignore the game for what It is, play at their own style and stay away from higher level servers / play modded servers
3. Or just simply quit
Personally, I did adapt and now love the competitive gameplay Chivalry offers along with the hilarious servers. This is just MY review, I would definately recommend this to new players, but I highly encourage to learn advanced tutorials on youtube. If you're looking for the medieval immersive game that this was meant to be don't buy it. If you are a competitive player who likes a challenge, you will highly enjoy this game. I think the developers should maybe increase the level cap for new players and teach the different weapon maneuvers. I doubt that would happen though, I do truly like this game and wish the community would keep growing, but this gap might just destroy Chivalry.

The Shadows of Amn portion of this game is pretty good, giving you plenty of quests to pursue from inside the main city and the areas you subsequently travel to. I spent over 40 hours in this section (and there were plenty of quests I hadn't pursued) and party members got to around level 20. This feels like the sweet spot in D&D rules for character power; you've hit the peak of your thac0 and saving throws, have access to your highest level spells, and get your first  taste of the high level abilities at 3 million XP. The main villain in this part of the game is the best one in the entire series, with good voice acting to boot.
In contrast, the final Throne of Bhaal portion is a very linear march through the final bosses, adding 15 hours of gameplay. At these few extra levels, your progression is mainly adding high level abilities and upgrading gear. Bosses get tougher since they start using HLA's on you, and casters are deadly if you don't keep pressure on them. The final fight has satisfying difficulty, but the story is far less engaging than Shadows of Amn.

Greetings fellow gamers! This is Gamer Guy (In a Suit) from the Echo Army YouTube channel! Today I am bringing you a review of Indie Arcade/Horror game Goodnight Butcher. Goodnight Butcher was released on Steam on December 18th, 2015 by Developer/Publisher Perfect Square Studios.
(NOTE: This game was NOT reviewed using a key provided by the Developer and/or Publisher, it was a game I purchased for my own account)
Video Review:
The "Too Long, Didn't Watch" Review:
IF you get it under a buck, ok. Otherwise, very meh. (Hopeful for future though) 1/5

Unfortunately, I was simply unimpressed with this little game. I figured at it's price, I would be ok. This came from a bundle I had bought before, and I am glad that is the case. I just cannot recommend this right now, as much as I want to like this game. The gameplay and graphics are simple but the music and sounds get old REALLY quickly. You find the meat locker, grab a carcass, take it to the saw, cut it down, then take each piece somewhere else to "craft" it into it's sellable item (hamburger, steak, etc), dump the bones, put meats in display, repeat. Avoid the ghost while you're at it. I mention it so casually because really, the fear lasts about 2 seconds, and that's it. The sense of dread, urgency, fear, anything simply isn't there. Sorry, this game just isn't doing it for me. Maybe if it was less than a buck I would feel different. I am hoping for updates, or a story that'll hook me or just some reason to care about NOT dying at all in this game. Meh. 1/5

Hmmm...a hard call, this one.  It's certainly not asking an unreasonable price for what it offers, especially on sale, and it's certainly not anyone's definition of "incompetent".  It is, on the other hand, a little hard to imagine just who I would consider "recommending" this game to, bar perhaps those masochists out there who think that constantly moving between rooms as instructed to perform myriad menial tasks, whilst avoiding the floaty ghosts of butchered beasties, constitutes something resembling "gameplay".  Hell, it would at least be a passable time-waster if the saves were regular, but every unspectacular death just means several minutes of getting back to where you were beforehand, and the satisfaction of a job successfully completed is marginal at best.
Now...I know that this arguably sounds like an awful lot of games out there, including some which I hold in incredibly high esteem, such as Outlast.  I guess I maybe just require slightly "deeper" gameplay if I'm not going to be served oodles of ATMOSPHERE in the overall package, and the fine line between "horror" and "retro"/"arcade"-style antics is perhaps a little too skewed to the latter for my liking in this case.  It really may just be a personal taste thing, though, and the vegetarian in me definitely wants to like the sheer perversity of this crazy little slice of madness.  It's really, REALLY not "bad" at all.  Maybe it's just not my bag, and maybe it will be yours.  Hence the recommendation...that, and the lack of a "neutral" button for me to push, because this game really is about as "middling" as it gets in my book.
Let me try putting it another way:  If you like super-duper old-school "arcade" games, with just a splash of horror (and the good old red stuff) to give it a bit of context, then you may well enjoy this.  I don't think it's going to hit anyone's all-time top-ten lists, but it may well be worth the two bucks or less if you're feeling suitably indiscriminating and just feel like killing a bit of time while you butcher a few cartoon carcasses.  For me, personally, its appeal ran its course pretty quickly.
Definitely NOT to be filed in the Lone Survivor/Claire-style category of genuinely "creepy" pixelated homages to Silent Hill, et al, though I guess it is at least marginally spookier than Commando or Pac Man.  The very definition of a "take-or-leave-it" proposition, methinks, and for now I'm choosing to leave it.  Good luck to the dev, though, as they seem sincere enough in their intentions, and who knows, may well go on to (much) bigger and better things...

I can only tentatively recommend this game because it is, indeed, very very flawed.
I preordered it years ago, when I had more money than sense but I don't regret it. The combat feels fantastic. It's quick and brutal, every hit has real weight to it and fights are over in a flash. The stealth mechanics are a lot better than you would expect. In the levels where it's relevant and viable, slowly moving from cover to cover and picking off the enemy one-by-one in brief flurries of violence is exhilarating.
The game doesn't have a very traditional health system. It's based on locational damage with the physics playing a big part. If you jump in the air and roll at just the right time, you can land on your neck in a funny way and it will break from the stress. That basically sums up how damage works in this game. Leveraging the environment and the physics engine to break your enemy's bones is how you win.
The control scheme is also unique. To attack you hold the attack button down and combine it with directional button presses to perfrom a variety of different moves based on your distance to the enemy. There's another button that, if held, can block enemy strikes but can also be used as a counter-throw or reversal if pressed at the right time. There's a roll button, but it's more effective to dodge by tapping a direction which caused you to smoothly hop out of the way of an attack whilst remaining in range to counter. Rolling is viable, too, and the roll button can also be used to duck, sneak and sweep kick. If you attack while jumping you can kick off of your opponent's face, sending you both flying. Doing this and smacking into a wall is another great way to break your neck.
The presentation is generally top-notch. It's not exactly a AAA game but it can be visually stunning all the same and runs pretty well on my fairly mediocre PC (I'm running a GTX 960 2GB, so more or less every PC gamer out there has a better PC than I do). The lighting effects can be gorgeous, the blood physics are maybe the best I've ever seen and the animation is beautifully fluid and strong. Sound effects are punchy and satisfying and the music sets the mood nicely even if it won't set the world on fire. Speaking of music, though, the song in the trailer is really bad, guys.
Sadly, at this point, I've run out of nice things to say about the game. Nine years of development sadly didn't yield many results when it comes to level design, pacing and writing.
Now, to be fair, this is a very small team who built one hell of a 3D engine from scratch by themselves. It has support for some excellent visual effects and physics and it is entirely unsurprising that it took so long to build. But that doesn't mean you should excuse some of the shoddy elements of the game itself.
The main campaign technically has a story but that story has absolutely no direction or purpose. The pacing is terrible and I genuinely thought the game was pulling some meta joke on me when it told me I'd finished the game. It just ends after a fight with a nondescript guard captain I'd never seen before right in the middle of what felt like the beginning of a new chapter in the story. It never feels like it's building to anything, it feels like nothing happens. It's a short sequence of none-events.
The difficulty curve is also none-existent. If you've had the game since alpha, like I have, none of the campaign will challenge you. It's not a very difficult game to beat once you're used to it The only reason new players tend to have such trouble is because it plays very unlike any other melee action game. You don't actually need to be any good at using most of the mechanics to be able to breeze through the game, you just need a basic grasp of its controls. The game never gets any harder than it is at the start. Enemies get a little tankier but the nature of the combat system and the plethora of bottomless pits and weapons make that a none issue.
The game is front-loaded with its best levels. It's a suprisingly fun stealth game, as I alluded to before, but stealth levels all but disappear later on. The larger enemy types that become common in the mid-late game just aren't that fun to fight either. Wolves are the worst. They knock you flying with every hit, cannot be counter-thrown and can even survive having a sword thrown through their face. They're incredibly vulnerable to the jump kick so they aren't hard to beat, they just throw everything fun about the combat system out of the window.
The first level in which you fight a wolf has a loading screen tip that implies you should just run away. This is impossible in game. The intent is clearly to impress upon you how powerful wolves are but it could be potentially confusing to new players who don't know that you can fight wolves.
There are several platforming segements in the game and they are a complete waste of time. Utterly linear in the worst way possible with extremely finnicky controls that will constantly kill you. During these sections, jumping to the "wrong" platform will instantly kill you regardless of height. Every platform you land on is a checkpoint. Most platforms are clearly marked but not always, and there is at least one section where it looks like there are multiple ways to progress but there are not. Some platforms are very narrow and your character has a tendency to just step off of them upon landing. I'm all for momentum in my platforming physics, just make sure your level design accomodates it!
These sections also frequently want you to use the wallrunning ability and it's just garbage. It feels horribly inconsistent and requires absurdly specific positioning to work. And when it does and you pull it off, it feels so stiff and so weak that it isn't even satisfying. Titantfall 2, this is not.
It's a shame because Overgrowth has so much going for it mechanically and every so often flashes of a truly excellent game shine through. It just feels like nowhere near as much care was put into the level design and pacing of the game as its technical aspects. The game has some very robust and easy to use modding tools so hopefully the community can make a campaign worthy of the game's mechanics but that's something that really should have come with the game.
Sadly most of my complaints about the Overgrowth campaign apply to the Lugaru one, too. At least the Arena mode is great to kill ten minutes with. And the combat is good enough that there is fun to be had with the campaign, even if the level design isn't quite up to snuff.

After 9 years of development, you would think they would have fixed some of the bugs and general bugginess in the game, but they haven't. Movement and parkour are satisfying 90% of the time and frustrating 10% of the time. The number of times when I grabbed a ledge but didn't want to was crazy, and I only played the campaign for 2 hours (before another bug finally crashed my game and reset me by a half-hour). There were plenty of other minor bugs too, like when I got stuck outside of the map, or when the map textures stopped rendering and every surface was black.
The combat is fun enough, though jump-kicking still seems overpowered compared to everything else. I think you can play split-screen which might be fun.
Other than that, the game sucks. The UI looks like something from ten years ago, and the dialogue is shallow and boring to read. Why am I reading dialogue in the first place? All of the parkour in the game ranges from mildly frustrating to very frustrating. I don't know why they thought platforming would be a good idea in an engine where you can't even change your course mid-air, but it isn't.
If you can find a copy for $5 or less I'd say go for it, otherwise don't bother. If they haven't fixed any of the glaring issues over the last decade, I doubt they ever will.

There’s a lot of potential here and it’s worth the asking price in it’s current state.
Pros--
1) Music and sound are great.
2) Map is simple.
3) Controls are simple and work well when navigating the game.
4) Graphics are retro and work with the tone of the game.
5) Overall sense of fear is there. I felt tense and scared when the sound effects to opening doors. One door in particular was scary, and I thought a monster would be waiting for me. No monster, but I was scared during most of my first play through.
Cons--
1) Story could be more developed and better. It would be nice if the butcher had a kid and/or a wife he had to provide for. Or, maybe someone will die if the butcher doesn’t figure out the mystery at work.

2) Lack of variant game modes or gameplay. I think if the story was developed more, the game could be better developed. Like having a metagame to take care of a sick child in a hospital, etc. Or heck, even a love interest who visits the Butcher during the day. Eventually, as I got better, the tension was less, and thus my fear lowered increasingly.
3) Lack of caring about if I die. It sucks “yes” that you have to start over if you are killed, but I just feel I have to redo the work I did before, that the only reason I want to live is to finish my work and not a meta game or a compelling story.
4) No Steam Cards or Achievements.
Update was promised in the community when I post this review, but steam cards wouldn't add to the game as other things could.
Again, I think this is rough version of what could be a better game for a higher asking price, and I hope come Halloween 2016 to see some major updates or even a sequel.

I randomly got this game on a sale, and tried to play it a couple times but couldn't get into it. The graphics were very basic, I didn't like the isometric view, and the gameplay seemed confusing and awkward. I just didn't get it.
Then one time I was bored so I decided to try it one more time. For some reason, this time it just clicked and it all made sense... and I realized this is maybe the best game ever made. I couldn't stop playing it.. after I finished it I was searching for D&D lore and more games like this.
I think the key realization is this: you aren't only "playing" what you see on the screen. When you play Skyrim or something like that, the immersion is based on looking all around at the sights of the world around you. In a game like Baldur's Gate, you have to think of the character models more like pieces on a tabletop. They are representing what's going on, but you have to engage your imagination as well.
When you get that, the whole world with its characters and rich storyline and lore come alive and you realize this is like stepping into an amazing fantasy universe where you are totally free to explore and talk to all kinds of people and have adventures. It's an incredible experience and BG2 is the perfect place to start!

Do not buy this game.
Don't get me wrong, I want to like this game, and I do like it to some extent, but the amount of content does not reflect its price or its development time.
There's less than 6 hours of content on the hardest difficult between the 'Overgrowth' and 'Lugaru' campaigns. Neither story is particularly interesting, though they have potential. Characters come and go, fights are just fights in different areas with little context.
The levels are varied. Some are beautiful, some are ugly, some are unoptimized. Some really make you feel like you are in this mystic, geometric world where animal people are fighting for their survival. Others feel like someone's first Unity project.
Combat is fun but largely the same as Lugaru. Enemies are smart: they gang up on you, they block repeated attacks, and they seek out and utilize weapons. But you'll never the less find yourself using the most OP move in the game: the jump kick. In Lugaru, enemies could potentially counter your jump kick, pulling you out of the air, and it was far easier to screw up the landing after a succesful hit. In Overgrowth, this mechanic is seemingly gone and now the jump kick has an extended range and auto rolls you so you almost always land on your feet. Hopefully this can be balance in the future.
I love the setting and I love the *idea* of Overgrowth, but it just isn't there. The comics are interesting. There's a world there that could exist and be expanded upon, but neither campaign does.
That being said, the game does have a powerful editor and supports the steam workshop, so the modding scene may keep this game afloat.

Alright, here we go.  I played this game only on singleplayer, and only with the Complete mod.  This review is meant for people who have played the two previous Stalker games.
Try to imagine Fallout 3 without the good story, and without the loot.  Yeah, it's like that.  You know, most games that start with a plot that's something like "You're a  military guy, go find out why your helicopters went down in the zone and evacuate the survivors if you can" would use it as an opportunity for something bigger.  Enter other circumstances.  Enter other characters.  It's done in every other game I've played that had such a simple plot.  Not this one, though.  That's what you've got.  The wholllleeeee game.
Although there are sidequests, many of which receive their own cutscenes at the end of the game, it's hard to ignore how painfully boring the whole thing is.  There are only three large zones this time.  Pockets of urban desolation are clearly marked, as are most sites of anomalies so you can collect artifacts.  The factions effectively do not exist.  Even the bandits won't shoot at you first!  The only de-facto human enemies are Monolith, and you won't even see them until the end of the game.
Did you enjoy the faction warfare of Clear Skies?  Gone.
There are a few new mutants this time around.  Some of the underground areas are creepy as all hell, but overall the combat is easier compared to the other two.
Parts on guns can now be upgraded incrementally.  The good stuff is no longer found on dead bodies though, you get it via special order from Nimble (the only NPC to be in all three games).  None of it really matters because the last mission is a cakewalk.  I think too many people complained about the difficulty of prior titles.  I went through on Stalker difficulty on all three, which was probably my mistake, but it does give me a perfect benchmark.
You now have one storage box in each of the three main camps, eliminating any guesswork as to where you can store your goodies.
This game in particular crashes wayyyyy more than the others.  Typically the old Xbug error which is usually associated with mods.
Bullets randomly and annoyingly spraying everywhere are a thing of the distant past.
In spite of everything I've just said, there's something that's entertaining, for awhile.  Emissions from the zone are intense and send you scrambling for cover.  Although ruins are picked clean, you can still find stashes.  Mutants are a little tougher and definitely have a sense of free-roam.  You'll still vaguely crave vodka when you play.  The game isn't much longer than the others, but somehow... you'll spend a little more time with it, voluntarily.
In any case, if you have the previous two, you'll buy it no matter what I say.  I'm sure the varying mods will help a LOT.

Contrary to what seems to be recent popular opinion (Looking at YOU and your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ review, Rock Paper Shotgun), Overgrowth is definately worth the buy. As a finished product, it doesn't feel like the smoothest game in the world, and it certainly isn't the most populus game in the world, but it's got beautiful graphics, and it really shines as far as fighting goes.
Spoilers below-
You play as a rabbit named Turner. It's unexplained, but to understand the Overgrowth story, you need to first have played Lugaru. In Lugaru, you are on a vengance fueled killing rampage, having your family ripped away from you by murderous raiders. In the end, you come to learn that your King has been selling your people to the wolves as food, and to the cats as slaves. Your final act in Lugaru is to exact vengance upon the king of the rabbits and the leader of the wolves, by killing ♥♥♥♥ing EVERYONE. In the end, it's a tragic tale about how revenge gains nothing, because even after killing the wolf leaders entire family, yours is still dead, and your nation is still torn apart.
Overgrowth picks up where we left off, however, instead of pursuing the cats, Turner has decided to sail to a different part of his home isle and pursue peace. Shortly after arriving, however, he comes to learn that peace just isn't an optino for him. The very same raiders are waiting for him, having sacked the town he chose to land at. One thing lead to another, and a few actions in the defense of the few turns into an overarching campaign to free the Rabbits from the captivity of the cats. In the end, you discover that just as before, the rabbits are politically fueled into an agreement with the cats, even with the old king dead. The lesson here is the same as in Lugaru, which most people seem to glaze over for. Violence solves nothing. Even after all that killing, all you did was put the people you liked into power. The people currently in power had families and friends all the same, and the murders you commit throughout the game have almost no consequence in the long run.
Enough about the story, though. Let's talk gameplay. And agreedly with most, Overgrowth can be a bit lacking. The platforming aspect is difficult to control, with alot of "I thought I had that's!" and "Really? I just broke my spine? ♥♥♥♥." But the combat, oh, the combat is where this game shines. It needs a more thorough tutorial, because the majority of the combat is left up to the user to discover. Most people default to the jumping attack, however as people complain, landing after the fact almost always ends poorly (HINT: This isn't unintentional! You aren't able to jump 30 feet in the air and land safely.) Instead of relying on the jumps, it's worth it to learn how you can chain disarms and counters to defeat your enemies. Enemies don't often throw weapons at you because they expect you to catch htem, and you'll notice they can catch almost anything you throw if they are paying attention. I won't spell out the whole combat system, because it is fun to learn some of it on your own, and I don't want to rob you of the experience, but I guarentee it has far more depth than the people who cannot use it properly claim it does.
So, in the end, if you're looking for a brutally violent game with stories that abhore said acts, and a combat system which is second-to-none the most rewarding to take the time to master, Overgrowth is for you. If you're looking for depth outside combat, such as in platforming or long and complex stories, seek entertainment elsewhere.
Happy Hunting!

It's not a game for everyone, due to its sheer complexity. If you're used to strategy games like Total War or Civilization, that's just training compared to this game. It has a ton of different interacting gameplay mechanisms that can be rather hard to learn at first, both due to the large amount of them and their complexity. I can safely say that there is no other strategy game quite like this. But, complicated game mechanics aside, what is this game actually about?
The simplest way for me to describe this is "Game of Thrones (there's a GoT mod for this game that's said to be very good) in medieval Europe". Just like in Game of Thrones, scheming, intrigues, sex and murder is all over the place, and the rulers do anything to secure more power.  Unlike many other strategy games, you're not playing as a nation striving for power and world dominance. Instead, you're playing a ruler in medieval Europe (if you have the relevant expansions, you can also play as Muslims in northern Africa and the Middle East, as well as Indian rulers, among others) in the time of the crusades. Rather than conquering others for more territory (which you can still do, of course), you aim to gather as much prestige for your dynasty as possible, while managing your life.
In order to secure a good future for your dynasty, you need to make sure you have good children (who you play as after death) and good relationships with your subjects so they don't turn against you. In your quest for prestige, you can find yourself playing in many different ways. If you want to play as an iron-fisted tyrant who executes anyone doubting him, you can do so, and if you want to play a kind and understanding noble, that's just as possible. Do you want to kill your brothers to eliminate competition for the crown, or do you want them to grow powerful on their own and help you secure more power? Do you marry your children to secure alliances, or simply to get them out of the way? The choice is yours, and sometimes, you might find yourself making morally bad decisions that turn out to be good for you in the long run.
Does the end justify the means, or is the most important thing to always do good? Crusader Kings II puts ethics and morals in an interesting perspective, and I think we can learn a lot from it, not just about history and how the medieval world worked, but also about philosophy and psychology. Perhaps we can understand the atrocities of the past by putting ourselves in the shoes of the ones in charge?
In summary, Crusader Kings II is a great (but complicated) game for all strategy fans, and I highly recommend it. Even if the expansions might be a bit expensive to buy all at once, I recommend it, since they all add so much to the game and make it better. It's an amazing and addicting game about awful things.

This is a game that has 3 main mechanics: Combat, which is the main point of the game, stealth, and platforming.
Combat uses an original and possibly unique system that is very natural, fluid, challenging, intelligent, and fast. For me it's extraordinarily fun and I've spent many hours just on straight-up pure combat alone.
Stealth: Not innovative like combat, but works fairly well. I enjoy sneaking around, learning the enemy behavior, and then coming up with a plan to sneak up on the enemies one by one and silently assassinate them from behind without anyone noticing.
Platforming: Supports basic parkour moves of jumping, running, grabbing onto ledges and climbing up, wallruning, and walljumping. There are some nice platforming challenges scattered throughout the Overgrowth Story Campaign.
The game currently has 2 campaigns: The Lugaru Story, and the Overgrowth Story. The Lugaru campaign is an HD remake of the Lugaru game inside Overgrowth, and as such the level design and graphical assets are nearly identical to the original Lugaru and are much simpler than the Overgrowth campaign. It's also significantly shorter.
The Overgrowth campaign has rich and detailed levels, and the levels feel big, like you can just go off on a hike anywhere you want, even though if you try you'll discover that the levels are actually small. They do a good job of creating this illusion of a big world, and then directing you where you're supposed to go so you never encounter the boundaries of the level. They do this by putting you directly in front of the place your supposed to enter, or on a path you're supposed to follow, and with a bit of dialog to focus your attention on your goal. The paths are marked clearly, either as an actual path, or with hints like fires, glowing mushrooms, or scratch marks from parkouring rabbits who passed there before. It's subtle and doesn't break immersion. There's also no wasted time traveling between locations and no filler content that exists just to stretch out the playtime. It's totally focused on doing its thing. There are minions to kill or get passed, and those you can deal with how you like. There are also many boss fights and some arena fights which you have to take head on.
The graphics aren't state of the art, but they are pretty enough. There is a nice variety of environments and locations.
The main weakness is the length of the Overgrowth campaign, which is only 29 levels, and I feel that the ending, while it made sense, came too abruptly. I finished the campaign in about 6 hours after dying many times in almost each level and almost each fight. There is also the issue of price. Right now it seems a bit high, considering the amount of content from the developer (although there is lots of community content, including whole campaigns), but then again it's a unique experience and for me at least it's highly replayable just for the combat alone. There's also versus mode for two players to fight each other and 4 arenas provided by the developer that can be enabled in the mods menu for fighting against various AI opponents, with the level of the opponents rising or falling to match your performance. I spent many hours just on that.

This is a great MOBA and combines it with a platformer very well. What's nice about this game, is that there are only 3 people per side. This makes every hero important, and doesn't allow much room for slackers. This also allows you to keep track of who is who and where they are much easier, as there are only three people. It's also much easier to find a group of people to play with, when you only need 2 other people.
Another great thing about this game is the fact that there are not tons of Awesomenauts in the game. Every MOBA has the learning curve part of it, but this game's learning curve isn't too steep. Each Awesomenaut only has 2 special attacks, and 1 regular punch(or shoot) attack, giving it a lot of similarities to Super Smash Bros. One thing that game did really well was its ease of adoption: it was easy to pick up and learn and play.
That's not to say there isn't depth. The game allows you to unlock new skills as you gain overall account experience, and this allows you to customize what skills each awesomenaut has, forcing you to choose to fit a play style. This allows for depth later on, but presents each skill one or two a time, allowing you to digest them and make sense of them.
Overall, a very fun and compelling experience. The online play isn't too tough at first, but ramps up as you advance in levels. Recommend to anyone wanting a MOBA with Super Smash Bros controls and aesthetic.

I've held off reviewing this one because I really wanted to find ways around its most cataclysmic flaw, but after so long trying I've got to conclude that I just can't.
The platforming, theming and level design are all interesting and fun. The music is awesome and memorable. Bosses, however, single-handedly put all that is good about the game to waste.
I certainly don't mind hard games, but too often it is artificial, particularly on the higher difficulty levels. To set the tone: Bosses generally kill you in 2-4 hits with spammy attacks that are very difficult to dodge, have a lot of health and provide VERY limited (and generally dangerous) vulnerability windows. Most of this is fine, though their health can get absurdly excessive at times and certain attacks have questionable hit boxes.
The problem is that some boss' attacks are decided by RNG and can become impossible (in the literal rather than exaggerating sense) to survive. If Gyalva wants to turn the arena into spikes forever and shoot you when you can't dodge, or if Istersiva wants to repeatedly spit out three laser-crystals until they fill the screen, there's genuinely no chance to win.
These are not controlled in any way; apparently the developers' idea of justifying this is the accessibility of the Retry button that appears when you die.
The need to compensate for often unavoidable damage means that, with rare exception on the highest difficulties, bosses become an aggravating marathon of perfection-demanding frustration that you would expect to see in a badly-balanced bullet hell. It is no small irony that the reliance on scripted attacks makes what is meant to be a tough final boss one of the easiest in the game.
The alternative is to spend an hour (again, not an exaggeration) before many bosses to grind a couple of levels extra, which dramatically reduces the damage you receive and makes them pitifully easy. To sum up the choices, you can beat your head against a wall or you can bore yourself to tears. Both options can only be considered anti-fun.
A far less critical issue is the controls: 3 buttons switch between and use magic, but there are only 3 different magics so they could have just got a button each. XInput support is lacking; controllers work but cannot be remapped. Xbox controllers access the menu with the right stick, while magic use (X) and jump (B) make life awkward as they are often needed together. There are also multiple complaints that jump button presses sometimes fail to register.
But this is a minor flaw compared to the boss problem, which could have been prevented. This is a Steam re-release of the original 2005 PC version. In 2010, the game received a PSP port which made a considerate reworking of bosses and provided a double-boost ability. None of that made it into the Steam release in 2012, and an otherwise great game suffers irredeemably for it.
