By far one of the best games I've ever had the pleasure of playing.  And as a big fan of Ys in general, I consider this to be the best of the series.  As with the rest of the Ys series, the world is built wonderfully.  Every area in the game feels very unique and interesting.  Every character in the game also has their own name, portrait, and a bit of personal character to them, no matter how insignificant their role is.  I've always found this to be a wonderful attribute to the Ys series, and makes character interactions feel more intimate and special than what you get in many RPGs.
The gameplay is also top notch in Felghana.  Each area is laid out very well and presents a challenge to overcome.  The bosses are also incredibly well designed, and some of the best I've seen in any game.  Boss battles are fast-paced and challenging, and despite the high difficulty, everything feels completely fair.  Every single attack is avoidable through practice, skill, and reflexes, no matter how ridiculous they may seem at first, which is something I absolutely love to see in my games.  While I highly recommend playing on the highest difficulty for Ys games to really get your blood pumping, there are also several easier settings for more casual players who aren't as good at fast paced action games, offering something for everyone.
Graphically, the game looks great.  Despite being pretty old (original Japanese PC release in 2005), the visual design and artstyle were done very well.  The colors, lighting, animations, models, and so on all just look fantastic, and I feel they'll hold up well forever.  Falcom just did a great job there.
The music is wonderful too.  Falcom games always have top notch music, and Felghana is no different.  They really did a good job with the soundtrack.  Unfortunately, unlike the PSP release, the Steam release doesn't have the option to change to the alternate soundtracks from the PC88 or X68000 versions of Wanderers of Ys, but this is a minor complaint that shouldn't matter much except to enthusiasts of the sound from those old machines.  The Windows soundtrack is phenominal to be sure.

tl;dr  Try the free version, if you like it, great, upgrade and keep playing; Be prepared for crashes
First off, their marketing strategy is great;
Free Version: Limited inventory, increase inventory by leveling (easy to level until level 9, gets you a nice backpack space of 11) Have to sell items to buy new items if full
Basic: Unlimited inventory, increase in G earned per match (you get to keep all your parts)
Premium: For those who just want to build and play
Gameplay: While the game offers customization, there are, of course, the OP, high damage builds that♥♥♥♥♥♥everyone else off who just want to have fun. One build in particular seems to always pop up in matches, and is annoying as hell since it is pure bullet spam and requires little skill; Using the double turret chassis + any damage support modules yields 4 secondary guns + 1 primary gun all being able to be fired at the same time. The 4 secondary guns can be gatling guns, rockets, lasers
(especially annoying due to their pinpoint accuracy and range, paired with a sniper, is able to 1 shot [well, 5 shots altogether] high armored players, and there isn't much you can do other than snipe back, or focus all of your attention on killing them every time they spawn),
cannons, sticky bombs, or if you REALLY want to be support, you can do quad heal guns and force those dipwads you call teammates to stay alive.
Last but not least, you have the build everyone gripes about, gatling gun + gatling gun supports + low lying body. While I like the low lying body for any build as it makes you harder to hit, the gatling guns just ruin most of the game. I like to play as mid-long range Vintage laser, mid-short range Revolver, or Bronze cannon just for the sheer joy of watching bombs randomly hit players behind me, above me, anywhere but the person Im aiming at, but the gatling guns just ruin it. Equipped on a quick frame, the game turns into blitzkrieg and "holding" a position just makes you an easier target for their bullet spam.
Now, there ARE counters to the gatling gun, equipping a heavy duty frame with a high damage gun (sniper, spear, big rockets, etc) will allow you to survive long enough to kill them a few times, it just isn't any fun to have to switch to that OTHER loadout to deal with the ONE person♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
Others will complain about the cloaked snipers in the game, and on one level, I agree with them, but in all honesty, they are really not that hard to deal with. The only annoying ones are as stated above, the double turret + sniper + 4 lasers that kills everything.
If you are really having that mutch trouble with a sniper, follow these rules:
1. Get killed once and figure out where they are (deathcam OP)
2. Equip a straightfire weapon (no fireballs, bouncing bombs, greyhounds, or slow moving rockets)
3. Position yourself so you can fire at the top of the building while still being below it (tanks can shoot further up, than they can down)
4. Fire at will (and chances are, the sniper wont change buildings... ever since there are few sniping points, so if you want to climb up there yourself, camp them all day long)
Some handy tips for building bots
Use the following for determining what "weight class" you should be in
Armor <100 Need acceleration >20
100<Armor<200 Need acceleration >10
200<Armor<300 Need high damage weps (cause you're not going anywhere)
For first buys:
Recommended Weapon: Revolver (pretty much a direct upgrade from default)
Recommended Chassis: Something light (you will weigh yourself down too much with even a medium armor chassis)
Recommended Propulsion: Spider Legs/Vintage Anything
Recommended Support: Heal Guns (aim at ground to heal yourself), Jump Jets (all the jukes + hilarious), Any high ammo, low damage support gun (helps maintain damage during primary shots, or when you run out of primary ammo)
Recommended Turret: The UFO, brain, flat, circle thing (I honestly don't remember what it's called) It has nice armor, low profile, decent weight, and looks pretty darn cool. OR if blitzkreig is more your style, go with Sputnik (made of aluminum).
Stay AWAY from:
Support Chassis: Low armor, medium weight, and the two support modules only turn with the tank
Bronze Cannon Weapon: Fun to use, impractical as t1ts on a hanar (kudos if you get the reference)
Mortars Support Weapon: Maybe just me, but these things can't hit a damn thing
A.N.T.I Weapon: Slow as molasses bullet speed, limited range, 50 damage only on direct hit, pretty much guarantees you wont hit a damn thing at even medium range. Has awesome visuals though :(
Wing Support Module: Useless without jump jet, cant jump with legs off of buildings to use, puts you in the air longer for people to shoot you (again, tanks can shoot higher up than the can down)
and that's all I had time to test.
Lastly, BE PREPARED FOR CRASHES!!! Holy crap this thing breaks more often than you get one-shotted. Crashes can happen at any time, from firing a weapon, to joining a new game, to buying a part in the store. To ensure that you can load the game again, start task manager and end the process from there (steam will recognize it as closed, and try to sync, enabling you to play again). If you don't do that, steam will constantly say you are still running the game, you can't exit until it's closed, and steam takes a steaming dump on you until your reboot your computer. (I tried simply deleting the appcache folder in steam, but it still wouldn't let me)
All in all a fun game when it works. While some weapons are a little unbalanced, and one chassis is obviously unbalanced, it's not that hard to gang up on those people and kill them. Closest I can describe this game to (this is NOT like robocraft, one is a voxel builder, this is a mix and match) is a simplified, tank version of Exteel (minus the awesome finishers as well)

After 62 hours playing, I can honestly say that I love this game! I would recommend it to all of my friends. I cannot wait until Aug 16th, 2017 when the new expansion comes out, and I would be very happy to see this game continue to be improved on by the devs.
However, all is not gravy(good) when it comes to Conan Exiles. First off, I would not say that I have the best gaming PC out there in the world, but it is well past the requirements for this game; it seems to me that no matter what I change the settings to, that the game continues to have major times of lag and instability, crashes, and just general un-optimization. This will happen most times when I play online, but can also happen even on single player. Don't get me wrong though, I know that this game is in early access; I am not complaining so much as informing.
Even with the un-optimization of the game, it is far from "un-playable" though, and I would like everyone who reads this post to know that. In fact, if you do pick up this game and can get past a few of the difficulties it can present right now in early access, I think that you will have a great experience. Especially if you like survival-crafting games, or just Conan in general. In my closing, I would also just like to give the devs of Conan exiles a final encouragement to continue doing what they are doing. I hear tell of mounts and other awesome things in the future for this game, so please keep up the good work!
Review Update* - August 19, 2017
As of August 16th, 2017 when The Frozen North expansion was released, and also since the following two patches where applied a few days later, the game has become much better optimized for me. Apart from the occasional server disconnections or game client crashes, I can now play with little to no lag, no matter where I am or where I go in the game. I can even play on Ultra settings, without anti-aliasing on! Great job DEVs!
Review Update 2* - August 30, 2017
After 135 hours of playing this game, and as of August 28th, 2017 I can no longer recommend this game. I do not know what happend, or why this game continues to screw me over, but I have had enough. Currently I do not recommend playing this game, because of all of the crashes; they have now made the game unplayable for me. I can deal with the equipment wheel when playing with a controller, the fact that running de-equips your weapon or tool, mob spawning glitches or bugs, server restarts, and even the multitude of other things that people have talked about.
However, I will not and can not deal with the crashes anymore; I have sat in the loading screen long enough, while hoping that my stuff is still around when I get back, because I died when the game crashed, only to find that it is not. I have grown tierd of having to knock out and rope another thrall because the crash made me lose it on the way back to the wheel. I am sick of switching my gear to a torch and crashing out of the game in the middle of a dark cave, while being surrounded by spiders. I hate swimming to escape a mob and then crashing once I hit the water, only to come back to find out that I drowned. And most importantly, I am fed up with having to craft a new waterskin every time I crash, because I rolled back to before I collected the grass fiber and lost it. I have crashed at important times, I have crashed at times when I am just standing around crafting, and I have crashed after I crash, after I crash. I am done. My final words of advice; Buy the game now while it is cheap, and then enjoy it later once it is in full release. Oh, and hope to hell that the crashes are fixed by then.

Is this a good game? Yes (if you like turn based RPG of course)
Is this better than the first? I would say no.
If I had to summarize :
+the game is beautiful, you can clearly see that the designers were inspired
+the story of the firt act is really good
-the armor system is frustrating, since it encourages raw damage over control, at higher difficulty this really limits the number of good builds. A single point remaining in an armor (for you or your ennemy) can change the outcome of a combat, not really fun
-for example ranger/sniper doesn't really work at higher difficulty (all ennemies have some sort of TP), and invocation is terrible
-mages have basically to specialise in one scool to be efficient
-two handed weapons is heavily favored for now, you can solo the game in tactical difficulty with a solo 2-handed warrior
-many things that worked in the first divinity original sin has been nerfed : crafting is more or less useless outside of runes, changing surfaces on the ground is sub-optimal (enemies like to put everything on fire, forget about poison and oil), etc
-initiative is only useful on one team number since there will be an alternance between your team and foes (hate the new system)
-the worst flaw of the game is the very weak act 3 (the last one) if you ask me (no spoil, but it is the worst of the three and the shortest)
-act 3 has by far the most translation's errors of the three, it feels rushed (for example description in the place of the name of the object and name in the place of the description or two times the same sentences in dialogue, not really funny)
-act 3 is also I think the one with the more bugs, at least it feels like it
So basically I am frustrated, it is quite a good game, but it feels not nearly as complete as the first. The end is rushed, the combat's mechanic is heavily damage oriented (forget about surfaces and such, it makes basically no damage and no control), and your life is basically useless, only armor really count (at least on tactical difficulty).
I don't know, it could have been so much better than I can't recommend it right now.

Edited: I'm leaving my original review below this new one as it shows my first impressions. However this new post covers my thoughts having learned to play it.
So this game is worth buying if you like micro managment, keeping track of dynasty and bloodlines, making sure your own family is kept in check as you slowly march through history in a attempt to re write said history. For me, I needed a friend to literally spoon feed me the game and its concepts. Forget thinking of this game as a rpg about one character. You are more of a guiding spirit that possesses a person and from there on you inhabit the body of the direct bloodline heir to your kingdom or whatever your in charge of.
The focus of this game is based entirely on what you want, you can shoot to make your own cleric the pope, to try and change the major world religion, to wage nothing but endless war through de jure claims and falsefied documents via your spymaster. Starting in Ireland is the noob location and to be honest I never moved past it except for 1 or 2 playthroughs where i started elsewhere in europe as a tribal. I found that the game in entirely unfair, but its upfront about that unfairness and why it is so.
Make alliances if you wish to live, hold territory that you took, or in general dont wanna get butt r@aped. Preferrably with larger nations that dont like your enemies. For me befriending and marrying off my daughters to the French and Holy Roman Empires rulers, proved a vital asset as england and scottland hate the Irish ( who knew? ). The game can be a great deal of fun but as time goes on it begins to drag on as so many of its key features and historical time frames are locked behind a pay wall.
The various DLC packages that you will find on the store page contain things from music, artwork, clothing hair and other things for the people in the protraits, dynasty shileds and what not. All of these things are arguably non essential and can be called not part of the main game.
However there are some DLC which are basically a part of the game and playing without them seems a bit redundent. I'm not sure why the company has decided to make all these things DLC as for me it just encouraged me to look for mods that would do most of these things without me having to pay for them, and where I couldn't find mods I at times I used hacks and pirated DLC.
The games devs simply want to much money for these various little things and honestly its a bit insulting to me as a consumer. Seriously just charge more for the base game and include all these things.
Overall my opinion of the game is a 6/10 its a above average game with above average dlc issues. If you hate micromanagment and little to no visuals to show you what you are building in your kingdom or doing as you wage war then this isn't the game for you.
If on the other hand you want a game where all of that is present and you enjoy minimal visuals then you should be fine. Many people have racked absolutly ridiculous hours on this game and I dont hold it against them for doing so. Some people really enjoy the things you can do with this game, but for me eventualy it just becomes a bit of a drag. Not to mention every time I tried to game with a friend the game would always de sync and we wouldn't be playing together anymore.
Also i'm a total save cheater and I cannot imagine playing the game on Ironman mode as so many times I was completly trashed by some seemingly random betrayal from a close relative who was suddenly backed by a neighboring country. This is something i ahted about the game, you will just suddenly be at war with other people. Its like its always a suprise attack, there is no negotiations or warning signs really. The farthest I ever got was becoming king of the Erie and holding a duchy in scottland via my queens family rights. Thankfully Scottland wasn't allied with England at the time because my daughter had been assassinated in the 3rd year of her marriage to the Holy Roman Emperor. France was in the middle of a civil war that it almost certainly was going to lose and would be no help to me.
I dont know how players are able to "clean house" of their various trouble making people as any time and everytime I wanted to execute, imprison or otherwise remove someone from my kingdom it would cause all my subjects to collectively hate me more which in turn leads to more and more in fighting and squabling. I get that these things make some people angry.. but everyone? Really that just doesn't make sense. How many times in history have Tyrants rules for decades at a time with no rebellions at all because their subjects and lesser lords are afraid of them? Quite a bit as I recall, not in this game though. Being a tyrant is out of the question as if you attempt to do so, nobody will ever like you, all assassinations attempts against you will succeed and more than likely you will have a very short game.
Also, for ireland the amount of income you regularly gain is very little. I'm not sure I understand the economics of the game as there is no trading or production of goods that can yield you better trade results or better income. All you can do is manage your taxes and try to control as much territory as possible and upgrade that territory as soon as possible by building cities and other locations that give you more taxes.

I've been following this games "progress" ever since inception in 2010. I was a Freshman in high school at the time. I'm a junior in college now. So was this game worth the seven years it took to make? No...
The combat is solid. The main issue with it is that the game has nothing in the way of tutorials. For BASIC MECHANICS.
You have to find out on your own that you can't block broadswords with a rapier. You have to find out on your own how dodging works. You have to find out on your own that you have to hold down the right mouse button to block thrown weapons. You have to figure out on your own how disarming works. The game simply doesn't tell you any of these things, and expects you to either figure it out with obscene amounts of trial and error or just do what I did and look up how the basic mechanics work on youtube...
The parkour is mediocre at best, and you'll often find your rabbit glitching onto invisible ledges or running off the side of a pillar due to the overblown momentum physics. If your character is going to skid half a mile before it stops, how about make the targets a little wider. Don't even get me started on the broken wall running...
The graphics were impressive. In 2010...
The story is, in a single word, boring. The characters are even more so.
Levels come in 2 forms. Get from A to B with the mediocre parkour, or clear the level of enemies. That's it.
If you're going to buy it anyway, I recommend the Therium 2 mod. It's a whole lot better than the vanilla story mode.
Edit: I forgot about the death messages, which actually do mention the timed block for thrown weapons (It might have more, but this was the only one I checked). The reason I forgot is that it will just spam the same message about rolling to your feet whenever you die during most fights and I just started to ignore them completely.
And you will die. A lot... At least until you give up on trying to legitimately fight, say, 2 wolves at the same time that poise through normal attacks and just abuse the leg cannon attack on them.
Pretty good game 8/8 would play again.

Awesomenauts is a very interesting and new take on the MOBA genre.
Instead of going into a mythical/fantasy setting, the game is set into the very very distant future, where robots have anger issues, aliens surf around and stab you in the back and talk in pop culture references and '80s movie quotes and technology is so advanced that it became sentient and created two factions to fight each other for the rarest material in the universe, little sparkly cubes called "Solar".
The art style and music is inspired by the american cartoons of the '80s.
The game currently features a cast of 16 (more to come soon) very interesting characters, each with their own unique abilities and ways of play and 4 maps to show off your skills in 3v3 battle arena mode (take down the turrets, take down the base, ????, profit).
It's worth noting that currently, there are a lot of balance issues, poor matchmaking that might put veteran players and new player in the same game (eventually leading to the rage quit of some players and leaving you with AI controlled bots, which are pretty good, most of the time), eventual laggy games and the leaderboards are a bit broken.
Unlike other MOBAs, Awesomenauts is a more casual game, with fast paced gameplay, the focus of the game being teamwork and fast reflexes. The majority of the community is pretty good and you'll be called mean things and asked to commit suicide way less then any other MOBA out there.
The game has very different mechanics from other MOBAs, players having to combine strategy with lots of jumping/platforming and shooting. I highly recommend watching a few tutorials first or trying out Practice Mode on highest difficulty.
It's worth nothing that you if you are the kind of player that likes to go solo, get high on the leaderboards and have highest stats, either this game is not for you, or you'll find it as being a serious challenge.
Bottom line: I personally found this game very enjoyable most of the times, the characters really funny and cool looking, the music is a treat, the gameplay really fast and addicting and besides the balance and matchmaking issues, all you need is a couple of friends to form a team and jump online and a few learning tutorials.

While this game was released before Ys 6 on Steam, it was actually released after Ys 6 initially. So you can tell there are some refinements.
First, instead of 3 different swords, you get the traditional weapon system from Ys 1 and 2, and the elemental attacks are replaced with three different magic rings. Fire Magic works pretty much the same as Ys 2, while the added Earth Magic and Wind Magic add another layer to your combat. Ys 6 lacked distance attacks and good way to mob enemies, while this provides just that. Earth Magic can be used to charge towards or away from enemies, which also provides another layer to combat. Overall, unlike Ys 6 where Brillante was pretty much the only sword you ever used, here, you find yourself using the three magics more or less balanced. There are also a lot of enemies that behave differently, especially the jumpers who make it harder to spam down stab like you always did in Ys 6, and some enemies requiring a specific magic to get through them easily, so the combat is overall an improvement, probably more than it initialy seems. The bosses are pretty fun too, though Ys 6 had good ones as well. As far as the final boss goes, this one trumps Ys 6's big time. Main combo being 6 hits instead of 3 also helps.
The dungeon design is, because Ys 3 was originally a sidescroller, flat, but in a good way. This makes the design a lot more comprehensible, and added with MUCH better platforming mechanic (no dash jumps, but also very forgiving gliding technic), it makes the dungeon design just much better. Of course, it's no Zelda, but then again, Zelda is built around dungen puzzles, while this game is about hacking away at your enemies, so it's not a fair comparison.
The problem is then the scale. There is only one village, and 32 NPCs. There are 6 dungeons, which I think is actually the same number as Ys 6, but it's overworld (if you can call it that) is pitifully small. As in, smaller than Ys 1. So if you are expecting Ys 2-esque, legit RPG with lots of characters to interact with, you are not going to get it here. Kinda sad, considering Falcom is usually really good at this stuff if you look at Trails series.

For some clarification: I have played this game since Open Beta around September 2011, long before it was released on Steam so I'd average around maybe 5,000 hours give or take a thousand.
This game used to be the greatest thing since sliced bread. The combat is phenomenol, still kind of is. The story is gripping although a little trope-y. Most if not all of the classes are unique in their own way, each having their own playstyle. Now why would I not recommend this game despite all the good things, it's only because the cons heavily outweigh the pros.
Let's start with content. Content is one of the biggest concerns I have had with this game for a while. The level caps have increased from 16, 24, 32, 40, 50 etc., with each cap including a couple of small 'nests' which are more or less instances with 4-5 bosses with some mechanics built in, a raid which is essentially like the nests only with 8 people instead of 4 and then the hell raid which adds a couple mechanics and makes everything stronger. Each cap lasts about 5-8 months with the exception of 40 cap which lasted nearly a year and some odd months. These months are filled with grinding the same dungeons and 'nests' week to week to try to get the best gear.
Now we'll talk about gear. Gear follows a familiar rarity system, Normal, Magic, Rare, Epic, Unique, and Legendary. Normal to Rare is highly disregarded when playing Dragon Nest, if you're seen wearing them you'll be kicked from a party without hesitation, but we'll get into community in a bit. Epic gear is obtained from doing the nests over and over again for materials to craft. There's usually 2 different Epic sets for each cap, one being for magic-based classes, the other being for physical based classes. Unique gear is obtained from completing the normal raid and getting it dropped randomly. Legendary gear is recieved from drops in the hell version of a raid. Essentially to get the best gear in the game you essentially have to just have immense luck, and not to mention a team which can actually clear a raid consistently.
Gear does not change any part of attire except for your weapons, so if you're looking to be a fashionista without forking over some cash you're out of luck. When it comes to making your character not look like the average joe, you'll usually have to pay 15-30 dollars on a costume. A lot of the time you won't be able to mix-and-match costumes to get the "ultimate" look just based on the fact that you'll lose a set bonus. These set bonuses get better the more you pay up, and if you ever do feel the need to mix-and-match you'll have to get lucky buying gachapon and getting the single item that allows you to do so, did I mention you need one for each piece of equipment you wish to alter? That's not all, if you're looking to get the highest rarity costumes you'll need to fork over even more cash to get sets and fuse those set pieces together for a CHANCE at a higher rarity costume piece. Good luck!
Class balancing is another of the bigger concerns with the game. Every so often there's a balancing patch, when this patch comes around there will ALWAYS be that one class that excells over all the others. This a lot of the time leads to people completely shunning other classes based on their tier list. And when it comes to nerfing a class, the nerf will just be making another class significantly more powerful than the other. If you're thinking about exclusively playing one class and still being able to join up with others then I'm sorry to say that's not the case.
Let's get to talking about the community. It's a fairly small game so the community is kind of scrunched up. A lot of the people are generally really nice, but when it comes to actually playing the game, personalities may be a bit skewed. A fair bit of players, especially the people who have been around for a long while, which make up a fair portion of the game, are elitist in one way or another. There is a list of requirements for joining parties ranging from having proper gear, the highest enchantments, the best gems, etc. It doesn't matter if you're trying to learn how to do the latest nest or something to that extent, you will be kicked on the spot if the party leader is not appeased by your gear. This game is without a doubt not friendly to new players, I hate to say.
PVP is one of the few things this game has left to offer, and even in that case PVP has had an incessive lag since the game was released till now.
I could keep going on and on about all the problems with the game, but I feel I've covered the bare essentials. A couple years ago I would've recommended this game, but unfortunately it just fell into the usual Korean MMO loop of unfortunate cases.

A surprisingly good little tank-em-up focusing on fast-paced action. One particularly neat thing I like about the game is that the parts you start off with with your starter tank.. aren't actually the "all-rounder" parts, for once! The starter gear is some of the fastest and lightest in the game, which is an interesting touch. (Although, first thing I'd say to a new player, upgrade that cannon, pronto.)
Another thing I really love about this game, it's not Pay to Win. At all. I've only spent about ~4 hours playing this game and haven't (yet! ;D) purchased the Basic Pack.. and yet, I can afford all the most expensive gameplay-modifying tank parts out of the Gold I earned during matches - the most expensive I've seen being "The Beetle" for 15G. For the record, you earn a minimum of 3G for a match victory, or 1G for a match loss - with +1G for every 10 enemies defeated and +1G for every 5 control points captured in Conquest mode. A good 8 matches and you can afford that Beetle. (Unless you're absolutely boss and win EVERY match ;U)
The only problem I have with this game currently is the weapon balance. In it's current state, snipers and gatling weaopns seem a bit TOO powerful at the moment (especially gatling cannons, which seem to have the accuracy of a sniper rifle, for some reason!) That, and the hull which allows a player to equip two turrets seems to have no drawbacks, considering that each turret has a weapon AND two Support Sockets. (My suggestion? Remove the two Support Sockets on the extra weapon! That's the Assist's specialty, not the Twin's!) -- I've seen some tanks using the Twin hull dealing ludicrous DPS for the sole reason that the hull gives 2 weapon slots and 4 support slots in total. Yeesh!

Definitely the best Survival game out there right now. It's shed it's EA bugginess and is a great core game, with the more interesting features being player building and housing looking very very good and melee combat, which is now smooth and reactive, although needed enhancements are due in the major patch this week that may bring it from OK to good. I found my experience was better playing with friends as you can diversify your crafting skills and specialise into areas that you might not reach on your own, as quickly.
It can be tough and unforgiving at the start on a standard paced server, but this hurdle is a challenge that makes progression more rewarding. However you can die and lose things by being unprepared or hasty or just careless, so the challenge of a dynamic world is ever present, which it should be.
The climbing and vertical building is unparalled. If you like building things, you have a toolset that can see you building bases on pinnacle peaks, along the sides of mountains, staircases up crags and chair lifts and so on. Falling or slipping you now have an option to grab and clutch at the slope - really cool if you can save yourself!
Housing has lots of furniture and visible crafting items that make home really feel like home. This should appeal to those that like having a permanent house in a dynamic public server. I know my wife loves this aspect!
Multiplayer, PvP and guild management is underdeveloped, primarily due to server number limits and a lot of "land grabbing" that can block areas of maps prior to climbing, unless the vertical sides are in closed ceiling, where there are some spots. The small server numbers affect a truly multiplayer experience, I rarely bump into other players, but it's nice to know you should still lock your doors at night :) I haven't played on any truly PvP servers and can anticipate some issues persist with that entire section of players, because it always does, however it is something the developers are trying hard with based on their updates and communications. Larger scale PvP might just be a pipedream right now, although im sure some have experienced it.
Magic is sorely missing. There are a few bugs or undesirable gameplay items that you tend to notice after 20-40 gameplay hours, but these are not detracting. The single Biome could be tiresome and lack of coordinated PvE content is something we will see added to, and needs more of. Especially something less end game that is more challenging, like rare monsters, random events and easier group content for the level 20's.
I've already hadd my money's worth before launch next year and I'm looking forward to new content as it comes. The developers are way more interactive than other survival games and have provided some limited roadmapping, and video devblogs. That's something i really appreciate as it gains my trust. I recommend this game to people who like this genre or for someone looking to try it out alike.

It's not a game for everyone, due to its sheer complexity. If you're used to strategy games like Total War or Civilization, that's just training compared to this game. It has a ton of different interacting gameplay mechanisms that can be rather hard to learn at first, both due to the large amount of them and their complexity. I can safely say that there is no other strategy game quite like this. But, complicated game mechanics aside, what is this game actually about?
The simplest way for me to describe this is "Game of Thrones (there's a GoT mod for this game that's said to be very good) in medieval Europe". Just like in Game of Thrones, scheming, intrigues, sex and murder is all over the place, and the rulers do anything to secure more power.  Unlike many other strategy games, you're not playing as a nation striving for power and world dominance. Instead, you're playing a ruler in medieval Europe (if you have the relevant expansions, you can also play as Muslims in northern Africa and the Middle East, as well as Indian rulers, among others) in the time of the crusades. Rather than conquering others for more territory (which you can still do, of course), you aim to gather as much prestige for your dynasty as possible, while managing your life.
In order to secure a good future for your dynasty, you need to make sure you have good children (who you play as after death) and good relationships with your subjects so they don't turn against you. In your quest for prestige, you can find yourself playing in many different ways. If you want to play as an iron-fisted tyrant who executes anyone doubting him, you can do so, and if you want to play a kind and understanding noble, that's just as possible. Do you want to kill your brothers to eliminate competition for the crown, or do you want them to grow powerful on their own and help you secure more power? Do you marry your children to secure alliances, or simply to get them out of the way? The choice is yours, and sometimes, you might find yourself making morally bad decisions that turn out to be good for you in the long run.
Does the end justify the means, or is the most important thing to always do good? Crusader Kings II puts ethics and morals in an interesting perspective, and I think we can learn a lot from it, not just about history and how the medieval world worked, but also about philosophy and psychology. Perhaps we can understand the atrocities of the past by putting ourselves in the shoes of the ones in charge?
In summary, Crusader Kings II is a great (but complicated) game for all strategy fans, and I highly recommend it. Even if the expansions might be a bit expensive to buy all at once, I recommend it, since they all add so much to the game and make it better. It's an amazing and addicting game about awful things.

I preordered this game a long time ago, and It's finally out! I've enjoyed reading the devlogs and occasionally playing the beta versions this whole time, it's been a lot of fun. I think that when you review this game you need to answer two questions: Is the game as good as nine years in development? The answer to that, is no. It's not. The second question is: Is it a fun game? The answer to that is a resounding yes! It's a lot of fun! The story is nothing to write home about, and similar to the first games story it's just a backdrop for some fun fights using a fantastic combat system. But if you want to play for the story, probably don't buy this game. If you want to have fun and learn a pretty deep and original combat system, then I would fully recommend this game to you.
The developers care about this game. I don't think that they could have worked nine years on it otherwise, and that love shows, all of the systems are advanced and interesting! However, it is a shame that the story mode isn't more fleshed out, and feels more tacked on than anything. I hope Wolfire takes their experiences making Overgrowth and turns that into a fully fleshed out new game, because even if the whole experience isn't there the amount of love they put into their work really shows, and I'll play anything else that they will make!

New Review:
In short-
I was watching the Great British Baking Show and they were making mirror cakes with layers of fruit and ganache. I suddenly found myself really starving so I got a bowl of organic vanilla bean ice cream, mixed in tons of fresh fruits like blueberries, banannas and madarins, topped it with dark chocolate syrup and liquor, and finally, heavy whipping cream. It was very satisfying and made me feel like I was right there, eating mirror cake. This game is NOT like that. It's like watching people making great desserts, and you knowing you might have a stale piece of bread in the kitchen that you could maybe put some peanut butter on, only you come to find out that you don't even have that. Not satisfying in the least. And on the contrary, playing this game is a tease, because it'll only let you down.
In reality-
My old review is below, and you can see that I was wrong to recommend initially. Some time has passed and this game has a release date for PC in less than half a year (May of 2018? now). HOWEVER, the most vital aspects of the game are absolutely missing. The developers keep adding more weapons and weather effects, but the game already looks beautiful, and we already know the 3D models and armor fits the ragdolls with no problem. Why do we need such ornate weapon models, actually, when we are essentially wandering alone in the wastes? Someone really doesn't waste time world-building. And (even more) dynamic weather is on the bottom of most people's lists at the moment. This isn't The Sims 4, with everyone griping about adding a Seasons pack.
Combat is still clunky, as if we were aiming for a game that played exactly like Elder Scrolls Oblivion. An enjoyable classic, minus all the portal closing, but  let's not aspire to emulate Oblvion's third person combat if at all possible.
For me, however, what's really missing is a socio-ecomonic simulation - even on a minor level. There is no story, and the game does NOT communicate a reason for you to be so alone in your struggles. Yes, in multiplayer, you can join clans and guilds, but we all know how these games go. No one really does that to any great extent. People just ask in chat how to do X or Y. In the gameworld, there are raider/bandit mobs all over, and yes you can turn them into thralls. But it's not very satisfying to do so after a short while because there is no consequences for your violence. There's no satisfaction in your power. I enjoy hoarding as many stones and palm fronds as possible more than I like gathering thralls. The kingdom you're building is essentially for you alone, because in single player, you're on your own, no NPCs, no story, no benefit you ruling over your thralls. I was going to call them minions, but that implies some recognition by them, of you. These are truely thralls in the same way that rocks are rocks and trees are trees. Both are there and there is no illusion of consciousness or suffering on their part. They can't talk to you, complain, and you don't feel like they are broken or devoid of life... they share the same AI as every mob in the game that just runs up and attacks you, like a wolf or crocodile.
It would be interesting if there were some kind of incentives in the game, or if you could have at least one NPC follower to share your journey with you, one whom would have some chatter about the world. Or what if non-thralls who would trade with you. Or NPCs who were slumming, just like you, it out in the elements? And they had a sad story to tell, or a fetch quest even. See how bad things are, that I'm wishing for fetch quests?
I know this is not really an RPG, but there needs to be more than just walking around harvesting materials, building a raggedy hut with a few rugs, capturing other human-looking mobs, and wandering around the wilderness. These  things are interesting, but you really can't shake the feeling that you want more.
I just don't understand how so much time would be sunk into working on a game, making the world look so enthralling, fine-tuning a robust and rewarding crafting system, and letting you outfit your character however you want -- then neglect fun combat, give no story to the player, no motivation for them  to care about the world, and no real objectives other than just build a base and catch some thralls.

I typically don't write reviews in total seriousness, but this game is a whole lot of disappointment and no matter how hard you try, you'll find to see this game as real and established as a 3 year old's drawing of a house.
I have not played Lugaru, but from what I understand, Lugaru was a good game, and Overgrowth was supposed to be a worthy successor. Though I haven't played Overgrowth from the beginning, I followed its development since 2012. The game was geniunely intriguing--Ninja rabbits that fight other rabbits, wolves, etc. But then after a few years of development, I thought this game would be dead.
Now that it was finally released, I was more than happy to try it and see what Wolfire had come up with.
The story is short, I finished it in one sitting of about 2 hours. That would not be such a big issue if the levels were good. I was expecting Wolfire to utilize all of their game mechanics better than any modder could, but all of the levels were cumbersome and while some of them were largely sceneric, they had absolutely nothing to do in them but keep moving towards a very easily seen pathway. A lot of the setting seems oddly fabricated--random chunks of blocks, very generic and robotic placement of landmarks solely made for platforming. This would be fine too, if the platforming was fun.
Now, I don't think Assassin's Creed style free running is very interactive or fun either, but at the very least they've made it fluid enough that you can go where you want to. Turner in Overgrowth will go where you want to, but the parkour is beyond frustrating in some levels as the wall running and jumping off of walls doesn't always connect. You'll expect to jump in one direction only to know you won't unless you get the timing to a certain millisecond perfection. After landing on a very small platform, sometimes you'll fall off, which is realistic as momentum can't disappear, and Turner's inertia would make it impossible to just grip onto a platform after falling on it, but the amount of times I completely missed platforms, and just slipped right off was ridiculous, either the platforms needed to be fixed or Turner needs to stop scurring after landing. As far as gameplay goes, the combat is as good as they market it, there are no click counters or easy combo finishers, just simple left click to attack, right click to dodge or get the timing right to disarm/throw. There is one problem in the jump kick being too powerful, if you want the game to be a breeze, just jump kick everyone, nothing can stop it. The stealth is okay, but clearly there are problems with detection as some enemies randomly turned their heads without any reason and noticed me immediately.
The game overall feels unfinished. Dialogs are just text, levels are completely and utterly unfinished and annoying. The story is short, and the free running mechanics seem unfinished. I realize this game has been in development for 9 years, so Wolfire has received money from early access buyers. I'm not certain how a game production company is run, but reciving payments of $29.99 USD over 9 years to finish a game should have allowed Wolfire to hire more and invest into this game enough to make it AAA level. Instead this feels like a base of a game left for modders to finish. I only hope that Wolfire uses the money from this game to actually hire a real team as it seems like only a few people worked on this game.

Seven years later, Overgrowth has finally left early access and finished development.  Was it worth the wait?  Frankly, no.
The plot is rather uninspired and shallow.  It tries to build up lore and development and characterization, but it fails to do anything.  You'll jump from segment to segment in the story and it'll feel less like you're going through an adventure and more like the plot was tacked on to give reasons for each jump between arena style combat and platforming levels.  Things will happen, but you'll be given no reason to care for anyone you meet.  You'll get no explanations or deeper development to the areas you go through, the factions you meet, the characters you talk to.  You'll have to fight characters that clearly know you, and rather than feel bad for them, you'll be confused as to how they know you.
It's coherent enough, but really doesn't contribute anything to the game.
The game presented itself originally as a mechanically skill based game, where timing, reactions, and thinking would decide whether you live or die.  You would have to make use of your full range of parkour abilities, on top of a diverse skill set of martial arts moves, to fight various enemies that required different approaches when fighting.  In reality, the game boils down to doing a jump attack that one shots most enemies or abusing the numerous weapons you're both given and able to find in almost every level.  Direct 1 on 1 combat almost never happens in the game, and when it does, it's against an enemy with a weapon or who normal attacks are ineffective on, so you're forced to resort to cheap tactics or abusing your jump kick like usual.  The mechanics for fun combat are certainly there, it's just the actual game isn't designed around it which is disappointing.
You'll mostly be frustrated if you try to play the game the way it was intended to be played.
One of the biggest things I looked forward to most in Overgrowth was the ability to make use of the interesting parkour movement you have.  I wanted to have giant towers to climb, mountains to scale, gaps to cross.  I wanted to run along walls and explore massive areas.  What I got however was mostly empty areas with almost no real need to make use of the amazing movement options you're given.  There are maybe 3 levels in the entire game that make use of the platforming parkour mechanics, and they railroad you into going specific ways, with distinct markings showing you where to go.  On top of that, a lot of the parkour moments just feel poorly designed, as if they were never actually play tested.  It can feel like a roll of the dice when you go from wall running to jumping to a ledge, as some times you just can't make it no matter how many times you try, or the character simply doesn't grab the ledge at all.
It isn't horrible, but it's boring at best, frustrating at worst.
The game is short.  Real short.  I played through both lugaru and overgrowth, as well as several different mods, and it took less than 4 hours for everything.  For 30$, I feel like you should get more than just a sub-par 4 hour experience.  Hell, if you're interested in overgrowth, you've probably already played Lugaru anyways, so you're getting even less value for your money then.
The game isn't all hopeless.  It has mod support, as well as steam workshop integration.  There are already several mods for the game built that fix everything I've found lacking in the game.  If you want more plot focus, better fights, or just want to platform, there's a mod that gives you just that.  It also includes Lugaru, the first game by Wolffire, which while it suffers from several of the problems I've already listed, is still a rather enjoyable game.
I frankly don't recommend this game.  It's expensive and you don't really get anything worth the money.  You'll probably enjoy more about the game than you disliked, but it'll still be unfulfilling and lackluster, and as it stands, the mods for the game don't really make up for what the game itself lacks.  Get it on sale if you're still interested, and I mean 10$ or less sale.

Overgrowth is one of the most unfocused and horribly mismanaged games i've ever played. Every facet of it is completely fine tuned to a mirror sheen: the graphics look great, the combat and platforming work well, and the editor is both complex and simple. Unfortunately, Wolfire forgot to make an actual game that takes good advantage of these features, leaving an experience that is extremely shallow despite having a feature list in the hundreds. This game has incredibly cool things like dynamic blood physics, dynamic bone/muscle density physics, dynamic throwing weapon physics, individual hitboxes so characters react realistically to blows, absolutely amazing support for mods, and a dynamic combat system that is both extremely dangerous and highly rewarding. Yet there is no real story mode to hold it all together, and the two campaigns that are available are a weak remake of the game Lugaru (which a much, much worse story) and Overgrowth itself, which is a horribly boring story filled with unlikable characters and weak, dry writing. Both are also very short, and will take you about 3 or so hours to complete. They're also terribly designed, though i'll get into that further down the review.
*Gameplay
This is the main draw of the game. Overgrowth contains a highly inventive and skill-intensive combat system that can incredibly fun. There are tons of moves Turner can do like leg sweeps and strong kicks, coupled with neat weapons that all feel different and have their own uses. Most notably, the game can be exceptionally brutal and punishing. Essentially, one good hit is all it really takes to kill someone: a thrown dagger to the head, a nasty kick to the neck, or a sword slash into the shoulder. Because of this small effort-to-kill ratio, battles can end deceptively quickly. That tough-looking dog armed with a greatsword can get a nasty slash across his neck, causing him to bleed out and die. The enemies are also incredibly smart, being able to gang up on you or chase you down with impunity, as well as being genuinely dangerous opponents. All of this adds together to create a dynamic and fluid combat system that rewards reaction time and ruthless brutality, and it feels joyously violent once you get the hang of it. Unfortunately, the combat system is often too overwhelming in many scenarios of the story mode: many of the rules that apply to you do not really apply to enemies due to their wicked fast reaction time. You simply will not be as good as the enemies due to their literally machine-tier reaction speed: I can vivdly recount an experience where I wanted to defeat a single rabbit opponent. I was at full health, approached him, blocked his sweep and was instantly killed when I was judo-flipped to the ground and kicked in the neck, killing me instantly. I had no time to react and little time to process what had happened. Enemies will also almost always roll out of the way, with can make followup attacks very difficult to do. While all of this is fine when facing one or two enemies, you'll be frequently tasked with killing upwards of three most of the time. While this is pretty cool, and keeps you on your toes, it also means that the games deaths feel very unfair at times due to being ganged up on and beaten down. This is only exacerbated by a horrible tutorial that teaches you very little, forcing me to check guides in order to figure out how to do things like catch weapons or even drop them (Note, you need to CLICK to block, holding does nothing). And low, the mighty Leg Cannon, an attack that is completely unblockable (for some reason) and does massive damage. This will most likely become your go-to attack around the midpoint of the game due to it's incredible reliability and relative lack of skill to properly use in comparison to the rest of the combat system. Would you rather fistfight that wolf that can kill you in two shots, or would you jump at it's head and kill it in two or three passes?  Turner himself also never upgrades his health or damage resistance, meaning he'll be fragile for most of the game.
Ultimately the combat system is well done, but the ruthless percision of the A.I and the story mode's swarming tactics make it both too punishing and too demanding to throughly enjoy outside of one or two on one fights. The game also has excellent mod support, and I am eager to see what people will create with the game's incredibly powerful editor.
The platforming is very fun and works suprisingly well, though some people report that it can be glitchy. I have faced no such issues, but be wary.
*Graphics
Overgrowth looks very good, and is optimzed well.... somewhat. Character models look very good, and the effects are nice. The animations also deserve special note, as they are realistic and make the combat fun when they work. When a rabbit whose throat I slit writhed on the ground in agony, I knew that this game had excellent animation quality. My framerate fluctuated rapidly throughout the game, and many assests are horribly unoptimzed (seriously, the grass in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing debilitating at times). This means that the game that has an inconsistent framerate and performance throughout the entire game, making the Overgrowth campaign a real chore to complete.
*Story
The game's story is flat out awful. The writing is boring and dry, characters come and go like the wind, and the only real character with personality is Turner himself. Despite this, Turner is an exceptionally boring protagonist, being cold and brutal from the outset. While this may be jarring for those who never played Lugaru (as his personality is in-line with the ending of that game), Turner undergoes little to no character development throughout the game. The game world is also exceptionally dark and features murder and enslavement by the bucketloads, with no real levity. You get unlikable characters in an unlikable world doing unlikable things, and I grew sick of it very quickly. Both of the initial campaigns are also incredibly short, and the ingame remake of Lugaru contains a butchered version of the original games' (actually not that bad for an early indie title) story.
Overall:
Overgrowth is too shallow to support it's myriad of interesting systems and has nothing to prop them up with, leaving a horribly empty experience with little in the way of interesting content. It's also $30 at the time of writing, which is ballsy to ask for when you make a game with as little content is this. If the modding scene takes off I could see this being a recommendation, but as it stands Overgrowth is an unrefined mess of feature creep that ultimately forgot to be a game.

The game play is very simple; you make a deck and then fight against other decks in order to win battles, placing one card down per turn. Some cards can be merged together to make stronger cards but only after you know what they make using the fusion tubes. Although it is a very simple game, I have found that it’s not exactly a balanced game. If the other character gets the upper hand, it’s extremely hard to catch up to the point you can get overpowered easily. The problem stems I think with the fact you can only place one card down at a time. This includes if you’re fusing a card together, being that the other card you’re fusing with needs to be laid down the prier turn. You also have to have a card in front of the opponent’s cards in order to block an attack to your life points and to destroy the other’s card. Cards cannot attack other cards adjacent to each other (unless they have a random power), only in front of them. If your opponent has a long stream of cards in a row and you only have one card to block with, you’re in a lot of trouble. It’s just way to hard to bring up your defenses in time before your life points are 0.
This came does have micro transactions (what game doesn’t have these now a days?) but it’s not a pay to win style. It’s easy to win coins and upgrade items free through doing the quests and just randomly going through the motions.
The artwork looks just like they jumped out of their cartoons into this dimensional rift place where they are fighting. It’s all still images which doesn’t bother me seeing as this is the norm in most mobile games. I think the pictures for the cards are taken straight out of the episodes and luckily they used high quality images. The backgrounds are common places that we see in the shows only on a floating island and based off of what character you’re fighting. Fight Peter and the Griffin house is in the background, fight Bob and his burger shop is behind.
Music is generic. I really didn’t pick out anything that stood out nor did I hear really anything that I could pick out as being from any of the cartoons. Weather they didn’t have the license for the music or just thought it would be a problem to bring it in, I’m not sure but I can understand why they didn’t really try. Most mobile games don’t have music that stands out or it loops over and over so after a while, I do tend to turn off the sound. We don’t even get the characters saying anything besides in speech bubbles so it’s not a big loss.
Overall, the game is alright, except for the problem with balancing. Even with the problem with balancing, I found myself interested in the strange fusions I could make and trying to level up the characters I could play as. It’s a pretty simple sit back game made to just have fun with it and waste some time, get achievements in steam or google play, and just have fun with your favorite characters.

There is much difficulty in reviewing a lot of Warhammer40K games because while most of them are functional, polished as a product, and arguably loyal to the tabletop lore (let's not get into Codex wars though, I'm a filthy Chaos Marine) they somehow lack an extra spark of fun that would distinguish them among the mediocrity.
Don't get me wrong, I love Warhammer40K. The only reason I joined Steam, originally, was to play the Dawn of War series. I would be the first person to sing my praise to high heavens for an Orks (and Nids) Must Die! set in Warhammer40K universe.
As a software, it functions: it runs smoothly on my 4 year old potato, there is no glaring glitch or bug, and while some may complain about the obvious port it does not assign R2 button to your melee command so there's that.
The problem, again, is that infuriating question of fun and lack thereof. Considering this is not a lore-centric title with the sole purpose of slaying Orks, it fails to deliver anything but disappointment--I mean, I had absolutely no expectations and I was still let down. Camera seems to exist only to fuel your wrath, power-ups and perks are as stock as they can be (because of how bland they are, the super-serious announcement voice for power-ups is all the more cringe-inducing), and the sound effects seem to nag you with existential, self-doubting question: why the hell are you playing this game where guns don't even sound like guns?
The whole project, from the announcement voice to uninspired gameplay to its mini-game length, has something of a business-like air to it, like the game was not something the developers wanted to make but a soul-sapping obligation on their contract to churn out an action-oriented Warhammer40K game. As a fan of the series, its universe, factions and Emperor-knows-what-else, nothing is more disheartening than this.
Co-op will not change the lack of entertainment or soul in this game, so don't drag your friend or family into this. If you want a good co-op Ork-slaying experience, play Orcs Must Die 2.
PRO TIP: When the game starts, just don't take the floating dagger.

When I tell people about 100% Orange juice, the first reply I receive is always something along the lines of "So it's kind of like Mario party?" and I can see why people would come to that conclusion, but in practice 100% Orange Juice is a completely different animal.
100% Orange Juice is a board-game inspired battle game in which players compete to achieve "Norma", a series of objectives based around either defeating various critters as well as the other players in battle, or collecting a number of stars. Stars are the only currency in 100% Orange Juice, and they are used to both fufill objectives and activate abilities that come in the form of cards, and this creates a lot of tough choices, while also preventing needless complication with alternate power sources.
The game provides many (Read: nigh-endless) opportunities for a comeback from players who are trailing behind, so unlike when someone has 5 stars in mario party and the turn limit has almost been reached, in 100% Orange juice you may find yourself winning at the last minute due to smart play, luck, or poor decision making from another player.
Initially, a lot of the content is unavailable for new players, but all of it is unlocked by playing the game. All new cards are recieved by buying booster packs with stars won from playing games. The basic booster pack contains most of the cards available, but later an expansion series becomes unlocked with a different variety of cards. The rarity and randomness of the card drops is a little annoying, but once you've recieved nine of any card, you'll stop getting it, meaning that eventually you'll get every card.
The single player mode is definitely challenging, and going in to a mission without a plan can make it extremely hard. Each of the four starting characters has a seperate campaign, and by beating all of them you'll receieve a set of extra scenarios that have interesting setups to create additional challenge for more experienced players.
I'd imagine most western players wouldn't recognise the characters used to make up the playable cast, but even if that's the case, it's still a very enjoyable game. Most people I gave the game to were capable of playing decently during their first match without much more than a brief introduction to the mechanics, so needing to memorise an encyclopaedia of rules, or knowing character matchups really isn't a hinderance to getting started.
All in all, it's a very solid game. I definitely recommend you play with other people, whether they be friends or otherwise. If you're having trouble finding people to play with, the official group chat generally has people playing or people who want to play, so stop by there and say "Hi!" if you're needing some friends to play with.
The support for this game has been pretty awesome. I normally buy doujin games expecting a somewhat finished product that won't really change much from its inital incarnation, but the patches released since 1.0 have really changed the game for the better. The character balancing and addition of playable bosses with unique mechanics gives the game a lot more longevity than was originally present. The character balance is pretty good, with the only questionable character having a toggle switch to allow them to be played in a lobby or not. Depending on who's asked, or whether a player is lucky or not, Tomomo will either be an unstoppable winning machine, or just above average with interesting drawbacks.
I don't like numeric ratings, but if I had to rate 100% Orange juice, I would give this game a 8.5/10. It's not perfect by any means, but delivers on everything I expected it to, while also providing a lot of opportunity for having a good time.
As an aside, the 4-P bundle is pretty awesome in comparison to a lot of other games, paying for a little more than two copies to get two more nearly free. Generally I'm offput by those types of deals, but if you want to get friends into the game it's a pretty good purchase.

This game is full of minor but very irritating bugs (especially the UI), none of which have been fixed since I tried it three years ago. I strongly suspect that the owners (who, I believe, are not the original developers) are in "Maintenance Mode", milking the game until players tire of it, but not adding any improvements or fixing any but the most serious of issues. Just on this basis alone, it is hard to justify sinking any money into it, which means you will be stuck with the sub-standard F2P experience.
Even if the bugs were fixed, though, the game utterly fails at narration: none of the characters are memorable. The missions, though ostensibly varied by their flavor text, ultimately feel very samey. How many times was I told to "defend your location"? In one of the last missions I did, I had to go deep, deep into a prison to kill a boss. It was hard to find him, and at one point I had to traverse a corridor almost literally packed with enemies, who stood there blankly while I murdered their comrades 4 meters in front of them. I finally got to the boss, the culmination of all the mission stories in the zone. There was no dialogue or confrontation; he just attacked me, and what ensured was a long, long fight (due to his massive amount of health) where I tried to cut him to pieces with my knives, while he shot me in the face with a pistol. It's too bad, because his story was kind of interesting. (He was cloning himself, and apparently one of his clones decided to lead the resistance against him.)
Combat is tedious, and (for my melee build) mostly consisted of holding down both mouse buttons while aiming the reticule at an enemy. This is made difficult mostly by the camera, enemies' poor pathfinding -- which frequently causes them to run around unnaturally before they home in on you -- and the facts that the game occasionally ignores your keystrokes and gives little or late feedback when it does detect your keystrokes.
There are good things about this game -- otherwise I wouldn't have spent as much time with it as I did -- but I'm not motivated to list them here, because mostly what I feel about it now is frustration.

So, I decided to try Gear Up the other day, just looking for something to pass the time, I seem to recall I'd passed over it once before, but this time I ended up downloading it.
And I found myself having a surprising amount of fun with it. After starting out the game and playing with the basic initial tank, I found myself buying a machinegun and using that to become more effective in battle, my ultimate goal being the creation of a heavy walking tank. And while the parts system was somewhat limiting, I realized my part storage was increasing with my rank, so I kept purchasing parts- building my tank and selling off parts that wouldn't fit with the design. After a few dozen matches, I had finished a tank worthy of note, all using the F2P model presented to me. I decided I'd like to try a new type of tank, and so ended up purchasing the 10$ beginner pack, which increased my part storage to unlimited, and gave me full access to color palettes for painting my tanks.
After about 14 hours of gameplay total, I've created a list of positive and negative points, and things I'd just like to seechanged or implemented in the game.
Pros:
- Tank Creation: By far the most interesting part of the game, build your own tank by purchasing and changing out parts. Most tanks will have a Hull, Turret, Propulsion, Weapon, and Support that can be switched around, as well as optional cosmetics and additional Turrets, Weapons and Supports. Swap out tank tracks for mechanical legs that can clamber over terrain, walls and ceilings. Switch your cannon to a minigun, or a fire-breathing dragon cannon. Note that all changes also affect the speed, weight and the amount of armor your tank will have.
- F2P Model: The F2P model in Gear Up is astonishingly fair for a game of it's kind. Playing matches of the game will earn you coins, netting you around 1-5 per match, depending on how you and your team play- sometimes as many as 2 just for being in the match. With coins, you can buy parts to swap onto your tank, and they aren't absurdly priced, about 5 coins for a basic part, 8-10 for some of the more advanced ones. Given that a match can be around 5-10 minutes, you can earn enough for a new part every 2 or 3 matches. Nothing is locked behind a paywall, even cosmetics are availible for coins. There is a limit to the amount of parts you can have while F2P, but the amount does increase with your rank, and parts can be used an unlimited amount of times once purchased.
- Gameplay: Gameplay, while simple, is rewarding, especially using a creation of your own design to roam the battlefield in the manner you choose. Combat plays as a third-person shooter looking out directly over your tank, with the tank's view following your cursor. Since this is a tank game, the actual aim of your weapon will follow somewhat behind your cursor as your turret moves, but this is shown with a small circle outside your cursor.
- Graphics: Graphics are simple, but fairly well polished, going for a more cartoonish look than realism.
Cons:
- As of now, the game crashes somewhat frequently, once or twice in several hours of gameplay. Twice it has crashed with a Runtime error that closes the game, but leaves the game "running" in Steam, forcing me to open the Task Manager and close a process used by the game manually. Keep in mind this is an early access game- however, also keep in mind that many early access games also haven't had full releases even after months of work.
- Maps are somewhat bland and far too open. Most teams (in a team match) have 2-3 tanks set up as snipers, because it's possible to spawn and either move quickly to a spot that can look over the entire map, or even snipe directly from your spawn. In a connected problem- capture points take far too long to capture solo, and almost all are completely exposed to snipers. Spawns are also in the open, and while you have a brief moment or two of spawn protection, it's possible for the enemy team to surround your only spawn point in an area, which frequently happens, making a one-sided match impossible to overcome.
- Lots of balance issues. Snipers nonwithstanding, most everyone in the game uses the Double Turret Hull, which allows them to carry both 2 main weapons, as well as 4 support weapons if they so choose. While main weapons cannot fire simultaneously, support weapons can, meaning a tank with twin turrets can fire up to 5 weapons at the same time. This also gives free-reign to sniper tanks, as they can simply equip a hard-hitting close range weapon to protect them at close quarters should an enemy actually manage to flank them.
Cannons- in particular the Heavy Cannon, have far too little range, and incredibly high projectile dropoff, making even an arching shot with these weapons impossible outside of medium range.
Capture points are easily shut down, as a small, fast tank can stand on an enemy point for less than a second in order to prevent the owners of the point from spawning at it again until someone makes there way over and re-takes it.

A 10/10 masterpiece.    For starters, the graphics are absolutely stunning, with Bobley himself being one of the most aesthetically pleasing characters this gamer has ever laid their eyes on.  Gameplay wise, you will find yourself constantly faced with daunting moral dilemmas that will make you question your definition of right and wrong.  The puzzles are delightfully balanced so as not to be too easy or too frustrating; just the right amount of challenge for everyone.  And the platforming, oh my the platforming.  What can I say other than that it's absolutely splendid.  It will remind you of classic platformers like Super Mario 64 and Jak and Daxter, all while still maintaining a unique feel all its own.
Then there's the story.  As already mentioned, the moral questions The Adventures of Mr. Bobley poses are very intense and profound.  If you are an innocent soul then this game might be too much for you.  I myself was shaken to the core by the time I reached the end, at which point I went on a month-long journey to find the meaning of happiness and self-worth and have never been the same since.  If you can find the strength to push through the hardship though, I promise that the rewards you'll gain will be life-changing.
Next up is the music.  This game features a soundtrack so heavenly and pure that it would put Mozart to shame.  My words really can't do it justice but you will fall in love with it, I guarantee you.
Lastly, I wanna talk about the technical integrity of Bobley.  A lot of times games like this have a variety of glitches and odd bugs as a result of being too far ahead of their time.  This masterpiece, however, is the most  stable game I've ever played.  44 hours invested at the time of this review, and not one problem whatsoever.  Everything works exactly as intended and runs supremely smoothly.
In sum, The Adventures of Mr. Bobley is about as perfect as any game can hope to be, and playing it has made me a kinder, wiser person.  To quote my friend Tin, it is an experience unlike any other.

Okay, So I gave this game a whirl despite mixed reviews and only after 36 hours. I have played just about every MMORPG Since Everquest and WoW on through to DDO, Conan Unchained and present games. I know a few things about games. Here is my honest assessment of Conan Exiles. Fanfreakingtastic!!! I am hooked; I am more than hooked. I have a dated machine by a few years and it still handles this game just fine. I did some tweaking for optimal gameplay with shadows and view distance on low, I placed post processing and texture on high, turned off anti and Vsync, and all other modes are set to medium. Without dropping $600 on a new card, I got the best bang for my buck. The world looks stunning, FPS holds just over 32 FPS (solid) so card isn't being overworked. I have seen this game on Ultra, there isn't that big of a difference; the keen eye might spot the candy. Funcom did a great job with the graphics on med on up settings, low is kind of a potato but not too bad. Okay, now for the game play; where to start. SANDBOX!!! Tower Defense, RPG, PVP, crafting, multi-level dungeons with bosses, (semi spoiler) open world (hehehe as long as you don't cross the cursed wall). Climbing beyond 'Skyrimming it' style. YOU CAN HOST YOUR OWN SERVER (tailoring the server to your play style). Chop off heads, eviserate, and clean corpses. Is cannibalism your thing? This is the game for you. Be a slave lord, be anything (even a boyscout or girlscout do gooder) although scouts usually get eaten by cannibals. Build entire cities and enslave NPCs to do your bidding. This game is everything the Fun Pimps should have done with 7 Days To Die. Don't get me wrong, I love 7 Days but take note Fun Pimps; this is a sic game. All disputes are being resolved with the new free expansion dropping on the 16th. Combat was a bit clunky; resolved with The Frozen North expansion. Watch the video for the new expansion and judge yourself. On a side note: just to let you know, do not run in balls out screaming death to all things you see; you will die if you do. Take the time to get a feel for the game, collect resources until you can build a weapon and then venture forth. Some people die and it's game over for them before it begins. So take caution and take it slow for a few levels. System specs my machine: AMD 6350 (6 cores) black edition, 8gb ram, GTX 760. I will be upgrading ram for faster load time. All in all, I could find worse ways to spend $30. Crap I have done it on some serious potato games. This game has promise, few miniscule bugs, it feels like it is a finished game although I know it is not. Everything considered; I give Conan Exiles an 8/10 rating among Sandbox RPG early access games.
In its current state, the expansion made a potato of the game, mechanics and immersion wise. I will still give it a thumbs up and pray the devs listen and address the issues over the next few weeks. This game makes you want to buy a ticket to Ukraine and tour Pripyat.  It takes the core concepts of the original game and pushes them in a direction that allows you to have a little more fun while exploring the brutal representation of a real-life scarred patch of earth.
The first game had a lot of elements of wanting to go somewhere, but the high radiation levels or heavy enemy resistance prevented it.  CoP opens up the world around you a little more and gives you some more room to do your own thing.
There are little touches that help crank up the entertainment level as well.  One of my favorites is the randomly occuring "blowouts" that will almost always (without the appropriate inventory items) kill you if you can't find cover in time.  Some of the greatest moments in this game exist when in the middle of a vicious firefight, or at the final moments of a task that has you hurt and running low on supplies, and then a blowout starts rolling in.
Get ready to feel like a badass.  Get ready to have moments where you're running for your life.  Get ready to drain hours of your life exploring the wastes.  Pripyat is calling.
