Overgrowth is one of the most unfocused and horribly mismanaged games i've ever played. Every facet of it is completely fine tuned to a mirror sheen: the graphics look great, the combat and platforming work well, and the editor is both complex and simple. Unfortunately, Wolfire forgot to make an actual game that takes good advantage of these features, leaving an experience that is extremely shallow despite having a feature list in the hundreds. This game has incredibly cool things like dynamic blood physics, dynamic bone/muscle density physics, dynamic throwing weapon physics, individual hitboxes so characters react realistically to blows, absolutely amazing support for mods, and a dynamic combat system that is both extremely dangerous and highly rewarding. Yet there is no real story mode to hold it all together, and the two campaigns that are available are a weak remake of the game Lugaru (which a much, much worse story) and Overgrowth itself, which is a horribly boring story filled with unlikable characters and weak, dry writing. Both are also very short, and will take you about 3 or so hours to complete. They're also terribly designed, though i'll get into that further down the review.
*Gameplay
This is the main draw of the game. Overgrowth contains a highly inventive and skill-intensive combat system that can incredibly fun. There are tons of moves Turner can do like leg sweeps and strong kicks, coupled with neat weapons that all feel different and have their own uses. Most notably, the game can be exceptionally brutal and punishing. Essentially, one good hit is all it really takes to kill someone: a thrown dagger to the head, a nasty kick to the neck, or a sword slash into the shoulder. Because of this small effort-to-kill ratio, battles can end deceptively quickly. That tough-looking dog armed with a greatsword can get a nasty slash across his neck, causing him to bleed out and die. The enemies are also incredibly smart, being able to gang up on you or chase you down with impunity, as well as being genuinely dangerous opponents. All of this adds together to create a dynamic and fluid combat system that rewards reaction time and ruthless brutality, and it feels joyously violent once you get the hang of it. Unfortunately, the combat system is often too overwhelming in many scenarios of the story mode: many of the rules that apply to you do not really apply to enemies due to their wicked fast reaction time. You simply will not be as good as the enemies due to their literally machine-tier reaction speed: I can vivdly recount an experience where I wanted to defeat a single rabbit opponent. I was at full health, approached him, blocked his sweep and was instantly killed when I was judo-flipped to the ground and kicked in the neck, killing me instantly. I had no time to react and little time to process what had happened. Enemies will also almost always roll out of the way, with can make followup attacks very difficult to do. While all of this is fine when facing one or two enemies, you'll be frequently tasked with killing upwards of three most of the time. While this is pretty cool, and keeps you on your toes, it also means that the games deaths feel very unfair at times due to being ganged up on and beaten down. This is only exacerbated by a horrible tutorial that teaches you very little, forcing me to check guides in order to figure out how to do things like catch weapons or even drop them (Note, you need to CLICK to block, holding does nothing). And low, the mighty Leg Cannon, an attack that is completely unblockable (for some reason) and does massive damage. This will most likely become your go-to attack around the midpoint of the game due to it's incredible reliability and relative lack of skill to properly use in comparison to the rest of the combat system. Would you rather fistfight that wolf that can kill you in two shots, or would you jump at it's head and kill it in two or three passes?  Turner himself also never upgrades his health or damage resistance, meaning he'll be fragile for most of the game.
Ultimately the combat system is well done, but the ruthless percision of the A.I and the story mode's swarming tactics make it both too punishing and too demanding to throughly enjoy outside of one or two on one fights. The game also has excellent mod support, and I am eager to see what people will create with the game's incredibly powerful editor.
The platforming is very fun and works suprisingly well, though some people report that it can be glitchy. I have faced no such issues, but be wary.
*Graphics
Overgrowth looks very good, and is optimzed well.... somewhat. Character models look very good, and the effects are nice. The animations also deserve special note, as they are realistic and make the combat fun when they work. When a rabbit whose throat I slit writhed on the ground in agony, I knew that this game had excellent animation quality. My framerate fluctuated rapidly throughout the game, and many assests are horribly unoptimzed (seriously, the grass in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing debilitating at times). This means that the game that has an inconsistent framerate and performance throughout the entire game, making the Overgrowth campaign a real chore to complete.
*Story
The game's story is flat out awful. The writing is boring and dry, characters come and go like the wind, and the only real character with personality is Turner himself. Despite this, Turner is an exceptionally boring protagonist, being cold and brutal from the outset. While this may be jarring for those who never played Lugaru (as his personality is in-line with the ending of that game), Turner undergoes little to no character development throughout the game. The game world is also exceptionally dark and features murder and enslavement by the bucketloads, with no real levity. You get unlikable characters in an unlikable world doing unlikable things, and I grew sick of it very quickly. Both of the initial campaigns are also incredibly short, and the ingame remake of Lugaru contains a butchered version of the original games' (actually not that bad for an early indie title) story.
Overall:
Overgrowth is too shallow to support it's myriad of interesting systems and has nothing to prop them up with, leaving a horribly empty experience with little in the way of interesting content. It's also $30 at the time of writing, which is ballsy to ask for when you make a game with as little content is this. If the modding scene takes off I could see this being a recommendation, but as it stands Overgrowth is an unrefined mess of feature creep that ultimately forgot to be a game.

Shadows of Amn is an absolute cult classic among RPGs, but despite its greatness one has to acknowledge its many flaws by the standards of today. For a strategy game, it is horribly unbalanced, as just the roll of one virtual dice (usually for one of the many overpowered magic spells/abilities) may completely eradicate your chances of winning a battle (because one or more of your party members die instantly), while on another attempt you might just get lucky and stomp every enemy in sight (because the spell is being resisted). In some situations, you simply have no chances of prevailing on your first attempt and you have to reload - knowing how to position your characters in advance, where not to go, or something like that. Inventory management is tedious (just so much stuff!), controlling your characters is prone to errors (casting spells is cancelled when the game is paused should you accidentally issue a move command, pathing errors), and some of the D&D rules employed in the game are just plain dumb.
So why play Shadows of Amn?
Because the game tells an amazing story, it has great characters and interesting locations, all of which alone warrant buying this gem from an age before fancy 3D graphics and well-thought out balancing. I have finished SoA at least 3 times in my life, and I’m quite confident I will do so a few times more before I die. And so should you.

Summary: What should be any furry's wet dream turns out to be just 'meh'. A regular gamer won't enjoy this for long.
I bought the game roughly eight years ago and I've been following design and development closely. I even went though the trouble of discussing some (possible) features on the forums. The trailers make this game look stunning, but it has improved little over the past few years. I actually hadn't played it in over two years, getting my hopes up it'd be awesome when released. After the release I started out with the Lugaru campaign, since I hadn't played that game before. I ripped though that in half an hour. The scenes only take a few minutes, even with retries. I looked at the scenes of the Overgrowth campaign and was already afraid this wouldn't be any longer that an hour. I wasn't far off, as I just completed it, totalling about 1.5 hours. The storyline is pretty much non-existent and characters don't carry any emotion. It's just random events with random fights and random conclusions. The fighting scenes aren't intense, as they are just frustrating. Fighting an enemy with a broad sword is practically impossible, since attacks and blocks don't seem to affect them - though when you wield a sword, enemies easily tackle you. Maybe I'm just a noob... who knows. The music is okay-ish, but it gets boring after hearing all three(?) tunes.
Also the fact there's still some annoying bugs (like muted sound effects) in the game after so many years of testing, baffles me. And last but not least: after almost 10 years of development, the graphics are highly dated.
I expected so much and it could've been so much. A deeper storyline alone would've improved this game tenfold. I guess the developers got "distracted" by other projects and basically rushed the game.
At least playing the arenas mod keeps me entertained for a few hours. Perhaps the devs will extend the story or use this engine as a scaffolding for another game. I'd give that a shot.
Other reviewers have pretty much summed up all the things I want to say about the technical aspects / fighting mechanics, so read those.

I purchased this game somewhere around 2011-2012. Back then, it was just a sandbox with little to do. Now, there's several things to do, but nowhere near enough to justify the full price.  $10 may be a better price, but I feel like that is still asking a little too much for how little I got out of the game.
The campaign is boring and lack-luster. It feels like a lot more was planned than what we got. You play as a Rambo-esque rabbit who goes around killing all the baddies, but never gets the character development of Rambo. The plot can be summed up in only a few paragraphs, and it'll only take your average person a couple hours to go through the story of both Overgrowth and Lugaru (the previous game, which is included for free). The loading screen quotes give the impression that the world and the story were originally supposed to be a lot longer and larger than what we got.
The music is large and grandiose. It kinda reminds me of The Elder Scrolls music, only without the large and wonderous game to back it up.
The combat is the star of the show, and one of its biggest pitfalls. In a one-on-one fight, it's stellar. There are tons of counters and throws and ways you can attack. It feels brutal, aggressive, and satisfying. However, once there's more than two or three enemies facing you, it gets quite tough. It becomes all too easy to fall back on the over-powered jump-kick, which everyone rightfully calls the Leg-Cannon. Later in the game, the Leg-Cannon is practically required. Some enemies require three-to-five Leg-Cannons to kill, whereas they can kill you in just a couple of normal hits. It almost feels like the game was balanced with the assumption that players were exclusively using this move.
The levels feel wide and open, but without much to fill them with. Most of the time your objective is just kill things or get to a high-point.
I like the ideas the game presents. I like the combat when it is well balanced and fair. Unfortunately, my enjoyment of both is hindered by the poor balance and the dull story. There was a lot of potential here, but it seems like nine years of development wasn't enough to make it the game it was supposed to be. Only get this game if it's on a good sale, or you really want to see the combat system. Even then, don't expect a stellar game.

So I’ve played the game through twice now and honestly I find myself unsure of where all these negative reviews are coming from. Let’s get the elephant in the room out first, NO Kill Team does not have online co-op and YES that would have made it many times better with hours of replayability. And no it’s not even close to the best WH40k game out there. But for $10 (or less if you get it on sale) it’s a perfectly fun little twin-stick using the 40k aesthetic that you can put around 4-5 hours into to beat the main plot, and around 10 if you want to round up the achievements. For me at least I got my monies worth, I agree things could have been done to make it better, but what is here is still quite entertaining for the duration its contents can provide.
There’s not much to say gameplay-wise, if you’ve played a good quality twin-stick shooter before you’ve played this game. If you haven’t then the genre is marked by constant action, using one stick to move and the other to shoot in a 360-degree radius at any time like a turret on legs (or alternatively the keyboard and mouse works too). Persistent upgrades you get through gaining points liven things up as do unlockable weapons, they mostly just make you more powerful but it’s still a fun little side-item to inject a bit of activity into the usual twin-stick formula.
Graphics are decent, outdated but the game is several years old having come out before Space Marine despite just now coming to Steam. Still they work and more importantly the colorful WH40k aesthetic is carefully rendered so even without eye-popping visuals it’s nice to look at. There are only the basest strings of a story here, usual fluff stuff; an Ork Kroozer is inbound on a Forge World and you have to stop them by shooting a billion enemies and occasionally blowing up some machinery, nothing complicated and it only serves to shuffle you from objective to objective.
So yeah, WH40k: Kill Team isn’t the best game ever, and the lack of Online Co-op is a negative. But what’s presented here should still keep any WH40k fan distracted for a couple evenings. And given the meager selling price for what you get I think all the reviews ripping it apart seem really entitled, like how dare they don’t provide a triple-A gaming experience for ten bucks!
Oh well. Anyhow I say go ahead and get the game if you just want a fun little time waster set in the 40k universe.

When I tell people about 100% Orange juice, the first reply I receive is always something along the lines of "So it's kind of like Mario party?" and I can see why people would come to that conclusion, but in practice 100% Orange Juice is a completely different animal.
100% Orange Juice is a board-game inspired battle game in which players compete to achieve "Norma", a series of objectives based around either defeating various critters as well as the other players in battle, or collecting a number of stars. Stars are the only currency in 100% Orange Juice, and they are used to both fufill objectives and activate abilities that come in the form of cards, and this creates a lot of tough choices, while also preventing needless complication with alternate power sources.
The game provides many (Read: nigh-endless) opportunities for a comeback from players who are trailing behind, so unlike when someone has 5 stars in mario party and the turn limit has almost been reached, in 100% Orange juice you may find yourself winning at the last minute due to smart play, luck, or poor decision making from another player.
Initially, a lot of the content is unavailable for new players, but all of it is unlocked by playing the game. All new cards are recieved by buying booster packs with stars won from playing games. The basic booster pack contains most of the cards available, but later an expansion series becomes unlocked with a different variety of cards. The rarity and randomness of the card drops is a little annoying, but once you've recieved nine of any card, you'll stop getting it, meaning that eventually you'll get every card.
The single player mode is definitely challenging, and going in to a mission without a plan can make it extremely hard. Each of the four starting characters has a seperate campaign, and by beating all of them you'll receieve a set of extra scenarios that have interesting setups to create additional challenge for more experienced players.
I'd imagine most western players wouldn't recognise the characters used to make up the playable cast, but even if that's the case, it's still a very enjoyable game. Most people I gave the game to were capable of playing decently during their first match without much more than a brief introduction to the mechanics, so needing to memorise an encyclopaedia of rules, or knowing character matchups really isn't a hinderance to getting started.
All in all, it's a very solid game. I definitely recommend you play with other people, whether they be friends or otherwise. If you're having trouble finding people to play with, the official group chat generally has people playing or people who want to play, so stop by there and say "Hi!" if you're needing some friends to play with.
The support for this game has been pretty awesome. I normally buy doujin games expecting a somewhat finished product that won't really change much from its inital incarnation, but the patches released since 1.0 have really changed the game for the better. The character balancing and addition of playable bosses with unique mechanics gives the game a lot more longevity than was originally present. The character balance is pretty good, with the only questionable character having a toggle switch to allow them to be played in a lobby or not. Depending on who's asked, or whether a player is lucky or not, Tomomo will either be an unstoppable winning machine, or just above average with interesting drawbacks.
I don't like numeric ratings, but if I had to rate 100% Orange juice, I would give this game a 8.5/10. It's not perfect by any means, but delivers on everything I expected it to, while also providing a lot of opportunity for having a good time.
As an aside, the 4-P bundle is pretty awesome in comparison to a lot of other games, paying for a little more than two copies to get two more nearly free. Generally I'm offput by those types of deals, but if you want to get friends into the game it's a pretty good purchase.

-=Hello=-
I have played the game for a few days now, and believe I am ready to write a review on it, so without further ado, here it is... I will be catagorizing the subjects in "Pros" and "Cons", simply because I enjoy keeping it organized that way.
-=Pros=-
1) Good background graphics! I have to say, I LOVE the background graphics. The light is very vibrant, and the colors are great.
2) Music! It took me a while to finally get to hear some of the tracks, as constant gunfire can sometimes get in the way, but I really need to compliment the music, as it makes you feel much more relaxed and keeps you from raging when someone annihilates your craft.
3) Movement! Very responsive, and WASD seems like it was made for games like this.
4) The building system! As much as I, and I'm sure many others, love RoboCraft, which I'm sure we can all agree this game got some inspiration from, I prefer this building system immensely over the voxel-based building of RoboCraft.
5) Gamemodes! I have to say, another thing this game is dominant for in comparison to RoboCraft is the different gamemodes it has, allowing for players with different skills to tackle the challenge of different gamemodes.
-=Cons=-
1) Music. Now, I know I just praised the music, and the beautiful tracks is not why music is put in this catagory. It's because of the fact you NEVER get to hear these nice tunes, unless you are huddled, camping under a bridge to avoid fire.
2) Vehicle limitations. Unlike in RoboCraft, equipment cannot be added wherever you seek fit to your vehicle. They have specific locations, and a set size is present for your vehicle, it being a very limited one at that.
3) Runs terribly. I know I can mostly excuse it at the moment, because it is still in Early Access, but still, I shouldn't be having parts where I am running 5 FPS, even though I have a fully-speced AlienWare, resulting in me making the screen resolution that of a Nintendo 64 Game.
4) Currency. The currency in this game used to buy anything, is so pain-staking to earn, that it's like the developers are putting you on a treadmill that they are slowly making go faster and faster with a button on the end of it, whilst they say "For only $19.99, you can push that button, and stop the treadmill...", so if you don't want to put the money down on it, you'll have to expect HOURS upon HOURS of farming.
5) Grinding. Since most of the game will be grinding to try and earn enough to get new robot parts, you'd think that atleast that part would be down. But no, grinding is nearly impossible with any gamemode besides Deathmatch, as any gamemode you have to be in a team with is nearly downright impossible, as the community aren't exactly "pros", and when you try to leave the match to find a new team, the game finally lets you know that if you leave, you get none of the rewards you just spent so long earning. Not to mention the rounds are very long. So, yeah. If your mum is calling you in for dinner, kiss your earnings goodbye.
6) Item disbalance. I feel like this is one of the most game-breaking. Unlike having to sacrifice whether you want your vehicle to be based on speed, power, defense, etc., like you do in RoboCraft, Gear Up has an obvious set of stronger items, that you need to grind to get to, so you can be flung into a group with people far stronger than you because they earned their cash faster than you, making it even HARDER to earn your cash to purchase upgrades.
-=Final Verdict=-
So in the end, I have to say, Gear Up is doing many things right, and unlike many people say, I don't think this game is 'copying' RoboCraft, I belive it is inspired by RoboCraft, and trying to take it's premise and improve it based on what RoboCraft's community likes and dislikes. The problem is how their executing it. Just click it then the "craft" button and it adds it to the crafting queue, as long as you have the required materials of course. Pretty much almost everything in the game has been crafted by another person. Whether it be vehicles or your favorite gun, or even that kebab that's been sitting in your inventory. Of course you get generated items through merchants or missions but this game allows for the better quality items to be instead crafted, thus relying on peoples ability to craft for a good economic system.
Lets see, what's another major characteristic about the game. Oh the pvp. Pvp/pve is pretty balanced throughout the game. Most places you are at are pve locations. You can turn off PVP (has a timer buff as to keep people from shooting and switching) and not be bugged in PVE areas. I barely see any of those "hackers" as kids like to call them nowadays. Most of time it's kiddie stuff like the auto bot script stuff.
I think that about sums up the major points of the game. I could go on more about it, just don't feel like it. :P I hope I have influenced atleast one more player to join. Could use a couple more newbies that I could pick on.

TL; DR: 'Learn hard to enjoy hard.'
That about sums up my thoughts on BG series, unless one is an original D&D fan and knows most of the rules and spells already.
BG isn't like the latest Blizzard games. It doesn't explain you much about anything, let alone a proper tutorial. There are dozens of status effects and you need to know how to counter them using the right spell which you might have or not if you didn't know about it. You have to pause a lot and make strategic moves, and I'm sure that this isn't rly familiar to younger generations unless they have been playing Dragon Age. This is definitely not easy to learn, thus you need to 'learn hard to enjoy hard.'
You might not like the term though. Why bother learning how to play this game when there are hundreds of other games that are much more newbie-friendly? This probably is the reason why the review score goes down every big sale; people buy it, doesn't get it, quit and thumbs down.
So back to the point. If you ask me why bother learning, this is my answer:  BG will let you conquer the game itself.
In Diablo, you will kill enemies using different weapons, and skills. It's not a matter of strategy, but a combination.
In BG, at first, you may step on traps. You may spend a long time to gear up different party members. You may be frustrated to control all characters at once. You may become paranoid at enemy mages, and be vulnerable against status effects.
After some time, traps wouldn't bother you anymore, and you may like it as a source of exp. You will learn how to gear up your party members properly. You will be using pause at a right moment and command all your characters at once. You will learn how to interfere enemy mages, and remove status effects.
After considerable amount of time, enemies will be stepping on your traps. You will minmax every characters in different save files and do funny things. You won't need to pause anymore. Enemies will be paranoid at your mage and status effects, while you will simply prevent bad status effects from your party.
As time goes by, the things that you've hated for the most will start to work on your favor, and you will be able to try different strategies. This feeling of accomplishment and variety is probably why people still like and play BG.
If you are ready for it, BG can be a historical masterpiece for you. If you are not, you might see it as an obsolete piece of drek. It's up to you, really. And as a fan of this game, I hope you give chance at it and stick with it a little more before you quit. You will see the turning point, as I did.

-Captured by Mind Flayers
-Find out What Happened to Montaron
-Find Proof of Mae'Var's Treachery
-Inside the Planar Sphere

-Seek Out and Investigate the Fallen Paladins
-Solve the 'skinner' Murders in the Bridge District
The above would be among the best RPG main questlines ever, but they aren't, they are SIDE quests! All for one game. One game that still stands in 2017 with a game world of unparalleled scope, atmosphere, and intrigue. Each of the above mentioned quests takes hours, but there's always more to do, even after you finish them.
The massive scope of Baldur's Gate 2 is decorated with mostly text-based dialogue (though the main story line is almost fully, and fabulously, voice acted). Despite the overwhelming quality and quantity of side-content, the main story is still the best part of the game. Featuring dialogue that represents the best writing the gaming industry has to offer. BioWare's storytelling in this game hasn't been matched for 17 years. Baldur's Gate is not a story about saving the world, like countless other RPGs, it is a personal story about one character's personal struggles, but it features everything else we all love about the best BioWare games. 20 deep and intriguing, well developed characters make up the cast of NPCs you get to choose from to form your party of 6. Each of those party members will banter with eachother, and will question your decisions, and sometimes your decisions will lead to them leaving you, or even trying to kill you. And if you manage to keep them all there's a classic BioWare style quest that is unique to each companion, and will ultimately shape your relationship wtih them, for good or for bad.
There's plenty complex gameplay that overlays a massive adventure here. How much more complicated, detailed and tactical could Dragon Age Origins have been if it wasn't dumbed down for console? You can find out by playing Baldur's gate 2. 7 races, dozens of classes, and hundreds of abilities and spells are all yours to experiment with as you clash with hundreds of different kinds of enemies and monsters, who all possess abilities and spells of the same complexity. Decorated with visually stunning spell effects and suprisingly immersive sound effects, this game still boasts many of the most epic RPG fights in the history of videogames. There's always something new to learn about the combat, so this gameplay will never cease to engage and interest you.
You'll find youself in a dungeon, trying to rescue a poor man's daughter from a dragon, but that dragon instantly butchers all of your tanky warriors as soon as you unpause. You'll find yourself in an ancient ruin with a demon that is immune to all forms of attack. The challenges are endless in this game, and they rival Dark Souls, but they are equally rewarding as well. When you finally figure out how to kill that Dragon, his loot will turn you into a demi-god, which is good, because you will have to fight a God in the next fight after that.
The main quest features many more characters besides the 20 NPCs that you get to choose. A quest that will take you on unforgettable adventures, not only through the Forgotten Realms, but through human emotion. Torture, imprisonment, war, death, suffering, betrayal, love, redemption, and atonement are all features in this wonderfully dark and gripping tale.
The mage Jon Irenicus, widely regarded as the best videogame villain of all time, tries to strip you of your powers, tortures you, and the questions he asks about your abominable and inhuman nature linger with you for the entire game, and often come up in nightmares. Because of his simple identity as a fallen human being with reasonable insights about human nature and society, yet his aura of pure evil and despicability, he reminds me more than a little bit of Heath Ledger's Joker in The Dark Knight.  He takes your friends from you, and he steals your very soul, and leads you on the most enthralling fantasy adventure that has ever been crafted, as you chase him through Elven forests, Catacombs full of vampires, alternate planes of existence, cities below the Ocean, Islands ruled by barbaric Pirates, Elven cities, The Underdark, and even to the Deepest circle of Hell.
17 years later people are still playing this game, and the only ones who wouldn't tell you it's one of the best, if not THE best RPG of all time, are the ones who haven't played it. It's better late than never to change that. No RPG has a combination of such a massive game world full of atmospheric detail and intrigue, combined with flawless and gripping writing, and extremely engaging and rewarding gameplay. And along with everything else, This games soundtrack will stick with you for the rest of your life, along with many of the characters, and many of the events.

So first of all, as a disclaimer, I haven't played the previous game. Also, I do love turn-based combat. But combat is what eventually will let me drop the game after about 20 hrs into it.
Two major issues I have with this game:
1. Side-quests are pretty much not optional. If you don't do every side-quest you can find and if you don't spend time fine-combing the environment for gear and XP (which takes considerable time), you will fail at the inevitable boss battles because you are underpowered. You can compensate a bit with clever use of skills and the environment, but at the end, you need to squeeze every bit out of the area you are currently in. In an RPG, I want to be an explorer and not an (XP) vacuum cleaner.
2. A lot of trial and error, especially in boss battles. For me, an RPG is supposed to tell a story. Battles should be challenging and give you a sense of reward and progression, but this should not rely on the players to trial and error through a fight, ideally with repeated dialogue that cannot be skipped. Throw in friendly NPCs with the AI of a rotten tomato that add an additional random factor to each fights progress and you end up with a time sink of enormous proportions.
There were other minor faults, like targeting in fights that could be overlooked, due to the interesting story and the engaging setting but sadly, I don't have the time to play Alexandar or Lady Vengeance fights over and over again until the stars of (friendly and hostile) NPC align in a way that the battle is won.
A lot of potential wasted, which is sad.

Very nice game. Combat is fluid and challenging, boss fights tough and engaging, story is adequate, and NPCs have personality and react to plot developments. If you've played Ys 1 and 2 and enjoyed them as I did, know that this third entry in the series is actually better in every way. Newcomers can feel free to start here because it's a standalone adventure.
The hero, Adol, is a swordsman who lives for the thrill of exploring new lands. In each game, he arrives at a new place, meets lots of people, earns their admiration for solving their problems and saving their lives, gets a girl to fall in love with him, and then leaves it all behind at the end to travel somewhere else. In terms of gameplay, Felghana has you platforming and hacking and slashing your way through varied environments (dungeons) filled with monsters, while trying to find treasure chests on your way to the next save point, after which there is a boss fight. It follows this formula all throughout -- simple and it works. You also have to keep an eye out for a few secret passages and a couple side quests if you want to get all the unique items in this game, some of which are incredibly useful in avoiding headaches later on. The soundtrack, as always in this series, is very good.
The main draw here is definitely the hectic combat, and the satisfying difficulty of the bosses is the height of what the game has to offer. The dungeon chests add an enjoyable exploration element, the story does a good job giving meaning to what you're doing, and the personable and reactive NPCs make you care about what's happening. Overall, Felghana is a very well put together package and a polished experience. Easy recommendation for anyone who likes what they see in the gameplay videos.

My hours are not accurate.
Overgrowth has an odd mix of wonderful strengths and crippling weaknesses.
+ Parkour is fun, and you jump really high.  This includes relatively realistic wall running, ledge grabbing, wall hopping.
+ Combat is intense, and in fair fights with other rabbits there are a large variety of moves and counters you can make.
+ Stealth and the ability to hide bodies in bushes is fun like in hitman.
+ The engine, the main thing devs worked on, is amazing, and can easily be modded to make way more interesting games than the included campaign.
- Parkour can be finicky on slanted or irregular surfaces.  Turn off auto ledge grab or be prepared to be confused.
- Combat degrades into a single jump kick that can always, and must be used once you fight some larger enemies.  These new enemies are interesting, have differential qualities, but cannot be stealth killed, countered, or even effectively rolled away from, degrading combat into a safer but less satisfactory run, jump, and kick fest.  Since the counters you use look like Judo moves, the larger enemies should be knocked off balance as well, but it is not the case.
- Stealth could be more dynamic, as all areas in the campaigns are quite open, only a few allow interesting thought put into how to stealth through them.  Enemies pull a short distance of friends to help them, and cannot lose your trail, so once you are seen, stealth is done.
- Both campaigns can be beaten within a few hours.
- The writing is not professional.  Think Rambo style character, that moves throughout the world, making a few allies as he kills all the bad guys, never feeling that any of them are a threat to him because he is so badass.  Unlike Rambo no time is even spent developing his character.  He is a one dimensional character in a flat world.
If you played Lugaru, you will be prepared for the interesting engine, paired with the lackluster writing, and short game.  This is more of the same, but with a vastly improved, easily moddable engine, with a great deal of potential, and more interesting parkour levels.
I do not recommend paying full price, especially if you are buying it without intention to mod or play multiplayer, there is $5 - $10 worth of singleplayer content included ATM.
Overall I still recommend this game if it is on a good sale, and if you plan to download or create mods.  It has great potential as an engine to make an amazing stealth, parkour, fighting game.  The in game campaigns are not terrible, but certainly not great at achieving this either .

If you love strategy games with a rpg touch like I do, then you will love this game! Now I am a little bias, but this game is simply the best stategy game of all time... OF ALL TIME!
You play as an individual, head of a preset house (created house if you get the ruler designer dlc). You ultimate goal is what you want it to be.
Want to start of as a lowly count/countess working his/her way up the social pecking order by getting the nobles of the realm to support your forged claim to your neighbor's title? You can do that! Or say you want a crown on YOUR crown, so you bribe the nobles of the realm to join your faction to force the King to change the inheritance laws of the kingdom from primogenture to elective so you can put your name up for nomination? You can do that too! Or say you want to start of as a King/Sultan/Caliph/Emperor and fight those very vassals who would try such a treasonous act, YOU CAN!
I can go on and on about the multitude of things you can do, from growing your family tree by marrying a wealthy duke's daughter so your son will have a claim to the duke's lands when he finally kicks the bucket. From growing old, dying and passing everything to you son, which as the new head of the house you will now play as. Say, what about your daughter? She is more capable than your current character's son! Change the inheritance laws to give you daughter a claim.
Use diplomacy to normalize relations, marriage to seal alliances, war to conquer you enemies, intrigue to assassinate your rivals, piety to gain the favor of the Pope/Caliph/Grand Priest, it goes on and on.
The rpg element is enhanced by a large and ever growing event system which helps form your current character's personality by gaining new traits, or losing them, based on your decisions. Educate your children yourself or have them assigned to a trusted retainer. Grow your influence and power by inviting talented people to your court and appointing them to your council. Hand out titles to your vassals to keep them loyal, or seize their titles when/if they plot against you. Deliver justice or Cry Havoc, and let slip the dogs of war!
This game has MANY dlcs, all of which expand the cultures, immersion, music, appearance, gameplay, features and possibilities in some way. I highly recommend the culture portrait DLCs, ruler designer, major gameplay DLCs like the Horse Lords, Old Gods, ect. But they are all good and imo modestly priced.

If you like fast paced action games, you'll probably enjoy this. I'd say this game is more action than RPG. It has elements of SHMUPs. It even has some light platforming elements.
Pros:
+ Very responsive controls and movement. There's no sense of sluggishness when you move, jump, and attack.
+ Fast paced action, favoring execution, reaction, and enemy pattern recognition over grinding and slower-paced strategic / tactical decisions. More like a SHMUP than a strategic action RPG.
+ aforementioned reaction-based elements are actually possible (at least for me in my late-20s). I've played games that have patterns that require unfeasible reaction speeds. So the patterns end up being, effectively, random amounts of damage because there's no reasonable way to avoid them (like the last boss in YS 1).
+ The way you get good at fighting the enemies and bosses in this game is by learning their patterns. As far as I can tell, there are very few situations where your ability to win or lose is based on randomness. There are some games where there's really difficult patterns or challenges that are so difficult that you won't be able to reasonably overcome them without spending a lot of time practicing. Take some of the bosses in the souls series - the process of learning each boss's moves can take quite awhile because they have a varied moveset, and there's often complications like cluttered level design and certain patterns that can't consistently be parried or dodged or predicted. That sort of stuff really frustrates me, especially when it takes awhile to get back to the boss. This game doesn't really have anything like that. You can pretty much learn the correct thing to do in any given situation in a reasonable amount of time, and it's very consistent. And, when you fail a boss, you can restart right at it without having to make your way back from a save point. To sum it up, I think that you can feasibly learn to fight every boss without taking any damage.
+ Difficulty options! Easy mode felt fun and not all that challenging for me. If you really want to play more you can replay on harder difficulty modes.
+ awesome music. Energetic, electric guitar, drums, + symphonic instruments. I believe the tracks use actual recordings and not samples.
+ World building. As you return to town during your adventures, the characters in town always have different things to say. It's nice when games don't have voice acting because it lets writers write a lot more stuff, and they've definitely taken advantage of that fact here.
Things I didn't like:
- towards the end, it seems there's a bit of an expectation that you grind to get more money and EXP so you can upgrade your gear, increase your max HP, and increase your stats. If you think that's okay, ask yourself if running back and forth between the same rooms doing the same repetitive task just to make some numbers go up is a really meaningful way to spend your life. Ask yourself if you'd go to bed feeling good about how you spent your day, having spent hours of it doing the same stupid task over and over again.
- overall, the grinding for EXP, money, and upgrade mats I think needlessly lengthens the game and gets in the way of the action-oriented gameplay. I hardly had to spend much time grinding, but I wonder what including stats and levels and stuff really achieves, from the perspective of just making the game fun. I think it hurts the fun.
- Partial controller support. You cannot map the menu button to a button on your controller. You have to have your keyboard there in front of you or you have to use an external tool to map your start button to ESC.
In short, there's not much I didn't like about this game. It's a nice, fast-paced action game with some JRPG elements. Although, I can't help but wonder what a game like this has to offer over actual "action-first" action games like Bayonetta, DMC, SHMUPs, etc...I feel like the thing that makes this game unique is its inclusion of JRPG elements, but I also feel like the game may have been more fun if it had just focused all on the action. The primary gameplay of this game is action-oriented, but if that's what you really want out of a game you have much better options elsewhere. The action in this game isn't as great as the action in other highly-polished action games. So why not just play those instead?
So, if you have no shortage of top-tier action games that you still enjoy (like Platinum games that you haven't yet 100%'d), I don't know that this game is worth getting. But if you're looking for something new and different, definitely check this one out.

I purchased Overgrowth back in 2012 and I've always been optimistic about the final product -- the fighting controls back then felt intuitive enough and there were myriad little details that I quite liked -- such as wounds bleeding in a natural manner and the ability to kill yourself by jumping and front flipping so you land on the base of your neck!
Over 5 years later and the game has finally been finished and.. it's disappointing. Back in the day there was a lot of promise and potential shown by developers who seemed to enjoy what they were doing and the mechanics were looking great - sadly though it never evolved past that.
The mechanics are still good but the game fleshed around it is poor. The "campaign" is linear with little freedom of approach and levels are basic map sections in which you must either climb or kill everything (Which is usually 6 enemies tops.) The campaign feels generally rushed and any attempt of characterization feels incredibly poor; it's almost humorous how often "friendly" characters will resign to killing each other without doubt.
>> "We don't have to fight, if we wor-"
>> "No. It has to be done this way."
>> "Er... Okay?"
The character quotes on the loading screens almost feel as though something more grandiose was planned but never gone through with.
The biggest challenge I personally faced in the game were mostly the controls -- tasks such as wall running seemed more difficult than the enemies -- You'd run along the wall with the intent of jumping to a nearby ledge only to fling yourself to your death. There are other map-manoeuvring options such as handing on edges to shuffle along though this is never actually used in the core campaign as far as I'm aware.
The end of the campaign is jarring too. I personally thought the game erroneously exited to the menu but nope -- I actually completed the game. No ending cutscene, no closing story, no credits -- just an exit to menu.
With good level design and story -- this game could have been something that is greatly replayable and enjoyable. Instead we've got a game that's just.. hollow. The mechanics are there and the lore is there, It feels as though the developers fell out of love with the project and just wanted it over and done with.

Wow, this game is really something.
First of all, if you've played The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim and you're expecting Oblivion to be like that, you'll be dissapointed.
Story:
Without spoiling anything, the story is very well structured. You'll be following the main quest. You'll find yourself running into Oblivion portals a lot. ( Duh. ) The story can be intimidating in the beginning as there are lots of Deadra warriors you'll be fighting. You'll have to be especially careful as a low level. I found myself spawning some Steel armor to help me through the first Oblivion gate. Also had to put on God mode once or twice. The game will get easier as you progess in your skills.
Graphics:
The Graphics are well done for it's time. You'll often see castle walls, river, lakes, and some towns. Even from a distance the graphics hold up. The faces of the CPU's are ( Mostly ) Normal. You may run into a few faces that just don't look human. ( And I'm not talking about Argonians or Kahjiits.)
Music:
The music for this game is incredible. Obviously, the main theme for all the Elder Scrolls games are the same. The music during battle is AMAZING. But when there is a serious moment, the music softens. You may have to turn up the music and turn down the other effects though.
Over all, the game is definitley worth getting. If you like Medievel games, you'll probably enjoy Oblivion.

At first glance it looks like the usual garbage that usually come out related to Warhammer 40K as of late (Dawn of War series excluded), however it is much more than that. The graphical design holds up well on low end systems and runs rather smoothly. The port itself onto PC is rather good aswell, however it does take a few deaths until the game decides to get you a tip on how to use a grenade right.
Levels can be repetitive but the 4 classes you can play as does give it a bit of life. But overall I believe the design of the game to be very good and presents a good challenge to the player. . . but not inn the sense you would expect.
Here is the big problem with this game: the camera. I don't know who programmed the camera in this game but whoever it is should take a refresher course. Level after level, I would reach the next section only to be attacked from the left side by a wave of Orks I didn't see due to the camera doing "look the fancy scenery" thingy. Getting the camera into a good position is a bit like a hungry child, wearing oven gloves, trying to get beetroot out of a jar.
While this game is basically a close up version of Dawn of War 2, I hesitate to say that as it just doesn't hold up in comparison, it just feels too much like a cash in on the license. I do recommend this game but with great caution as the camera makes the game much harder and frustrating than what it should be.

I love challenging games. I play lots of retro games, quite a bit of which I master. But one of the thing a truly hard game needs, along with a lot of other stuff, of course, is a steady and even difficulty curve and a steady sense of progressions. When the player loses, it's always good if at the same time it feels like they're learning something. When one plays a game like the 8-bit Ninja Gaiden 3, one might lose a lot and be forced to restart the game, but each time they get a little farther and learn to beat previously beated parts a little more efficiently. This brings a sense of progress that, in my opinion, can often make or break a truly challenging game.

Man, what do I even say about DN... I've been reasonably committed to this game since September-ish of 2015, and have just broken 2.2k hours. We've been through a lot of changes in that time - 90 cap made leveling a breeze, but dropped the bottom out of the game and left us starved for content; with 93 cap we were released from the withered claws of Nexon but dropped into the bottomless, ravenous maw that is Eyedentity games.
I'll begin with some of the things I must warn new players about, so that I may end on a more positive note. Firstly, while Eyedentity may on the face of it seem like a company that wants to make players happy, they are not to be trusted. I don't mind respecting and admiring the fact that they brought us this game in the first place, but I am always wary of the decisions they make and their inability to follow through on things like customer support and general player feedback.
Something else to be wary of with this game is how everything is RNG and everything costs gold. It's something I maintain a general disdain for - gear repair costs being exorbitant, enhancement costs being downright disgusting, and crafting costs being at odds with the ridiculous amount of materials one must grind for in order to craft an item in the first place. The systems in place themselves also continue to irk me - I could spend 3 or 4 weeks grinding for enough mats for one attempt at a certain item, and because the stats are random, there's a 70-80% chance that it will be completely useless. And enhancing gear, god damn, I'm just not even gonna go there.
There's more I could complain about, but I don't actually want to drive people away from this game, so I'll start on the positives. First and main thing I must mention is that the combat system is easily my favourite that I've ever played on. Seriously, after playing Dragon Nest, every other combat system feels boring. You've got this enormous range of different subclasses to choose from, and they all have unique and interesting ways to dish out amounts of damage that will make you squint and shake your head in disbelief. The game will have you combo-ing until your fingers fall off and your eyes implode.
Second thing that really keeps me involved is how after a certain amount of time, the game environment feels almost homely, in a way. It's down to a combination of the anime-ish, low-poly-but-still-detailed-enough-for-pantyshots graphics, the musical arrangements, and the funky English dubs for all the character voices. There's a definite charm to how it feels unpolished in regards to these things, and in amongst it all, there is also a really good story quest line if you should so choose to follow that. The story quest does become very text-heavy after a certain point, but it's pretty riveting and quite complex, so it doesn't become a bore.
I should also mention that I wouldn't have gotten nearly as far in DN as I have without the help of the friends I've made. The community may be small and continually shrinking, but the people that are left are on the whole some of the nicest, funniest and most lovably sideways weirdos I've ever come across. When I was just starting out all the way through til the present day, at no point did I ever feel like there was no one around that could help me or give me advice. There is always someone ready to share their knowledge or run a dungeon with you to lighten the load.
So I guess in summary, I would recommend giving Dragon Nest a try, but be very careful, and keep your expectations low in regards to good server management. If you're unable to spend any real-life money on it, be prepared to feel underpowered for quite some time, but if you enjoy it as much as I do, stick with it for a while and see how things go for you.
Oh, and if you see a Windwalker called Sylvaera hanging around in Saint's Haven, feel free to drop me a like or say hi. :)

Sometimes, video games can attract attention just because of their names. This is likely the case with 100% Orange Juice, even if the primarily response is confusion. After all, it sounds more like the description of a drink than any game! But 100% Orange Juice is very much a game and quite the fun one at that. You’ll just have to spend a bit of time learning about its rules to truly enjoy it.
The name of the game is 100% Orange Juice. Why? I don’t care, and I don’t think the game does either. The strange name is only the beginning, however, of the bizarre realm of 100% Orange Juice. Because I can’t pass up the opportunity to make a citrus joke here, the game is definitely sweet, but at times can appear very sour. In fact, I am pretty sure this game hates me.
100% Orange Juice is, at its essence, a simple board game. While it may take a game or two to fully grasp everything, it’s fairly simple, but also fairly brutal. Four players are placed on a board and must roll a die or dice to move forward either playing passively, trying to quietly and quickly obtain as many stars as you can, or aggressively, out for blood and attacking enemy spaces and opponents around every corner. The way the game challenges you to choose and alternate these styles of gameplay is what makes 100% Orange Juice an excellent game, as the player must be apprehensive in the face of the unfortunate circumstance where your strategy, and the world itself, has seemingly failed you.
100% Orange Juice is far from perfect, but it’s still an exceptional virtual board game that really pushes your buttons. With some tweaks to the formula, specifically changeable difficulties, more consistent stage design, and some tweaks to the general presentation to help make the on-screen madness a bit more legible, 100% Orange Juice could really pick up speed with a phenomenal little series of board game titles. All the elements are there: charm, strategy, and madness.

The Adventures of Mr Bobley is a surreal, psychological thriller, following the misadventures of the eponymous character, Mr Bobley.
After a frightful accident at his workplace, construction worker Mr Bobley must pass through different stages of his mind in order to wake up from a terrible coma and return to his wife and son - Mrs and Master Bobley.
Right off the bat we're thrown into the terrifying experience that we imagine Mr Bobley experiencing. The way in which the developer conveys the harshness of his injuries is through the control scheme, which is ♥♥♥♥ing annoying. However, this was introduced as an artistic conceit on the terrible condition of Mr Bobley's mind and how discombobulated he is due to the brain damage he induced (and I did after playing this for one hour).
Another amazing artistic choice is that of the extremely bland and nondescript world which this is set in. Every colour is white and washed out, conveying two things:
1) That this is set in the 1940's Germany, where White and Aryan supremacy exists. Mr Bobley - a construction worker who creates autobahns - is discriminated due to his red nose and was castrated by Hitler himself. Unfortunately, Bobley just created the aforementioned Master Bobley, who hides under the floorboards of his house. Master Bobley, therefore, has a ruined spinal column due to the fact that he is forced to hold a fetal position for the rest of his life. This fetal position can also be observed within the game, as Mr Bobley is capable of entering this position. Perhaps these are the memories of his son entering the comatose dream? Besides, this adds serious depth and motivation to the character of Mr Bobley, as he attempts to break free from this nightmare to save his son from the Nazis.
2) The 'artistic' style conveys the misery of Mr Bobley and his family, without having to show them. This kind of visual imagery and metaphorical symbolism can be viewed in such great art films as Citizen Kane and Paul Blart: Mall Cop.
Finally, one brilliant feature of the game that I observed was that of the uninstall button. This is perhaps the only button on the control scheme that works properly and is extremely satisfying to use.
In conclusion, Mr Bobley is a masterpiece in video game storytelling. Should this garner the necessary attention, I believe this good make society finally accept gaming as an art form. Or they'll think 10x worse of it. After all, it took 10 years for Citizen Kane to be realized for its brilliance.

Jet Set Radio is a game from a different era. It's a game from a time when it was considered a good business strategy for a major developer to throw money at an unproven concept. However, it's also unique even among its peers for its sheer cohesion. Every part of the game - from the core gameplay to the aesthetic to the plot (what little there is) - is screaming "you gotta live free!" Therefore, I would describe Jet Set Radio as a true work of art. The game is certainly not perfect, however; the controls are slightly wonky, as is standard for the early 2000s, and the overall pacing and progression of the game has some rough patches as a consequence. Overall, I'm still more than comfortable calling it a game everyone should play once and an absolute steal at only $8.

JET SET RADIOOOOOO!
I never had the chance to play this little gem of a game growing up, and I was very pleasantly surprised by what I found. This game is platforming extreme sports fun with a twist - easy to learn, but hard to master. First time you Jet-Rank a level is a great feeling, especially after hours of wanting to throw the USB controller at the wall in frustration at *those damned Noise Tanks being way too fast goddamnit why are the rivals hard to catch why are the controls so laggy for me GET ON THE RAIL AND GRIND GUM why why why?!*
That said, the controls for doing tricks are excellent for this game's age, and for the most part, tight and responsive - especially with some characters more than others. The graffiti controls take some getting used to but are simple to understand once you get the hang of it. That could be said of most things in this game - not too tough once you get used to it. This is definitely a sign of the age of this game - the game can be unintuitive due to its age sometimes - the maps are confusing, the occasional glitch happens (I had Mew standing horizontally on the side of a barrel in Kogane-cho once, which made me giggle), and the physics can occasionally do something funky. The AI can be ruthless, and the precision needed can be a little ridicuous at times - it took me way too long to unlock Garam because I couldn't get Beat to do what I wanted him to do (the rail, rail, wallgrind sequence at the end is rather tough). I also still for the life of me can't figure out how to beat the races for some of the characters, and it's driving me up the wall - in the non wallgrind way, I mean.
Oh, and about the controls - this game is extremely tough without a controller. I ended up buying a rather nice wired Xbox One controller for cheap just to play this game. Of course, it will be useful for other games too, because some games just do not work well with WASD controls. JSR was not meant for play on a PC; sports games like these do not work well with keyboard and mouse. It *is* possible to do, a few people in the community hub mention having beaten the game with keyboard and mouse, but I would really suggest just biting the bullet and finding, or buying, a USB controller for cheap.
But back to the positives. Did I mention the art style is great? Because the art style is great. The music's top-notch too, although I admittedly do have my favorites. Being able to use custom graffiti is fun, too, and I've been messing about spraying images of Cthulhu everywhere in Tokyo-to for grits and shiggles. The characters are unique and lovable; Garam is a personal favorite because for some reason, the controls feel tighter when I use him. And as for unlockables and achievements? Yeah, I'm going to be here a while, and even then I'm pretty sure I won't get every single one due to toughness for some of them. I'm a gamer, not a masochist, JSR. I have a life and you make my wrists hurt more than a sad virgin's living in his mother's basement.
If you haven't played this yet, why ever not? It's free from Sega. It's fun, it's challenging, it's addictive, and it has a style all its own. It's funky, it's cheeky, and it's a refreshingly different take on extreme sports games as well as on platforming. It's Jet Set Radio. I mean, JET SET RADIOOOOOO!!!

In the world of Free To Play games, we have a sea of options nowadays. With big publishers pushing out successful F2P Battle Arenas, First Person Shooters, or MMORPGs, it's become more and more difficult for the little guy to get a foothold. Gear Up feels like one game that's found it's grip, all while incorporating a little from each genre.
On the surface, Gear Up looks like a cutesy arena brawler on wheels. The idea isn't new, but the extent that they've taken their customization, and the overall amount of polish at this early stage is a little staggering. The sky is really the limit, and you can take that literally by reducing the mass of your tank, swapping treads out for hover fans, and then putting a wing on your tail end. The options in the game are inspirational, and it feels like I've always got my next upgrade in mind.
Don't let the game's aesthetic fool you. As cute as it is, the skill ceiling is rather high, and I've found myself impressed by some of the players out there. This is one of those games that is great to pick up, put a few rounds in, and come back later. In a day and age where we're putting 45 to 60 minutes into matches, this has been a breath of fresh air.
Sadly, the game is not without it's faults. As it's still early in it's release, there has been a light amount of bugs and glitches, but nothing entirely game breaking. Weapon balance in a game like this seems like a nearly impossible task, and while they've got it close, it feels like it may be some time before they hone it in perfectly, especially as more updates are put out.
My only real gripe with this game is it's business model. Each time you level, you're awarded an extra slot to store items in on top of the 8 they give you initially. This seems fair at first glance, but as I near level 8 at my 12 hour mark, space has become irritatingly limited, and the XP gaps between levels has soared drastically. It really does feel like the developer intends to twist your arm into shelling out $10 for their Basic pack, which at this juncture may be a completely fair price for a game with heart and soul put into it, with a quickly expanding community. I just wish that it didn't force me into that decision.

**It should be technically noted that I got this game with the implementation of the gem system with steam and managed to 'win' this for the equivalent of $5ish? dollars.**
So, firstly I wouldn't recommend this game at the price being charged. 29USD is more money than the usual person will likely get out of this game. Ys III was a weird game. It was the first in the series to swap from the top-down bump system to a 2D platformer. It was also outsourced to many, many different devs and systems. The series later swapped back to their original system for Ys IV (And presumably V) and then started using a 3D platformer engine for VI and beyond.
Yet this is my favorite in the series.
Oath in Felghana is a 1st-party remake of the original. With remixed music, completely redone areas, and superior gameplay. I would honestly list this among my top 5 RPGs of all time.
Ys TOiF is an Action RPG/Hack&Slash 3D platformer. You have four main abilities. Obviously: Attack combo, Jump, and Magic. But you also have a boost, which charges over time, gives you a quicker, stronger combo, and halves all damage taken. (In the PSP version you get a second boost which also gives HP Regen.) There are plenty of moves, like plunging attacks, rising blades, and such. The gameplay is generally very fast-paced. Grinding is made easier with a combo system that awards an XP multiplier based on how long you can keep a combo going.
This game is VERY hard. You shouldn't have too much trouble beating it on normal, but I'm currently in the midst of an Inferno mode playthrough. Dodging attacks is very necessary, though you get an ability later that negates all damage and serves as a guard.
One of the game's strong points is it's boss fights. All challenging, tense, and require a dedication of learning patterns and when to attack (Especially in higher difficulties). You really feel accomplished when you beat them.
Oooohhhmygodthisgamehasamazingmusic.
Falcom loves putting metal remixes of the original songs in their games. I'm serious when I say that literally every song on this soundtrack is amazing. Please just give it a listen even if you don't want to play the game. It always fits with the area perfectly.
This game picks up a few years after Ys II leaves off. Monsters are still rapant even though demons and magic have been eradicated. And a small trading town is hurt severely by the rule of a tyrant noble. It's a pretty decent story, and the intended emotions towards all of the characters get carried over very well.
Overall, I love this game. It's one of my favorites of all time, and likely the best in the series.

After months of wondering if I'd lost interest in video games, this one got me hooked from beginning to end. As a long time gamer, I enjoyed Y's 3 back in the day on the SNES. This is a great example of a re-imagining done right. The people who worked on this game seem to have a deep understanding of good game design and know what keeps a player interested without adding any fluff. There is plenty of new content that wasn't in the original, and all of it improves upon the old foundation.
If I had to suggest improvements, I'd ask that the easy mode was a little bit less easy (maybe 2/3rds damage instead of half damage from enemies. There is an included "Very Easy" mode after all.) Normal mode required a bit more dying, grinding, or perfect pattern memorization than I'd prefer, and bosses often had a few moves that seemed to be unavoidable. It would have been great if the original soundtrack was included as well, but I wouldn't hold that against the game.

Pre-ordered this game in 2011 and in it's alpha stage it was pretty fun to mess around for a short while. Though there wasn't much to it in terms of variation or content so I decided to wait for the final release.
And after all these years of development I still have the same feeling about Overgrowth. Like others mentioned the game feels more like a tech demo of the engine.
The combat seems fun until you discover the JUMP KICK. You can kill countless wannabe "bosses" with a single jump kick if they get pushed on something which usually casuses them to break some crucial bone and die. And after this discovery the (short) game becomes a series of spacebar presses followed by LMB clicks. I know the devs put a lot of work into these systems but from the player's perspective they could just as well use something a lot simpler, as the gameplay doesn't flesh them out at all.
Levels feel very empty and cheap, usually there are only props in the center of area and the further away from it you go the less there is. And even in the most "cluttered" parts it all goes down to a ground texture, a square building and three vases near the wall. Seems like no attention was paid to the level design which is unfortunate because the general art direction is really nice.
The story is presented in a form of "cut-scenes" before each fight / platforming section. During those scenes you can observe text-boxes taken straight out from a cheap Ren'Py vn game. Camera is set in weird angles and the characters use only a few clunky animations (idle and talk) waiting for their turn to say "look! a lot of enemies! let's get reinforcements!" or "nah, i despise the bloodshed but will take them down all by meself" over and over again.
The world outside the fights feel empty and artificial. You can't interact in any way with the NPCs, the only time they do something is when you enter a trigger to play the next cut-scene.
It's all a shame because I thought this game will turn into something much greater. I'd rather see the game play more in an open-world style, walking around well crafted locations, talking to different NPCs, hunting down your targets, etc.
At the moment I'd say it's a wasted potential but I hope the team will hire more devs and make a great game out of these promising fundaments.

Ys is a remake of a classic RPG that has been around for for almost three decades. It is one of your more standard JPRGs. There's a lot of grinding involved and a lot of back tracking as well. Ys is one of those RPGs that don't always tell you where you need to go or what to do. Most of the game's story progress is based on in game events, so you may find yourself wandering around and then having to back track in order to actually get anywhere.
As a standard JRPG there isn't anything too bad about it, the graphics are good, for it's age, it has a decent sound track and there's some very nice hand drawn animation as well. One of the bigger problems with Ys is the fact that while it's a standard action-rpg, it incorporates platforming elements that can be tedious at best, infuriating at worst. There's been several times I have actually had to quit playing the game due to this issue.
If you are a fan of difficult JRPGs, then Ys will do fine by you, if you aren't a huge fan of massive grinding or back tracking, this won't be your cup of tea. People who want to play RPGs "for the story" are going to find they are going to have to slog their way through Ys difficulty and BS in order to get to the meat of the story.

This game is my significant other.  The one I go back to when I'm bored with the latest AAA title... the embarrasingly large number of hours on record stand testament to that.
I could give you a run down of one of my campaigns.  There was the time I played a Norman Count recently installed after the Battle of Hastings.  I played it nice with William, was made Duke... then overthrew his son as soon as he died and crowned myself King Edmund (Blackadder).  There was the time I rebuilt the Roman Empire, reunified the Christian Church then imported the Save into EU IV and took Rome to the New World.  There was the time where I built a great Welsh Empire that emcompassed all of Great Britain then took the fight to the Mongols.  Then there was the time that I encountered the Persian Joan of Ark who led my armies to victory in India... but I won't go into details of those, instead I will tell you why you should grab a copy of CKII as well as a few reasons why you might not want to.
The Pros:
*CKII is a very complex game that gives you an unparalleled level of freedom to shape your dynasty.  Along with the usual diplomacy and warfare your character will encounter all manner of interesting random event and can embark on all manner of interesting personal quest - erect a runestone honouring your mother or seduce the King's wife then convince her to help you murder him... or dump her, seduce her daughter and catch sypholis.
*The game is very well supported by Paradox and there is a constant stream of new content (some of which is free and some of which you need to buy).
*If you do manage to get bored the Modding Community has created some truly exceptional pieces of work that will completely overhaul the game.
*Offer the French King up as a human sacrifice to appease the Norse Gods.
*If you like Diplomacy this game models it in a far more satisfying manner than any other game I have played.
*Capture the Mongol Khan in battle.  Then castrate him and send him back to his people.
*This game will run on most PCs.
*Claim the throne... then get murdered the very next day.
The Cons:
*CKII is a very complex game.  It has a steep learning curve.
*Getting a complete copy of CKII is not cheap!  Paradox has released a lot of DLCs since this game was released.
*If you love Total War style cinematic battles, CKII does not do that.  You have no direct control over your generals.  You can watch them and see what strategies they are employing which is often quite fun but which can also be irritating when you watch your troops massacred through the flagrant incompetence of your commanders.  Applaud as your massive longbow volley devastates the enemy ranks, then cringe as your general charges his own skirmishers then hesitates at a crucial moment... and suddenly everyone is running away.
*The game will slow down towards the end-game as it follows the lives of the thousands of characters who are living, dying and murdering their way through Eurasia and North Africa.  If there are too many it can become a little unstable.
It's a good classic style RPG game!

Okay, where to start. I figured that there was no need for me to review this game as it is so successful, but, as always, All the Steam reviews on the front of the store page are one to two sentenced jokes instead of something actually helpful. Please thumbs-up this, if you like this review, for visibility.
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is the sequel to the critically acclaimed The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind. Knowledge of prior storylines are not needed to enjoy Oblivion, though a working understanding of TES world lore will always enhance your experience in any of The Elder Scrolls games. A good idea is to just read some of the in-game books, from time to time, as you play the game. Some of the fictional books are amazing little detours from the game world. Oblivion and Morrowind are less fantasy experience and more-so a virtual world that you
in. With mods, this experience feels more real to me than some of the Dungeons and Dragons campaigns I've played. It's incredibly easy to get immersed into this work.
Oblivion's main story leaves some to be desired. You are a prisoner who meets the Emperor (voiced by Patrick Stewart) and his guards as he flees a rumored assassination attempt through hidden tunnels in the Imperial City prison. Suffice it to say, that its' not really a spoiler that you witness the Emperor's assassination. Before the Emperor's death, he tells you that you are fated by the gods to save the Empire and "close shut the jaws of Oblivion". Long story short, you flee the tunnels and are sent to track down the Emperor's last remaining illegitimate heir (voiced by Sean Bean) as well as pretty much single-handedly repel the invasion of Daedra from Mehrunes Dagon’s hellish plane of Oblivion.
However, in classic Elder Scrolls fashion, the main quest isn’t even the largest part of the game. The entire Imperial province of Cyrodiil is open to you for exploration. There are many guilds to join, whether or not you want to be a mercenary, a mage, a thief, an assassin, or a holy crusader. There is an abundance of miscellaneous side and freeform quests for you to do. I recommend the purchase of a strategy guide, not so that you’ll have a walkthrough, but because you’ll need some way to keep track of where everything is! There are many quests and areas that you will miss if you don’t scour the world for them. You can easily spend around 350 hours if you finish all of the main, side, and faction quests as well as the DLC. Many people just wander across the world, not even touching the main story.
The mechanics have long been applauded as an improvement over Morrowind, level scaling aside. Morrowind offers a better story and atmosphere, while Oblivion offers a more modern experience. The graphics are a bit dated by today’s standards, but I still sometimes catch myself stunned by the beauty of Cyrodiil. Skills are a lot more streamlined than Morrowind, which I consider a negative trait, although it does make the game friendlier to newcomers. Combat is not as bad as so many people claim. To me, it really feels like I’m actually swinging the sword. The magic system is a lot simpler than Morrowind’s but a lot easier to use. It is not as good as Skyrim’s magic system, but still useful.
The DLC The Knights of the Nine and The Shivering Isles
trump Oblivion’s main quest. Knights of the Nine puts on a holy crusade to fight against Umariil the Unfeathered, an ancient Ayleid elf who has come to try to enslave men once more. The Shivering Isles sends you to the frankly breathtaking realm of Sheogorath, the Daedric  “Mad God”. Most of the dialogue in The Shivering Isles will have you chuckling to yourself and smiling. And the atmosphere of the realm brings nostalgia from Morrowind to mind.
Now, I am going to discuss mods. Oblivion’s modding scene is unparalleled by Morrowind or Skyrim. There are enormous overhaul mods, plenty of lore friendly stories, and enthralling and immersive stories and factions. You can even reach an added five or six hundred more hours if you play through some quality mods. Morroblivion, brings the entire landmass of the previous game, Morrowind, as well as all of it’s quests, items, NPCs, creatures, etc. You can then travel between the two provinces with your same character. Other mods add some of the other provinces from Tamriel. And a few mods have been so well rated that they’ve become known as unofficial expansion packs.
Oblivion is an astounding RPG that will draw you in and stick with you for a long, long time. The replayability of Oblivion is excellent. The game was released eight years ago and I am still playing it to this day. You will not regret buying this game. Get the Deluxe pack for $25 that comes with all the DLC, themed player lairs, and, yes, even horse armor. It is well worth the price and you will get your money’s worth over and over again.
