A nice, straight-forward third person shooter based on the WH40K universe, marred by several silly issues that do affect the overall enjoyment of the game. First off, the save situation - or the complete lack of it. Progress through a mission, broken up between checkpoints and that's fine - whilst you continue to play the game. Quit the game during a mission however and your progress within that mission is totally lost. There's no ability AT ALL to save within a mission. You either play it through completely - or redo the entire mission when you relaunch the game. Silly.
The progress through the level can at times be ludicriously hampered by a failed camera system. You have no control over which way or elevation that the camera maybe be pointing. I've 'lost' the camera several times, often wandering off into the darkness of tunnels that I cannot see and blindly reaching a point where the camera decides to catch up. Again, a silly oversight. Why hasn't the player got control of the camera?
Then there's the fact that the enemies appear every single time at exactly the same the point. On occassion when I've died, I've reapproached the same point of the level - firing into blank space, knowing full well that a bunch of orcs are due to appear. Sure enough, they do.
I've yet to play this co-operatively and I think that's where the game will truly shine. Though god-knows how the camera issues are compounded in that mode! Also, the game itself looks to be very short - though I've not completed it as yet.
Overall, a taster really of what type of game this really could be. Different factions of marines, much more choice on equipment and weaponry - and a random element of the opposing forces sent out to stop you. All would make this game much more appealing and enjoyable in the long term. As it is, 6/10.

The deal breaker: This game crashes constantly. All the issues with this game are outside of gameplay. Which is good, maybe they will eventually get fixed. The game crashes when loading a map, at random times while on the map, while changing graphics options, when you spawn, when you die, when returning to the menu, when clicking through the menu. The game also appears to have a memory leak. It starts at around 450MB usage in the menu, 460MB while in a map, then over time goes up to 2GB usage while in the menu.. Probably higher if you can go long enough without crashing.
Other thoughts: There is no party system, and the "invite friend" system is broken. It's still easy to find friends in matches. I don't mind not having parties, I like playing against my friends as much as I like playing with them, this is a positive in my mind.
TL:DR____________
Fix the crashes and I'll give this game a solid recommendation. The gameplay really is there for a fun way to blow off some steam and mess around. But it causes as much frustration as it lets out at the moment.

Honestly, I loved this game with a passion. Splendid soundtrack, wasn't TOO much of a pay-to-win game, it was well made, the combat system was AMAZING, there were several classes with some really neat specilizations you could choose from when getting to a certain level, on top of that, levelling up your character wasn't too particularly hard. The game was just... excellent.
That is, until the update came. The update that removed some very important things. Such as quests on the message boards, stages that had high rewards, which, without those it's significantly more difficult to actually make a decent profit off of level completion, sometimes even after one you could potentially lose cash from repairing your gear. Sure it added the level 90 cap, and the players were waiting for that for months on end, but were soon to realize it was more of a disappointment than something nice.
However, they are still updating the game and not abandoning it, which is awesome, and when they add new classes, I am sure to hop on and check them out. The Dragon Nest team has created something incredible, and I really wish for it to only get better, but honestly with that update, I'm not so sure it will happen.
I really do recommend this to people who are looking for a quick time-killing game, but I would not suggest becoming a hardcore fan that wastes all their time playing this one game in particular. You'll just end up disappointed, like I was.
In the end, I still like Dragon Nest, I do play occasionally, and it is definitely one of my all times RPG's, but it's just not... that great anymore.

So I could barely run Overgrowth on this laptop but whatever, I got it working and now here we are. Should you buy Overgrowth? No, you should not. In fact I would say that nobody should buy Overgrowth, because it's thirty bucks for four hours of mediocre levels slapped together in a lazy fashion, bad platforming, and lame arena fights.
Or, in fact, it's three hours of that and one hour that's just Lugaru again but in HD.
On the surface, LUGARU IN HD seems like a neat bonus but, ironically, I think including that was a bad decision. This is because, first of all, it makes the actual overgrowth campaign look♥♥♥♥♥♥in comparison and, second of all, it has a bunch of costumes for Turner for no reason, illustrating the entire problem with Overgrowth in microcosm: nobody working on it gave a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the actual levels. There's lots of art here; every enemy has its own model and outfit and design and they all move very fluidly. But the actual levels are all just a bunch of crap boxes stuck together with no rhyme or reason. Sometimes they're pretty and ornamented. Sometimes they are actually untextured and just sort of sit there, an existential nightmare world of floating blocks for Turner to awkwardly jump at. Have fun falling the ♥♥♥♥ down!
Sometimes you can kill yourself by jumping near a wall: Turner will hit the wall and his spine will snap. Seems legit.
Also, don't bother with the combat unless you've got a proper sword. The knife is useless and will always be parried by your enemy, and unarmed combat only works with people your size or smaller since wolves can't be thrown and instantly kill you if they touch you. The actual secret is just to jump up and press attack near the enemy, which will jump kick them into a nonsensical ragdoll state and throw them across the room. Every fight can be handled this way, and some seem impossible unless you do it. Jump kicking counters all weapons, since they drop them, and it can't be blocked so it works on the bosses too. So the combat's compromised and kind of naff. What else we got?
Well, the actual story is barely there, but even that is wrong. They build up the story to killing this cat slaver lady, which entails an awful and endless tournament arc which lasts half the game, and then you kill her instantly by jumpkick and run away. Which would seem like the end, but instead it's followed by the worst platforming sequence in the game to climb a tower, at the top of which are four generic rabbit enemies and a "boss" which is just another generic rabbit. He has not been introduced, he has no real presence, and he's not even exciting to fight since you can just stab him with a sword and kill him instantly. Or, as happened in my first fight with him, he may jump at you and fall down the tower to his death, but I assume that was a bug. Game design, however, is not a bug, and the design here is laughable.
Overgrowth didn't take nine years to make. It took nine years to stop being made.

A spiritual successor to
, Overgrowth is one of the games that predated the concept of Early Access in late 2008, but sadly didn't predate the concept of having nothing to show for it in 2017.
Often referred to as "a glorified tech demo", it might as well be. The Engine it runs on was built from the ground up to enable more-or-less fluid fighting mechanics and is equipped with a bunch of admittedly interesting scripting systems, A.I. behavior and movement features, yet the developer set out to not actually do anything with them besides expecting its community to.
Let's go through what you get out of the box when buying this, though:
All in all, after all these years, it's clear Overgrowth should have long changed its marketing from offering a gaming experience to being a community sandbox of sorts focused on the customization thereof, as modders managed to make more worthwhile content for the game than the developer did across the entirety of the development cycle.
It failed to recognize its weaknesses in order to make up for them, and didn't even bother trying to make the most out of the mechanics and features they set out to work on for so long. Nothing guarantees that the content (mods) that are actually worth checking out will stick around if you buy it, but you still could surprise yourself if you're creative and patient enough.
A game with a strong creative mode that is ironically overshadowed by a very uncreative and unimpressive singleplayer experience, dodgy mechanics that give no justice to its predecessor, and a business practice that heavily relies on its modding community doing work without admitting it (i.e. being thankless).
Unless you really like quick brawlers and you're into making/sifting through amateur work, just avoid this rabbit hole of an attempt at a game concept.
If the mechanics alone entice you, do consider trying out the better developed games:

itself.

If you love strategy games with a rpg touch like I do, then you will love this game! Now I am a little bias, but this game is simply the best stategy game of all time... OF ALL TIME!
You play as an individual, head of a preset house (created house if you get the ruler designer dlc). You ultimate goal is what you want it to be.
Want to start of as a lowly count/countess working his/her way up the social pecking order by getting the nobles of the realm to support your forged claim to your neighbor's title? You can do that! Or say you want a crown on YOUR crown, so you bribe the nobles of the realm to join your faction to force the King to change the inheritance laws of the kingdom from primogenture to elective so you can put your name up for nomination? You can do that too! Or say you want to start of as a King/Sultan/Caliph/Emperor and fight those very vassals who would try such a treasonous act, YOU CAN!
I can go on and on about the multitude of things you can do, from growing your family tree by marrying a wealthy duke's daughter so your son will have a claim to the duke's lands when he finally kicks the bucket. From growing old, dying and passing everything to you son, which as the new head of the house you will now play as. Say, what about your daughter? She is more capable than your current character's son! Change the inheritance laws to give you daughter a claim.
Use diplomacy to normalize relations, marriage to seal alliances, war to conquer you enemies, intrigue to assassinate your rivals, piety to gain the favor of the Pope/Caliph/Grand Priest, it goes on and on.
The rpg element is enhanced by a large and ever growing event system which helps form your current character's personality by gaining new traits, or losing them, based on your decisions. Educate your children yourself or have them assigned to a trusted retainer. Grow your influence and power by inviting talented people to your court and appointing them to your council. Hand out titles to your vassals to keep them loyal, or seize their titles when/if they plot against you. Deliver justice or Cry Havoc, and let slip the dogs of war!

When I was getting tired of WoW, a friend recommended Oblivion to me. I'd never played any of the Elder Scrolls games, but I quickly got caught up in this one. I'd never experienced such an immersive RPG experience before, where I could sneak into locked fortresses, steal from neighbours' houses, assassinate people if I wish, advance the specific skills I want, freely travel about a virtual world and engage in countless conversations with NPCs who have a tremendous amount of vocal acting (rather than the standard text of WoW.) This game was also darker, bloodier and grittier. Another difference is that it doesn't play online with other players, just on your computer. This means that you don't have annoying personalities to deal with. The NPCs and quests are so engaging, who needs them?
What made me fall in love with this game however was the modding. At first I felt intimidated by modding, but after watching a couple YouTube tutorials on it and following the mod installation instructions, I quickly picked up on it and I fell in love with it. Oblivion was designed to be mod-friendly and it is amazing how this allows you to improve the game in exactly the ways you desire. Want more lush colours? More NPCs? Companions to keep you company? New lands to explore? New quests? Weapons or armour, it's all available for free download! (Just be sure to download Oblivion Mod Manager to better manage your mods.) The modding community is what keeps this game alive and I hope it never dies. I love what mods bring to this already stellar, epic game :)

This is this game in it's released form? Really? After 5 long years of waiting, they give us this campaign? I'm so sorry wolfire, I really am. I know how much blood and sweat went into this game, but it's fundamentally flawed.
Overgrowth is a fantastic tech-demo. It's got a beautiful combat engine, which is hard to find these days. Here's the problem: The rabbit kick is completely broken. Once you learn how to use it (which I did during the techdemo years ago) the game becomes a cakewalk on the hardest difficulty. Weapons become irrelevent.
Also, the only hard parts were just excruciating jumping puzzles. They aren't fun in the same way trying to swat a fly isn't fun.
The story isn't great, and the way it was presented was worse. The jokes aren't funny, and the attempt at comedic timing is aggressively unfunny. The characters aren't memorable. After this, I know nothing about anyone in the story. I ended up just skipping the 'cutscenes' near the end because I didn't give a rat's @$$ about the story anymore.
Every mission is one of three things: Fight this series of guys, fight this one big guy, or climb this giant pillar. After a while, that gets monotonous. The combat would be great, if they did something with it. Again, the rabbit kick is OP throughout the entire game, and trying to use anything else just makes me want to use it. It feels broken. Everything you do is immediately followed by the thought 'Was I supposed to be able to do that?'
TLDR: I killed the final boss with two kicks. It lasted all of 8 seconds. It wasn't fun or satesfying.
This game is NOT WORTH $30. Hell, It's barely worth $10. When it goes on sale during a humblebundle, pick it up then. Set up a 1v1 with AI and ramp up their difficulty as you progress. That's fun. The rest of the game is not.
I'm sorry wolfire. Aim lower next time.

Kill Team is a decent game, which is first and foremost recommended to the WH40K fanbase (purely for collection at the very worst case scenario if something in this title doesn't fit your liking) as well as any player who loves a simple, straightforward shooter with the top-down camera perspective. Warhammer 40,000: Kill Team has a well designed atmosphere, and by immerging the player into it, the game easily incinerates time at a fast and fascinating pace. Slaying hordes of xenos is what this game is about, and the title says it all. As an action shooter set in a legendary universe where there is only war, Kill Team does a decent job for depicting and brining forth what the 41'st millenium is - Death and Carnage
On the downside, the game does possess a certain feeling of inflexibility to it, a feeling of an old-time shooter which could of been a bit more openworld, but this can be merely my subjective opinion, especially considering the fact that this is a shooter, not an RPG with a freedom of movement and action. Still, always knowing what will happen next, even if this was not inteded to be so by the developers obviously reduces the element of unexpectedness, which for this type of a game is a bad thing. There could have been more weapons, skills (each class of the space marines only has one unique skill, thus making 4 skills in the whole game) and content. The lack of "flavour", however, does not only affect gameplay; The interface too feels somewhat mediocre in it's seemingly formal minimalism - in this game, you won't find detailed icons of weapons, items or various skills, reducing the interface (which often has an important role of adding a distinct image to the game) to simple text and primitive looking "buttons". The enviorment detail of the levels is nearly, if not completely, unchanging throughout all of the game, with minor differences in the palette color and doodads between levels at it's very most. This is justified though, because the game is set on an Ork Kroozer - a galactic warship of leviathan proportions (my apologies for the spoilers).
This game would be so much more immense and awesome if it would have some type of a Team Deathmatch or Deathmatch multiplayer mode, this is where the game would actually shine, and shine bright at that. Alas, this was not to be, because the only closest thing to multiplayer in Kill Team is a 2 player Co-Op mode, by either playing the whole campaign (which consists out of 5 levels, and they aren't that long) or by playing Survival Mode which, to no surprise, is about survival against endless hordes of greenskins. Again, there could have been more levels, but there isn't enough proportional content, and if the game would be, let's say, twice as long, then it would simply become stale and repetative. Out of the other, more minor downsides, sometimes the camera angle becomes annoying, with the player having no possibility to rotate or alter it in any way whatsoever.
Warhammer 40,000: Kill Team, in my opinion is a good, absorbing game which should undoubtedly be played and experienced by any WH40K fan, with it's atmosphere and it's simple yet addictive gameplay being the titles most evident upsides. This game is great if you and your friend want to have some simple fun and blast through incoming tides of the menacing greenskins in Co-Op mode, or if you just want to indulge in the opportunity of steeping into a little bit of WH40K lore - the choice is always yours.

Why am I torturing myself for so little benefit?  Is it fun to suffer from anxiety?  Is it fun to always strive for perfection?

It's a fun game, and I will continue to play it, despite everything I'm about to say (the first combo I put on the table was "Condom Chris," and I was hooked).  This game, like most P2W however, is geared toward folks who have way too much money or way too much time.  For the rest of us, we can grind, persist, and then kick the nearest concrete wall.
Pros:
1) It's free, and you don't have to spend any money on it (this is also one of its downfalls, as I'll mention later).
2) It's really fun if you like CCG's.
3) Linking to #2 (hahaha!), you get a lot of nostalgia from all the different cards and combos.
4) There's a ton of combos out there for folks to play with, and the different abilities they afford (for tactical and strategic purposes) are quite varied.
Cons:
1) Refering to #1 in the pros, this game is gated for those who are not willing to drop real money.  The reward system is set up to pamper the elites with more elite cards at a more lucrative rate, and this becomes exponential.  It's like the worst Ark server you can imagine, but a CCG - if you're not rocking mythics, then you'll never be able to qualify in competitions to reap things to unlock mythics (unless you pay).
Anyway...
2)  Some of the combos make ZERO sense, yet they're dominating.  A fat fish can destroy the captain of a starship?  I don't care how German it is - I CALL SHENANIGANS!!!
Conclusion:
Get ready to grind some flour, or you'll have to pony up the dough.  Either way, you're going to run in to a group of Zack Brannigans using nothing but legendary combos.  If at any point you feel like you're starting to do well, you're about to get an uninvited dose of reality up the ♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Sometimes, video games can attract attention just because of their names. This is likely the case with 100% Orange Juice, even if the primarily response is confusion. After all, it sounds more like the description of a drink than any game! But 100% Orange Juice is very much a game and quite the fun one at that. You’ll just have to spend a bit of time learning about its rules to truly enjoy it.
The name of the game is 100% Orange Juice. Why? I don’t care, and I don’t think the game does either. The strange name is only the beginning, however, of the bizarre realm of 100% Orange Juice. Because I can’t pass up the opportunity to make a citrus joke here, the game is definitely sweet, but at times can appear very sour. In fact, I am pretty sure this game hates me.
100% Orange Juice is, at its essence, a simple board game. While it may take a game or two to fully grasp everything, it’s fairly simple, but also fairly brutal. Four players are placed on a board and must roll a die or dice to move forward either playing passively, trying to quietly and quickly obtain as many stars as you can, or aggressively, out for blood and attacking enemy spaces and opponents around every corner. The way the game challenges you to choose and alternate these styles of gameplay is what makes 100% Orange Juice an excellent game, as the player must be apprehensive in the face of the unfortunate circumstance where your strategy, and the world itself, has seemingly failed you.
100% Orange Juice is far from perfect, but it’s still an exceptional virtual board game that really pushes your buttons. With some tweaks to the formula, specifically changeable difficulties, more consistent stage design, and some tweaks to the general presentation to help make the on-screen madness a bit more legible, 100% Orange Juice could really pick up speed with a phenomenal little series of board game titles. All the elements are there: charm, strategy, and madness.

Gear Up is a game with a lot of potential but with a serious lack of content, matchmaking, balancing and overall variety.
>> Pros
-nice art and design of the map and tanks
-amazing sound effects
-fast-paced
-funny types of weapons (like a harpoon or a flamethrower for example)
-easy controls and great gameplay, it runs smoothly
-average number os maps
>>Cons
-no matchmaking ("find a room" concept)
-with no matchmaking, you rarely have balanced matches STOMP OR GET STOMPED
-lack of variety (for a game that stimulates criativity when you are going to build your own tank, you dont see many ways of changing the style of it. You are always going to have two types of weapon, wheels and its body. Even with this,  you don't have enough different types of items)
-heavily inspired on robocraft but not on the idea of starting the tank from scratch (decreasing variety this way)
-impossible to creat a party with your friends and join a room (as for 1/03/2015, the button to invite your friends is not working)
-when you win a match, it doesn't feel rewarding at all. you just have to wait 3 more seconds and one more will start. because of this (and other factors listed here), you can't expect to play for weeks this game
Gear Up, as said before, is a game with a lot of potential. IF the developers use this and other's feedback to improve tha game, it has the chance to become a great game afterall

As much as this game looks pretty and interesting, its full of bugs and bad programming. Ruins the fun. Install and play for 5 hours to satisfy your desire to play a game that looks fun and interesting, then uninstall and forget about it.
Examples:
- The number of players does not sync properly. My brother saw 5 people in the match, I saw 4 people in that same match. We compared who we saw and who was missing. There was a guy playing on this server that my game did not show, in the scoreboard and in the game world. I could have literally bumped into him and not know he was there.
(Makes you wonder what the programmers are doing, how can you ♥♥♥♥ up that bad?)
- In team deathmatch, team scores is not synced properly. My brother saw 18:0, I saw 18:1.
- The score does not count properly. We were being destroyed, and the enemy's score stayed at 1 (or 0 for my brother)
- The time left in a game does not sync with the server. I was playing with my brother and the time left on his screen was 30 seconds less than on mine. When he ran out of time, his game proceeded as if the match was over, rewarding him with the goodies and what not, then showed a loading screen. Meanwhile I was playing for 30 seconds longer on that same server, and the issue resolved itself so that my brother had to wait at the loading screen while the match REALLY ended. Again, how can you ♥♥♥♥ up this badly?
- No team balance mechanic. A lot of games were 6 against 2. No manual balance mechanic, you cannot change teams, even if you wanted to.
- You can change the layout of the tank midgame, in the field, while getting shot at. That's not fair, logical or balanced.
- When you run out of ammo, instead of going for an ammo pickup, you can change your gun to something else, then change it back and have full ammo again. Takes you 5 seconds. Ammo is supposed to be a big deal in this game.
- Balance is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Like mentioned by other people, you'll see only a handful of tank layouts that excel. I haven't seen at least 50% of the parts available used in any game so far.
- Hits are calculated on clients, not on servers. This means any player with lag can in fact kill you after you have killed him. I'm not talking about his flying rocket that he shot just before I killed him. I'm talking about a guy looking away from me when I killed him, then I get destroyed by him. How do you ♥♥♥♥ up that badly?
- Rubberbanding of people with lag. No way you can hit them. Not all that rampant, but reveals the level of bad programming.
- Tanks sometimes appear under ground, with just the top part sticking out.
The artists and the model designers all did a very good job, but the programmers on the team put zero thought into everything they made. Any person with common sense would have programmed it differently. If this was a game in alpha or beta, it would be acceptable. Not acceptable for a game in full release.

Divinity: Original Sin 2
is a game I have already sunk in 59 hours playing and have enjoyed every minute of it. If are looking for a game with deep RPG elements with a very indepth story and plenty of side quests to keep you busy for hours this game is for you.
Warning: Expect to die a lot unless you play it on Explorer mode of which I have not touched.
Do not expect any kind of hand holding, walk your way through battles or just a quick game to breeze through in a few hours. This game will make you invest time, learn strategies, and figure out the best way to beat enemies that might only be one level higher than your characters.
Replay value- (Super high)  Many quests in the game do not get answered or you do something which ends the quest early. This leads to wanting to not only try the game again and see what road that takes you but also not using their pre-set characters will make it extra enjoyable.
Other Modes:
Game master mode- is fun and enjoyable. Allowing the player and his friends or whoever might want to try out a true D&D feel.
Arena- is pvp based where you are pitted against another player. ( Not really my thing but plenty of people to try out your skills against.)
Overall the game is a joy and a fresh breath of air from the other mundane strategy based rpg's currently out there. This should be GoTW for any RPG based PC player and if this ever comes to console it would probably get pretty close also.
If you are on the edge and thinking of buying this game don't hesistate it is worth every penny and then some.

So, I've played both  D: OS1 and now D:OS2.  I didn't hear about D: OS1 until it was in SEA, at which time I bought in to it right away because I've enjoyed their earlier games.  The way in which Larian went about their development in SEA for their first D:OS game was very impressive, it was on point, always with regular updates and susinctly launched right when they said it would.  It was a professional, well-oiled development machine.  That reason alone is why I made sure to follow them and when they launched their Kickstarter for D:OS2, with the inclusion of different races,  I didn't even have to think about it, I wanted in.
Long winded backstory aside, when I saw that one of the many Kickstarter tiers was to hire on Chris Avellone to be brought on as head writer, I was even more stoked.  As far as story goes, the first game had its issues, it was 'ok', but that's about. With the addtion of Chris, and as a fan of Planescape: Torment, the minute I started to play the game after launch, it was immediately engaging and I was sucked in, just like I was when I played Planescape so many years ago.  You can't fake writing talent and Avellone is without a doubt, one of the very best in the gaming industry and it shows in this game, boy does it ever.
The addition of the other races was another big draw for me.  The only downside to that is, for me at least, it gave me a big case of restart-itis, which isn't the game's fault at all, it's just me being flakey and indecisive with so many options.
Each race has a gender specific origin character that has a storyline tailored for them, you can play one of them or just play a custom character and include any or none of the origin characters in your party. I have to say, I was a bit disappointed in how origin characters were handled. In hindsight, it makes sense but when it was first described in the Kickstarter, I guess I was expecting it to be more like you create a character, are asked questions about your character (kinda like how Bethesda used to do it, back when Bethesda wasn't the corporate hack job it is today) and your own unique character would have the benefit of the origin backstory, etc.  Well, it's not like that at all, but I can deal with that.  I can safely say it's still fun to play a custom character, at least I find it to be so.
Oh, another addition for D:OS 2 is that modding has been incorporated into its development from the beginning.  So there's potentially no end in sight for all of the custom adventures that can be had, so much like Neverwinter Nights, as long as the creators are there, the game will live on. That's just so damn cool.

This game is a masterpiece, so far.
I've put a few dozen hours into 1 save with a few friends. Progress is slow, but there is so much to do and so much to learn and explore.
The graphics are good, but they don't matter in the long run. What matters is the gameplay.
The turn based combat is phenominal. I wasn't so sure about it when I was considering the purchase, but I've fallen in love with it. Taking your time to strategize and really understand the situation, trying to understand an opponents range or abilities--all of it, is just exhilerating, and battles are never repetitive.
Out of combat gameplay is intensive.
Movement feels a bit slow, but there is so much to loot and interact with that it almost doesn't matter, and waypoints are placed in areas to make your travel less tedious. Conversations are great and depend on your 'tags' and species, and it's really nice to try to play to the character you're interacting with based on which one of your characters you think would be wisest.
Persuasion events seem...off. There doesn't seem to be any roll system here aside from just choosing the correct option, and a character with 0 persuasion can win persuasions easily, and I'm not sure if I'm just getting lucky or if there's something I'm missing, but either way, it doesn't impact the game experience negatively in the long run.
This game, and I can not stress to you enough, is BIG.
In my save with my friends, we spend about 12+ hours in the first zone. Sure, we tried to find and do everything, and you may not be one of those players, but I'd recommend it as sidequests you do may help you in ways down the line that you wouldn't expect.
But that does bring something up. The quest marker system is incredibly odd. There's no indication of what a yellow/red marker means, and some markers are on objectives already completed, and it makes it hard to decipher which is where and where is what. Eventually you get a feel for the map and know if the direction you're going is making sense or not, but it is a tad annoying.
I haven't played this with random public lobbies, but I almost wouldn't recommend it based on the fact that I'm terrified someone would be a Dbag or something.
There is an intensive GM mode where you can create levels, quests, storylines...it's really big. I want to take the time to craft a good campaign, but note for anyone who wishes to do so, it'll take a lot of time, more than a normal DnD campaign creation I'd assume.
All in all, I briefly touched the surface. There is just so much, and everything seems well polished and thought out. No sidequest seems bad or unfit, the storyline (so far) is intriguing and immersive, and the gameplay is phenominal. I would fully recommend this game.

When I was getting tired of WoW, a friend recommended Oblivion to me. I'd never played any of the Elder Scrolls games, but I quickly got caught up in this one. I'd never experienced such an immersive RPG experience before, where I could sneak into locked fortresses, steal from neighbours' houses, assassinate people if I wish, advance the specific skills I want, freely travel about a virtual world and engage in countless conversations with NPCs who have a tremendous amount of vocal acting (rather than the standard text of WoW.) This game was also darker, bloodier and grittier. Another difference is that it doesn't play online with other players, just on your computer. This means that you don't have annoying personalities to deal with. The NPCs and quests are so engaging, who needs them?
What made me fall in love with this game however was the modding. At first I felt intimidated by modding, but after watching a couple YouTube tutorials on it and following the mod installation instructions, I quickly picked up on it and I fell in love with it. Oblivion was designed to be mod-friendly and it is amazing how this allows you to improve the game in exactly the ways you desire. Want more lush colours? More NPCs? Companions to keep you company? New lands to explore? New quests? Weapons or armour, it's all available for free download! (Just be sure to download Oblivion Mod Manager to better manage your mods.) The modding community is what keeps this game alive and I hope it never dies. I love what mods bring to this already stellar, epic game :)

Man, am I glad I stayed within the 2 hour mark so I could refund this game.
First off, I gotta say, I had been looking forward to the release of Overgrowth for a long time. For as far as I can remember, I found it about... Five, maybe six years ago, and really liked the look of it. Now, after pretty much forgetting about it, and seeing posts about it every now and then - it's finally out!
But, it's far from worth the price. The mechanics and combat of the game are truly fun for an hour or two, but you can get bored really quickly. (In my opinion.)  The story mode is... Eh. That's honestly the best word I have for it. It tries to throw weird mythology about the bunny-people, dog-people and their Gods and whatnot, but all I could find myself thinking during the 'cutscenes' (which are pretty much almost just stills with a weird angle) was: "What the ♥♥♥♥ is this?"
So, the first 10-20 minutes are pretty neat. Discovering the idea behind the game, and the mechanics of the combat system. This whole combat system immediately falls apart when you discover the bunny kick. You jump in the air, and launch both your bunny feet at the opponent. There's a chance this'll kill them in one go, and if it doesn't: Just do it again. No reason to use the other, now-clunky-looking combat options there are.
I would not buy this game at the set price of 30 bucks, nor would I buy it at the promotion price of around 20 bucks. If you have some cash to spare, this might not be so bad- but after 9 years in development, this is what the team pushed out? This? No thank you.

Awesomenauts is your perfect game for competitive platformer!
At the moment, there is 15 free characters to play and one in the DLC. 4 more are confirmed for the next year, in that same DLC. Each of them have a basic attack (gun, blade, bite, rocket, laser), a jump (double-jump, thruster, jet-pack, frog-jump) and two skills (rage, tongue grab, dynamite, goo, dash, bomb drop, suicide drones, trap, nuke, sniper-shot, cocoon, etc...) Each character is free and unlocked very soon in the game.
There is almost no common items. Each character have 6 item/upgrade for both skill, 6 for the basic attack and 6 stats (almost the same for each). You have 4 on each categorie available when you unlock the character. The missing ones unlock as you level-up (wich is almost one per game, out of a little bit more than 100 levels. They raise pretty fast, I got prestige 2 after 50 hours.) Before each game, you choose 3 items per categorie. This is your build, or your loadout, these will be the items available in the shop. The missing items wont undergrade you, you'll just be a little bit limited in build when you'll begin to play.
Each team of 3 awesomenauts is recruited to take controll of a specific area by destroying the minning core the the opposing team, defended by few layers of towers and periodic rounds of droids, while defending their own core. Each of the four maps (the fifth one is confirmed to come in the DLC) have a special features like a jungle boss, bonus drones, a giant worm or a invisibility buff.
A lot of peoples complain about the balance of some characters. My answer is: be quick, swift and dodge that lightning ball!
I love the gameplay of the game. They even added full controller integration few month ago (but I customized it because it wasn't convenient to play). If you like competition and platformers, go for it!

Unlike Clear Sky, CoP features all-new locations, which is one of its greatest strengths. It also features refined core mechanics, making it a true and worthy sequel to SoC in most ways.
My only real criticism when comparing this to the other games in the series is the story. I won't post spoilers, but I felt as if the eerie and unsettling mystery that you unravel in the first game utterly trumps the story in CoP, and while the game certainly looks and plays better than SoC, the story falls quite flat by comparison. Which, given that (like the other games in the series) CoP doesn't hold your hand and other than the narrative there's not much to assist your sense of purpose in this open, desolate environment, means that I felt like I had less direction in this game than in both previous games.
In saying that, it's a far more polished experience than Clear Sky, both in terms of the basic optimisation of the game and in terms of the game world. On top of that, the sound design is as fantastic as always (voice acting excepted), and the creatures are still ♥♥♥♥ing terrifying. So while I don't think this is the best game of the series, it is certainly my second favourite after SoC, and is absolutely a worthy sequel, and worth your time if you enjoyed any of the games before this one.

I've played for a little bit, so my review should only be considered by people who want a look into the first few moments rather than an in-depth look at the game. The game looks like it will be a battle between the 5 shows listed, and there may be some sort of supremacy, but I did not see that upon entering it. The "introduction" to the game looked like something from a mobile game and felt too simple to enjoy. The mechanics of the card game itself were disappointing; you place down a character card on your turn, nd on your next turn, you can place another character down or add a power-up card to a card currently on the field to make it stronger (Example: Bullock+Alcohol: Drunk Bullock). The two stats are attack and health, similar to games like Magic the Gathering, but there isn't any depth to attacking. The game auto-attacks for you, so as long as you outnumber your opponent, you will always win. The game also pushes for "research", allowing you to unlock new combinations of power-ups and characters. This seems like a decent mechanic to keep things balanced, but the use of microtransactions in order to feed corporate interests ruins the integrity. There are also challenges to tackle, but they are hardly interesting. Also, the lack of music from the shows themselves or any type of voice acting makes this game oddly quiet and boring. My opinion isn't based on hours of playing so you do not need to take my opinion to the highest regard, but from a first-look standpoint, it was not worth it. I would not recommend this game.

but all combined it's a decent game and i would recommend it if you like board games

Man, am I glad I stayed within the 2 hour mark so I could refund this game.
First off, I gotta say, I had been looking forward to the release of Overgrowth for a long time. For as far as I can remember, I found it about... Five, maybe six years ago, and really liked the look of it. Now, after pretty much forgetting about it, and seeing posts about it every now and then - it's finally out!
But, it's far from worth the price. The mechanics and combat of the game are truly fun for an hour or two, but you can get bored really quickly. (In my opinion.)  The story mode is... Eh. That's honestly the best word I have for it. It tries to throw weird mythology about the bunny-people, dog-people and their Gods and whatnot, but all I could find myself thinking during the 'cutscenes' (which are pretty much almost just stills with a weird angle) was: "What the ♥♥♥♥ is this?"
So, the first 10-20 minutes are pretty neat. Discovering the idea behind the game, and the mechanics of the combat system. This whole combat system immediately falls apart when you discover the bunny kick. You jump in the air, and launch both your bunny feet at the opponent. There's a chance this'll kill them in one go, and if it doesn't: Just do it again. No reason to use the other, now-clunky-looking combat options there are.
I would not buy this game at the set price of 30 bucks, nor would I buy it at the promotion price of around 20 bucks. If you have some cash to spare, this might not be so bad- but after 9 years in development, this is what the team pushed out? This? No thank you.

Pros: Good engine and art direction
Cons: Everything else.
Edit: Here's an actual review, in case you like reading rants.
Edit2: The developers of this game are awesome, many of the issues I had were addressed in the comments. I'm talking to you kavika, you're the bomb.
Combat and parkour feel really, really poor. Like the least of the concerns were the players themselves. As jack the ripper said, let's go one part at a time.
Combat feels unresponsive, frustrating and unsatisfying. getting ragdolled into oblivion is not fun (Not true, you can still block which prevents you from getting pummeled, it's pretty janky tho). Ragdolling an enemy and then him magically standing up to block feels cheap (It does, but you got the same thing going for you). I know the focus of the game are the fast and relentless battles, like hotline miami. The issue arises when the rules don't apply for the players and the npcs alike (Not true, it may feel like it, but that's not the case).
Then there's the lack of control over your own character. Armor in the game protects characters from weapons when hit in that zone, it's infuriating to hit and your character keeps going for the armor. I know I have to just go for hand to hand combat, forgetting about blades and such. But here's the thing, weapons sometimes do hit in the right spot. Which leads me to just go for it and pray for my character to do what I need.
And worst of all, the jump kick. After beating the game I don't have a single doubt in my mind that the game could be beaten with nothing but this overpowered move. And jumpkick being the only way to beat wolves it's just a joke, a "boss" enemy shouldn't be handled with a cheap move. I'm fine with a 1 hit ko for me, getting killed by trying to block, totally fine too. Here's an idea, let me actually fight the wolf with those two things going against me. Force me to dodge and counter, that's a challenging way to handle the fight. Forcing me to cheap a fight it's not the way to go. The removal of the jump kick would make everything better for the game (Still true on my end, but it helps unexperienced players get through, but I don't feel this is the way to handle this issue).
Oh, and I almost forgot, I checked the controls and there didn't seem to be a way to get rid of a weapon you're carrying, you need that, sometimes you want this or that weapon instead of the one you're carrying (My bad, there is a way, you have to crouch+look down+Q. I do believe there should be a better way to do it).
And now for the parkour. It's lackluster, there's not much going for it, and the little there is ends up ruined by the physics engine (the map itself). Falling from a safe height to a slightly rounded object makes you bounce off the plataform to your own doom (This will get patched with playtesting. Submitting examples of this to the developers at
will help them iron out this issue). Taking away the collisions of these objects would fix it in a pinch, or maybe adding a flat invisible surface on top, I don't know, those are just ideas I came up with by checking the editor.
Then there's the lack of control over the ledge grabbing, the character does it every single time without exception (There's a button to disable it, I'm just a dum dum). There's even less to do while jumping around, and it does get in the way of fights. I remember the alpha, where you had to hold right click in order to hold ledges, I wished I had that several times during my playthough, at least the option to disable the autoclimb (Yes, there is an option for that).
And finally, It was really hard to know where to go during climbing, the scrach marks worked well, but that was the only clue. I would have appreciated lights subtly poiting me in the right direction, or maybe some marks to help me look here or there (Once again, the developers take feedback and this will probably be adressed in the future).
All in all, the game lacks focus on what's supposed to make it fun and memorable. I really hope some of these issues get addressed in some way or another. I'm no game designed, I don't know what should be done about all of this. And this is just my oppinion, maybe I don't know what I'm talking about. With this in mind, I just didn't like what the game offered (But I'll probably change my mind once everything gets ironed out). My suggestion would be this one: Focus on the core mechanics and gameplay, make them the best they can be (And I don't have a doubt they'll get there. The developers are clearly pouring their hearts and souls into the game).
PS: I will absolutely check every major update in this game and change my review accordingly.

No nonsense ARPG. This is what all RPGs should strive to be. No melodrama. No sissy boy main characters. No overly dramatic crap. No desire to be a movie masquerading as a barely playable game. No "OMG look at these graphics" to distract you from how much crap the rest of the game is. Here it is the rest of the game that wows you.
The plot is simple and I like that. It doesn't take itself seriously. What this game does take seriously is the gameplay. The combat is fun. You can avoid enemies. No random encounters. No crap loot either. Everything has a purpose. You don't need to waste your time doing inventory management. No useless items. No useless spells. It is a finely balanced game.
After playing this game, I wonder, why the hell are all other games not like this.
Where other games randomly generate crap loot for you to search through. This game has a very very limited inventory, all useful during the time they are available to you. You don't need to manage inventory, wondering if you need to drop X to make room for Y.
Where other games randomly generate dungeons for you. This game gives you hand crafted dungeons that require some good platforming to get hidden treasure.
Where other games throw a million abilities and spells at you; half of which are useless against the majority of enemies, this game gives you 4 abilities. All of them useful.
This game is a masterpiece. You cannot take away anything from it without totally ruining. And if you were to add anything you would probably just ruin the precise balance of it.
If you enjoyed Dark Souls/Demon Souls. These games are a level of precision above those.

Unlike Clear Sky, CoP features all-new locations, which is one of its greatest strengths. It also features refined core mechanics, making it a true and worthy sequel to SoC in most ways.
My only real criticism when comparing this to the other games in the series is the story. I won't post spoilers, but I felt as if the eerie and unsettling mystery that you unravel in the first game utterly trumps the story in CoP, and while the game certainly looks and plays better than SoC, the story falls quite flat by comparison. Which, given that (like the other games in the series) CoP doesn't hold your hand and other than the narrative there's not much to assist your sense of purpose in this open, desolate environment, means that I felt like I had less direction in this game than in both previous games.
In saying that, it's a far more polished experience than Clear Sky, both in terms of the basic optimisation of the game and in terms of the game world. On top of that, the sound design is as fantastic as always (voice acting excepted), and the creatures are still ♥♥♥♥ing terrifying. So while I don't think this is the best game of the series, it is certainly my second favourite after SoC, and is absolutely a worthy sequel, and worth your time if you enjoyed any of the games before this one.

Not since Geometry Wars Retro Evolved have I been this addicted to a one-life score attack game. Instead of twin stick shooting, however, Devil Daggers looks back toward the jumpy, floaty FPSes that only '90s kids will remember. This game, however, manages to use a nostalgic genre to create something entirely fresh.
The art is spooky and cool. It's not the vague retro-ish style that I've come to expect from this sorta game. Sound design is impeccable and headphones are necessary because the aggghs and skull bounce noises are your best way to determine how close enemies/spawners are located.
It's also neat that the game lets me watch replays of players near my skill level.
Worth the five bucks so far. It's really refreshing to play a game without persistent upgrades/XP bars. I definitely prefer leaderboards for my replayability carrot-on-a-stick.

This is a dirt simple reflex arcade game -- watch the arrows, GTFO, repeat. In short order bigger badder arrows pop up, the screen shakes, and everything goes to hell. It's cheap simple mindless reflex action, it's mildly addicting, and to some people that is FUN. Once you get a bit of rhythm in it, you can go far. You've seen everything it has to show you in the first ten seconds, and that's just fine.
There are some serious polish problems -- like the fact that once it goes to hell you can't actually SEE what the next wave will be, or that once in a while you get hit with an undodgable combo, both of which should have been fixed before release -- but despite that, you can get lucky and quick and hit some achievements before you scream bloody murder at the TV, and isn't that all there is to live?
If you're splitting hairs over whether it's worth a buck or 50 cents or just 10 cents, just stop, your time is worth more than that. Either you'll like it enough to pay a pittance or you won't.
PS: Use Joy2Key if you want gamepad support.

Kill Team is an isometric shooter set in the Warhammer 40,000 universe, where Humanity's last hope rests upon the shoulders of  genetically engineered super soldiers defending against xenos and heretics  such as Orks, Tyranids, Chaos, and quite a lot more, too. Even if you are not familiar with the universe, you may have some fun with this game. However, if you're big into the lore/tabletop game, you should definitely consider a purchase.
In Kill Team, there are four classes, two melee, two ranged. Although they all practically play the same, it is interesting to experiment with different classes for each mission. Power-ups dot the landscape of each level, which enhance your character for short bursts of time.
The campaign is as you'd expect, run around and blow stuff up real good. Don't buy the game for the story, though. If you're expecting Dickens, you're in for a nasty surprise.
There is also a survival mode, where a relentless wave of enemies charge at you, and you ( and preferably a friend) must push them back. It's mindless fun, but an excellent distraction as you do whatever is in your power to top the leaderboard on your chosen map.
And finally the co-op. It may only be local, but it is great fun when you've got a friend to kill some time with.  Just remember you need at least one controller for co-operative play.
Overall, Kill Team is arcade fun only made better by a friend. If you're into Warhammer 40,000 it is definitely worth it.

With an unbelievably rich story and exciting battles, as well as allowing you to enjoy simple things like doing more personal quests, grabbing a drink in a tavern, reading books or taking some time to laugh at a hamster's "squeek" (you will meet Boo!), Baldur's Gate II has a unique balance that makes you get lost in its world without getting tired of playing at all (one of the original loading screen tips said "while your character doesn't need to eat, remember that you do").
You can actually feel empathy or antipathy for each one of the characters, their pasts and their personalities (this can even be one of the determining factors for who you're going to let into or to kick out of your party). Even common people may have interesting things to say, or just something to make you laugh. Quests may be only waiting for you to talk to someone in a corner.
The locations, though particularly "small" by today's standards, are many, well designed and diverse, which gives a real sense of travelling and adventure. The game also features a nice day-night cycle, and not only the sceneries change, but some monsters, animals and NPCs may appear only at night or during the daytime, as well as some quests. Oh, and party members get sleepy, so be sure to find an inn or another safe place to spend the night sometimes!
All these things, in conjunction with the game's substantial lore, help build up an incredibly immersive atmosphere. Have no doubt that a lot of characters and places will stay in your memory forever.
On top of that, as far as the Infinity Engine goes, every corner of Baldur's Gate II has impeccable art (besides those awful character miniatures in your inventory xD), from the menus to the spell effects. In my opinion, to this day, the environments are very beautiful and pleasing (this statement MAY be nostalgia talking, but reviews are kind of personal, so... :P). Also, an extremely nice and beautiful feature is the fact that every item has its own hand drawn sketch scroll to go along with its written description.
Dialogues go from the trivial "g'day, sir!" to the most philosophical questions about who you are in the story and what you'll do with your life and with the ones around you. The voice acting is impressive! Besides, you have the liberty to answer a "good day" with a sword in the throat, as well as a "will you save his life?" with a heroic action. The answer alternatives are really well thought and have true impact on the quests - it's not an illusional free choice, as we see in other RPGs. This allows you to fully and faithfully roleplay your character all the way, by the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons 2nd Edition's rules.
The freedom you possess to determine your party's reputation is absolutely amazing too. Your doings may have good or bad consequences not only to the story and to the world (for example, people in towns will react differently to your presence, depending on your reputation), but to the integrity of the party itself, as all members will have their own points of view about your actions (yes, you can end up losing party members because they don't agree with what you're doing or with the time you're taking to do something, or simply because they don't get along well with each other!).
The combat system can be turn-based or real-time (the choice is yours), and the variety of possible actions you can take is almost infinite, from a myriad of spells (coming from your character, from scrolls or from magical items) to a brutal two-handed sword reckless approach - or maybe by sneaking through and simply avoiding the situation, who knows? This allows you to get into the same battle by many different ways and create your own unique strategies, which means that, even if someone can't handle a certain combat at a certain time in the game, another person (or even you, later on) could end up sorting it out, making the combat skill-rewarding, intelligent and exciting.
You can follow the main storyline straight to the end or you can take your time to do side quests (lots of them). And, by the way, it's not uncommon to find yourself bumping into ultra powerful enemies when you're just not even a little bit prepared for the fight. You have to really work your way to strengthen your party before being ready for some of these quests. And the harder ones are trully rewarding. Well, the whole combat system is rewarding, as a matter of fact. So, if you face and kill a dragon, know that (besides feeling like a boss) the loot will be fantastic!
The soundtrack will stay with you forever (nostalgia hits me every time I open the menu), and all tracks fit every scenario like a glove, finishing the immersion with a flourish. The orchestration is a work of art. Just listen to the first trailer's opening! That's Viconia's Romance Theme.
If that isn't enough, well, rest assured no playthrough will be the same as the previous one! The replayability is infinite (specially with friends, if you have the chance!).

It seems all the reviews I've read for this game are all bad, but I actually quite enjoyed the game. It's not a bad port, but neither is it a good one. The best you can do with options is change your resolution (Contrary to popular belief, you /can/ use widescreen resolutions), enable V-sync and windows to fullscreen. Some people complained about the absence of mouse sensitivity options, but for me it was just right.
The game itself is essentially what I would say is Alien Swarm with Space Marines. You have two melee oriented classes, which are the Librarian and the Vanguard Veteran Marine. The VV Marine is more focused on killing essentially everything in sight with melee, whereas the Librarian is a good support class with an area of effect explosion special ability, which is good for taking large groups of enemies at once.
You also have two ranged oriented classes, which are the Techmarine and the Sternguard Veteran Marine. The Techmarine is good at holding positions due to his Tarantuala Turret deployable ability. (You'll have to hold a fair amount of places in the game, and the Tarantula Turret helps a lot with this.) The SV Marine is a ranged version of the VV Marine, with the focus fire ability which increases damage and fire rate to great effect when dealing with continued hordes of enemies.
The game also features power-ups, giving the game a more arcade-style feel to it. There are several ranged based power-ups, some of which increase the amount of bullets fired (Shooting two at once, etc.), or how fast the weapon is firing. There is also an invincibility power-up, which gives about 20 or so seconds if invulnerability to all attack. The health power-up automatically heals a portion of your health then begins auto-regenerating until the timer on the power-up runs out. There's only one melee oriented power-up, the Righteous Fury, which increases damage, and increases speed as well.
The storyline is rather basic, you crash into the Ork Kroozer, intent on destroying it before it reaches the Imperial Forge World it was headed for, by destroying generators and finding power cells. The narrarator is fairly monotone, but he has more expression in his voice than people who actually talk monotone. It's pretty short, about 3-4 hours when played casually,  I would bet around 1 or 2 for a speed run.

UPDATE: The developers of this game are great and are always releasing new versions with bug fixes or even free additional content. As such, they've added support for higher resolutions and as far as I can see (can't confirm this 100% yet, but it seems to be the case) the problems I faced below appear to be fixed. I can only recommend this game now. I'm starting to play it again and they've even added chat support in multiplayer. It has a nice community and it's fun to play online. I'd recommend using the casual mode for the single player campaign though. Any higher setting and the dice rolls are pre-determined I believe.
---
If you have a dual-screen setup, reconsider. If you don't, this is a fun game and you should buy it. However, it has serious crash problems for dual-screen (or more) players. Most of the problems lie in the fact that if you click a pixel off the game's full screen, it starts flickering like crazy and after about ten seconds, closes. This is because it doesn't have any kind of mouse cursor locking; in other words, the mouse cursor does not stay in the game window.
This problem can mostly (I've had crashes unrelated to this) be averted by using the smaller windowed mode. This is not an option for me, though. I use my computer for non-gaming purposes in my lounge, but when gaming I play in my cinema room on the sofa. The card descriptions are very low resolution, and since I don't have the option of bringing my head close to the screen, I can't read the text unless using full-screen mode. On that note, I use a 2.4GHz mouse to play the game since it doesn't support gamepads.
If you have a single monitor or you're happy with windowed mode, go for it. This is just a warning. It's a fun game (a bit masochistic when the AI cheats) and the reviews speak truth. The developers are also friendly and responsive. However, until they fix these problems, I don't think I can play this game. It ends up as a waste of time with crashes near the end of long games, etc.

I have played Baldur's Gate I & II since release way back on early 98 or something lol, i'm now 27 and still love this game with a passion and still develop for it, the graphics were unique but decent for their time and the mechanics were again unique and amazing, classic D&D style and i recommend this game to anyone who likes Medieval/Fantasy RP Games, Mobas, or general strategy games.
The game offers micro-management on a fair scale with a.i. capabilities that come in handy considering how difficult the game can be.
Now don't let the games graphics fool you, this game is fast paced when it comes to combat and you need to know what you're doing, this isn't your typical hack n slash or kick back cast and nuke, some enemies have immunities, some enemies have buffs or shields that could send your spells back at your party, they could be immune to the weapon they are using, 1 well-placed spell in this game can determine an entire battle remember that.
The updates for the game have been amazing and beemdog are still hard at work although a shared files system would be nice, GameSpyArcade in it's days had just down, download and use the files of the host of the server, very cool feature i think BG is missing these days but still a great game, networking does need some improving still.
The new chat system isn't all that, fairly small and if the group you are playing with is not very social it can be easy to lose track as it is hidden in the top right and to be honest i think having a chatbox above the console with no visible background or border would be much cleaner for the interface, or have it on the top of the window, just a suggestion.
The new character borders are nice, at first i thought it looked a bit too toon but over time i've got used to it and its become a nice change.
I think considering the patches that were released for ToB before EE to fix bugs that still exist in !EE! is madness, they were released with source codes so why were they not implemented in the EE release.
(Thank you beamdog for fixing the cutscene crash/disconnect bug) that was driving the community of this game mad for so long.

Possibly the most elegant FPS devised. Every element serves a purpose. From the scraping dry laughter to the red glint of gems. Devil Daggers is lo-fi poetry in motion.
The eponymous weapon combines doom 2's double barrel shotgun and Hyperblaster into a single devstating instrument of death. The movement system is straight out of Doom, Quake and Painkiller. Strafe running, strafe jumping, bunny hopping, it's all there. But don't let that speed go to your head. While you can accelerate faster, the enemy has higher top speeds. But their swarms cannot turn as fast. The demonic swarm also has exploitable behaviors, notably they will try to avoid your daggers. This allows you to carve paths of destruction, splitting the demonic hordes as you punch through. With sharp target prioritization, skillful shooting and the grace of a satanic, bullfighting ballerina you can eke out extra seconds of life as you climb the leaderboards. And speaking of the leaderboards, they have a wonderful demo feature. Every scoring run is recorded. Probably the best anti-cheat feature possible for a leaderboard, as well as a wealth of information and techniques.
Sure to fall flat with the cinematic shooter crowd, this is a love letter to ID's glory days, right down to the gritty textures of the low poly models and the palettes that color them. There is no story to tell or goal to achieve except the tale of your own mastery. A total emphasis on skill, no margin for error and absolutely zero downtime (even death holds no loading screens) is this game's hallmark. Devil Daggers demands nothing less than your total attention, and while razor sharp reflexes will serve you well, you need to have an even sharper grasp of position and target priority. Hell has many lessons to teach. It communicates so well there is no need for a HUD. All the information you require is in the motion of your enemy, the sound of bone scraping on stone, your own momentum as you strafe the edges of this platform suspended in the void.
Devil Daggers is a purposeful distillation of what made the greats so compelling.

Warframe is a sci-fi loot n shoot, with a bit of a twist. Rather than randomized drops with incremental upgrades, or something akin to Borderlands "millions of guns", characters you play as (frames) and gear you equip are primarily crafted items. You purchase a blueprint, farm materials to craft them, and then you build the weapon or frame. From here, rather than finding a slightly better version of the same gun, you find "mods" that you then equip to that frame or weapon that make it stronger. As you play the game, your weapons and frames will level up, increasing their mod capacity, raising their potential strength significantly.
The core gameplay loop reveals itself rather quickly. You run missions to get blueprints and crafting materials, allowing you to craft new weapons and frames, which you can then level up. You level them up by running missions, which gives you more crafting materials and blueprints, etc. It's simplistic, but the basics of moving around feel good, the tilesets are pretty varied, and most importantly, shooting feels great.
The free to play elements can look pretty crappy at first. One of the first things the game introduces you to is the market, and if you click around, it wont take long to find weapons can cost $5 each, and buying a new frame can be as much as $50, depending upon how new it is. But you never have to pay for power - for 95% of the the usable weapons and frames, you can buy blueprints with in-game currency or obtain them as drops, and farm the materials yourself. Access to new weapons and playable characters provide strong incentives to progress, as there's always the feeling of something exciting right around the corner.
The real "gotchas" are all tied up in cosmetics. Most of them cannot be earned, and are only available through the in-game store, using a currency you buy with real money. However, there is a player market, and you can sell items you've obtained in-game to other players for credits or platinum (the real money currency), which you can then spend on whatever you see fit. At the end of the day, the free to play model is far more ethical than it appears to be at a glance, as the entire game is playable without spending a dime. Those that are truly dedicated can play the market system to get platinum from other players, allowing access to cosmetics and blueprints you otherwise wouldn't be able to get.
As someone that has recently nearly completely exhausted all of the PvE content Destiny 2 has on offer, I find myself with a strong urge to return to Warframe - there's far more to do, and many more reasons to play. If you are evaluating both games, I think Warframe wins out here, especially for players that aren't particularly interested in any sort of PvP experience.

I need to preface this stating that if you see the game is on sale, or if they ever add online multiplayer, I'd reccomend picking it up.
I bought the game in 2014 and three years later at full release, it seems to be 90% identical. While they were constantly adding new content in that year, it seems the only thing they have added now is a very short campaign. The combat seems identical, the weapons are the same, and they haven't added any new mechanics or animals.
The combat system is unique and while it feels good at first there's no real 'strategy' to it. It seems extremely random as to wether or not an attack will land or not, sometimes when hitting an enemy that doesn't block, you won't do anything. Other times an enemy will block and your attack will one-shot them. While there are various weapons, your character has a jump attack that one shots almost every enemy so there's no point to using most of them and if you ever start losing a fight you can just jump kick and instantly win.
In addition, the game is extremely buggy. The first time I loaded the campaign the game crashed, and numerous other bugs have been found. If you pick up a spear, the game will not let you equip any other weapons, but you can pick up two other weapons first and then get a spear, and then its fine. You also cannot de-equip a spear or switch it out for your other weapons unless you throw it, and the game won't let you throw it until an enemy is in range.
In addition, the game has platforming sections. While I remember there being features like this in the EA version three years ago, it feels much worse now. It seems like every time you jump it's randomized wether or not you will actually climb a surface you hit, and the wallrunning tends to stop after a split second so I died about 30 times on a platforming stage just because halfway across a wall my character would suddenly switch to a fetal position and hurdle to his death.
In summary, while I am happy the game is finally considered 'done' and out of early access, it certainly doesn't feel done. It feels like the exact same game I played three years ago but they added dialouge in between the fights. The story consists of 'Oh look a bunch of enemies, let's get reinforcements' 'No I am a cool guy I can kill all of them myself' over and over to the point were I wonder why the allied characters even have to suggest getting backup. The combat system, while very dynamic and fun at first, is in fact very basic and efficiency is random at best.
I would reccomend if the game was cheaper, or if there was perhaps online multiplayer to make use of the combat system, but as it stands I don't think the game is actually finished and as it stands now if I was to buy the game as it is I wouldn't spend over 10 dollars.

Spikit is described as a bullet hell game where the player must dodge a constant bombardment of spikes and obstacles in an ever-changing 2D landscape. Spikit is a tricky game to classify; while it doesn’t fulfill the traditional bullet hell criteria, it’s not much of a rhythm game either, as the obstacles do not fully interact with the beat of the music. With that being said, Spikit is a fairly primitive form of the genre with only one beat sequence throughout the game and  no method(s) of introducing your own [music] to the mix.
You start the game with one life and a small box as your environment. The music begins and spikes [hence the name] began shooting out from various sides of your screen. Being struck by any one object will cause your score to reset to “0” and automatically starting you out at the beginning again.
During the course of the game, smaller square blocks will randomly appear, which can be collected and used to purchase minor cosmetic changes such as changing your square’s “face” or the color scheme of your of the overall game screen. There’s not much use to them other than personal appeal, though I did find the dark purple color to be easier on the eyes and kept obstacles from bleeding together after longer playing sessions.
There is no end game to Spikit, nor does it really create any purpose aside from besting your own personal skill or the global leaderboard for those that are interested. Due to the game’s overall lack of popularity, it’s not entirely difficult to crest the top of the leaderboards with a bit of practice. At the time of this writing, I was within the top 30 players; a feat that sounds more impressive that it really is though. Those looking for a challenge might find it momentarily engrossing, but there’s not enough substance to keep you hooked.


Overall, Spikit could have been much more than what it turned out to be. It’s a saturated market that requires innovation in order to stand out, but Spikit doesn’t quite deliver anything new or interesting. While I can’t give a negative review for Spikit, it doesn’t deserve a positive one either; Spikit sits comfortably in the middle of mediocrity.

This is simply one of the greatest RPGs of all time. the characters are absolutely fantastic in every way, from comical to depressing. The storylines run the gauntlet from short and surprising to sweeping epics of betrayal. The world is so much deeper and richer than almost anything else that has been released since. You will find yourself sent on small errand quests that uncover plot twist after plot twist and now you're fighting a subterranean old god under the sewers. You will be infiltrating thieves guilds and trudging through the underdark.
It is also one of the least linear gaming experiences you will ever have. At times you're only given long term goals like "you need to pay X amount to gain the help of Y group, here you are in this city, go find a way to make tons of money"
Yes, the rule set can be a little daunting in the beginning as it is based on old 2nd edition d&d, which is widely known to be highly unintuitive and even, at times, contradictory. Fortunately it really only takes a few minutes to learn the basics in the form of, lower armor class is harder to hit, higher saving throws helps you avoid things, do more damage to kill things faster.
Honestly just give it a chance, explore a little bit and you're almost guaranteed to be hooked.

I plan on playing Fallen Earth for a while to see how it goes, and as such, this review will see updates from time to time when I see big changes.
*REVIEW*
As a player starting off in Fallen Earth, you're greeted by your Character Creation Screen. Everyone seems to have the same kind of build, with height being the main difference. Good choices for customisation and whatnot, but nothing ground breaking.
The Tutorial is straightforward and simple. There is no "Hand-Holding" as such in it, just the basics of gameplay and combat. Here, you are introduced into what seems to be an OK story.
Why is the story OK? Well, it's corny ("You are special" is what you're told, but yet your just an ordinary guy by the looks of it) and a bit narrative. You don't need a Ph.D to figure out the story from what every NPC tells you, who seem to be devoid of opinions and just state facts.
Controls-wise, it seems ok. WASD, 1-0, Shift+1-0 etc. Pretty standerd stuff, but that's not a bad thing. The controls are quite nice to play with, and I haven't decided to re-bind any keys which is a boon.
Combat is simple enough from what I have seen, but has possabilities in the perks and skills you unlock. IMO, Ranged Weaponry seem to have the dominancy in this game. The rifle you find in the Tutorial is a staple weapon and really easy to use.
The voice actors seem to be good in this game, and they add an air of professionalism to the game.
*Verdict*
All in all, a solid game that looks good from the get-go. The €0/$0/£0 price tag is nice, so I would recommend everyone try this game for at least 30 minutes, just to see how things pan out.
