I cna't really stand MOBA style games. I've tried League, I've tried DOTA, and I just can't get into them. Awesomenauts, though...that's different.
Firstly, let's talk graphics. I frequently describe this game as being similar to playing an 80's cartoon. It's over the top, colorful, and more than a littly crazy. Characters range from big robots to small demon children, rapper frogs and mafia fish, french chameleons and ice-cream paladins. Locations range from space stations to alien forests. And unlike the majority of other MOBA-style games, which rest firmly i the fantasy genre, Awesomenauts is unashamedly sci-fi.
The gameplay? It's a 2D action sidescroller type of deal, meshed fairly well with classic MOBA gamestyle. If you have the expansion, you can creat custom games, changing how the game flows, turning it into a deathmatch, even changing characters randomly on death, giving a wide variety of things to play.
The sound in this game. Fantastic. Each charater has a unique character theme, and that theme has a pumped-up version that plays in-game while on a killing spree. Every song is great. Every. One. The characters all have great voice acting, too. It's funny, sounds great, and fits the characters well.
The one thing that needs work is matchmaking. I'd say that I have a negative matchmaking experience 25% of the time. Of course, these experiences are typically more memorable than the ones that go well. Sometimes you'll be matched with a couple of people who just started, who don't exactly know what they're doing, and you'll be facing a team of 3 friends who know EXACTLY what they're doing. Even then, though, the majority of the time, it's cool. The community in this game is damn near always positive and friendly, in the game to have a good time. There's some friendly trash talk, yes, but typically people are more than willing to give tips to someone who is struggling.
The DLC might be considered lackluster, for the most part. The majority of it is character or announcer skins, yes. The soundtrack is worth far more than it costs, for sure, and i would recommend it heavily. The expansion, Starstorm, adds a bundle of 5 new characters, which are all just as amazing as the rest of them, and is very much worth the cash. The announcer skins are amusing, and if you want a voice other than the default announcer, they're pretty nice. If you play one character a lot, and you like the look of a skin, go for it. Other than that, there's not a ton of purpose to them.
Overall? This is a MOBA you can play with your siblings, SO, parents(?), and have them still have a good time. It gets regular updates, sounds and looks great. 9.5/10, if you want a number from me.

Basically every aspect of this game feels like BETA-quality. The worst offenders are surely the camera and checkpoint system. It's so easy to fall or get killed without clearly seeing what is happening only to be forced back to the beginning or halfway point of a level. I'd wager than half my time spent playing was traversing areas I'd already cleared because I kept falling at some bizarre jump point miles away from the checkpoint.
Also, the "weapon upgrades" in this game are very strange. There's no way to switch between them without physically picking them up from the stage-select world. Also, by the time you unlock 2 of the 4 unlockables, the game is basically over. There's also no nuance in that there's no reason you'd ever want to use an ability other than the most recently unlocked.
Hard to believe I just complained about nuance in a game called Woodle Tree Adventures, but it is what it is. It's just poor design.
Speaking of, this makes me wonder: who is this game made for? The visual style (perhaps the best part of the game) seems to suggest children. And yet, there's no way small kids would be able to play through some of these stunningly awkward jumps with a♥♥♥♥♥♥eyed camera angle.
Or at least...they shouldn't be made to be. And niether should you.

I can tell you about the difference between it and ETS2. Each game has it's own charm.
-ATS is newer. Better graphics.
-ETS2 has more trucks. Way more and slightly more upgrades. ATS only has like 4. 2 brands and 2 types of truck for each.
-ETS2 has a much bigger world. ATS is still young so getting max Distance perk cannot even be applied as you only go between 3 states. ETS2 is full Europe now. Including GB where you should remember to drive on the left side of the road. ;)
-ATS is smaller because it actually has all the world realistically planned. Roads barely ever repeat. In ETS2 you can think "hey, I've been here before. Or not?" or "one more clover highway spread... sigh..." while in ATS it's always something new wherever you go. And you feel the warmth when you come back to familiar places.
-ATS has long straight highways, relaxing and enjoyable. Not too boring, not too extreme. ETS2 has very sharp and plentiful turns. Whatever you prefer. Personally I love ATS. You still get enough turning off the highway, in the city or on narrow roads.
-ATS has amazing scenery here and there. Makes you wanna go everywhere. ETS2 is repetitive. The price for being that huge.
-ATS has view zoom!!! =D To look out for police. =P
-ATS has very strict speed limits. I think it can be turned off but... Do I really want to do that? I left it on. Speed limits are actually pretty sane. You may crash if you break it. ATS fines for speed violation are much higher. And you're watched by police mostly, less often by cameras. So you a) have to look around to see if there's police nearby, b) you have to watch your speed and current limit, c) you can decide if you want to keep your money or pay a lot for a questionable right to break the laws. Wanna be a rebel? Go ahead. =D  Overall it adds to the gameplay very well. Surprisingly well. I hated speed limits in ETS2, they were stupid and cheaply fined and meh.
-ATS offers more options for parking. More exp for difficult position, less for fast simple one, none for just ditching the trailer at arrival. Small bit but also adds to the game score.
-ATS has slightly better traffic AI. In general it's just refined and polished more.
So ATS has a great potential and can one day beat ETS2 in all aspects. For now I can enjoy both, depending on my mood. But, I must admit, I love ATS more. It's an upgrade, after all. ^__^

I really tried to get into this game, given the 10/10 scores and consistent positive feedback. The promises are all there. Multiple branching pathways, full voice acting, and battle mechanics. The problem is, the game is simply not fun. On normal difficulty level, the game simply does not provide you with the means to empower your characters and overcome main questlines without resorting to spamming/exploiting game mechanics like pickpocketing and stealth. Virtually everyone I've heard playing this game has had to resort to the same strategy in act 1 and that is not good role playing mechanics if the level threshold has been set so high that the player cannot explore and act freely.
I get that this is not a game for casuals but at least developors like Bioware give players more content and choices through which to grow characters and have a fighting chance against higher tiered enemies.
The inventory system is beyond archaic, I've literally spent one third of this game having to sift through menus and bags. It's 2017, is it too much to ask for shared inventory and filter options?
And lastly the writing...it's okay, but again, for game getting all of these coveted perfect scores, I was expecting characters and story which were a bit less tropish.
I'm not saying Origina Sin 2 is a terrible game and as I stated before, you do get all of the features and promises as stated on the box which is rare in games these days. The problem is the game just turns in to a slog where you are constantly quick loading because of high level thresholds for quests in which you have NO means whatsoever to grind a little bit or do side quests to accomate for the difficulty.
It's very clear that a lot of work and care went into making this game, but ultimately it just isn't fun and relies too much on it's gimmicky battle systems.

Picture this example: you're working on a puzzle for, say, 20-30 minutes now. The "solution" requires stacking containers and crates, and you're struggling against the (rather bad) physics engine but overall making progress. And then due to some random not-your-fault physics bug, a key element of the puzzle just flies off of the building and is not recoverable. You must suicide your Mr. B and start over, effectively forfeiting these 20+ minutes of work. How would you react?
Because if this would make you angry (and honestly it should) then stay well away from this game. This kind of thing happened to me, and more than once. But the strange thing is, I found the game amusing enough that I managed to plough through all of this and actually enjoy it. But that's just me: I enjoy quirky (bad) games.
And there is a lot of "quirkiness" here indeed. The graphics are plain terrible, even by my (lax) standards. The crazy physics simulation is your worst enemy. The music, while decent, is some sort of open source thing because I am 99% confident I heard it in another Unity game recently. Controls seem kinda floaty yet are suprisingly precise if you have the patience for them. The level design is... pretty good sometimes; it has its moments. I'd recommend getting this only at a significant discount. There is some weird amusement to be had here but extracting it is not for the faint of heart.

text:
I bought this game 2010, when it was basically a sandbox engine where you could fight with rabbits. Over time they added weapons and cool features. But now, after a total of 9 years in developement, the full game is just... nothing.
The "story" mode, if you can call that is maybe 2 hours long, and half of the stages are mainly about fighthing, the other half is more platforming. The fighthing stages are great, the highlight of the game, but they are basically the same, just with different coating. The platforming stages are absolutely horrible, the camera is way too zoomed in for any kind of platforming, the grabbing mechanic is almost broken, it will automatically grab on random things, like the side of a rock in a cave, but sometimes wont grab onto an actual ledge. This becomes incredibly obvious on the last stage, where you're forced to do a climb, but you can't see well. It's incredibly frustrating.
In those 9 years, the Wolfire team made an incredibly impressive engine with amazing features, but somewhere along the line, durning these 9 years, they forgot how to make a game. Even with the added remake of Lugaru, this is still bad. This is not worth the full price (27.99 EUR), or the discounted -30% price. Basically this is feature crawl: the game. I had more fun when this was in beta and all you had was a sandbox, you could make your own fights and that was fun for an alpha version of a game, but this is absolutely ridicilous. Don't let my playtime fool you, I've played this a lot when this game wasn't even on steam. The graphics are pretty, but sometimes they look buggy, you see the underside of some models that you're not supposed to see, and if you did buy this years before and played around with the level editor, you can see how many obvious mistakes there are in the stages. Some of the promised features are also missing, or not implemented in the main campagin, like the aztec weapons (but I think the rats use the aztec dagger?), the scabbards, that weird spear-like rabbit catcher weapon, etc.
I'm incredibly dissapointed, the only reason why I'm not asking for a refund, is because durning the 7 years I had this game, I easily played enough to warrant the then paid 20 euro price.
Buy this game if it goes on sale for like 5-10 EUR, or just buy Reciever on it's own. Maybe if they add more content, like an actual multiplayer, instead of that weird screenlocked mess, or a good campaing. If you do buy this, you'll probably have the most fun messing around with the level editor, creating your own scenarios, or if you mess around with mods.

Let's preface this review: It's not that I dislike this game or the idea behind it, but Steam doesn't have a "neutral" setting for reviews. I'm glad I backed it when I did, but you can get through both included campaigns in 2 hours, and that's just not worth the asking price of 28€.
If you're one to mess around with the game engine itself, play around with the powerful creation tools contained within, then this might be absolutely justified, but if you're just the average gamer, here to consume a quality game, you'll get it, but it's a very short and repetetive one.
I bought this 8 years ago from the Wolfire page, it was an interesting one-man engine developement project that was very interesting to follow. But the human attention span isn't really suited to keep up with something that goes on for this long.
What you're buying isn't so much a game as it is an engine with an editor, while the story of a bloodthristy medieval rambo-rabbit is quite cute, there isn't much of it, and it serves mostly as a template.
So if you're fine depending on user-generated content, or have an interest in creating mods and storylines yourself, then this might be absolutely worth your money.
The engine is quite impressive, it was visually absolutely stunning almost a decade ago, and it has aged quite gracefully.
But the main meat is in the animation system, the combat can be quite thrilling and looks spectacular, it can be over very quickly and in unpredictable ways, there's no HUD which makes the experience particulary immersive and a pleasure to look at.
To sum it all up...
The good:
+ Looks decent
+ Great combat
+ Cute short story
+ Powerful editor
The bad:
- Not a lot of content
- Very reliant on UGC.
- Price to value ratio is not in favor of the average gamer.
I got the game through a key so my "negative" review won't affect the overall score, but it's important to me that you know what you're getting for your money and to me it's just not worth it at the current price-point.

I hate Devil Daggers but I love Devil Daggers and unless you don't like brutally hard games that are quick to play and reward lots of practice, you should probably get it.
The concept is simple. You're thrown into a small arena where you will face off against an ever-increasing endless barrage of Hellspawn creatures and need to survive for as long as you can. The only scoring metric is time and you're fighting for top placement on the leaderboards. Sessions are usually very quick (most people will be lucky to survive a minute) and things start hard and only get harder fast. You have unlimited ammo and can fire either a continuous barrage or if you tap your mouse button, blasts similar to a shotgun. There are only a handful of upgrades available, some of which are obtained by collecting red gems the enemies drop and others that you just get automatically for surviving certain amounts of time. That's basically it.
The leaderboards also allow you to view anyone's run. This is a great feature that will not only keep people honest and point out cheaters but is also a great teaching tool, allowing you to glean strategies and ideas for how to improve your own runs. Devil Daggers is all about iterative progress so be prepared to die a lot and to need to play hundreds of times to get good.
Devil Daggers runs on a custom engine and purposefully uses a graphical style similar to old DOS first person shooters like DOOM, Duke Nukem 3D and other Build Engine games. It won't be everyone's cup of tea but as a huge fan of those games, I thought it was a really cool throwback.
This game is cheap, dead simple to understand but brutally hard to master. You'll hate it and love it at the same time. I highly recommend it.

Arguably the greatest game in the Ys series.
Ys takes nearly all the extraneous elements of RPGs and tosses them all out in favour of a super streamlined action battle system with some of the greatest bosses gaming has ever seen. I'm not exagerating here, Ys really does have some of gaming's greatest bosses.
There were 3 ys games to use this style of engine. The ark of Napishtim (which was the first), The oath in Felghana and finally Origins.
Felghana has the greatest soundtrack of them all and arguably the second strongest soundtrack in the entire series (In a series famous for it's soundtracks (look for a psp or psvita for Ys 7 if you want the best soundtrack)).
Felghana, on it's hardest difficulty has some spectacular bosses. However the game doesn't put it's best foot forward at the start. Initial bosses are pretty simple and hardly inspiring, which is unfortunate because the later bosses are absolutely spectacular. Thematically unique bosses all with their own interesting quirks and unique mechanics make each big baddy feel wholly unique and incredibly satisfying to down.
In fact Felghana and Origins are spectacular examples of good boss design (with a few very obnoxious exceptions).
There's also a bit of exploration and secret discovering involved in Ys, and because a number of your abilities give both combat and traversal options there is some fun platforming to be performed in the game.
So this all sounds super positive, are there any negatives then? Actually yeah, quite a few.
This game isn't pretty, I mean let's be fair it's old (2005) but that's gonna be a turn off for some people.
Then there's the plot, Ys' localization is about as good as it can get (Xseed is really good at that) but this isn't a plot that's likely to do anything for you, and not much time is spent on either it or its characters.
The game is also very grind heavy, especially on it's higher difficulties. Levels and weapon upgrades in Ys make a huge difference, to the point where a single level can make your attacks do almost twice the damage and can turn some boss fights from cruel jokes into fun encounters. but there are humungous experience penalties once you start over levelling, and even then you're going to have to farm normal mooks just to avoid being underlevelled, which may have been alright except for the game's final weakness, fights that aren't bosses.
Ys's combat is simple, but the way it blends with each bosses unique mechanics make it incredibly satisfying. This doesn't occur with normal enemies though, which means for many, normal combat in Ys isn't very satisfying, which is unfortunate because you'll need to do a fair amount of farming basic enemies to be able to afford upgrades and avoid
being underleveled.
So to sum up:
+ Awesome soundtrack
+ Awesome bosses after the first couple of dungeons
- Not very pretty
- Grindy on higher diffculties
- Fighting basic enemies isn't that fun
- Playing on easier difficulties wont let you appreciate it's great bosses properly
Ys will appeal extremely strongly to a certain crowd, and that crowd absolutely SHOULD play it, because it's one of the best examples of it's genre. But most other people will likely find the game to be more trouble than it's worth.

Devil Daggers, to put it bluntly, is a masterwork. An elegantly designed arcade style arena FPS that not only is an example of a simple idea done well, but its posterchild. From the introductory screen onward, the bleak Gothic atmosphere takes hold, clearly worshiping at the altar of Quake, with stark colors and industrial edged background music. Starting the game, the goal is simple: navigate and combat a horde of demons as they spawn into the arena. The longer you survive, the higher your score, and the higher your place on the leaderboards. One hit however, and it's all over. The game is punishingly difficult, but not unfair. It provides you with a plethora of tools to deal with the onslaught. You have incredible fluidity of movement, that allows you to bunnyhop and dodge and weave your way through enemies. You have a single weapon, the daggers, which are actual projectiles (as opposed to hitscan) with two alternate fire modes, a spraying rapid fire which must be well timed and lead, and a shotgun like blast, that requires twitch accuracy for maximum effect. You can use that blast to catapult yourself into the air, a "rocket jump"-esque maneuver. These abilities not only skyrocket the skill ceiling, but the excellent pace of the game allows you to learn without becoming comfortable, pushing your ability constantly. Once in motion, this is where the visual and sound design shine brightest, both from a mechanical and artistic standpoint. Artistically, the game is one of the most cohesive and focused visions I've seen in games recently. The monster design is impeccable, managing to be both complicated and clear, grotesque and horrifying, and how everything is rendered evokes the days of the old school shooter. On top of that, the 3D sound allows for complete immersion, with each monster giving off it's own call until the arena is crescnedoed into an orchestra of foul clicks, jittering, and crys. Mechanically, these same things give the player all the information they need to move about the arena: monster silhouettes are easily distinguishable, and the host of audio cues not only tell you where the monsters are, but what kind of monster it is lurking outside your vision. But even with all that, the game will kill you. Thankfully it never steps into frustrating territory. The game allows to you instantly restart a run at any time, placing you back at the beginning in less than a second. This ease of access prevents frustration to set in between attempts, and greatly increases the draw of an already addictive formula. And to top it all off with a nice little bow, the leaderboards feature a replay system. Not only will you be able to watch back your own high score, to either show off, or to see how you did it, but anyone on the visible leaderboard will have a replay available of the run that put them there in the first place, enabling you to study those ahead of you simply by clicking an icon. It's a brilliant package, but understandably not for everyone. The steep difficulty paired with the admittedly low amount of content will be enough to put some off, and that is understandable, but at five dollars it's difficult to argue against its value. Wholeheartedly recommended.
(Steam Awards 2 Edit: 30 hours later, still a masterpiece).

Ys games are all action RPGs where you control one character (usually Adol, though Origins has no Adol and I think Seven has multiple character options?) against the world in a story-moderate environment. (moderate compared to Falcom's other RPG series, Legend of Heroes) Grinding is generally expected to some extent, but that'll only ease the pain so far -- especially as you get to the end bosses. They're also known for their amazing rock/metal soundtracks.
As for this particular Ys game...one word: Brutal.
I've played Origin, I & II, and VI on Steam and this one still annihilates me...on NORMAL. What separates most of the difficulties is simply damage caused by enemies and enemy health, and the enemy patterns can be difficult to make out after your first 10 or so attempts at a particular boss. Just a fair warning -- you need to be in the zone while playing to stand a chance...or you just need to be better than this reviewer.
Aside from that, it's a loose remake of Ys III, the one "platformer" of the series and as such, this one has a lot of platforming elements. Thanks to the fixed camera, though, the 3d platforming is pretty simple and straightforward.
One disappointment worth noting: Some PSP features like New Game+ (which itself was very minor) and refining gear up to level 9 are gone from this port. Seems strange, especially since the achievements beg "replay", but it's not anywhere near a deal breaker.

I seriously tried to get immersed in this world...I really did.  I played Shadow of Chernobyl many years ago and found it enjoyable with the immersive music and semi difficult gameplay.  Call of Prypiat (COP) is almost the exact opposite.  From the get go you are thrown into the extremely small map in search of your 5 objectives, crashed helicopters.  The music is there, the scariness is there...but the game just lacks something that its predecessors had.  I can't quite place it, but the game feels rushed.  I know its european but they can make some really great games.  First off, you get way too much ammo initially.  The game is fairly easy on the standard difficulty however, you will die from cheap deaths over and over and over forcing you to quick save like every 5 minutes lest you die and have to load something from an hour ago.  For this game to be enjoyable graphically these days, you pretty much have to download a 3 year old graphic mod that improves lighting and shadows while also improving a few textures here and there.
Edits:  A few things I forgot to mention that are really tedious:
Your character gets exhausted after 10 seconds of running!  This leaves you being very slow and open to attack...very annoying.
And finally the engine crashes every so often leaving you reloading a previous save. So again, save often. At least every 5 minutes.
For me, I think it's just the size of the map initially that put me off.  Its just a giant circle with your objectives on the outer sides and keeping the quest hub in the very center.  It's pretty stock gameplay design if you ask me and pulls from the immersion.  There are Stalker fan boys on here that have sunk hundreds of hours into this game and the series in a whole and will probably scoff at this review.  I just couldnt get into it.   For 20 bucks I'd say this is definately NOT worth a buy.  Wait for it to go on sale which it does quite often and get it for half off.  Today, there are just better shooters out there like the Metro series which has far superior graphics.  Obviously...the game is 5 years old so the graphics arent going to be stellar.  IMO to enjoy this, download the misery mod to make the game really hard and immersive.
I think also, if there was a skill system in place it would make me feel like i'm progressing. Instead I just get better weapons if I search in caves and such.  Eventually, from what i've read, people get so powerful from farming resources for cash that they have all the best loot in the game and are pretty untouchable...even with the misery mod.  This probably takes time but whats the point after that?  I'd rather have a skill system in place or at least attributes that improve the more I run, fight etc.
Yeah, as far as I can tell, this is Dota 2d for the kids ... people keep killing me :'(

I played Fallen Earth pretty extensively from their site before it moved from Steam.
I downloaded this game to my steam library to write this small review.
The game has a ton of content. Lots of quests and lots of items.
You get a free horse. But since there are so many horses, you have to name it Horse34532 because literally every name has been registered.
The map is big. And there really are a lot of places to go and to see.
There's lots of guns and things to kill and to see.
It was an amazing game when it came out in 2009.
.... But now.. In 2015? With the standard being set so high?
The player base is all but dead. Mostly Non-English speaking people play this game. Even in the American servers I'd say one in five people over the course of a week spoke English. And almost NO ONE replies to you because they're too busy running around doing repetitive MMO tasks.
Outside of the newbie area the game is dead. There's literally no one. I maybe ran into one person a day wandering the wastelands.
The quest system is incredibly broken. And the NPCs are terrible.
The Crafting system is awkward, confusing, and feels ancient.
The UI feels ancient.
The game is not properly optimized. And even with a good rig it won't run well. Even at 80 fps it just doesn't feel "smooth."
The combat feels delayed, even on good Internet, and the gunplay is stale and clunky.
The AI is terrible. Even six years later after the game's had plenty of time to update.
So why did I recommend this game? Several reasons.
It's still a lot of fun to explore the post apocalyptic world, and there are still a lot of cool places to go see. And it still feels detailed and immersive.
There aren't that many post-apoc games right now.

Honestly, I'll say the things I find good, and the rest will be both opinion and (I think) Fact of what I think it really needs to do. I have played it enough to know enough about what I'm talking about.
1)Good controls, Easy menu, simple interfaces, reasonable choices in the game shop, free to play.
Now, I realise it was only realised a month ago, but it really does have some things which it seriously should have sorted out before hand.
2)Uneven games - I was playing a game where there where 27 on my side, and 48 on theirs! And they got more people as time passed, meaning less for our side! This really should have been sorted before hand. Making sure there are even number of players is essential.
Uneven games 2 - I was playing on a game which said "Average rank, 2.2" Now when I played on said map, I was being kill by players who where 1 shotting me no problem, if not two shots. That is crazy! If I join a game with average ranking of 2.2 when I've just started, I should be able to have a chance! This also needs to be sorted out quickly. As robocraft is the main comparison, it should sort it like that, people playing in their respective ranks like robocraft does tiers.
I also noticed that when I killed a total of about 14-16 people across 4 games, I only got 4 G! This was not only crazy in my mind, but also very unsatisfying (personal opinion). I would recommend at least multiplying the numbers by ten. Including the cost in store to level all that out.
Speaking of the store - I really didn't like how I could get a much better gun for 6G, and a worse gun for 10G. Why? That's ridiculous, and needs to be sorted out.
I also dislike the idea of having to pay to have more that 6 things in my inventory in a "Free to Play" Game... Microtransactions are one thing, but that's basically pay to win in my book.
OVERALL! I would recommend this game, but only if you don't mind the downsides I mentioned, and are patient enough to wait for their updates in the future. I will play it in a few months and write a new review. But until then. Here.

The Adventures of Mr. Bobley is great as it mostly an adventure through many building sites using the environment to get from one site to another. You use many engines such as cars, fork lift, crane and many others. You can interact with many part of the environment. So it's mostly a puzzle platforming game with some simulation features. Bobley have a special ability, he can't be hurt if he jumps and make himself as a boulder before landing. One of the great feature of this game are some additional camera in some part of the game that let you see what's going on around you. Also there is some pretty fun levels such as a maze, a football match played alone, a frogger like game (the game where you help a frog to cross the traffic jam) and many others.

I pre-ordered the game about 5 years ago now to get the alpha and I enjoyed it a lot. I stopped playing for a couple years because there wasn't much to do and decided to wait until it was released.
Well the release day has come and I have no idea what changes they have made. To be fair, I only played for about 30-45 of v1.0 but I am already bored with it. The story is meh and very short from what I've heard. There aren't any big changes in graphics or gameplay from what I can tell. I don't know what the developers did when they worked on this game for almost a decade, but it doesn't feel any different to from what it did 5 years ago. I'll get around to playing more later, but $30 just seems like too much.
Edit: I've played the game more but this time I did the Overgrowth story instead of the Lugaru story. The Overgrowth story is way better. I still cannot recommend this game, however. There isn't much content (9 years in development) and runs poorly. In most areas of the game, it runs fine. But if there is a lot of grass, frames will drop. The graphics aren't even amazing. Don't get me wrong, the game is pretty still, but not by 2017 standards. Also, the game has crashed multiple times on me.
If you are just discovering the game, it is worth picking it up on sale. $30 is too much for what it offers. The game can still be fun and each level has good design and the settings are cool. Story is very "meh" but you can't really expect much from a game about fighting rabbits. But if you were following this game for a long time and were super excited for it, I can't recommend it. If I remember correctly, the graphics and gameplay still look and feel exactly the same as it did 5 years ago.
Sidenote: it's 2017, why is it so frustrating to pick up weapons in a videogame? You can't drop a weapon in your hand unless theres a close by enemy to throw it at. If you're holding a stick but want to pick up the spear so you can stealth kill the enemy, you're screwed.

A simple reflex/response tie based mini-game game, Ninja Reflexes fails to interest beyond simple attemps to improve one's score.  They slowly introduce you to variations on 6 mini games, unlocking them as you achieve new "belts."  At each level, you must complete the same minigames you did on the previous belt with slight increases in difficulty along with a new challenge modification for that level.
If this is some kind of brain/reflex training game, then I can see some merit, but as just a game to play an have fun, it fails in that regard.  It's too simply, too repetitive and the controls never quite feel right for a few of the games. Targeting and then throwing ninja stars just doesn't work with a mouse.
I can't really recommend this game, even under $1.

I always say Warframe is the best example of a game as a service. It has been constantly updating and evolving over the last 4 plus years. If you picked the game up in 2013 and came back today your head would spin with all the changes. Big changes to core gameplay elements like the movement or damage systems. Just for the simple fact that it needed to be changed to enhance the player experience. An update happens at least once a week even if its just for bugs that pop up. Every few months there is a new prime frame, new frame, several new weapons, and cosmetics. Not to mention the big updates like story quests or overhauls to old systems/designs.
The free-to-play model works so well because the premium currency (Platinum) can be traded among players. Which means you can get a lot done in the game before you spend a single dollar. Farm Prime parts, trade to other players for platinum, and buy what you want from the market. Which is usually just cosmetics, weapon/frame slots, etc. The only thing that is stricly cash is the user created cosmetics, Tennogen. Part of the reason for that is because some of the purchase goes back to the artist.
Although the game can be a grindfest most of the time it's a satisfying grind. Mainly because the controls are tight, the action is fast paced, adn the variety of Warframes always spices things up. One day you could play Excalibur and wreck enemies with blinding light and energy swords. And the next you could run around all stealthed as Loki or Ivara. You don't have to juggle multiple character accounts to play with the 34 characters and hundreds of weapons.
For the low price of free you might as well try it out.

The campaign is not engaging, it lacks pacing and worldbuilding. The transition between the levels doesn't even exist and the dialogs are forgettable as well as the characters u will meet. Pretty quick u get a feeling of playing demobuilds for the purpose of showcasing the engine graphics, which are indeed not bad created and realized - Exept the UI which is just uninspired, lame and not appealing to the eye... no motion graphics at all. Sadly the gameplay gets quickly very old too and soon u notice that it is not fully fleshed out. For example u could think that using weapons while fighting multiple enemies is a big gamechanger but it is not because there is no crowdcontrol at all. The weapons just make more damage than your fists or is a onehit-kill. The most efficient way to combat is to go for the enemies one after another. Otherwise it is just a timingbased clusterfukk of blocking and pressing directional keys while being defensive and rolling around the place. Another halfbacked feature is stealth which is reduced to slicing throats while avoiding getting detected. U can actual hide bodies but since ur character take ages to drag the body around it doesn't even work out or is valuable. That is a shame because the AI do recognize their fallen m8s and call for aid while actively searching for you. There is no much room to fool the AI like in all the other stealth games u know and love to play.
I am disappointed of the game because after all these years of the development and all the ideas, which the devs showcased in their art asset/alpha videos, the release 1.0 leaves u alone with a bitter irony that they were infact just ideas of a game what could have been a great game. I seriously tried to get immersed in this world...I really did.  I played Shadow of Chernobyl many years ago and found it enjoyable with the immersive music and semi difficult gameplay.  Call of Prypiat (COP) is almost the exact opposite.  From the get go you are thrown into the extremely small map in search of your 5 objectives, crashed helicopters.  The music is there, the scariness is there...but the game just lacks something that its predecessors had.  I can't quite place it, but the game feels rushed.  I know its european but they can make some really great games.  First off, you get way too much ammo initially.  The game is fairly easy on the standard difficulty however, you will die from cheap deaths over and over and over forcing you to quick save like every 5 minutes lest you die and have to load something from an hour ago.  For this game to be enjoyable graphically these days, you pretty much have to download a 3 year old graphic mod that improves lighting and shadows while also improving a few textures here and there.
Edits:  A few things I forgot to mention that are really tedious:
Your character gets exhausted after 10 seconds of running!  This leaves you being very slow and open to attack...very annoying.
And finally the engine crashes every so often leaving you reloading a previous save. So again, save often. At least every 5 minutes.
For me, I think it's just the size of the map initially that put me off.  Its just a giant circle with your objectives on the outer sides and keeping the quest hub in the very center.  It's pretty stock gameplay design if you ask me and pulls from the immersion.  There are Stalker fan boys on here that have sunk hundreds of hours into this game and the series in a whole and will probably scoff at this review.  I just couldnt get into it.   For 20 bucks I'd say this is definately NOT worth a buy.  Wait for it to go on sale which it does quite often and get it for half off.  Today, there are just better shooters out there like the Metro series which has far superior graphics.  Obviously...the game is 5 years old so the graphics arent going to be stellar. I have been playing this game since 2013. I have been on hiatus many times, but whenever I get back to the game, it's a blast :)
Awesomenauts is a really cool MOBA plattformer. As with any MOBA, you play with your hero (an Awesomenaut) and try to push against the turrets of the enemy lanes until you reach the drill (the nexus/the ancient) of the enemy team. Once you have destroyed the drill, your team wins the game.
You have a good variety of different heroes that you can pick. In total there are 3 heroes on every team. There are many different maps that you can play (which is different from Dota 2 or League of Legends).
The community is small and overall okay. Sometimes it is difficult to get into a match, because not enough people are online. But the game is still far away from being dead.
The content of the game clearly shows that this is a work of love. Each hero has a unique style and soundtrack, that shows that the team behind this game put a lot of thought into designing each Awesomenaut. And while doing so, they did not take themselves too seriously, so that you will discover some jokes and weird shop items.
Overall a very enjoyable game. Definitely worth checking out. The game also features a good tutorial to get you started and you can also play against and with bots if you would like to try out new Awesomenauts in a safe environment.
Oh, and did I mention the really cool soundtracks? Love listening to these.

Updated 8/16/17 - The third (and also canonically the last) of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, Call of Pripyat is considered the least difficult of the three games. This is due to the obssession Shadow of Chernobyl has with instant death radiation, and Clear Sky's fixation on bandits with impossible shotgun accuracy.
Call of Pripyat is also the most refined of the three games, featuring the fewest bugs of all the games. You play as Major <Redacted>, who was sent in as an undercover agent to find out about the <Redacted> and the Zone in general. Throughout the game you will encounter random spawning mechanics via the A-Life system, leading to some interesting situations.
Playing Call of Pripyat with some gun-improvement mods is recommended, not because CoP is bad in that department but the graphics could really use an overhaul. For those who want to experience CoP 'properly,' getting the AtmosFear and Absolute Nature mods (they work together) is a great way to pretty the game up some without affecting gameplay elements.
As with all S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games, it is recommend that you play it on the MASTER difficulty. The game really shines when everything can kill you, and paired with the complete and utter insanity that is the A-Life system strained to the limit, can lead to moments of hilarity. Anomalies are just as dangerous as before, but they have well-defined areas compared to SoC and CS, so it is easier to avoid them when necessary. Radiation is significantly less lethal than SoC and less prevalent than in CS, so walking in water is unlikely to make you surge up to 600+ rads and die of internal organ failure. Because of this much safer environment, the primary danger now comes from significantly more aggressive mutants, who will now all attack you at the drop of a coin.
The invincible-while-invisible bloodsuckers are now gone, so feel free to fill up that blur full of bullets while it's running at you after doing a marathon with a gas mask on. Controllers are now significantly more dangerous, being much tougher than any of the previous incarnations and with extremely lethal melee. Burers are just as cancer as before if not even moreso. Although anomalies early on are less lethal than in CS, all later anomalies will pretty much consign you to instant death, especially since most anomalies of the instant-death kind do not have artifacts that can sufficiently protect you like in SoC.
There are a whole host of mods that change and overhaul every aspect of CoP, so once you get bored of doing story-based exploration you could try some of those out. Call of Chernobyl in particular stands out for me, since it turns the whole game into a free-form roaming experience. Other suggested mods would be the STCoP weapon pack (russian-made) to give your bang some extra glam, and if you really hate yourself try the Misery mod. The health-wall enemies there will be sure to annoy you some, if that is your thing.
This game is definitely worth playing, with excellent atmosphere and environmental cues that explain the story in place of dialog. Where SoC was about GET OUT OF HERE STALKER and CS was Slav Squatting Simulator 9000, CoP is about running through an entire field of anomalies with the bolt out while being chased down by a bunch of snorks. Such is life in the zone.

This is a review of the game from a technical/gameplay standpoint
a review regarding the storyline, graphics, etc. I am writing this review for those that wish to play the Ys games in chronological order.
For those of you that didn't know, Origin, Oath in Felghana, and Ark of Napishtim use the same engine. However, OiF and Origin were released after Ark of Napishtim, in that order, and thus were "tweaked" or "improved," rather, in terms of combat, stat growth, and money gain. Playing in chronological order means playing Origin, then Oif, then Ark, and getting used to things that might be missing, as you go through the series.
Now, I've played Origin all the way through on all characters on Nightmare difficulty, and the first thing to compare between Origin and Oif, is that Yunica and Adol play similarly to each other, without being exactly the same. For example, while Yunica and Adol's fire spells function identically, Yunica gets her fire magic from a sword, which does slightly more damage than her normal weapon, but swings slower. Other than that, their attack patterns are pretty similar, with Adol doing more thrusting as opposed to Yunica swinging her axe about (which makes sense, considering you don't stab with it).
In Origin, your dash attack has a chance of lowering the enemy's defence, including bosses. This is incredibly helpful as it can be chained into your normal combo. In OiF, you still have a dash attack, however, instead of lowering the enemy's defence, it is a quick 3-hits, that can be chained into your normal combo. That being said, in Origin, it's imperative to learn how to effectively use your dash attack, where as in OiF, you can almost completely disregard it, and get by just fine.
The second thing to note, OiF and Origin have a thing called Boost, which functions similar to a Limit Break, if you will; while it's active, movement and attack speed is increased, while damage is greatly reduced. However, Origin added an additional power to that, called Burst, a special attack that, when activated, will use the remaining time on your Boost. The attack varies for each character, but is nice to have, as it's essentially a panic button, to go along with your Limit Break. You don't
it, but it's nice to have, in the situations where you are surrounded by enemies with 3 HP, and no way out.
Regarding the difficulty as a whole, of both games, Nightmare is incredibly hard, even frustrating at times, in both Origin and OiF. The difference, however, is that OiF has boss fights that are much more demanding in terms of snap decisions, timing, and reflexes, whereas the dungeons leading up to said fights, are a fun challange. Not particularly terrifying or anything. The first boss, Ellefale, is both a perfect representation of what to expect later on, as well as being a nice throwback to Ys 2, where everything died by fire. If you try to dodge her attacks too early, they will chace after you, and you'll get hit, and likewise, dodge too late, and you get hit. For a first boss, having to learn the timing right then and there is incredibly demanding, especially when you die in 2 or 3 hits. Boss fights like Gyalva and Gildias very much felt the same way, requiring precise timing, quick thinking, and not using every tool in your arsenal will cost you your life.
On the other hand, Origin had much harder dungeons, yet had less demanding boss fights (not to say that they aren't exactly "harder"). I found myself dying quite a bit, as trash mobs used their numbers and large attack power to hit for all I'm worth. The Water Prison has you fighting enemies that can only be destroyed with your earth power, while trying to navigate underwater, looking for more oxygen. The Silent Desert has enemies that, when you first get there, can't be permanantly killed, all the while traversing quicksand, while they come from the ground and dance around you. At times, I felt myself traversing these dungeons with a sense of caution, as the next batch of enemies, and a wrong move would be the end of me. While poor planning will also get you killed in dungeons in OiF, it felt a lot more frequent in Origin.
Boss fights, however, were a lot more fair. The dodging you had to do from enemy's attacks would prepare you for this moment, because a lot of the bosses have projectiles, or attacks that reach large sections of the field. Jenocres' attacks feel very much like playing a shoot 'em up, for example. Which leads to one of the more noticible changes between Origin and OiF; You see the entire battlefield, and always have eyes on the boss, at all times. During the course of the fight, lightning strikes will come down in the area where you are standing, indicated by circles on the ground. You have to keep running, until the lightning is finished chasing you. Being able to see where  Jenocres is, as well as the entire arena, while dodging attacks that reach every corner of the screen is keeps you from running into another attack, after dodging the last one.
This, cannot be said for OiF. With the exception of Gildias and Ellefale, you do not normally have constant sight on the boss, the entire arena, and Adol, at the same time, without keeping within a certain distance of the boss. The arena in which you fight is about the same average size as the ones in Origin, however, the camera is focused on Adol, zoomed out for the boss fight. What this means is that to see all of the boss's tells and attacks before they happen, you must keep within a certain proximity. However, the result of that is a smaller margin of error for dodging and reacting to attacks.
To compensate for the lack of traditional shops, Origin has a system implemented where you can buy powers, named Blessings, which allow your character active passives such as boosted ailment resistance, reduced damage from terrain, or things such as increased item drop rate. However, on Nightmare, all SP (the currency of the game) is worth 1 SP. With the occasional treasure chest giving SP, you will have just enough SP throughout the game to increase the defence on your armour, and obtain 1 to 2 extra skills, depending on what you get, and assuming you are leveling normally. The lack of shops also means that you will find all of your weapons and armour, and any items you obtain must either be found, or otherwise obtained from the story. OiF does not suffer from this, as it does use the traditional shop. You do still find weapons and armour during your escapades, however, you can also buy weapons, armour, and expendable items. Thankfully, unlike in Origin, currency in the land of Felghana is a lot easier to come by, so there is no worrying about saving for just the right moment.
Upgrading weapons and armour requires two things: money, and Cleria Ore. In OiF, ore comes in abundance, dropped by enemies, along with gold. Every weapon and piece of armour requires both gold, and ore to level up (stat increase), with better equipment being more expensive. Origin has simplified this process, in accordance with the shop system and/or money drop rates. Weapons are upgraded specifically with Cleria Ore, however, they are scattered throughout the game, and power up your weapon enough to last you until the next upgrade, and armour is upgraded by spending SP.

In the game's current state, I don't know if I would recommend Woodle Tree Adventures to anyone, as there are a few things that break the game for me.
The camera system is flawed. You have no control over the camera, and for a 3D platformer like this, it makes it almost impossible to play the game. Fixed cameras in games like this are fine if they are done right. Unfortunately for Woodle Tree Adventures, they aren't. In some instances, you have to run toward the camera, not knowing if you're about to walk off of an edge or into an enemy. Using the recommended 360 controller, the triggers and right thumb stick are not mapped to anything. Using those to control the camera would make the game much more playable and enjoyable.
I had an instance where I paused the game and accidently hit a button, and the game just disappeared leaving only the skybox. Music, objects, platforms... all gone. The only option I was left with was to close the game.
The game is pretty straightforward, but it would be nice if it gave you more instruction, or told you what you were supposed to do other than collecting water. There are fruits or nuts that you collect, but from what I've seen, the game doesn’t tell you what they are used for. Another reviewer said they were used to upgrade your weapon, which is a giant leaf, but all of the enemies seem to die in one hit, so I don't really see a point.
All in all, Woodle Tree Adventures is not a bad game. I paid $0.74 for it, and if the Dev patches/updates the game, I will change my recommendation. But in its current state, I give Woodle Tree Adventures a 2/5.

If you're a fan of other 40k games chances are you'll like this.
5 campaign levels averaging at about 25 mins to complete each level.
Survival modes for each level once they have been completed in campaign.
Same story that tends to be in 40k games; we're space marines so kill everything GG.
Gameplay is reminiscent of old top-down shooters like Loaded and Gauntlet where you hold on the fire button, collect powerups and do what the narrator tells you.
4 Different classes, though in my opinion they don't feel massively varied; Each class has a secondary weapon and an option of 1/3 primary weapons (2 of which must be unlocked first) which basically have the same animation but slightly higher damage than the last weapon.
Each class also has a unique ability (Rapid fire, AoE explode, turret, dash) which charge up and can be used fairly often.
A couple of negatives; The camera angle is determined by what is happening in the game and where you are stood, you have little control over it so sometimes it can be difficult to see where you/the enemies are. Also due to the game having control of the camera your reticule will sometimes move to the wrong spot meaning your shots will fly harmlessly past enemies.
Cutscenes can't be skipped so when replaying or respawning you have to watch them over & over (alot of which don't show anything important).
Co-op is local only so you'll need a gamepad and friend/warm body to play that mode with.
Overall it's a fun couple of hours with replayability if you want to play through the campaign with each class.
For the price they're asking, it's not a bad invesment.

Dragon Nest is a fast-paced MMORPG based around dragons (of course) where you have to save the world from the darkness like usual and mostly gather a lot of things.
Gameplay:
This is the points that makes the Dragon Nest what it is:
- Fast-paced
- Good variety of skills with good animations
- Combo skills very well
- Terrible crafting system based on gambling mostly
- Kind of Pay 2 Win if you aim for the top (or you will just grind your existence)
- Grindy for meager rewards
Story:
The story is nothing amazing but it's not the boring type if you compare it with your average mmorpg game I would say, it's fun but not worth praising as it's the regular "save the world from the darkness" kind of story like you would expect. However they give you some cutscenes and you can solo it without troubles so it feels more alive than doing the side quests that are basically fetch quests.
Graphics:
I would give a good thumbs up for the animations but the overall appearance of the game is pretty lackluster, it feels outdated even when it came out. I can understand the desire to make it anime-like but you can make look anime without having such low resolution.
Audio:
It's average, you can't change to get other languages with english subtitles to make it feel more anime if you get what I mean and the english voices are not that fitting sadly.
Overall:
It was good before, today servers are getting deserted gradually as better games come out I played quite a bit in the past but stopped since the end-game wasn't all that great for me. But I really enjoyed flying around and going fast in this game for a long time still would enjoy doing it but I would not play again. I recommend it since it's not a bad game but it's not that great of a game anymore they would need major updates which is pretty much making another game instead.

For example u could think that using weapons while fighting multiple enemies is a big gamechanger but it is not because there is no crowdcontrol at all. Another halfbacked feature is stealth which is reduced to slicing throats while avoiding getting detected. U can actual hide bodies but since ur character take ages to drag the body around it doesn't even work out or is valuable. That is a shame because the AI do recognize their fallen m8s and call for aid while actively searching for you. There is no much room to fool the AI like in all the other stealth games u know and love to play.
I am disappointed of the game because after all these years of the development and all the ideas, which the devs showcased in their art asset/alpha videos, the release 1.0 leaves u alone with a bitter irony that they were infact just ideas of a game what could have been a great game. The first game, Shadow of Chernobyl, was one of the best games I've ever played. Clear Sky, the second installment to the franchise and a prequel to the first game, was an overwhelming disappointment. I was skeptical when coming to Call of Pripyat, but I can say without a doubt in my mind, that this is one of the greatest video games of all time.
STORY
Where Clear Sky faltered with a dull story, Call of Pripyat brings forth a new, compelling, and interesting story that spans throughout untold countless hours of gameplay. For the first time, optional missions and side quests have their own stories, ranking among my favourites in RPGs. Memorable missions such as sneaking through a lair of sleeping Bloodsuckers, joining a team of hunters to kill a massive Chimera, overseeing a trade of information between enemy factions and then sniping them from a distance, and discovering the secrets hidden throughout the Pripyat area make the side missions a wonder to play through. While the central story isn't as deep and strong as the first game, it can be expanded upon through hundreds of optional missions which alone give the game far more replayability. A cast of new and surprisingly memorable characters filters into the game, all with their own distinctive and unique personality traits. For the first time, we finally get to go deeper into the city of Pripyat, to explore the old ruins of the world's biggest ghost town.
GAMEPLAY
Strong gunplay against intelligent enemy fighters and nightmarish mutants with a set of their own unique attacks ranks Call of Pripyat among some of the best FPS games I've ever played. Weapons will jam after prolonged use and wear, enemies will relentlessly and savagely attack you, flanking, taking cover, reacting in new and dynamic ways, even traveling around the world and engaging in fights among themselves. Suits and weapons can be seamlessly upgraded through assisting characters. This is undoubtedly the strongest of the series.
GRAPHICS
Much like Clear Sky, the visuals just seem to fall flat. They're beautiful, most certainly, but there's simply little to no immersion like the first game. While there are haunting environments and surreal moments when you reach the dead city, I simply didn't get the same feelings that sparked through me as I assaulted the Brain Scorcher, fought waves of charging mutants, and battled my way inside the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Shadow of Chernobyl. Visually, the game does look quite good, though I am sorey disappointed to see that the beautifully detailed and ominous cutscenes present in the first two games are suddenly and without warning absent from Call of Pripyat. The jerky, awkward in-game cutscenes are laughable at best, and the slideshow cutscenes in the beginning and end of the game are groan inducing and all around pitiful attempts to recreate the CGI of the first to games. Nonetheless, graphically the game is stellar, and even running at medium settings the game still looks great.
MULTIPLAYER
Unfortunately, I have never seen more than one other person playing the multiplayer of this game, and therefore cannot make a full review on that particular portion. However, from what I've tested, the game modes look fun, gameplay is very much intact, and the new maps look interesting and well-detailed. If you have a few friends who want to play, a private lobby for this game looks like it could be unending fun.
VERDICT
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat is a well polished, fun, entertaining, and overall incredible game. It took me nearly 17 hours to complete the main story, and I still haven't even scratched the surface of the overall package with the wealth of optional missions and exploration available to the player. While the story may not stack up to the mystery and horror of Shadow of Chernobyl, and while the survival/horror gameplay present in the first game is still quite lackluster, Call of Pripyat proves itself to be a fantastic experience. Had I not owned a PC of my own at the time of my playthrough of this game, I would have sold all of my consoles soley to play Call of Pripyat. A strong modding community keeps the game fresh and exciting, and I highly suggest that before playing, everyone install the S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat COMPLETE mod, as it enhances the visuals and adds a few new and fun mechanics that blend seamlessly with the central game. I didn't think anything could beat the first game, but this alone proves me wrong. The only true complaints I have are minor and do not derive from the full package. This is a game that I will be playing for years to come and still will find it new and fascinating each and every time I play. This is money well spent and perhaps one of the greatest video games ever made. With that said, the final verdict of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat, is an astounding 10/10. Now, if you'll excuse me, I'll be trying to figure out how to kill all of these mutants and keep the bandits off my back.

OK, this game is brutal.  But it is brutal in a great way.  It punishes you, but not in a cheap way.  When you die, you die through your own faults.  Not paying attention, not listening to the audio cues that tell you death is eminent, not strategizing on which enemy/spawner you need to take out first, and failing to take out said spawner in enough time before the other several spawners on the floor start spawning more monsters.  There is no delay in controling your invisible protagonist.  It will take one to two attempts of playing the game to get a feel for how the daggers (your only weapons) perform.  Every I played, I managed to get just a little further in.  As I have progressed, its difficulty has scalled up and up and up.  Glorious, and engaging.
Gameplaywise, this game is solid.  Easy to understand controls, easy to understand mechanics, and really easy to jump in and jump out regarding game play.  One session or an hours worth, you can put as much time as you like in this game and continue enjoying yourself as long as this sort of action FPS horde mode game is your cup of tea.
The enemies keep coming, and they keep you on your toes constantly, with virtually no breaks to catch your breath.  Which brings me to really the only thing holding this game back from general players.
There is a limited variety provided by this game.
You have one weapon, while it does evolve as you progress (hoovering blood crystals or what ever they are), it is still the devil daggers by which the game's title implies.  As you progress through the waves, the enemies increase in number, but seem to be limited to around 10 total types of enemies (this is as much as I have seen through my playthrough and others playthroughs.)
There is also only ONE dimmly lit arena (that you can kill yourself by falling off the edge), that can leave you wishing it was just a little bigger.  If the game ends, I have not seen the ending yet (at the time of this review).  This unfortunately sets the game with a very small amount of content provided for its cost.
I understand how this sort of thing can be a turn off to people.  As far as I am concerned, this game is simply addictive and amazing in the vein of a solid arcade title.  If the developers decided to add more to the game, it would be amazing, but I personally feel it is not nessesary to maintain a level of interest that will keep me coming back.
Given its price tag, I would advertise this game as an arcade gem, and well worth the investment.

Highly recommended for those who like games that involve strategizing, challenge, and character building. Some reviewers are angry with the skill level of the game and the necessity to repeat fights: Yes, the game is more difficult than others, and the "normal" setting is more akin to "hard" elsewhere. However difficult, Divinity is most certainly beatable without cheats, mods, or other cheese techniques, and is all the more rewarding for it when you overcome difficult encounters. I hardly have an optimal team, with most of my characters melee and one a shielded tank (many players recommend near all range teams), but I have made steady and relatively smooth progress without playing on the easiest difficulty. If you like spending time thinking about battle plans, getting items, and approaching tactically demanding boss fights, then you'll very much appreciate what Divinity has to offer.
In addition, the game has some pretty cool environments, a load of equipment, and a pretty solid number of skills. Again, some people have complained about what they perceived to be few actual skills in the game: Play into the "second act" and you'll soon find that there is a number of higher tier spells as well as craftable and hidden skills. You cannot use ALL the skills available in the game during battle, but this again compels you to think strategically about your character's role. You also have quite a bit of flexibility in how you build your characters: You can build paladins, two-handed warriors with necromancy, thieves with fire spells, summoners with bows, and so on and so on. There's many opportunites to personalzie and maximize your character to your likings; not too far into the game you will also be able to respec for free an infinite number of times.
I have spent a huge number of hours in this game, yet I have hardly finished all the quests, played all the class combinations, and still have a few companions whose story I never pursued.
My complaints, however, are the story, which I don't find as compelling. Fane has an intriguing background, but the main storyline just does not hold my attention. I tend to be excited for the battles, items, and chances to explore rather than in advancing the storyline. I also have performance issues despite running a pretty powerful PC, though this may have to do with some issue in my hardware and not so much the game.

This game started out like a cat on fire on the charts. Has been awaited with great expectations for awhile before the lauch too, since the fanculture was quite big, in the first place, since the other Conan-games were relatively popular, and ofc, the movie and lore of the world appealed to many of us oldtimers in the survival/sandbox-genre.
Many a streamer/youtuber jumped at this game, when it got released on EA in STEAM. It offered refreshing new RPing-elements, that got very popular, very fast, after people saw it on displayed by the streamers/RPers. It boosted sales and got the game rolling, very fast.
I played it on solo, regular MP and in RP-whitelisted servers. And spent a good deal of hours in it, enjoying it quite a lot. Even with the limited content it had, back in the beginning, the bugs, glitches etc.
A game of this magnitude and resources, takes time to develop, for sure. Funcom was pushing patches out, every week, the first couple of months, catering to the multitude of comments and feedback they recieved. Which I saw as a good thing. Compared to other developers, Funcom actually took heed of our feedback, and was very focused on NOT being like other EA-games, where the Devs seem to hate you, if you dont praise their game 100%. And I hope that pays off in the end.
To this date, the game has added a ton of content, fixes and optimizations, and the prospect still looks quite cool, afaik. Ive taken a break from the game, the last couple of months. But I WILL be jumping back into it, once they get the game a little closer to release, or when some new large content is added. It deserves the attention, still, imo.
The main negative points about the game, is still evolving around a central element of the game: Combat. So far, the Devs are being a little evassive, when confronted with this argument. They claim that they wont be doing a huge combat-change, which is why many streamers stopped playing. And thats sad, tbh. But I kinda understand it.
Conan is a world of melee and combat. Or at least its a very integral part of being in the world. And as such, the simple "spam the left button" and the occasional dodging/blocking, seems under par with other titles in the genre.
Overall, I love the game. And Funcom seems to be good at nurturing their community etc. Im hoping the game will have success in fixing the flaws and maybe taking another look at combat. If not Im sure itll still be popular, although I DO think it would have had a much larger and stable following, if the VOIP and combat gets more focus, in the future. Or maybe we have to wait for the modders to fix that for them... I recommend it, though. Its definately worth at least 200 hours of playtime, and maybe more, if you find a good community to be part of.

I love the game, more so than I did Euro Truck Simulator 2. In part because of the long nose Peterbilt 389 that comes with the game and the long nose W900 that comes with it too.
The game does like all simulation games get very repetitive, but that is to be expected because you are driving 2 lane roads, interstates, etc. to pick up and deliver your loads. It can be made to simulate real life truck driving to an extent, very small extent in my opinion, but still its nice if you are a big rig enthusiast or have ever liked semi trucks in the past it works out well in that regard.
Now, I will say this, this isn't all about likes, I do dislike that its better to play this game with more than 2 monitors (aka 3 or 4 monitors). Also, the limited amount of official trucks is bad in my opinion. You can get more, but they are custom mods that you can download from all over the net, and in this day and age, I rather not and wait on SCS to eventually release more trucks. Currently there 4 official trucks 2 from Kenworth (aerodynamic T680, or the classic W900) and from Peterbilt (the aerodynamic 579 or the classic looking 389).
I highly recommend at least starting the game out without mods running so you can get a few laughs like when I first saw Penny's (which real life company would be Wendy's) and Wallbert (which well you know, Wal-Mart), etc. :) It gave the game a little giggle factor at first, but it doesn't last.
I love some of the classic long nose trucks (W900 and 389) customizations, the stock ones are nice, and even some of the mods are even better too for it. If you like looking at show rigs or show trucks, then expect to spend loads of time bouncing around from a Peterbilt 389 that you customized to be all show truck like and a Kenworth W900 that you made into a show truck too. Sadly, you can't take them to shows in the game, but use them as work horses. :) At least you don't have to worry about all the road grim and all when it comes to truck wash time.
I would like a few changes to the game. Expanded roads and less drain on graphics when you go to Vegas. With a i7 4770s + GTX 980 and 3 1080p monitors, the graphics would drop from 60 to 45 and sometimes lower FPS, yet maintain 60 FPS when driving practically anywhere else, but maybe LA.
The other change I would add, is to make the game a bit more realistic by allowing players the option to turn on the ability to keep log books, at least simulate greasing the fifth wheel, and simulate doing the pre-trip check list and the post-trip check list. Among other things. This then would make the game a bit varied than just the same old pick up load here at point A drive and park load at point B. Then it be like check truck for all maintenance issues first, drive to point A, check in with gate guard, back in and pick up load, inspect trailer and load to be secure as well as truck if necessary (pre trip), then drive out verify things with gate guard, go to point B and do the same stuff but to drop the trailer off... (post trip stuff)... lol be a lot more involved of a game then...
However, even as is, I still recommend this game because its just fun for all of us that like big rigs. Reminds me of childhood and dreaming of driving trucks one day even though I never got went to do that once I got older. :)

It's hard to explain what there is about this game that makes it so much fun.  It's pretty simple, and there are only a handful of very samey maps, but overall I've really enjoyed the couple hours I've played so far.  For one thing, it's free.  There aren't really pay walls. There's basic for 10 bucks, which has upgraded inventory space (you also get upgrades to storage through ranking up as you play, if you have patience).  And with premium, you'll unlock all the parts instantly which normally you must save in game currency to do.  Part of the fun is unlocking parts, but I can understand someone with 20 bones to spare wanting to just play and have fun with it.  People complain about snipers and machine guns in a lot of the reviews I see here, but I armed myself with a fairly decent heavy armor and speedier treads, and a shotgun with basic rockets, and was having a blast sneaking up on those snipers and blasting them in the face for a one-hit.  And it
take a certain amount of finesse to play.  I bought the simplest spider-type legs and realized the mass of the body of my take really made them viable, especially with the powerful-only-at-very-close-range shotgun equipped.  There are enough parts to keep you busy configuring, and you can swap them during a match if you're not happy with your loadout.  I see a lot of potential here, and the graphics are vibrant, everything looks like it's molded from soft plastic.  It would be nice to see more particles or pieces fall off tanks the more damage they take.  And one gripe is that no matter how many kills or towers you secure, you get no additional points (G - used for buying parts) for doing so.  3 points if your team wins, 1 point if you lose.  Not a big deal, but why even list stats if they don't matter?  I'd like to see my skill getting me paid.  Perhaps have a separete unlock/monetary system for flare, which you can only buy racking kills and holding towers?  Hats.  For tanks.  It'd give us more of a reason for wanting to do better each round.
At any rate, the game is fun as it is, and I look forward to seeing where the devs take it in the future.  Recommended.
Plus, it's free, so why not give it a shot?

Pros:
You can pick your chapter marines (select few).

Wow. Absolutely blew me away.
First of all, especially given the price point, YES, it's worth your investment. Think of this game as mixture of Unreal Tournament, Doom, Magic Carpet, and Geometry Wars. The intensity, addictive quality, and horror are all top-notch. Of particular note is the SOUND DESIGN and direction. I'm an extremely jaded survival horror fan, and it's tough to impress me with audio - or scare me with it, given that I'm a noise musician in my spare time - but the relentless, terrifying soundscape that this game includes grates on you and psychologically fatigues you in the best possible way.
It's truly a refreshing experience and a ton of fun. A brutal challenge but sooooo worth the money.
Now, DEVS: If you're reading this, I think you have an amazing formula here and I hope you expand on it. I could see this functioning very well as a stand alone title. Part of what makes it so unique and cool is that it's not bloated with a million additional add-ons, and seems like a genuine labor of love. Another reviewer described it as a nearly perfect game, and I agree. HOWEVER, I'm concerned with the game's longevity. I would appreciate a few power-ups and/or additional weapons along the way. Maybe a minimalized system like Binding of Isaac's character selection, where you can eventually unlock some different abilities or something like that. I would totally respect you if you disagreed with that opinion - in fact, I would admire your commitment to your aesthetic! However, that might be the difference between me playing this game for 5 hours or for 50 hours.
Ultimately, I'm glad this game exists. I very much hope you will entertain the possibility of making a sequel or some DLC to expand on the ideas you have. You have an incredibly solid foundation and I hope to see it grow. Then again, if it doesn't, I'll love it all the same.
In fact, I like the game so much I would be happy to volunteer to work on it. Not that you guys need the help, but if you're willing to point me in the direction of a way to mod the game, I'd be happy to prototype some features - I have some experience with game design and coding. I guess what I'm saying is... this game gets me excited about making and playing games! I hope that serves as a compliment - it's certainly intended as such!
