What makes this game so fun is also what makes it so replayable, the ability to write your own alternate history.
There are so many ways you can play out your characters. Often unexpected events lead to very interesting, challenging or downright hilarious scenarios. Very often various characters that you plays as (somtimes even those you don't plays as) will end up endearing themselves to you, as you painstakingly try to guide them succesfully through the political quagmire that the feudal system can become.
That being said, this is by no means a simple game, it is complex and can be daunting at first.
The graphics are functional, and only serve to convey information for the most part.
The majority of the storytelling will be going on in your imagination, since there are no cutscenes and events appear as a text popup with some artwork. Personally I love coming up with elaborate character stories, so this isn't even a factor for me.
Battles are simplistic in nature, essentially clashes of numbers with some factors thrown in, like commander skills and traits, terrain and so forth.
In conclusion, if you like grand strategy, I absolutely recommend it.
Edit:
A note on the DLC:
A number of it is purely cosmetic, so unnecessary unless you like to have updated sprites/portraits.
Other DLC is mostly concerned wih expanding playable dynasties, like Sword of Islam for muslim rulers, Rajas of India for Indian rulers and most recently Jade Dragon for Tibetan rulers.
These are only necessary if you want to play in a specific region and experience different mechanics.
Finally we have DLC which I would consider core to the experience, which add options for everyone or the at least the majority of characters, like Way of Life, Sons of Abraham(sort of), Conclave etc. Of course others might have different opinions of what is core or not, don't be afraid to pop by the Paradox forums and ask if need be.
My recommendation for purchasing DLC is this: If you feel it adds value to the game than buy it; on sale or otherwise.
If you feel the opposite, vote with your wallet and don't buy it.
In multiplayer you get to enjoy the same DLC as the Host anyways, so this isn't splitting the community either.

TL;DR: I wish there was a middle rating for recommendation because I don't think the game is bad enough to be a Thumbs Down but not good enough for a Thumbs Up either. I would recommend this to any Ys fans but personally I was kind of underwhelmed. I'm not even sure what it was that underwhelmed me but I liked Ys Origins a lot more. Maybe it's because it feels like you only need to beat it once and then move on to another game. Save the other Ys games for after you've beaten this one for a more rewarding experience.
[Difficulty - good]: As with the other Ys games, you have difficulties for everyone to be able to enjoy the game although there are at least 2 bosses that are annoying no matter what you choose.
[Story - average]: Pretty standard stuff but I liked the little touches here and there to make the story more than just a standard issue "Evil being awakens and you happen to be nearby to slay/seal it for the villagers" story. I don't know if Ys Ark of Nepishtim would explain why Adol and Dogi are traveling together but not being able to own and play it may explain why I feel so disconnected from Felghana.
[Characters - good]: As with all the other Falcom games Steam has, the attention to details about every character's personality and lives is always a pleasure to read about. The merchant trying to get fame and fortune, the hardworking townspeople and a surprisingly kind countess are just a few to name in adding layers to the otherwise cookie-cutter plot.
[Graphics - average]: It's a matter of personal tastes on this one. The characters look great to me since I prefer the 2D anime style over full 3D characters. The cinematics are as lovely as I've come to expect from any Falcom game as well.
[Music - excellent]: One thing this game has no problems with is the music, my favorites would definitely be the world map and clock tower music. Not to say the rest wasn't memorable though.
[Combat - good]: It uses the same combat and magic system as Origins which makes playing one then the other very easy to transition into.
[Length - average]: It may be a good length for people who prefer short games but as for someone with tons of spare time and expectations of RPGs to have decent length and content in them...it was disappointing how quickly I chewed through it. That disappointment also leads to my rating for...
[Replayability - bad]: Unfortunately there is almost no reason to replay this game except to get Steam achievements. The version we Steam players got is lacking all the extras the PSP version players get for beating the game and time attack mode.

I have been playing Crusader Kings 2 on and off almost since the vanilla launch. This game after several years manages to keep me coming back. Paradox are constantly even now a few years on pumping out DLC which have for the most part really added depth and fun to the original release of Crusader Kings 2. I almost don't know if I could play the vanilla version of the game now knowing how much has been added to the game with the DLC so really keep that in mind if you intend to buy this game.
The game is a wierd mesh of a RPG cross Real Time Grand Strategy cross Fuedal Politics simulator that can be paused and is open ended like sandbox type games. Yep. However it is an insanely clever game that really makes your decisions meaningful. Never in any other game have decisions I made become so important until sometimes I sit there for 10 minutes especially in difficult situations just thinking about the ramifications of that decision.
The game is nicely styled with graphics that are keeping well for a game a few years old. The audio is phenomenal with the score being honestly one of the best in a game I have heard in a long time. The sound effects are nice but do get occassionally annoying especially if you happen to be playing a Muslim character with multiple wives...those babies just don't stop coming! The game is also very stable and has never really frozen or crashed or bugged out. Paradox are pretty on top of bugs and issues for the most part.
So onto the actual game itself... Well in short you pick a character, any, it could be a Count or a Duke, King, Emporer and then run and maintain their dynasty. So of course this would involve marrying, raising children, educating children, organising an heir to your titles and so on and so forth. However being a Count or Duke or any other character means you also need to deal with the demands of your kingdom, duchy or County. You may need to contend with jealous relatives or you may just have your own goals of taking over all of England and becoming King. This is where the sandbox nature of the game kicks in. You do have in game goals you can aim towards however the choice is yours and the game can be taken into any direction as long you plan and work towards it.
The game once learned is easy to pick up and play anytime. But seriously it will take you a good 20-30 hours and a few play throughs to really grasp how to play the game correctly and to start making the most of the in game mechanics. But don't let that scare you off because Crusader Kings is in all honesty one of my all time favourite games. It is just one of those games I keep coming back to. You know, you can look at the menu as long as you eat at home type of games. As much as I play other titles I just keep coming back to this one.
I completely recommend this game whole heartedly and hope you have as much fun as I have had!

WARNING: MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS TO SHADOW OF CHERNOBYL. READ AT YOUR OWN RISK!!!! Call of Pripyat is the third installment in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series of survival horror, single player games. It directly follows up the events of Shadow of Chernobyl. The path to the center of The Zone is open for all. The military sends in five helicopters all headed to the CNPP. The mission is designated Operation Fairway. But they all mysteriously crash. As Major Alexander Degtyarev, it is your job to find what caused Operation Fairway to fail. I won't go any further into the plot than that. The gameplay is mostly similar to the previous games. The controls are pretty straightforward. Though you can change them to fit your liking if you're not happy with the default settings. Most of the same mechanics are still there. You still need to eat and watch your radiation meter. Artifact hunting is a bit more fun and interesting this time around. In Call of Pripyat, you get an item called a detector. And it does exactly what it sounds like it does. The first one you start off with isn't really that great though. But the more advanced ones will display exactly where an artifact will spawn in an anomaly. Side missions in Call of Pripyat are a huge improvement over the last two games. They are also much more rewarding. You might be given the coordinates to a stash hidden in the forest, or a discount on weapon and armor repairs/modifications. But those aren't the only rewards for completing missions. There's also a bigger emphasis on exploration. Simply while exploring abandoned buildings you might come across some documents. And here you have a choice, you could sell the documents to one of the local traders for a hefty price to upgrade your gear and maybe buy some much needed medical supplies. Or, you could give them to the leader of one of the many factions in The Zone which could in turn lead to some extra missions which could possibly have a much larger reward. It's completely up to you. There's also some pretty incredible anomaly formations where there could possibly be some very valuable artifacts just waiting to be found. The graphics in this game are beautiful. Even without mods, the game still looks incredible on max settings. Each area in The Zone has its own look and feel. Probably should've mentioned there are three large areas to explore; Zaton, Yanov, and Pripyat. From the abandoned streets and apartment complexes of Pripyat, to the rainsoaked swamps of Zaton, each area has its own atmosphere to it. Speaking of atmosphere, Call of Pripyat isn't as scary or intense as Shadow of Chernobyl mind you. But there were a couple moments that had me on the edge of my seat, with my heart racing. In one mission, you assist a hunter seek out the reason for recent S.T.A.L.K.E.R disappearances which leads to the discovery of a Bloodsucker lair filled with sleeping Bloodsuckers. I could feel my heart beat in my chest as I crept past them, careful not to make a sound. For even the loading of a shotgun could awaken the beasts. You do not want to get trapped out at night and accidentally walk right into the lair of a Chimera. As far as bugs go, I have yet to actually encounter any. Not to say there aren't any. Final verdict: Call of Pripyat is an amazing game. I would highly recommend it to any fan of post-apocalyptic, survival horror games. 10/10. P.S If you beat the game and feel like playing it again, I HIGHLY RECCOMEND THE MISERY MOD. But do not use it on your first playthrough. I strongly discourage it. Unless you like a huge challenge.

TL;DR Kind of tricky to recommend. Overall it'd be worth it, in my not-so-objective opinion, for maybe $20 or so.
What the game does well: A basic, but highly mobile, fighting system that is fairly fluid once you get into the rhythm of things, though there is a few issues with some aspects. The platforming portions are also well done and only twice in my time thus far has the camera been a hinderance. The game's ledge grabbing detection is also very forgiving, which is nice most of the time. Many of the level designs are also very well done and look good, if dated. The added single levels, Versus and arena mode, and the previous game definitly are a good content addition to the game.
What isn't so good: The graphics, as I mentioned, are dated. This game has been in developemnt of just over 9 years and it definitly shows here. Most noticable in the rather muddy and bland world textures. The story is basic and the levels are individual set peices. Character development and interaction is minimal and restricted to pre and post level in game cut scenes.
What is really annoying/bad: There are some intresting physics interactions in combat. Where this rears its head the most is with the jump kick manuever. If you have a lot of momentum going and you land a solid hit, you're going to going flying a kilometer in some direct. If its straight up, you're pretty much guaranteed to die on impact. The dual use of some keys will lead to frustation in some areas. Trying to pick up or throw something is bound to 'Q' and there will be times when you try to pick up a second weapon in combat and end up throwing your first. Also the tendency for your character to auto-grab ledges can be fatal in combat when you're jumping around a lot.
Not good, Not bad: WIth about 2hrs in I'm having fun, but reaching the point I'm thinking "now what?" I think the long term viability of the game is going to rest with the dev and community adding levels and content. I'm finding the game itself is rather basic, but is a good parkour type with a melee fighting system. Good level designs being added are whats going to keep this game going.
Overall: A solid combat platformer game, but one that feels a bit dated and with a few flaws. Enjoyment of this game past a few hours is probably going to rest with what is added post release.

Too Long, Didn't Read: Unless you REALLY want this, wait for a sale.  And even then, I'd advise passing this up.  There are many games that do this genre better.
A twin-stick shooter set in the Warhammer 40k universe.  That sounds excellent.  Lots of shooting and bloody combat and fast faction.  For $10 bucks, how could you ask for more?
This game just doesn't hold up to the price in my opinion.  The game is nearly 3 years old and originated on the XBox 360 market place.  After not bringing the game to PC for such a long time, you'd like to think they did something special like maybe updated the graphics, added online play, or at least polished the controls!  But no, there's none of that here.
The game uses assets from Dawn of War 2: Retribution, models that look wonderful when viewed from half mile from up in the sky like it was in the original RTS format.  In these cramped and confined quarters though, everything looks really bad.
The controls work with mouse and keyboard, but there are some peculiar oddities such as running not seeming to work well and melee attacks often missing due to the odd way are "fired".  At least the developer was kind enough to change the XBox button prompts to pictures of Keyboard letters.  That's a small bonus that MANY games forgo doing.
Finally, while I understand this was a couch-co-op game for Xbox 360, that niche doesn't really exist on the PC market.  You might expect some for of online co-op, but from my wanderings through the menus, I found no such option available.  I hope you like a friend crowding your computer desk with another body, because it's local co-op or solo.
Many more minor annoyances exist, and I'm nearly shocked that this is the same price as when it first came out nearly 3 years ago.  If significant content were added, and the game was more finely ported to PC, I could understand such an asking price.  But I almost immediately regretted paying full price for this game.  Even if I paid $5, that might be too much for me.  My advise is wait for a steep sale or just pass this by for something better.

I love the game, more so than I did Euro Truck Simulator 2. In part because of the long nose Peterbilt 389 that comes with the game and the long nose W900 that comes with it too.
The game does like all simulation games get very repetitive, but that is to be expected because you are driving 2 lane roads, interstates, etc. to pick up and deliver your loads. It can be made to simulate real life truck driving to an extent, very small extent in my opinion, but still its nice if you are a big rig enthusiast or have ever liked semi trucks in the past it works out well in that regard.
Now, I will say this, this isn't all about likes, I do dislike that its better to play this game with more than 2 monitors (aka 3 or 4 monitors). Also, the limited amount of official trucks is bad in my opinion. You can get more, but they are custom mods that you can download from all over the net, and in this day and age, I rather not and wait on SCS to eventually release more trucks. Currently there 4 official trucks 2 from Kenworth (aerodynamic T680, or the classic W900) and from Peterbilt (the aerodynamic 579 or the classic looking 389).
I highly recommend at least starting the game out without mods running so you can get a few laughs like when I first saw Penny's (which real life company would be Wendy's) and Wallbert (which well you know, Wal-Mart), etc. :) It gave the game a little giggle factor at first, but it doesn't last.
I love some of the classic long nose trucks (W900 and 389) customizations, the stock ones are nice, and even some of the mods are even better too for it. If you like looking at show rigs or show trucks, then expect to spend loads of time bouncing around from a Peterbilt 389 that you customized to be all show truck like and a Kenworth W900 that you made into a show truck too. Sadly, you can't take them to shows in the game, but use them as work horses. :) At least you don't have to worry about all the road grim and all when it comes to truck wash time.
I would like a few changes to the game. Expanded roads and less drain on graphics when you go to Vegas. With a i7 4770s + GTX 980 and 3 1080p monitors, the graphics would drop from 60 to 45 and sometimes lower FPS, yet maintain 60 FPS when driving practically anywhere else, but maybe LA.
The other change I would add, is to make the game a bit more realistic by allowing players the option to turn on the ability to keep log books, at least simulate greasing the fifth wheel, and simulate doing the pre-trip check list and the post-trip check list. Among other things. This then would make the game a bit varied than just the same old pick up load here at point A drive and park load at point B. Then it be like check truck for all maintenance issues first, drive to point A, check in with gate guard, back in and pick up load, inspect trailer and load to be secure as well as truck if necessary (pre trip), then drive out verify things with gate guard, go to point B and do the same stuff but to drop the trailer off... (post trip stuff)... lol be a lot more involved of a game then...
However, even as is, I still recommend this game because its just fun for all of us that like big rigs. Reminds me of childhood and dreaming of driving trucks one day even though I never got went to do that once I got older. :)

Overgrowth is a game that has encountered many roadblocks in the public eye. Whether it was the long development time or the product itself, there's something about the game that doesn't necessarily lend itself well to being recommended. With that being said, I'd argue that that distaste or distinterest stems from a lack of understanding.
At it's core, in my eyes, Overgrowth is what happens when somebody decides they want to make something really cool and unique. If you look at the comics that have been done for Lugaru, there's some interesting world building that goes on, and this is shown in Overgrowth via it's Lugaru campaign and it's Original campaign. It's a world with anthropomorphic animal martial artists that attempts to carry a heavier tone / weight. I think the tone is communicated well, despite the campaigns being a little lacking in length, but Wolfire designed something that was fun to play.
And fun to play is, in my opinion, one of the most important elements to a fighting game, because you see, there are very few fighting games with a robust, engaging singleplayer. Hell, if you look at my profile I have about 100 hours in Skullgirls and about 1 hour of that was online with a close friend of mine. Part of enjoying single player fighting games comes from an appreciation for the art, fluidity of the combat, and the flow of navigating the game itself.
For what it's worth I think Overgrowth navigates this well. From my understanding, after 17 hours, the maps are designed to be incredibly large and fairly sparse. This leads to a feeling of emptiness, but that only reinforces that exploratory feeling you get from running and leaping across vast swarthes of landscapes. There isn't necessarily a lot of nuance to it, but it looks beautiful and it's fun. Audio FX like the wind rushing as you fall are very solid and the polish in general is pretty good.
Combat is also unique in Overgrowth, because from what I could parse it's more management than it is execution. To attack you hold down the attack button and your character takes a combat stance and will attack when an opponent enters attack range. From there you can move different directions and your directions will influence the move you end up doing on your opponent. I couldn't find a way to get 100% reliable results for the attack, but it's not about executing specific moves, it's more about having a game plan. You can parry, parry into judo throw, or matrix dodge attacks and through this system Overgrowth becomes a challenge of predicting your opponents moves, reading their animations to react, and finding a way to land some blows. This system is made more extreme when weapons are introduced, because most weapons are a 1-2 hit kill. I could understand how someone could argue that the fighting system is bland because it uses a minimal amount of buttons, but this just makes it easier to execute strategies in a consistent manner and I never found it to be boring, because all of your attention has to be focused on the opponent.  I'm a big fan of the combat and I only wish that encounters lasted longer, because there was nothing more fun than trying to run during a story mission until you get a favorable location and then resuming the fight.
In terms of flow, Overgrowth functions quite well. There are infinite arenas to partake in and they look pretty darn good, and although the campaign is short, it's fun and challenging. I haven't spent as much time with the release build as I'd like, due to being busy in my personal life, but I adored the beta build that I've played with over the years and I feel confident recommending it on that alone.
It's not that Overgrowth is perfect, but I think many of the criticisms for the game come from a lack of understanding. I haven't even touched upon it in this review, but there's an incredibly comprehensive editor that accompanies the game which lets you make intricate levels with triggers and all that stuff. Honestly, Overgrowth just requires you to be content with making your own fun. You could argue that at it's base price you need more than a playground to have your own fun,  but I'm sure that as the games lives on the list of good mods will grow. It's not like that gives it points, but if you see Overgrowth at a price you find reasonable, then I highly recommend picking it up and playing around with it. This game reminds me of cuphead insofar as that it was a game that was in development for a really long time and it's official release is cause enough to celebrate. That joy hasn't influenced my review, but I felt a sense of genuine joy when I realized that Overgrowth is "complete".

The story of your lost brother unfolds as chapters in a book are read. Other reviewers noted that if you're experienced at HOG's, this game probably won't be much of a challenge to you - and I do agree with that assessment.
However if you (like me) are new to HOG's and trying to determine if they are a type of game you want to play, this is an excellent "starter HOG" for beginners to try out.
I had not done a shape based HOG before, and I found it a nice change of pace from the word based HOG I had previously played.
I did not like petri dish puzzle, but the rest of the puzzles were good - they made your brain think a bit but it wasn't too much of a challenge - mostly relaxing fun.
and of course, who could forget ... Bloodthirsty Penguins FTW!! LOL
I got this game as part of a bundle, and for less then $1 I feel it was a good value and I was entertained. If I had a friend I wanted to introduce to HOGs, I feel this would be a good game to gift if it was available at a similar discount.
I do feel the current price ($6.99 USD at the time of this review) is too high for what you are getting.
Since there's no "meh" rating, I'm giving it a positive but *only* if it's available to purchase at a discount.

I really tried to get into this game, given the 10/10 scores and consistent positive feedback. The promises are all there. Multiple branching pathways, full voice acting, and battle mechanics. The problem is, the game is simply not fun. On normal difficulty level, the game simply does not provide you with the means to empower your characters and overcome main questlines without resorting to spamming/exploiting game mechanics like pickpocketing and stealth. Virtually everyone I've heard playing this game has had to resort to the same strategy in act 1 and that is not good role playing mechanics if the level threshold has been set so high that the player cannot explore and act freely.
I get that this is not a game for casuals but at least developors like Bioware give players more content and choices through which to grow characters and have a fighting chance against higher tiered enemies.
The inventory system is beyond archaic, I've literally spent one third of this game having to sift through menus and bags. It's 2017, is it too much to ask for shared inventory and filter options?
And lastly the writing...it's okay, but again, for game getting all of these coveted perfect scores, I was expecting characters and story which were a bit less tropish.
I'm not saying Origina Sin 2 is a terrible game and as I stated before, you do get all of the features and promises as stated on the box which is rare in games these days. The problem is the game just turns in to a slog where you are constantly quick loading because of high level thresholds for quests in which you have NO means whatsoever to grind a little bit or do side quests to accomate for the difficulty.
It's very clear that a lot of work and care went into making this game, but ultimately it just isn't fun and relies too much on it's gimmicky battle systems.

Grab Civ 5, Mount & Blade: Warband and the Sims series and you get this game. So far it beats every strategy name I ever laid my hands on and I only have 200 hours in it as of yet.
The learning curve is long and painstaking, but it's definitely worth it.
Many people complain about the immerse amount of DLC's that should be included in the vanilla, but once you grind your teeth and decide to buy some of them, (besides they are on sale rather frequently) you won't regret it as each one of them give something to the game that you otherwise would have missed. For instance (dlc's I have so far):
- Legacy of Rome: Retinues and the Byzantine Empire
- The Old Gods: the struggles of tribal people, conquering your way to feudalism/republics, also, raid europe to pieces
- The Republic: start out slow and have huge armies, even as a single county ruler... or even just as a patrician vassal
- Horse Lords: it's bloody hard, still just learning, but the hordes you can recruit are amazing
- Charlemagne: another +100 years of (IRL) gameplay + tons of new tribal characters
- Sword of Islam: another take on feudalism, plus roughly 1/3 of the map unlocked to play with
- Way of Life: all the character focuses and the events they generate give the game so much more... the Seduction focus seems to be hated by the community, but it's fun, especially when you play with your friends. :P Also, don't be surprised if you die of syphilis.
- Sons of Abraham: Jewish characters unlocked and some extra gold to be borrowed in times of need
- Conclave: Your own council becomes your worst enemy, imo makes the game slightly harder
All in all, a great game, the only thing I could see it being better is if Paradox made multiplayer more stable, my friends often complain they've lost control over their troops and the game client needs rebooting, also whenever someone drops from the host, everyone has to reboot the client, as the multiplayer button is greyed out. Now this wouldn't bother me much, except sometimes you have to do it multiple times in a row until everyone can play again.
So for me, single player 9/10, it's almost flawless, but for multiplayer it's only an 8/10, still a great experience (the other day we were laughing our♥♥♥♥♥♥off on a lunatic character's horse councillor, then I murdered it), but some fixes need to be done to make it perfect.
I'd definitely recommend if:
- you like sandbox strategy games
- you like history and want to be part of it
- you'd like to know more about medieval hierarchy
- you'd rather lead a dynasty rather than a nation
- you just want to watch the world burn

WARNING: MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS TO SHADOW OF CHERNOBYL. READ AT YOUR OWN RISK!!!! Call of Pripyat is the third installment in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series of survival horror, single player games. It directly follows up the events of Shadow of Chernobyl. The path to the center of The Zone is open for all. The military sends in five helicopters all headed to the CNPP. The mission is designated Operation Fairway. But they all mysteriously crash. As Major Alexander Degtyarev, it is your job to find what caused Operation Fairway to fail. I won't go any further into the plot than that. The gameplay is mostly similar to the previous games. The controls are pretty straightforward. Though you can change them to fit your liking if you're not happy with the default settings. Most of the same mechanics are still there. You still need to eat and watch your radiation meter. Artifact hunting is a bit more fun and interesting this time around. In Call of Pripyat, you get an item called a detector. And it does exactly what it sounds like it does. The first one you start off with isn't really that great though. But the more advanced ones will display exactly where an artifact will spawn in an anomaly. Side missions in Call of Pripyat are a huge improvement over the last two games. They are also much more rewarding. You might be given the coordinates to a stash hidden in the forest, or a discount on weapon and armor repairs/modifications. But those aren't the only rewards for completing missions. There's also a bigger emphasis on exploration. Simply while exploring abandoned buildings you might come across some documents. And here you have a choice, you could sell the documents to one of the local traders for a hefty price to upgrade your gear and maybe buy some much needed medical supplies. Or, you could give them to the leader of one of the many factions in The Zone which could in turn lead to some extra missions which could possibly have a much larger reward. It's completely up to you. There's also some pretty incredible anomaly formations where there could possibly be some very valuable artifacts just waiting to be found. The graphics in this game are beautiful. Even without mods, the game still looks incredible on max settings. Each area in The Zone has its own look and feel. Probably should've mentioned there are three large areas to explore; Zaton, Yanov, and Pripyat. From the abandoned streets and apartment complexes of Pripyat, to the rainsoaked swamps of Zaton, each area has its own atmosphere to it. Speaking of atmosphere, Call of Pripyat isn't as scary or intense as Shadow of Chernobyl mind you. But there were a couple moments that had me on the edge of my seat, with my heart racing. In one mission, you assist a hunter seek out the reason for recent S.T.A.L.K.E.R disappearances which leads to the discovery of a Bloodsucker lair filled with sleeping Bloodsuckers. I could feel my heart beat in my chest as I crept past them, careful not to make a sound. For even the loading of a shotgun could awaken the beasts. You do not want to get trapped out at night and accidentally walk right into the lair of a Chimera. As far as bugs go, I have yet to actually encounter any. Not to say there aren't any. Final verdict: Call of Pripyat is an amazing game. I would highly recommend it to any fan of post-apocalyptic, survival horror games. 10/10. P.S If you beat the game and feel like playing it again, I HIGHLY RECCOMEND THE MISERY MOD. But do not use it on your first playthrough. I strongly discourage it. Unless you like a huge challenge.

Game is completely unplayable for a large number of people.  Many people get stuck at loading screen with their character in the game being killed.  When it works it is alot of fun.  90% of the time the game doesn't work and the only fix is to wipe everything and start over, or start on a new server because you can no longer log in to your character. That being said I still have hopes for the game.  Just can't reccomend it.
Pros:
-Beautiful game world.  I love the graphics and exploring.
-Great building system (Albeit very buggy).  you can build some nice stuff when you are not having torubles placing a wall, ceiling, or stair.
-Nice crafting system
-The one dungeon is fun but really short.
Cons:
-Very buggy, many are near game breaking including a login bug that can occur if you log out in the wrong place and can prevent you from ever logging in again on that server unless a admin resets/deletes your character.
-Lots of placement issues when building.  Often depends on moving a few feet then trying to place something in the exact same location and orientation to get it to finally accept it as a valid placement.
-Poor combat system.  Very basic with no strategy, just spamming attack.
-Almost no PVE content
-PVP base raiding is so easy that it is not worthwhile to build nice bases as even tier 3 bases can be raided or destroyed with minimal effort.
-Poor mapping of blocks.  Decorations and NPCS often end up partially or completely in your buildings.
-Very little equipment to craft
-Loot tables are poorly constructed so no useful loot can ever be found in PVE.
-Unoptimized graphics.  The game is a graphics hog.  My Geforce Titan X chokes on the game at high graphics.  Regulary drives my graphics card to near max operating temperature.
-Very small map (expansions to the map are eventually coming)

I remember playing this game at my friend's house on his ancient Dell computer, and to my surprise, it still holds up to this day. The voice acting and plot are excellent, and miles above more recent RPGs like Skyrim and even Witcher. Don't get me wrong, Witcher 3 is incredible, but Geralt is honestly a monotonous slug. He sounds like Bat-Bale grumbling in his sleep, but even quieter, somehow.
Baldur's Gate doesn't have this problem, with memorable voice actors who bring life and vibrance to the characters they play. Even the personailities you hate will stick in your head long after you finish (coughMinsc), and main villain Jon Irenicus is still one of the best antagonists in any video game. He doeesn't have time to stand around monologuing about his evil plans of world domination, he's too busy experimenting on humans and/or blasting them into red mist. I'm pretty sure he wipes out half the wizard population all by himself over the course of the game.
You should absolutely play this if you enjoy old-school RPGs, and especially if you're a D&D(2e) fan. The replayability is amazing, as most quests can be solved in multiple ways, often good or evil, and each class gets its own unique missions to acquire their base. The main story is long, but if you try to completely every side quest alongside it, you will be looking at well over a hundred hours on just a single character. Better yet, I can't remember a single fetch quest, and even the simple "retrieve item for person" quests had an interesting backstory to them. It's a lot of content, and more importantly, it's all quality stuff.

**Updated 25/08/'17**
What's changed: PvP is slightly better, but still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Human AI is less buggy, but still extremely easy to exploit to the point of rendering thralls utterly useless. Gear disparity is only made worse with the new "expansion".
I have a much more in-depth criticism of the game here:
tl;dr: If you like building, and don't mind rebuilding/changing location every day, and have a good deal of patience towards griefers, get the game. If you don't like building (OR) want to do PvP (OR) want to do PvE, don't buy the game.
PvP - The PvP has some worth, now that the devs added a dodging system. It plays like a very poor dark souls, primarily due to two reasons. The first, is that the hitboxes are very out of whack. You may dodge an attack before it hits you, but since the attack animation has started playing, you get hurt. In otherwords, you don't dodge attacks. You dodge when you think they're going to attack. Which is complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
And if you are losing a fight, all you have to do is sheath your weapons, and then run away. You can sprint when you have weapons sheathed, but not when they're equipped. The reason why that's implemented, as that the sprint mechanic is overpowered; before the change, the meta was to sprint and spam your left mouse button.
Now, the meta is to spam your left mouse button, sprint away, then edge closer whilst spamming your left mouse button.
If a player with a warhammer attacks you, even if it's made of stone, and you are not wearing the best gear the game has to offer, you will be stunlocked into oblivion.
Damage is still very messed up. If the enemy has armour, the solution is to make an Ancient Khopesh (easily attainable), and then spam left click. You can kill an end-game player in a couple seconds. But lo' and behold, the devs have added in two new tiers of damage! Now you can kill players in record time with a star metal sword, which is easily attainable for alpha clans, and very hard for solo players. Great, more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t level and gear disparity.
There is no block, unless you use a shield, keep your distance (which nullifies the whole point of a shield in the first place), aren't lagging, your opponent isn't lagging, and the server isn't lagging.
Building - Great building system ruined by extremely unbalanced raiding system.
The building is fantastic. If you loved Fallout 4's settlement system, which I did, you'll love the building in this game. Sure, most people make box houses, but you have the ability to make all sorts of awesome architecture. Viking long houses, stilted tribal villages, sprawling medieval fortresses, slave camps, gigantic altars, it's all possible and a joy to make.
But it's extremely easy for players to make your effort null. Kill a few dead-in-2-hits enemies (baby dragons) for some material that's supposed to be rare and hard to come by, make it into explosives, and plop it down at somebody's base. Bring a couple spare for destroying the more advanced continers, and you've just robbed a player of everything he owns. In under two minutes.
PvE - Terrible. Take the AI from Wurm, and make it janky, stuttery and unable to make a meaningful number of attacks. Never mind the accuracy of 'em.
With the new update, the human AI is at least not as prone to stuttering. But still very easy to cheese and exploit. If you position yourself above a human thrall, they will not be able to hurt you, whereas you can still attack them; they have only one aiming direction, and that is forwards.
Archer thralls are pathetically short ranged. It's only an effort of tedium to stand far away from an archer thrall, and shoot it to death. Repeat ad nauseam for all the archer thralls in your way, and proceed to loot the player's base.
Visuals - Superb.
Performance - Terrible. If the devs use instancing and/or robust batching, it sure doesn't feel like it. And the LOD only has a couple levels; high detail, and med-high detail. GPU Performance plummets in the more attractive parts of the game.
The server software is also mostly single threaded, and the server runs all of it's connections in one main thread. This is extremely bad, and it shows.

I'm going to start this off by saying that I've never played any truck simulator before this. I decided to grab it after seeing a YouTuber playing it. I have to say that I am not disappointed.
This game is incredibly relaxing. Driving across the Southwest while listening to 90s country is just an incredible experience. It's a great way to unwind after a long day.
The trucks handle well, but I'll also add that I've never driven a truck in real life, so I can't say whether the handling is realistic. I'd highly recommend using a steering wheel with this game. Keyboard or controller use is possible, but you'd be missing out on a huge aspect of the game, in my opinion.
The graphics are okay. They won't blow you away, but they are acceptable. If graphics are a major factor for you, there are mods that help with this. I'd also recommend a sound mod, as the default sounds are somewhat lackluster.

I have now owned Overgrowth since its days in early development back in 2013, and i have to say, although progress had been slow, it has come very far for such a small development team. And I have to say, the wait was worth it for the finished product.
Pros: 1. Its fun if you enjoy ragdoll physics, throwing blades, and beating the bazzingas out of
your enemies in general.
2. The graphics are gorgeous, and the music is really well made and enjoyable to listen to.
3. The main story is a decent one, although it could be improved in some areas near the
end.
4. The combat and climbing system is extremely interesting and fun, and let me add how OP
the jump kick is.
5. The gore is good.
6. Levels look good and are made well to suit the parkour.
7. The workshop feature is good for once you have done the main stories, and the extra
arena battles are fun little
things to waste some time on.
8. At the time of writing this there are two storylines to play.
Cons: 1. The main story is quite short, I beat it in just under two hours on medium difficulty, which
wasn't hard at all- although take that with a pinch of salt considering I've got the hang of
the combat system.
2. Sometimes performance will drop a lot if the level has rain or snow falling, although not
all the time.
3. The combat system can be exploited rather easily with the jump kick, as you can one
shot enemies at the end of the game when they are meant to be challenging.
4. It does get quite repetitive after an hour or two or solid gameplay, so it's better off played
in little go's.
Overall I  recommend this game if you want a fun little fighting game, with a decent storyline, nice fluent controls and combat, funny ragdoll moments, and lots of blood too.

EDIT 8/15/2016:
As of the date above, I am changing my review of this game from positive to negative.
The game is falling apart.
I don't know what the developers are doing, but alot of the game's content has been removed.
Specifically the "Nests" - Special dungeons that used to be run in party's to get decent gear and drops for your level bracket.
They have removed nearly all the nests except the ones for very high levels (dont quote me on this) but I believe any Nests under level 70 or 80 have been removed entirely.
Also, board quests have been completely removed from the game (bonus quests that you could pick up to turn in for xp. Posted on small boards before dungeon entrances). Those board quests made grinding an option, as many were repeatable for xp. They also gave people the option to not have to run through any quests but the main story quest line. Now you are actually forced to go through numerous npc side quests for reasonable xp. This is a very frustrating point for people who have more than one character and dont wanna have to re-read the entire storys content/ menial side content.
I've noticed large portions of the game's dialogue is now showing up in korean. I know this is a korean developed game, but everything in this version was originally properly translated and coded into english. It's very frustrating now to click on things like NPC's or boards only for it to come up completely in Korean and you have 0 idea whatis being said.
*THIS GAME NO LONGER HAS A DIFFICULTY LEVEL. THERE IS NO DIFFICULTY!
Yes folks, you read that right. After taking hiatus from this game, returning, and making a new character on the newely released silver hunter class- I was legitimately shocked, and disgusted at how easy the dungeons were.
I was able to basically 2 hit everything in the dungeons. BUT IT GETS BETTER!
As you level, nexon gives you this free special level up chest you can open which often has 5 to 7 day costumes and acessories you can equip to make your character look nice. But guess what? Those sets give stat benefits.
Literally be amazed as you equip your costume and go from 2 shotting, to 1 shotting literally everything in the dungeons- INCLUDING the boss of each dungeon. I kid you not, 1 skill was all it took me to defeat bosses, and it gave me 0 satisfaction.
I brought a friend who was new to the game to try to play with me, and even he complained about the game being too easy. He said he didn't feel like he really was doing anything.
Even hard mode still poses 0 challenge, even if you have sh*t common gears and weaponry.
I also heard the highest difficulty setting for the dungeons ABYSS mode (which also dished out the best xp and rewards for completion), was removed completely for all the low to mid level dungeons and are only reserved for very high level dungeons (again i believe somewhere above lvl 70 to 80 but don't quote me). I can only confirm that there was no abyss mode for the lower level dungeons anymore, as I was too disgusted with the state of the game to bother logging on the my higher level alt to check the other dungeons.
But as usual, the character models, attacks, specializations, and effects are still pretty awsome.
HOWEVER.
This game is far from the fantasy MMO it was when i first picked it up. If anything it is more of a hack n slash PVP game. Literally PVP is the only redeeming thing left in this game, and to PVP decently you have to level.
All of the basic fundamentals of what used to make this game great for some reason have been made exclusive to high levels or people nearing the level cap, leaving little rewarding content for the rest of the majority of the game. This has caused many people to abandon the game all together, and i've definitely noticed a decrease in the number of players.
In it's current state I would absolutely not reccomend this game.

I can't believe that I haven't played this sooner, but at least I do now. Warframe is something I have seen a long time ago, ever since it's release actually, but never really gave too much attention for it mainly because it was so rigid at the time, and so it was dumped with the rest of my never to be seen video games again list. That is until there was a massive uproar about this Plains of Eidolon update. That was the call that made me come back to Warframe to check what all the fuss is all about, then I noticed it, for the past couple of years since it's release, Warframe has been constantly updated to the point of it being able to go toe-to-toe with other AAA video game titles. This has a lot to say to the developers of Warframe. Warframe wouldn't be Warframe today if it wasn't done by such dedicated developers.
One thing I love about Warframe is that it doesn't spoon-feed you at all, excluding the tutorial of course. It lets you discover what is beneath its surface by yourself. Now this isn't something that is for everyone, some prefers for all of the video game's functions to be taught to them right off the bat, but for me and possibly others as well, the sense of accomplishment when one discovers something is exhilirating. The tutorial teaches you basic movements like how to sprint, crouch, slide, and jump. And you might think that that's it, but no. The longer you play Warframe, you might accidentally press your crouch button while you're sprinting, that in turn makes your character slide, then you'd press your jump button, then you'll notice something, your character just spun forward like a torpedo, then you'll try it again, and again, and again, until it becomes part of your way of traversing.
But that is just the movement part, I haven't even talked about the variety of Warframes and arsenal of weapons and mods offered by Warframe. And all these three caters to everyone's style of playing. Warframe doesn't tell you what Warframe to choose, what weapon to prefer, and what mods to install, everything is entirely up to you. Warframe doesn't dictate your pace. It is also worth mentioning that everything in Warframe can be earned entirely for free without spending anything aside from your time and patience for grinding.
I would also like to talk about Warframe's customization. The customization of Warframe is outstanding. You can customize everything, from the Warframe that you are using to your very own ship. And you don't just pick one color and that's it, every part of everything you own can have a different color. You can also choose different skins, and some of them if not most are not just re-skins, but actually have their own design.
Lastly, there's still a lot more that I want to add in this review, but I fear that it's now far too long, I even doubt that someone would read this. I want to talk about the community of Warframe. From the developers, Digital Extremes or DE, to the players themselves. I just want to say that DE is a group of developers that actually listens to their players, the interaction they have with the community is what made Warframe really enjoyable because they know what we want. Kudos to them as well for not being a greedy group of developers. They have done a tremendously great job for a free-to-play title. Warframe has a quality the far outclasses most AAA video games, and it's still being updated constantly, yet everything remains free, everything can be earned by grinding, even the premium currency, Platinum. As for the players, since Warframe is a PvE focused video game, everyone is really kind with each other, and from my experience, even the most experienced players are really willing to help out beginners such as myself when I first started out.
Warframe is certainly not for everyone, but you wouldn't know if it's for you if you don't try it yourself.
This concludes my review for Warframe.

Despite hints of its pay-to-win nature, I initially felt I’d been a little too harsh on the game after completing my first impressions video.
Then I played for a couple more hours…..
At this point I was locked out of all the game modes apart from practice. I either had to purchase more energy or wait a number of real-world hours.
(My first impressions video)
The pay to win rears it's head when you’ve played for a couple of hours and have access to research. Research lets you create combo cards (the games only interesting mechanic which they’ve ruined) but you have to wait 8 hours for them to complete. You can pay real money to speed up the process.
Combo cards are powerful and usually take 2 turns to play. Researching a combo card lets you drop it in one turn. This lessens the RNG when playing and means if you get a decent combo card down early you’re likely to win, until you reach a player with a better combo card or a higher level character. This game is not skill based that's for sure.
You can also upgrade cards to make them more powerful and all of this can be done more quickly with real money. Hence, the more you pay, the more likely you are to win. This game is after your cash, nothing more. Steam is flushed with free CCGs at the moment and a lot of them are not only far superior games, they have a fair fairer business model too.
Stay away.

What makes this game so fun is also what makes it so replayable, the ability to write your own alternate history.
There are so many ways you can play out your characters. Often unexpected events lead to very interesting, challenging or downright hilarious scenarios. Very often various characters that you plays as (somtimes even those you don't plays as) will end up endearing themselves to you, as you painstakingly try to guide them succesfully through the political quagmire that the feudal system can become.
That being said, this is by no means a simple game, it is complex and can be daunting at first.
The graphics are functional, and only serve to convey information for the most part.
The majority of the storytelling will be going on in your imagination, since there are no cutscenes and events appear as a text popup with some artwork. Personally I love coming up with elaborate character stories, so this isn't even a factor for me.
Battles are simplistic in nature, essentially clashes of numbers with some factors thrown in, like commander skills and traits, terrain and so forth.
In conclusion, if you like grand strategy, I absolutely recommend it.
Edit:
A note on the DLC:
A number of it is purely cosmetic, so unnecessary unless you like to have updated sprites/portraits.
Other DLC is mostly concerned wih expanding playable dynasties, like Sword of Islam for muslim rulers, Rajas of India for Indian rulers and most recently Jade Dragon for Tibetan rulers.
These are only necessary if you want to play in a specific region and experience different mechanics.
Finally we have DLC which I would consider core to the experience, which add options for everyone or the at least the majority of characters, like Way of Life, Sons of Abraham(sort of), Conclave etc. Of course others might have different opinions of what is core or not, don't be afraid to pop by the Paradox forums and ask if need be.
My recommendation for purchasing DLC is this: If you feel it adds value to the game than buy it; on sale or otherwise.
If you feel the opposite, vote with your wallet and don't buy it.
In multiplayer you get to enjoy the same DLC as the Host anyways, so this isn't splitting the community either.

Alrighty, so I've got 30.4 Hours into this in 2 weeks. I spent $5, mostly out of "Well, I played for 30 hours, I owe them SOMETHING."
What I don't owe them, is a positive review.
There should be a "I don't want to play with people who spend more than $10 on this game" mode, because I've hit that wall 30 hours in. Warframe has shown me that F2P can be amazing, if done right. This game has given me arcade fever. It feels like Quake with more hellish legions. The sounds and visuals are stunning, the rounds are fast and brutal, and the controls are super tight. There's just enough momentum in your hopping and shotgun-jumping to make tight maneuvers challenging but rewarding to pull off. Each round lasts about 60-90 seconds (for me) and they always get me pumped. I'm not really someone who's typically driven by competition, but the challenge this game presents is too tempting for me to turn down. It's an incredible bullet hell that's devilishly satisfying to play.
One of my favorite features is how you can download and watch replays from the people topping the leaderboards so you can learn some of the tactics they use to stay alive. And in a game like this where mechanical mastery and knowledge of the challenges you'll have to face are key to survival, that's an amazing feature. Even the top-scoring run is less than eight minutes long at the time of writing this - which means the game is incredibly challenging - but there's a lot of nuance in understanding the enemy design and movement, so having an opportunity to see the game from the perspective of someone who clearly has a level of mastery beyond your own is invaluable.
The game almost feels minimalist in design. There's one game mode, and the core of the gameplay is super simple to learn. But it's brilliant in execution. It's extremely satisfying. I'm addicted to trying to beat my friends' scores. I cannot recommend this game more highly for the price.

I have been playing Crusader Kings 2 on and off almost since the vanilla launch. This game after several years manages to keep me coming back. Paradox are constantly even now a few years on pumping out DLC which have for the most part really added depth and fun to the original release of Crusader Kings 2. I almost don't know if I could play the vanilla version of the game now knowing how much has been added to the game with the DLC so really keep that in mind if you intend to buy this game.
The game is a wierd mesh of a RPG cross Real Time Grand Strategy cross Fuedal Politics simulator that can be paused and is open ended like sandbox type games. Yep. However it is an insanely clever game that really makes your decisions meaningful. Never in any other game have decisions I made become so important until sometimes I sit there for 10 minutes especially in difficult situations just thinking about the ramifications of that decision.
The game is nicely styled with graphics that are keeping well for a game a few years old. The audio is phenomenal with the score being honestly one of the best in a game I have heard in a long time. The sound effects are nice but do get occassionally annoying especially if you happen to be playing a Muslim character with multiple wives...those babies just don't stop coming! The game is also very stable and has never really frozen or crashed or bugged out. Paradox are pretty on top of bugs and issues for the most part.
So onto the actual game itself... Well in short you pick a character, any, it could be a Count or a Duke, King, Emporer and then run and maintain their dynasty. So of course this would involve marrying, raising children, educating children, organising an heir to your titles and so on and so forth. However being a Count or Duke or any other character means you also need to deal with the demands of your kingdom, duchy or County. You may need to contend with jealous relatives or you may just have your own goals of taking over all of England and becoming King. This is where the sandbox nature of the game kicks in. You do have in game goals you can aim towards however the choice is yours and the game can be taken into any direction as long you plan and work towards it.
The game once learned is easy to pick up and play anytime. But seriously it will take you a good 20-30 hours and a few play throughs to really grasp how to play the game correctly and to start making the most of the in game mechanics. But don't let that scare you off because Crusader Kings is in all honesty one of my all time favourite games. It is just one of those games I keep coming back to. You know, you can look at the menu as long as you eat at home type of games. As much as I play other titles I just keep coming back to this one.
I completely recommend this game whole heartedly and hope you have as much fun as I have had!

Animation Throwdown is another Pay to Win card game based on the smashup of 5 different American TV shows. The shows are Family Guy, Futurama, American Dad, Bob's Burgers and King of the Hill.
The objective of the game is to race to knock your opponent's lifepoints to 0 before they do it to you. The gameplay is fairly simple. You have a hand of 5 cards and you choose 1 to play on your turn. You either play it on the field or combine it with a card in your hand/field. When you play it on the field, it cannot be activated yet, similar to summoning sickness in Magic the Gathering. When you combine 2 cards, the combo needs to be researched first. At the end of your turn, you draw back up to 5 cards. The game keeps on going until one player runs of life points.
Conclusion, you may skip this P2W game. It is a plethora of money sinking methods that have been used for the gaming market. The only one that they are currently missing is Gachapon. The best price is 10,000 gems + 500 Mythic Stones for $99.99.
Notes: This is a collaboration by Fox Digital Entertainment, Synapse Games, Chinzilla and Kongregate.
1. Semi-interesting sauce
Some of the shows are interesting in real life.
1. Pay To Win
Gems, Mythic Stones, Gigittywatts, Legendary Stones. The best price is 10,000 gems + 500 Mythic Stones for $99.99. Use the gems to buy upgrades for your cards and bypass the Gigittywats grind. Starter pack costs $4.99 for 800 gems, 100 Gigittywats, 5 Energy Refills,1 L5 Professor Farnsworth, 1 L1 Paintball with Guns, 1 L1 Manger Babies
2. Super Rarity Creep
The cards are tiered into Common (Grey), Rare(Green), Epic (Blue), Legendary (Purple) and Mythic (Gold). Legendary cards have way superior stats compared to a Common. E.g. 4/10 Legendary to 4/4 Common
3. Designed to be a Time Waster
Want to do a combo? Research it for 24 hours. You need to buy a Research Accelerator for $9.99 to boost the research. Want a larger Adventure Energy Cap? Pay $9.99 to boost the Adventure Energy Cap by 25.
4. Game Mechanic Paywalls
Want more inventory space and add 50 card slots? Pay 250 Gems.
5. Crafting
1000 Mythic Stone to craft 1 Mythic Card. A Mythic card is just 1 OP card that helps you win the game. You can also look for 250 fragments and spend 5000 coins on crafting a Mythic too.
6. Upgrading and Fusion
WTF? Use Gigittywats to upgrade the cards and then fuse 2 cards of the same name and level together for the next upgrade? How much time wasting is this?
7. Bad Connections
Game always disconnects mid-game due to "Slow Connection" error.
8. Research Combos
Another WTF? In order to combo your cards, you have to research them first. Common Combs take 1 hour, Rare Combos take 8 hours. You can imagine how long more it would be for the Mythic ones.
1. Automated Combat
While I am typing this review, the game is playing itself. All I have to do is turn on automated combat. While this is a stupid feature to put in the game, I realise there is a benefit to automation. Thus, I am neutral on this.

What could I say about this game?
The game has a lots of potential, which could go well beyond what originally intended. It is a first person survial game in the surface, but with the possibility to be a roleplaying game (if players on the servers agree or you run your local server with dedicated friends). It is definietly the adult version of minecraft - the building is amazing, with mods that extend the possibilities. It is easy to make new cities, castles, even dungeons if someone creative. I haven't tried it yet, but I can immagine to be able to make player made dungeons with NPCs (thralls) as enemies or guardians to make some story/quest to others without dwelling and learning some modding.
I think the key here is to know what do you want out from this game, and seek that kind of community online. In theory the server selection offers a loads of option to you to able to find what you are looking for. There are categories where you can set PvP or PvE feautures, the community type (from roleplaying to purist), and you can read the set up small details (the progression rate, the ability to damage buildings, etc). If you still unhappy, you can make your own server with your own settings.
The game is great for someone who loves Conan or sword and sorcery, but I seepossibilities to extend beyond that. WhileI am not sure (but I think) one can make their own map with modding, it might be possible to make your own setting. I can clearly see a Dark Sun setting made with extended modding in this game for example - desert settings are there, so does the hunger and thirst rules, crafing, slavery, etc.
There are problems with the ame, perhaps the greatest challenge for me comes from a positive aspect of constant updates, as it does affect the games already started, So if you want to wait something stable, wait until the final release.
Otherwise go ahead and find your cross Exile.

This was the most enjoyable FPS I have ever played. After trying out various mods for this game, I eventually went with Misery Mod 1.0 (2.0 was too much for my wimpy laptop, but I personally think 1.0 was better anyway). I also completed the game on Master difficulty.
Modding aside, CoP is a brilliant open-world shooter. While there is a story that the player eventually needs to progress through, the open-world element puts you in control of the pace of the game so you can explore/merc all you want and then perform the essential plotline tasks when you're ready. I loved the idea of three gigantic levels taking the places of seven or eight smaller ones. The gunfights are technical and challenging. The finale of this game is terrific - probably the most intense gunfight I've experienced in a game.
By the time I was done with CoP's prequels, I was craving more difficulty, so I installed Misery, which was pretty unforgiving in the early game. It also creates a bleak atmosphere, adds new weapons, and changes the sound a bit. The mod also tweaked the random events, keeping the player on edge. I HIGHLY recommend this game with the Misery mod.

BUT if you do find a cheap 2nd hand copy of this game with it's expansion, or even the 4 disc of both 1 and 2 and thier expansions (which would probably play much better on the current crop of OS's), you'd be a fool to pass them up.

For first time players, who did not play the PSP/Vita release, it's a worth picking up. Released way back on various consoles and computers as, "Ys 3: Wanderers from Ys", it was brutally hard and I'm sure led to many a controller tossed in frustration. Back then it was only a 2-D side scrolling platformer, though in this go-around it has been given a massive facelift and brought into the 3rd dimension. There are lots of pretty visuals, excellent music, and the game play can be tailored in difficulty for the meek or the seasoned. It's got a good storyline, a lot of content, and great graphics.
Now, for those of us who DID play the PSP or Vita download versions of this game: they cut out a lot of content. Not game or quest-wise, but you'll notice that the people of this Redmont have a lot less to verbally say than their PSP counterparts. There is no way to program your controller to your liking, and the special bonus pictures and such you could earn throughout the game are gone. If you already own this and are thinking of getting it for the updated visuals and such, know they're NOT widescreen, and honestly, they don't look much better than the PSP in my own opinion.
So, if you don't have a PSP or Playstation system you can play it on, it's worth getting. Especially on sale. If you have the PSP version, stick with that one, you're not missing anything really.

I'm going to start this off by saying that I've never played any truck simulator before this. I decided to grab it after seeing a YouTuber playing it. I have to say that I am not disappointed.
This game is incredibly relaxing. Driving across the Southwest while listening to 90s country is just an incredible experience. It's a great way to unwind after a long day.
The trucks handle well, but I'll also add that I've never driven a truck in real life, so I can't say whether the handling is realistic. I'd highly recommend using a steering wheel with this game. Keyboard or controller use is possible, but you'd be missing out on a huge aspect of the game, in my opinion.
The graphics are okay. They won't blow you away, but they are acceptable. If graphics are a major factor for you, there are mods that help with this. I'd also recommend a sound mod, as the default sounds are somewhat lackluster.
As of now, the choice of trucks is lacking a bit. There are only two brands in the vanilla game (Peterbilt and Kenworth), with two trucks each for a total of four. This is not the fault of SCS, however, as they are having a hard time obtaining licenses to use other brands, so I can't fault the game for this.
Overall, this game is pretty great. For the price, it's really hard to go wrong (unless you're just not really into truck simulators). It is very relaxing and a great way to pass the time.

I'm not even sure where I got this game. But anyway, here we go.
The game has a very simplistic style. The art style is cutesey, kind of mario-worldy. Everything has beady little eyes and your character makes cute noises. Combat is very simple -- Enemies either throw things at you or attempt to run into you. You defeat them by wooshing them with a leaf. Enemy AI is as basic as you can get. When you die you are put at a random place in the world, somtimes back at the very beginning.
Your goal is to collect berries (apples? What are they?) to unlock other worlds and to gather tears to finish the current world. The beginning has a few spelling errors and there's real no rhyme or reason to what you're doing. You seem to be a tree stump trying to give water to a bigger tree, so that's your ultimate goal.
The camera, at best, is atrocious. You have a few options: Super close to your character, or super far away. There is no rotation and sometimes being put behind things causes your camera to freak out and either go really far away, or drop to ground level.
The music is nice, the style is nice.
If you are looking for a calming puzzle/platformer to play in your free time, find something else to play.
Overall score, 3/10. Definitely not worth the 3 dollars it's selling for.

After keeping an eye on this project for nearly a decade it was a profound pleasure to finally play its first release outside of beta/early access. This game became somewhat legendary for its long time in development and I saw too many people surprised at this 'final' release to count. Sort of a Redwall-meets-Mirror's-Edge, the unique fantasy atmosphere mixed with crazy fighting and parkour is really unique. The love from its development team definitely shows, but plenty of aspects can be fixed and there's so much room to grow.
Overall, Overgrowth is composed of two types of sections: combat, and parkour. Both are excellent, and the graphics and sound back it up. Physics bugs occasionally muck down the experience in both sections and the 'game' doesn't make much of an attempt to become more than just a series of levels consisting of one or both of those parts. While a lot can be improved, the foundation is solid and fun.
+Fighting
Certainly the main draw and for good reason, the fighting is varied and fun. The options in many areas to choose between stealth or going in also keeps things fresh. Enemy AI is very capable, and it was surprising and awesome to find guards chasing you up walls and on top of buildings.
+Animations
These are excellent. Character animations are very fluid across your various movement and attack options.
+Music
The music in Overgrowth is fantastic and matches each level well. Lugaru is hobbled pretty hard by its stale music, which was massively improved for Overgrowth.
+Graphics
The scenery is gorgeous and the effects added really bring everything to life: raindrops, snow, sun, and the fade of distant objects.
+Ragdolling
The death ragdolls are AWESOME.
~Physics
Where the most workable improvement can be found is in the game's physics itself. The game's fortresses are fantastic for parkour, but organic surfaces don't handle very well. Jumping around rocks or tree branches will inevitably lead to you dangling off of invisible surfaces as the game tries to rectify the situation. It never 'breaks' the game at all but it interrupts the gameplay enough and looks awkward enough to detract.
-Balance
Swords are incredibly overpowered, whether by serious intent or otherwise. Often a OHKO, both on you and on any enemy, including 'bosses'. I had one end-of-scenario fight in particular end in under a second just by clicking a few times because I started with a sword. Jump kicks are also super powerful, enough to warrant ignoring all other combat if you choose.
-Transitions
I'm not sure how to categorize this other than "everything besides the gameplay itself". The game moves along fairly abruptly, which is likely a shortcoming with the current engine. The repeated sequence of text box/kill some enemies/text box/loading screen, repeat ad infinitum, leaves the game feeling lifeless. With what was shown I don't think this is possible to improve without some change in the foundation - the main story was clearly just a set of maps with either the goal of killing the enemies or free running to the end or both. The story itself isn't bad, but a video game can't just present itself as a series of text boxes attached to different set pieces. I could be missing the point of Overgrowth when I say this all, but such a unique engine really deserves more. The ending especially is super abrupt, and while maybe Overgrowth was never intended to be a full game the ending really throws that feeling in your face.
I was hoping for more out of a single-player Overgrowth experience but I can't say I'm dissatisfied at all. While I'm sure the modding community will come up with incredible maps I hope either this or a different single player mode are developed further than simply a series of maps with story text. The game is too fun to play on a base level to leave it as is.
(Note: my actual play time is on a non-Steam version)

My traitorous cousin sits shackled, rotting in the dungeon. He asks for mercy, but I instead send him to the oubliette. My victorious armies are out on campaign, lead by my militarily savvy brother, and are poised to conquer neighboring territory for the Kingdom. Wedding bells are ringing in the churches of my capital ; my niece has just been married to my son. Yes, its just another regal day in the game of Crusader Kings 2. One of Paradox's latest entries in the grand strategy series, CK2 boasts an enormous amount of options and freedom in player choice, giving you numerous ways  to make your mark on medieval Europe.
The core of the game surrounds your control of a Medieval dynasty, and their ascent through the ranks of nobility over multiple generations. With a great deal of historical accuracy put into CK2 (you can even access the Wikipedia pages of historical characters in-game), you can choose from any number of dynasties that reigned during the course of the game's covered history (1066-1453). Not only does this give you the ability to tailor the game experience, but it adds a great deal of replayability .For example, newer players can choose to start as one of many lowly counts, while more experienced armchair monarchs can jump right into the dynastic action as a King.
On it's surface, CK2 is an intimidating game. You may want to brush up on your understanding of the feudal system, and you will definitely be learning a lot of geography from the massive map that spans from western Europe to the fringes of Asia. A distinct lack of tutorials will leave you flustered at first, wondering how you can achieve your goals within the mechanics of the game. It doesn't help that several of the games more useful features are accessed by clicking on obscure buttons.
Thankfully, once you do get a grasp on the fundamentals of the game, it is a truly rewarding experience. It is extremely satisfying when you can use the sandbox nature of the game to its full potential. Marrying into families to gain territory, installing your kinsmen on the thrones of other kingdoms, and forging empires based on your conquests are just a few of the things you can accomplish with a little guile, and the right timing.
Even as a purely single player experience, CK2 is a very strong title. But what makes the game truly entertaining, and downright dripping with potential for those who like to game with friends, is the multiplayer. The multiplayer essentially gives all the freedom of the single player experience, but with a friend, allowing you to go to war together, intermarry families, and generally have a great time taking over Europe. Few multiplayer games offer you the fun that can be had in teaming up with friends in CK2, and it adds to an already staggering amount of options when it comes to starting up a new game.
Crusader Kings 2 is not for everyone. If you hate history, this is going to be a boring game, and for the hardcore FPS fans ; you are probably wandering a little too far out of your genre. However, for the rest of the gamers out there, this is a must have title that is constantly being updated and tweaked by developers, and modded by fans. Whether you're a history buff, or just enjoy highly strategic games with a lot of depth, this one is definitely for you.

I have no idea what to review about this game. So here are instructions to tie a noose:
1)
Place the rope on a flat surface in the shape of the letter "C." Find a durable rope that is at least three feet long.
2)
Form an "S" shape with the rope. Leave the lead of the rope (the bottom part of the "S") long so that you can tie it to something when you've made the noose.
3)
Compress the "S" shape. Compress the "S" shape until all three rows of rope are nearly on top of each other, with only a few inches in between them.
4)
Pinch the three lines of rope together in the middle. Pinch them tightly until the ends fan out to create a bow-tie effect.
5)
Take the top of the original "C" and wrap it around the pinched space. Wrap it from the right side to the left, leaving about three to four inches of the rope unwrapped. You should be left with a loop and a string on the left end, and just a loop on the right end of the "bow tie."
6)
Poke the end of the rope through the top of the loop left by the "S".
7)
Pinch the coiled part of the rope. Use your thumb to hold down the short piece of rope that you just worked through the loop on the left-hand side so it bends over the loop.
8)
Pull the loop on the right-hand side of the bow until it closes the loop on the left. If this part of the loop begins to pull on the free rope instead of the loop, pull on the other side of the bow.
9)
Adjust the noose. Adjust the noose until the coils look nice and tight and the loop is the size you wanted.
There you have it! A noose :)
