What makes this game so fun is also what makes it so replayable, the ability to write your own alternate history.
There are so many ways you can play out your characters. Often unexpected events lead to very interesting, challenging or downright hilarious scenarios. Very often various characters that you plays as (somtimes even those you don't plays as) will end up endearing themselves to you, as you painstakingly try to guide them succesfully through the political quagmire that the feudal system can become.
That being said, this is by no means a simple game, it is complex and can be daunting at first.
The graphics are functional, and only serve to convey information for the most part.
The majority of the storytelling will be going on in your imagination, since there are no cutscenes and events appear as a text popup with some artwork. Personally I love coming up with elaborate character stories, so this isn't even a factor for me.
Battles are simplistic in nature, essentially clashes of numbers with some factors thrown in, like commander skills and traits, terrain and so forth.
In conclusion, if you like grand strategy, I absolutely recommend it.
Edit:
A note on the DLC:
A number of it is purely cosmetic, so unnecessary unless you like to have updated sprites/portraits.
Other DLC is mostly concerned wih expanding playable dynasties, like Sword of Islam for muslim rulers, Rajas of India for Indian rulers and most recently Jade Dragon for Tibetan rulers.
These are only necessary if you want to play in a specific region and experience different mechanics.
Finally we have DLC which I would consider core to the experience, which add options for everyone or the at least the majority of characters, like Way of Life, Sons of Abraham(sort of), Conclave etc. Of course others might have different opinions of what is core or not, don't be afraid to pop by the Paradox forums and ask if need be.
My recommendation for purchasing DLC is this: If you feel it adds value to the game than buy it; on sale or otherwise.
If you feel the opposite, vote with your wallet and don't buy it.
In multiplayer you get to enjoy the same DLC as the Host anyways, so this isn't splitting the community either.

I have been playing Crusader Kings 2 on and off almost since the vanilla launch. This game after several years manages to keep me coming back. Paradox are constantly even now a few years on pumping out DLC which have for the most part really added depth and fun to the original release of Crusader Kings 2. I almost don't know if I could play the vanilla version of the game now knowing how much has been added to the game with the DLC so really keep that in mind if you intend to buy this game.
The game is a wierd mesh of a RPG cross Real Time Grand Strategy cross Fuedal Politics simulator that can be paused and is open ended like sandbox type games. Yep. However it is an insanely clever game that really makes your decisions meaningful. Never in any other game have decisions I made become so important until sometimes I sit there for 10 minutes especially in difficult situations just thinking about the ramifications of that decision.
The game is nicely styled with graphics that are keeping well for a game a few years old. The audio is phenomenal with the score being honestly one of the best in a game I have heard in a long time. The sound effects are nice but do get occassionally annoying especially if you happen to be playing a Muslim character with multiple wives...those babies just don't stop coming! The game is also very stable and has never really frozen or crashed or bugged out. Paradox are pretty on top of bugs and issues for the most part.
So onto the actual game itself... Well in short you pick a character, any, it could be a Count or a Duke, King, Emporer and then run and maintain their dynasty. So of course this would involve marrying, raising children, educating children, organising an heir to your titles and so on and so forth. However being a Count or Duke or any other character means you also need to deal with the demands of your kingdom, duchy or County. You may need to contend with jealous relatives or you may just have your own goals of taking over all of England and becoming King. This is where the sandbox nature of the game kicks in. You do have in game goals you can aim towards however the choice is yours and the game can be taken into any direction as long you plan and work towards it.
The game once learned is easy to pick up and play anytime. But seriously it will take you a good 20-30 hours and a few play throughs to really grasp how to play the game correctly and to start making the most of the in game mechanics. But don't let that scare you off because Crusader Kings is in all honesty one of my all time favourite games. It is just one of those games I keep coming back to. You know, you can look at the menu as long as you eat at home type of games. As much as I play other titles I just keep coming back to this one.
I completely recommend this game whole heartedly and hope you have as much fun as I have had!

I am so very torn by this game it's unreal. I can't love this game and yet I want to, I can't hate it and yet I want to. I suppose I was just so excited at the premise of an open world shooter set in Pripyat, the idea alone is worth so much and yet I find myself ambivalent. It's really fun to explore the dark, depressing but not tense world of post-Chernobyl Pripyat (and the outlying areas, you don't actually REACH Pripyat until much later) but it feels so sparse. I know you'd expect that sort of thing from an irradiated area but it feels like a few meagre locations interspersed with mostly identical grassland with the occasional swamp or trees or anomaly, it works from a canonical standpoint but I feel it cheapens the whole "open world" aspect. The almost utter lack of voice acting prbably wouldn't have bothered me so much except it makes it impossible to distinguish people. They have no personality of which to speak and whatever voice acting you DO get is at best okay (sometimes you can CLEARLY hear the same person switch between two different voice actors, one in English and one in Russian), I really feel as if the NPC's in this game are a serious impediment to the enjoyment of what is otherwise quite a fine game. Gunplay is a bit turgid, the guns don't really have much feeling to them and there's no real discernible differences in firepower within the same class of firearm. All the pistols are like peashooters to most enemies, shotguns are okay and so on, although I kind of liked the Gauss Rifle which brings me to another issue in the area of sound. Most of it is actually quite good, especially at night when it gets actually really atmospheric with rather haunting animal noises, crickets and a bit of fairly repetitive but good background music. But a lot of the audio sounds so uninspired and boring, especially gunfire (with particular note to the Gauss Rifle, it sounds terrible), item noises sometimes don't make sense and can get repetitive (although that is understandable). The ending was also really abrupt and very unsatisfactory. Yet despite its many failings this game has quite a bit to offer the discerning gamer, even if I can't quite elucidate my reasons for liking it. All I can say it's atmospheric, the world is pretty good looking if sparse and the concept of anomalies and stuff in Pripyat is interesting and quite engaging. This game might not live up to its potential but it is worth your time. I sincerely hope they get some experienced devs to make the sequel this IP deserves.
EDIT: I suppose in retrospect this review looked quite negative, but this is a really engrossing game at times and the fact that there's no hand holding or explanation of which to speak means that it's on you to figure everything out and that's always a plus for immersion. If it's ever on sale do buy this game, for all its flaws it is still a good game.

When games are good, but fall short in very obvious ways, it's always a little disappointing. The game is fun! But it takes too long to get started. There's somewhere around 10-15 minutes from pressing New Game to being let out into the world. Around 4-6 hours into the game, you can get an item that lets you regenerate health if you stand still. This is a needed mechanic, since you're going to have to beat up on a lot of enemies to level up for the boss fights, but standing still is not fun. The game has a 'Boost mode', in which you deal extra damage and take less damage for a limited time, after you fill up a gauge that fills up as you take and deal damage. Why not tie the regenerating health to damage done in boost mode? That would set up a dillema for the player: Do I keep fighting since boost mode is almost full, or do I not take the risk and teleport back to town to heal? Instead, if I find myself in danger after clearing a room, I just stand still for 30 seconds. Somewhere in Falcom, a ball lays on the ground, dropped.
JRPGs get a lot of flack for grinding, and there's plenty here to go around. It's really not that bad, since only monsters that pose a threat give good experience and gold. I died several times while grinding, since I thought I could go just a little more before having to heal. It's a lot more tense and exciting than beating up Rattata outside Pewter City's gym. The story is cliched and filled to the brim with classic JRPG tropes, which I can sort of forgive for a game released in 2005, but I wouldn't hate the Ys series if it took a less serious tone in it's story department, maybe something like Half Minute Hero.

Gameplay: 8/10
+Bots handle very well, and firepower feels just right.
+Good physics engine allows bots to collide, fly, climb on walls, and experience believable recoil from massive guns.
+Bot customization has a significant impact on your play. Such variety. Many cool. Wow.
-Strategy is dominated by snipers. The only way to beat spider-tank snipers is with more snipers.
+There are so few problems with the gameplay that I have to nitpick about snipers so I don't seem one-sided.
Free-to-play model: 9/10
+Good overall. Free players level up quickly, earning enough points to buy a new part every three matches.
+++No microtransactions that I can find. Seriously, Doctor Entertainment is credit to team.
Uniqueness: 5/10
+The art style is cute. I get a serious micro-machines vibe, which hits me right in the childhood.
-The market has robot-building games out the wazoo. Robocraft, Terratech, From the Depths, AirMech, M.A.V., Guns and Robots, and the list goes on and on. Gear Up seems to be just the latest to jump on the bandwagon.
-This feels like War Thunder meets Robocraft, but without the customization, strategy, or destruction physics of either.
-As robot-building games go, this one really has little customization.
Technical: 2/10
---The Traktor game engine may offer nice physics, but its performance is a travesty. On a decent PC (80+FPS on TF2), with the graphics all turned down as far as they'd go, the game ran at 15FPS (measured with FRAPS, not the in-game utility, which falsely reported over 100).
-15FPS.
-Brutal crashes. Don't try to change the texture quality. Just... don't.
-15FPS.
-Load times indicate the use of hamster messengers for data transfer.
-15FPS.
+Good audio options. You can change ambient sounds, vehicle sounds, and music independently.
-15FPS.
+Fully customizable gamepad. About time more developers started doing that.
-15FPS.
Summary:
If you really like the artstyle and direction this game takes, and that is enough to lure you away from the endless stream of other Robot Wars wannabes, then yeah. Take a look. It might just captivate you.
This being said, I can not recommend investing in this game until Doctor Entertainment shows that they can get their engine running better.
-15FPS.

The number of hours I've played this game on Steam are a mere tithe of the numbers I've spent playing my boxed CD edition - probably as many as I've spent in Skyrim (more than 1,000). This was my first ever video game, and it was so good that it converted me into a gamer.
Although Oblivion lacks the intense conversations and interactions, and superb VA, of games such as Dragon Age: Origins, it has a great deal to bring to the table.
* It is a vast, open world game - it isn't linear at all (not only can you do the main quest first and keep playing, or leave it until last, you can simply not do it at all).  If you love exploration, it's hard to beat an Elder Scrolls game.
* There are a number of good DLC that add more content.
* It lacks the limiting class systems of so many games, allowing you to play your characters as you choose: a warrior who can cast healing spells on themselves and others; a cloth-wearing mage who can fight effectively with weapons when they run out of mana (if they train with them); a stealth-based character who can kill while undetected, go toe-to-toe with melee weapons if need be, and can use magic too. The skills your characters become good - or great - at are those they use or train in.
* Difficulty of particular quests and areas scales with character level. Some people hate this - I don't.
* There is a huge modding community that can make a great game even greater.

When I first played Oblivion (on a console) many, many years ago, it would have been an enormous understatement for me to say that I loved the game.  Oblivion was the first time I had ever ventured alone into an open-world game, and after those first few steps I was hooked.  I was forging my own path through this immense and shapeable world, and it felt great.  The game consumed my free time; I spent dozens of hours across multiple characters fully immersed and invested in in this game, this world.  Returning to Tamriel was always a sweet experience, even as my devotion lessened.
Now, it's been a solid few years since I last played Oblivion.  Since then, I've made my way through and have had a blast within several other open-world games, Skyrim of course being one of them.  Circumstances recently brought me back to Oblivion after all these years, and as the game installed I couldn't help but ask myself: is this going to be the same game I remember?  Several hours later, and here I am.
I'm not here to try and compare this game to Skyrim or Morrowind, even though some comparisons will be necessary.  I'm not here to see if this game holds up to the standards of today's industry because, when it comes down to it, I know it doesn't.  Rather, what I am doing is reviewing this game as an old fan who's come back after a long time away.  I want you to know whether or not Oblivion can still provide a genuinely fun experience even after all these years.
And to cut a long review short: I do.  But not without some big catches.
Oblivion is a solid roleplaying experience at heart, and I think that's the most important aspect here.  I will never, ever get tired of exiting that sewer system and asking myself: what am I going to do in this world?  I will always be charmed by the life, color, sound, and music of the game's world, especially when contrasted with the frozen tundra of Skyrim.  The people of Cyrodiil, while infamously hideous, are enjoyable to listen to and worth "knowing."  It almost feels as if there's something worth knowing about every individual NPC, and I think that's a wonderful bit of charisma that isn't as prominent in other games.
That said, the immersion of Oblivion's world is largely the only quality of the game to have endured the test of time.  Despite all the warmth Cyrodiil provides, Oblivion's vanilla gameplay experience will feel very dated to anyone who decides to give it a shot.  Your character simply never feels powerful due to creature level scaling and other tweaks, and becoming a "master" at the game does not aid in your ability to overcome a system that is, generally, unfair.  Wonky animations, corny voice-acting, and lackluster combat don't help, and it is for these reasons that I highly suggest using mods to tweak Oblivion to a much more enjoyable level of playability.
Simply put, I do honestly think Oblivion needs to be modded to be enjoyed in this day and age.  So many other games have come along and done it better at this point that Oblivion does really feel as if it needs a crucial update, and mods are the only way to go.  With mods, the game can become a vastly better experience, but this does mean that those unfamiliar with modding have several hoops to jump through before the game reaches its highest potential.  The obvious incentive though is that everything you love about Oblivion can be enhanced, while everything you hate can be fixed.  I believe modding is a must for this game, but of course the degree of necessary changes is largely up to personal preference.
Overall, I do recommend Oblivion, but not as a vanilla experience.  Time and modders have proven that Oblivion is a game that needed fixing and that it's capable of much more than its original design.  This is not to say that the vanilla experience is completely "not fun," but it is the foundation for what could be a much more refined experience.  That said, to return to an earlier point, there will always be a charm to Oblivion that I don't see in its successor or competitors.  The world has humor, charisma, life.  It doesn't really take itself too seriously, and consequently a lot of those wonky little flaws (like ugly NPCs and weird animations) sort of come to enhance the fun of the game rather than completely distract from them.  In a way, these qualities of the game are just as familiar to me as the landscapes and cities, and to see them again is honestly a welcome sight.
Oblivion still has its charm, and I believe that is what matters most.

It took me a long time to properly write out this review as I honestly did not know what exactly to say about the game.
Overgrowth has been in development for nearly 9 years at this point and is finally in its final beta stage. Over the years, the game has changed drastically with its level design and editor. However, the core of the game has remained mostly the same. The same parkour, the same combat system, the same enemy AI with a few small tweaks. This means that in the last 9 years the developers have only added two campaigns and some arena maps (which are in the campaign). While I have never made a game myself, this seems like an incredibly long time for the content that's there.
As previously stated, there is not much content to play through. The Lugaru story was a simple port but was still practically an entirely new portion from a game design perspective. It can take around an hour or two to complete. The main Overgrowth story, a sequel to Lugaru, can take a little longer - probably around three hours - and the writing is above average at best and mediocre at worst. The arena maps are all practically the same and get boring after a while. Besides the sandbox levels and the local only versus, that's it. From the vanilla content, you'll get around 10 hours of gameplay if you
push it. Obviously, there is workshop support, but that is not representative of the product the devs are selling.
This is easily the game's best feature. The combat here is some of the best in any game I have ever played. Even games like the Arkham series do not reach the amazingly fun and satisfying levels of this game. There is so much about this combat that is done right:
In addition to this, the game has some light stealth mechanics which allow for pacifist choking-out of enemies, throat slitting, and dragging bodies. Despite all of this, there is one fatal flaw with the combat system...
This is the most overpowered move in the game. It allows for an instant kill on some enemies and incredibly high damage on others. While it is difficult to execute at first, you quickly get the hang of it and realise that there is no point in any other move in the game. Why have a tense and stressful battle with the enemy, dodging attacks and getting a hit in whenever possible when you can avoid combat altogether in one simple move? This issue can be solved by playing as other creatures, such as cats, but these do not have the same free-running abilities as rabbits. Speaking of parkour...
While the parkour in this game is not as complicated as that of games such as Mirror's Edge, it is still incredibly fast and fluid, allowing for fun parkour portions or even full maps. It also combines well with the combat, allowing for fast-paced free-running encounters. However, the enemy AI seems to have not quite worked out how the parkour works, as it will mainly just jump in the direction of the player - even with bottomless pits in the way. This definitely needs some work before the final release (though I doubt the devs would make such drastic changes so close to release).
I really
want to recommend this game, but I simply cannot in its current state. It lacks the polish and content required for a full release. Especially for the current price of £22.99, this game is - sadly - not worth your money.
EDIT: Though I may have got a few things wrong, such as the way the damage system works (just look it up), these points still stand after release.

First impression after 16 levels: annoying physics puzzler/3D platformer.
Please note that most positive reviews have rather short play times; only 3% of players even got the first achievement or finished the game, and judging by the "Global Leaderboard" here on Steam, those are 12 (twelve) players in all. Why is that? Isn't the game aimed at children familiar with "Bob the Builder"?
Well, in theory that's the case, but in practice the game suffers from its unpredictable physics; if you had hoped for a sandbox-y experience, there's little opportunity of that, and the game does punish exploration by making you drop through the floor or otherwise fail in many "wtf" ways.
Sop you follow the obvious path through a level (which is most often the only path the camera angles actually allow you to see), doing the obvious forklifting/craning, with obstinate controls (rotating crane control is especially weird: instead of rotating the crane and moving the trolley, you move the position of the hook up/down/left/right, which can result in some erratic movements). Stacking crates one atop the other with the forklift is practically impossible; it works when the base is wide, i.e. one crate rests on two others. Sort of. Stuff just goes wrong or behaves unexpectedly a lot.
The physics interactions in this game are quite few; if the devs had not gone with a general physics engine, but written code for these interactions separfately "oldschool" style, the game would have been a lot better. Crates and vehicles don't need to topple over. The crane hook doesn't need to swing around at the end of "fake" cable. The physics code should've allowed the player to execute a solution plan in a predictable fashion. Currently, that's just not the case.
So who is the target audience for this game? It can't be small children because of the wonky contrrols (no gamepad support) ; it can't be puzzle players because the puzzles are easy; it can't be physics game fans because experimenting with the physics in this game is rarely rewarding.
Get this if you like games that are sort of weird and sort of bad and sort of cheap. You won't miss anything if you don't.

Animation Throwdown is a card collecting game incorporating five Twentieth Century Fox Television animated comedies: American Dad!, Bob’s Burgers, Family Guy, Futurama, and King of the Hill.  Game is also on Kongregate, IOS and Android.  Gameplay is similiar to other free to play CCGs, but has some different features.  You have a deck with a limit of 35 cards, which give you enough chances to get the cards you want out.  PVP arena is the only place where you can level up your deck hero and unlock other deck heroes, you get random chances of receiving xp for a random hero.  The game is Pay to Win so don't expect to win much verses a P2W player, if you don't Pay or didn't grind it like a job.
PRO:
- Has Consecutive daily login reward system that give out resources and items that help F2P players out ( including Mythic stones, 8hr research speedups, arena beers, gems, gigitybits, golden turds, hero token, legendary stones.)
- Has a Daliy quest that rewards gigitybits and gems, that is easy enough for everyone to do.
- Has some funny sayings, but some have colorfull langauge.
- Great graphics that looks like the media it is based on.
- Fans of the five comedies will find something to like here.
- Looks like you can play the game for a while free if you have patience, willpower, and smarts.
- You can get 1 random card for 1000 in-game money, you earn quite a lot of this currency.  There are other currencies you can earn by playing to buy card packs.
- You can get more cards for rewards from PVE campaigns, event rewards, PVP rewards.
- If you know what you are doing, you might win more matches.
- Has a simple tutorial to get you started.
- Has PVE events to play through, separate from your energy limit, the energy recharges the fastest with PVE campaign.
- Has 30 PVE campaign tiers with 3 opponents each that can be played again to advance the difficulty of Bronze, silver, gold, black.  Each get progressively higher difficultly as you go up in number.  Some have set decks that you have to figure out how to beat.
- Has guilds that provide buffs to members, and guild vs guild battles that give more rewards.
- Has auto-battle toogle using  AI and speed increase toggle and instant complete button and surrender match button.
- Has asynchronous PVP with ok matchmaking, when you increase your win streak your chances of getting matched to a P2W player increases.
- PVP opponents is AI bots using the player's deck, no real PVP and no bad sportmanship.
- You can reroll your opponent in PVP arena by paying 100 pennys, and you can look at their hero details. so if you notice a hard player you can skip them.
- You can practice battle with players in PVP arena and with other guild members.
- Match conditions change over time, called Battleground Effect, changes every month.
CONS:
- Is Pay to Win, since there is PVP between players and what you can buy in the store can give you an advantage over players that don't spend money or as much money as you spent.
- Players that started playing at the Startup of the game, Will have the advantage over everyone else.
- The chances of getting the cards that you want and need are lousy.  You will have to make do with what you got.
- You are limited to holding 200 cards in your inventory at start.  Have to buy 50 card upgrade for 250-500-750-? gems.  You will be spending your earned gems only on increasing your inventory space.  You need your inventory space to hold all the cards you get to make the various builds needed for various match conditions.
-  You will be making hard choices on what cards to destroy for upgrade resources and free up inventory space.
- Some card combos are overpowered.
- Some deck builds are overpowered.
- Some cards are overpowered.
- Has PVP, so there will be matches you lose just from bad matchup with higher level or P2W player.
- Does not have in-game Help.
- The auto-battle AI misses better moves than what an knowledgable player would do with their deck.
- Has many progressively increasing timers and energy system, so you might have to stretch your playing out.
- Free to Play Players will take a long time to earn enough points to get just 1 Mythic card, need Mythic cards to compete with P2W players.
- Game Not for young children, has some bad language.
- Game does not have chat built into it, you chat through the Kongregate website.
Try it, maybe you might like it.  Don't pay money for this game. Quit when you tired of it.

When games are good, but fall short in very obvious ways, it's always a little disappointing. The game is fun! But it takes too long to get started. There's somewhere around 10-15 minutes from pressing New Game to being let out into the world. Around 4-6 hours into the game, you can get an item that lets you regenerate health if you stand still. This is a needed mechanic, since you're going to have to beat up on a lot of enemies to level up for the boss fights, but standing still is not fun. The game has a 'Boost mode', in which you deal extra damage and take less damage for a limited time, after you fill up a gauge that fills up as you take and deal damage. Why not tie the regenerating health to damage done in boost mode? That would set up a dillema for the player: Do I keep fighting since boost mode is almost full, or do I not take the risk and teleport back to town to heal? Instead, if I find myself in danger after clearing a room, I just stand still for 30 seconds. Somewhere in Falcom, a ball lays on the ground, dropped.
JRPGs get a lot of flack for grinding, and there's plenty here to go around. It's really not that bad, since only monsters that pose a threat give good experience and gold. I died several times while grinding, since I thought I could go just a little more before having to heal. It's a lot more tense and exciting than beating up Rattata outside Pewter City's gym. The story is cliched and filled to the brim with classic JRPG tropes, which I can sort of forgive for a game released in 2005, but I wouldn't hate the Ys series if it took a less serious tone in it's story department, maybe something like Half Minute Hero.

The game has been out for several years now, and this won't be a review on the game itself.
Rather this is a review of the excellent MISERY 2.1 mod I had installed recently.
MISERY is a "hardcore survival overhaul" mod for STALKER: COP, which sets out to do just that. And it does.
Guns that you loot from enemies are now in very poor condition, it's FAR more expensive to repair them or to buy new guns/ammo. NPC's will meet a gruesome end during emissions, which force you to take cover in a good-sized building or meet that end yourself. To top that off, emissions are frequent occurrences in the game, breaking out every 9-12 hours of in-game time.
Furthermore, stealth is vastly improved, all character voices are Russian rather than English. And you can even specialize in one of 3 classes added by the mod, each with their own required playstyle.
The list of changes added by the mod is too large to list here in a review, so I'll include a link to the mod's guide below.
MISERY turns STALKER into an enormous challenge, and I highly recommend it if you have the nads for it :)

I beat the Japanese version of this game with a fan translation weeks before this was announced to get an official translated release on Steam, so please disregard the hours here - I have absolutely 100% this game in the past.
An amazing game that has some core issues that prevent it from realizing its full potential:
1. The levelup system is a waste of time. When played on the default difficulty (which is what I encourage, otherwise the game is so easy its boring or so difficult it's unrewarding), you gain XP from monsters until you're on par with their level, at which point killing them becomes completely pointless. This means that you have to grind each zone just to make your character be able to survive that stage, because of this I feel pacing would've been better if you could just play from start to finish with *no* leveling system because in its current state, it does nothing but pad out game length.
2. The backtracking is annoying. I enjoy the Metroid aspect when it's done well, but in this case, most of the things you backtrack for aren't even optional unlockables for boosts, they're story-related items that you need to find in order to progress. It just feels like another way to pad game length, by making you redo areas you've already seen in order to get to the next one.
3. Bosses battles are really well designed, but insanely punishing. Whether this is an issue or not is really up to taste. You don't get to use any recovery items, when you're on-par with the level of the boss (which is only whatever's possible on the default difficulty, since "grinding" only gets you to "par"), it only takes a few hits to die. Some boss fights can go on for upwards of 5 minutes, even if you know what you're doing, and if you get hit a few times, you die, and have to start the fight from the beginning. Some of the fights are really interesting from start-to-finish, others start repeating mechanics really quickly, which makes them get boring very fast, as they become battles of tedious endurance as opposed to interesting battles.
4. There's almost too much dialogue in a game that seems to be focused on being an ARPG, and really, I didn't find myself liking any of the characters.
However, the soundtrack is absolutely stellar, is is most of the stage design. It's really just some of the old-school mechanics being too old-school for their own good, but considering this is a remake of a game that came out in the 80s (Ys 3 - 1989), that kind of explains itself, and as far as remakes go, this is one of the best that's ever been done (not as good as Resident Evil 1 on the Gamecube, however) - it took the game from 2D to pseudo-3D with much better boss encounters and stage design.
It still plays like an old PC game though, and I wouldn't recommend checking this out unless you have the time on your hands to dig through some RPG history. If nothing else, you should check out the soundtrack. This has some of the best tracks you'll find in any RPG.

Duration: 8 hours
3 hours for tutorial campaign and 5 hours for main campaign.
Legions of Steel is a computerised version of the 1992 board game.  It is very similar to Space Hulk and pits marines against machines (instead of genestealers).
There are some nice options such as suppressing fire and advanced "overwatch" options. But it does feel like a lesser version of Space Hulk lacking in-depth customisation, alternate squads and close combat.
The tutorial teaches you how to play with some almost puzzle style scenarios (where shots always hit) to learn the rules.  Although I never did used advanced overwatch targeting in the main campaign.
The main campaign had some fun scenarios, and most can be played in less than 15 minutes.  The campaign and missions did feel to lack depth.  There is multiplayer options which I did not try, but I don't believe there is much action to be harnessed.
Overall, I'd have to recommend Space Hulk:Ascension over Legions of Steel.

Oblivion is a game I truly and honestly hate. One of the only games in existence I hate, in fact. Be warned before you begin reading this. This is not an unbiased review, nor is it baby's first review, nor am I someone who is paid money to like games that are objectively bad. I'm proud of my strong bias on this, actually. Any bias against one of the worst games ever made is good bias in my opinion. Not having a bias against Oblivion is like not having a bias against Adolf Hitler. Straight up.
Oblivion.
Oh Oblivion.
Where do I begin?
There are so many things wrong with this game I legitimately don't even know
to begin. There's so much bullѕhit in this game it'd make Penn and Teller jealous.
Let's start with a basic description on what this game is.
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is an open-world fantasy RPG ("RPG"), much as would be expected from an Elder Scrolls game. Here begins the first of Oblivion many failures. Despite the fact that Oblivion is meant to be an open-world, non-linear game where the player is encouraged to explore, the game features a "fast travel" system that the player can use to essentially teleport to any place they've visited in the past. While that's not especially despicable in and of itself, the problem rests in the fact that every main city in the game world is available to fast travel to from the beginning of the game. This basically amounts to making exploration/travel useless and obsolete, as the player can instantly travel to any area in the province at no cost or risk. That's obviously the best fucҝing choice for a travel system they could have used, even though TES games before Oblivion, like Morrowind and Daggerfall, had well-developed and senseful systems of travelling that worked well and could have easily fit into Oblivion's world.
Now, this review isn't about making Morrowind or other TES games seem better by comparison (they do a good enough job of that by themselves), but we need to recognize that Oblivion isn't a standalone game; it's a sequel. And as a sequel, certain things are expected of it that otherwise wouldn't be, were it a standalone game. The only real "improvement" I can think that Oblivion has over Morrowind is the combat system. Morrowind's combat system was indeed one of the game's shortcomings, but it's been covered well enough before that I don't feel the need to describe it in this review. Oblivion attempts to rectify problems players had with the combat in Morrowind by removing all RNG from it, and making it into more of an action game system where the player simply needs to hit the enemy with their weapon in order to do damage. While the concept is fine, the actual result in Oblivion is laughable. Oblivion combat has absolutely, positively no depth or required skill. It is literally "click until they die" with occasional menu digging to swallow potions. On top of being horrible from an action game standpoint, Oblivion's combat is also bad from an RPG point of view, as actual skill points put into weapons do nothing besides unlocking a "special move" every 25 points and making the player do a negligible amount of extra damage every skill point.
Magic in Oblivion is more user friendly than in Morrowind and easier to get into, as spells can no longer fail and the player can now equip both a spell and a weapon at the same time. However, the magic system has been absolutely butchered in depth, with a lot of magical effects from Morrowind being removed, and there being vastly fewer vanilla spells built into Oblivion
vs
The ability to create custom spells is retained, however, it is arbitrarily locked behind the player having membership in the Mages Guild, which requires a fairly lengthy quest line to unlock. Furthermore, the Enchanting skill was removed from Oblivion, meaning that the player is now required to go to a specific location in order to be able to enchant their gear. At least you can't fucҝ up while enchanting and destroy your ѕhit anymore.
Well, let's move onto the core gameplay of this game. As we have already established, Oblivion is not a serious, hardcore roleplaying game experience. Nor is it remarkable (or even slightly noticeable) as an action game. Oblivion has about as much depth as a half-filled bathtub. A bathtub that someone pіssеd in for a good period of time and then didn't drain. With that being said, Oblivion is still an active attempt by a group of people (probably unfrozen neanderthals) to create an RPG. Now, Oblivion does employ a good amount of traditional RPG mechanics one would expect from an RPG. Unfortunately, they are almost all badly implemented and a problem of some sort can be uncovered within each of them. The attribute system is fairly simple. There are eight main attributes. Two are chosen by the player character to correspond to their class and gain a starting bonus to them, and every attribute is tied to a skill and gives a benefit to that skill as it rises. The attributes kind of overlap, though, and the same benefits are give by several of them. For example, fatigue is increased by agility, endurance, strength, AND willpower. Hilarious enough, despite being increased by so many attributes, fatigue is almost completely useless, and regenerates so fast anyway that it never has any presence in gameplay. Similarly, the player's starting max encumbrance is so high that the player would never have to invest any points in strength while playing, regardless of class. Well, the weight of equipment increases linearly depending on what it's made of, leading to scenarios such as elven swords perplexingly being heavier than iron swords, for example.
The game's more or less entirely linear, computer-generated equipment statistics lend to making Oblivion feel even more like a soulless, uninspired blob of a game.
"Uninspired" really does define Oblivion very well. Absolutely nothing about this game will challenge you, change you in anyway, or push the norms or expectations put upon video games by any means. TES games were known among the video game industry for being impressive and innovative in many ways, being one of the first series of RPGs to actually do an open-world successfully. Oblivion inherits none of these traits, and even manages to baѕtardize the open-world gameplay that the Elder Scrolls series capitalized on beforehand.
TESIV is unimpressive in aspects of both gameplay and design, with this game's art being comparably dull and lacklustre as the gameplay. If I showed you a screenshot of Oblivion
would you be able to pick it out from any of the games you see here?

I thought this game was bad.
I thought this would be just a generic ninja-ish shooter.
I was wrong.
Warframe is unique. Very unique.
This game has space and calm only if you actively try to not do stuff.
When you get in a mission, you're already in the action and everything is fast.
But even if you think this is just some parkour simulator, you're only half right.
Because this game is incredibly fun, has a lot to explore and more is being added every couple of days or weeks.
Oh did you hear or read that it's grindy? Again, you're only half right.
If you're familiar with Monster Hunter and other similar games, you'll know what i'm talking about:
The grind is the game. Getting, building and trying new stuff IS the fun.
So yeah, it's grindy. Overly grindy? In no way.
You can get everything in the game for free. YES, EVERYTHING.
Buying the ingame premium currency, Platinum, does indeed help, but it's not necessary.
If you do try and enjoy the game, you might want to buy some plat to help the devs and speed up a little the start of your game.
Or you know, get some cool and flashy cosmetics. They look great, i can recommend.
You can trade with other players for their Platinum, so even a free player can get all of the above.
The missions are usually quick and objective-focused:
Get in. Do your objective. Get out.
Some will be done in a few minutes.
But later, will might want to farm an endless survival for an hour or two.
So the time-consuming factor depends a lot. You might play 30min, 1h or even 6h per day and get satisfied.
Nice to note that the community is far more accepting, respectful and helpful than most games.
The developers also show great care for the game and try not only to keep it fresh and exciting, but actively try to make the players happy with those choices.
Warframe has bad sides? Yes, sadly.
The new player experience could definitely be better.
The game won't hold your hand and tell you specifically what to do, which might be a plus in some cases, but it also somewhat leaves you wondering "what do i do now?".
Also, trading for Platinum early in the game when you're still getting started sucks a reasonable amount.
If you manage to survive these early problems, you can be sure you'll have fun. And that's worth it.

I wish I could recommend it because the core gameplay is pretty good but there's not nearly enough content at this point. I've played it for 3 hours according to Steam and that includes the earlier alpha tech demos I checked out once in a while. With the full release (edit: not exactly full but the beta release which added the main story so mostly feature complete, when I first wrote the review the full release was to come in like a week so with barely any changes to what I'm writing about here) I have finished both its story mode and the included Lugaru story mode (that's an enhanced version of the developer's older game put into this new engine I believe) and did a bunch of arena fights too (those are just for fun, there's no score or ladder or anything else at all, it just keeps restarting the fight with different enemies and weapons though only a handful of variations exist).
The story mode is way too short without the levels ever realising the potential for stealth and action they could offer. They're all extremely basic in layout and encounter design and there's not much else to do after that.The story mode also includes a couple of levels that focus on platforming and I found those annoying more than fun, the wall run into a jump didn't seem to work reliably either but it was only needed for a handful of places and the checkpoints were frequent so it wasn't too big of a problem.
The fighting mechanics are in fact superb despite being simple and the main attraction of this game. I do have a few minor complaints however:
I think for example after the air kick if you have some momentum your character jumps off waaaaay too far both unrealistically and in a way that's not fun, while the system isn't really suited for the many against one fights it keeps setting up so you just run around trying to pick them off one by one or if possible use stealth to reduce their numbers before going all out. Finally, the wolves didn't seem to play by the same rules as the player and other enemies, I just cheesed them with the air kicks since countering and what not seemed impossible.
Anyway, I don't think many will keep coming back to this game unless more and more intricate levels, campaigns and modes are added, it's a shame but there's basically no meat to it at this point, you'll have seen all it has to offer after an hour and then play one or two more just to get to the end of the plain stories and try out other modes.

I backed this game long ago, and sure, the development has been
slow, but what you want to know is whether to buy it.
The story is bare-bones and very simplistic. We're talking childishly simple—but this isn't really trying to sell you a narrative. It's right there in the description. This is an action game, and with that in mind, the short dialogues that outline the story do a fair enough job to give you some context for your wolf, dog and cat-slapping.
The gameplay is on point! The control scheme is unlike most games, but you get the hang of it quickly. Despite the few buttons involved, there's an immensely high skill ceiling. New players will be able to look good fighting, experienced players will find plenty of room for skill. The simulationist approach to attacks and wounds makes it feel as realistic as any anthropomorphic rabbit-fights-dog simulator ever could.
There's no replay value to the story itself, but I myself can't get tired of the gameplay. I'm not gonna get tired of deflecting thrown weapons, stabbing dogs in the crotch with spears or killing myself by rolling mid-air and landing on my neck. I also really appreciate the lack of a UI, which makes stealthing around or fighting feel really nice. It's a good example of a zero-UI game that works.
The game takes well to mods, so you may want to check out the steam workshop to see what people are cooking. There is a very basic but fun arena mode, too. I don't know what my hours here say, but I've played it a bunch before it hit steam.
Should you buy it?
For the story? No. For the gameplay? Maybe? I know that I keep coming back to it and feel I'm getting my money's worth. I also know that plenty of people feel games need a lot of story/mission/level/whatever content for them to feel like the game is worth their money. I'd recommend you just look at the gameplay vids and ask if you could see yourself kicking the legs out from under a dog and then stabbing him in the buttocks with a spear. If the answer is yes, give it a bash.
It's a good example of a game that's the best it can be within its own limits. It's not trying to be anything more than what is advertised, and it's damn good at being exactly what it says it is. You'll be disappointed if you expect an epic story or a lot of activities. You'll have a good time if you're looking for a well-designed and simple simulationist/"realistic" brawler.

"STOP RIGHT THERE, CRIMINAL SCUM!" These are words that summed up a game that cannot be possibly described in words. Building off the success and standard set by Morrowind, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion far more than its predecessor sucked us into a rich, breathing world filled with breath-taking scenery, towns with believable NPCs with voiced dialog, factions to join, houses to purchase. horses to ride and a vast amount to see and do. Oblivion like Morrowind before it was a game you poured hours into and could still not have seen even a fraction of the game's content. The sheer fidelity, quality, and scope of Oblivion set a standard for Western RPGs to come and heavily influenced the development of Fallout 3. Patrick Stewart even lends his talents to provide the voice of Emperor Uriel Septim.
Once again, the reason why Oblivion has remained its legacy is the mod community. Oblivion has strong mod support and  countless mods have been created that add to the game and change the experience in significant ways. Among these is an Oblivion version of MOG*MOD. There is a wealth of content in this game, and with both expansions included, there is a lot to lose sleep over in this game.
Out of the most recent The Elder Scrolls games, Oblivion to me seems to have aged the least well. Part of this is due to the way the leveling system can work against you, especially if you're a new player and make poor decisions leveling and allocating points. This leads to the "leveling problem" where at high levels you have an underpowered character but all other enemies have leveled appropriately. The other issue is the models themselves where most NPCs have an uncanny look to them and the odd decision not to include modeled facial hair (which was rectified in Skyrim). Thankfully there are mods to fix both these problems.
Overall Oblivion is a fantastic and almost perfect game, overshadowed only by its successor Skyrim.

Devil daggers is a supercharged shooter that is very close to games like the original quake in terms of speed and super hexigon due to difficulty. The game itself just starts up with you standing in front of a dagger and once you pick it up you are immidiately attacked by an array of 3 types of enemies which only get more and more difficult as the timer goes on, it can be extremely difficult for some people to even pass the 60 second mark.
Outside of that the game has no story, no secrets (unless you count figuring out how the game mechanics work) and nothing but the challenge of the game. Devil Daggers is an arcade scoring FPS. While this review is negative, it only means that I do not personally recommend the game. It does not mean that I think that this is a terrible game, so please do not vote me down just because you are a fanboy defending your game.
That being said, Devil Daggers consists of surviving as long as possible in a (very small) square where darkness reigns, while killing hundreds of skulls thrown at you. That's all there is to the game, no levels to beat, no permanent or temporary progression, just occasionally a new enemy type makes its appearance while the skulls keep swarming and swarming.
Tentacle pillars dispense skulls and need to be disposed of quickly after their first batch before they vomit an overwhelming army. Flying skulls are quick, they home in on the players, and are a CONSTANT pain to deal with. Very rarely there is a moment to breathe, which means that the pacing of the game is very intense, and in my opinion completely off. It feels tedious and repetitive. Moreover, always the same enemies are coming at the same moment, so unlike roguelites the player does not learn the systems and then adapt to different situations: here, the sequence is the same, so the player has to do the same thing over and over until they learn the partition of the music they play (although there is no in-game soundtrack).
I would compare this game to Super Hexagon: play the sequence over and over until you get good at mastering it, and then get farther into the game.
Conversely, I suppose that some very skilled players would be able to get quite far without needing to learn the sequence, just by sheer skill of shooting and moving, The shooting consists of pressing once for shotgun or keeping the finger of the mouse for machine gun fire. Collecting gems from enemies (stop shooting to attract them like a magnet) eventually upgrades the firepower. Shooting feels good, just too bad that I am fighting swarms of skulls and not interesting enemy types that come in waves inside a bigger arena.
A very interesting addition to this game is the ability to watch the replay from anyone in the leaderboard. Very useful to learn or just be mesmerized at the graphics without focusing on surviving.
To me the main draw of the game is the art style and atmosphere (although there is no in-game soundtrack). The graphics and gameplay throw back to Quake, and will probably attract the same kind of elitist crowd. Sadly, the content is too simple and repetitive.

This weekend had been fairly unpleasant. I’d come down with something awful, sneezing and coughing like crazy as I lounged around trying not to infect every inch of my home and the people who share it with me. I was all but forced by my body to do nothing but lie in bed wondering what I’d done to the universe this time, as I cycled between barely conscious and hyper alert and all the while failing entirely to distract myself from whatever was ailing me.
I needed something to occupy my time and give me something to write about (which has become a rather therapeutic activity for me). Metamorphabet couldn’t have released at a better time.
I imagine I’d have enjoyed it whenever I decided to play it, but being cooped up inside for days with a rabid fever, it came as an even more potent concentration of pure joy and creativity that I desperately needed. Every screen bounced to life with enthusiastic wonder, creating scenes and characters and bizarre anomalies out of letters that become increasingly esoteric yet perfectly fit within the game.
And suddenly I was smiling and laughing, almost forgetting I was sick at all as I toyed with the shapes before me eagerly wondering what they might turn into next. I could barely talk because my nose and throat hurt so much, but if didn’t matter because I suddenly felt like I was a wide eyed toddler let loose in a dreamland where clouds turn into dogs and an elephant balances atop the Earth.
In all honesty Metamorphabet should be more disturbing than endearing. Certain letters can take shockingly weird turns, sprouting animal heads from fingertips and having disembodied legs grow feathers and fly away. I think it manages to overcome its weirdness though by how it never so much as hints at a hidden layer of cynicism or unpleasantness. Being a game focused around the alphabet it could be easy to get the impression Metamorphabet is a game for kids, but when I actually played it any doubts that I was the wrong audience immediately faded away. It doesn’t feel like a game that’s been hamstrung into something kids can play the way so many children's games do, or that had all the life sucked out of it because its creators don’t care enough to create a kid friendly game worth playing.
If anything Metamorphabet goes out of its way to never box itself into a certain demographic. It’s full of the sort of universal love and joy that I can’t imagine anyone with half a heart wouldn’t find at least a little delightful regardless of their age. It introduced me to what I imagine my baby niece sees and feels when playing with simple blocks and stuffed animals, simple toys becoming outlets to unleash her imagination in a world that probably doesn’t make a lot of sense but is full of amazing things if only you could see them like she does.

First of all: I only played single player. So I can't and won't say anytrhing about exploiters and all this stuff. I don't find it enjoyable to invest hundreds of hours into a game only to get my base destroyed by some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, so... no, not for me in general. (Also I am 35 now and don't have hundreds of hours to put in a game anyway.)
So I played this game when the early access began, though to myself "ah, there's potential!" and then came back to it after six months.
The good stuff: It's pretty, it playes well and it is friggin Conan. Gathering resources is kind of addicting and it is genuine fun to build you base and advance in level.
The bad stuff: First of all, the combat system is utter♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Yes, you can do rolls, you can do strong attacks, you can block but everything feels just so clunky you'll just smash the mouse button anyway and block ranged attacks with your shield. That is, if your shield isn't destroyed immediately by the first attack... Yeah, of cause this game usas a durability system. And generally speaking, these kind of mechanics can work, even though they're just there to make you gather even more resources - which is pretty stupid in a game where my goal is to build a base with lots of stuff anyway imho. So my personal view is: screw durability mechanics completely. And if you use them, don't make things break after just a few uses. Which Conan does. Especially on earlier levels your resource income sometimes almost perfectly matches the cost for repairing your weapoons making progress painfully slow.
But that's not the biggest problem,. Oh, no! My biggest complaint with this game are the NPC enemies. The aggro range in Conan Exiles is hilarious. Enemies spot you from almost hundreds of feet away and directly charge you. They even try to beat you if they're incapable of hitting you at all. Let's say you fled from some spiders and jumped down a crevice. That stupid thing will sit above you on that rock and try to hit you no matter what. This is until you move a mile away or so.
It would be nice if creatures and enemies would calm down in situations liike these. It would also be nice if not every friggin creature would love to kill you instantly. Why is every hyena, every spider and every crocodile in this game on a constant murder spree?
It would be half as annoying if the music wouldn't ramp up everytime an enemy wants to kill you. The first few times your heartrate shoots up and it's exciting. But after the one hundredths time that battle music kicks in, you're just irritated.
Also it would be nice if not every human NPC charactern was a murderous ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Yeah there are a few tearchers here and there who don't attack you, but let's say you'll find an elaborate settlement of dudes somewhere in the desert. My first reaction was "Oh, great, I'll say hi and maybe trade some stuff if that's possible" No, it's not. They'll just kill you. And if you kill them, they'll respawn after some time and try to kill you again in an infinite loop of dorkness. Guess that's not really a bad thing but a wasted opportunity and quite honestly I don't know if something like that is planned or will come in the future. It sure wasn't implemented in the last six months.
Then you have the balancing issues. The bow is almost useless (because deer needs two or more shots and runs away before you can hit it again, which makes bow hunting pretty tedious). Wooden shields and even the next tier shields get smashed on one single hit. Animals like crocodiles are immune (!) to first tier weapons (as if immunity in common enemies was ever a good idea) and then there are.... the spiders.
The spiders attack you more often than not in packs up to three or more creatures. They are plenty, they are quick and you often see them a little too late to avoid them (remember what I wrote about aggro range?). Now, if more than one or two spiders have spotted you, you're basically dead. Spiders poison you with two different poisons: normal poison and crippling poison. While crippling poison slows you down, the normal poison deals damage over time. Poison can also stack. So let's say some spiders team up and try to kill you. The forums smartasses will now tell you to "carry some antidotes" or "use your shield to block the poison attack" (remember what I said about durability in this game?). What I reply to these people is: No. Antidotes are not as common as spiders. I will not visit the guy who can teach me the Set religion to build a Set temple to craft the ceremonial dagger to sacrifice human hearts to get the antidote. Because I died fifty times of poisoning until then!!!
Call me a ♥♥♥♥♥, call me a newb, call me whatever you want. But this game is just poorly balanced. And I wouldn't be so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥if this was six months ago. But the inability of the devs to fix the most basic balance issues and gameplay mechanics of their game speaks volumes in my opinion. I don't see this coming, to be perfectly honest. If you are not able to half poison damage and durability effects in six months, you tell me you don't want to.
Gladly, this game supports mods and there are mods that at least fix the durability issues. But I haven't found anything for the enemy behavior and poison-mod I once used doesn't work anymore. Anyways, you should rate a game by its vanilla state. And I am frustrated too often to give this thing a thumbs up.
Maybe I'll update my review after the game was launched.

As a big fan of all 3 Final Fantasy Tactics games, XCOM 2, Vandal Hearts as well as less tactical turn based RPG's(Final Fantasy X and earlier, Baiten Kaitos, Xenosaga, Skies of Arcadia) I've got to say this is hands down the best RPG of all time. There are so many options, the environment reacts to you(and your enemies) and if you're not paying attention to what you're doing you could end up zapping and stunning your entire party, setting them all on fire, poisoning them, or accidentally healing them to death. The voice acting, narration and story are pretty good, but not perfect, it's hard to write a unique story because just about everything has been done in some way, shape or form. They did a fairly good job though, there were even some moments where the narrator describing the disgusting things my character was doing even made my stomach turn a little
. Another note, I love that there's an actual narrator. Instead of investing in fancy animations and visuals for much of the scenes, you're told the story and left to let your imagination run wild. And the vocabulary! Wow! The dialogue was clearly written by intelligent people...no mention of anybody's face being tired!
This game doesn't hold your hand, there's a steep learning curve, you really need to pay attention to what you're doing and don't forget to quick save before going to a new area. If your favorite "RPG" is Skyrim or Fallout 4 this game isn't for you, move on. You won't like it and you'll just complain about it being "too hard". Not saying fans of those games will definitely not like this, but if that's what you're preferred RPG is like, you most likely won't like this. Do a little research on games before buying and you'll avoid getting games that aren't your style.

If I had to choose between the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games, I'd pick Call of Pripyat. Many good features from the previous games have been polished such as trading, upgrading items, combat, artifact detection and collection, and even questing. The plot and ending really got to me.
The open world is an issue. The pacing of progression between questing areas is a bit of a different flavor from previous games. In Call of Pripyat, your progress between zones is limited by story progression. This is in contrast to SoC where your exploration was (mostly) only limited by progressively more difficult opponents and anomalies. On the other hand, while CoP locks you into a zone, it's not exactly a small space. Later in the game, you'll even find yourself with reasons to go back to previous areas for bonuses and min/maxing.
The RPG element has been well polished as well. The importance of your equipment choices cannot be understated. With a wide variety of weapons, armor, attachments and modification trees (like talent trees!), consumables, and artifacts(stat altering) your options are quite vast. There are many situations in the game where the proper equipment can turn a fevered fight for survival into a even back and fourth or perhaps little challange at all.
As a STALKER game it would be poor form for me not to comment on the atmosphere. This is something I feel Call of Pripyat, like it's predecessors, did very well. At a glace, some may see only a melancholy dystopia sprinkled with shock and a little horror, but there's so much more to it. While the darkness and gloom are very evident, beneath the surface lies the subtle thrill of being on the edge of an unexplored frontier with somthing to discover around every corner. You never know who or what you'll run into next.
The themes behind the game and STALKER in general are fairly mature. For all the good in the game, it's still (IMO) dark, gritty, and brutally honest about "might" and it's connection to what is "right". There is good in this world, but it's few and far between. As for the plot, it certainly helps to have experience in the previous games. From the get-go you're aware your character's motivation is ethically dubious at best. To his credit, the MC grows and confronts these issues making him seem more relatable.
If you want a full experience I recommend you play the previous STALKER games first. There are plenty of references and even an important character or two. Problem is, I don't believe any of these games have aged particularly well graphically or mechanically. But if you can suffer though some imperfections, the experience is worth it.
One final and important note, there are some good mods for Call of Pripyat as well as previous games. If you manage to get though the game, modding is definitely a way to expand re-playability.

Legions of Steel PC Game Review by
The Past has hit the Present with an all new way to play the classic board game, Legions of Steel.
This game was released yesterday ( July, 16th, 2015) on the PC.  I heard about it last night, and instantly started doing research about it.  As mentioned before, I tried to help with the Kickstarter and after it didn’t go through, I was bummed.  Yes, I probably could have tried to keep up with the Legions of Steel news and watched it develop, but I didn’t.  Call me lazy, or busy, but for whatever reason it dropped off my radar.
Right now I’ve played multiple hours of the game.
Holy crap is it fun!  I didn’t even bother to run the tutorial or the rules, I wanted to approach it with the rules I learned when playing the board game all those years ago.
Let me tell you, while it’s not identical to the board game, it’s really damn close!  I mean, it would be impossible to mimic every element of the board game, but to be honest, some of those rules were thick to understand to begin with.  This PC version takes the guesswork out of it and inject pure fun into your eyes.
The graphics are wicked cool, the music is haunting and exciting at the same time.
The Setting:
The Future.  Okay, we just took the Past, mashed it with the Present, and now we are flinging it into the Future!  Whhheeeeeeeeee!!!!!
The League of Aliens and the United Nations of Earth (U.N.E.) have teamed up to keep at bay a new threat to the galaxy, The Machines.
GamePlay:
Legions of Steel is a tun based game.  Each unit has it’s own set of skills and characteristics.  Different weapons can be used and sometimes you have to use the map as a weapon itself!
You can also choose to play singleplayer missions or go against another player in multiplayer mode.
In the board game’s set up, players took turns setting up snap together cardboard tiles that created the scenario you were to play in.  As best as I can tell so far, you do not do that here, all of the maps are premade.
Platforms:
Right now Legions of Steel is available for the PC and iOS.  At the time of this writing there is no release date yet for Android but I will update with one when I find out!
The Cost:
You can purchase it for a measly $18.00 from Steam or from the iTunes store!  EIGHTEEN bucks!  That’s dirt cheap for this wicked cool game!  Hell, the board game itself was about $60.00!
Bottom Line:
GO GET THIS GAME!

One of my all time favorites and the game that got me into the Ys series which I criminally ignored until a couple of years ago. Great hack and slash game with tight controls and high replayability. You're definitely going to play this more than once.
Be advised though, this game is HARD. As in, don't start it on the hardest difficulty if this is your first time playing as this game is actually an old game, not something that was made in the last 3 years. This means this game was developed back when "hard mode" actually meant HARD MODE and not just a slightly harder normal mode where you still pretty much streamroll through the game. I cannot put enough emphasis on this, this game is HARD and you're going to die over and over and over until you finally learn to get good at it.
For people who hate JRPGS and whatnot don't worry, this game, much like most of the Ys series games, is anti grind so you'll never be underleveled. You also don't have to fiddle around with a bloated inventory or anything like that as your character's progression is pretty straightforward (You don't get different type of swords with different properties, just better swords with more attack power so you can just ignore your old gear).
The soundtrack is easily one of the highlights of this game. It's probably one of the, if not THE game with the best soundtrack in the entire Ys series and a pretty close contender for game with the best soundtrack ever.
Getting 100% completion is something only the most hardcore players will be able to achieve due to how insanely hard the last difficulties are, so be ready to invest a huge amount of time on that task dying over and over.
Special note: Don't pay attention to the store images, the game actually has full widescreen support which was added shortly after the game came out so it won't look as bad as in those screenshots, don't worry.
Bad stuff:
* Cutscenes. You can't fully skip them, you have to hold a button to autoskip every bit of dialogue and waste tons of minutes doing nothing. This is especially aggravating when you're on your 3rd playthrough or so.
* Xbox 360 controller support: Game has no native xinput support so your left and right triggers wont work. Easily fixable by using joy2key or something but to be honest you don't even need those buttons to begin with.

I'm going to give this a very neutral standing view point, with an honest review.
Gear Up is fun. It definitely has a lot of potential. Weapons and Mods for your tank are purchased via gold, where most games (if you're a decent to great player) can average 3-5 gold per game (1 if you lose or 2 if you win, 1 for enemy kills, 1 for taking towers). Side Note: People are saying "I can't get gold no matter how many I kill!" That's a lie. They're just not good enough to do it. It's 10 kills per gold. 20 will net you 2.  Anyhow, it's either that or you can unlock everything for the $20 blah blah. The thing is, you're restricted to how many parts you can have as you level (starts at 7 I believe, rank 5 allows 10) so you'll have to constantly delete things and pick what you feel is best. Also, you don't have any loadouts unless you purchase the game (which I suppose is acceptable). You can, however, hit escape and change your vehicle during the game, but this leaves you vulnerable to attack. Hit boxes seem to be good for the most part, I'm still trying to figure out how they calculate speed to weight ratio, but everything as far as controls and movements feels great. There's only 3 modes, Conquest, Team Deathmatch, and Deathmatch, so don't expect tons of options aside from vehicle customization.
My gripes are simple: the game needs some serious tuning, which is understandable given it's Beta state.
What needs to be done:
Match Optimization. If you're starting out, you'll be stuck with some high level players instead of players your own level.
Ability to choose servers by ping. Currently there is no way to, and it's noticable
Menu bug. When searching lobby games, it'll bounce you back to the top of the list when you're scrolling. Rather annoying.
Ability to party with friends on the same team.
Ability to report players.
Test Section (to test your build)
Spawn protection. Spawn camping is kind of big right now.
Has a few runtime errors from time to time (Win 7, i7 4800 MQ, 32GB RAM). You have to cntrl/shift/esc and end the process Traktor.Amalgram...exe. Why it's run via Traktor (a DJ program) I haven't the slightest idea.
Conclusion:
All in all the game is a lot of fun and has some good potential. Just gotta hope they polish it up really nice and iron out all the kinks/lackings first.

My new favorite board game. Also, a lackluster TCG and fast-paced RPG.
Do not be fooled by the cutesy graphics. This is a very well-developed game.
Starting with the trading card game elements, there aren't very many cards and there's no trading. Still, this game uses a rather clever solution for balance: each player picks a handful of cards from their own collection and those get put into a communal deck to be used by any player. When selecting cards, you have to weigh the value of how much it can help you if you get it against the impact of it being used by another player. Card types include "boost," "trap," "battle," and "unit" cards.
On the RPG side of things, there are a few selectable characters who each have their own short, comedic story, but these stories aren't really focused on enough to be factored into the decision to purchase the game. Each character has different stats; one has +0 to all stats while another has +2 attack and -1 defense and evasion while yet another has +1 to all while having reduced HP. These stats can only be changed temporarily by using cards; there are no stat level ups, which helps keep things from getting too imbalanced. Having low values for all these stats helps make combat go faster. The stats are added to the value of die rolls to determine damage, and when you only have ~5 max HP, every point matters. Each character also has their own unique "hyper" ability that is activated by cards in the communal deck.
During combat, the attacker rolls first. The defender then chooses whether to defend or attempt to evade. After the aggressor's attack, the victim then counterattacks with the same mechanics if they were not slain.
While the characters do not gain experience, stats, or abilities, you (the player) do. Each match played online gives experience based on how well you ended up doing and level ups unlock more stuff to purchase in the shop including more characters.
The boardgame mixes strategy with luck. There's enough luck involved that a player who is down is not truly out until the game's finished, and a player with a large lead is not safe until landing on the finish. I've seen many examples of come-from-behind victories and large leads falling to pieces, and these ups and downs help keep the game fun and interesting when playing with other players. As far as strategy goes, you can pick routes when the path branches (altering the distance to home), you pick when to play cards, and when passing another player you can choose to stop on their square and battle them with victory awarding you half their stars and +2 win points. The goal of the game is to meet an ever increasing goal of either stars or combat wins (player's choice) and reach a home point to turn in that goal (and thus reach the next goal tier, with 5 being the final tier, earning victory when cleared). Wins always go up but can be difficult to get while stars are easier to earn yet just as easy to lose. There are also plenty of boards with very different layouts which helps the game stay fun after multiple play sessions.
The game is mostly suited for online play (though it does have a single player campaign and free mode), and it has a few things of note in that area. The game uses Steam servers to form lobbies and you can have a match with random players. During a normal turn, you get 60 seconds before the AI takes over for you, so it's not too much of a problem if players leave their keyboard for a bit. When attacked, you are given 40 seconds to decide what to do, but the other player's clock freezes after they make a choice, so you can't outwait them for the sake of taking advantage of enemy AI. When doing a revival roll, you are given less time.
Addtionally, Fruitbat Factory has been quite active in the community as well as busy adding content and rebalancing things.
Verdict:
The game looks quirky enough that I wouldn't normally recommend it, but it makes for one heck of a cheap party game. If you and up to 3 friends are looking for a casual game to play online in which all players remain on equal ground and can get this cheap, it comes highly recommended. If you do not have 3 friends, bots or random players will fill in the missing spots.

Sometimes you'll punch, kick, roundhouse kick, and you'll never choose which. So if you and your enemy are low on health and you want to do a quick punch after a dodge, well too bad - your character decided to rondhouse kick and your enemy punched, so he won. Versus mode is the best experience in my opinon, playing with a friend makes the combat system less frustrating and makes the full use of the parry/dodge system.
