Ignore hours played, this game does not like the Steam overlay and for whatever reasons hasn't recorded my game time.
So Earth 2150 is a fairly standard straightforward real time strategy game with some unique ideas, especially for it's time. First off, you can customize units over the course of the campaigns. Though your options are fairly limited in the beginning, you can upgrade your units with stronger weapons and defences, this goes for some of your structures as well.  With that you have numerous playing fields which consist of your main base and the mission area. Both these features truly make this a unique experience. However upgrading building units does come at a cost of precious resources, as your main mission which spans the entire game is to collect enough resources to basically build something of an Ark to leave the dying Earth.
Now onto the technical side and the games age showing. This game does not support resolutions of modern computers properly. As far as I've seen, there aren't any real mods for the game to fix this, so know you will have to play at a much lower resolution. Now note the game does function at higher resolution, some of the in-game menus will cause crash to desktops to occur when you open them. As far as I've been able to see, there is no fix for this. Otherwise, the game runs like a charm and runs just fine on Windows 10 and Windows 7 OS.
Now when it comes to gameplay, this game will make you think and strategize early on. Resources are very limited, enemy units are not joking around, units (both owned and enemy) can run out of ammo on the field which requires constant supply deliveries in the mission area, view for units can be obstructed by time of day and weather. Earth 2150 was ahead of its time. But of course, it doesn't have it's drawbacks. AI in general isn't particularly smart and will require an immense amount of babysitting and careful cooridination, as units will tend act a bit silly and blindly roll into enemy fire when using large groups.
Pros:
-Excellent real time strategy
-Compelling story
-Gameplay has aged well
Cons:
-Technical limits due to age
-Dumb AI
Overall, this is a good game and worth buying if your up for a challening real time strategy which falls into the same vein as Homeworld. Just be prepared to deal with feel of working with a much smaller resolution. But trust me, this game is worth playing, even if it's a bit blocky.

Crusader Kings 2 is one of the, if no the, best strategy game i have ever played. At the beginning of the game you are shown an accurate political map of europe for the start date you choose to start in, you then choose a character to play as, you may start as the grand basileus of the Byzantine Empire and fight back the invading Seljuk sultunate in a glorious battle with the varangian guard at your side, or simply a lowly count of devon trying avoid the norman and norwegian armies attacking anglo-saxon England (in the 1066 start date).
I have played over 200 hours of this game so I am speaking from experience and I strongly recommend you ignore the reviewers who have played between 1-10 hours of the game as it it NOT long enough to repect the game for what it is.
Positive aspects of the game:
1) very historically accurate characters and nations at the start of the game
2) many different events to keep the game interesting
3) many different interactions with your' subjects
4) with no dlc there is 400 years of medieval history to play through, with all dlc there is 700 years!
5) In depth medieval politics and accurate feudal, iqta, tribal and nomadic government systems
6) with all dlc activated you can see more mechanics, subject interactions, alternative history events (sunset invasion) and new eras to play in, however this leads to my first gripe with the game...
1) the DLC, so many DLCs, now first things first i dont mind the dlc in the game thought there is a lot im perfectly fine with the major add ons, however i think it is pure greed that after you pay the £15 for the newest expansion you have another £4 to pay for the new unit sprites and portraits that come with it!
2) not for those who want a complete historic experience, because as the game goes on you will see more and more alternative history events take place, like the norwegians taking england not the Normans in 1066.
3) to get the best experience out of the game i recommend the full game with all dlc, however this is very expensive so i recommend getting it from a discount site or in the sales.
Finally, this game is the most accurate medieval grand strategy game I have come across and I definately recommend it to anyone who likes strategy games, but as previously stated it is very expensive for the full experience so if you are a die hard strategy gamer i fully recommend the game, however if you are new to the strategy genre i would recommend a more welcoming game and a less expensive experience.

Ahhh VectorPark. These guys really do have a way with animation. Whatever sort of engine they are using for their work, and whatever sort of methods they use, it cannot be denied that anything that comes out of them looks as though it is filled with life and joy. Having only one game previously on steam called "Windosill", a short, simple puzzle game about going from room to room as a little car, and solving the puzzles in the room, all while watching and interacting with the environment, VectorPark decided to try their luck again with this "game", Metamorphabet. So, does it hold up?
Well... yes and no. I'll say it like this. If you're expecting anything that gives you any sort of challenge, look away. If you want something with replayability, this aint it. If you want something that can at the very least keep you occupied for more than an hour... I'm sorry, but this just isn't what you are looking for.
Metamorphabet is exactly what it advetises itself as. An interactive alphabet. It really is that simple. Letters appear on the screen, you click the letters, and stuff happens. Stuff that you can interact with further. For example, you could click the letter "S", and 2 striped socks that cover both sides of the letter itself. What happens if you click on the S again? The S becomes a snake, which you can now move around, and after a few seconds, the snake gets a shadow, which mirrors it's movement. S, sock, snake, shadow, you can see the pattern. It's like this with every letter. I'll try not to spoil much more, because that really is all the game has going for it for anyone who already knows the alphabet. Every letter has maybe 5 or so ways that you can interact with it. Some of these ways include dragging things, using vacuum cleaner, unzipping things, all fairly simple things, but there's a fair bit of variety with each new letter. There's usually stuff you can play with on the screen that doesn't actually affect the game, which is fun, if limited.
As for sound and visuals, the sound is nothing special. Things sound as you would expect them too. A drum sounds like a drum, a door opening sounds like a door opening. There's hardly any music, which I believe is a good thing, since the game does have sort of a relaxing atmosphere. As for visuals, it's VectorPark. If you expect anything other than beauty, then I don't know what to tell you. Everything reacts to what you do with fluid movement, and it all looks gorgeous.
So, if the game offers no challenge, and you can finsh it in under 20 minutes, is there any reason to spend money on it? Well, if you have a child just learning the alphabet, I suppose this can be a useful tool, though I feel like children who can't speak the alphabet wouldn't really know how to use a computer. I could be wrong, as the controls are really simple, but even if they could use the mouse, it's not guaranteed that they wouldn't just be distracted by all the stuff happening, instead of learning anything. The game is entertaining for what it is. With every letter comes a new surprise. Sure, the surprise only lasts a few seconds before you get bored with what's in front of you, but it's neat nontheless.
Can I recommend this game? Well, check out the trailer. It gives you all the info you want. I personally don't really see why this company, who have proved the can make good games that challange players, decided to make an interactive alphabet (probably just for fun, which I can respect), but for what it is, it's good. It's pretty, it's entertaining, and it's resonably cheap, though for $5 there's not really much value for your money. I personally enjoyed windosill a lot, and love anything that comes out of these guys, so I hope they keep making games/animations. I just hope that in the future, they make actual "games" that challenge players in some way.
The game doesn't lie about what it is. It's an interactive alphabet, and that's it. The interactions are nice, it covers every letter in the English alphabet, and it looks beautiful. If that's enough for you, then sure, pick it up. If you're looking for a something challenging, maybe try Ninja Gaiden or something.

Very good game. I would reccomend it to anyone who likes post apocalyptic Role playing games. The enemies and AI groups are very interesting and worth delving into, to learn more. The combat system is very well done, with the various side affects from bleeding to the durability of weapons and armour. The weapon armor upgrade system focuses on a tier built system which are unlocked through finding Toolkits (either through side quests or exploring the world.) There are Several factions in the game: Loners, Bandits, Mercenaries, Scientists, Zombified Stalkers, Military, Monolith, Duty, and Freedom. Each having quests and a relationship system, however the zombified stalkers and Monolith are mapped to hostile to the player. There are more things to fear than men and mutants which prowl the land. Emissions (powerful electical and radioactive storms) will occur throughout the game while you travel the land and are sometimes very beautiful to stare at. However, these emissions will kill all who do not take shelter and remain outdoors. You can however survive the emissions by using various specialty drugs and watch it pass. There are atifacts which can be found throughout the world which act as personal upgrades to your character stats and abilities. Most are modular and can be used in conjunction with other artifacts, or multiple artifacts of the same kind can be used to multiply their effects. Once you finish the game you can free roam where you want and complete all the quests you missed.
I recommend you play the game first in english, to understand the plot. But to aquire the most out of the game, i would recommend using its native russian audio (as the english voice actors with russian acents are to par-se for me).

Oath in Felghana is a phenomenal action RPG. It is the third game in the Ys series, and a remake of the original Ys III. While the original Ys III was a good game in its own right, it was also a flawed game in many ways (don't take that to mean it wasn't a heck of a lot of fun). Oath in Felghana not only rectifies every flaw of the original, it also improves upon Ys III in every way, all while remaining faithful to the core essence of what made Ys III such a fun and memorable game.
Pros:
- Phenomenal soundtrack
- Great battle mechanics
- Unique boss fights
- One of the best Ys stories
Cons:
- The beginning feels a bit slow
- (No Volcano)
- No easy way to access bonus bosses (even if you beat them)
A distinguishing feature of all Ys games is outstanding music, and this is true even for the original Ys III. In Oath in Felghana, the music has been upgraded to entirely new levels of awesome. If the soundtrack was the only good thing about this game, I'd still recommend it at full price. Fortunately for us, the music comes with an awesome game as well.
The gameplay mechanics of Felghana are some of the best, with controls that are tight and very refined. There are difficulty settings for every kind of player, be they casual or hardcore. Regardless of setting, the game is very encouraging of exploration, but for any difficulty above easy, it's loaded with intense action. Even some strategy comes into play concerning certain enemies and scenarios. Boss fights are varied and unique, and each boss requires a different method in order to defeat them. At higher difficulty levels, boss fights can be very challenging. While there is a random luck factor, for the most part, beating the bosses is a little bit of know-how accompanied by pure mad-skills (and it's very satisfying once you beat them).
Oath in Felghana is a bit of an oddball in regards to story. Most Ys games begin with Adol washed ashore after some great struggle. Here, Adol leisurely sails into Felghana with his long-time friend Dogi. Most Ys games feel epic and grand from the get-go. Oath in Felghana feels like a sidestory you could skip over (you’ll regret it if you do though).
The story has a pace that is uniquely its own, and VERY different from any other Ys game (that I’ve played at least). It ends on a powerful note, but it takes its time getting there (despite being a surprisingly short game). Even though it feels slow, there is always a driving energy that pushes the story forward; you can always feel the hidden danger, even if you don’t fully understand it. And when the story finally hits the turning point, everything comes together perfectly, leading to one of the most powerful moments in any Ys game.
Ys stories have depth, but they go by so fast that you may miss some of the more thought provoking themes and ideas being explored. Oath in Felghana, in particular, is an exploration of human weakness. The theme is explored through several characters, all of them strong individuals. And all of them having fallen to human weakness. That said, it is not just the strengths or failures of these characters that make them, in particular, so interesting.
Like the game itself, the story doesn’t give any answers; it shows you what you need to know, and leaves the rest to you.
While the slow pace of the game is one of its good points (it matches perfectly with Dogi returning home to family), it has the consequence of making the beginning feel too slow. This is because the beginning isn't interactive enough to offset the slow pace. More interaction means more immersion; experiencing rather than watching.
If you've had the opportunity to play the original Ys III, then you might remember the Volcano in the background of the Illburns Ruins. And it was AWESOME! I know this isn't really a 'negative' per say, and the Felghana version of the Illburns Ruins is clearly amazing without it. But... this should have made it into Felghana because it was just that cool.
While more of an annoyance than anything, there is no easy way to access the bonus bosses, even if you've beaten them before. It would be nice to have a means by which to easily access the two bosses once you've unlocked them. What makes this more annoying is that the bosses are quite fun and challenging, and not deserving of such obscurity.
Oath in Felghana is available for both the PC and the PSP. The PC version is, decidedly, visually superior to the PSP version. However, the PSP version has some exclusive content that should not be overlooked.
PSP Exclusives:
- Voice Acting: While mediocre (sometimes hilarious), it definitely has its own unique charm. And for the most part, I liked it. Unfortunately, the voice acting choices made for the final boss destroyed the atmosphere; it gave the boss more ‘human’ qualities (made it less monstrous) when it should have done the opposite.
- PSP Version is More Forgiving: Double Boost (regenerates health after boost), Room Retry (retry in the room you died in), Retry Boss at a Lower Difficulty.
- Selectable Soundtrack: You can choose between the Oath in Felghana Soundtrack or the Original Ys III Soundtrack.
- Inferno Time Attack: With double boost, this is probably about the equivalent of Nightmare Time Attack for the PC version. By the way, am I the only one who things Inferno Time Attack should be added to the PC version?
- Easier Access to Bonus Bosses: (Random Eye Twitch).
- Museum: This is a collection of unlockable art for the game (not unlike the Ys VI Materials Collection).
- Prologue Novella: As it turns out, the manuals for the Ys games included a Prologue to the main story. I actually think the Ys prologues should be included with their respective games is all cases (even if it’s as a PDF in the game folder) since they are a part of Ys lore.
While the PSP version decidedly has some nice exclusives, I don’t believe it has anything that makes it ‘superior’ to the PC edition. Both is an excellent choice (I might be evil).

Ah, The Oath in Felghana...
Many people like to say that the Resident Evil Remake is the best video game remake of all time. I disagree. While that game is amazing in its own right, the original Resident Evil was already a good game to begin with. Oath in Felghana, however, took an irredeemable pile of dogpoop and turned it into a masterpiece.
Back when I first played this in late 2006 I generally had reservations about it, since my experience with the original Wanderers from Ys was not a very good one (read I threw both cartridges I owned out the window, I'm dead serious), however after finishing it I was so satisfied with it that it instantly became my second favorite Ys game of all time and it still is (I & II will always hold top place in my heart for as long as I live).
It is generally agreed among the fans that Ys: The Oath in Felghana is, in terms of quality, the best game in the entire saga and for very good reasons (Originbabbies need not apply here, your game is good but it has far too many flaws to be called best of anything. I'll talk about it some other time and incur your wrath then).
Now let me tell you why you really should play this game even if you aren't an Ys fan.

Around a year after the events of Memories of Celceta legendary adventurer Adol Christin and his longtime companion Dogi the Wall-Crusher are traveling around mainland Europe when they hear rumors that Dogi's homeland, Felghana (located somewhere around real world northern Germany) has fallen on hard times. After a young fortune teller from a passing gypsy caravan confirms their suspicions, they both decide to head to Felghana and investigate. Arriving by boat they soon discover that the land is overrun by monsters and so begins their next adventure...
Compared to the legendary Ys I & II, which had an amazing story, the original Ys III (which wasn't even developed as an Ys game to begin with, but that's another topic) barely had a coherent story to it. Like, it had something similar to a story, but it was all very flat and underdeveloped in comparison to its predecessors. The localised versions we got here didn't help either, all of them, to put it simple, were terribad, which was a huge step down after the extremely high quality PC-Engine localization of Ys I & II.
Oath in Felghana, thankfully, fixed all that. The story has been vastly expanded from barely being there, to a very enjoyable one, even if it won't break any grounds in video game writing. The amazing world-building autism that was born with Ys ETERNAL is once again present although not to such extremes as the above-mentioned game. In typical Falcom fashion every single NPC in the game gets new lines of dialogue as the story progresses, so if you want that extra bit of immersion while playing you should take the time to go back speak to everyone every now and then.

Felghana uses the same engine as Ys VI, so from a technical side it doesn't really look much different from it. The sprites and models are of higher quality this time around, but the game won't break any graphical records. Fancy graphics has never been Falcom's goal and I'm thankful for that. XSEED added native widescreen support with the Steam release, but be advised the game was never designed for widescreen monitors, so there will be some small oddities if you do decide to play in widescreen. I originally played it in 640x480 on a virus-ridden Windows XP piece of scrap, so 4:3 doesn't bother me.
Performance-wise the game will run perfectly even on a toaster, so you shouldn't have any concerns about that. And as usual it runs at 60FPS.

The only saving grace of the original Wanderers from Ys was its soundtrack. It's amazing and for a long time was considered to be the best Ys soundtrack of all time. This also applied to most of its ports (aside from the NES and SNES ones, if you thought those sounded good you're clearly deaf). The PC-Engine version in particular was so amazingly amazing I feel all warm and tingly inside every time I hear it.
Felghana, however, managed to not only match the PC-Engine soundtrack, but outright surpass it (though this can be debated). In both musical quality and technical quality, Felghana's soundtrack is godly. While both Ark and Origin suffered from the use of lower quality synths, Felghana completely lacks this problem. I've heard that Sound Team J.D.K. used live instruments for this one instead of synths, but even if it was synths they are extremely high quality.
In short: Oath in Felghana's soundtrack is simply perfect. It does its job perfectly in-game and 11 years later I'm still actively listening to it even outside of the game.

While Ys I & II were unique in their own right (I'm gonna punch the next person who calls them Zelda-likes, go do some actual research) Wanderers from Ys was nothing but a bad Zelda II clone. And being a bad clone was the least of its problems. The whole game was a mess especially when you started comparing all the different ports it had. It was so bad Ys IV went back to the style of I & II to prevent fans from burning down Falcom HQ.
For Oath in Felghana Falcom went and rebuilt everything from scratch. While all the areas of the original game are present here, everything has been vastly expanded and infinitely improved. Ys VI was used as a base for the gameplay and in the process they ironed out all the flaws Napishtim had and perfected it. The combat system is simple, but effective. The gimmicky dash jump is gone and Adol controls extremely tight and responsive.
The main complaint I hear from people who diss Felghana is the difficulty.
I won't sugarcoat it, this game is brutal. Even on normal difficulty it can destroy you if you aren't careful (for reference I have nightmared every single Ys game that has nightmare difficulty aside from Felghana, I've only made it up to hard.) HOWEVER this game is completely and utterly fair. There are no bullsh*t ways to die, every death will be your own fault.
The boss battles are the highlight of the game. I consider Ys VI's bosses to be extremely easy (not Ys V levels of easy, but close), but here it's the polar opposite. The battles are very intense, you'll need to learn how every boss works to survive and utilize your whole arsenal to achieve victory, especially once you move past normal difficulty. For people coming from the Souls series (because they are mainly the ones who brag about difficulty these days): forget everything you know, you'll need every bit of GIT GUD you can get to survive here. There's no hiding to take a sippie or summoning NPCs to help you, you get one life bar and that's it. You die: you start over.

Ys: The Oath in Felghana is an amazingly fun game and the perfect example of how a video game remake should be done. The only really bad thing about it is that it's also responsible for ruining the Ys fanbase by giving birth to the Felghana purists and later the Originbabbies (I'm not dissing Origin fans, only the fanboys who praise it as the second coming and sh*t on everything else).
It has an enjoyable story, good world-building, an amazing soundtrack and despite its difficulty it has addictive gameplay with god-tier boss battles. The amount of love put into this remake is outstanding and I highly recommend it to anyone who is truly passionate about video games.

There is also a PSP port of this game, but unless you really want to play it on the go I suggest you stick to PC. It does have some extras like NG+, a prologue novella, an extra opening cutscene, voice acting which ranges from good to awful and was also localized by an idiot who completely ruined the final boss (hope they got fired). However the difficulty was considerably lowered due to the ability to heal during bosses, it runs at 30FPS and generally looks and feels worse than the PC version.

LEGIONS OF STEEL is an incredibly well polished graphically gorgeous and game mechanics stunning science fiction strategy war game where your squad of futuristic Commandos are tasked to protect the universe against cybernetic organisms known as The Machines.
The sleek sci-fi artstyle and mechanical ambient music merge to create a dark surreal galactic canvas bathed in deep red slaughter. The look of LEGIONS OF STEEL conjures up comic book memories of ALIEN LEGION and games i used to play on the Commodore Amiga 500 which delivered the whole package in a very visceral satisfying potent way. Its a fun kind of tough where even losing feels exhilarating all the while learning from ones mistakes and going back into the fray to attempt to do better.
In LEGIONS OF STEEL combat flows with graceful lethal elegance as units move in a battle ballet of death seeking to achieve the most advantageous tactical position to annihilate their foes. Engaging the enemy means knowing when to do certain command maneuvers such as a strafing attack where the combatant steps out into the open to blast the Machine enemy with metal shredding fire then fade back into cover with such speed one forgets this is a turn based marvel of strategic controlled chaos as they would say in the old ALIEN LEGION comic books.
Player and enemy turns are geniously done via table top style dice roll to see who wins the intiative to decide which side moves first. This adds another level of strategy as the player with the initiative roll may decide its better to let the enemy move first as they wait for that right momemt to engage in a ambush maneuver. Before each firing encounter the player can click on the fire panel to see what modifiers are effecting their chances of getting a hit or not thus allowing them to make a decision to fire, move to a more advantageous location or wait until they are in a better situation to engage such as when grenades with different vision and area effects are making for a difficult successful shot or one of your fellow Commandos is in your line of fire thus making for a penalty modifier to hit. Ah wonderful wonderful modifiers!
Then there are throwable weapons like the force wall which comes in extremely handy in desperate situations when the enemy needs slowing down or their line of sight blocked buying the player some time to gather their wits and launch a counter attack or retreat to more advantageous ground. The Machine enemy also have their own plethora of grenade weapons which effect the battlefield or just outright kill those who stand against their all consuming might.
Have i mentioned yet that there are also ballistic and energy weapons?
Animations compliment the futuristic art style perfectly giving inhuman alien menace to The Machines and vigilant heroic stature to The Commandos. Storyboard screens are rich with comic book artistry alive with violently valiant imagery urging the player to continue their war against The Machines.
There is both a lengthy campaign mode and skirmish mode where you can play either as the desperately fighting for survival Commandos or the indomitable relentless Machines. For those who desire for more fleshlike opponents there is hot seat as well as multiplayer for your.. special needs.
Music and sound effects transform my reality into unreality as i suddenly find myself in a science fiction audioscape as if out of the movies FORBIDDEN PLANET and ALIEN among many other forboding paradise nightmare worlds. Truly audiophile elite level of quality.
LEGIONS OF STEEL table top majesty in a digital age where screaming metal and liquified flesh fill the battlefields of tomorrow. Buy it! Play it! Decimate in terror all before you!

However, the Misery mod for Call of Pripyat makes it an absolute hardcore survival masterpiece. It is by far the toughest, most fully-featured, and mercilessly dreary single-player survivor shooter out there - nothing comes even close. It always walks that fine line between jaw-droppingly challenging, frightening and just kind of stupidly insane, and that definitely makes it not everyone's cup of tea. The name doesn't lie - you can say a lot of things about Misery, but it's hard to call it "fun". It is a game out to murder you, both with bullets and monster claws, AND with its complex inventory/item/health/trade system which forces you to think about a lot more than just armor and bullets. Maintaining your health, stamina and the state of your gear isn't simply a matter of walking up to a couple of stations and spending some currency - oh no, this game throws one of the most arcane inventory/item/stats management systems out there at you while providing virtually no instructions, charts or stats bars, only vague indicators. For every new nifty acquisition there is a price - cheap food is radioactive, suits with gas masks constrain and muddy your vision, and carrying more than just bare necessities makes you constantly run out of stamina, even from just walking. It gives you few cues on who is friend and foe, and foes will drop you with deathly-accurate fire from long range. You will die. A lot.
But in the process of making you miserable, Misery inspires not just respect and curiosity for the Zone (like STALKER games are wont to do), but sheer awe and terror of the place. It's a game that, many times, made me basically forget everything I was doing and RUN for my (virtual) life, as far as my realistically-puny stamina would allow - not through scripted setpieces like horror games do, but through sheer incidental immersion in the gameworld, which I knew at that moment just happened to be randomly trying to murder me. Even after many days of play, it repeatedly turned me into a lowly scavenger, hunting mutated pigs for something to eat, racing NPCs to a dead bodies just to get some loot off it before they cleaned it all up, and spending as much as 2 weeks of game-time just to scrounge up enough cash for a brand new gun that - gasp - actually works and doesn't jam all the damn time!
So yeah, while I think Call of Pripyat by itself is just barely recommendable as an alright game, I give a very hearty recommendation to the Misery mod - with the warning that it takes a certain kind of masochistic player to properly enjoy its hatefully hardcore survival charm.

Well, well...what to say about "100% Orange Juice"...well for starters, it's my favorite drink and it's extremely nutritious.
THAT WAS A JOKE, THANKS FOR COMING!!!
Now time to be series about this review.
100% Orange Juice is a really fun game, especially if you can get 3 friends for a full-game. It's like Mario Party (a dice board game) but without the mini-games, and instead added the element of Cards (like items but with multiple uses) and the element of constant battles. The battles are simple and a double-edged sword. When you pass someone you get to choose whether to just pass by them and continue along, or fight them and regardless of win or lose, you stay on the space they were on.
In a battle, the attacker/approacher rolls 1st to determine his bonus attack added to his base attack. The person being attack is put in defense mode and chooses either to roll for bonus DEFENCE or bonus EVADE points. Defense just reduces the damage based on the roll but always guarantee you take one damage. Evade is a hit-or-miss. If you have MORE points than the attacker, you dodge all the damage. If you have less, you receive ALL the damage.
Now here's the double-edged part.
If they failed to kill you (or even damage you), it becomes YOUR turn to ATTACK. You have the possibility to damage them or even KO them for attacking you. If you win/lose a battle, you gain a lot of the opponents stars (I think you take half) which are used for leveling up (reaching Lv.6 is the objective for winning the game) and are also used for the cost of playing cards.
To level up and reach Lv.6 to win the game, you must reach the "Norma" (better known as "The Objective".)
There are 2 ways:
The 1st level up is the same for everyone, gain 10 stars. After that you have the option of doing "Collect X star" OR "Defeat X enemies." Once you achieved the "Norma", you must LAND on a "Check Panel." If you reached the Norma, you will level up and then get to decide which Norma objective you would like to do next to level up (Collect Stars or Defeat Enemies). Everyone has a "Home Check Panel" on the board. YOUR home check panel gives you the option of stopping on it regardless of your dice roll. It heals you 1 HP if you decide to stay on it.
Overall, this game gets 9/10 for me.

[Warning, Walls of text incoming, also, this is gameplay only, I had a much longer review planned]
The Gameplay
This is easily STALKER's strongest point. To put it frankly, it's awesome. The open world is fun to roam around, the locations are all unique, the way they handle the difficulties is very cool, and using the guns feels very nice, even if some of them do sound like pea-shooters. To go in to a bit more detail:
The game starts you off with a bit of food and medical supplies, a light vest, a gasmask, a pistol, and an AKS. All equipment has a durability meter. Now don't worry, that's just equipment, so your grenades, medpacks, and food will remain in tip-top shape. Lower durability means lowered stats, and if it's a gun, it may jam at the most inconvenient times. Durability lowers either by taking damage, or shooting. Do yourself a favor and shoot in single fire mode, as that helps you both control your shots better, and saves on durability. Your inventory consists of the storage, your helmet and armor slots, and your 2 gun slots. Do note that certain armor takes up both the armor and helmet slot, so watch what you wear. Your 2 gun slots can carry whatever you want, it's not limited to primary and pistol. You could have any combo, the choice is yours. Your inventory automatically extends, so you can carry what you want. The only thing that will get in your way, is the weight limit. At the beginning I think it's about 50kg. Going over that limit over-encumbers you, causing you to move slower, and sprinting drains your stamina really really fast. Going 10kg or above the weight limit will cause you to stop moving all-together, meaning you'll have to drop some items if you wish to move at all. You can, however, get drugs that temporarily increase your carry weight, and you can upgrade certain armor to increase the carry weight. I'm pretty sure some armor comes with a base carry weight increase, though I haven't taken the time to check that out. Throughout the game you will battle Zombies, Snorks, Burers, Blind dogs, Boars, Pseudo-Dogs, Rodents, Bloodsuckers, etc. Sure, there's Flesh monsters, but what you do to them is more akin to Genocide than Battling. You'll also encounter Anomalies. These are rather odd entities that, depending on the anomaly, can do all sorts of things. Some are simply pillars of flame triggered by movement, others do such crazy things as teleport you, or even trap an entire squad in a world of emptiness. And by the way, that's a side-mission that you can easily miss. Most of the anomalies are found in, quite obviously, anomaly fields.
Now you might ask yourself, "Well why would I go to an insanely dangerous area filled with the oddities of an already strange world that could practically rip me apart?" Well the answer, is Artifacts. Artifacts are strange items scattered throughout the world. They are found only in Anomaly fields, with 2 exceptions. Exception 1 is certain scripted artifacts, exception 2 is when you get the prototype detector. With the prototype detector out, you can detect them out in the open, albeit very rarely. Artifacts are extremely useful in that you can either sell them for varying amounts of money, depending on how rare they are, or you can equip them, if your vest has the slots for it. The only downside to equiping them is they usually give a fair amount of radiation every second, so it's best to get some radiation-reducing artifacts before working on the more useful ones. The upside is a lot of the artifacts have some rather good effects, just make sure to mouse over them and see just what they are. But what do you do then? What do you do when there's no more Artifacts to find? Well, that's where Emissions come in. I mentioned these earlier, but now I'll explain what they do and what they are. Emissions are the result of the Zone basically releasing any excess energy. They happen every day at a random time, and when they begin to form, you'll hear all sorts of crazy sounds, and see the clouds forming in a strange way. Seconds later you should get a PDA side-mission telling you to find cover, along with a radio broadcast telling all stalkers an emission is approaching. You have around 2-3 In-game minutes to find cover, which is marked on your minimap, before the emission hits the land. Anyone caught outside either dies, or turns into a zombie. Another way to tell an emission is approaching is monitoring the mutant activity. Mutants spawn more often both before and after emissions. You can survive these while outside though, you just need Anabiotics. If you survive 3 emissions with these, you'll be immune to them, though they will drain your health like crazy and you will black out. After an emission is the most important part though. After any emission, artifacts have a very large chance of respawning at Anomaly fields, empty or not.
Now that I've covered Emissions, let's move on to something I mentioned while I was talking about them. Achivements. These are not normal achivements though, these ones have in-game advantages and disadvantages. One gives you medical supplies every day in your personal box, another gives you AMMO everyday, but spawns more dangerous mutants, and another spawns rarer artifacts much more often, but causes bandits to sometimes fight you. Of course there is some that are just there to be achivements and nothing more. One in particular was supposed to do something, specifically the one you get for exposing Magpie, but because of a programing error, it doesn't do anything. So far, it hasn't been fixed, and seeing as GSC Game World was disbanded, I don't expect a fix anytime soon.
Now going a little deeper in to how the game works, everything has Stats, technically making this game an Open-World RPG. Guns have the usual stats like damage, accuracy, and even Flatness, which decreases the arc of the bullet. Armor has stuff like radiation resistance, psy resistance, armor, chemical protection, et cetera. A nice feature is that certain guns can have attachments. You know, the usual, like grenade launchers, scopes, and silencers. As for movement, it's all the usual, but with a few tweaks. For instance, you can lean left and right with Q and E. You also have 3 stances, but the last one isn't the one you expect. Standing, crouch, and low-crouch, which is basically prone but a slight bit faster. And no, there is no prone stance. For fighting mutants, and especially humans, it's best to try and get headshots, as they'll 1-shot most humans and do a good chunk more damage to mutants. If YOU get hit, you have a large chance to Bleed, which will drain your health until it's fixed. There's 3 color-coded degrees to bleeding. Green, your health goes down slowly, and you can just leave it and it should fix itself up in a couple of seconds, yellow is when you should apply bandages, as your health drops faster, and red is when you HAVE to apply bandages, as your health will be gone in a matter of seconds. The game also has hunger, so on top of the emissions, the mutants, the anomalies, the bandits, and your equipment's durability, you gotta make sure you had your mini-wheats for breakfast. Thankfully, they downplay it quite a lot, so you only really need to eat either when you sleep for more than a few hours, or if you are adventuring for a LONG time.
<Score>
And that's really the basics [and a bit of the advanced] of the gameplay, I don't really know what to say other than, it's STALKER's strongest point, with atmosphere being VERY close behind it. It's easily a 10/10.
<Final game score>

Having played this game on the dreamcast and its sequel on the xbox classic, I can assure you that the Jet Set Radio franchise is definetely a unique one as you won't find anything else quite like it. (aside from that one indie game that's supposed to be its spiritual successor)
Firstly, the gameplay can be pretty quirky and you may have to fight the controls a bit in order to do what you want to do  but its not TOO quirky, and honestly it keeps the gameplay from getting dull for me. This game takes 3D platforming to a whole new level. Jumping on walls, riding wires, and trying to reach certain platforms aren't easy, but to make it all the more difficult, the cops go from 0 to 100 real quick so you always need to be on your toes as they move fast and hit hard so you need to act hard and smart if you're going to survive the armored swat teams and helicoptors. This game is actually pretty difficult but it rewards you with a sense of satisfaction everytime you accomplish a mission, earn a new player, or perform a certain trick you couldn't get quite right after many tries.
Now for the music. Jet Set Radio and its sequel both have some of the best soundtracks I have ever heard in a game. There are very few soundtracks that I would put on my phone and listen to them while I go on walks or do homework, and the game's soundtrack not only fits the game perfectly, it also provides a neat soundtrack to a lot of everyday life activities. If you liked the soundtrack to Sonic Rush its the same composer.
If this game has anything at all, its style. From the voice actors, animations, cell shading, even the grafitti itself has style. You can also draw your own grafiitti in the game if you want to be creative but I don't find it as the easiest thing to use, but if I'm not a perfectionist I can create some things that aren't completely ugly at least.
Overall, I can definetely recommend this game. It's not perfect, not by a long shot, but it is definetely fun, exciting, stylish, and one of my favorite franchises of all time.

Rulling over a series of vassals or independant counties is fun and all, but there's not much to this game. You always feel as if you could do more to work your way to the top, but overall you stutter your way through the development side of ruling land. Spending in-game decades trying to fortify some tiny cities, only to defend yourself from overly powerful neighboring areas. Cultivating your own offspring is even terrible because most of the time your kids inherit whatever bad traits you may have.
Quite a few flaws and less actual control then what is displayed. WIthout the DLC, this game is giving a max of a few hours of real gameplay.

You mostly waddle around slowly, ride slow elevators or drive slow vehicles. In between you solve physics puzzles which will probably not challenge anybody above age 4, except when trying to execute the solution. The physics and camera are the real challenge in this game and will test your frustration tolerance.
- nice music and it's available for free from
I really like four of the five tracks used in the game:
Call to Adventure, Radio Martini, Run Amok, The Builder
- some parts of the physics work really well. I only managed to glitch through one closed door that was supposed to be an impassable level border during the whole playthrough. Jumping onto crates is assisted, making it really easy
- good variety of challenges, most of which sadly suffer from playing like Surgeon Simulator
- nice setting, family friendly. All you do is make your way through a huge construction site. With smoother edges and more variety it would even look good
- some of the puzzles are fun, even if they are easy. I especially liked the balls through pipes puzzle (level 22 or thereabouts)
- bad camera: it's incredibly difficult to exactly place a pallet on top of something, jumps are hard to judge (the jump target marker is frequently wrong and absent for the deliberately difficult jumps)
- bad physics: Imagine trying to solve a series of puzzles with Surgeon Simulator controls. Add to that a bunch of glitches: balls that are supposeed to roll somewhere get stuck, stuff sinks into the floor a lot making it impossible to pick up with a forklift, good luck trying to pick up a flipped over pallet or putting it right side up again, vehicle tires can get stuck in miniscule gaps, vehicles tend to get completely stuck on top of empty pallets, and so on
- the puzzles are a joke. The two times I was stuck for a while were both cases of not finding/recognizing a piece of the puzzle right away
- walking simulator: you spend 90% of your time crawling around the level, and most other actions are equally slow
- Mr. Bobley is the ugly, geriatric brother of Bob the Builder, complete with red nose and a waddle that suggests serious pelvis displacement. The man needs a doctor

As someone who has seen some Early Access blunders, Conan Exiles seems to me like the perfect example of Early Access done right.
After a few stress tests and optimization to keep the game running, the developers have been adding content non-stop.
What started as "yet another generic survival game" is slowly being fleshed out as a unique and interesting Conan game, with a fun and engaging world full of beasts where the greatest dangers often come from other players.
The world of Conan Exiles is ruthless yet appealing, and FUNCOM really seems to be doing its part here.
Though there aren't many quests planned, I found that this isn't a problem, as many times those are created by the players. I got into a situation where I helped a clan to defeat another one simply because they had taken over a mountain path and blocked it to all other players, or some other times I went to a dangerous zone to gather ingredients so that one of my friends would craft an armor for me. Though single player is engaging, this game IS a multiplayer game, and it is playing with others what makes it feel the way it feels.
But, if you find that adventuring and exploring is not your thing, building bases and crafting items is becoming quite an art after last updates. Drawbridges, elevators, spike traps, burning oil and armed or artisan thralls will bring your city to life and protect it from intruders... though the enemy currently has trebuchets and explosives, and things like siege towers have been planned. The developers said it so themselves: no base will be unraidable.
Still, anyone who buys this game needs to take into account that it's still Early Access, and by no means a finished game. The developers said they will add better AI, combat, sorcery, a city-system, mounts and a main quest among other things. Many players decided to buy it now or when it gets cheap and then stay dormant until Early Access ends. I personally enjoyed it, but it's not for everyone.
My favorite part of the game is the detail put into the world, which makes it very immersive, especially thanks to the music. Be it on its eerie deserts, its jungles, boiling with life or the many caves and dungeons filled with unspeakable creatures, one can't help but to feel Howard's world comes alive in this game. It is a world filled with mysteries and stories that you must discover, through the paths of sword and sorcery.

By itself, Call of Pripyat is alright and mostly recommendable - way better than Clear Sky, but still far from delivering on the original promise of the STALKER concept. As all of them, CoP is genuinely at its best when you're left to roam freely, explore, scavenge, pick your own battles and soak in the atmosphere. The linear parts of the game are forgettable and the graphics, well, I guess there the engine is starting to show it's age. But it's pretty alright.
However, the Misery mod for Call of Pripyat makes it an absolute hardcore survival masterpiece. It is by far the toughest, most fully-featured, and mercilessly dreary single-player survivor shooter out there - nothing comes even close. It always walks that fine line between jaw-droppingly challenging, frightening and just kind of stupidly insane, and that definitely makes it not everyone's cup of tea. The name doesn't lie - you can say a lot of things about Misery, but it's hard to call it "fun". It is a game out to murder you, both with bullets and monster claws, AND with its complex inventory/item/health/trade system which forces you to think about a lot more than just armor and bullets. Maintaining your health, stamina and the state of your gear isn't simply a matter of walking up to a couple of stations and spending some currency - oh no, this game throws one of the most arcane inventory/item/stats management systems out there at you while providing virtually no instructions, charts or stats bars, only vague indicators. For every new nifty acquisition there is a price - cheap food is radioactive, suits with gas masks constrain and muddy your vision, and carrying more than just bare necessities makes you constantly run out of stamina, even from just walking. It gives you few cues on who is friend and foe, and foes will drop you with deathly-accurate fire from long range. You will die. A lot.
But in the process of making you miserable, Misery inspires not just respect and curiosity for the Zone (like STALKER games are wont to do), but sheer awe and terror of the place. It's a game that, many times, made me basically forget everything I was doing and RUN for my (virtual) life, as far as my realistically-puny stamina would allow - not through scripted setpieces like horror games do, but through sheer incidental immersion in the gameworld, which I knew at that moment just happened to be randomly trying to murder me. Even after many days of play, it repeatedly turned me into a lowly scavenger, hunting mutated pigs for something to eat, racing NPCs to a dead bodies just to get some loot off it before they cleaned it all up, and spending as much as 2 weeks of game-time just to scrounge up enough cash for a brand new gun that - gasp - actually works and doesn't jam all the damn time!
So yeah, while I think Call of Pripyat by itself is just barely recommendable as an alright game, I give a very hearty recommendation to the Misery mod - with the warning that it takes a certain kind of masochistic player to properly enjoy its hatefully hardcore survival charm.

[Warning, Walls of text incoming, also, this is gameplay only, I had a much longer review planned]
The Gameplay
This is easily STALKER's strongest point. To put it frankly, it's awesome. The open world is fun to roam around, the locations are all unique, the way they handle the difficulties is very cool, and using the guns feels very nice, even if some of them do sound like pea-shooters. To go in to a bit more detail:
The game starts you off with a bit of food and medical supplies, a light vest, a gasmask, a pistol, and an AKS. All equipment has a durability meter. Now don't worry, that's just equipment, so your grenades, medpacks, and food will remain in tip-top shape. Lower durability means lowered stats, and if it's a gun, it may jam at the most inconvenient times. Durability lowers either by taking damage, or shooting. Do yourself a favor and shoot in single fire mode, as that helps you both control your shots better, and saves on durability. Your inventory consists of the storage, your helmet and armor slots, and your 2 gun slots. Do note that certain armor takes up both the armor and helmet slot, so watch what you wear. Your 2 gun slots can carry whatever you want, it's not limited to primary and pistol. You could have any combo, the choice is yours. Your inventory automatically extends, so you can carry what you want. The only thing that will get in your way, is the weight limit. At the beginning I think it's about 50kg. Going over that limit over-encumbers you, causing you to move slower, and sprinting drains your stamina really really fast. Going 10kg or above the weight limit will cause you to stop moving all-together, meaning you'll have to drop some items if you wish to move at all. You can, however, get drugs that temporarily increase your carry weight, and you can upgrade certain armor to increase the carry weight. I'm pretty sure some armor comes with a base carry weight increase, though I haven't taken the time to check that out. Throughout the game you will battle Zombies, Snorks, Burers, Blind dogs, Boars, Pseudo-Dogs, Rodents, Bloodsuckers, etc. Sure, there's Flesh monsters, but what you do to them is more akin to Genocide than Battling. You'll also encounter Anomalies. These are rather odd entities that, depending on the anomaly, can do all sorts of things. Some are simply pillars of flame triggered by movement, others do such crazy things as teleport you, or even trap an entire squad in a world of emptiness. And by the way, that's a side-mission that you can easily miss. Most of the anomalies are found in, quite obviously, anomaly fields.
Now you might ask yourself, "Well why would I go to an insanely dangerous area filled with the oddities of an already strange world that could practically rip me apart?" Well the answer, is Artifacts. Artifacts are strange items scattered throughout the world. They are found only in Anomaly fields, with 2 exceptions. Exception 1 is certain scripted artifacts, exception 2 is when you get the prototype detector. With the prototype detector out, you can detect them out in the open, albeit very rarely. Artifacts are extremely useful in that you can either sell them for varying amounts of money, depending on how rare they are, or you can equip them, if your vest has the slots for it. The only downside to equiping them is they usually give a fair amount of radiation every second, so it's best to get some radiation-reducing artifacts before working on the more useful ones. The upside is a lot of the artifacts have some rather good effects, just make sure to mouse over them and see just what they are. But what do you do then? What do you do when there's no more Artifacts to find? Well, that's where Emissions come in. I mentioned these earlier, but now I'll explain what they do and what they are. Emissions are the result of the Zone basically releasing any excess energy. They happen every day at a random time, and when they begin to form, you'll hear all sorts of crazy sounds, and see the clouds forming in a strange way. Seconds later you should get a PDA side-mission telling you to find cover, along with a radio broadcast telling all stalkers an emission is approaching. You have around 2-3 In-game minutes to find cover, which is marked on your minimap, before the emission hits the land. Anyone caught outside either dies, or turns into a zombie. Another way to tell an emission is approaching is monitoring the mutant activity. Mutants spawn more often both before and after emissions. You can survive these while outside though, you just need Anabiotics. If you survive 3 emissions with these, you'll be immune to them, though they will drain your health like crazy and you will black out. After an emission is the most important part though. After any emission, artifacts have a very large chance of respawning at Anomaly fields, empty or not.
Now that I've covered Emissions, let's move on to something I mentioned while I was talking about them. Achivements. These are not normal achivements though, these ones have in-game advantages and disadvantages. One gives you medical supplies every day in your personal box, another gives you AMMO everyday, but spawns more dangerous mutants, and another spawns rarer artifacts much more often, but causes bandits to sometimes fight you. Of course there is some that are just there to be achivements and nothing more. One in particular was supposed to do something, specifically the one you get for exposing Magpie, but because of a programing error, it doesn't do anything. So far, it hasn't been fixed, and seeing as GSC Game World was disbanded, I don't expect a fix anytime soon.
Now going a little deeper in to how the game works, everything has Stats, technically making this game an Open-World RPG. Guns have the usual stats like damage, accuracy, and even Flatness, which decreases the arc of the bullet. Armor has stuff like radiation resistance, psy resistance, armor, chemical protection, et cetera. A nice feature is that certain guns can have attachments. You know, the usual, like grenade launchers, scopes, and silencers. As for movement, it's all the usual, but with a few tweaks. For instance, you can lean left and right with Q and E. You also have 3 stances, but the last one isn't the one you expect. Standing, crouch, and low-crouch, which is basically prone but a slight bit faster. And no, there is no prone stance. For fighting mutants, and especially humans, it's best to try and get headshots, as they'll 1-shot most humans and do a good chunk more damage to mutants. If YOU get hit, you have a large chance to Bleed, which will drain your health until it's fixed. There's 3 color-coded degrees to bleeding. Green, your health goes down slowly, and you can just leave it and it should fix itself up in a couple of seconds, yellow is when you should apply bandages, as your health drops faster, and red is when you HAVE to apply bandages, as your health will be gone in a matter of seconds. The game also has hunger, so on top of the emissions, the mutants, the anomalies, the bandits, and your equipment's durability, you gotta make sure you had your mini-wheats for breakfast. Thankfully, they downplay it quite a lot, so you only really need to eat either when you sleep for more than a few hours, or if you are adventuring for a LONG time.
<Score>
And that's really the basics [and a bit of the advanced] of the gameplay, I don't really know what to say other than, it's STALKER's strongest point, with atmosphere being VERY close behind it. It's easily a 10/10.
<Final game score>

As a big fan of all 3 Final Fantasy Tactics games, XCOM 2, Vandal Hearts as well as less tactical turn based RPG's(Final Fantasy X and earlier, Baiten Kaitos, Xenosaga, Skies of Arcadia) I've got to say this is hands down the best RPG of all time. There are so many options, the environment reacts to you(and your enemies) and if you're not paying attention to what you're doing you could end up zapping and stunning your entire party, setting them all on fire, poisoning them, or accidentally healing them to death. The voice acting, narration and story are pretty good, but not perfect, it's hard to write a unique story because just about everything has been done in some way, shape or form. They did a fairly good job though, there were even some moments where the narrator describing the disgusting things my character was doing even made my stomach turn a little
. Another note, I love that there's an actual narrator. Instead of investing in fancy animations and visuals for much of the scenes, you're told the story and left to let your imagination run wild. And the vocabulary! Wow! The dialogue was clearly written by intelligent people...no mention of anybody's face being tired!
This game doesn't hold your hand, there's a steep learning curve, you really need to pay attention to what you're doing and don't forget to quick save before going to a new area. If your favorite "RPG" is Skyrim or Fallout 4 this game isn't for you, move on. You won't like it and you'll just complain about it being "too hard". Not saying fans of those games will definitely not like this, but if that's what you're preferred RPG is like, you most likely won't like this. Do a little research on games before buying and you'll avoid getting games that aren't your style.
Larian Studios, you have restored my faith in modern RPG's. I acquired this game through..."other" means. Judge me all you want, I just don't trust developers these days. After getting off the island I realized I had only scratched the surface(and only did maybe 3/4 of what was available on that island...in 31 hours). Woke up the next day and purchased it for full price. That's how you know you've made a great game.
The one con I've found in over 125 hours invested, is the split screen. It's an abortion. Even on a 96" screen(via projector) it's just not good. I don't know how console players can stand playing the first game with a controller. So by having such terrible split screen, you've got me to buy a 2nd copy(opted for the Eternal Edition for my 2nd copy). Still don't feel ripped off.
And no, you don't have to abuse teleportation to suceed ;)

My nomination for the 'Test of TIme' award as years later I find myself coming back to this beaut and still love the characters and the world you play in.
Thanks to a little tweeking by the guys at beamdog, this game still holds up pretty well, dispite it's 2D world limitations. Where as games like skyrim imerse you with a 3D world you can explore. Here you are pulled in by not only the rich story telling centred on the main character, but the quests and dialog of your supporting party members. I remember the first time 2 party members started talking to each other, and I thought, 'hey, where's my bit?' but then realised that these characters had their own thought/agenders, that didn't make my character the centre of the universe.
Game play is pretty solid with a respectable learning curve. New game modes allow you to change the difficulty to however easy or difficult you want. Magic can take some getting use to, so it's important to read what spells do and track combat text through the feedback window. However with the game being out so long you can find any number of useful guides online to help explain spells and debuffs etc.
The soundtrack include one of my favorite games themes to date, which is good if like me you want to spend your first hour roling the perfect human paladin.
Overall this game is perfect for anyone who wants to see where Bioware got their reputation from, long before they made 'Mass Effect' of 'Dragon Age'

Before I say anything, 10/10. If you have ever played and liked Mario Party, Fortune Street, Dokapon Kingdom, or any real or digital board game, this game should be given great consideration.
100% Orange Juice goes into the long tradition of combining characters from different series by making them all into a single card game most recently done on Steam with Card City Nights or a board game most similarly done like Fortune Street. This game decided to do both. What I really enjoy about this game is that it is basically the first of its kind on Steam. It combines many core elements from Dokapon Kingdom like combat and different stats, Fortune Street for “promotions” and board control, and Mario Party for stars and the 3 item max system (no minigames unfortunately).
The main objective of this game is to get 5 normas. Normas are objectives that you need to achieve by either collecting stars or killing enemies. Once the objective is met, you need to land on an enemy orange or pass your own that you can automatically stop at even if you overroll. Each Norma will give you an additional level up star, from a start of 1, and caps at 5 for the 5th norma is victory. Higher stars mean you can use more powerful cards to help secure victory.
A dice is rolled at the start of each turn. Like other games of its kind, you can also use applicable items at this time, which this game implements as cards. Each card, as mentioned earlier, does have a minimum level requirement, so overly strong cards will not come out till late game. Across the board are many spaces. Green draws a card, red fights an enemy, yellow gains stars based on roll after landing, blue drops stars based on roll after landing, purple warps to another purple, and the orange marker is each corresponding color’s base that can automatically stopped at to get a norma if it is your own or landed on for the same purpose if not your own and can be used to heal. There is also a grey space that does nothing :(.
The combat in this system is really reminiscent of Dokapon Kingdom. In this game you can choose to fight whenever you pass an enemy or have to fight when another player fights you or you land on a red space. Each player only gets to do one attack and one defend each encounter. You can use applicable cards before combat if you have any that apply. During combat, the main decider of things is how high you roll for an attack and what defensive stance you take. When defending you can either defend, which will reduce the attack into their roll minus your roll with a minimum of one, or you can evade, which will completely avoid the attack only if you roll higher than the opposing roll. There are also boss battles that sometimes occur on red spaces that drop a lot of stars. If you reach 0 hitpoints, you will have to roll a dice to revive. It requries a roll of 5 or higher and then goes does by one each turn you fail. You also lose half your stars upon death and these go to the oppoment if defeated by that person.
This game is a lot of fun and you should strongly consider it. The only complaint one may have is this game contains a lot of pulp. Hours upon hours of "pulp".

An excellent action-RPG that will grind the meat off your bones make you love every moment of it.
This game is a remake and expansion of the Sega Master System's Ys III: Wanderers from Ys.  Combat is fast-paced and difficult, and boss fights are complex and brutally unforgiving -- but in (almost) every case it's readily apparent what you're doing wrong, and you feel like such a badass when you eventually make that one clean run and come out on top.
There are a few notable flaws, mostly on the highest difficulties.  Certain boss mechanics (Chester's teleport spam, or Gyalva's tile flipping on Nightmare) can randomly screw you and there's not always any clear difference between a failed run and a flawless one.  These are very rare, however, and a solid battle plan and execution will get you through almost everything all the way through the highest difficulties.
For those less adept at the genre, don't be afraid to start out on Easy.  Ys is a series rooted in the 8-bit era of difficulty, and this game's idea of Easy is right about where most other franchises would place Normal.

The Earth 2150 Trilogy is an excellent game series that remained true to real-time strategy conventions but still offered many interesting features, such as the ability to construct original units from component parts.
Those of you who haven't experienced the science fiction of Earth 2150 have missed some good gameplay, highly realistic environments, and an exciting plot. All of these features satisfied even the most demanding RTS fans. What we can say for sure is that the outstanding atmosphere presents the most appealing aspect of Earth 2150. Changes of night and day, weather conditions, and highly detailed landscapes proved that the guys at TopWare really take their work serious.
Each of the three organizations features more than 50 units, weapons, and structures in its arsenal, many with upgrade components, prerequisites,and specific properties. Weapons and technology range in power from simple chain guns and cannons to earthquake generators, weather control centers and shields. Structures run the gamut from energy supply facilities and mines to research centers and base defenses.
Single-player campaigns include a carryover resource system from mission to mission, so maintenance of a home base is mandatory and requires transportation of units and resources to and from specific mission areas. Skirmish mode offers access to campaigns and battles created with the built in map editor, and serves as a practice field for multiplayer training.
The Earth 2150 Trilogy  is one of those games series  that make you wonder why others in the genre don't have the same features. Then again, a RTS game with good graphics, good artificial intelligence, and good unit balance is quite uncommon. But the Earth 2150 Trilogy meets all these demands: The graphics are distinctive, the computer opponent is good enough to give even experienced players a tough time, and each side plays differently and has its own advantages.

I began playing Chiv a few weeks ago after a friend suggested I buy it due to my interest in medieval themed games. As an online multiplayer game I wasn't sure what to really expect, so as per usual I began with the tutorial. I had been rather curious as to how the combat system would work; non-target based etc. I was intrigued by what I had learned in the tutorial, the system is rather complicated from the view of someone who hasn't played the game but once you get used to it you'll find it's all about timing and strategy. It's not just running in and spamming the mouse with clicks.
The classes are fairly different: Archer, Man-at-Arms, Vanguard and Knight. All have their advantages and disadvantages, archer as an example is significantly weaker compared to other classes and yet using a crossbow you can one hit someone with a headshot. I've played all classes, some more than most and I can say it's useful to change up every once in awhile as it can get boring sticking to one. It can be fun learning the other classes, and it may help you to better understand your opponent in the sense of how their class works, how fast they are and what strategy your enemy may use.
All together I really enjoy this game quite a bit from what I've played, it can be a lot of fun and I'd suggest  not necessarily taking it all seriously. /Most/ of this game is about teamwork, and I'd suggest you work well with the team you join. Don't focus on running off and getting as many kills as possible on your own and pay mind to your comrades. If you're not careful you can kill your own team mates, and receive the repercussions. (Longer respawn time, getting kicked etc.)
-----------------------------------
* Interesting/complex combat system
* Great online
* Affordable
* Still a few bugs around, nothing too major
* Limited customisation
* Might take awhile for newer players to get used to

Start off by saying, it's a survival game like many other survival games with its own twists. With that said, so worth a try because the twists Funcom has are actually preat cool.
Pros:
Creativity
* Sadly characters are not majorly unique but they are actually very good quality
* For buildings, if you have played ARK, it's what ARK dreamt of but Funcom created with less bugs and more streamline
* The map is a big and dangerous place with things that attack you and things that can't attack that want to attack you
* The map is getting bigger coming soon in August with a new biome (loving the look of it so far)
* More of a realistic survival in a way (in some ways not so much but completely amusing for those instances lol)
* The graphics for an early access game actually are very well done
* Base builders: Most games only give you structures with nothing to put in them, this game gives you accessories along with those crafting stations to make your buildings stand out and more unique (pillows, flasks, tables, chairs, etc). There is a teir system not just for buildings but also those accessories. There is not just one chair but many.
* Component building system: Some things cannot just be made out of rock or wood like in many other survival games. Many require wood to be turned to planks and than those planks to be modified with twine and wood in addition (a bit more elabrate but not so much to be confusing to no end). Brings a bit of a game to those just looking to build.
* PvP: Some will say it's broken or there are flaws. Each game has its flaws but this one in the survival game genre seems to put a lot of thought in to the combat system (it is also getting a revamp to add some features and take away some restrictions such as an ability to dual wield being added soon).
* Cimbing: Not static climbing like the Forest where you need to have a static rope or specific area that it's allowed. The world is your oaster, so long as you have the stamina for it.
Cons:
It's in beta so take these with a grain of salt and know the dev team is working on many of these.
* Imagine someone that has been on medication for taking their wisdom teeth out, the after effect of the dazed glazed over look? Yeah? The AI for some of the animals and npcs belong to that dudes friend the stole the medication that already wasn't exactly the most bright. (This is a hit or miss as some patches the AI is fine while other patches they spin around in circles. Amusing though).
* There are rubber banding issues across many servers both official and unofficial. It is what it is though. It's a beta.
* The animations of some of the beings in the game are not exactly, worked out yet. Hyena's sometimes run at you full speed....while laying down. That or Funcom has made the most dangerous hunter in the world.
* As many pros as climbing has, the hit box for the jump that activates it isn't exactly "smart." There will be times that you will not grab on to anything while dropping 100 feet to your death. At other times you will grab on to the ledge that hangs 3 feet from the ground like the water below will mealt your toon. (Please be aware, climbing was JUST added lol). This has also caused me to have to destroy a few structures because instead of just jumping from behind an object after respawning from death, my toon was hyped up on human flesh from the gods of Yog and decided he was going to make his best impression of the exorcist climbing all over a wall strategically to small to be able to get unstuck. Please not, my toon feels much better now.
Typical life of a newly created toon that hasn't played before:
Make toon, laugh at toon because their "attachments" are stupidly overgrown.
Cry because your toon has outragously large "attachements" than yourself.
Get over this downfall and enter world but not before reading your evil reasoning behind being put on the cross for crapping on a statue.
Scare an animal by said "attachment" than punch a few imps in the face
Die because you ran out of water or food
Respawn back in the desert (still haven't learned your lesson though)
Get back to where you were and realize you really do need to find water and food. HEY! these bushes give you bugs that you can eat! Ewwwwww (nom on some bugs regardless).
Die because that innocent turtle looking thing just Orge smashed your pathetic level 2 naked toon (worth the humor)
Respawn (odds are, still haven't learned your lesson)
Make an axe, find sad turtle to avenge yourself

*Repeat this about 9 more times until you have learned your lesson well enough to move on*
Lastly.... ? After this point, you get to test what you like in the game and not like. It will shape what you enjoy in the game.

I love this game! It has a dark, moody feel that is great. Very bleak and somber. It drives home the feeling of being a lone soldier trying to push on and finish his mission no matter the costs.....or is he just tossing all that and going STALKER on his own?? :) I was trying to narrow down one thing that really made the game for me and, while I had a hell of a time doing it, I think the thing that really sold me on the atmosphere is that the game doesn't use subtitles. You're playing someone who doesn't speak Russian so why should you understand anything? People joke and sing and carry on conversations around you and you have no idea what is said (assuming you don't speak Russian of course). To me this really drove home the idea of being on your own, even though you are surrounded by people. You of course find folks who will assist you on your way, vendors and such. But, beyond that you are on your own, literally. The very first time I fired the game up, I spawned and lurked around maybe thirty feet or so before an event happened (think, big radiation outburst from the reactor that happens randomly), and I didn't know what was going on other than it must be bad. I died of course and then had to go read up on some of the story arc.
Gunfights are pretty straight forward with pretty realistic damage models vs humans. The mutants can vary from being one hit kills to requiring several RPG rounds or more. My only real pet peeve is that to me some of the mods are a bit silly. Though I'm not sure if they're trying to get around copyright issues there or just being a little different, dunno but I looked past it and found it enjoyable eventually.
After you finish the game you can choose to remain in the area if you like and basically become a full time STALKER. I did this and even with all my gear there are STILL things that I simply run from lol. You can take most anything down by then, but at times it simply isn't worth the expenditure of resources.
The graphics by today's standards look dated, as you might expect from an older game. But I find that it fits in with the gritty, moody and run down atmosphere just fine actually. Oh sure there's no hyper realistic stuff but honestly, you don't notice it once you get immersed in the game. The rain effect is still one of the best I've ever seen actually.
So, overall I'd say to give it a try. There are some mods out there but try it first without them, if your system gets grumpy with crashes (it does happen sadly), then go look for a few mods that help a lot.
