Second no one has yet to follow where they went.
I am not going to give a game review but give a review of why no one has followed its foot prints.
The games give 3 factions in that it follows others but where it changes is that each faction has a strong point.  The lurnar group is hover low armor/high shield output, the ED are heavy tanks with high armor/low shields, and the UCS are robot mechs with a med armor/shield output.  This gives a 3 factions that play in their oun way.
The vehical system is where this game blows the rts walls open. Make a vehical tha way you want it not the premade idea some one thought up. Like rockets add that to the tank, like heavy guns change it to heavy guns then build it.  Want a combo? Yea heavy guns with a rocket on top, it dose that(for real!!! best tanks for ED)  The weapon combo system with a med weapon system added on top of a large weapon makes for vehicals that are your liking.
Then they put ammo in, you need to reload your vehicals with air drops from cargo choppers linked to supply depo's.  With energy weapons needing time to recharge, lasers, spark cannons, sonic guns(hate that aoe), it makes for a good balance.
Save your crew, this isnt much in the muti player but in any campaign if you keep units alive you can transport them back to a main base and reuse them on the next mission.  This leads to the exp, as you keep units alive they make kills and gain more armor,hp, and damage with each lvl. The quick way to see this is make a unit with a banner, it adds 2 lvl's to units around it, very use full early but wont add past lvl 4 if a remember right.  This will show give an example of the added damage/hp a unit has at higher lvl's.  The next thing is a unit that will let you upgrade units with new tech, better shields ready add it on and upgrade it. Some units you cant, but that up to you to find them the starting unit types.
The game was ahead of its time and I dont think any rts has come close to following the way it plays.  The line that describes the game with 150 missions and 9 campaigns is true but thats ED,UCS, and LC X3 games so each game has a campaign for each group.  I would start with ED on ESCAPE FROM THE BLUE PLANET to learn the game, it has the easy start, the UCS and LC through you in.

Overall the game is very fun, with the best third person hand to hand combat system i have found, only a power attack would make it complete. The damage dealt feels right. Both you and your enemies have very little health. Blocking is expertly implemented and timing is completely key, a fourth of a second too late can mean death. As well as blocking you can roll out of harms way and dodge back, right and left with the ASD keys. Combat feels visceral and deadly.

The setting is basically non existient, which is sad because all of the levels are pretty, they just do not have much of a layout to them.  All dialogue is set up in a still frame format without any voice work. While the campagin is still in the works the ported story from the previous game by these developers is very short and each level feels very separate from the next in terms of pacing location and dialogue. The levels feel too open ended(due to lack of layout and size) to be linear but not connected or long enough to be an open world game. Its a strange middle ground. I feel like the developers nailed the gameplay much more than the story and setting.

I'm not all that sure that this game will ever become good.
After quite many years of obviously active development, the core mechanics do not work (movement is glitchy, fights are chaotic to the point of being useless, climbing stuff is just frustrating, loading is frequent and load times are downright atrocious, etc), yet they've spent time on content instead of getting the core mechanics right - content that depends on how the core mechanics work, so fixing one requires fixing the other.

This is a non game.
There is so litle agency involved in what you can do in a turn,  this is a CCG made by someone that never understood CCG's but saw someone play one once.
I feel like a conversation between a dev and his boss went like this:
"ok, so I think there's two values on all the cards, one is the fight and the other is.. I duno health? and some cards have special abilities, but those would be hard to program, so just use a set of simple ones that a bunch of cards can have"
"Ok how do you want to show attack? like a fist or a sword or a boxing glove?"
"a hammer"
"but how does that-"
"Make it a hammer, Bill"
The design choices to explain abilities is... odd, below are some conversations that I'm sure took place between some poor designer and his overbearing boss:
"ok, how about this ability that damages a random enemy, should we show a die to demonstrait the randomness? or a dart?  Or maybe a rocket to show it can hit something that's not in front of it? Or maybe a-"
"Boxing glove"
"but how is that-"
"Make it a boxing glove"
"Isn;t that confusing when we have a more abstract gliph to represent attack ?"
"The hammer is perfect Bill, we've already had that conversatation, make it a boxing glove"
"Oh, ok what about the health drain? Maybe a fampire or a leach or fangs?"
"How about those brain sluggy things form the futureshow?"
"The brain slugs from futuramma? umm they don't reall drain-"
"But they stick to ya like leaches! make it that!"
The game is super geared towards microtransactions, which honnestly I was expecting, but it doesn't get its hooks in you so there's never any motivation to spend real money.  A well designed fremium game dangles that *one* thing you *just* need to beat this enemy, if only you could have it now you woudn;t have to wait... maybe just spending 5 bucks this one time wouldn't be so bad.
But this gae has none of that, this is mostly because you don't see a wide vareity of cards or have any idea which cards can drop from what. Not to mention that a core mechanic in teh game is leveling up your cards. BUT packs contain once level one card each  so there's no reason to even entertain the idea that "Buying a pack will improve my chances"  Because from experience you will get a level 1 card that you will never use.
You just hit a wall and rather than thinking "ok, if I had this one card I'd be fine" it feels like "oh, I guess I'd have to buy like 50 packs and hope I get *something*  and then level up maybe two or three cards I get and then maybe I'll win?"
Had someone spent actual money on marketing research to understand consumer behaviours, the developer would have a much more profitable product as it stands only a real idiot will ever spend money on this.
But the biggest problem is overall This game feels rushed, and the amount of advertising being put into it makes me feel like a lot of money went into it and I kinda hope that that's money that isn't going to be made back. I can't respect this as a game, I can't even respect it from a business perspective since it's so poorly designed from a profitibility angle.
The art on the cards looks like someone screenshot a 240p rip on youtube of the episodes,  and not even the best shot of a given moment / character. It's as if they took an unpaid intern and said "here's a list of all the images we need,  get them before tomorrow"  and all he had was a computer, a crappyt internet connection and a few cupps of coffee. ANd when he handed in his slopy rushed unfinished mess they said "PERFECT, IT'S GOOD TO SHIP!"

Normally, I wouldn't bother writing a review, but this game is an absolute state and people need to be warned against purchasing it.
Firstly I need to mention this games huge technical and performance issues. It has a massive memory leak and cannot be run for more than a few hours without requiring a complete reboot of your PC. The games optimization does not exist. Even if you have the most powerful, expensive PC on the market, you're going to have to turn all of the graphical settings down and even then you will still get huge frame rate drops.
If you attempt to play online you will suffer for this. Due to what I assume is poor netcode working together with poor optimization, whenever your game has to receive new data from the server, it will freeze, frequently at that. Opening the menu will cause a freeze of several seconds, moving around too much will frequently cause freezing, and god forbid you enter an area that has many player structures because that can result in freezing that exceeds 20-30 seconds.
With the biggest issue out of the way, lets talk about bugs. The game is full of them. I have not ran into any game breaking bugs during my play time, but people assure me they exist. That being said, I ran into so many small bugs during my play time that they negatively impacted the entire experience of the game.
To name a few, enemies clipping through stuff, enemies spawning inside the games terrain, enemy AI is so bad sometimes enemies just sit around and do nothing, hitboxes are wonky and a lot of the time you'll swing at something and hit thin air, equipping multiple things in the same hand, being unable to use tools even though my character is holding them and has stamina and lots of small graphical issues that happen like ghosting/a weird after image and low resolution graphics that failed to properly load in.
Now on to the actual game it's self.
The gameplay is pretty bad. Movement is floaty, combat is spammy and attacks feel like they have no weight or impact, building is horribly awkward and positioning things correctly is a pain (roofs in particular refuse to be placed correctly) and if you make a mistake you cannot replace the object.
The game is also grindy. Hilariously grindy. Building even a simple structure takes a huge amount of resources which require a long period of time to gather. As you progress through the tiers of the game, the grind just becomes absurd. Your gear breaks with almost no use at all, but requires a lot of materials to repair and these materials are not only spread across the world but require time to harvest, make into another material which is made into another material and finally used to repair your gear. You can spend an entire day gathering materials and blow through it in minutes of actual playing.
The games design is pretty bad too, and it feels as if the development team either don't play the game or don't know what to do with it.
The amount of grinding in the game implies you're suppose to work as a group to achieve things. Yet the game world is too small to support many players, server player caps (even official servers) are tiny and I just honestly doubt the game could handle large numbers of players in a single world due to technical issues.
The world it's self is actually impressive and well designed. But it's designed like a MMO, with clearly designated areas and level ranges. This does not lend it's self well to a survival game as survival is never going to be an issue if you simply avoid areas above your level.
Additionaly, the design of the world does not work well with the structure of the game. Building is clearly a big aspect of the game and without building you essentially cannot do anything. Building requires much time and effort. Yet the worlds design has a clear route you are suppose to take through it and it makes little sense to settle in many areas of the game because they have nothing in them.
Likewise, until you're a high level and established, where you build a base is very restricted. You will not choose a location for it's resources, but for what enemies are around. Even if the resources are nice, a low level character cannot survive in a high level area where all enemies are damage sponges that will 1-2 shot him.
The game also has many very questionable design choices. Entire stacks of food rot before your very eyes with no way to preserve it. Equipment and tools all have the durability of wet paper and break with minimal use. Most content is locked behind a level wall instead of having any kind of natural progression (IE, you cannot make steel until you have iron, this would make sense for progression, in Conan Exiles you cannot make steel and use steel until level 30, no exceptions).
The game also lets you choose a religion which will break the game depending on which you pick. One provides an infinite source of easily obtainable food that doesn't perish and is the best food type in the game, another provides an infinite source of very easy to obtain healing items that make combat trivial, the final religion provides easily obtainable arrows of death, though these at least take a bit of effort to unlock.
Content is also a problem. The game doesn't have much of it at all. The world is small and not particularly hard to explore, enemies are so dumb and unresponsive that you can for the most part just run around and ignore them. Enemy variety is pretty bad, most are just reskinned versions of weaker enemies. They do not have anything that makes them unique, even materials obtained from them in most cases aren't unique.
Stuff you can craft comes in three tiers. Each new tier is objectively better than the previous tier. Weapon, armor and tool selection is very limited and in most cases the only differences between them are that the newest tier has superior stats. There is no thought or tactical choices needed in selecting your gear, you wear what is best.
The game almost feels like Funcon where developing another game, and for whatever reason it was cancelled. Rather than call it a complete loss they decided to repurpose what they had into a survival crafting game because those are the in thing right now. It's a shame it didn't work out well.
This game just feels bad to play. It isn't enjoyable and there are other, cheaper alternatives that do everything this game does but better. The only draw it may have is for fans of Conan, though honestly even that is almost none existence in the actual game. Robert E. Howard is probably turning in his grave at what Funcom have done to the Conan brand.
Does the game have potential? Will it be good in the future? I don't know, I can't see into the future, but given Funcoms track record, I seriously doubt it.
Avoid this game for now. If it's not good within a year it's probably never going to be good.

Another problem that happens to me is that I'll kill part of a group of guys and the other part will escape. Devil Daggers is an endless arcade shooter that's incredibly challenging, yet satasfying.
It's best suited for short burst gameplay, around 30-60 second rounds, but of course if you're capable, even longer. Infact that's the real goal. To survive as long as possible.
The mechanics are pretty simple. You can shoot a stream of "devil daggers" or tap your shoot key for a shotgun-like burst. You can also collect red jewels as you kill larger enemies to improve your devil daggers' strength. It's all about micromanaging your spatial awareness, and priority in what to kill.
Though the premise is simple enough, the challenge is incredibly high. You'll get overwhelmed with enemies very quickly if you're not careful. Surviving for longer than a minute per round is a true achievement. There is an addictive value to the game's design loop with "one more game" as the initiative to replay over and over again.
The game's visuals are striking and stylized. With an eerie Gothic horror look, rendered in a pixel-3D aesthetic. The sound design is disturbing and compliment it's visuals quite well. It presents a moody atmosphere that drew me in.
The game can certainly be considered repetitive, and with only one mode to play it dosn't help it's repetition. After playing just a few rounds I quickly understood why the game was so cheap at $5.00 USD. There really isn't much content here. Luckily for us, what is here is addictive, challenging, and satasfying.
Overall, Devil Daggers is a cheap, grotesquely gorgeous endless shooter that is well suited for score attackers. It's short on content, but makes it up an addictive designed gameplay loop.
Pros:
- Atmospheric visual and sound design
- Incredibly challenging
- Very addictive
- Appropriate price tag
Cons:
- Short on content
- Might not be for everyone

If, before playing the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games, I had described in detail my perfect gaming experience, I doubt I'd have arrived at anything close to Call of Pripyat. Sometimes things fill a gap we never knew we had. Like Pascal's "God-shaped vacuum in the heart of every person", there was a S.T.A.L.K.E.R.-shaped hole in my Steam catalogue.
Shadow of Chernobyl, the first game in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, is often (and rightly) touted as a flawed but ground-breaking masterpiece. The second, Clear Skies, is all too often disregarded. Call of Pripyat, IMHO, is one of those rare instances when the third in a trilogy improves on what has come before. Some have pointed to a superior story in Shadow of Chernobyl, and this is a natural impression given by the novelty of the first in a series. The burdens heaped on the difficult third of the trilogy's shoulders (following an already classic first and an almost universally panned second) were daunting. That it can stand alone as a masterpiece, and take pride of place in the trilogy that birthed it, is truly impressive.
The sandbox, free-roaming FPS skeleton of the game is all but flawless. Gone are the irritating and frequent zone-transitions of the first two games - the map is divided into three instanced zones, but within those zones the travel is seamless. It is a rich and believable world, but you will require a fast CPU and/or installing game on an SSD to avoid micro-pauses every so often as you move through the map. Mob AI is vastly improved upon, and, despite all three games in the series using the same "X-Ray" engine, CoP's graphics are an improvement beyond what could be expected.
Call of Pripyat's cast of weapons and armors are as loveable, believable, and as almost-touchable as the characters. Weapons are almost all faithful renditions of the NATO and Warsaw Pact arsenals, with nods and developments to the alternate history STALKER narrates. No min/max table lurks behind the equipment; no backwards-engineered dps spreadsheet. Instead, a well-balanced cast of items, with pros and cons emerging naturally from the real-world items they reproduce.
Like the two S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games that preced it, Call of Pripyat mods extremely well. The modding community has developed a catalogue of astounding size, quality and diversity. As is usual for a well-modded game, some mods almost inarguably improve on the game, some add extra content, while a few simply break the experience. I recommend playing through without mods first.
After gauging the experience, I recommend either MISERY, a massive and thorough reworking of the game; or if you prefer to retain the gameplay and difficulty of the vanilla game while improving on the graphics, a combination of mods such as Atmosfear, Absolute Nature and Absolute structures, and Particle Paradise will yield excellent returns. Although the "Complete" mods are sound for the first two S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games, I cannot recommend the CoP Complete Mod. It significantly dumbs-down the combat, while implementing graphical tweaks either similar or inferior to those previously mentioned.

Great open-world game. If you like Fallout 3, then consider the STALKER series Fallout on steroids. Combat is intense, against both humans and mutants alike, and a single headshot from an enemy is enough to take you out. You have an absurd amount of freedom in this game. If you want to shoot the guy giving you a mission, you can. If you want to shoot the guy who just rewarded you for completing a mission, you can. I've already been playing this game, CoP for about 15 hours and haven't even started with the mainline story missions, there's so much else you can do.
Not to mention this game is so DYNAMIC. Enemies get into firefights if they're in opposing groups, or mutants against humans. Bandits and other stalkers will loot dead bodies after killing them. Wounded enemies can either be healed with one of your medkits or executed. Wild packs of mutants will kill human AI and drag their bodies off to be eaten. And anomolies don't discriminate against who they destroy. These are things that were in all of the STALKER games, mind you.
If you do decide to get this game, be sure to download either the complete (better graphics, improved gameplay, bug fixes) or the Misery (same as Complete only a LOT harder) mods. They're a good pick for even a first time run through, though I would only do Misery if you are really patient and don't mind dying a lot.

Earth 2150 redefined the notion of having mixed feelings from a game on Steam.
Beeing a trilogy,it has the original game and the two standalones.
To review this game, as a whole package ill use a list of Pros and Cons,and I’ll leave you to figure out if its worth it or not.
PROS:
-	You can “create” your own type of units by combining chasis with addons
-	Structures can be updated with turret defenses
-	The three factions are very unqiue and attractive to try out
-	Story has an interesting premise that keeps you engaged initially
-	You can reshape the terrain and build tunnels/bridges as part of your strategy
-	You always have a main base and a mission base
-	Music is better than in Earth 2140
-	360 degrees rotation and zooming on the game screen
-	Feels like a “deeper” Command&Conquer initially
-	Game mechanics are really well done (probably the best part of the game)
-	Each unit has a depleteable ammo stack and needs to be supplied with more ammo
-	The research tree is quite impressive
-	Game can be played with air ,ground and tunnel fights
-	There is a transport vehicle that moves units from main base to mission base
-	Day/Night cycle and weather system
-	Each faction has unique superweapons
-	You can queue unlimited units/research and resources will be consumed gradually for them
-	Units can be assigned scripts
-	Lost souls has an actual chronological story
-	The concepts were unique and breathtaking for its genre and quite ahead of their time
-	The news reports,build up slowly but they give a sense of danger regarding Earth’s fate
-	Buildings leave debris after you destroy them
-	Earth progressively decays with the advancement of the campaign
-	Weather affects units and buildings
CONS:
-	It has not aged well at all, the graphics being really washed down
-	Tutorials are very tedious and not straightforward
-	The path finding is horrible
-	The voice overs are annoying and too cheesy
-	The story becomes forgetful because too many pointless gather x minerals missions
-	Learning curve is too steep
-	Missions seem too hard even on Easy difficulty
-	Music is too repetitive
-	Too many missions are gather missions (especially with ED)
-	The unit limit seemed small
-	Figuring what to do is too hard. I had no idea what to do half of the time I played
-	Game play feels too slow and sluggish
-	The ammo sluppying while interesting,it gets boring really fast
-	To me the AI seemed too hard because of the steep learning curve.
-	No real sense of achievement after completing several missions
-	Each mission is a big time sink and becomes boring
-	Your army can be immediately killed if it is facing some type of enemies
-	The fighting targeting is horrible because of the path finding
-	Your units will keep being hit and move around to position themselves before attacking
-	There is a lights on/off on buildings and units which seems completely pointless
-	The maps are too big and annoying to navigate through
-	The minimap layout is extremly horrible,rotation makes even more confusing
-	The minimap is basically uselss,as it doesn’t help you at all during missions
-	The multiplayer is obviously dead and its  game modes are severely outdated
-	The story fails to deliver in the end
-	The cinematics are pointless and too cheesy. They don’t add any value to the story
-	Game feeling bounces from really like it or really hate it too frequently
-	The expansion moon project  worse than the original game in most aspects : especially story
-	The terrain and movement on the terrain is agonizing to look at and wait upon
-	Unit selection is faulty when you have a lot of units on screen
-	The game feels too often like a chore than actual fun
-	Missions rarely vary from gather resource/destroy enemy base/escort transporters
-	The fighting music is too irritating and repetitive
-       The ending for each faction felt anticlimactic and non emotional.
-	Last impression was that game missions take too long and don’t have enough to keep you wanting to come back
Overall,I cannot say that I would recommend this trilogy. It has its PROS but it also has too many CONS for me to really like it. You can make your own decision, but I for one,really forced myself to play and experience as much as possible from this game.

I
to like this game. I want
to like this game. But some flaws keep it frustrating instead of being truly enjoyable.
First, let’s talk about the
: On the whole, the
! The whole look of Jet Set Radio is really cool with its cell-shaded aesthetic. It gives it a unique style and sets it apart from today’s grimmer crop of games. The
and even include several people of colour which you still don’t see much of over 15 years later.
The whole shtick of the game, running around, spray painting graffiti, is a great idea and aspects of it are fun. The spray painting mechanic, in which you follow on-screen prompts, is forgiving and pleasing as your masterpieces materialize before you. And even the
designs themselves are interesting and varied. You can even create your own!
What really drags the game down are the controls, especially when it comes to fine tuned movement. When you’re skating around without a real destination in mind, everything feels fine. However, as soon as you slow down or get stopped (by falling off of the level, getting shot at, etc) you begin to struggle against the controls to move exactly where you want. Basically, it lacks the precision of something like Tony Hawk.
There are also some design aspects that are maddening. For instance flying enemies can shoot you while you’re doing your graffiti and there’s no way (that I know of) to get a reprieve other than spray painting during your invincibility frames. Finally, even though I really like the different characters, I can’t tell much of a diference between them when it comes to their stats. Sure, power is easy to spot with their smaller and bigger health bars, but Technique and Graffiti don’t seem to make much difference in how they play. Some characters can carry 40 cans of paint, whereas others only get 15. But it doesn’t change how many it takes nor how quickly they can tag a spot.
The music is all right, for the most part, but the repeated tracks can certainly wear on you after repeated listening.
I played it enough to get through the 3 chapters and beat the game and honestly, I’m not really chomping at the bit to play again. Try it, see if I’m wrong, but I think you could spend your time and money better elsewhere.

If you have lots time to spare and willing to put effort in to learning a very complex game, with a very high skill ceiling; you will get lots out of this game. Chivalry is often in a sale at 90% off for £1.89, and at that price it is a steal.
Be warned, Low rank servers are servers that place you against people between ranks 0-15. This will last the average player about 20-25 hours of
gameplay.
Once this time is up, and you reach rank 16- you are placed into a non ranked public servers. This means that you will be fighting people from someone who has just installed the game as well as people who have thousands of hours on the game and have been playing it for years. This accounts for the large numbers of people who leave negative reviews as they reached the section of the game, believing that the game contains a large number of "hackers" who are in actual fact people who have a couple hundred hours in the game.
At this point you will be able to decide if you enjoyed the game, or if you want to take it further. If you buy this game on a sale, you will easily get 25 hours of enjoyment even as a causal player for merely £1.89.
My advice it to avoid low rank servers all together as it forms bad habits early on which can be hard to get out of, and by doing this you will not be lulled into the false sense of security of low rank servers, to then be shocked as the average skill level shoots up when entering the non ranked servers.
Having said this, I love chivalry and I believe that if you keep on giving the game another chance, and do not quit at the first face of defeat- you will get lots and lots of enjoyment and pleasure out of this game.

I paid 50 cents for this on sale, which is the only reason I'm not asking for a refund on it.
If you pay less than $1 it's an interesting gimmick game, I suppose. But I can't really recommend it, and it's most definately not worth anything close to the $4 regular asking price.
This is a walking simulator with jump scares, that's it. The story is one sentence long and you read it off the main menu.
You spawn into the game with no memory of who you are, or why you are there, or what's going on. And: there's no way to ever find out.
You wander around  a lab in the dark with a broken flashlight that barely works (and only for a few seconds at a time). You pray to find a few flashbang grenades. There's no other weapons.
It has an interesting atmosphere to it, but it's a rather small one map game with nothing to actually... do.
It seems to want to be a stealth game, but the stealth mechanics are limited to "you see the enemy first and avoid their line of sight".
If you don't avoid their line of sight, you can flashbang them (if you've found any) or ... they touch you and you die. The end. No lives, no tips, no progress, just dead and start over.
Basically this feels like it might have been a tech demo built to show the start of an idea that was never finished. Or just a weekend project by a student game developer learning to use unity assets.
If you happen to get it on sale or just want to support the developer who made it (an independant who has made a few other decent games), then more power to you. But it's really hard to recomend this as a game when it feels barely started, let alone complete.

I received this game for free, if I recall correctly, for donating to the development of Natural Selection 2 in 2008.  2 years later, they offered keys for Overgrowth.  Then in Alpha, I didn't pay it much mind.  After noticing recently that it has hit Beta and making noises about leaving Early Access, I installed it and gave it a play for the first time.  I'm suitably impressed.
**Currently the game consists of a Tutorial and a remake of the Lugaru campaign (the predecessor to Overgrowth)**.  The Lugaru campaign is a little rough, as is the client itself.  The gameplay and mechanics are quite far along, but little things like level-loading and transitions between story segments are a bit rough.  You'll find yourself abruptly kicked to a black screen with terminal text scrolling by telling you what's been loaded, then abruptly kicked into the stage.
The game itself is a joy.  The anthropomorphic rabbits do terrible things to each other.  The melee combat requires timing and distance estimation, and the enemies don't screw around.  It's a good thing the levels are sort of small encounters since, especially if you attempt to go in direct-and-noisy, you're going to get the crap beat out of you (or more accurately, kicked).  Speaking of, there is no HUD, no health counter; however, as you take damage your bunny protagonist will become dynamically bloodied.  If slashed, he will have a slash on his chest.  If wounded in the shoulder, he will clutch it in his idle animation.  While showing a friend I even deliberately jumped and mis-timed a mid-air flip so my character would fall, hitting the ground hard and momentarily ragdollizing.  When he got up, his head was bloodied, a stream of blood dripping down his neck.
The graphics may be a little rough, as may be the stages, but it's tough to say if that will be indicative of the final product, as not only is there just the Lugaru port to go through, but the game is most certainly still a beta and in-progress, not a beta-but-basically-finished-just-not-released.
It took me a little under an hour to make it through the tutorial and half way through the campaign.  Depending on how much the difficulty ramps up, I'm expecting another hour and a half at least out of the campaign.  Additionally, I'm expecting mods and just screwing around in the game itself to amuse me beyond that until the full release.  It's just a joy to walk up to two guards, throw a knife into the neck of one, running jump over his soon-to-be corpse and flying bunny-kick his partner in the head so hard that, with a loud *crack*, the game goes in to cinematic slow motion to show his lifeless ragdoll flop on the ground.
So far, the game is difficult but in a fair way.  Dying doesn't set you back too far.  Additionally, you are skilled but not a super hero: being outnumbered 2-to-1 is genuinely not great odds, especially if you screw up an attack and get your knife stolen.  A stealthy approach appears to be viable in most cases, as the game seems more natural than most others: you are given tools and challenges, but the challenges don't force a solution on you.  Two guards at the front of the compound, 3 more patrolling inside.  Do it however you want/can.
So far, I'm rather impressed.  The developer, Wolfire Games, is somewhat prolific with YouTube updates about the game and changes with each iteration, so their YouTube channel is a good place to go for information and footage.  They also made Receiver, a game which has an interesting take on gun mechanics that I *wish* were in a full-fledged multiplayer game.  In a way, I see the same spirit in Overgrowth/Lugaru.  Holding your hand to teach you, then hands-off when it's time to put it into action.
Check it out and see if it's your kind of game.

Woodle Tree Adventures is a 3d action platforming game in which you play as a small Tree stump wielding a leaf collecting fruits and water drops in your backpack to save the world.  It is a game with lively and colorful graphics, reminiscent of many of the favorite games I played as a child on the N64, however that's about where the games charm ends.
Pros:
-Beautifully designed and vibrantly colored worlds and characters which are cute, whimsical and well designed bring back fond nostalgic memories of old school platformers.  The areas seem fairly well designed and are really a treat to look at.  The character designs are really cute and unique.  These qualities present a lush and intriguing platforming environment that you actually want to try to explore.
-Great controller support which implements itself without need for setup.  The preset button configurations are simple and intuitive.
Cons:
-Horrible animation quality, the characters seem to half walk/half glide across the screen, animations are slow and choppy.
-Poor camera control creates problems within the game where you can't see where you are trying to go, or enemies and platforms are blocked from view.  Often times it's difficult to grasp where you stand in relation to the platforms and enemies around you, leaving you swinging your weapon and finding the enemy is to your side rather than behind you, or much farther away than you thought.  This is a real killer as much of the game requires reaching that next platform and when you can't see it, the result is quite frustrating.
-Poor performance causes this game to run extremely slowly and rifled with lag.  You'll feel more often than not that you are about as quick as a snail... and this alone makes you want to close the game.
-enemy death animations are slow and drawn out, however as they are dying they still manage to attack and kill you while you attempt to slink away.
-the sound quality is really mediocre, some sounds are drastically louder than others, most of the sound effects sound like they do not belong in the game and make no sence at all.  The music is ok, but it really doesn't feel like its in the right game.
Overall I can't recommend anyone plays this game.  Adventure/platformer games are all about the gameplay, and this game has a horrble implementation of anything resembling gameplay.  Its so gruellingly slow and buggy you want to ragequit after just a few minutes.

I know this game is always going to ride the fine line because you have the cup half empty and the cup half full types of people out there. I see and have heard alot of debate about this game. I have many friends that like it and some that don't or those who have avoided it all together. I have the types that have been bought the game from a friend put 15-20 hours into it and gave up on it entirely. (IMHO you have to play it much longer to give it a proper try mostly because of the leveling and armor system. The first 20 levels you are fairly squishy)
I also realize you could easily focus on the negatives. You could say the most common thing:
It's ARK without the dinosaurs, in a different setting with magic and slavery.
But it's immediately evident that this game gets certain aspects right 100% from the gate. THOSE particular aspects if (and when) taken further... can give this game the longevity it deserves.
The best aspects of this game in order:
1.) Exploration
2.) Lore
3.) Building
I would also like to give and honorable mention to Crafting. While it's good and perhaps similar to many other games...
it needs a bit of balancing on time and rates. When it does get that balancing down it too will be on this list.
Exploration:
In this game exploration & mystery are paramount. There's a lot of dungeons and areas to explore that are wildly different. This adds for many many hours of game play to both find and explore all of the interesting places that exist.
That too should go hand in hand with mentioning the AMAZING world design. The wildly snaking topology, towers, aquaducts & encampments are some of the best design I've ever seen. There's alot of cracks and crevices, tunnels, dungeons, peaks, valleys and biomes to see and explore.
There's also alot left to the map they can yet add to so there is ALOT of room for expansion.
If this aspect is leveraged properly it will add to longevity and replay factor of the game.
Lore:
This is a no brainer. Granted there is a ton of pre-existing work to draw from so there's alot that can be added to the game. But the existing lore at present is actually quite interesting if you give it your full attention. There's alot there that can add to the mystery and exploration factor as mentioned above. This too is something that has to be properly used to it's advantage.
Building:
Great building block setup from the gate. You have to level up and unlock the ability to build the pieces as you go. The polygon, triangle, angle, and cone pieces are the most welcome addition to a building setup for any game. This adds alot more possibility and variability to the building styles and really gives you alot more freedom in design. They are not 100% perfect there does need to be a few additional pieces added imho and some tweaking to the snapping of pieces, etc. But overall it's a really nice setup and if this is expanded on it will also add for alot of logevity of game play.
Final Recommendations:
Do yourself a favor IF you play this game. Play it with good FRIENDS, play it MORE then 20-25 hours. Up till LEVEL 30 at least to give it a proper chance. <=====
Get to know the map. Pay attention as you go and use landmarks for reference points, Use the cardinal directions N S E W as reference points.
Don't get attached to your stuff at a lower level. You ARE going to die. You ARE going to get one tapped down to 10-20% of your health early on.
Back off & pace yourself during fights. Give yourself time to let your health re-gen.  Use ambrosia if necissary.
Put alot of ticks into GRIT. Stamina can and will both save and kill you if not used proerly. in and out of fights.
Use the buddy system. Don't go out alone and explore too far without someone with you. They can keep you alive and also help you navigate back to your body in case you die.

It's... Eh. I'm really on the verge between recommending and not recommending it. I've decided to mark it as not recommended because there isn't really much content and the game's challenge level is mostly a test of patience. As you can see from how many hours I've played this game, it's a test I myself could not endure.
I would have recommended this if it was a free game or extremely cheap. While it's not really an expensive game, I can't recommend it at its current price. If you really want to play this, I'd recommend waiting for a discount.
Basically, you'll be in a randomly generated area, walking around, finding generators to reset and flashbangs, waiting for a countdown to end so your memory returns, while also having an oxygen meter going (and I haven't really found out how to recover oxygen, I'm assuming it has to do with resetting generators). You'll be trying to avoid three monsters - you know the monkey is nearby because of a blipping sound it makes and you can use flashbangs to slow down the doctor and his wife. Your flashlight depletes quickly - it recharges automatically when it's off, but you'll need it on quite often. And the oxygen meter depletes more quickly when you're running.
And that's about it. You just keep avoiding these three monsters, trying to maintain your oxygen level and waiting for the countdown to end. If one of the monsters catch you, it's game over.
It's decently scary because you never know when one of the monsters is going to just jump at your face, but there really isn't much content besides what has been mentioned.
It seems like the game's being constantly updated, so who knows - maybe in the future things might change and I might be able to recommend it. Not at its current state, however.
Also, for some reason, this game causes a very bad coil whine on my PC - no idea why. I've had coil whine from other games before, but so far this has been the worst.

I'm probably nor going to sell this game very well but I like to criticize things I love and I want any reader to understand everything I've encountered and use it to determine wether spending their hard earned money is a good desicion. It's good visually and I only have gtx 960, but I've run into a lot of visual bugs and frame drops just by looking in the wrong direction. As with any survival game, this game isn't for everyone. You have to have a lot of spare time and dedication if you want to succeed in this game. I recommend you have at least one friend who is willing to play this with you because it can get boring fast if you're alone. The game has a TON of different server varities, including RP and PvE, they even have a ranked option where you climb up in rank by killing people on the server and then it gets wiped in 30 days. With this many options there comes a downside... It's impossible to find any server other than PvP. Call me a nerd if you want but I like RP servers but almost none exsist and the ones that do have exp multiplyers out the♥♥♥♥♥ Singleplayer is fun and you can make it so you can invite friends (if you have any) but will most definatley get boring fast. The AI in this game needs a major overhaul because you can be spotted by a Thrall from across the map and Hyenas run in packs of 50 and will most deffinatley destroy you unless you are armed to the teeth. You can lynch the AI by building a small base and leading them to it and then hit them through the door frame because they dare not enter you masterly built hut. I recommend you select what you want to be in advanced because the tier system is limited to 50 levels and you can not unlock everything. From what I know your religion doesn't really matter unless you want to spend 100+ hours trying to summon a god to destroy everything (Unless you pick Yog because that is the best god you can summon) There are a suprisingly large amount of armor variations but I wish some of them did something other than just protect you. In conclusion this game is in early access for a reason and it has a lot of potential to be one of the best survival games out there. Even if you played excessive quantities of the original games- as I did- this is well worth a revisit, if only to be able to play through such an experience again in multiplayer with friends.
The whole series comes strongly recommended, though I feel Baldur's Gate 2 and Throne of Bhaal were the true masterpieces.

Probably one the hardest Action RPG's with the exception of DarK Souls. It's not as insane as Dark Souls but it does have quite a bit of frustrating moments. At moments it does require the player to grind to get through the tough boss battles. The boss battles are intense but do give a sense of reward after they are defeated. The good thing about the gameplay is that if you die at a boss battle you don't have to go to your last check point but at the boss fight itself. Once you nab the pattern down for the bosses they are much easier but they do require a bit of skill and luck to defeat, including the final boss which when I saw it fall gave a huge sense of satisfaction.
If you're not really good at these kinds of games, I would reccomend playing on Easy instead of Normal. I did complete the game on Normal but the challenge was almost to the point where it started to interfiere with how fun the game was. Though it does give a great sense of satisfaction, so if you like challening Action RPG's, this one should fit the bill. Even if Normal is too easy for you there are other difficulities which I will personally never try but they're there for those who are into that.

Then I find this stalker shadow of Chernobyl game and think generic knockoff. After going through stalker 1.0 with all the weird bugs however, I soon realized this was fallout on steroids.

Walking around the metro shooting ghouls with the terrible shotgun whilst paused in v.a.t.s. pales in comparison to going into the labs around Chernobyl. Chernobyl had zombies but also included cloaking bloodsuckers lurking behind you, snorks ready to pounce, a behemoth flesh creature, along with mutated dogs, poltergeists, and various other startling abominations.
Clear sky brought in the interesting concept of modifying weapons and factions. That was about all Clear Sky offered save for an upgrade to the Xray engine. Oddly enough, the factions were lost with the next installment
Now with the most refined version of Call of Pripyat what was interesting before is even better.  Hunting in anomalies for artifacts using a detection device and throwing bolts is a very interesting way of essentially mining the environment. Secret stashes that can be found at any time without prerequisite was a good addition.
Call of Pripyat also saw a better structured campaign. SoC was too loose, CS was to linear, CoP to me is just right. Though don't get me wrong the game in all iterations is open roaming, but CS felt like walking through levels and SoC had areas of no interest.

I recommend anyone interested in good games to play this.

===
Legendary. There is no other word for it.
Divinity Original Sin 2 (from now DOS2) is the second installment of the Original Sin saga, developed by Larian Studios first time a couple years ago. Veteran RPG makers as they are, they come a long way since they made the first Divine Divinity back in the early 2000's, and also the following chapters which all were good games (No, Beyond Divinity never existed, shhh). DOS2 is a real time RPG with turn based combat, with some new twists in the classic mechanics to keep it modern.
===
There is so much to say about the gameplay of DOS2, there really is. First of all, the thing that astonished me the most among all the good ones, which are really a lot, is the incredible freedom given to the player in all his actions and interactions with NPCs and eventual co-op players alike. The freedom DOS2 offers is as close as it can get to pen-and-paper RPG level of freedom transported in a videogame: every NPC is killable, everything can be stolen, companions will react on what you do based on their alignemtn and may even become your enemies (and so can do players you fplay with in multiplayer!), there are a myriad of different dialogue options suitable for any alignment you might want to roleplay about, unique dialogues for each of the story NPCs, unique race-based ones, unique background-based ones, reputation based ones... so i mean, there are so many unique combinations and things that can happen that every playthrough will be very different as far as interactions go, it's all about what you do and who you are, in this Larian did a wonderful job and very few other RPGs ever have been at the same level of depth in interactions.
Other than this, gameplay is pretty much straightforward and like any other classic RPG: explore a very vast world composed of 3 huge areas, plus all the dungeons and secret places of course, loot from randomly generated pieces of gear (except unique ones, those are always the same), fight a good variety of enemies each with its own features, and mind you enemies are very different from one another in this game so you will have to use new strategies a lot, solve quests in various ways depending on your alignment of just on how you feel like doing, but remember everything has some consequences.
If i was to explain in detail all the gameplay, this would be a very very long review and would go over the Steam word limit, so i tell you this: there have maybe been 2-3 RPGs in the whole history that match the depth this one offers, don't miss it.
Combat in DOS2 is turn based and very much classic style. Every character starts with a fixed AP number each turn (excluding buffs and debuffs of course) and they are used for both movement and actions. There is no Mana in Divinity OS2, just cooldowns for all skills, and for some, a special type of energy is required.
The new mechanics Larian decided to introduce in OS2 are mainly about how armor works: in DOS2 there are two types of armor, Magical and Physical, which act like additional health bars and nullify any debuff or damage from that specific source (magical armor counters magical damage and magical debuffs, and so on) as long as it has 1 point at least. Once an Armor is depleted it can be regenerated with some skills and potions, but while down, Debuffs and negative statuses will always afflict the targeted character, there is no such thing as success percentage, it just matters if you have still Armor or not. The elimination of RNG this way is a quite clever gameplay change, but also comes with some issues we will discuss further on.
Other than that, rest assured, there are plenty of skills and fighting schools for all tastes, from warriors to healers to summoners, there are something like 150+ skills around to build your very custom characters the way you want.
Immense. There is no way you can do everything in one playthrough, you will have (and want to) play this game multiple times to get all the interactions, quests, and so on. To make just one play it can very well require above 85 hours, to complete the game 100%, can require more than 200.
There just is one but quite serious issue with balancing: based on how the Armor mechanic is structured, it is logical to think that a party basing all its damage on either Physical or Magical would defeat enemies much quicker than splitting damage between example, 2 magical and 2 phyisical characters. And it is exactly how it is: a party based on just 1 type of damage is much more efficent, maybe too much, in combat and can defeat most enemies with much more ease than a "standard" party with some magical and some physical damage.
Tactician difficulty, the hardest, is a serious challenge if taken without the proper respect. Badly built parties will be wiped with ease and requires planning, strategy in combat and experience. Some fights really impressed and got me on the brink of madness, let me tell you, and i play RPGs since twenty years! Luckily the unlimited and free respec at your base and adjustable difficulty will make the game beatable even for the less experienced.
===
Enviroments and art of cutscenes are really well done. Bear in mind this game does not make graphics one of its priorities, still the visuals are quite stunning in certain environments, particle effects are well done, character models are alright, armor and weapon models are made with particular care.
The world on DOS2 is vibrant and alive, the ccharacterization of the various environments and locations is marked very distinctively, it all contributes to the immersion feeling you already get from the roleplaying part.
It is to mention that Larian decided to voice act EVERY SINGLE DIALOGUE of this game, and there are a monstrous quantity. The voice acting is also good. This alone is a huge plus. other than this, the music and sound effects are at very good standards for an RPG, no really, they are good.
Performance is alright, the game is optimized well enough but can become heavy for low to mid end machines because it renders and makes all the characters in a whole area work together at the same time so it requires some computing power some machines might not have to run everything smooth.
Also when saving the game has some inexplicably huge frame drops.
DOS2 is not really unstable, it crashes sometimes, it is bound to happen, but rarely. There are no particular stability problems.
Enemy AI is one of the best i've ever seen around. They will execute complex manouvers to get the most efficency out of just about everything. Think of this: enemies will get shoulder attacked to walls to avoid being backstabbed if they are supports or ranged units and there is a rogue in the enemy team. How often you see this? Never. This is the level of AI i'm talking about, the same AI that curses you with healing is damage to bypass your shield and kill you with your own healing the next turn.
Prepare to be impressed.
Inventory management and interfaces are generally good, but one thing is really bad: picked up new items will constantly clutter your hotbar and having to always clean it is a chore... there is a mod that solves this (blessed modding!) but as far as the vanilla game goes this is an issue.
Sometimes enemies will jsut get stuck in combat if the pathfinding becomes too complex or if they are teleported / thrown / whatever in locations they cannot walk down from. In Act 3 some voice lines and dialogues are broken and do not work properly.

At the height of the Sega Dreamcast's popularity, there was a tension brewing in the air as the 21st century began. No, it wasn't Y2K. This was something much more serious.
The year 2000 was surprisingly beneficial for SEGA as a company, with more people buying into
subscriptions, and a near-complete lack of bad games for their platform. They still weren't pulling numbers for hardware sales like their competitor Sony was, but they were on the right track as far as making up for their poor business/marketing decisions in the mid-90s went for the 32x and the Saturn. And then Sony unveiled the Playstation 2. "Oh." said SEGA. This inevitably would spark debate over which console was going to be the future of gaming, but Sony's DVD/DVD-ROM support would be the deciding factor in the long run.
While the SONY HYPE TRAIN was starting to gather steam with the Japanese release of the PS2 in early 2000, the SEGA defense force was desperately seeking quality titles to rub in the face of Playstation fanboys. One of the very biggest being a colorful roller-blading action game from Smilebit- Jet Set Radio.
"JET SET RADIOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO" the game howls at you from the menu. DJ Professor K is just as amped as you are that you're playing it. And rightfully so! The game is a delight. Getting that out of the way right now because I know that since you're reading this review on a universally praised game and seeing a thumbs up next to it, it's a foregone conclusion what I'm gonna tell you.
The game's good. No♥♥♥♥♥♥
But the question is- why? Why does this game get the praise it does? Why are you reading this and not playing it for yourself and letting some idiot on the internet tell you why you SHOULD play it?
Right from the get-go, the game's aesthetic and world itself is established- colorful, crisp, and full of wonder despite being a lampooned vision of modern-day urban Japan. Definitely not counterculture, but more as satirizing what Japan's vision of a police state would be. You've got cops chasing you up and down the streets as you shove rival gangs out of the scene and cover up their graffiti with your own, with the captain of the police force shooting you with a revolver the size of Texas. Can't say that isn't
law enforcement.
One of the most striking things about the Jet Set Radio games that people will talk about is the music. The soundtrack consists of a medley of fun, danceable tracks by the one and only Hideki Naganuma, but also playing second fiddle is Deavid Soul with a mountain of terrifically sampled tracks that are just as fun. I'm not sure if all of the tracks are in every version of the Steam release these days, but back in the day they had a few region-specific songs. Most notable were the North American extra tracks that were mostly featured in chapter two of the game, which had a more hard rock/post-grunge sound to them. Not sure about these tracks being very... tonally-fitting, but they're fine. I still think it's hilarious to see someone go wide-eyed when you tell them that there was both a Rob Zombie and a Cold song in Jet Set Radio. Nobody who looks at this game on a surface level is going to expect that. I think the only track that isn't in this release is Deavid Soul's "Yappie Feet", and that just straight irritates me that the only song missing is one of my favourites.
The core gameplay for Jet Set Radio is strong, and encourages a lot of replayability- even moreso now that the HD re-release has online leaderboards. Good platforming with an emphasis on speed and style that's complimented by the spraypainting mechanics. Proooobably would recommend a controller with that, given that the spraypainting involves a lot of twirling of the analog stick... it doesnt quite work on a keyboard. There are some obvious shortcomings that you're going to feel with the gameplay though, and whether you feel like you can adjust to them or not is liable to be a dealbreaker to a fair chunk of people- most notable of these being the directional jumping. Where the skating and grinding has a pretty intuitive momentum system, jumping can't help but feel floaty and imprecise by comparison. With hops on the mind, one real weird thing is the fact that all of these white kids can actually jump? Weren't really going for that realism commitment, were we now.
Not being a bigot, tbh- I'm as white and as beardless as an Arcade Fire concert.
Now, one big thing that has also completely baffled me about the gameplay is the fact that there is a metric ton of characters to unlock, yet there is absolutely NO MULTIPLAYER to speak of (that would eventually be corrected in the sequel, 2 years later) and just as well, there's no real "endgame" aside from the fact that you can just replay each stage as many times as you please.
Graphically, this is what you'd expect from a mid-life Dreamcast game polygon-wise, but it makes due with beautiful textures and an incredibly potent style from the environments to the characters to the graffiti you're spraying. The visuals strike a chord with me that appealed both to me as a kid to me as an adult. The game looks terrific, and frankly has been done a service with its HD resolution.
With everything said and done, you've got a game with solid gameplay, despite the iffy control quirks- beautiful visuals, stellar soundtrack, great aesthetic, and a mountain of replay value, even with the lack of multiplayer. Do yourself a favour and play a piece of history today, you won't regret it.

To be honest, I did not expect to find a game that is on par with Cargo 3 and Devil's Share in quick succession, yet, I managed to do so. Interestingly, of all 3 this is the one that can be considered the "best" as it does not have any floating enemies nor does it give you the impression of being able to make progress while keeping the gameplay very repetitive.
Here you do not make any progress. You start out at the very same place in a barely lit maze all the time without any hints as to what happened to you and why you are there. Cargo 3 at least tried to include a "cutscene" by including some artwork telling you some basic background story that made you think the devs had spent a decent amount of time with the development. What TL gives you is exactly what the store page synopsis says - no more, no less.
While the videos showcase a monkey (in fact, most of the gameplay videos on YouTube have this antagonist) during the 20 minutes or so I spent with TL I only encountered the so-called "Doctor" and his "Wife". While they look decent their one-hit kill makes the game very irritating and next to impossible to complete (if there's a chance to do any walkthroughs here, that is), yet, the dev (in one of his most recent updates) claims the difficulty is now perfect. Now, this one-hit kill practically consists of a scary voice / sound effect coupled with the close-up view of the antagonist's face who suddenly turns away and is on to his / her business. I guess what they want to say is "Tag, you're it!" instead of killing you - either this or another famous playground game is used here: Hide & Seek.
You are given a couple of minutes "free roam" when there's a sudden music change indicating your dearest friends started coming to look for you. This also means that they will definitely find you - the AI is programmed in a way that it will find you regardless of what you do. Except for one thing - if you hide behind two machines they cannot go into the same narrow space so you're pretty much safe - until your oxygen runs out. If you run this chemical element leaves your body even faster - thank god you can find generators that fill you up quickly.
As for weapons: the game gives you flashbangs but using them blinds not only the "couple" but also yourself. The effect is a reddish something that can easily make you dizzy. Talk about nausea: since you run out of O2 the sensation of unease and discomfort is just perfect! You also have a torchlight but it runs out of battery very quickly. Quicker than in any other game in video game history. It's a shame as the game is extremely dark.
There are some other machines that can be interacted with but I forgot what those were and why I should even be bothered by them. In fact, I had a hard time forgetting about the main menu that pretty much gives all the info you need without any options to offer any changes in audio or graphics. I know it's a Unity engine game and prior to launch you have that pop-up for the changes but what purpose does it serve if you can play the game only on "fantastic" quality? So, you only have the "New Game" option with also the controls and in-game tips and instructions but written in an English language that will make all grammar nazis stay true to their beliefs. Oh, and there's no pause - hitting esc brings you back to this screen which has constant, irritating music that you (guess what?) cannot turn down or off.
Terror Lab offers a short-lived gaming experience with cheap jumpscares and the fact that the developer is constantly trying to let you know that your opinion matters and will shape the game makes you pose the question: Why isn't this still in Early Access? GenomGames may be an ambitious indie developer / publisher company but the fact that they  have released 3 games so far in half a year or so (all with pretty much identical quality / approach) does not bode well.
PS: While the great number of positive reviews is not necessarily bad (everybody's entitled to their opinion) what is alarming is that they are too short, far from being factual and there's an odd similarity of their command of English to that of the game's main menu.

If Woodle Tree Adventures was given to me as an assignment for a game development class, I suppose I would give it a passing grade.  Functionally, the game works fine.  That said, as a comercial project, it just falls flat.  Woodle Tree Adventures begins with Not The Deku Tree telling... Woodle, I guess?  It's never clear on the player character's name.  Anyway, you have to gather-up water drops.  The story is told and then forgotten about, both by the player and by the game.  So clearly we're here for the gameplay, and that's just fine.  There are so many games that are determined to make you sit through hours-worth of cutscenes to tell their terrible stories, so I'm just fine with having a quick summary and then onto the game.  It's just that when you get there, you almost want to know more about the story.
The game advertises itself as harkening back to the days of Super Mario 64 or Banjo Kazooie, and to that respect it's fairly accurate.  Taking place on levels that seem to be inspired by Nintendo's recent 3D Mario titles, your objectives are two-fold.  Collect berries to unlock more powerful ranks for your leaf, and collect the three water drops to bring to the end of the level in order to complete it and unlock a new one.  Basically instead of coins and stars, you have berries and droplets.  Fair enough.  I can dig simple.  The problem with the levels isn't so-much in lack of things to look for, but more in how the levels are delivered, and in how Woodle (I'm just assuming that's his name) controls and fights.
First, the levels.  As design goes, they're competant-enough.  However, the developer rules over the camera with an iron fist.  The player is only allowed to control the zoom of the camera, which only sometimes allows the player to get a better look at the area they are navigating.  This creates a common problem in most levels where the player is expected to navigate, explore, and even platform along a 3D environment while the camera insists on parking as low as possible in order to give the player a strictly 2D view.  This is a particular problem on a level where the player has to navigate up a wall of honey combs, but there's a pit hidden from view behind what otherwise looks like could be flat terrain.  Then there's the ice level with the obligatory slippery terrain, and the player is expected to navigate and platform up a thin line of stairs.  Too far back, and they fall into the pit and back to the beginning of the level; too far forward and they fall onto the ledge below and have to start over; all while dealing with slippery controls because of the ice.  Then there's the problem of only
levels having any check points.  Die on the wrong level, and it's all the way back to the beginning to re-navigate any annoying obstacles (and it seems it's always the levels with annoying platforming segments that have no checkpoints) in order to catch back up to where the player died in the first place.
Woodle himself seemed content to add to the frustrations.  The game's physics are kind of weird in that Woodle seems to maintain momentum, even after running into a flat surface.  This lead to a common problem where, after running into a wall or something, I would jump and find Woodle projecting himself forward despite no input on the analog stick.  This lead to more than one occasion where Woodle seemed to take control of himself in order to find the nearest pit, and back to the beginning of the level (or if I was lucky, to a checkpoint).  The combat in the game is equally uninspired.  There are enemies, and they will attack Woodle to try and send him back to the beginning of the level.  Thankfully, they're also painfully easy to defeat; especially once Woodle gets the leaf that sends-out a projectile.  Not only are they no threat, but killing them doesn't even feel rewarding.  They all make the exact same noise, fall over, then disappear.  By, aren't we getting stimulated.
Normally this is the part where I'd say that the game was clearly designed for children, so it's okay if it isn't exactly game of the year material.  There are two problems with that defense though.  Firstly, the advertising specifically appeals to nostalgia by referencing games from about 20 years ago, meaning that anyone who played them (especially during their prime) is going to be 25 or older.  Secondly, there are just better games that are child-appropriate.  Steam has thousands of games available to choose from, and there's also the option of acquiring (or dusting-off) an N64 in order to have their kids play the very games whose appeal this game uses for marketing.  Granted that children tend to have lower standards, but when games are available that are child-appropriate AND entertaining for older audiences, why settle?
Sadly, I cannot recommend.

A deeply immersive game where placing your dynasty on the different thrones of Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa is the main goal. You accumulate score based on the number of empires, kingdoms, duchies, counties, and baronies controlled by your dynasty. The base game allows for nearly 400 years of gameplay in the base version, with close to 300 more years added in DLC.
The base game starts in the year 1066, around the time of the historic Battle of Stamford Bridge. You can start playing during any month and year between 1066 and 1337, choosing any historic ruler you like. You can choose to play as any christian ruler all the way down to the county level, (you can unlock all other religions and cultures with DLC) and you work your way up the ranks. Your ruler's traits determine how much your vassals like you, how much land you can hold, how effective he is as a military leader, diplomatic relations, etc. Marry daughters or sisters of kings for alliances, and have children to ensure the success of your dynasty. You will want to groom your heir as well as you can, but beware of assassinations and other freak accidents.
My only complaint is the amount of the game that's cut out and made into DLC, but when they add DLCs they also add a large amount of free content to base game users, so its not that bad.

Ok.. so I bought this game after mulling over the decision for a few days. Read a lot of reviews of it, some good, many not. I'm not a huge fan of survival games, mostly because I hate the epic ♥♥♥♥ing grind they become. Oh you need to make a metal cup to consume water? Go mine 1,500 iron from that mountain and then mine 5,000 coal for the smelter. 10 hours later yay! Cup! However I DO enjoy building and crafting -just not when pointless, endless mining♥♥♥♥♥♥is confused as "gameplay".
But Conan Exiles had three things going for it: It's advertised as a decent solo game (and this review is strictly from solo play), it’s in a fantasy setting, and NO ♥♥♥♥ING ZOMBIES. I'm really not a huge fan of zombies and it seems every damned survival game these days is a zombie game. So I thought what the hell, I'll grab it. ~25 hours later I write this review.
The Good
The environment in this game is superb. The sounds and music fit right in (thought the music does become a bit repetitive as the tracks aren’t very long). The game draws you in very early. Graphics are good overall, though the textures and flora meshes look dated up close.
The skill progression system is interesting. You don’t unlock skills or abilities, you unlock parts of the crafting trees to craft new stuff. Base building in Conan Exiles is pretty damned good. Very easy to place structural components and very easy to undo what you did if you made a mistake. It’s actually one of the better base building systems I’ve seen. Lots of nifty things you can build too if you’re interested in really roleplaying in the Conan universe, and some interesting contraptions available.
Crafting items themselves is pretty straight forward, nothing groundbreaking. Select recipe, put req. resources in inventory or crafting station (forge, tannery, etc.) click craft, wait.
The Bad
The progression right now is really out of whack. By default, levelling past the first few levels in painfully slow and harvesting the required resources to craft anything beyond the basic recipes takes a very long time. Now, here’s the caveat: You can tweak all these values to your liking. So you can increase the drop rates and XP rates so the later levels don’t feel like a chore. The problem there? You make the beginning of the game stupid easy, which in turn makes the rest of the game easy as soon as the environment is no longer a threat. Playing solo this isn’t too bad as you can adjust on the fly, but I’m still trying to find a good compromise for a co-op servers.
Playing solo there isn’t much to do beyond building up a bit and wiping out different camps. In later updates this will be changed as the devs have stated bases will eventually get raided by mobs, too.
The AI is also dumb as♥♥♥♥♥♥right now. It poses practically zero challenge once you’re geared and levelled up a bit and learn the “tricks” to defeating it. Though in fairness the crafting recipes are still unbalanced and will likely be changed. This is the third Ys game I have played up to this point and its definitely my favorite one so far. I haven't played Ys origin yet or any of the PSP ones but this one is the best combat of the Ys games IMO. While my knowledge is only from ys 1 and 2, I think oath in felghana has a better combat system due to the fact it has an actual combat system.
While it centers around one area only they're still things to do even after you complete a certain dungeon. The main reason for return to each area as you progress through the game is the metroidvania like system that's implemented. As you gain new powers new areas that may have been inaccessible open up (Like a higher platform) and most of them have really cool treasure locked away.
Main story features Adol the Red and Doji returning to Doji's homeland and things soon get out of hand for the Duo (Like usual). Adol is seemingly stripped of everything at the start yet again, but from a gameplay perspective I understand why. I would have liked if they featured his last games armor and weapons as the basic starter items though.
The combat system is miles ahead of what ys 1 and 2 had with a combo system, magic built in, multiple magic moves that have charging attacks as well, can jump in the air and do air combos and downward slamming attacks.
A lot of the enemies in the game have some strong defenses in one category but may be extremely weak to another category (Strong vs attacks, weak vs magic). Once you figure out each enemies weakness they become slighty easier to kill off.
Bosses are really awesome in this game and most of them feel bullet-hellish (To a minor degree, nothing insane) and require you to learn the bosses patterns to beat them effectively. Some bosses do become pushovers if you overlevel an area via grinding.
Music is badass like usual with electric guitar and electronica sounds mixed into the game for a bunch of memorable tunes. Also another nice feature is no more grinding an enemy over and over again for its bestiary (Only have to beat it once for it information).
Positive:
Great combat system
Interesting combos both in the air and ground
Multiple magic charging attacks
Really interesting boss mechanics
Negative:
Stripped of everything at the start
No voice over

I would give this game a 100% yes for a recommendation and then some. I honestly have barely made it passed lady vengeance part and that's after dozens of hours of playthrough, and I've barely scratched the surface of the game. For those of u just starting out in the game, here are several different tips for you to browse through before delving into this gem of an rpg.
1. You will die whther u like it or not. Be sure that every character in your party has a ressurection scroll trust me. Evenetually u can get a reviv skill later down the line
2. EXPLORE EVERYTHING! If one of your guys happens to have the lucky charm civil skill, I'd recommend looking through every single crate and barrel.
3. Races kind of matter. Lizards can dig without shovels, dwarves can get into hard to reach areas, undead can pick locks without the use of lockpicks, and elves can eat body parts which allows a part of a quest to continue, or actually gives you an ability
4. Although it uses a point, be sure to get the pet pal perk. It's fun in general to engage in dialogue with pets, and allows you to go through quests more easily at times.
5. Through personal experience, I find that the summoner skill is one of the most useful skills in the game. It does not require that you put points into intelligence, thus allowing for it to be used with any kind of character. All you gotta do is put points into the summoning skill itself. Another cool thing is once u get it up to 10, the incarnates you conjure will be colossal incarnates doing more damage and such. I currently have a fighter that is pretty much pure tank, but also has the summoner skill as well, which goes along well with my tank through personal experience.
Few cool little tricks I'll list as well.
1. If you wanna steal, have one person engage in dialogue, and then switch to a different character that has the thievery skill and pickpocket them. (Make sure you leave that specific area where the theft occurred, or the npc u stole from will try to search you)
2. You can combine spell tomes. Might be some combinations that the internet has not found out yet, so try all kinds of things
3. Combine boots with nails, and you won't slip on icy terrain.
4. If you can, bring a poison barrel with you on the go. You can actually combine weapons with the barrel to give them a slight edge with a bit of poison damage, and you can do this an unlimited amount of times. Be aware that there are a LOT of undead in the game though and they regen from poison, so be sure to bring a different weapon as well just in case.

- AT deluxe has a lot of features content wise , AT 2 gold just added the features in AT 1 as dlc.
So yeah Airline Tycoon 2 was a disaster of a sequel none of us AT 1 fans wanted to see but at least we have the first game back.
