One of the more innovative gaming concepts of it's decade and one that has a lot of charm in the design of the characters, the music and the gameplay itself.
One of the best things that SEGA did besides NIGHTS.
Gameplay
The gameplay consists on a very simple concept, in which you have to spray graffiti on the walls in order to complete the stage, that sounds meh, but here's the interesting concept, you do this while grinding on rails, walls, and other things in the city. Which adds challenge to the setting and does offer some tricks and quirks so that you'll be engage on your mission of spreading your art.
By having the ability of grinding in order to reach to certain places combined with the pumped up music and the interesting design of the levels you're into a fun ride doing tricks while you paint the walls. Although not everyone is happy with that since you'll be chased by policemen or gangs that will try to prevent you from doing that. Which are relatively easy to avoid.
And in some cases you'll have boss battles where you'll fight a gang by spraying on their backs, which is also fun and does require some skill to perform.
Controls
Since this is a port the controls will get screwed, so if you don't have a controler you'll have a hard time since it's not optimized for keyboard.
As for how it plays in the game (assuming you have a controller (preferably a 360 controller)) it plays well and the controls are tights.
On a keyboard though it's a big mess.
Story
It mainly consists on a group of graffiti artists and their main mission to gain territory by "fighting" the other gang members by spraying over their graffiti. Which sounds ridiculous but it's not one of those games that the story matters.
It's only there for the sake of having a story and not one to take seriously.
Graphics
Since it uses cell shaded 3D models it does look quite good even in this age where games from 2000 normally tend to look bad. It's aesthetically good, it does have it's charm and does help it to differenciate from other games, making it very easy to remember it and to see certain iconic things from the game. So it's not an issue and you'll probably like it.
Music
One of the strongest points in the game since it does fit the nature of the game and of them being young, similar to the 90s where these themes were seen as cool and hip and they help you to have a good time while you perform your missions.
And since they're very catchy you'll probably look for them on youtube after playing it and you'll probably remember some of the songs that appear in the game. My favorite ones being on the bowl and grace and glory.
Overrall
A game that you must have and one of the most important ones in gaming history, since it's a concept not done before (as far as I can remember) and innovative. A very engaiging gameplay coupled with a god tier soundtrack will make this experience one that you'll never forget.

My king is childless, a weak ruler of a great kingdom spanning the length and breadth of Britain, where his family have ruled unquestioned for two hundred years.  His barren wife hates him and he's got the pox from knocking off a maidservant.  When he dies, all of his titles belong to the king of France, a nephew from an ill thought out marriage, and not of the family.  The succession laws insist that all the vassals ratify any changes, and 3 dukes and a duchess have just been imprisoned for rebelling against the crown.  They don't feel like being helpful right now. To rub salt in the wound, the King's faithful dog just died.

Crusader Kings II is the ultimate strategy game, eschewing fancy graphics and total war-esque battles for the big picture, assuming the big picture can also include how to shag a maid servant and get the pox.  You'll spend most of your time skim reading messages and weighing up the cost of roleplay choices, before deciding to declare war on a mad king with a gimpy leg who happens to be threatening your borders.  You'll laugh, cry, scream with rage, ponder your morality, and♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself when the nanny hangs herself over your strange ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child who you just know is responsible for the accidental death of your nine year old heir.
"Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown"
What's good:
* nice graphics
* intense roleplay
* sense of strategy other games can't give (I'm looking at you Rome II)
* challenge and a sense of achievement
* the messaging can be adjusted
* massive replayability
* the omen kid
What's not:
* UI is at times frustrating
* the endless messages (see above)
* unforgiving learning curve
* weak tutorial (but don't we love the deep end)
* Hugo, The King of France

As someone who has played this game since it originally came out on mobile, I can say with confidence and the utmost sincerity, avoid this game at all costs. Back in the first few months of the game, the divide between f2p and p2w was managable. There weren't game breaking cards back then, so the majority of decks were made of 90% farmable cards. Then the box (paid) cards got better. Wildly overpowered pre-combo cards that, if pulled on the first turn, is akin to getting Exodia. It means your opponent automatically loses. If you started back in the begining of the game, you had the ability to farm story levels. As of about 2 weeks ago (at least on the mobile side, idk if this version has it too) you can no longer farm. This makes the divide between the 2 sides infinitely more expansive. There are, however, a few things that I can positively say about the game. While almost 95% of the best cards used to be locked behind a paywall, now, through the use of challenge coins, you can actually get some valuable box cards, which is an improvement. This game, unfortuantely, works on the idea of '1 step forward, 3 steps back'. If they give us challenge coins to give f2p characters box cards, then they have to take away farming, make new players disadvantaged by making their research times be 4 times what a paying players are, and make even more insanely OP cards that only the fattest of whales could ever hope to obtain. I understand that when managing 5 big IPs like the shows in this game, they need to make a pretty penny just to justify the games exsistence, but this is ridiculous. Take it from someone who has spent over $200 in this game in its prime, if you know what's good for you, avoid this game.

I'm not a huge JRPG guy, but I absolutely adore the Ys (pronounced "ease") series, of which this is the 3rd entry.  The Ys games are all extremely fast-paced action RPGs with rockin' ADVENTURE METAL soundtracks, and they all star Adol Christin, a dauntless adventurer who makes the ladies melt with his flaming red mane.  The stories the games tell are very simple, sort of like epic fairy tales, and they thankfully lack that chirping, cheap fakeness that hangs over most JRPG narratives like a pall.  There are always archetypes to be sure (the angel-pure but troubled maiden, the grizzled old battlemaster), but Ys possesses a sincerity that appeals on a deep level.
Even though this game doesn't have the frenetic "bump" combat of the first two entries (a mechanic that really turned me on, gamerwise) Felghana's push-to-slash fighting is every bit as frenzied and quite a bit more strategic.  Also, with the exception of the Azure Statue in Tigray Quarry (the first level), the bosses are spectacular.

I have played this game for over a year now(close to 2 years). I started out off of steam and then downloaded it through Steam.
I have multiple characters, 3 max leveled and the rest still working on. I focus primarily on PVP but I also have experience with the nests & Dragon Raids (PVE).
I have never once felt the need to purchase items through the Dragon Vault to play the game:
>You do not NEED costumes as they are null and void in PVP, and the effect they have on your stats are so minimal that you do not notice a difference in Nests or Raids. (I purchased 2 because I liked how they looked on my character)
>You do not NEED a dual skill scroll, I survived with out one (A hybrid build) all the way till recently when I got a free dual skill scroll from an event.
>You do not NEED any extra talisman slots, crest slots, etc. (I can do everything max lvl w/o these)
>You do not NEED a pet (you get one for free through achievements anyway)
>You do not NEED a fancy mount (you get one for free through the main quest)
With all that said let's realize something. Nexon gives the players multiple Dragon Vault objects for free as you level up and through seasonal events.
>You receive free skill reset scrolls at 15 through Irene, and when you approach each "previous level cap" level (40,50,60,70,80) your gift box gives you a free reset scroll. Each of these items are worth $15 or 15k NX yet you receive multiple ones just in case you're new and mess up.
>You receive a free mount through the main quest Brownie Joker or Mocha Sugar, yes they are not the must extravagant mounts (They're just horses) they still do the job of allowing the player a quicker way to move. You can also farm for more fancier horses through the higher level nests for free.
>Any time there is a technical problem you will most likely receive compensation for the server troubles or problems. Most of the time it involves Dragon Eggs (a small amount but RNG can be merciful). Also Dragon Eggs of any type are just RNG models. Your chances of getting rare items is static. Spending more money will not increase your chances.
>Through seasonal events I have received free resets, free dual skill scroll, free costume parts, free pets and more.
GAMEPLAY:
The Gameplay is fast and entertaining. You must learn how to dodge and be aware of your surroundings for higher level bosses, Raids and Nests. You should know how your moves work (Super Armor & Super Armor Break).
It is instance based not open world and therefore the dungeons can be repetitive.
The main story I find to be very enjoyable and entertaining.
PVP can be difficult due to certain unbalances between classes and frustrating just like every games PVP. PVP is normally equalized or partially equalized so you do not need top gear or any gear to pvp (Unless you are doing Ladder pvp which is more rank based)
My advice would be to take the game slow. Try to do the nests at each level avaliable. Level with friends or join a guild it's more fun with a group. Don't specialize in one aspect. Be able to do both PVP and PVE.
Hopefully this helps,

I don't want to give the game a thumbs down, but at the same time I can't really recommend it as it is. There is a lot of potential here, but the problem is that the challenge is non-existant and the game is more of a time sink than an actual game per se. Once you've figured out the basics, haggling and combat become far too easy to win every single time. I had hoped this game would be something along the lines of Oregon Trail on the Arabian peninsula, but the challenge and depth is not to be found here. The only time any of your characters can every possibly die is during combat, or if you run out of water and they die of thirst. But it is far too easy to win at combat once you've figured it out, and it is not terribly difficult to stock up on water to prevent dying from thirst either. I feel that taking inspiration from Oregon Trail and having things like injuries and diseases, and the requirement to bring along medicine and other essential items in the event this sort of thing happens would keep players on their toes. To be fair, there are healing potions in the game, but if you have a sage in your caravan then they can take care of that for you for free.
In fact, everyone in your caravan does their work for you completely free of charge. Why aren't they being paid wages? The only thing you give to them is water, without which they die, but other than that they are doing all their work for you completely free of charge and this is very unrealistic and the only overhead you have is the cost of the water. Oregon Trail   requires bringing along provisions, and you could even hunt for more in the wild if you need to. Why not have that in this game? There is a scout class which I honestly never even used (except to get the diversity achievement), but it seems like it could have been something very useful if this class could help forage supplies in the wild. And as with Oregon Trail, how about a hunting mini-game to hunt antelope or whatever sort of game exist in Arabia? That would be fun.
Anyway, this game is not bad as a casual time sink, but there is not a lot of depth or challenge to be found here, and that is a real shame because the premise is interesting.

Save Scumming (Noun, pronounced /sāv skəmiNG/)
The act of repeatedly reloading a previous saved game, in order to benefit yourself.
When you die in Divinity: Original Sin 2, you don't come back in a town, or respawn, or even have a "re-load last waypoint" option. You just go back to the main menu and re-load your last auto save. (which could be 3 hours old, because auto saves are based on when you enter unexplored areas, not every X minutes)
Got one-shot by a hidden trap? re-load your last save and avoid it this time.
Mob too hard for you? re-load your last save and avoid them this time.
NPC didn't like a dialouge option you chose? re-load your last save and choose something different this time.
Loot crate had medicore contents? Create a save before opening it, and save scum until it spits out something really rare.

My king is childless, a weak ruler of a great kingdom spanning the length and breadth of Britain, where his family have ruled unquestioned for two hundred years.  His barren wife hates him and he's got the pox from knocking off a maidservant.  When he dies, all of his titles belong to the king of France, a nephew from an ill thought out marriage, and not of the family.  The succession laws insist that all the vassals ratify any changes, and 3 dukes and a duchess have just been imprisoned for rebelling against the crown.  They don't feel like being helpful right now. To rub salt in the wound, the King's faithful dog just died.

Crusader Kings II is the ultimate strategy game, eschewing fancy graphics and total war-esque battles for the big picture, assuming the big picture can also include how to shag a maid servant and get the pox.  You'll spend most of your time skim reading messages and weighing up the cost of roleplay choices, before deciding to declare war on a mad king with a gimpy leg who happens to be threatening your borders.  You'll laugh, cry, scream with rage, ponder your morality, and♥♥♥♥♥♥yourself when the nanny hangs herself over your strange ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child who you just know is responsible for the accidental death of your nine year old heir.
"Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown"
What's good:
* nice graphics
* intense roleplay
* sense of strategy other games can't give (I'm looking at you Rome II)
* challenge and a sense of achievement
* the messaging can be adjusted
* massive replayability
* the omen kid
What's not:
* UI is at times frustrating
* the endless messages (see above)
* unforgiving learning curve
* weak tutorial (but don't we love the deep end)
* Hugo, The King of France

There's a lot going on with this game.
When you start, you have nothing, and know nothing about what you're about to walk into. With the world map being one with enigmatic terrain, it's sometimes difficult to get from point a to point b without a diversion, but it's all about exploration. Even being a fan of the Conan books and graphic novels for years and years, I'm not always sure what's going to be around the corner, or if the person I see at a distance is a friend or an enemy, just like in the books. Any turn can lead you to extensive caves filled with anything, a previously unknown water source, a ruined temple, or the crumbling road to a mysterious abandoned city. Even when learning crafting recipes, it's not always clear what the advantages or disadvantages of any decision is until it's made - there's no real hand holding here and that's what makes it so difficult to walk away from.
Finding the right server that is set up for the way you play is a little tricky at first and you may have to start over on different servers until you find the right balance. I was lucky enough to find a PvE server that's very laid back and filled with helpful people - this was a great way to get familiar with the game. Going straight to PvP and not having an idea of how to get around or where certain strategic resources can be found won't let you last long, and is bound to be frustrating for the first ten or so hours of gameplay.
I'm giving credit where it is due, this is early access and there will be more content and polish as we go on, and I can't wait to see how this game evolves over time. I'm already sucked in to the drama of the landscape, interesting NPCs, and feeling like I'm discovering something new when I just walk towards something flaming in the distance. Though, along with the no hand holding thing, there's no map coordinate system, no minimap, no way to mark locations for yourself, and going off and exploring can result in not being able to find your way back to where you started, which for me is just part of the fun.
I really appreciate how this game stays true to the Conan stories and mythology of the world. It is brutal, dangerous, sometimes confusing, erotic at times, and ultimately gratifying. The crafting element is the most time consuming, followed only by trying to find food and water, and then combat. Crafting yields some really impressive structures, arms, and armor, allowing for the imagination of the player to run rampant. You can only go out looking for more wood and stone making hundreds of trips back to your shelter to keep building so many times before it does feel a bit repetitive, but you can always venture out and almost always find something new to explore. It's a great game now, and it will only get better as it is developed above and beyond what it already is.

In the spirit of EA Survival games, Conan is extremely divisive. The combat is a bit jank, and there is plenty of old school clipping. The wild life is bountiful and murderous and the dehydration unrelenting. You will start in a wasteland next to a water bottle you will ignore, and only visual cues on the horizon as to where to head. Ignore these cues at your peril.
The building mechanic, while blessed with its own failings, is more flexible and interesting than its closest competitor. You could ignore the rest of the game and focus quite happily on simply building if you wanted.
Progression is slow, but all the settings for the game are editable in the admin console.
Would I recommend it if you are a lone survivor? No. Like other survival games, Conan is like a night out at your local crappy club or bar. It is not where you are that makes it fun, it is who you are with. If you can find a core group of friends that have enjoyed breaking your legs on a step in DayZ, or reliving your Jurassic Park fantasies in Ark, then you will almost certainly enjoy experiences in Conan while they last.

While this game is still far from perfect, it has done an amazing job so far. Based on my experience, this game can either be a bad experience or a good one depending on the community you play with. Choosing the right server for YOU is essential to getting the most value out of your purchase. The game certainly has its limits in terms of content but with each new patch, the game becomes a little better. If you don't think it's a good deal right now then hold off on your purchase, the game might be worth revisiting after more content has been added.
What the game does right is providing you as the player almost complete freedom of gameplay as any survival game should, there is no guide or tutorial. You start off as a nude (if you choose that option) character in the middle of the desert and survive from there, there is no quest, no freebies, no blinking icon telling you what to do. Playing the game on vanilla settings is probably the fastest way to regret your purchase, having friends play with you is the best way to go. As I have said earlier, playing on the right server is everything, it can vary from increased xp rate, harvesting rates and even mods to help enhance the overall experience. Don't worry if your alone and none of your friends wanna play with you, the better servers usually have the most welcoming communities around. You will sometimes come across servers with an abusive admin or toxic players, if the better admins do not ressolve these problems then it is time to move on to another server. Its better to rebuild and start over than to put up with it, prolonged exposure to toxic people will greatly demotivate you to continue playing.
Combat is still pretty basic with a limited amount of weapons and armor to choose from but they have plans to better it. NPC AI too is pretty basic and sometimes dumb, it can create for some uninteresting fights. That for me is the games biggest weakness, it does not promote much tactical thinking in combat when it comes to pve and pvp is a giant mess where everyone swings their sword and hammers wearing the same heavy armor with the occasional dye variant if they bother. But I won't lie, running with your clan to raid, fight another clan or even explore certain parts of the map is an amazing experience.
This game may not be for everyone, don't buy it if you want a clean and finished product, an amazing story and gameplay experience. Buy it if you wish to try something new, be creative on survival and building, be ready to accept that the game is still in early access and have fun at it.

So let's get into the pros and cons...
PROS:
- The graphics, considering the style of game, are good although simplistic;
- The sound track is awesome
- The game reminds me of the old game Taipei, and if you still remember Taipei and you enjoyed that then you'll enjoy this
- The user interface is easy to use
CONS:
- The combat mechanics, which is a nice idea, needs to be implemented with more complexity along with a major improvement in the AI tactics behind it.
- The random events when moving between towns need to be more random and the user to be forced to take more combat actions as opposed to the ability to avoid combat 95% of the time.
That said, the combat system does work and so does the events that come up, I'd just prefer further complexity inside both.

It's goooooood.
There's not much else to say.  It's a simple game where the few moving parts are made beautifully.  You have one gun, the Devil Daggers, that can fire like a shotgun or machinegun.  You shoot the weakpoints and collect them to upgrade your fingers. WASD movement.  Survive long enough to get on the leaderboards.  That's it.
Except that isn't just it.
It's a game about making a million binary choices every second.
The first enemies you face are a tower that spews a swarm of fast moving skulls and one bigger one that just kind of runs away.  Do you destroy the tower quickly, or clear the mobs first?  Depends on the moment. Destroy a few and a massive skull spider shows up.  You need to destroy it quickly or it'll send out a bunch of spider hatchlings.  But wait, the larger skulls from earlier just flipped over, have 5 times the health, are chasing you now, and are cackling maniacly.  Do you destroy the laughing skulls and risk the spiders hatching?
Maybe you just want to run away.  Game's got you covered.  You can bunnyhop easily by jumping every time you hit the ground, making you slightly faster than the swarms of skulls.  Of course, then you can't turn easily.  Do you want to risk bunnyhopping when it could lead you into a swarm you could easily avoid on foot, or will the speed be your best bet at the moment?  Need to just go backwards as fast as possible?  Or possibly up?  Use the shotgun blast to rocketjump.  You got away!  Of course, you might accidentally launch yourself off the edge of the arena.  Is going backwards worth that risk?
See?  Just a bunch of simple risk/reward choices.  But you only have one health, so every choice matters.  And even the first enemy makes you make 3 of those decisions the moment you set eyes on it.  Should I bunnyhop towards it or not? Should I shoot the crystal to destroy the tower or focus on the swarms.  Should I try and kill the larger skull it spawned that's leaving me alone at this moment?
And every enemy just starts piling these choices on.
More and more.
Faster and faster.
It's the risk/reward of Galaga with the graphics of what Quake wanted to be.
If you like arcade games:  GET THIS.
P.S.  The ability to download and watch the replay of anyone above you on the leaderboard makes improvement much easier.  Great feature.

At first I was hesitant at getting this. It looks great, and like a lot of fun, but maybe not worth the price. I thought maybe I'd pick up the game on a sale or something.
But I'm very glad I got it.
The story is very rich and there's so many ways to play. I'm excited for my second and third play throughs.
You can steal from anybody, kill anyone, befriend NPCs, talk to your followers if you choose to have them, and each story is different from character creation. Each race is treated differently, you have different dialogue options if you're an Outlaw, or Scholar, or even if you play a smart Wizard, you can persuade people with your smarts, or intimidate people with your strength.
The combat is very fun, and comboing spells and attacks is awesome.
Classes aren't really set in stone either. If you're a Fighter but decide you want to shock people, or grow some wings, you can very much do so.
And the GM mode is amazing.
As a Game Master for D&D games, I've always wanted a game to play it in, to immerse the players, and let them explore with out having to explain every small detail. And this game does it very well. You can create custom items, NPCs (even down to what hat they wear), allies, and customize the pre set maps the game gives you. I would honestly buy a DLC that includes more maps. But there are plently right now, I'm just afraid that through multiple play throughs we'll all think "Oh, this map again."
This game is a masterpiece, but it's not perfect.
The combat is very hard, even on the easiest difficulty it sometimes feels like I need to kill a couple NPCs who don't deserve it so I can level up and continue the story. And sometimes this makes the game feel linear. I don't know if I'm missing something, or I chose bad classes for my party, but either way that's a big down side for me.
That being said, at the time of posting this review I'm 71 hours in, and I havent even completed my first play through, which is a good thing. I'm taking my time, exploring the world, talking to every NPC and living the world.
UPDATE (very minor spoilers):
I finished the game, and I have to say while the ending was good, it was very buggy. I was unable to use res scrolls, enemies would teleport everywhere, and some other minor things.
Arx also felt very bland for what it could have been. Driftwood and all of Reaper's Coast felt huge, and there was so much story there, but Arx... You were there for one thing, and that was to beat the game. I tried to find more to do there, I tried to find side quests, just anything, but there was nothing. Maybe I missed stuff, maybe I didn't. Either way I feel the game no longer deserves my original score of 8.5/10.

Alright. This may as well be a rant but I'm going to break this review down on some subcategories. I've been playing this game for a while and recommend it to new people. CATEGORY 1: Graphics

CATEGORY 2: Gameplay (Combat, Movement, PvP, PvE)
Gameplay is...it's...it's alright. The combat is either 1st or 3rd person; and personally I would rather go 3rd. 1st person is extremely wierd and awkward, and rather dull as well. I was left STRANDED IN THE MIDDLE OF NOWHERE  with a horse that eventually DIED on me (No it didn't literally, but it may as well have with the speed it was going). I commonly found myself GRINDING THE♥♥♥♥♥♥out of high level enemies just to rank up. Took me HOURS and loads of cash for ammunition.

The community is alright, but nothing different from any other MMO community out there. You're going to have those OBVIOUS dickwads and terrible people. Don't hope for the best from this community, 'cause you ain't gon'na receive♥♥♥♥♥♥

While this game is still far from perfect, it has done an amazing job so far. Based on my experience, this game can either be a bad experience or a good one depending on the community you play with. Choosing the right server for YOU is essential to getting the most value out of your purchase. The game certainly has its limits in terms of content but with each new patch, the game becomes a little better. If you don't think it's a good deal right now then hold off on your purchase, the game might be worth revisiting after more content has been added.
What the game does right is providing you as the player almost complete freedom of gameplay as any survival game should, there is no guide or tutorial. You start off as a nude (if you choose that option) character in the middle of the desert and survive from there, there is no quest, no freebies, no blinking icon telling you what to do. Playing the game on vanilla settings is probably the fastest way to regret your purchase, having friends play with you is the best way to go. As I have said earlier, playing on the right server is everything, it can vary from increased xp rate, harvesting rates and even mods to help enhance the overall experience. Don't worry if your alone and none of your friends wanna play with you, the better servers usually have the most welcoming communities around. You will sometimes come across servers with an abusive admin or toxic players, if the better admins do not ressolve these problems then it is time to move on to another server. Its better to rebuild and start over than to put up with it, prolonged exposure to toxic people will greatly demotivate you to continue playing.
Combat is still pretty basic with a limited amount of weapons and armor to choose from but they have plans to better it. NPC AI too is pretty basic and sometimes dumb, it can create for some uninteresting fights. That for me is the games biggest weakness, it does not promote much tactical thinking in combat when it comes to pve and pvp is a giant mess where everyone swings their sword and hammers wearing the same heavy armor with the occasional dye variant if they bother. But I won't lie, running with your clan to raid, fight another clan or even explore certain parts of the map is an amazing experience.
This game may not be for everyone, don't buy it if you want a clean and finished product, an amazing story and gameplay experience. Buy it if you wish to try something new, be creative on survival and building, be ready to accept that the game is still in early access and have fun at it.

Fast forwards to 2017 and, through sheer perserverence as well as rigorous updates, the developers have managed to push passed this obstacle.

Warframe is a grind, but it's a fun grind. I even purchased Platinum to support the developers despite the fact that I could have earned it via trading crafting components with other players, which is actually one feature that rekindled my interest in the game.

Undoubtly one of, if not the best RPG games of all time, it was a instant classic when it was released many years ago. It covers around 200hrs or so of playtime depending on what all you decide to do in it, with tremendous replay value in the form is multiple choice dialogue, character creation, party selection, and branching storylines.
Storyline
Being of the strongest aspects of the game, it is rich in nature and varied to some degree depending on your choices in the game, which can have a real permanant impact on how it unfolds and certain events that can occur later. The main story covers about 50hrs or so of the game, so it is a small piece of the much larger game with dozens of sidequests and optional areas to explore.
Characters
There are about a dozen or so base characters in the game, each with their own unique look and personality. Everyone of them interact with other party members and some may even outright refuse to join you if they see a particular person already with you. Lots of instances in the game have reactive choices as well, meaning they will either comment on your actions or depending on how extreme may even outright leave you. Romances are possible in the game with three standard female options to choose from and one male.
Gameplay
The gameplay is largely based on the DnD 2nd edition ruleset, though you really don't need to be particular familiar with this in order to be able to play it. You are able to either create your own entire party from scratch, which can be a lengthy process if you aren't familiar with the game or choose from existing templates. Battles can be highly tactical in nature with many having numerous ways fo being handled depending on your composition, spells and gear. Some encounters will also be different depending on what level you get to them at, being far more difficult if you aren't properly prepared.
Sound
The voice acting in the game is top notch and there are thousands of lines of dialogue to go through. Not all of it is fully voiced, but all of the important scenes in the game are. Music sets a good pace as well, with some of them being able to indicate a tell tale pace as to what type of encounter you are facing, with major ones playing certain tracks which you will come to know and associate.
Overall
If you are any kind of a fan of RPG games, this is a must play. Deep character development, storyline, relantionship building, roleplaying elements and sheer replayability will have you spending many hours in this classic. And with the ability to download mods for it to add more quests, characters, romances, items and new areas; the possibilities are staggering.

Ys: The Oath in Felghana is a rare beast on the PC... well it is to me. Before I broke down and bought it I stared at its gameplay video in steam. I stalked the title for months on end. I was delighted to see a JRPG on Steam. Would my delight be broken, or would I take the oath and never look back?
First off I must say I played this game to completion with a gamepad. I never even once tested out the keyboard ad mouse controls. This type of game just screamed use a controller to me haha. The game controls perfectly with a gamepad. Every little command I used worked, and never were the controls broken. A++ on that.
Sound design in Ys is all about the music. The sound effects are very basic and serve the game well, but do not stand out at all. The musical score on the other hand does stand out. Each piece was moving, and the guitar driven battle themes fit perfectly. Never once did I feel like I wanted to put on my own soundtrack while playing the game. If it's any testament to the games music, I would even go into the options menu just to play the games soundtrack a few occasions.
The story of the game is its weakest area. The game uses nearly every JRPG trope. I knew of every upcoming plot twist and action. This made me really sad as someone who enjoys a good narrative. I must admit though that not once did the narrative become convoluted. It served its purpous rather well, and that was to transition from dungeon to dungeon and the awesomely addicting gameplay.
The gameplay of Ys is where it's at. A simple mixture of semi strategic hack n slash with a dabble of platforming and RPG light elements. Combat is fast, fluid and when you get hit it's ultimately you're fault. The game doesn't offer that much in terms of different combos. You can perform only basic ground and air combos. You can't knock an enemy into the air and combo them further. What you can do is cancel combos to get in more hits. There are 3 magic in the game, but playing on normal I didn't find much use for them. The most useful if magics is the earth dash as it nullifies enemy attacks. Once you get this magic it'll be you're go to magic. This is because the game doesn't feature a shield or dodge roll which some may find annoying, but I understood it as part of the game.
Level design is simplistic and yet very well done. That being said, there are a few areas where you can enter a new screen keep holding the same direction, and move yourself back into the previous area. It's a personal annoyance to me. These areas are few and far between so it's not that big of a deal. The platforming segents mainly located towards the end of the game are well thought out. I initially believed I was going to have trouble with them until I realised your character shadow does appear on the ground. This way you could at least tell where you might land. For people who fear platforming there is a mode in options to make it even easier, and even at that there no fall related deaths in the game.
The bosses are where the game really shines. Each boss fight presents a new challenge and build upon eachother as the game progresses. You're first time playing the game the bosses will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ unless you're an uber-gamer, don't get discouraged. Their attacks hit hard, and require precise timing to dodge. There is also limited time to hit the bosses. That window becomes less and less as the game goes on forcing you to get better with your attack dodging. This type of progression is saught after by me, because no matter how much someone could power level, you still need the skill to back it up. Speaking of leveling in this game, I didn't have to grind more than one time, and the combat is so fluid and fun it didn't even feel like grinding and lasted all of thirty minutes anyways.
Ys: The Oath in Felghana isn't an expierence I'll soon forget. Nearly all elements of the game blend harmoniously into a polished hidden gem just waiting to be stumbled upon. I thought I was risking $15 paying full price for the game, but my apprehension was laid to rest quickly.

Ys: The Oath in Felghana is a very easy game to jump into storywise, even if you have not played any of the previous games in the series. It has its own epic tale to tell, and knowledge of previous events is not required. A fair warning though: if you have never played a Ys game before, start on Easy or Very Easy. I'm not trying to scare you away, but Oath is without a doubt one of the most challenging games to hit the market in recent times. If you choose normal, prepare to die a LOT during the massive boss encounters. That is not to say that the game is cheap or unbalanced, as often tempering your equipment or simply gaining another level will even the playing field. The reward lies in the challenge, and you WILL feel a great sense of accomplishment each time you finally triumph over your foe.
One way to describe the gameplay in Oath would be to imagine an amped-up Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past. Add blazing speed and the ability to jump into the mix,  and toss with a heavy dash of well-executed platforming, and you have a hearty recipe for gaming success. Don't just go rushing in headfirst hacking away at your foes with reckless abandon however, the combat in Oath requires a fair bit of strategy. You will have at your disposal three elemental rings, and the powers they bestow upon you are necessary to dispatch your foes with efficiency. Always be on the lookout in hard to reach areas, as you can always find hidden chests containing upgrades and new equipment, as well as the Raval ore needed to temper your gear at the smithy in town.
Back to the topic of combat. The boss encounters in Oath are epic in scale, and they take a fair bit of thinking to overcome. Simply flailing away with reckless abandon is sure to get you killed. Don't be afraid of failure however, if you die in a boss fight you will be given the option to retry as many times as you wish (though beware, dying 10 times to the same boss and the game will mock you with an "achievement"). The key to success is to study the bosses patterns, and use the proper attack for the job. If all else fails you can grind a level or two, or temper your gear as I pointed out before.
It truly is a grand day for the Steam Community and Ys fans alike now that one of the finest games in the series has hit the platform, and with promises of Ys: Origin on the horizon. Oath will definitely fulfill the wishes of anyone who desires a solid JRPG experience on their PC. With an epic storyline, badass bosses, masterful music, gorgeous graphics, and all around gratuitous gameplay, Ys: The Oath in Felghana does NOT disappoint. With unlockables such as higher difficulties, time attack, and boss rush modes, players will be entertained long after the main story has wrapped up. What are you waiting for? Go get your Ys fix now!

Awesomenauts is a very charming Multiplayer Online Battle Arena game.
Awesomenauts pits two teams of three against each other with the sole objective of destroying the other teams base. Very few games have this much replay value to casual gamers such as myself, by far one of my favorite video games to play with friends and family. Its game mechanics are simple enough for an 8 year old to play, but entertaining enough for middle aged adult to take control of one of the very quirky and fun characters in the game.
There are 14 very distinct characters, with more to come and 4 levels. For the most part each character has 2 seperate skins that you can buy not with in game currency, but actual money.
The only drawbacks of the game are that all skins for every character are around $2.50 each. While I actually did buy one it seems like cosmetic changes to a character aren't all that worth it. Also it can get really repetitive if playing single-player, majority of the bots youre put up against are usually the same variation of 5.
Overall, gameplay is solid, graphics are lovely and rarely do I ever get disconected from a match. A solid game and for only $10, worth every penny.

I've played two of the however many levels of the game, and I have to say - I don't get what all the hate is about. It's a cute little platformer that doesn't try to reinvent the genre. The story is that you were brought to life specifically to collect Fairy Tears and bring water to a land - the Fairy Tears acting as your MacGuffin, like the crystals in a Crash game. You collect them throughout simple platforming levels that are surprisingly long, but never overstay their welcome. Along the way, you pick up Wumpa fr-, err, berries, which serve as sort of a score/unlockable counter - every so often, you unlock a new item for your little Deku Scrub. There also seem to be a level that requires 600 berries, but I'm not sure how grindy getting that is. The game overall is rather easy, however; enemies serve little to no threat, and the platforming is simple. The thing that's most likely to kill you is the camera screwing up because you backtracked. To fix a camera screw up, you just go past the point you were just at - but it's still irritating. So far, I give it a 6.5/10, another .5 if it gets a controllable camera. The June 29th update claims you have camera control, but it's not distance that's the problem, it's angle. The price is right, as it seems like a rather short game.

Is Woodle Tree Adventures a great platformer?
Probably not. Let me explain why:
The camera, god, the camera. The game features an automatic camera and it just doesn't work properly most of the time. Then, we have the not really accurate jumps. Is really annoying, having to fall countless time for cliffs just because the jumps aren't as precise as they should be. Because it's not supposed to be like that, it's not like the game says "You jump and you stay in motion till you hit the ground". Nope, you can freely move while you're jumping, but you're still gonna fall of a lot of cliffs. That, and the game has a few bugs.
Even so and counting all that, I really liked this game. It's... nice. The art design is really nice and makes you feel comfortable all the time. The music is calm and nice. The level design, the simplicity of the game, etc, etc. It just makes the game feel nice.
I don't think that's enough to 'save' the game, but it's certainly not bad. The game is short, I finished it in maybe two hours. But it was a nice play. So, do I recommend this game? If you're just looking for a good platformer, there are plenty out there that are better than this. Even so, this is a nice game at a low price. I hope the game gets better via updates, because I really  think it has potential.

I recommend this game, but only to creatives looking for somewhat intesting take on the RPG genre.
As an actual game, I cannot recommend it in its current state. It simply lacks the polish (and I am not talking about the graphics, they are fine for an indie game at this price point).
A good example is the combat. Like many modern RPGs, it has a time-dilation effect during combat., but due to the limited control you have over your group (limited even further by the way the interface is implemented), this effect is often far more annoying than it is useful.
The game really needs a way for you to control your group members without having to track them down in 3D space (and hope nothing is obscuring the buttons on their heads). Something as simple as putting the three buttons next to the icons in the group slots on the left of the screen.
Some other little quality of life items that would go a long way to making the game playable:
- A quest journal, and removing quests from NPCs once completed.
- The ability to sell items to vendors beyond their inventory capacity (this is debatable, but due to the way purchases are implemented it is kind of necessary in this game).
- Better check pointing (I gave up on the game after constantly being pushed back three major fights. The save slots seemed to do nothing).
- Allow the time-dilation to be disabled. As much as I can see that this is meant to be a major part of the game, there just isn't enough control over the group to make it worth it. Leave it for people who want it, but make it optional. It would need a complete overhaul to bring it on par to the time-dilation in other group based RPGs.
- A proper targeting system. You really only have 1 direct attack spell for most of the game (lighting strike), and it is extrodinarily hard to target at monsters that aren't on the same level to you, or who are far away. A more traditional RPG action system of "click to target, numbers to cast" would be much more workable.
- A better way to compare item's stats / more consistency in the colour coding of items.
Having said all this, I do give props to the developer for the ambition and combination of ideas. I think it is a stretch to call any given element of this game innovative, but the combination of mechanics is interesting.
The tower defence / vaguely-MOBAesque elements mixed with a more tradition group based RPG present some interesting possibilities, and while none of those possibilities are fully realised within this game (or the parts I have seen), they were intriguing.

So, the revealing portrait of the protagonist you see in the store page only appears on the title screen and when you use your ninja magic. I think it's cute. I don't really care what other people think of it. Now, let's talk about the game.
Our heroine is a plucky ninja with a secret crush on a samurai, who gets kidnapped Double Dragon style in the opening cutscene by a rival ninja. She sets out to rescue him, and to kick any butts standing between her and her true love.
This is a pretty simple platformer, which seems to be aiming for the style of the old school platformers like Shinobi, or maybe the original Ninja Gaiden. The art is chibi style, the sound is basic but functional, and there's gamepad support.
You explore several worlds of three levels, with a boss at the end of each. Various types of enemy ninja are out to stop you, but can be easily dispatched with a few throwing daggers, or you can use a ninja magic scroll to fling a shower of daggers in various patterns, which can hit enemies you would otherwise have trouble reaching wihout getting hit first.
Spikes and other enviroment hazards abound, as you might expect, and some are a real challenge to avoid completely. Skillful use of jumping, crouching, and wall clinging is absolutely necessary to get through some areas successfully.
There are three folded kimono in each level, which you need to collect 100% if you want to get the best ending, but this can be done over multiple runs. Since the levels are timed, you will not always want to go for all three at once, but re-run the level to get ones you missed the first time. Any kimono you're holding when you reach the exit don't need to be collected again, they'll be greyed out on later runs through the level, to let you know which kimono you can skip.
I'm honestly a bit surprised I was able to finish this game 100% (with the keyboard!) as quickly as I did, since I'm not that good at platform games. (I have trouble finishing the original Super Mario Bros. for crying out loud.) A few of the later levels and boss battles were very tough for me, but for the most part it's just patience, practice, and persistence.
I was using keyboard controls, so I can't speak to the problems some people are reporting with the gamepad controls. (I had no working gamepad to use at the time.) The control system felt tight enough to me that I never felt cheated by it.
Overall, I feel like I got my money's worth out of this game. It didn't take that long to finish, but it was a cute diversion.

Some noises that the enemies make sound like people trying to imitate airplane and car sounds, which isn't as funny as it sounds when you consider that you are supposed to be fighting demons in an environment that could only be described as "nightmarish".

Hello here my review for Divinity Original Sin 2
The game is a downgrade from the first one in all terms.
Most attributes dont mean jack anymore. Wits for example. In the first game your initiative was bases upon it. Who acts first in battle. With high wits your entire team could act before the enemy. Here with high wits and luck one of your character can act first, then a round robin system takes over. You act, one enemy act, you act and so on. Wits = useless stat now.
The power progression is incredible bland. You get 2 attributepoints and 1 skill point per level. A point in strenght gives you 5% more damage for str based weapons. So 10 points in str give you 50% more damage. A point in constitution gives you a little more hp. Int is for spells and int based weapons. Finesse is for ranged and finesse based weapons. Str increases carry capacity. Memory increases spell slots. That is it. Evasion is not governed by your attributes, initiative is useless, you have no mana points, there is no attribute to get more action points. That is just so annoyingly streamlined and simple it makes me angry.
The combat is way too difficult on normal difficulty. You have to upgrade your equip every level to have a chance in the battles. There are way too few battles to get xp in the beginning. Without cheesing and min maxing to the extreme you do not have any chance in one battle. You come to the starter island and have like 3 battles to begin. First you fight against some cockroaches, easy battle. Then you fight against 3 crocodiles that can 2 shot your party members. And you have no tools to overcome this. Even on explorer mode the battles are unfun and too hard. You are a level below the enemies no chance.
The combat system is non-tactical. There is an idiotic armor system working that sucks the fun out of every fight. As long as the enemy has physical or magical armor you can not use a control spell on them. So you have to pick at their armor before you can do use control spells. That takes any kind of tactic out of the fight. You just hammer the enemies and it is good. The control spells when working are too short. It is way better to just outright kill enemies with your hardest damage spells.
Every skill has a cooldown. Yo so fun. You have the healing school water magic. The enemies dish out a lot of damage, so you have to heal your party. But your only healing spell in water magic has a 4 turn cooldown. So you can not heal your party up. What is that kind of stupid design.
So you play a pyrokinetc mage, but your main damage skills have all cooldowns on them. After shooting your damage spells like fireball and fire daggers, you can not do nothing but waving with your want at the enemies for low damage until your spells are ready again, 5 turns or 4. What are doing MMO like cooldowns in a supposedly oldschool roleplaying game?
Enemies get much more action points then your party. They dish out a ton of damage you can only dream of in the beginning and midgame. Later it gets worse and worse. The enemies get tons of armor and hp, dish out more and more damage.
Skills are not explained, all mechanics in the game are not explained at all. You have to find everything out yourself through try and error.
It seems like every mechanic in the game is just made to annoy the player. The battles are stupid. You can not hold aggro, they have zero tactical elements thanks to the armor system and the only difficulty tool the developers use is HP bloat and damage output of the enemies. The enemies magically know that healspells work on your undead character. But you are hiding the fact that you are undead carefully. Is that immersion?
The story is your standart you are the chosen one stereotype go save the world run of the mill fantasy garbage. The highly praised roleplay system with warrior, barbarian or scholar tags context in dialoges is more annoying then anything. Without the right roleplay tags you can not interact with npcs and have no clue what would be working. You miss a ton of content without a guide. For some people this would encourage to replay with another character. But for me the combat is so frustratingly difficult i will just not play the game at all. Roleplaying means that you decide how your character behaves and acts. Here the tags decide how you can react to npcs. That is not roleplaying anymore. It takes away player freedom, which can not be a good thing in my eyes.
The skill system is just bad.
Itemization is very bad. You find an epic item, wow cool for you. But in one or two levels it will just become obsolete because of the power creep of items here in this game. It is a diablo like itemization without the tons of loot opportunities through combat. That is just screwed up. Items in Shops reset every level. Wow so much immersion. So you nearly have to upgrade your equip every level on each of your characters to stay inline with the insane power creep of the monsters. Just insane. And equip costs a ton of money too.
Without knowing and abusing every powerfull skill and every tool you can use in the game you will just have no fun in this game. Even the explorer mode is too difficult. Monsters a level or two above your paygrade? You will loose, tactics do not matter.
Okay you could read guides to know what is good and lower the frustration a lot by playing cockie cutter builds, but where is the fun in that. Do i have to replay the first 3 starter island fight until a find a combination of skills and classes that have a remote chance of getting through the game. It seems to me the game was only made for expert fanatic fans, not the normal player.

So I got this game as it was recommended for liking The Long Dark. Being that I was lacking an economically-focused survivalesque game I chose to purchase this.
Frankly, the game becomes very simple to beat, not just because you can grind your way to victory (as all markets may go), but that the true randomness of the game is lacking. Every farm you'll come across will have a man begging you to buy 2 wheat for 30 drachma (always a good deal), every cave will either have nothing, 1 hides (3 with a sage sometimes), or 3-4 Ghouls. Merchants will always fake having a broken down cart just to backstab you. Also, Scouts get you free horses, so much so that you begin wishing you could SELL horses.
I'd be happier if the game came with an (unlockable or not) endless mode that could amp up the difficulty, not in the combat or the haggling (that's very binary to begin with), but with the world itself. Auxiliaries bring next to nothing to the table for needing to beat the game (get at least one for your Sage if you want free heals and you're set.) The storyline is short, and that's fine, although it happened very suddenly, and with very little information or understanding.
The point is, I enjoyed this game for what it brought, more than what it failed to bring, but feel it's not worth $13 (let alone $15 when it's not on sale).
I'd like to see the developers work on this game more to justify the price, and to perhaps bring up replayability.

Overgrowing With Possibility!
ALERT! THIS REVIEW CONTAINS MINOR SPOILERS!
Before And Now.
When I first bought Overgrowth there was only the Lugaru Campaign, Arenas to fight in forever, Sandbox Levels to explore again and again, and finally Versus which I've never played since I have no-one to play it with. It's safe to say doing all of that, even with the addition of mods made the game a bit boring. But now that's changed with the Overgrowth Campaign (or "Story" as it says in game.) And with this new campaign to go through and the addition of choosing difficulty it's no longer the same game, it's starting to feel like a real game with story, though it's not a masterpiece just yet...
Up's And Down's.
+Great and simple to understand combat mechanics, though will require a lot of training to get down.
+Hardcore parkour where a single mistake could send your bunny bun falling 200 feet to their death, though the game does give you hints as to where to jump and climb next.
+Some parts of the game are really hard, not Cuphead hard but it made spew to profanity from time to time but it never made me ragequit which makes it an up for me.
+Bunny/Rabbit moon jumping... You can jump really high and far is what I mean by that.
+The graphics.
+The music.
+The freedom of modding and map creating.
+It's anthro animals fighting eachother in hand to hand combat, with daggers, swords or even claymores, that is fu****g awesome.
+If you pay attention to the dialouge you'll be able to piece together a story which connects both campaigns.
-Even I can't overlook how long this game has been in early access for, it's quite absurd, but it is nice to see progress is being made.
-Bunny kicking (Left clicking while jumping) is the easiest and fastest way to kill any enemy provided you don't have a claymore.
-Bugs I've found include: Climbing on things don't look climbable, not climbing on things that do look climbable, and a single fatal error.
Final Rating.
As the title suggests this game is overgrowing with possibilities and there's plenty of room to expand it further, the new campaign has fed new life into this game and updates in the furture will surely do so too. Now for the actual numbers, my fluffy self gives Overgrowth an 88/100.

First, I want to say that I understand that this is a game developed by a single person, I think it has some promise, and I absolutely support developers learning the ropes and trying to make it. So despite the fact that I can't recommend the game, I applaud the developer for his effort.
The game is a Super Mario 64 / Super Mario 3D Land style 3D platformer where the world is made up of a bunch of connected geometric objects. You're a tree. You can run, jump, swing a leaf to attack... and that's about it. The objective of each level is to get three water drops and get to the end of the level; there are also berries scattered around (around 100 berries per level or so). You don't need to collect berries to finish the game, but if you collect 200, 400, or 800 you can "upgrade" your leaf, at 850 you get a headband for your character which seems mostly cosmetic, and there's an optional hidden level at 600 berries. There are 6 main game levels plus the optional level. Each level takes about 8-10 minutes. Personally I 100%ed the game--that is to say beat all levels and unlocked all optional content or unlocks in-game--at 71 minutes.
The issue is that much of the core gameplay loop doesn't work very well. Your default walk speed is far too slow, your default run speed is far too fast to be controlled for precise jumps. The game also never tells you you can run, so, PRO-TIP: You can. Underwater, everything is too slow and the physics don't adjust at all besides movement speed. Jumping is not controlled very well and I frequently missed pretty easy jumps. There are clipping issues. There are almost-but-not-quite making a jump and getting stuck in the lip of geometry and having to jump again to get unstuck issues. There are also issues where you feel like you've picked up a berry but you aren't inside its hitbox, so you sort of wander back and forth until you pick it up. You almost never get good feedback--the "feel" of the game is a real problem.

When you die (you will, frequently, enemies AI is basic, many enemies are stationary, the rest move in fixed patterns, but clipping is generally poor and it's difficult to tell if you're going to hit an enemy when you swing your weapon), you respawn instantly either at the beginning of the level or at a checkpoint, but you can't see where the checkpoints are and in my experience they're rarely where they make sense to be; but because enemies and items don't respawn when you die, you basically run through an empty level until you get back to where you died.
The camera is the biggest problem. The camera angle is frequently no good; for example, in a 3D platformer the camera should never be directly on your level facing straight, because it ruins depth perception entirely. The camera should never be so close that it obscures the action, and yet it is. Worse, as you collect berries, the bag your character holds gets bigger and bigger, so the obstruction is actually worse at the end of levels than at the beginning. You should never have to run towards the camera and take leap-of-faith jumps to get to platforms unless there's some visual indication that you ought to.
It's an hour long game, so obviously if you want to play it, you'll deal with the frustration. But it's pretty rare that you're playing and something isn't going to be bugging you.
The music's composition is not bad (it is a little simple, and it's not really catchy), but the author chooses very very very chintzy, cheap sounding samples for almost every instrument. In particular there's some sort of harpsichord used as one of the main instruments and it sounds really terrible. Sound effects are rare, to the point that the game feels a little unfinished because there are times where you expect sounds and don't get them.
You can't quit the game from inside the game without doing an Alt+F4 or Apple+Q or whatever. There's no main menu to go back to. When you beat the game, it sits at the end of the credits section. This is very frustrating to me. There's also no Steam Cloud support, and although the game is multi-platform, achievements don't work on the Mac or Linux versions.
It's a pity because the graphic side of things is very good. The enemies and your character are cute. The visual style is simple but colourful, and reminds me favourably of Mario 64 or Super Mario 3d Land. There are lots of little touches in the animation. If I had to guess, the guy is probably an animator or an artist who made a game, rather than a programmer.
I don't want to dissuade the guy from continuing to make games and there are occasional hints of promise, but it comes off more as the kind of thing that would have been free online in the late 90s / early 00s, or the kind of thing that would be released on Desura. I am confident that before Steam changed the approval process to be more open last year, this game would not have seen release. Moreover, the dev is still actively patching the game, but a lot of what he's adding in seems to be stuff that would be typical of a 1.0 release, which makes it seem even more like a hobby project.
It's definitely an earnest effort and I hope the dev keeps trying, but I don't think it's /there/ and besides supporting the dev, I don't really feel like there's much to recommend here.

First Impressions, decent casual trading game that caters to a specific type of player.
Primary goal is to build up your caravan while trying to survive the wilds of Arabia. Prologue starts off quite slow, as shown in the video above. Personally felt a bit lost after the intro as there was no primary quest marked to progress. Just needed to guess which left me feeling somewhat disconnected from the story. Ultimately not a bad thing as it's less linear and more about how much time you want to take accumulating fortunes.
Each town holds different npcs, all of them have traders and a place to fill your water. Guildmasters are located in larger cities where you can level up or buy new slaves and companions. Values on trade items change over time but after a playing a while it's easy enough to figure out which items trade best along with where to buy and sell them. After much trekking back and forward trading goods, dealing with fresh produce decaying and keeping my water levels up while fending of random bandit attacks, I've made it to chapter 2, Huzzah! Onwards Soldier!
Visuals are lovely, soundtrack was fitting and I had no issues with performance. Game is all mouse driven so there are no controls to remap. SFX can be adjusted separately. 4k res wouldn't display but 1440p seemed to work fine. Overall I'm giving it a thumbs up, just be aware there are other games out there that give a similar experience, some of which are free. It's not really doing anything new with the formula but it's polished product none the less. Cheers.

I tried BorderZone despite the endless amount of negative reviews because I wanted to experience the gameplay for myself. I gave the game a chance, I really, really did.
If you like RPGs and action adventure games, you will probably still dislike this game.
The aesthetics are lacking - the character models and detail in the backgrounds are weak and bland. The different armor and weapon types available, however, will actually appear on your characters - which is something I appreciate. The music is easily the best part of the game, but it fails to carry the experience into a positive one.
The controls are a bit sluggish, and there is no tutorial to guide you through the game mechanics. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with action RPGs. You will probably spend a bit of time trying to understand how the menus (especially the inventory management) work, and the interfaces are not very ergonomic. One of the most annoying things for me is the lack of feedback regarding item stats - I end up swapping shields based on what looks cooler, since I have no idea which one is actually better stat-wise.
Both combat and dialogues are lackluster - I played around with the character creation mode, hoping that different specializations would alter my gameplay a bit, however, I was always disappointed regardless of the character I rolled/made. You also are not given much feedback if you choose to make your own character from scratch.
Honestly, I would strongly recommend you invest your time somewhere else, as this game fails to compete with most alternatives. I also strongly advised against the game Space Hack (to which I received a lot of negative reception), however, I would even encourage people to waste their time playing that game before trying BorderZone.
Even after the patch, the game remains fairly buggy, and is prone to crashes. Would suggest staying away, unless you are able to get this for free.
DO NOT recommend.

TL;DR Game is hard but not engaging. It feels nothing like Doom/Quake - the ONLY weapon you get is boring to use, there isn't a proper level to run through (just a wide open room), and the beginning enemies are so monotonous that you won't feel a drive to even excel at the game. If you want a hard FPS throwback game with a bit of roguelite, I'd recommend
,
,
or just go to the source and get Doom and Quake.
Devil Daggers might claim to be inspired by 1990s FPS games, but make no mistake: this is nothing like Doom or Quake.
You're dropped onto a wide open circle of ground and enemies spawn randomly on the edge, spewing tons of flying skulls when they do. If you get hit once, you die. There is nowhere to hide and the area is dark so some enemies will be hidden in that darkness. In Doom/Quake, a lot of the gunplay came from moving quickly through cooridors, finding secrets, ducking in and out of doorway cover and being surprised by a monster closet opening behind you. This game only spawns monsters around you with very little fanfare, and you'll spend most of your time simply bunny hopping and circle strafing. That's it. This might be a fluid movement system but it does not supply an enjoyable nor interesting space to use it in.
The difficulty is very high, as you'd expect. I can appreciate one-hit difficulty, but frequently you'll die because something spawned behind you without much or any warning, or one lone skull did a Tokyo drift and nipped your ankle, or something else altogether. The game won't give you feedback about WHY you died. Probably a lone enemy snuck up on you? Who knows. There are tons of floating skulls everywhere but it simply isn't fun or interesting to fight them or die to them. In the end, the game killing you doesn't feel frustrating or terribly unfair really - it's just kind of boring.
The only weapon you get is the devil daggers. If you click mouse-1, you have a weak shotgun attack that is nothing like the boomstick from Doom. It feels like a nerf gun. If you HOLD mouse-1, you get a minigun like weapon that actually does feel good to use.  I don't know why they chose to tie these firing modes to the same button (you can't remap this either!) - it feels clumsy to use and it often will not work at all, simply giving you a one shot from the minigun instead of the shotgun. Combining the weakness of the shotgun shot with the unreliability of the controls, I'm not sure why you'd bother to use it. Apparently the game gives you homing daggers for mouse-2 at SOME point, but I honestly never played enough to get there before I got extremely bored.
Normally in difficult games, you'll have a desire to get better at the game, to learn from your mistakes, and last a bit longer next time. I didn't have that feeling in this game. The gun (dagger?) play felt so dull that I just accepted each death and tried again. 45 minutes later, I felt like I only got marginally better but had no desire to try again. There are 10 more enemy types that I never got to see, but I simply don't care enough to play longer to get to that content. I also never got any double jump, nor homing daggers, or any upgrade.
Finally, you can watch replays of the top scores on the leaderboards, so you can watch people who have mastery over the game play. It's a lot of circle strafing and holding mouse-1. Not the most riveting gameplay to watch, but you can appriciate how good these people are at the game. I'm just not sure why they feel driven to achieve that mastery when it just doesn't seem interesting to get there. There are better, deeper games out there that fill this niche.

I’m almost completely split in my opinion of this game, but I’d say that I’m 51/49, trending to the positive side. I wouldn’t necessarily say that I’m actually recommending the game to everyone, but I think that the good outweighs the bad by a very slight margin. Strangely enough, the good stuff is almost entirely in the art direction and style column, and the bad is almost entirely in the gameplay column. It really depends on what you think is most important in a game. I’ll talk a bit about the game’s strengths and weaknesses, and then you can decide for yourself.
First of all, everything about the game’s style and presentation is out of this world. The art direction, the character designs, the timeless cel-shaded graphics, the graffiti, the look and feel of every environment…it all just has so much flavor and personality to it. The soundtrack is unforgettable (“The music just tuuuuuurrrns meee on!”) and there are so many tracks that you’ll be humming for days on end. The voice acting is really great - Professor K is the man! The overall project just has an incredible sense of attitude that perfectly captures this particularly late 90s atmosphere of hip hop, street art, skater culture, dance clubs, punk rock, and weird postmodern advertising.
Unfortunately, and I hate to say this, the actual experience of playing Jet Set Radio is a chore. The controls are so stiff and there’s no sense of speed to your movement. The game puts so many obstacles in your way that prevent you from getting into a really nice grinding groove. It feels like the developers wanted you to be fast and stylish, but then at the last minute they decided to make things as clunky and rigid as possible. You have to make these really precise jumps but the game doesn’t give you precise tools to pull it off. The controls are an actual obstacle that you have to overcome, and they make the missions kind of frustrating. Every level takes way long than it should because of how difficult it is to get the hang of simply moving around and tagging stuff. As if this wasn’t bad enough, each mission has a time limit.  If you can’t complete everything before the timer runs out, you’ll have to do it again. When a game uses a time limit system, it can’t afford to have bad controls…that’s just a major gaming sin right there.
I absolutely love what the designers were going for with Jet Set Radio, but I feel like the idea of the game is better than the execution. When you look at its style and personality, you think you’re in for this great sense of action, speed, and style, but the game itself is clunky and awkward. So why am I ultimately giving this a “recommended” review? Even though I have many issues with the game, I’m glad that I own it. I’m glad that it’s in my library and that I get to return to it and experience its world, style, music, etc. It’s a stylish, compelling, weird mess that you can’t look away from because it just oozes so much energy and coolness. That being said, I probably won’t play it very much, because it’s not fun. So where do you stand? Do you care more about style and attitude, or do you care more about gameplay and tight mechanics? I think that's really going to determine how you feel about this game.

Where to begin with this game? As you can easily infer from the store page, this is a platformer starring a red-headed ninja. The gameplay is relatively basic: just run, jump and shoot kunai at enemies until you make your way to the end of the stage on the right.
The game has five zones divided into three acts, each with three hidden kimonos for you to find. This is probably the only replayability the game has, which isn’t too much. If you explore the levels, my guess is that you’d find most, if not all, of them on your first playthrough. The kimonos are placed in pretty obvious locations, save for maybe one or two.
Despite the levels having an in-game timer, you’ll be hard pressed to die due to a timeout. Even on levels that took me longer than I felt like they should, I still finished with thirty seconds to a minute on the clock.
Graphically, the game isn’t very nice to look at. They tried to go for a retro style which isn’t done very well. The disproportioned characters were probably meant to be cute, but just come off as amateur. Then you have these bosses which appear to be hand drawn that really stick out from the rest of the game. Probably the only thing I think looks graphically fine are the cat statues.
The music is all stock royalty-free music. The same song will play through each zone’s three acts with a boss theme when you reach the boss in the third act. It can get somewhat tiresome relatively quickly and some of the music doesn’t seem very fitting to the zones in which they’re supposed to represent.
The controls are one of the areas this game really falls apart. Akane is simultaneously slippery and stiff. She walks at a snail’s pace and takes a moment to decelerate when you want to stop moving. The slow movement speed makes it frustrating to avoid some enemies’ projectiles in later stages and her jump is relatively useless.
Speaking of enemies, this is another area where the game falls apart. The first three zones of the game are pretty simple. The fourth zone, and especially the fifth, are the zones where the poor control plus the enemy layout become the bane of your existence. You’re probably going to want to memorise enemy layouts and ration your special so that you can get through what would be otherwise controller-breaking frustrating areas.
The only difficulty comes from some bad game design choices that add up to create an unfair challenge. This game isn’t NES hard. In fact, I’d say I only got stuck on one act the entire game. However, I couldn’t help but feel the deaths were because of the cheap design as opposed to my own fault.
Overall, this is probably what you would expect from a budget title. It’s very inexpensive and going on sale makes it even less of a gamble. If the game had some more refinement, it probably wouldn’t be bad. As it is now, it makes it hard for me to recommend. If you just wanted to try something different that will keep you entertained for a couple of hours, give it a shot. Otherwise, if you want to play a good ninja platformer, I’d just stick with Ninja Gaiden.

A one-of-a-kind game where the main point against it is exactly how good it is at what it sets out to do.
"Clunky controls" gets thrown around a lot to describe maneuvering in this game, but it bears in mind that this is a game (partially) about riding around on inline skates. The game is really, really good at making you control like a person riding on inline skates. Momentum plays a key role in your ability to maintain traction and smoothly get from point A to point B, so a loss of that momentum can be like hitting a brick wall. While sometimes jarring, it's sort of an extension of the premise and ultimately, you merely have to be extra mindful of your surroundings--an exercise made much easier by the inclusion of camera controls to the second analog stick.
I'd highly recommend this for being a game that doesn't have anything much like it before or since (besides the sequel), but be warned that it can get punishing. This is a short game that emphasizes trial and error to lengthen play, like old "Nintendo hard" titles back in the 8-bit era. Racing missions, though sparse, get especially brutal. But an arcadey, play-it-in-bursts format makes that the perfect direction for it to take.
