It's one of the better Early Access titles out there.  Most of the negative reviews are holding the game accountable to a final product's standards.
1. If you play on a public server without knowing the server rules you're going to have a bad time.  The public servers are garbage.  Every server has tons of customization, same as Minecraft.  Examples are hunger, thirst, length of day / night cycle, toughness of enemies, respawn times of items / nodes, durability of armor, etc.
2. If you want to have a good time you need to play on your own server with friends.  There are AI humans to fight, and AI camps to raid if playing against other real humans is too difficult for you.
3. It runs about a hundred times better than ARK ever will, and the devs actually update it frequently, sometimes as often as 2x a day.  They listen to feedback and post updates on Twitter stating exactly what they're working on.  The game is far from abandoned.
4. It's Minecraft for adults.  It doesn't hold your hand.  Expect to die a lot, especially as a solo player.
5. The difference between Minecraft and a game like this is the resources are NOT clumped together.  In Minecraft you can find everything you need in the square area of a football field.  In Minecraft you can dig all the way down to the bedrock and get diamonds in five minutes.  In Conan there is no "digging" and you have to run all over the map to gather all the different kinds of resources you need.  If you play on a server with groups of people this will instigate conflict, as differing camps will be guarding separate resources.  If you want to progress in the game you need to get XP via combat to learn recipes, and then explore to gather all the parts you need.  This is the biggest issue players have, and it's why it's extremely difficult to grind to the top and become overpowered in some secluded area without being bothered by anyone.  You may have all the rocks you want but no trees for wood, so guess what, you'd better start walking around to find some trees.
6. Most of the negative reviews complaining about "rubber banding" and "poor network optimization" aren't completely wrong, but then again, it's an early access title and as the devs continue to work on the game these bugs are constantly being ironed out.
7. The Conan universe is a brutal one and this game doesn't pull any punches.  If you want to cry about "being raided by griefing Asian gangs on public servers" then I suggest you create your own server and turn all the cheats on.  The game is designed to not only build but to destroy.  It's part of the game.  The only reason you don't see it streamed on Twitch as much lately is because there are so many updates it's difficult to stay on top of keeping the private servers updated.
If you are that impatient and can't handle playing with strangers you can always go back to Minecraft.

UPDATE 08052017:  Conan Exiles has undergone several updates since my original review and now on the brink of it's first major update/expansion let it be said it has progressed leaps and bounds in the way of performance and some game content.  The climbing mechanic in the game is a very welcome addition although it has garnered some criticism from those on pvp servers.  I think it is awesome on a pve server as it brings a way to explore, evade, and infiltrate that has not yet been seen in any FPS or survival game.  From tall trees to mountain sides to enemy strongholds, with enough stamina the player can climb like spiderman and jumb onto vertical surfaces like you're in a scene in Impossible Mission.
The optimization of the game has progressed very well.  I'm now able to run at a constent 61-74fps with highs around 112 and lows hitting 56.  The heat on my video card reaches 44-47° with an average of 44° and highs of 51°.  I'm running a Titan X Pascal on a customized AIO water cooler.  Controls are responsive and the game runs butter smooth.  Animation still need help however...Read my original review below!
It's better than I expected but it definately shows signs of being an early access game.  I am eager to see what comes of this game and hope to see the devs come around to seeing it come to full fruition.
First off, like so many of the early access titles Conan Exiles is begging for optimization.  The game, although beautiful in scenery regarding landscapes, flora and fauna, the graphic quality still needs a lot of help, so for the little amount of FPS and high heat created by playing this game it's a sure sign the game code needs to be opimized.  The graphic shaders need attention as well as the game, in it's current state, resembles sort of a cartoony landscape populated with somewhat cartoony creatures and avatars all housed within an otherwise grim and savage wastland.  Graphically the game looks nothing like the snapshots and I'm hoping that changes becasue the snapshots look awesome.
Animations are wonky for some creatures but not all.  The rabbit or hare for example, runs and leaps sideways a lot and does not always move in the direction it's body is facing.  Also, there is a lot of pop-in across the landscape of the game, meaning at one instance there is nothing within close proximity to the player and in the blink of an eye there is.
The crafting system is simple and to the point but quickly becomes a grind.  This isn't so much of a bad thing as there are rewards to be gained sooner than later, be they small or large.  Starting out, you can count on dying.  A lot.  The survival aspect of it is not very balanced especially for those starting out as almost anything and everything that decides to attack you will kill you.  I found myself running and looking for places to hide all the time starting out, but eventually was able to craft some very basic equipment to help defend myself and provide a better means to acquire even more resources.
The character creation at the beginning of the game is great but not spectacular.  I personally prefer a very detailed approach to creating my avatars and although Conan Exiles is closer than many to realizing that preference, it still falls short in quite a few aspects.  I would like to see more  body and face morphs, as well as better skin textures and shaders, and far more hair styles, eye colors, scars, and tattoos.
So far, I can see this game being at the top of my all time favorite survival games.  I believe there are a few things that can be learned from Ark Survival which is now set to leave early access in August I believe.  Still, both titles need work, and with Conan Exiles being young in it's development I think it's off to a good start.

While I like the premise a lot, the game falls flat in many ways.
After playing couple of hours, I've noticed that actual trading isn't in a big role at all. You make much more profit from random combat encounters and quests.
The combat system is simple, and the AI is bad, or even worse, nonexistent. The combat is boring as it is, there's a shared pool of dice that you use to boost your combat stats that are compared to opponent's combat stats. AI doesn't even try to win though, it just picks dice completely randomly. It doesn't take the objectively better dice at all, just a random one.
You have henchmen that you link to your chosen heroes that boost their abilities and stats. However, if you want you can use an ability that gets boosted by having a henchman (For example main character has an ability that reduces water consumption for 5% per henchman), then trade that henchman to another hero and do the same. I avoided doing that, but the fact that it's possible shows how little thought the system has been given, at least in my opinion.
Also if you have henchmen linked to your fighter (You only ever fight with 1 character and if you lose it's game over. Dumb I know) you instantly lose them if you take even 1 hit point of damage in combat. It happens very easily even if you win, so I pretty much had to keep zero henchmen linked to my main character, or I'd just lose them easily.
Even in my 2 hours of play, I encountered the same random event (A salt merchant) at least 5 times, if not more. Most other events I saw like 2 or 3 times. Gets very boring very fast.
That said the plot is quite interesting, but the gameplay is just too boring, repetitive and random for me to continue the game.

To start this off, I'll say this doesn't SEEM like a bad game. It doesn't even look so bad either. It only occurrs to you how bad it is when you start playing it. And this pisses me off the most. It could've been a good game, all it needs are some minor fixes...
In a nutshell, what good can be said about the game:

It doesn't seem so bad, right? And that's the problem. This COULD'VE been a decent platformer. That makes it even more irritating - the small things that could've been fixed and polished, but weren't. The things that makes playing (and attempting to finish) this game a bad, almost masochistic experience:

Dear Haruneko, you could've made this a game about a nimble ninja, quickly disposing of enemies. You could've. THEN the time limit for levels would make sense. Heck, you could've even lowered it by a whole minute for some levels then, why not? Would be a good challenge. That is, IF and ONLY IF you made your character a nimble ninja, moving quicker than currently (or have a run button - hold to run), with slightly more air control, and of course made the controls more responsive.
Or, you could've made it a game about a crafty stealthy ninja, who has to slowly progress through the levels, avoiding getting hit as much as possible, taking out enemies one by one. In this case, you could even take away one heart from the life meter, but you MUST drop the time limit then, since it no longer makes sense to have a time limit in a game where you are supposed to progress slowly and carefully. Your movement could be more realistic then, not as nimble.
No.
None of this.
Instead, you made a game is a godawful combination of the two. Your character moves like she's on slippery wet floor at ALL TIMES. The controls aren't exactly responsive either. Please play some acclaimed 2D platformers and see how responsive controls can be, how nimble a character can be. You can compare to titles such as Jazz Jackrabbit 2 or Electronic Super Joy for nimble characters, or LIMBO for more realistic movement. This is the biggest bug in your game, and one that seriously hinders it, along with other terrible mechanics mentioned in this review.
It pains me that this could've been a decent platformer if you got these few things right. Knowing you won't fix any of this (it's been quite some time since the game came out and recieved numerous negative reviews) I can not recommend this game to anyone.
Do not buy. Especially if you like platformers, there are plenty good ones out there. Don't waste your time and money on this one.

This game is really one big disappointment, sadly.   The art style is very cute, but that's about the only positive thing I can say about it, as the game suffers from some major flaws that just kill the game:
The camera angle is horrendous.   In a 3-D platformer, having a fixed camera angle is both baffling and frustrating.   It makes jumping and moving an exercise in frustration.   I tried to give the game a fair chance to make an impression on me, but the camera angle alone was enough to cause me to cut my time in it short.
The story, or lack thereof, is very thin and not engaging in any way, shape or form.  It doesn't provide any motivation whatsoever to keep playing.   After a few minutes roaming around, instead of it feeling like there's a greater purpose to my actions, it becomes a case of "Meh.  WHY am I doing this again?"
Movement in this game is a major downfall.   It felt like traversing any distance was done at half the speed of smell and it made the whole experience feel more like a chore than something done for fun.
There really isn't much of a challenge to the game, other than contending with the camera angles and movement issues.  The enemies are incredibly passive and it was insanely simple to avoid them, considering that they did little to nothing that would make me want to attack them instead of just walking by them.
All of these combined to make this game a rather tedious and completely forgettable experience.   Whether it was an isuse of inexperience on the part of the developers or simply a lack of effort, there are just so many issues with the game that even if the art style is somewhat endearing, it's not worth playing.

First of all, I usually don't make a habit of writing a review before I have spent some time with the game in question, but this particular time I get the impression I could have written this review without even playing Devil Daggers (quite an irritating title, don't you think? That „s” in particular.  I tend to call it Devil's Dagger whenever I mention it to anyone and then immediately correct myself), because the game is exactly what it says on the tin. And is pretty damn good at it.
To describe the presentation, let me quote on Shakespeare's: This game is such stuff as dreams are made on”. Not the particularly good dreams though. Pretty nightmarish ones to be honest, and I feel in an hour or two I'll be rather unhappy with myself having decided to play Devil Daggers in headphones, with lights out and home alone. I mean, the game looks like the classic DooM's best moments mixed with the Silent Hill 1- tier disturbing sounds and glued together with the best looking blood I have seen in some time in games (and I've gone to the control panel and shoved some AA and Triple Buffering down the satan's throat - they don't do game much good, but if I'm in hell I could as well play by my own rules).
Not like you will get chance to enjoy the views since Devil Daggers is actually fast and unforgiving. And we're talking here Quake 1 fast. As far as the „unforgiving” part is concerned – one hit and it's over. And no, it's not an uncommon sight to have 30 or so enemies onscreen at a time. Imagine Serious Sam series (sounds awesome) with one hit point. Got the image ?
My major (and by major I mean the only, but rather significant) problem with the game is the lack of diversity. I mean, the only thing that really changes are the kinds and the numbers of enemies on the screen. Ok, to be fair you can improve your weapons one or two times (and trust me, they look and sound -just like everything in this game – nightmarishly gorgeous) but still, I have felt tired with the game after the first hour. Which isn't good. But there are strafe jumps and rocket jumps which is.
To be honest, if you enjoy arena shooters and beating your and your friend's high scores you could completely disregard my complaint. From that standpoint, the Devil Dagger's pricetag is more than fair. I am well aware that I enjoy my games mostly for the storyline and character development. At this point you should probably ask why the flying ♥♥♥♥ am I buying and reviewing the game utterly devoid of the elements I like and my answer would probably be that I want to support the developers. I definitely enjoy the game's aesthetics and I hope that the game sells well enough for the authors to introduce some variety in the content patches. And maybe some randomly generated dungeons and some excuse plot the next time we meet? Please?

I recommend to buy it ONLY if you want some frustrating yet satisfying platformer experience :)

Jet Set Radio (Originally Jet Grind Radio) is a SEGA developed game originally for the Dreamcast released June 29, 2000 (Japan) and October 30, 2000 (North America).
The camera controls were good for an early platformer game. In comparison to modern 3rd person games they were absolute trash, however, for the era the camera controls were useable and not that bad. As is customary, the left analog stick controls the player character while the right sick is the dedicated camera control following the character. The controls in this game often feel like controlling a tank. The turning isn’t so tight and the player character often glides upon releasing the movement analog stick.  Though, this is to be expected because the player characters are on roller skates.  When not manually controlling the camera, the default action is for the camera to stay centered behind the player character. I tried to play for a bit without using the right stick but I found controlling the camera more enjoyable. When up against a wall the camera would shift up to a bird’s eye view awkwardly showing the wall I was against as well as the player character. This issue caused the camera to be snappy at times and put the player character at odd angles. One modern technique that has improved this letting the camera have complete movement freedom. The fix for this would be to make the environment slightly or completely transparent as the camera moves into a wall or past an environmental object, as seems to be the case for modern 3rd person games. One other technique would be to take camera controls away from the player. This was quite common with early 3D platformers before the popularization of two analog sticks on consoles. For instance, The Legend of Zelda titles on the Nintendo 64 gave the player very little camera control. It was controlled by the Z button, the trigger for the index finger of the left hand and the R button to lock onto enemies and points of interest. In doing this, the player was more focused on traversing the environment rather than moving the camera around to view the environment.
For 2D platformers the main object generally lies off to the right of the screen, the player is compelled to move right to the end of the level towards completion. However when games moved into the 3rd dimension one common issue is how to get the player to go in the right direction. In Jet Set Radio, the player is led to objective by floating spray paint cans and convenient bright red arrows point down from above graffiti spots.  The player must collect these spray cans in order to spray their own graffiti over that of rival skaters. Other techniques used by the developers are different rails and ledges to grind on. Each level in the game is designed in a way that the environment is open for the player to explore and finish objectives. In this aspect the player is given the freedom to explore the level and confront the obstacles in it. It also provides a challenge for the player to find the different areas required to pass the level before the time limit runs out. This aspect of the game provided to be quite frustrating at times. Though frustrating at times, I appreciated the design and openness of the levels.
Though an old game, Jet Set Radio has aged particularly well.  Though controls were not as good as modern 3D platformers and the graphics were obviously dated, the game still played exceptionally well and looked awesome. The Soundtrack was great and added to the entire vibe of the game.

Many a time I've wished that some classic Commodore 64/ZX Spectrum games were available on Steam, and for some reason, my mind always goes to the Codemasters library. The Dizzy series and their imitators, BMX Simulator, Steg the Slug, Rockstar Ate My Hamster, Tilt...
And then we get a Codies game released on Steam, in more or less its original form, and... it's Slightly Magic. I'm not sure if I had any prior relationship with this game. I think I owned it at some point, but maybe it was one of those tapes that rarely loaded properly. Maybe I gave it a try but was immediately put off by the apparent difficulty and oblique puzzles of the first few screens.
Having given it more of a chance, to make the most of my Steam purchase, I'm a bit more taken with it. It turns out there is more to it than getting fried by the dragon right at the beginning. The puzzles have a logical progression to them. The platform jumping seems fairly sophisticated and forgiving, but I suspect that's an aspect of the remake rather than the original. Overall, the game certainly has that 8-bit charm. It's just so good to play a game with that white sprites, black background Spectrummy look. For a Dizzyalike, Slightly Magic has its own unique style.
Is this worth a purchase if it doesn't hold any nostalgic appeal for you? I'd like to urge yes. It's certainly more worthy than a lot of Steam indie games. At full price, it might be asking just a little bit much. This is a game that cost 3.99 on release (inflation, I know). Achievements and trading cards would do a lot to add value.
I hope between this and Deus Ex Machina, this is the start of seeing a lot more games of this era on Steam. While this release seems to be a one-off project by Colin Jones, I'll keep dreaming of that Atari Vault style collection of Codemasters classics.

I played the original Slightly Magic on the ZX Spectrum back in 1992-1993, when games came on cassette tape and took 10 minutes to load. I loved the gorgeous (for the time) graphics, the Dizzy-esque gameplay and the sheer ruddy charm of it all. This updated version keeps all that intact while also adding a new soundtrack and insightful, informative commentary from creator Colin Jones. If you were old enough to have played it back in the day, pick it up and feel like a kid again. If you aren't quite old enough to remember it, or if you were a mere twinkle in the eye of your local postman at that time, Slightly Magic is a sweet, charming glimpse at the golden age of the UK "bedroom programming" scene.

Or if you're interested, hear me out:
To be fair, I've enjoyed parts of Akane: There's some descent music and solid sound effects that make hitting enemies feel right. And sometime the game shows that it wants to be fair and reasonable: There's three Kimonos to find and collect in each Level, but you don't have to find them all in one take, you can just get them one at a time and then finish the level after having found the last one, which is pretty generous. Also your invincibility phase after getting hit is long enough to get out of trouble, which is pleasant too.
But still, as it stands, I can't recommend the game. Here's why:
My first impression after firing this up was that the game looked generic and the sprites lacked animation or expression. The following "achievement" - a thank you for watching the intro till the end - didn't exactly make the game seem confident about itself. Sure enough you'll encounter all four enemy types in the very first level already. So variety is also a slight issue here.
But more profoundly: Everything you do in Akane the Kunoichi has a delay to it, be it jumping, shooting or just plain walking. Once you do start moving, you'll find that it's way slow and sluggish, which doesn't make you feel like an agile Kunoichi at all. You also can't shoot many times in quick succession or walk while shooting. This will likely lead to enemies walking into you while you mash the shoot-button only to realize that you can't fire fast enough to kill them in time.
When it comes to jumping you have very little control over the height of your jump, which complicates making precise shots. Your walljump is even more problematic, since you have to push toward the wall and wait until your character sticks to it. When jumping off the wall there's again a lack of control, especially with the distance of your jump which for example makes the platforming in the beginning of 4-2 way harder than it needs to be.
The game does get challenging in parts, but mostly for the wrong reasons, the controls being number one. Some levels demand precision that the controls don't provide, like the last three stages with collectables placed between spikes.
But also contributing is the unfair leveldesign in general. Enemies will spawn right in front or almost on top of you, sometimes even four or six at once. In Level 3-2 for example there's a spot where, when you reach it for the first time, two spawning ninjas will likely push you right back into a bottomless pit. Some other levelparts that I wouldn't consider unfair are at least more annoying than they would have needed to be, like a climb-section in 3-2, where the moving platforms block all of your projectiles but not those of your hat-throwing enemies. Blind falls are also pretty common, sometimes into a bottomless pit like in 3-1, sometimes into spikes like in 5-2.
Most of the boss battles are uninspired, though they get the job done and provide a fair challenge. But the final battle is very anticlimactic for it's easily the least interesting of all:
You jump on skates and spray cops with paint 11/10 would Listen to rad music again.
It's like H.P Lovecraft designed a shooter during a fever dream, after he was pulled into the bowels of the Stygian abyss.

So a word of warning ahead of time Divinity Original Sin 2 is probably my favorite game of this year and probably one of my favorites of all time, although the year's not up and despite my 80 some hours in the game I'm still powering through Act 2. This is an incredibly biased review (just like any review I guess) ALTHOUGH I do have complaints at the end I swear.
So first of all there is so damn much voice acting in this game, literally the ♥♥♥♥ing rats are voice acted its absolutely bananas. The massive amount of voice acting allows me to sit back and relax and let the story sink in rather than other games in the CRPG genre that have minimal voice acting and what feels like 4 bible's worth of literature and don't get me wrong I love those games but this particular departure is probably the most stand out feature of the game that for me personally has kept me playing for hours on end until my girlfriend comes out of bed at 5:00 am and asks me if I've been up all night four times before I respond because I didn't hear her because I'M PLAYIN ♥♥♥♥IN DIVINITY AND I CAN'T STOP.
Beyond the amazing amount of voice acting in the game the next stand out reason I would reccomend you need to get this game is the customization of your class, there's a ton of freedom here with your build. Say you chose the wizard class at the character screen, by no means does that have to imply your character is a caster at all, you can completely mix and match skills from the start and truly make it your own class. As you level you can put points into your different skills like fire magic or polymorphing or warfare moves and based off that skill you can learn skills from skillbooks that you purchase (or just steal) from NPC's. As you progress further into the game you gain the ability to respec your characters from the ground up, even in appearance, at any time for free. The only thing that remains the same are the learned skills the character has learned up to that point. I suppose it's worth mentioning that in single player you basically have 4 characters at once of course. I also love the fact that the civil skills were sepperated from the main combat skills. What I mean is that you have a complete seperation of your combat skills in the game like casting or fighting and your more in town or well civil ability to steal, persuade, or barter (among other things) as an example. So your tank could be your lore master and your cleric can be your thief.
The amount of sheer content is noteable, beyond the MASSIVE campaign theres a few other modes in the game. There is an arena mode where you choose 2 random characters and fight another real person. I haven't really gotten much mileage out of this mode but if they ever let me bring my own characters in that would make it fun for me. There is a "Game Master "mode where you can litterally make your own campaign and have your friends play in it, even so far as to include a digital D-20 and vinigettes to partitian your adventure and let the group make decisions. I'm not saying this replaces D&D night but ♥♥♥♥ I'd run a session on it eventually with the right group. It's just a faucet for more content from the community at worst case scenario. The game is every kind of co-op there is, including splitscreen using controllers or drop in drop out online games either private or public. Currently the modding scene is growing day by day and there's already a crap ton of new cool junk to find there as well. I would like to have the ability to bring my characters into another friends game though.
Finally the combat. Ohhh the combat, this game harkons to old school dnd in some ways, you have action points that you can spend on movement or spells and attacks. The difference is the game is on a cooldown system for your active skills and there isn't much rigidity in your class. The elemental interactions are really great as well, if you have a fire on the ground and put it out that makes a steam cloud, that you could shoot with a lightning bolt and make a thunder cloud, which you could bless and make a healing thunder clound of godly power. The interactions go on and on and I could talk all day about that but I won't because you're not dumb and you get my point. The actual fights are difficult and not for the lighthearted to say the least. You will make great use of the quicksave button and quite a random encounter has taken a full hour of my day to keep as many of my party members alive. But it's kind of the same rush I get from killing a boss in Dark Souls where you feel that real sense of accomplishment at having overcome a really difficult task.
There is a ♥♥♥♥-ton of loot in this game and some how a giant majority of it doesn't feel useless, and rather awkwardly I don't know how to say this but that is kinda a con. All of the loot you get feels like it has a use or you could craft some crazy recipie because in your head it just makes sense and for the most part thats what you see but on the other hand... There is SOOOO much bag sorting you're gonna do, and if you do get this game LEFT SHIFT + CLICK is a shortcut to automatically sort something into wares. I will have carpal tunnel when im done sending all my items to Ifan, my designated barterer, when I need to sell my junk, I would really like to see the game automatically assume that my barterer if in my party and chained to me is handling all of the buying and selling so I don't get scalped on the prices rather than making me spend literall hours doing bag management. Thank you for the auto sort button though :)
Ok so on that note there really isn't much of anything that I could complain about here to be candid. BUT. I will say there are some bugs I've encountered in local multiplayer; one where the game froze on my turn and would not allow me to take an action, we ended up having to reload the game and restart the fight all over which was torture because it was hard as balls. Starting the game is always an issue for me and for other friends of mine as every time I boot it up the game stalls for about a full minute and then fails to connect to Larian servers to allow me to share my game stats for their bug fixing junk, ironically, before it launches just fine and runs like butter. But even past all of that, back when my buddy and I encountered that annoying bug while yeah I'll admit we were frustrated we still played for like 4 more straight hours without realizing it anyways... so what does that tell you?

It's too bad the Ys games aren't more popular, because they're a ton of fun. Although I can understand why this is the case; if you want a deep story with well-developed characters in a rich, vibrant world, you're probably better off looking elsewhere. (Or you could read a book.)
However, if your cup of tea happens to be runney-jumpey-hackey-slashey-swing-your-swordey-things-get-deadey gameplay where you mow down swarms of monsters, all building up to fights against gargantuan, screen-filling bosses with heavy rock music playing in the background, then you should totally give the Ys series a try. Like I said, they're a lot of fun.
I haven't played all the games in the series, but out of the ones I have played, I feel that The Oath in Felghana is pretty good game to start out with. I & II are fun, but very much showing their age; Seven is a good one also (and was actually my first Ys game), but it's only for PSP. I would actually argue that Origin is better than The Oath in Felghana, but being a prequel, it does have some spoilers for Ys I, and it doesn't have everyone's favorite mute redheaded berserker.
Every Ys game also comes with multiple difficulty settings, so if you want to let off steam by making everything that looks at you the wrong way your ♥♥♥♥♥, there's Easy and Very Easy. If you like a really good challenge, there's Nightmare and Inferno. And yes, holding down your jump button (at least I think it's the jump button, off the top of my head) speeds up the text scrolling in the cutscenes.
Speaking of buttons, if you have a USB controller, you're definitely going to want to dust it off; in my opinion, Ys games weren't meant to be played with a keyboard.

Note: This review is a bit outdated (It was made at around 70 cap). Some of my complaints might have been addressed at this point but I have not played the game recently so I cannot tell for myself. Fundamentally this review is still accurate though.
My steam time for this game is not accurate. I likely have at the very minimum 1,500~ hours in game.
tl;dr: Gameplay is solid and suprisingly good with a reasonable amount of depth. However, the grind from lowest level to max level (even with someone grinding you) can be nigh unbearable. The games optimization is hit-or-miss with many players computers as the optimization seems to be based on CPU power with it hardly if at all utilizing the GPU. In terms of class-to-class balance, the actual devs are fairly incompetent at making sure one class doesn't completely dominate the others.
In depth
Gameplay:
The gameplay of Dragon-nest is primarily fast-paced combat with heavy reliance on reflexes, ability to predict the enemy movements, and knowing your own skills. The combat has no casting bars rather relying on animations which makes you feel as though you are 'in control'. Many of the higher level skills do a satisfying amount of damage in PvE and a reasonable amount in PvP. In my experience, the end-game content (Dragon nests) often devolve DPS races to blow up the boss before it has a chance to do any of it's harder mechanics. Simply getting hit by some of these bosses could result in an instant death for you. Note: In the end-game content, after you die, you are dead until the raid (called 'nest' ingame) is complete or your entire party dies.
PVP:
PVP deserves it's own section because for many players it is simply all that matters in the game. PVP is largely player-skill based as a highly skilled player can easily combo the other player to death, giving the other player no opportunities to fight back. There are a few types of PVP in Dragon Nest which I will describe quite simply. There is Ladder, Endless, 1v1, and blacklisted 1v1.
Ladder is what many players might call 'competitive' mode with a rating, but in reality, it is simply an infestation of a single class. Gear plays a role in this mode and for many PVP'ers, no one actually cares about it, since gauging it as a metric of skill is completely stupid.
Endless is simply 8v8 combat. Given its playercount, it is easily the laggiest mode for many players and, simply put, is a mind-less cesspool of high AOE skill-spamming. Gear does not matter.
1v1 is what it is. Gear does not matter.
Blacklisted 1v1 is different from what you might expect it to be. To give it a bit of a background, many players view some skills as overpowered compared to other skills (example: A mercenary's 'Iron Skin'). Most classes have a few of these skills and players will mutally agree to not use these skills. For some players, Blacklisted 1v1 might include entire classes or very specific rulesets and for many players, what is blacklisted to someone might not be blacklisted to the other. Most 'legitimate PVP'ers' play this.
One other 'important' aspect about PVP is PVP rank. PVP rank is arguably important because there is an icon associated with your rank. Initially, it is a brown egg icon next to your name. As you PVP more, you get more experience and the icon changes. The other icons are blue (silver) and yellow (gold). However, be warned, the blue and yellow icons are EXTREMELY difficult to attain as they are exclusive to a certain rising XP threshold. It is difficult to describe in words but simply put, if you were to attempt to become the player with the #1 amount of experience, it would easily take you a year of pvp'ing to get even close to it.
Sound:
The sounds of Dragon Nest are fairly average I would personally say, although, one of the key issues many players seem to have is that the voice-actors for some of the classes are borderline cringeworthy, prompting some users to completely disable the voice or download a foriegn language voice mod. Another one of the issues and to many players and advantage is that most if not all the skills have their own special voice-line for casting that spell. This means when your Adept (that's a class) casts Inject, every single time you are going to hear what sounds like a child say, "This might sting a bit!"
Graphics:
The graphics are good and fantastic for many of the skills. However, some classes and raids (nests) in particular have crippling effects on many player's computers. One class in particular, the Alchemist, has a few spells that are strong in PvP simply because for many players, casting it is 'like opening six movies at the exact same time', resulting in a crippling half-second burst of lag.
Community:
The community of Dragon Nest is fairly odd. A mix of Anime fanatics and normal people coupled with a loud creepy population. The population seems to be a mix of 12 to 19 year olds with some guilds greatly skewing this margin. I highly recommend finding a guild that suits your playstyle rather than joining one of the ones that you get invited to right off the bat. The best way to do that is make a friend in-game and try their guild.
Server & Game Issues:
The server occasionally seems to have frustrating issues with lag. Sometimes these issues are extremely frustrating as they might completely void and entire 'nest', leading to a player missing out on loot. One of the most notable issues is the completely unavoidable 'Hackshield', and instant kick from the game resulting in the failure of the games anti-cheat. It is not detecting a false-positive, merely it just messes up.
Pay-to-win Factor:
Suprisingly, this game isn't nearly as pay to win as I expected. The only pay-2-win'ish factor seems to be Dragon eggs and, even then, the only good thing that comes from them is wings which boost your characters movement speed in everything but PVP. When it comes to costumes, 'green' costumes boost stats which can pretty much only be purchased through NX (real life money). However, 'blue' costumes which boost stats much greater than 'green' costumes can only be reliably purchased through large amounts of ingame gold.
Overall: The game is suprisingly good but has a good few problems that detract from some of the good parts. The game seems to have a large issue when it comes to grinding of either money or levels. There are minor issues with the community regarding it's vocal immature side.

Oath in Felghana is actually a remake of Ys III: Wanderers of Ys, which was released on many consoles during the 16-bit era. It was a side-scroller, played a lot like Zelda 2. However, it received a lot of backlash from fans, but Falcom took notice and eventually remade Ys III in the style of the previous game (released before Oath in Felghana), Ys VI: The Ark of Napishtim, but greatly improved on its' engine. And not just that, but the story was retold in both a different and yet similar way and the music was given a complete overhaul as well. It's easily my favourite game in the series, I highly recommend it for anyone who loves a challenge. And Zelda-like games.

Baldur's Gate 2 received a good update compared to the original game. It's not such a big update compared to a modded version of the game, but that's the point, it stays true to the original and only improves on where the game lost strength in time. There is new content, there is interface scaling, there is native widescreen support and there is support (the game receives updates).
Although I have not experimented heavily with mods I think this version (the enhanced edition) is better than what you get if you mod the classic game. Cloud saves are also a big advantage. The game runs fine, the zoom function is good, the new rendering abilities of the engine are nice (compared to the old version) and loadings are instantaneous (if you played the original you remember the long lasting circular loading screen, it's completely gone).
I don't know why this game received so much hate, the original Baldur's Gate 2 is the best western RPG ever made, and this update makes it a viable choice in 2016, especially if you never played it before. The learning curve is steep and you'd have to either read the manual, or watch tutorials on youtube, but once you do that, the gameplay is as good as any game today.
If you like turn based tactical combat and fantasy rpgs get without hesitation.

Rating: 9/10
IF YOU BUY THIS GAME DO NOT KEEP YOSHIMO(it's a spoiler if I tell you why). Yes, he's a really awesome pure thief. Still not worth it.
Overall: I really like this game. I have fond memories watching Baldur's Gate II over my dad's shoulder. So, there is some nostalgia involved for me. In short, I'm biased. Baldur's Gate II is tied to the original(as in you can import your character), which I recommend over-and-above the sequel. BGII is an old-style D&D videogame. Reading is required, and pausing the game to issue commands is a core part of combat, especially if you are fielding spellcasters of some sort. I have started the game multiple times, and recommend looking at all the classes' abilities before you exit character creation. You do have to save a lot in this game. The auto-save system isn't that good.
Plot: Fairly decent. The political intruigue of Baldur's Gate I was more enganging to me. In this game you chase an egocentric, manipulative, creepy, evil wizard who made your life miserable and abused your sister to hell.
Bugs: At worst, a quest may not trigger properly, and you have to load to five minutes ago. This game runs fairly smoothly, bug-wise.
Difficulty: It's unforgiving at times, and you may have to load again and again or save constantly fighting a monster with an immunity to all but one of your party members' spells or a particularly difficult enemy group. The difficulty is adjustible from 'being handed to you' to 'the game mercilesslessly laughs as you are slaugthered by a +1 skeleton'(or something to that effect). I play on the 'core rules' setting, which is, more or less, 'veteran', but easier than 'hard' or 'legacy of bhaal'(insane).
Graphics: The graphics are horrible. Don't buy this game if you need amazing visuals. The scenery, however, is rather pretty, especially outdoor forests and water. This is not a graphicially demanding game. You will not lag on this game unless you magic missile from every party member who you built as a mage/sorceror. There may be slight 'lag' when fighting one of the dragons. They are seperate fights, and are at the end of dungeons. I haven't had the game crash, ever.
UI: It's a mini-menu popup system there are numerous menus, from 'map' to 'journal' to 'inventory'. There are others. The UI was redesigned. Fans of the old system(which I agree looked better) did not like that. I like the clean, new interface. If you want the classic interface, sorry, it was scrapped. If you don't care, then this is a non-issue.
Party System: If you are playing normally and not 'hosting' an 'online' game and playing with a party you build yourself(which you can do, that's completely vaild, the interjections by BioWare NPCs serves to freshen the otherwise semi-stale dialogue), there is a single "Playerchar", and five extra NPCs. Banter and other random quest interjections makes the game a lot better. While it is realalistic, I don't like it that party members, even if you support them, will leave if your party reputation goes to the extremes. 1 and 0 are super-evil, 19 and 20 are super-good. Evil characters leave if you go above 18. Good characters leave if you go below 2. Neutral characters don't leave. The most interesting characters are good or evil, in my opinion. Also, certain party members, if left together for long enough, will try to kill each-other. The game does not have a modular system like mass effect, it's more of a 'team selection' mechanic. If you want to change your party, you have to re-find the character in question. Also, since this is a D&D game, levelling is important and shapes your character. Characters outside your party auto-level. The auto-levelling system in the game is insane, and makes stupid choices. It's best to find your five, and stick with them. I would recommend looking online at the party members and making it a priority to run around the world and find them as soon as possible.
Note on 'romance' system. Thre three original 'romance' options for a male character will get into verbal cat-fights over him. If this annoys you, you either have to deal with it, or only have one of them in the party at a time. Also, these three are the best NPC healers in the game. If you want multiple healers, and play as a dude, do it yourself, or put up with the snit-fest. Female player characters do not have this issue. However, they're stuck with a traumatized gooody-two-shoes fighter-cleric(likable if you can get past the arrogance).

CK2 is an extremely complex –
– easy to learn and hard to master game.
When starting a game you step into the role of a duke/king/emporer that rules a designated demesne. This is where the hard work begins at all. Not only head of your county/kingdom, etc. but also head of your family, your actions are required in all terms: Marriage policy, heir management, title and fee organization, regional and national politics, war management, neighbor relations and foreign politics as well as building upgrades to your cities, castles, etc.  and while doing so, keeping an eye on your income, your prestige and piety.
The easy part is to enter all these actions. The menu is quite intuitive.
The more tricky part is to plan the future actions and try to see whats coming to be prepared.
Over the decades this is a thing that gets harder and harder, due to the size of the land you rule and the number of vassals you have.
Considering all this CK2 offers a variety of things that differ from attempt to attempt and it also offers hundrets of duchies to start with. Which makes it attractive over a long period of time and makes you want to play it again and again.
10/10 Atmosphere
6/10 Graphics
8/10 Sound
10/10 Game mechanics
8/10 Balancing
10/10 Depth
10/10 Fun
CK2 is a game for everyone that likes management, menus and for everyone that likes to perfect things. The game requires a lot of time. A lot of management, but it also reflects your actions very well.

The Mooseman is a beautiful walk through the myths of the Perm Chud tribes, of whom I knew nothing before playing this game.
You play as Mr. The Mooseman, one of seven The Moosemen Brothers, and a shamanistic figure who can (a few minutes into the game) see freely into the spirit worlds. You are tasked to go through three worlds, discovering the ways your spirit vision, and later another ability, can help you solve puzzles and move forward. There are some skill-based challenges, but they're very gentle, and if you just want to see the way everything plays out the puzzles you *need* to solve to get to the end are pretty simple. Things get a little more complicated if you want all the collectibles, with more exploration and observation of subtle environmental cues needed.
The art is wonderful throughout, with a simple but scratchy, handmade feel. The music is gorgeous as well, and has the very welcome habit of breaking out into choral arrangements of folk songs. But to me the real star are the myths themselves, which are not just great but beautifully told and extremely well integrated with the game. One recommendation, whenever you walk by any totems (which function as checkpoints), make sure you read the lore they unlock; these lore bits add a lot to the experience, and are usually tied to whatever you are doing at the moment.
It's a short ride - longer, if you want to find all the collectibles, but as with many of these type of games its short duration works well; there's a lot of variety here, but nothing feels like padding. It does an amazing job of making you feel immersed in a folk tale; if you enjoy reading about mythology it's a no-brainer.

The first and most damaging is the fact that you cannot control the camera. In a 3D platformer where it's very easy to mis-time your jumps, that's a quick road to frustration. Even worse, sometimes the game will change your camera angle for you, making it hard to see a jump that a moment before was perfectly visible. Add in the fact that if the character's pack is full it enlarges so much sometimes that you have trouble seeing past it and you can see that earlier potential just start to bleed away in a flurry of missed jumps.
The second flaw doesn't directly affect gameplay, but it affects immersion a lot. That is, the character animation. For the most part this is fine, and I really do like little touches like being able to jump until Woodle is upside-down. Charming. But when walking about the world, I noticed very quick that the walk animation doesn't interact at all with the ground. The speed at which you move seems independant of the motion of the legs, giving a feel of sliding about which may not seem like a lot but since you have to look at this for the entire game, it gets a bit bothersome. And to a degree, since you can't really tell speed from watching the character, sometimes it's hard to judge jumps and you're down into the abyss again.
The third is the general lack of explanation of anything. I've played up to where I was able to buy a second leaf mainly by accident. I had no idea why I was supposed to gather fruits until I pretty much randomly wandered outside the house for a bit. I'm not really sure what it does yet, since there's no explanation when you get it, so I guess trial and error? In any case, the game doesn't really give you anything to tell you that upgrading your leaf is significant, so it almost feels like the game doesn't care. Even a little fanfare would be nice.
Overall, I'd say maybe a 6.5/10. Barely recommend, mainly based on the remaining charm and the knowledge that updates seem to be planned. Hopefully they'll fix some of these issues.

I can describe this game in three simple words: Pure. Platforming. Fun. Wait, why would I not recommend this game if I enjoy this game, mixed messages galore! Well, if you are sticking around to read this, I wouldn't recommend this game to
Why? If you look at the most popular games sold, they are creations of commitment to spending hours and hours exploring, killing things, playing online with friends to continue the rampage. This game has absolutely none of that, the only people I would ever recommend this game to are those that don't play many games, those who don't really have time to play a game, anyone that that wants a very small game to enjoy or maybe a little sibling or relative who is just staring off playing games.
You are Woodle, you must collect berries and fairy drops...not much story beyond that. You travel through eight worlds to collect these things, in each world are three drops that you must collect. There are a few weapon unlockables, but other than that, this game finds its charm in jumping, exploring, and enjoying the very vibrant world created by Chubby Pixel. As I was playing this, I was reminded of games like Banjo-Kazooie or even Gex 64: Enter the Gecko, it was such a great trip into nostalgia, that I didn't mind that it took me a little over an hour to beat, but in my opinion, it was extremely worth it.
Now on to the bad stuff: the camera is jittery and sometimes in the wrong place, there isn't any sort of GUI and the enemies aren't really...smart. Again, this is why I would not really recommend this game to an average gamer who would rather play something like Skyrim or Dark Souls II. Another thing I want to point out is that this game is much easier played using the 360 controller instead of mouse and keyboard as controlling the character is sometimes difficult.
However, if you are like me and just enjoy small or even have time to commit to some 60+ hour adventure, I highly recommend you at least watch some gameplay footage of it. To the average gamer, though, who has that sort of patience and willingness to venture out to become a Dragonborn, crunching numbers, calculating statistics or wanting to see that KDR ratio on your leaderboard, this game is definitely not for you.

Upfront, I'll say this game does have some fun gameplay at times. However a litany of problems make me give this a negative review.
- Dumbfoundingly inconsisent difficulty. Battles range from entertainingly fun to stupendously, insultingly difficult. Seriously, you should never have to go into a battle knowing EXACTLY what is going to happen in order to have a chance of surviving (not winning, just surviving). And the only reason you know what's about to happen is because you've tried it half a dozen times and failed each time.
- Weak story compared to D:OS, and heavy use of sad, tired and predictable tropes. Half the time it wasn't even clear what we were trying to accomplish, and who/what we were fighting against or for. And when major plot points did occur, most of the time our response was "Really? We're doing this again? Sigh..."
- For a game that encourages you to forge your own way, it punishes you for not following some pre-assumed path through the world. Heaven help you if you choose a different direction - enemies do not scale with level, and gear that would help you manage is prohibitively expensive. So if you head west when the game expects you to head east, you'll struggle.
- Battles that break the game's own pre-established rules. Examples: repeat casting of abilities which have multi-round cooldowns, and stacking identical status ailments. Case in point: The Sallow Man's Airborne Plague, which bypasses all armour (physical and magical), stacks with itself (I was at -15 Con at one point because of three repeat casts) and can be cast EVERY ROUND.
- Inconsistent lore/world impacts: you can kill someone and consume their soul, only for them to show up again later, apparently none the worse for wear. (Yay, that achieved a lot...).
- Multiplayer feels like two single player games occurring simultanously, with some quests not progressing or closing because the wrong player spoke to the quest giver. To add to that, if the speaker doesn't have the required item for a fetch quest, too bad - having it in the party isn't enough (but the game doesn't let you know that, does it? That would be too much to ask...)
- Quest system is broken. Somewhat repaired with a patch, but if you'd progressed past a certain point, the damage was done. The Tarquin side-quest was just a balls-up.
- My partner, who was using a controller (I use keyboard/mouse), had endless difficulty with target selection and interactions with the environment. Certain skills just wouldn't work (no reason was given - you just can't select this character because we say so). The controller interface also made line-of-sight hard to gauge, so several times critical actions were lost because of some unseen obstacle.
- Multi-stage boss battles: stop, just stop with this tired, over-used and just irritating chiche. This has been done so many times it's just not interesting, exciting or surprising.
- Some puzzles have an exact solution required, but the game gives you absolutely no guidance or hints. Another case in point: the Cursed Revenants in the Lizard Embassy. We gave up trying to solve that and just left them there. We got around them enough to finish the quest, but they'll be sitting there in the ruins till Judement Day.
More on the battle difficulty: if you're at the correct character level for a given encounter (ie a L5 party against L5 opponents) I don't think it's unreasonable that your party members are able to survive the opening salvo. I GM a Pathfinder group and so understand that some encounters are meant to be more challenging that others, depending on their importance in the plot progression. However, given that in 95% of encounters one or more of the opponents invariably go first, the number of times one (or more) of our party members were one-shot killed or disabled before they've had a chance to act is kinda ludicrous. This ties back into my previous point where you have to know exactly what is about to happen in order to have a chance of getting through the battle (which I consider meta-gaming in a cRPG). Sure, give the enemies superior starting positions and outnumber the party, but don't compount that by making every mook immediately superior to the whole party.
For a game that we've spent over 100 hours on, this has left such a bitter taste in my mouth that I can't say I've enjoyed it. We've given up trying to win the final battle, and to be honest I couldn't care less about how it ends. There were occasional moments of fun, but the negatives outweigh them.

THE STORY: This is by far the most densely rich lore I’ve played through from any game I’ve played, where almost everyone and everything is connected in one way or another. Creating a living and breathing world, where one’s actions and decisions will affect their adventures through Rivellon. The part where this game shines the most, is how it gives the player choices on how they want to advance the story in any way the player chooses to play. Choose to be good, evil, just or whatever mood you choose, this game adapts to it and guides you to the end that your choices led to. While I’ve only completed Fane’s Story (in the moment of writing this), the endings it gives you will satisfy however you played. While you can choose how your adventure ends, the game lets you know how those actions will affect Rivellon in the future. The reason why I love this story is how grim and real this story plays out, no one is truly good or evil, it’s all a grey area, but it’s your choice on how you want to navigate in it.
THE COMBAT: There was never a dull moment every time I went into battle, or stumble on to one. While combat is turn-based, pre-battle is when things become interesting. Some approaches I found to be more fun is laying out traps and pre-emptive attacks on unknowing enemies. I can go into combat with my enemies clinging on 5% health and wipe them out with one attack. This is true liberty that this game gives to players, it gives you the tools and it’s up to you on how to use them. And this is just combat, skills can give a creative twist to combat. You can chain attacks to deliver devastating blows to your enemies or toy around with them by unleashing various Statues Effects and skills that can either immobilize them or transform them into chickens. All this creates a simple yet complex toy box you can play with. Finding out what seems fun and effective will make you want to seek out the next battle and unleash your battle plan.
THE MUSIC: I do not, in any way, have any complaints or criticisms about the music. The only thing I can say is that it is Divine. The music makes Rivellon and in turn makes you believe that it is a real place and these characters who live in it are part of a giant play. The 4 instruments that you can pick (while you build your character) creates the mood in how you want to play and you can change it any time you want.
This is the best RPG for this generation. While there are quite a few bugs the developer needs to fix, this doesn’t affect how much I love this game.

So many hours of playing, modding and more playing, I appreciate the old Bethesda leave fans do the modding and focusing on developing new games. There are so many mods out there that never seize to amaze me. This healthy modding community has been exsisting for so many years I wish it survive this 'Creation Club' apocalypse.
Anyway Oblivion itself is an awesome game. Huge maps, tons of dungeons, multi-layout cities with none-radiant quests, all of these had set standards for RPGs by the year 2006. the Thief's Guild and the Dark Brotherhood still remain as my favorite factions. The final quest of the Thief's Guild was a brilliant design, a true test of player's thief skills, and a touching ending to think about. As for Dark Brotherhood, almost all main assassination missions have an optional objective, and the rewards for completing it might be useful on the next mission. It is a very considering design. And also, Lucien Lachance, so much truama surround this charater I doubt I will ever forget him.
Moving on to Oblivion expansion the Shivering Isles, yes I said expansion because it truly is. A new land full of weird and beautiful plants. The island is a reflection to the mad daedric lord so everything happens there is funny and outside the box. Solving prblems for the clone village residents. Participating in the political espionage between lords of Dementia and Mania. Breaking the never-ending loop in the ancient ghost ruin. All of these remind me a game has so much freedom, can also be fun.

CK2 is an extremely complex –
– easy to learn and hard to master game.
When starting a game you step into the role of a duke/king/emporer that rules a designated demesne. This is where the hard work begins at all. Not only head of your county/kingdom, etc. but also head of your family, your actions are required in all terms: Marriage policy, heir management, title and fee organization, regional and national politics, war management, neighbor relations and foreign politics as well as building upgrades to your cities, castles, etc.  and while doing so, keeping an eye on your income, your prestige and piety.
The easy part is to enter all these actions. The menu is quite intuitive.
The more tricky part is to plan the future actions and try to see whats coming to be prepared.
Over the decades this is a thing that gets harder and harder, due to the size of the land you rule and the number of vassals you have.
Considering all this CK2 offers a variety of things that differ from attempt to attempt and it also offers hundrets of duchies to start with. Which makes it attractive over a long period of time and makes you want to play it again and again.
10/10 Atmosphere
6/10 Graphics
8/10 Sound
10/10 Game mechanics
8/10 Balancing
10/10 Depth
10/10 Fun
CK2 is a game for everyone that likes management, menus and for everyone that likes to perfect things. The game requires a lot of time. A lot of management, but it also reflects your actions very well.

Move around with WASD, look around with mouse, hold LMB to fire a continuous stream of "daggers" and tap LMB to shotgun more "daggers".
Easy to understand your only objective is to survive as long as possible with the constant demon barrage and that's it! You get a leaderboard that shows the best players in the world as well as your friends to brag around.
My only complain is the minimalist options available. You can only decide mouse sensitivity, volume level and if you are left handed or not. I wish there would be an option for resolution as to me it appeared as a good old 800x600 scaled up to my monitor. At least it ran a constant 120 FPS no matter how many hundreds of demons were sprawling around my screen.

I have backed this game since day one... i don't even remember how many years passed by... and i am confused as to where it is going... and if it's gonna be enjoyable. As of now ( lugaru campaign ) as soon as you get to weapon fighting, everything gets boring, random, frustrating and unpredictable. You can spend a whole fight holding left click and end up killing your foe. Or you click 2 times and get your weapon stolen after an unpredictable parry and disarm( Same NPC after a load, btw ) Weapon throwing is suicidal and bunny kick ends up being the only thing i used before Alt+F4ing my way out of there.
I still like a lot of stuff, but most of it is technical stuff
-The physics feel great
-Animations are amazing
-Hand to hand combat is satisfying
-Particle and blood effects are impressive.
-Controls are simple
-Editor is easy to learn
But on the other hand, i did have no fun at all playing the Lugaru campaign
Weapon combat is horribly random. With a knife, you hold left click until the enemy grapples you and takes your knife out of nowhere.
You can throw your weapon... but you end up giving it the the enemy since it's not an instakill anymore. He can also just grab the weapon in mid air... just like that.
The way you parry a knife wielding enemy is so unprecise and confusing ( Since the enemy slashes you 3 times a second, you rarely have the time to react ) You end up dead before you even manage to grapple and steal the weapon back.
Knife on knife fights usually goes like this: Hold left click until your weapon, or your enemies weapon just fly off after impact, then the armed one chases to win.
If there's a melee fighter near you while you are in a knife fight, prepare to get wrecked cause you can only slash your low damage knife and the melee guy can kick you so hard you backflip to oblivion. All of that, while the other guy stabs you.
Then you get to Staff wielding enemies...
One strike, you are on the ground bleeding. If you even manage to get back up, good luck trying to disarm him, as the disarm system is still the problem. Random as hell and hard to manage.
The only thing that seems to work well and predictably, is hand to hand and stealth, and those are really satisfying.
I still believe mods can save the combat system... but for now, i have to say Overgrowth lost all the hype i had for it. Weapon fighting is really broken and i hate it. It's not fun. Something like that, where you can die as easely as in one strike, should be predictable and allow you to read movement and actions.
Sadly, most of it seems, and feels random.
I nominated Speedrunners, because I have a lot of fun, while playing this with my friends.

The Mooseman is an atmospheric side scrolling almost religious experience. I am somewhat hesitant to call it a game, as this label lessens the depth of what the authors tried to achieve.
The core game loop consists of progressing through various natural and supernatural environments, with some mild puzzle solving along the way. As you proceed through the very strongly stylized environments, the core takeaway of this experience is revealed to you: the myths and believes of people native to the area of today’s Perm. Don’t be alarmed, there is no preaching here. As far as I am concerned this is an excellent non-intrusive way of preservation of days past of nations vanishing from the present. A decent amount of lore is supplemented with visual story telling. While the experience is rather short clocking in just above two hours, it is instantly memorable and best of all sparks your interest. Luckily the Internet is here to help you. Don’t be surprised if you find yourself reading up on the various tribes and historical events. I know I did. I firmly believe the authors can be proud of that. Now when the Komi, the Mansi people or Anbur is mentioned, those who partook in the experience will immediately recognize these.
A very distinctive feel of The Mooseman is amplified by the excellent use of ambient sounds and thematically appropriate music, in key moments amplified by an elated choir. The composer managed to very accurately supplement the visual style of the experience, which in turn is distilled from the various historical artifacts from the area. The way historical artifacts are obtained and presented is one of the few items that fall squarely into the “gaming” category, as the player needs to unlock each artifact by finding it’s hiding spot within the world. Contrary to this, the entirety of the lore is accessible from the start. The catch is that all of it is written in Anbur, an Old Permian Script. Each snippet is only translated to your language, once a certain totem is reached on your journey. I must commend the authors for taking the flow of the experience into account and making some of the puzzles optional. While enhancing the game aspects of the piece, I feel it would have considerably detracted from the experience.
Overall, I have a single minor quality of life level complaint. Artifacts and lore are presented in a paginated list of items that resets to the first page after a stage transition is performed. This is truly a minor point, as both categories only have several pages.
I would recommend The Mooseman to those who enjoy focused audio-visual narrative experiences. Especially considering the price of admission, as 9 whatevers nets you the soundtrack and a comprehensive art book.

Growing up, I guess I never realized that Wanderers From Ys was kinda...crappy. You don't really think about how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tty games were back then when you were a kid, you just thought that taping the attack button down in the first dungeon and coming back later when you're at max level is just a thing you do. Most of the Ys games don't hold up really well, and that's why I'm glad Falcom has continually revisited the series while progressing it over the years.
This remake of Wanderers from Ys is completely top shelf. Sure, the story's still about as dry as it ever was, but the game is just a damn joy to play. Fast-paced, breakneck combat cut with (almost always) just the right amount of punishing difficulty and the spectacularly responsive controls make it a joy to play for those of us that like a good bit of twitch reflexes and pattern memorization. There's rarely ever any need to grind like in the original either, given that each dungeon is set to level you up appropriately before each boss encounter.
My only real issue is that the game's balance can be a bit wonky and a few boss encounters border on unfair and completely luck based. It's just really weird how a few times simply gaining one level or piece of gear will suddenly cut enemy damage down by 50-75%, and a few bosses can get really cheap in their patterns by either canceling their vulnerable states with attacks you simply can't dodge or unleashing a combination of attacks that trap you in a way that's really unfair.
Even with its slight flaws, Oath in Felghana was a treat to roll through and I felt satisfied with my victory in the end in a way modern games don't really strive for anymore.

I'd like to recommend this game, but there are problems with it.  The most notable is that the "Free to Play" aspect is severely limited on this particular release.  You see, this is a port of a mobile game, and it is available on a Kongregate (a Flash portal) as a free to play PC release.  The thing is, both the Mobile and the Kong versions use advertisements to give a benefit in game.  This includes increase drop rates, increased money, and the ability to open crates that give extra turns.
Steam does not allow for ads like that to be used in games on their platform (which is a policy I support).  To work around this, the game offers a subscription-like fee in "VIP Passes", which give you some premium currency every day, a higher energy cap (this is a game on a timer for plays, hence the 'extra turns' above), and thanks to the Steam release, the ability to get all the ad bonuses without watching ads.  Even if you link your accounts, and watch the ads on another format (Mobile or Kong), they do not impact the Steam version at all.  You simply don't even get the crates to drop without the VIP Pass, to open elsewhere.  You cannot get the added drop chances, and increased in-game gold.
Beyond that, if you want to utilize the game's chat, for talking with your clan and the like, the game just shoves you off to play the Kong version anyway!  It doesn't open it up in-game, like it does with Mobile.  No, it points you to a place where you can play a more complete version, and have chat open while you do so.
Animation Throwdown, on Steam, is not worth playing because of these issues.  If you want to play it for free, do so on Kong, where you can get the full benefit.

This is a rather pretty looking exploration of a Sápmi myth, and it's quite atmospheric with some great music that is very fitting for the setting, but sadly this is a boring game. The story of the game is told mostly through lore-collectibles that unlock somewhat poorly written text (at least in the English translation) that's accessed through plain-looking menues, and through text-cutscenes; the main story is actually told in the lore-collectibles before you reach it in the actual story progression, which takes away the value of the narrative of the game, since you already know it by the time you reach it.
The game tries to be atmospheric, by having a slow movement speed, which is suitable for the sensation and the myth that it is trying to deliver, but the controls of the game are quite bad, and often lead to repeating puzzles as you fail, and the slow movement it is then less atmospheric and more frustrating. It would have been less infuriating if the puzzles weren't for the most instant kill on most occations, requiring you to repeat the same sequence again, with the same poor controls.
I had great hopes for this game, but they all fell short. The delivery of the narrative is uninspired; the myths, culture, and stories of the Sápmi people are told in such a grueling way that it soon leaves you not bothering to read more of it. And the game is extremely short, clocking in at around 90 minutes, and that was with several repeats of sections as the miserable controls made things more difficult than they should be.

It always felt to me that this series never got the love it deserves. While the (de) original Blob was a good proof of concept,
is pretty much what I'd call a
.
It improves on pretty much every aspect of the original. The levels, models and textures are much higher fidelity. The menus are easier to navigate. Gone are the button mashing (press X 50 times) to update landmarks - replaced by new, 2D puzzle levels. There are no more arbitrarty mission time limits. The controls are much tighter. The loading screen comics make more sense. The compass design is improved. Animatics are hires... you name it.
It's a great game for those who enjoy colectathons, or who just want to chill and play a not-very-challenging 3D puzzle platformer where you paint bleak dystopia into graffiti-inspired colorama.
If I had two pet peeves - it would be: 1. Lack of proper graphics options (the game runs at the desktop resolution, but menus don't scale well on all resolutions). 2. The length of the levels. As far as I know, you can't pause mid-level, save and return to the game later, instead having to complete each level from start to finish. Given a level can take anywhere between 40-120 minutes to complete (especially to 100%), that's quite a long chunk of time to have to reserve.
Fortunately, it's a fun, colorful time. Highly recommended - especially if you enjoyed the first
but wished it was better.

Oh boy did I love this game when it came out on the Wii back in 2011 (6 years!). Needless to say, my love for this game hasn't changed a bit! This review may be a bit biased, but I'll try to highlight lesser points of this game as well.
The game is very colourful (kinda obvious since colouring is literally one of the objectives of the game) and has a beautiful artstyle. There's plenty of content (even a small multiplayer mode!) and the level design is good.
But what totally makes you fall in love with this game is the soundtrack. Not only is it amazing in general, it also adapts based on the things you do during the level! The more you colour a section, the more energetic the music gets! Enter an area that is filled with ink or blanc houses, and the music will take on a much slower pace. Each colour (7 in total) also adds unique sound effects that blend in with the soundtrack upon painting something with that colour!
There are tons of collectibles, which either increase your final score, allow you to upgrade Blob (making you stronger), or unlock gallery items (which are definitely worth checking out!). It's also possible to see how many of these collectibles you have already collected in a single level, meaning that there's no need to replay all levels just to find that one last collectible.
However, as with any game this game is not perfect which hurts me to say. Depending on how good you are at 3D platformers, this game is too easy. There may be more difficult sections (some of which are just enemy-spam-near-ink-pools), but overall it's not that difficult. (That being said the main audience for this game is probably way younger than me, so that might explain)
I take it that this game mostly focused on chill platforming, rather than tight platforming (which in my opinion is an entire genre on its own!)
Also, it might feel somewhat tutorial-y at some points. (Shut up Pinky I know I can duck to dodge those things!). You might enjoy avoiding the red challenges and just colour a section at your own pace to get rid of this feeling though, which is how I played this game.
