UPDATE Dec 11th/2017;  Cranked Animallica up again after not having played in a few weeks and Im as impressed as I was when I first played it(or more).  The devs have begun to institute the story and did a major engine/graphics overhaul that should make the game run better on "lesser" machines(hope that doesnt sound too elitist lol).  For my initial review, I thought the game had already been switched to Unity because the game ran quite well for me but I guess they did the Unity thing only recently.  Other than upgrading the game engine and adding some story, theyve also added some other content as well.  I get a kick out of certain reviewers who state that the game "has been forgotten by the devs" or "abandoned".  The game just got an 11.5gb update!  Some people are just clueless lol!
Animallica(weird name but anyway...) is actually a great start on a survival/crafting type game and Ive enjoyed what Ive played of it so far.  From what I understand, "you" wake up in a bunker years in the future after a viral apocalypse has occurred.  The virus that caused the apocalypse has made most humans and animals sick and/or mutated and often aggressive/dangerous.  Your job is to gather animals to your very large and expansive "base" to cure and save them.  The base has numerous huge areas where you will keep and raise your animals.  I dare say that there is probably going to be breeding as well since I just captured a dog and the dog has "traits" listed and is specifically described as "female".  I say "From what I understand" about all this because there is no tutorial in the game yet and Im pretty sure that the story part of the game hasnt really been implimented either(at least Ive seen nothing that explains any kind of story anyway).
Dont be discouraged by the fact that the story hasnt really been implimented though!  The game still has a ton to do!  Ive explored just a couple of the maps so far but there are many(and many more to be implimented) and each map is fairly large.  There is also a very large number of crafting recipes that Ive only just scratched the surface of.  At first I thought the crafting had not been developed much either because you start out able to craft just a handful of items.  But then you build a workshop and your list of craftables explode.   Ive also discovered that the player will be able to craft "themed" items.  For example, I just found a book in the game that teaches me how to craft items in an "Asian" style.  This leads me to believe that there will be other "styles" in which you will be able to craft as well.  Yeah, so there is already a ton to do and many large maps to explore.
Other stuff Ive noticed;  The Uninfected animal AI seems OK.  Uninfected animals generally fear you and run away like real animals would.  To capture them, I assume that you have to tranquilize them and use a "taming potion" on them.  You get a couple of both kind of potions at the start and learn to craft them later but I havent played enough to have figured out the capturing and taming mechanisms(Maybe its not implemented yet? I think it is though).  Enemy AI is pretty basic.  If an enemy sees you, it attacks.  The enemy hits you, you hit the enemy and after getting hit enough times, one of you dies.  Its pretty much that simple so I hope the devs try to do a little more in that department as the game goes along.
Graphics are passable but nothing to get excited about.  The game is still in Alpha though so graphically it could and probably will get better.  I did not find the game to have any performance problems either.  Apparently a number of people have complained that this game is a "resource hog" but, as I said, I didnt find that to be the case.  I run it on ultra without the least bit of an issue.  I can even run other stuff in the back ground while I play and still have no problem.  The game could run fine for me for one of two reasons(or both?); First, I have a monster system that I over-built specifically to be on the ultra high end of Virtual reality qualifications.  Second, the devs were supposed to be switching their game engine to Unity, so maybe theyve already done that since the other reviewers complained about performance issues.  Either way, the game seems to run pretty nicely now.  I didnt even encounter any noticible bugs during my initial 3.4hrs play time.
Oh, something else Ill mention is that the player is going to be allowed up to 5 companions at a time while playing(in game animal friends I assume).  I saw that message scroll out during a brief loading screen I believe.  That will be kind of fun.  I also like that the main charector is female and only female(at least right now).  So sick of survival games where I HAVE to play a guy(The Forest, Far Cry and so on).  Dont get me wrong, I love "The Forest"!  Its one of my favorite games.  I just wish that I could play a charactor in it that I could relate to better.
Thats about it for now I guess.  If you dont like change and get all bent out of shape because of bugs or other adverse issues of game development, please dont buy this game.  Im getting so sick of people buying early access games and then complaining that early access games play like they are early access games.  This game is pretty good for the point of development its in right now.  There is a whole lot more that needs to be fleshed out but even so, there is a ton of content to keep almost any player busy!  Ill be watching this game with much hope and anticipation.  Since there is already a good deal to do in the game, I REALLY want to see how the story fleshes out!

Bam. You're a prisoner. Then what? Oh, its just PICARD TELLING YOU YOU'RE IN HIS DREAMS. SECRET. PASSAGE. HE DIES (OH NOES) TAKE THIS SEXY AMULET. GET OUT OF THE SEWERS. EXPLORE FOR 100+ HOURS.
Well, you can already tell this game will be incredible.
But seriously, this game starts off very strong. You're a prisoner, with your crimes unknown to you. As long as you don't abuse the character creator (hehe...) you'll be able to mold your ideal elf, human, or orc... or cat... or lizard. But yes, many great awesome things happen in the first few minutes within the game. You may think the game is linear... until you exit that sewer.
"Can I go anywhere?" "Can I follow this road?" "I want that horse. Can I steal it?" The answer to all this is a glorious "yes". Oblivion is at it's best when you're wondering along the vast land of Cyrodiil, exploring multiple dungeons, mines, and towns. Oblivion is outdated, but still pulls you into the world.
Quests are great. Some surpass Skyrim's as far as story goes. (The Thieves’ Guild quest line is so much better.) There are both your typical quests with markers, and a well mix of a few. Ranging from some puzzle solving, to even being a detective, it'll keep you entertained. Help out a town by shutting down an Oblivion Gate (which furthers the main story), and now you can buy a house there, and buy upgrades for it, just for playing the main quest. Kill an innocent person, and have a very unique visitor appear, and follow a very dark path. Either way you'll be getting into all sorts of crazy situations, and it'll be a delight.
Gameplay is more complex than Skyrim, yet not quite like Morrowind's. I consider it a perfect balance, as its tough, but very rewarding. If you're a weakling, maybe you shouldn't steal that horse just yet. Oblivion in a way pushes you to a certain type of major, as if you’re taking college classes. Keep shooting that bow, and you'll advance specially in that skill set, and use your experience to further develop this. But if you pull out a sword after not using it for three levels, well you might want to rethink what you're doing. It’s not hard, but the game defiantly wants to pick one type of combat and stick with it. This is fine to me, as I love dedicating my character to a specific type of combat. If I want to be good with a sword, and have some good magical ability as a side dish, I can do that. It'll just take time.
This game probably has the greatest DLC ever. The horse armor has so much value... well not really THAT specific DLC, but Shivering Isles is a MUST HAVE. You're getting another free game when you purchase this. Knights of the Nine is harder to get access to due to the slow leveling progress, but is also pretty great. Get GOTYDeluxe, its worth the extra $5, you penny pincher.
Mods, mods everywhere as well. There are some greats ones. In fact, this game taught me how to mod. I might of ruined my first save file(s) tough doing that, so be warned; there's no silky Steam Workshop bed waiting for you upstairs. You must use either your brain, or a Mod Manager application.
For those complaining that it isn't working on Windows 7; The Steam (digital) version seems to work fine, and there's a mod called "Unofficial Oblivion Patch" which solves many conflicts and errors, and is stupidly simple to install. Get the latest version patched for your game as well. In fact, before even launching the game, you might want to do all these things I've mentioned. Also have the latest video drivers installed (derp).
Oblivion may be old, but you shouldn't stick your nose up at it. It's great, and will always be great.

I hate this game. I've tried so hard to like it, to learn the ins and outs, the underlying nuances. I've spent hours on tutorials, even more hours in learning scenarios, and I STILL can't wrap my head around why so many people would play this game. As a war game, it's too slow, as a diplomacy game, it's too complicated, and as a political intrigue game, it lacks substance.
I consider myself a well rounded gamer with reasonable expectations. Based on positive reviews and awesome stories told by reviewers, I came into this game expecting a Game of Thrones-esque experience that would give me a minimal amount of kingdom management and more interactions involving a council and backstabbings and plots. What I got was an uninteresting map simulator that changes colors, a bunch of historical icons with Wikipedia pages, a slew of complicated menus and charts that fail in helping you manage your kingdom, and scripted events that pop up every now and then telling you how close you are to getting wrecked. A majority of the reviews here recommend getting DLC to make the game more fun, but if the core game can't get my attention, there's no point. So if you're the sort of person that likes clicking around menus and playing with game speeds, go ahead and get it, but I'm done.

The first day at school can be stressful, especially for a blind kid. Eight-year-old Ian is happy he can bring his guide dog North along, and he will direly need him as things turn ugly during the preparations of Blue Norholm School's centenary celebration.
Luckily Ian is not alone but has North and the player to help him find his way to the library, the gym, up and downstairs, the cafeteria...
Hampered by tank-like controls and a rigid camera angle like in an old-school horror game, we pilot North either with or without Ian by his side.
Actions in game are limited to the necessary: sneaking, running, barking, to explore every section and lure enemies away to open up the path for Ian.
The tightly defined camera and controls are no real default but another means to increase the retro-ish tension through gameplay alone, adding to the macabre atmosphere visibly drawn from Tim Burton movies such as Frankenweenie.
Yet don't let yourself blind by Ian's Eyes' eye-catchingly cute graphics for the game gets difficult right after the start requiring a strong learning curve to continue, and playing until the suprising end takes quite some patience plus lines to be added to the merciless death counter.
Ian's Eyes can be tough, but overcoming the most difficult sections with strategy and skill is rewarding in itself for players that like mastering challenges. Sindie Games’ debut title certainly merits being played and enjoyed.

This is a largely needed clarification. People complain about ‘glitches’ or weird moves. Firstly, these ‘glitches’ are not glitches. They are intended mechanics supported by Torn Banner (the developers). The glitch or ballerina name was coined by amateurs who refuse to properly learn the game. These mechanics add depth to the game. Without them, the game can literally be mastered in a week. This superficiality would most likely not appeal to anyone. These mechanics are necessary for the enjoyability and progression of combat. By this I mean, it is impossible to land hits against a good player without utilizing these mechanics. If you want proof, go to a duel yard server (not duel mode server. The map is called duel yard.) and ask the highest level player to not attack you and just block your attacks. I guarantee you, you will not land a single hit without using these ‘glitches’. It should be obvious then these mechanics are required for players to actually hit each other.

Ian’s Eyes, is a game in which you play a guide dog called North, with your little buddy Ian. A blind 8 year old who starts his first day at a new school, when things conveniently start to go awry. The concept of the game was intriguing enough to want to get my hands on it and with an aggravated sigh at the completion, I was thoroughly disappointed.
Ian’s Eyes had a high start, with it’s Tim Burton style art and quirky music, it felt like a game that was going to take a loved style seen in Don’t Starve and Limbo and mix it with an interesting new game concept. However, my opinion started to sway some what, when I looked at the ‘How-to-play’. It was an extensive look into how to play the game, with a dash of stabbing the corpse over and over again, Overkill. It explained the basic methods of moving and controlling your character, along with every single aspect of the game you could possibly want to know. I felt like I was being told how to breath, it’s as if the developers expected people who had never played a game before to be their audience. Whilst there is the saying “No stone left unturned” that doesn’t necessarily mean you should turn over all the rocks on a pebble beach.
However, the majority of gamers will avoid looking at the rules, adopting the “I know what I’m doing” attitude as their confidence is high, they are then met with what can only be described as an amateur voice actor. The voice of the Narrator and Principal was hard to listen too as he often didn’t pronounce his words correctly, or said the wrong words alongside the subtitles. It was even harder to understand as they seemed to use a poor quality mic, plus his obviously heavy accent made distinguishing words almost impossible. This was even more befuddling when you heard the voice of little Ian, he was clear and quite professional, albeit annoying, but there was still a stark difference.
You are then forced to listen to the Principle, Mr Bates, talk during a short tour of the school, it is here that I discovered the controls for myself. Reading them in the broad rules section was quite different to actually using them, they were clunky and fiddly, each direction had to turn your character at an agonizingly slow pace before you were even able to move. Getting used to those controls would take some time, but as soon as you were, they would change up on you, you could no longer move backwards, you now had to wait for the same slow turn. It was like finally getting used to writing “2009” at December, only for a month to pass and now having to write “2010”. Combining this with the Resident Evil style fixed cameras that would change at the most awkward intervals. You were in for one hell of a ride. This would eventually be the cause of a multitude of deaths and a number of profanities muttered under your breath in aggravation.

Ian's Eyes is a puzzle, strategy, and stealth game. You start off going to "Blue Norholm Primary School, it is the first day of school. Ian is blind, so it obviously harder for Ian. Ian beginning his school day with his seeing-eye dog names North. There are "cassette tapes" that bring the story to life. They give you chills, and help you understand what is going on.
PROS
The music in the game is incredible. It has a nice creepy "Tim Burton" feel in the beginning, while going quieter during the gameplay giving you an eerie anxious feel. The background sounds of crickets, footsteps and growling really give it an extra eerie feel. While you play the game, you will randomly hear SCREAMING and banging on lockers, loud noises, and much more. It really makes you feel nervous!

The game can be played with a controller, or keyboard.
I enjoy the easy visuals. There really isnt any violence shown. You will see "dead" children lying around, and thats really creepy! All the children look "hypnotized" and "zombie-like". There are random posters up in the school that make you go "hmmm?", and I love that about this game! People can be critical about graphics, however, no game is perfect! It's an Indy, so some angles you can see thru a wall, or head. It's not that serious!
Game runs smoothly, and I have had no problems! I have seen complaints about it being broken, it is not! Make sure your PC is up to par!
Death tally screen. LOL it's HUGE!

CONS
The camera angle can be difficult at times, changing often when going around corners or running farther down the hall.
Can be quite redundant and you will get stuck in the same spot for an hour, with lack of direction or ability to review objective.
Not great to stream as you can get stuck in the same place for a while!
OVERALL:
I love this game! I would recommend as the story is intriguing, and induces a sense of fear and anxiety while you play. The gameplay can be frustrating while you dont understand what to do, but it also gives you an overall feeling of accomplishment when you do make it to the next objective!
Ian's eyes is a refreshing gaming twist, and I am addicted! I will be making some walkthrough videos if I have time!

I never thought I'd ever see a Falcom game here on Steam, let alone an Ys game!
I played this game years ago and if you know anything about Falcom games and Ys, then you know this game is going to be good.
It's pretty much an awesome remake of the original Ys III, that came out back in 1989 for the NEC PC-8801/9801, MSX2 and X68000, then remade in 1991 for the Famicom, Super Nintendo, SEGA Genesis and the TurboGrafx-16 CD (which was a first to include animated cutscenes and voice dialogue) and remade again in 2005 for the Playstation 2.
Ys: Oath in Felghana was released for the PC in 2005 and was the first of the Ys III remakes to have a 3D world. It also has a perfectly remixed soundtrack that does not take the feel away from the epic original.
Plus, the addition of Cloud save and Steam achievements is a nice bonus!
Highly recommended for fans of Falcom games.

While I LOVE Phantom Brave, this iteration is nothing special and I urge you to find a legal PSP emulator and dump a cd copy of PB:HT onto it to play with better quality on visuals and on gameplay.
--minor spoilers--
There are several downgrades from the PSP version, and the problem is that there are many options that are removed from the game that were added in the PSP version, but were not added in the PC version due to the game being a fork of the WII version of the game. The team has had ample time to add these features back into the game, but being a busy game design company as NISA/NIS is, NISA/NIS have decided that they will not be making any more money off of this game if they update it.
It is odd that the game was not prioritized towards making more of the features previously available in the PSP version for the PC, while still adding code to the game that changed mechanics from the WII version. The most notable of these differences being that the icons stating the elemental type of an attack has been removed; however, there are moves that need these icons to make the damage system make sense, like the space/time type move that occurs late in the game. Also, the special items that are not supposed to be available to the player, were available to the player so long as they were able to cheese the system. Items like the magenta core and Marona's seashell are now permanently unavailable as the devs decided to hardcode the inability to take these items home from battle as demonstrated by videos in the community.
I bring up random updates like this to showcase the refusal of the NISA/NIS team to prioritize their updates for the features in this game. Players wanted better graphics and upscaling and the players got a bicubic filter, instead of actual updates to the game's maps; which are desperately needed in the game currently, as sprites are constantly being shoved UNDER the maps. Also, spheres denoting the player's ability to hit a set amount of characters are not representative of the player's ability to hit a set amount of characters, just approximations. IIRC The spheres were correct in the PS2, WII, and PSP versions of the game, but not now.

I never write negative reviews. I love supporting companies by providing positive feedback and encouraging people like Beamdog to remaster our favorite games. This review isn't about the game or any of the gameplay mechanics. Nooooo, this review is about something so much worse than I let on. I have played Baldur's Gate 2 since I was 8 years old and it has been so near and dear to me that I cannot begin to express how elated I was at owning the remastered version, which is practically the only readily available version left online. So this review isnt about the game, but about the company and their "liberties" they have taken on our beloved classic-- A classic game so timeless, it is frequently listed as one of the best games and RPGs of all time.
Beamdog, I want to personally and come out and say for all fans of BG2  that bought your game..
This game became less about remembering about the times we played it when we were kids or young adults, and more about putting Beamdog's dreaded arbitrary personal stamps all across BG2's UI.
1. Reconfiguring the spellbook (this just ripped my soul out of me)
2. Entirely scrapping the character portrait screen and replacing it with  uncountable nuances that make it hard to even describe what was there before.
3. Changing the map display
4.Changing the inventory screen
5.Changing weapon icons
6. Simplifying item statistics
7. Changing the journal
8. God just too many to count...
Making this game more accessible and user friendly isn't what fans of BG2 want. We want the challenge we remembered and the time consuming, rewarding experience of this perfectly crafted game. The game simply has little room for improvement on its original construction, besides some of its outdated graphics. We want all the quirks of the original game, and the massive game that Black Isle created, not Beamdog.
But they matter more than one single change that was made for "optimal" organization or helpfulness. Baldur's Gate 2 isn't supposed to hold your hand and it shouldn't be changed like this. People that buy this game, including me, that are disappointed, will personally go out of their own way to make this barely recognizable classic fail and your company to lose the privledge of meddling with a piece of art so valuable, it proved to be too much for your company to responsibly manage with respect, and care to the creators, as well as the die hard fans.
Art is often said to belong to the public once it is crafted, because it exists with flaws, and is in our memories. We connect with these pieces of work on a level that we can see in ourselves, and our past. Everyone that enjoyed this game when it was released played one of the greatest games of all time.
Beamdog, do yourself a favor and fix this trash or let some other capable company fix what you have destroyed, because this isnt art anymore, its trash that I have to tolerate. Im a positive person and have always tried to be, but this is just awful.
Whatever you do...

This game is not very good. It starts out ok despite the terrible floaty jumping and dumb wall grabbing mechanic and you feel like you can still manage.....until you start advancing through the levels and the game exploits the awful controls and becomes exhaustingly frustrating. Everything about the controls is dreadful: sluggish movement, inaccurate jumping, unintuitive wall grabbing, unresponsive button pushes. Even crouching takes longer than it should.
When you're trying to walljump you can't immediately jump to the next wall like in every other game. First you have to jump on a wall and wait until you "stick" to it, then press the direction of the wall you want to jump to but before you can you have to wait until the game lets you which is indicated by a visual cue from your character -- her eyes will look behind her -- then you're able to walljump. It's tedious and takes way too long. You also can't cancel the wall jump and just drop down. You either have to slide down the entire wall or walljump off.
The game will punish you further by adding slippery mechanics like waterfalls going down platforms or snow on platforms, as if the p!ss poor controls weren't torture enough. Then add enemies that throw projectiles at you from annoying angles where they can hit you but you can't hit them. When you get hit you get knocked back which will most likely make you fall off the platform. The hardest part of the game is not the boss fights. It's getting through the levels.
In a platformer bad controls almost always results in a bad game. This game is proof positive. It could have been decent if the controls were tight and responsive. But they're not and it isn't. Skip this game it is not worth it.

This is an RPG focused on tactical combat and not so much on background and character development unless you use one of the premade charaters. Let me clarify that. You can advance your team almost however you want within the limits of skills, traits and stats, but if you're looking for the kind of rpg that focuses on how you feel more than in how many ways you can use an oilbarrel in a fight against an undead squirrel, you may not get your fill here. However, this game has a very nice storyline that gives you multiple options in how you wish to get from A to B. You may have a hard time trying to play as a pacificst hippie with some sort of social disorder but if that ever worked in a computergame, I wouldn't be surprised if that worked in Divinity.
Another thing that I've seen alot of people complain about is that the game is somewhat challenging. For me, this is one of the absolutely top reasons why I enjoy it so much. If you play like I monkey, the game will punish you for it. Not to the extent that a monkey can't get through it (there is after all a savebutton for those of you that can't own up to your misstakes), but enough that you look at a fight mid way and ask yourself if this wouldn't have gone better if you just used your brain before charging headlong into a lvl 25 Dreadbeast of Doom, Destruction and Dogtreats (TM).
I must say that you will probably get the most out of Divinity if you play it solo, but the option to bring up to 3 friends along in the multiplayer mode is a very nice addition. It's been long since I've laughed so hard as when I first spend 15 minutes telling my mates how to stop being useless in combat and then accidently stunned half the party with and ill placed lightningbolt from my staff. I strongly recommend you practice a bit on your own before getting your crew together. It will most likely be a better experience for everyone...
One final tip, also regarding the mutliplayer mode. In my experience, you should never leave the game open for strangers to join. I've tried it a few times but had to throw away the savegame after someone joined in, attacked some random bystanders and then left the game. It's just not worth the hassle.
Hope this was helpful, now stop wasting time and go play!

A decent port of a classic Dreamcast platformer with support for true widescreen and higher native resolutions than any other port. The graphics haven't been "improved" but their cel shaded style is still striking.
The game mechanics are unfortunately tied to a 30fps cap and there's a few minor transparency related flickering glitches which aren't present on Dreamcast but exist in every version of the HD port.
In terms of framerate, PC is probably the best way to play the game. The Dreamcast version would stutter noticeably when moving between districts in a city or when things got really hectic & both versions for Sony hardware have bizarre slowdown in the Bantam Street level. On PC, during gameplay, I don't think the framerate ever noticeably dropped.
You can now control the camera with the right stick: something the Dreamcast controller lacked.
It's a real shame it's not possible to map the camera reset button separately from the tag button. You can disable it entirely but it's a useful feature to have; just not when it's mapped to the tag button. You need to press tag a lot, sometimes even mid-jump, which makes frequent camera resets disorienting.
The game's audio holds up well. It's missing two songs from the European soundtrack but it's possible to mod them back into "story" missions crudely yet fairly seamlessly using Audacity if you happen to have the original Dreamcast version's audio files handy.
It's also missing Dunny Boy from the initial Japanese release but I don't think it could be restored so easily since the song order in that version was too different.
Something seems to be wrong with the US-exclusive tracks too. There's supposed to be a 50:50 chance of them playing in both Grind City story missions, the only time they can be heard during gameplay. They show up just fine in Bantam Street but I've never managed to make Grind Square play its American soundtrack. This issue didn't exist on PS3.
The port has five Hideki Naganuma songs from the game's sequel as bonus unlockables but unfortunately there's no way to use them in-game. It's a real shame they can't at least show up in Jet levels.
The PC port is also probably the easiest to insert your own custom grafitti into, thanks to mods.
There are Achievements but they're mostly stuff you'd get if you were aiming to complete everything in the original, with the possible exception of Detached.
It should be noted that a mandatory patch introduced a (fixable) bug that breaks saving and broke the game's configuration tool at resolutions below 1080P. Other than the configuration tool, the system requirements are very low.
My laptop is too weak to run either of the Sonic Adventure games on Steam at full speed but this game runs comfortably, perhaps a benefit of the 30fps cap.
The game's not for everyone. It's an early 3D platformer, not much newer than Sonic Adventure, meaning it has a lot of camera issues and clunkiness. A controller is highly recommended. I've never even considered playing using a keyboard.
In fact, even for the time, the mechanics take getting used to. The fact remains that you can get used to them though and, once you do, I still think the game is very enjoyable. I didn't regret playing it to death again even though I'd already done so on Dreamcast and PS3. Multiple times each.

With almost 250 hours in game, I feel it is time to review Animallica. It is a SINGLE-PLAYER (co-op is a future possibility, according to developers multiplayer IS NOT, please stop clogging discussion page with the same repetitive question, "Is this game multiplayer?").  It is an open world, animal-themed crafting game.  The developers created the Animallica mod for Skyrim previously.  As it is a post-apocalyptic setting, animals are diseased and must be captured and cured. They can then be released or kept as companions or put in enclosures. Animal interaction is still somewhat limited, but breeding, and possibly genetics, are planned. Currently, there are around 15-20 different animals including many of the large African mammals.  Additionally, there are enemies which consist of mutant animals and bandit humans. These are found randomly and around spawning nests.
Crafting is accomplished through building increasingly complex stations including a science lab to cure and heal animals. The variety of craftable items is currently somewhat limited particularly in relation to unnecessary to game items like furniture and decorations. Resources are the typical wood, stone and various ores. Additionally, rare multicolored shards allow upgrades and other perks.
Exploration, discovery and resource collection are primary at present. While some people call it a survival/crafting game with an animal theme that is a little misleading. After initial gameplay, survival is rather easy particularly after acquiring armor. Food, water and stamina come into play but do not hinder the experience, all readily available or craftable.
Without doubt, this is one of my favorite current games and one of my all time favorites. Remember, it is early release and content is continually added (15 updates in first two months of availability). Updates always address bugs but content is also regularly added. The visuals on this game are stunning and on my newer system I notice very little lag. Have not done a fps analysis, sorry.  There are numerous biomes to explore each having a different theme and availble loot and animals. The developers are readily available and regularly respond to questions related to bugs and gameplay as well as reasonable suggestions.  For an early release game it is one of the best looking, well developed ones I have seen in a long time. If you like an animal theme, great graphics and a responsive development team, give this one a chance.

I saw that the Tinkerer can summon a giant robot and hit things with a giant wrench, which reminded me of Max from Dark Cloud 2, so I made one. When I got to choose a Job Specialization, my friend had previously made his an Engineer, so I made mine an Alchemist. This is when I really dove into the game, finding out that most of the Alchemist’s abilities are really fun to use. At level 45, I got to choose a second job specialization; the Adept’s increased Fire and Ice power or the Physician’s increased Poison and Healing power. I chose Physician because I like playing healers. Now I have 350+ hours in the game and probably not stopping soon.
I like it mainly because it’s an action RPG with fast-paced fighting and I love action RPGs. This game is not a freemium at all and very little pay to win(costume items give very little stats, and you can buy item protection jellies and revives with real money).

I really enjoy this game. I find the gameplay fun and interesting with a high amount of replay value. I would suggest people to at least try it out to see if you like it or not. This is a good game to delve into if you are bored, so I pretty much recommend this for people to play.

I hate this game. I've tried so hard to like it, to learn the ins and outs, the underlying nuances. I've spent hours on tutorials, even more hours in learning scenarios, and I STILL can't wrap my head around why so many people would play this game. As a war game, it's too slow, as a diplomacy game, it's too complicated, and as a political intrigue game, it lacks substance.
I consider myself a well rounded gamer with reasonable expectations. Based on positive reviews and awesome stories told by reviewers, I came into this game expecting a Game of Thrones-esque experience that would give me a minimal amount of kingdom management and more interactions involving a council and backstabbings and plots. What I got was an uninteresting map simulator that changes colors, a bunch of historical icons with Wikipedia pages, a slew of complicated menus and charts that fail in helping you manage your kingdom, and scripted events that pop up every now and then telling you how close you are to getting wrecked. A majority of the reviews here recommend getting DLC to make the game more fun, but if the core game can't get my attention, there's no point. So if you're the sort of person that likes clicking around menus and playing with game speeds, go ahead and get it, but I'm done.

I liked it very much. Since the moment that you enter the school the story of Ian’s Eyes gets you completely. It’s not another game about zombies, it has a very original idea. Aesthetically is very well made, very coherent, and both textures and lighting are carefully treated. Animations are very polished and when the zombies chase you they turn out quite funny, hahahahaaa.
The only downside I’d point out is that the sudden camera changes makes the controls a bit confusing even though they give the game an extra strategy depth as you have to consider those changes to have a clear picture of what to do in each moment. On the other hand, if you play with a gamepad instead of keyboard it gets better.
One fairly interesting thing is that you can overcome each phase in different ways as a puzzle with several solutions: you can run, go stealthy, use barks or combine everything. Thereby both playability and replayability are increased. It’s also great the fact that there are quite a few moments where you’ll have to squeeze your brain and design a good strategy in order to success, it’s not just about the controller skills. All in all it’s a very funny game.
Highly recommended if you like amusing games with an original proposal.

I could finally play Ian’s Eyes and the truth is that I has really wanted to try this extremely original game. That’s precisely its main strength: the originality of what’s proposed, a story that attracts the player and tests his ability with the controls (and occasionally also his nerves).
In general the game is delightful in terms of entertainment, and both Ian and North are designed with charisma which is something key in the indie video game industry. As to the creative part and ambiance a great work is also noticed (illumination is very slick to create such a dismal atmosphere at certain moments).
And we get to the main part, controls and movement. There are certain things that are somewhat exasperating, not so much for the skills that the player may have but because there are things that are kind of shocking for how it is programmed. With the number of times you get to die (this is a trial and error kind of game after all) you end up realizing that you can perform an action over and over in the same way and maybe one of them is successful (a mistake or it’s that you have to Split hairs), sometimes it’s not clear the detection ranges of certain zombies, or the dog controls that are a little messy when you have to move a box for example. On the other hand, I think it’s a great idea that Ian may die if North is away for too long, and also the different zombie types you encounter which causes the game to turn into a very entertaining and a strategic map.
Summing up, an indie game highly recommended for all audiences, that will enjoy and ge ton the nerves (in a good way). Don’t get fed up on dying, it’s worth it!

Not the most graceful or elegant implementation, but a completely functional way to play a board game you don't see online often.  Mind the rough edges*, but if you want to play Senet, you can.
* Fullscreen mandatory, no resolution options.  Graphics include one or two egyptian-themed backdrops, one of which flashes on the screen somewhat at random towards the end of the game without explanation, and some cheap color filters applied to game pieces to show which ones can move.  How-to-play segment seems to be a raw text file that was put into a scrollable window with a default windows font.  Options panel includes two unlabled buttons, purpose unclear without experimentation.  Gives the impression it was put together on a deadline, or an assembly line, or by someone whose interest just ran out somewhere between alpha testing and the final polishing.
Note : None of these issues impede gameplay.  So, good for boardgame enthusiasts, or someone in need of a solitaire alternative.

I got Woodle Tree Adventures for free so I really can't complain. This game claims to be a homage to 3D platformers, and as a person who grew up when these kinds of games were in their prime I can say that this game fails to mimick them. While its cute and colorful, there are a lot of things missing that don't quite qualify it to be on the same level as, let's say, Banjo Kazooie or DK 64 - both games I consider to be the epitome of 3D platform adventures.
Bad news first, I'll start with the negatives.
- It's plain, a little too plain. The cute and simpleness is nice at first but you get bored with it fast. The last two levels are at a beach and a snowy mountain which seem like a nice change of scenery but they also seem to get boring quickly.
- The music is bland and repetitive.
- It has some unfixed glitches. One time I fell through the world because I got stuck under a moving elevator. Another thing is the spawn points seem completely random. If you die, sometimes you're spawned back at the beginning of the level and other times you're spawned near where you died. One time I spawned underneath the level with no way to get back up and had to restart the game and play the level over again.
- The camera perspective can be your biggest enemy. There is a way to control the camera but the only thing it seems to do is zoom in and out. This game seems to depend heavily on parkour skills in terms of difficulty. A lot of 3D platformers do this, but when you can't change your perspective, making precise jumps becomes more frustrating. You will most likely die a lot.
- There is no typical item counter, status screen, etc. It really isn't needed, especially in this game, but you're playing a platformer that has a huge focus on item collecting you want to know how many of that item you've collected in the level so far and how many are left. After you exit a level you can see how many berries you've collected overall but there's no way to tell if you've collected all of the berries in one level and how many you have collected in a particular level. There is also no health bar or lives because there are none. One hit kills you and you have unlmited lives, so there isn't much of a penalty for dying.
- There are no boss battles, every enemy, big and small, takes only one hit to kill. You only have one weapon in the game that can get upgraded depending on how many berries you've collected.
- Very short, it took me about an hour and a half to complete it, and that was with me dying... several times.
There's a lot of negatives but there are some good things about the game:
- Decent control. I didn't have a hard time controlling the character. Most of my deaths were really just because of the bad perspectives and not because the character was difficult to control.
- The game seems to be expanding more and more so there seems that there is possibly room for improvement.
- Despite the large amount of negatives I can't help but find it charming. I actually kind of liked it, but the negatives make me feel like I shouldn't reccomend this game.
- The price is fair. $2.99 is not that much for a game that is still expanding. But at the moment, even with that price I can't reccomend the game. I think it would be best to wait for major updates if someone is interested in buying this game.
- It seems like only a handful of people, maybe just 2 or 3 worked on this game which is an achievement all on its own. With the small size of the staff I think they've actually produced an enjoyable game despite all its flaws.
Overall, Woodle Tree Adventures feels more like an alpha demo of something that is in the works to becoming a full-fledged game. It definitely feels unfinished. It also feels like the age group is geared towards children rather than older, 90's 3D platformer fans. Its simple and virtually has no penalties for dying so it feels like a younger audience would be more interested in a game like this.
It seems like this game is still being updated and I'll probably continue to check out any major updates because as I said: oddly enough I like it, but at this point I would not feel right saying I reccomend it for it feels unfinished.

Senet is a classic board game that’s been around. The game claimed it to be one of the oldest as well. I remember playing it as a child, though failed to understand the gameplay since at that time I was still counting fingers.
The game provides a clear and concise tutorial (Labelled as ‘Rules’ on the menu) on how to play. It’s quite simple really, and you can play on 3 difficulties: From easy to hardest it’s Novice, Egyptian and Pharaoh. All the game requires is the use of a mouse too, so it’s quite easy to get into the gist of things.
Its theme goes in accordance to Egyptian art, as established by the opening sequence (which I also liked). Even the board game was fashioned with this style. The rough textures and shading helped on giving that ‘ancient’ feel to it, plus the design was very detailed. This especially applied to the hieroglyphics, and tiles on the ground. The paintings and art overall, looked wonderful.
The audio also compliments to this theme. There's a BGM or sound effects whic hare present with your actions like clicking the sticks or when moving one of your pieces on the board. It's nothing too unique but still adds to the bigger picture.
I thoroughly enjoyed playing Egyptian Senet and would likely play it again in the future, whether single or with another player. At the time I am posting this review, the game is at 80% off too, so I do highly recommend buying this game.

First off i'd like to say i'm having a lot of fun with the game. I'd say that it's one of the few games on steam that you can just shut off and enjoy some mindless tank-fighting action, though there's plenty of  interesting things to do and make should you ever wish to delve deeper into the customization of your vehicle.
The payment and free-2-play model is very well done, if not a bit pricy. Most f2p games behave more like free2be cannonfodder, which this is not. The starting tank is very capable and will introduce you to the mechanics of the game. You'll get tokens for completing objectives in the game with which you're able to spend in the parts store.The great part is the fair pricing of the parts, the best only require a couple of games to play. The limiting factor in the f2p version is tthat you're limited to 7 parts slots, not unlike hangars in robocraft. With each level you gain, you'll get an extra slot, though you can sell parts back to make room (though you won't get much back). The first purchasing option allows for unlimited part slots and the second unlocks everything as well.
I firmy disagree with the top negative review, which mostly seems to be griping about certain loadouts (some of which is valid, others not so much), all that can be countered by clever tactics and select weapons. I find that mortars and wasp missiles to be very effective against snipers on top of roofs. At the end of the day it all comes down to skill, knowledge, and placement.
Pros
-fairly mindless
-deep customization mechanics
-fantastic balancing
-very fair free-2-play integration
-vibrant art style
-very fun
-2 ways to buy the game
-fun and silly weapons, each viable.
-hats
-plenty of people play so that there's always a server open.
Cons
-fairly expensive purchasing options
-limited gametype and map selections
-very bright [distance fog?]
-freind invite system is very iffy, and caould be much better
Other thoughts
-Although very well balanced, certain parts can be taken advantage of to come up with min/max builds that can be hard to counter, namely the twin chassis and turrets. Most of these issues can be solved by reducing weapon ammo by half and not allowing support items.
-Extra gametypes need to be added in order to keep things interesting. Conquest and TDM are fun, but not all the time. I'd like to see a Forge-esque map and gametype editor at some point
-The freinds and invite system don't really work. If you do manage to get a freind in you will most likely not be placed on the same team, even if there are available slots.
-The price is fairly steep for what the game contains; i'd like to see a 25% reduction for both packages to truly make me consider it.
All in all i'd say try the game for a bit, it's good fun and you've got nothing to lose trying it out. if you want to support the game the $10 package is generally woth it.

I do recommend this game, but I'd suggest you take my words with grain of salt, as I'll list few major problems with the game. If you think you can play through these problems, then you got your self a nice and simple 2D platformer that'll give you couple of hours of play time, if you are veteran in the genre or few hours, if casual in the genre for completion. It took me about 2 hours or so to complete everything. My play hours are high, because I left the game on over night.
Wall of text incoming.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
First, the positive aspect of the game. The game holds the basic essentials of a platformer, which will allow the players of the genre to be familiar with the mechanics, so they can play without being lost.
-Standard projectile attacks
-3 types of special with skill icons that clearly shows the effect.
-Wall grab and wall jump. You can hang on the wall and able to slide down by gravity or drop faster by pressing down. You can also fire projectiles to the opposite direction by facing the direction as coming down. Simple mechanics, but there is a flaw to this, which I will explain in the cons.
-Touch sensitive jumps. Hold longer for higher jump. Tap for short.
-Different types of platforms to give players challeges. If you played any of the side scroll Marios games, you'll recognize them immediately. Again, small flaw within the game's mechanic diminishes good of this a bit. Noted in the cons.
-Extra objectives for challenge. Each stage has 3 Kimonos (Japanese traditional garment) that you can grab for achievement and special ending.
-Low price
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now, for the cons of the game. This is where the potentially a solid platformer stumbles down. These issues really frustrated me during my play, which made me think, if the developer purposed created them to further challenge the players.
-Controls are rather stiff at times yet slippery? To elaborate, the control itself is quite simple, but it's the way the character reacts that causes a misconception that the controls are clunky. When Akane begins to move, there is a very brief period of acceleration for attaining her normal movement speed. This can easily be mistaken for delay in controls, but it's not. Same issues happens when she stops from moving. She'll take extra couple of steps, which will likely cause a notion that you may be sliding. Normally platformer characters have a fluid and snappy movements, but that's not the case here. My assumption is that, the develooper tried to emulate an actual human movements for Akane. If true, such emulation is unnecessary for 2D platformers like this. If must be done with fluid and snappy motions.
-Wall grab. Nice mechanic to have, but it falls short here. If you like to hold forward little extra long, perhaps influenced by other platformer, well you may become annoyed by wall grab, as the grab take action by pressing towards the direction of the wall and side surfaces in mid air, while right next to it. You'll often end up grabbing the walls and side surfaces even when you didn't mean or want to. This can be easily overlooked if you can let go of the wall instantly, but only way to let go of the wall is to wall jump or press down to come down slightly quicker.
-Platform layouts really created frutrations for me the most. Usually there is an extra 5-10% room for you to make it up to the higher platform, but here the highest platform gives almost no extra room to make it up there. You'll have to perfectly time your jump from very edge of the bottom platform with maximum jumping height to barely make it up. You'll often fall down or grab the side of the platform if off by the slightest. Some may like this feature for purpose of challenge, but this is unnecessary if the stage layout is more complex.
-Bug? In the water fall stages, if you end up getting pushed against a wall with water flowing in the same direction below, you'll be practically stuck there, as you'll barely move against the current. In that case, jump out is the only option. Sometimes enemy's attack will hit you when you are on a moving platform and hate throwers attack goes through the terrain in certain areas. Minor annoyance.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Though I made the problems sound quite bad, but they are something you can get used to without a huge effort. I did and still had fun, as well as some frutrating moments.
Overall Score: 6/10 Average

A potentially great RPG with solid fundamental mechanics, which is currently lacking polish and quality of life features and that can make it an extremely frustrating experience. This is mind boggling considering how long it was in early access. Below you can see just some of the issues which can infuriate you. When/if the devs fix these, I'll happily recommend the game to every RPG fan.
1.Whenever I start the game, it resets my controls. Every. Single. Time.
2.Inventory management is clumsy AF. You can't move around multiple items and that's a royal pain the♥♥♥♥♥ which is only exacerbated by the fact that each of the characters in your party has their own inventory and they can't use consumables or gold from eachother unless you manually transfer it between them. Might work in co-op, but it sucks in single-player.
3.Civil skills are character-specific instead of party wide. So you may have pumped a bunch of points into persuasion for 1 of you characters, but if you don't specifically click on them to initiate conversation, it'll be wasted as the game will only check the persuasion skill of the char who started dialog. This is made even worse when NPCs start the conversation, because then you have no control over which character will be involved. Another example is with the bartering skill. Since traders only look at the skill of the char talking to them, they'll have worse prices for everyone else. So you only have to pick up items with your barter guy, unless you want to either be screwed with the prices or manually transfer every single item one at a ♥♥♥♥ing time between chars. Again, might work in co-op but it's horrible in SP.
4.Crafting screen doesn't give you any information about the items so you don't know if you want to craft them or not. How much does a medium healing potion heal? Is a primitive harpoon ranged or melee? WTF is a glowing idol of rebirth? No clue.
5.Autosaves only happen once when you stumble onto an area where the game thinks you might die. But if you wander off and only run into the encounter later, you won't be covered. Or if you accidentally click on a 0 value spoon because the NPC you wanted to talk to moved and now everyone hates your dirty, thieveing guts and you thought "damn, i should reload" - well, your last save may be an hour ago. It should have autosaves on area changes and timed every 5-10 minutes in addition to the encounter specific ones.
6.Everything that can be used directly in some way gets tossed on your quickbar as soon as you pick it up, cluttering the ♥♥♥♥ out of your life. Scrolls, potions, skills, booze, ♥♥♥♥ing bedrolls - everything.

I really enjoyed Ian’s Eyes, it is a mix of old school Resident Evil camera game with a very difficult one, which gives you an amazing feeling when you can go through a tough puzzle.
Now I will analyze it in depth.
First of all, the game design is strongly immersive, you really can feel how your bonds with Ian are growing while you go into the story. Also the learning curve is accurate to a game like this, the challenges presented to you are balanced with the possibilities that North and Ian can do. The first part is quite easy but when you get further in the game… wow, it can make you angry when you did everything as planned and then a little red hairy zombie girl surprises you in a corner, I hate those ones.
When you see the game in an artist way, the feeling that you are in the 80’s comes easily, those “Tim Burtonish” style with all the posters as easter eggs from nice movies makes you empathize with the game.
The zombies are well treated and you can easy know who is who when they come to kill you. The school is a nice place to see when it has not a lot of zombies, after that, some places are scary to hell (again the zombie girl lying in the bathroom). Ian and North make a nice couple and they seem to belong to each other in every way possible.
The animations are well made and suits fine with each of the characters, one of them that I like the most were the animations of North pulling and pushing the box, those were nice and fun to watch.
The game is fully enjoyable and has no big bug issues, it has some minor sound time fixing in the kinematics but the rest comes fluid as water. When you think that you were killed by a bug remember that, it is just you being not able to do it right.
To sum it up, Ian’s Eyes is an experience that I will recommend to every person. It has difficult and perfectly timed puzzles (other way you die), nice art, catching story and charming characters. You should buy this game if you like all that!
Finally, I am eager to see what Sindie Games will do in the future, they begin with a brilliant game.

To preface about myself, I've been playing this game since beta, and have well over 500 hours logged on this, since the switch to using Steam for Dragon Nest was relatively recent.
I have a great time playing this game. It recently got revamped to make leveling from 1-50 easier, although it will still take time. It's definitely possible to finish the story line with just the gear you get from quests, although getting really good gear will definitely take time and in-game currency. While there are people who trade NX for gold and vice versa, this game is most definitely not pay 2 win, but there are many costumes and cosmetic customizations that you can purchase within the NX store. While those cosmetic items do indeed have stats, they're definitely not needed to be well-geared for raids.
Class elitism doesn't exist for the most common things, such as nests, although once you start getting into raids and other really tough things to clear, people will definitely have class preferences. That said, it's good to visit the forums on
and read about different classes, as well as do some googling on what's easiest to gear, what class is cheapest to get good at, etc, before jumping into this game.
Most people I've met were extremely friendly, and it's never hard to party up and work with people for nests and quests. Guilds are also awesome in this game. There are many, and different types exist for different players, so everyone from casual to hardcore can find guilds to suit them. The market is also really well done now, and buying/selling is a smooth process.
The fighting system is real-time and 3D, which makes for an AWESOME gameplay. It's super fast and has pve and pvp within the game, with reward systems and ability to acquire weapons by doing either. It's not all about stats - your ability to dodge monsters' abilities, other people's abilities, and the whole cartoon animation style is great.
The one con that I would mention is that once you get really high level and your power runs out quickly, the game can get somewhat boring unless you have a guild or a group of friends to do raids and nests with. Being purely a solo player is a lonesome and boring life once you hit 70, and grinding does exist for the last 10-15 levels until you hit the cap.
Overall I'd rate this game 8.5/10. It's solid,

Ian's Eyes is not very good at all... which is a crying shame. An interesting concept and a cool Coraline-y (albeit low fidelity) aesthetic is ultimately marred by some bewildering game design choices, awful voice acting, an uninteresting story, unlikable characters, and ultimately poor, repetitive, unfun gameplay.
A lot of love when into this one, though, which makes this a difficult review.
But I digress.
It's Ian's first day of school, a Jimmy Neutron lookin' young man voiced by Elijah Wood if Elijah's voice went through some kind of horrible modulator that made it more grating and awful. You're his seeing eye dog, North, a... Golden retriever, maybe? I don't know, he's small and has creepy eyes and a stingray mouth.
You're given a brief tour of the school by Principal Bates (henceforth Principal Masturbates because I'm immature), who looks like Captain Ahab and is voiced by Tommy Wiseau after a botched lobotomy (the tour works like a tutorial, showcasing gameplay mechanics). Now this first day is special because it happens to be the centenary of the school's establishment. Unfortunately for you and your human, something goes terribly wrong and everyone, staff and students included, turns into mindless, blind zombies. As North, you have to guide young, obnoxious Ian out.
And ♥♥♥♥ me sideways if that just isn't the biggest, most boring chore. If you were thinking this might be a scary experience you'd be mistaken: when you're caught it quickly fades to black and you're greeted with a tally of your deaths. Then you're back at the last checkpoint, which are blessedly fairly frequent. However, if Ian had a bit of dialogue before your untimely death, every time you come back he utters his dialogue again AND AGAIN in case you'd forgotten. And if it's a particularly challenging hallway to navigate anticipate having “we have to get to the library, North!” or something burned into your frontal lobe.
The dialogue, as badly as it's delivered, is written poorly. "We have to wait for help, North," is uttered by Ian and, in the same breath, "I guess help isn't coming." JUST CHILL DUDE, MAYBE HELP IS STILL COMING. "Let's wait for Principal Masturbates," he says to North. "BARK," North replies, his creepy mouth opening and closing slowly as he struggles to presumably breathe as he is the unholy byproduct of golden retriever and stingray copulation. "You're right North, Principal Masturbates is not coming back." WHAT? WHY? NO! This happens A LOT, and near the end there's a hilarious exchange with Principal Masturbates that tries to be powerful and is anything but.
It may have been my favorite moment in the entire game.
Let that wash over you.
The baddies, who travel on preset paths, notice you if you're too close or loud. You can use North's sick barking skillz to lure them off their paths – sometimes they wander back, sometimes they stay where you've lured them. And that's the primary gameplay. Going from room to room, hallway to hallway, avoiding the same five or six kids and teachers. I encountered one (now two! Except the second one might be broken!) lazy puzzle in the library... and I think that was it? I'm currently stuck in a particularly hellish room but I don't think I'll press on for my own sanity. (Author's Note: TOTALLY got past that bit and I'm at the very end. There's a classic (read: hastily googled by dev) riddle puzzle but the game absolutely refuses to register my answer... and sometimes the event doesn't trigger at all after reading the passage. Soooooo I guess I'm definitely finished now! Not that the ending could save this drek - it could dispense ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, world peace, and cakes and it would still be awful!)
If the game was even a little fun it'd be fine – I love a challenge. It's boring. Running up and down a hallway, giving blind kids the slip as you go from one side of the school to the other to find out if a door is locked? Not fun. Wandering down a hallway and blundering into an enemy because the fixed camera deemed it necessary? Not fun. Navigating a narrow hallway populated by a half dozen enemies using weird, clunky, not-super-responsive controls? Not fun. Worst of all, I don't give three blind mice worth of asses about North or Ian or Principal Masturbates Furiously. The whole damn plot is them trying to leave the school and... that's it. I guess there's THE MYSTERY as to why the kids and staff went all EVIL, and there are cassette tapes to collect that... might glean on that? But it isn't worth the headache.
Ian's Eyes could have been good... maybe a bit more time in the creative oven, with a few more people working on the project? This wasn't the case, and good intentions only count in horseshoes and hand grenades.
Or something.

The community has embraced these exploits and the developers have left them in the game on the grounds that they take practice or "skill." I think it's necessary to split the review for this game into two parts: the story part (as most people do, in fact, play games for the story) and the gameplay part. I think both of them are great, as far as japanese SRPGs go.
The story revolves around a young girl named Marona who's lost her parents and has a spirit guardian named Ash filling the role of her older brother and sort of mentor/protector. Ash is a ghost whom only Marona can see, and the only being who cares and looks out for her. Most of the people Marona encounters consider her an abomination for seeing ghosts and talking to them. She also gets incredibly brutal and unfair treatment because she's seen by everyone as an orphan girl with a freaky and dangerous power. Despite that, she never gives up. No matter how harsh the people treat her, how difficult and unfair her circumstances are, she endures them all, and when you play the game, it feels incredibly genuine and not just because Marona is "such a nice and friendly girl!". Her willingness to help those who are treated even less fairly than she is, those who are struggling, is genuine and heart-warming, and it's Marona's own way to cope with all the harsh treatment and loss she has to endure. It's a tale of a very selfless girl whose kindness knows no bounds, and perhaps her kindness would inspire the players in turn.
The gameplay relies heavily on grind, which is a staple for Disgaea series and its spinoffs. However, the gameplay takes its own unique turn with Marona's abilities to summon spirits, or "phantoms" who fight alongside her, as well as picking up stuff scattered around the stages to use as weapons, alongside the usual weapon choice like swords, spears and staffs. Even a measly rock and a random weed have an incredibly power lying dormant in them! Which is, of course, pretty awesome. Leveling up weapons also offers the player an opportunity to completely break the game because you're free to make them as overpowered as you desire. The phantoms can only be summoned for a limited number of turns, and Marona can only summon a limited amound of those from her roster, so you have to plan out many of the more difficult fights ahead (or keep replaying till you get them right). The stages also offer your units opportunity to more or less free roam, which is slightly more confusing when it comes to positioning compared to grid and more predictable and fixed positioning.
Difficulty level expects you to grind a lot and can get pretty brutal if you don't commit enough to grind, and straight out impossible if you choose to neglect grinding altogether. If you don't enjoy grinding, this isn't the game for you.
The soundtrack is incredibly nice and has an easy-going, yet somewhat somber and melancholic feeling to it; it's never about pure carefree joy, which further enhances the general direction of the story and Marona's character. It also makes even the sloggiest of the stages and the grindiest of grinds a better experience.
The graphics, however... Well, the 3D part of the stages looks ok, as well as the backgrounds; unfortunately, pixel sprites are blurry and feel very out of place because of said blurriness. The PC version is pretty much an emulation of the PS2 game, which PB originally was, and it's definitely not meant to be viewed on modern HD monitors. Which is a shame, because the sprite work is really detailed and varied, but it turns out to be such a mess on the actual screen.
Overall, the game is really good if you're willing to commit effort to grind. The only downside I can really point out is the blurry pixel sprites, which is a glaring shame on a game that's otherwise pretty much flawless.

Initial play review here. I've only played one round against AI so far. However, here is my constructive critique of the game.
First off, allow me to say that obscure, archaic board games are something that fascinate me. I just saw this on sale, and could afford it, so I grabbed it. I'm not particularly picky about graphics, music, or visual interface. As long as it more or less does its job, I'm happy. Yes, the interface and graphics are simple, and the music isn't amazing, but that's not a concern for me. The gameplay mechanics, from what I can tell, function as they should. Senet is a game of luck. There is a little bit of strategy with whatever moves you end up being permitted to use. It's more like thinking ahead, or even prioritizing. Mostly, however, it's luck.
Try not to be intimidated by the game at first, given the lack of a tutorial. There are instructions, and yes, those instructions are a little bit difficult to comprehend in the manner it is written. I encourage you to give it an initial play-through against AI. Just dive in, and do it. My first playthrough started with me knowing little to nothing about what to do. But within minutes, I was picking up the pace between moves and turns, and soon found myself almost instinctively getting a feel for the game. My first playthrough was a victory.
Pros:
- Very light weight file size
- Very low system requirements (aside from requiring at least Win7)
- Simple and straight forward interface
- Easy to learn gameplay
- Game is based almost entirely on luck; some but very little strategy involved
- Personal opinion: Being based upon a real life ancient Egyptian board game is entertaining
- Single player (vs AI) and Two Player modes
- Different difficulty levels vs AI
- Different interface text language options.
Cons:
- Lack of screen-resolution options
- Lack of window-mode options
- Lack of in-game volume slider (sound toggle and music toggle only)
- Lack of guided tutorial.
- Readable instructions are present, but difficult to comprehend at first.
Overall, if you enjoy obscure, archaic/ancient board games, and don't care too much for trivial matters such as graphics, this is the game for you. It indeed does play with a very casual atmosphere, but I feel that perhaps that's what is intended with board games, especially from ancient times. I feel that they were likely used as simply "something to pass the time when feeling dull and bored". It's definitely a great boredom killer, and even more fun for history and mythology buffs.

If you're familiar with Nippon Ichi's other Strategy RPGs, most popularly Disgaea, then you should already have some idea of what to expect here.  The game does feature several fundamental differences, however, the major ones being that the game isn't grid based and instead lets you traverse the map freely and that the introduction of the "Confine" system means that rather than summoning characters permanently from a base you instead summon them using items on the map via the main character, Marona.
Each of these things come with their own pros and cons.  Having your phantoms on a timer seems annoying but it adds another layer of strategy to the game and whether that's better or worse for you really depends on how you vary your regalia.  As for the lack of a grid, this freedom can lead to some odd behavior and questionable AI logic at times but it clearly allowed them to make gameplay that was more dynamic than something you would get out of a Disgaea or a Soul Nomad, largely thanks to terrain effects and physics.
As far as the story is concerned, starting out you have two options:
and
.
is a standalone story that was introduced in the game's Wii port,
, and because it includes characters and allusions to the main story, it's best to save this for after having beaten the game at least once (it can also be accessed through the New Game+ option after beating the game, though it's best played starting at level one).
Starting a new game, you'll run into an unskippable tutorial and unskippable cutscenes.  Don't let these leave too big of a negative impression on you because in general the game's cutscenes are short and all of them past the first are skippable, so it's mostly replay-friendly.  You play as a chroma (basically someone who deals in various types of odd jobs) named Marona, an orphan who can see and summon phantoms.  While some would consider this a gift, most see the girl as a witch who is possessed by phantoms and is filled with malintent.  This couldn't be farther from the truth, of course, as Marona is about as pure as her age implies and all she really wants is to help others.  While a character and setup like this could easily be annoying, it's played to pretty great effect as Marona is torn down over and over again before it looks like she has any chance of standing on her own, and this is made better by seeing how the mail that she gets reacts to current events (and the mail is probably some of the darkest content in this game, which says a lot more than it sounds like).
Much like Disgaea, Phantom Brave is a level-based Strategy RPG that takes place over a series of maps.  Put simply, if you like Disgaea's gameplay, you'll like this after you get used to it.  And then you'll like it more when you realize that each different type of item that can be found on a map has its own skill set.  Then you'll like it more when you realize you can use the Fusionist to combine items together to give them really interesting skills and stat buffs.  And then you'll like it even
when you realize just how fun and satisfying giving custom titles to your characters and their items can be.
Phantom Brave's gameplay is by no means perfect and has a fair few imperfections, some of the more major ones I mentioned above, but the emphasis on customization and use of the environment as well as generally interesting map designs just makes it one hell of a fun romp that isn't much like any other game NIS has put out, even its spiritual successor, Makai Kingdom.
As for the graphics, they're ugly as sin.  Absolutely ugly as sin.  Normally, I would just say they're dated, because that's what they are.  Normally I wouldn't be so hard on the game.  But normally a game like this that didn't even have all that big of a following doesn't get 3 subsequent ports over 10 years on variably stronger hardware without anyone doing anything about the fact that the game looks like it was made for the PS1 after the PS2 had already been out for 4 goddamn years.  Thankfully, the UI fonts and textures have been brought up to date, and though that does make the sprites feel even more uncanny, it's at least nice to see that some effort was made.
And finally, the music.  It's always amazing to me how Tenpei Sato manages to make his games feel unique.  If you blindfolded a NIS fan and played tracks from several different NIS developed games, they'd somewhat easily be able to tell you what was from Rhapsody, what was from Disgaea, and what was from Phantom Brave, because the guy tailors his sound to his series rather than to the situation or any one style for all of his work.
And here, his work shines just as brightly as it ever has. Because Phantom Brave is one of the more somber and melancholic games he's worked on, rather than the usual frantic or chaotic melodies heard in Disgaeas 1-3, here we find that songs his are generally slower and themed based on context.  This might seem like it betrays my previous statements, but that speaks more to exactly how the characters and maps of the game are designed than anything of himself.  But rather than trying to convince you with words, I'll leave these here and let you be the judge.
If you're a fan of Disgaea then you probably knew whether you liked this pretty early off.  If you're new to SRPGs or just want to try something different, Phantom Brave's worth checking out, largely because you won't find much else like it (even if you look to its cousins) and it gets cheap pretty often.  If you get into the game's systems and invest a little time, you'll probably be dozens of hours in before you even realize it.
