TLDR Version - Newbies should buy, Veterans (and Newbies who have access to the originals), should probably avoid.
After further tweaking (and finding out it is compatible with mods) I have come back to this game and its prequel, but I cannot change my vote to a recommendation: It's solid, but derivative. I am very, *very* glad for its existence, but I cannot recommend veterans to pick it up.
Get both Baldur's Gates (the second is not as fun without an imported character, and the first is not as fun without the BG "tutu" mod) and mod them. While I love bioware, and *did* gladly pay again, unless you have *both* never played Baldur's Gate before *and* are skittish or unaware of the modding community, it's not worth your time.

This game is a real blast from my past! I remember playing this as a kid, and revisiting it years later, it still holds up really well. If you're here for the mix of dark and silly humor of the Disgaea series, you aren't going to find it here. Sure, the story has its funny moments, but for the most part it's a bit more on the serious side, and there's nothing wrong with that. Great characters, nice voice acting (my man Steve Blum's here, and that always helps!), and a decent story to move you through the gameplay.
Gameplay is the real reason to be here, though. Simple yet deep, Phantom Brave shines in inviting and personalized combat and team structure. Tons of different unit types to start and even more to unlock makes it easy to customize your team exactly the way that you want. The only equipment that you need to worry about is your weapon, but you can use everything from standard RPG Swords, Axes, and Spears to weirder options like Books, Scrolls, and Logs, to things that don't make sense like Trees, Trolley Cars, Weeds, and even other units! Tons of special attacks, lots of units specialization through the Fusion system, and easy access to almost every item make it easy to try and blend everything!
Combat doesn't take place on a grid; instead, your units have a circular distance count and can move anywhere on the map on their turn within that circle on their turn, making positioning more fluid, and position strategy is as precise as you want it to be. This is helped by your deployment system: Rather than having a whole army on the field, you have your main character, who summons units (Phantoms) into objects on the battlefield. After a few turns, they'll vanish, leaving room for another ally. So you can have as many allies on standby as you want to make, and pick the best for any situation.
This review doesn't truly do the depth of the game justice. But it's a great, deep, interesting game with a lot to offer to anyone who's a fan of the genre, and is looking for something fun, but different in terms of gameplay and customizeability.

This will probably be a game you get addicted to (as you can no doubt see from my playing time). A few notes for a first-timer:
- Even if you've bought the DLC packs, I nevertheless recommend starting as a Christian. They tend to get a few more of the features to work with, such as extensive variations on the inheritance laws and CAROUSING. Also, it can be far more interesting to have only one wife - and many mistresses (or if your character is so inclined, male lovers).
- I also recommend starting at duke-level. You can then get in some experience of both lording it over a fun number of underlings whilst still having the challenge of (eventually) seizing the throne ahead of you.
- Keep one game going for at least a century. You might be tempted to suddenly flick your game as a Catholic French duke over to a Sunni Persian Satrap but the best games are the ones where you can see the full fruits of your labours.
- Don't be tempted to cheat. Believe me, losing wars, running out of money and ending up with an idiot drunkard son can sometimes be much more fun than having everything coming up roses.
I would recommend getting the DLCs just to add a tad more complexity to the game and some more variables in those occasional periods of eventless calm you get (and can fast forward through) between assassinating your nephew, appointing your new drinking buddy chancellor and recovering the Necronomicon from a desert hermit. I particularly recommend The Sword of Islam (letting you play as a Muslim ruler), The Old Gods (pagans and VIKING RAIDERS), Sons of Abraham (for those Poperific features and excellent events) and the Customisation Pack (yes, you CAN name that city Candyland and make your dynasty shield into a badass rainbow). Rajas of India and The Republic are perhaps best for later-game players who would enjoy the new variety an Indian Raja or Venetian Doge brings to the game. The portraits packs are also quite good, with the Turkish, Persian, African and Mediterranean faces being practically mandatory in my view.
Paradox is still continually fiddling with things and adding new features in both DLC and free patches - from the looks of it the DLC arriving tomorrow, 'Conclave', will be a must-have for any serious overlord - so there's plenty of new growth in this baby yet.
There are also a great and ever-increasing number of mods, from the mandatory Game of Thrones mod to ones enhancing the core game (CK2+ and Crusader Kings Expanded) or adding new features (the ever-popular Personal Castle mod and the Zun Invictus expansion of Zunist paganism).
Now, if you'll excuse me I have to go defend Sultan Hussayn II 'The Mad' of Filastin from a Byzantine attack (hopefully whilst getting one of my decadent and greedy younger sons killed in the process), secure a dynastic alliance with the Shah of Persia, arrange a trade mission to far-off barbarian lands and assassinate the Pope. All in a day's work...

The game is fun and great, until you leave the first island.
Once you leave Fort Joy, the games quality takes a sharp nosedive as it starts throwing encounters at you way out of your league without a warning unless you notice a single corpse laying on the ground and conjecture there might be enemies that will be spawned on you. Then there are so many glitches in the game it's extremely frustrating, such as the game straight up lying to you on who actually goes next in a turn based system. Such as MC, Party member #2, then #3, then #1, oh but wait, the boss gets a turn not shown on the UI and kills two of your party members because "Didn't expect that did you?". Then there's the extreme ramp in difficulty and scaling which puts MMO's to shame, from levels 1-10 you're increasing your damage by two or three points every level, but once enemies start hitting 11 and 12, their damage skyrockets by a hundred points.
The difficulty is all over the place as well. You can easily take on a 4v4 hidden hero encounter at level 9, while all the other enemies are level 12, and auto-revive into stronger versions with relative ease and tactics. But you talk to the wrong person, they forcefully initiate a fight 4v1, summon a monster in the middle of your entire team, and deals enough damage to OHKO your party members with a basic melee, and can opportunity attack. So you just fought a hidden boss encounter at level 9 and had a tough time but did eventually win it, and now you're getting OHKO'd by a simple minion a single character can summon multiple of?
It's fun, but manually save every three to four minutes, before you talk to anyone, before you walk into unknown territory, and after every single fight. The games autosave does a rather poor job of autosaving, and will make you lose hours of progress because "Oh you talked to this person and didn't know it was going to be a fight." There are a lot of forced encounters, save often, know what you're getting into before you get this game and learn it will throw artificial difficulty at you.

I first played this game back when I was 13. This was the first Elder Scrolls game that I was subject to (I was slightly too young to be interested in Morrowind at the timeit was released).  I had never played a game that allowed for such open-ended exploration and freedom.  This blew my mind when I first played and it seemed like there was always something new to find out in the world.  As a kid obsessed with this new experience, much of the flaws never really surfaced.
Fast forward 10 years.  For nostalgia's sake, I take another trip down memory lane.  It isn't as fantastic as I remember it (but nothing is as good as the first time).  The exploration is still the best part of this game (as it is with all Bethesda games), but the problem is, once you've seen everything, a game can get old quick when it relies heavily on exploration.  This is the problem with all future Bethesda games (but that's a conversation for another time).  The quests are what elevate Oblivion.  There are still some fetch quests, but I think those are few and far between in this game.  If there are fetch quests, they dress them up and throw in plenty of twists to make it interesting.  The best part is there are tons of quests in this game.  Reliving those, or trying out new ways to complete them made this second playthrough incredibly enjoyable. Oh, and do yourself a favor and play through the best DLC/expansion Bethesda has ever made.  Shivering Isles was so diverse and included so much content that I feel like I still haven't done everything to do there.
Downsides: Bugs, no real controller support, potato faces.

Based on an early board game played by Ancient Egyptians as early as 3100 BC.
The rules are simple, based on the notes of historian Timothy Kendall.
The gameplay itself is part strategy and part luck.
Strategic moves include moving in groups, blocking your opponent, and even knocking them into the House of Water.
Luck is based on dice roles, or in this case, stick throws.
Instructions on how to play the game are available from the main menu.
It supports local multiplayer, but sadly no online play.
Although it could technically be played with a screen sharing app, with one player moving the others players pawns based on verbal instructions.
Overall, I enjoyed the game.

Crusader Kings II (CKII) is the most tactical strategy game of all time. From the producers at Paradox, it incorporates a number of features missing from most strategy games, and provides a robust modding experience allowing players to rewrite history on their own terms. As a person who detested Paradox games, I went into CKII expecting to be turned away, but instead, I was sucked in to an intricately unique character development system.
Unlike most strategy games focusing on war and city-management, CKII's character development system sets the bar for future grand strategy games. Literally every character in the game has traits. These traits culminate into a character's statistics, and their behavioural A.I. For example, characters with the ambitious trait are aggressive in pursuing actions to further their own personal agenda; however, characters with the content trait tend to be passive. Characters who are lustful pursue multiple relationships, deceitful characters are more driven to betray others.
As your nation's leader, you must juggle between these behaviour types, and more, to create a peaceful and large country amongst threats from various warring fronts. You have rebels, political strife, assassinations, the Mongols, the Pope, and simply ill-fated events, such as the plague. Age is also a factor, and as you and your council grow older, your favorite characters are more suspectible to illness, and negative traits, such as being infirm. One day, my talented leader died because his heart wasn't healthy enough for sex. The game is profoundly deep, and you'll feel like it accounts for everything.
Speaking of sex, the game dives into very controversial taboos that would make some developers squeamish. There is imprisonment, torture, concubines, bi-sexual relationships, pagan religions, cruelty to children, making someone eunich, and that's just the original CKII content! Intrepid modders have already added slavery, assassinating your own children, and fantasy content, such as Succubi, werewolves, and vampires. The game is what you make of it!
CKII also has an ambitious Game of Thrones mod. It includes a customized map, and all the characters from the show with their corresponding behavioural traits, events, and more.
CKII is a ground-breaking ambitious title setting the bar for future strategy games. It's character-driven concept is fresh and innovative, and I hope Sega's Total War series embraces some of its ideas.

BEAMDOG, WHAT THE HECK!?
For old players returning after a long absence, you will immediately recognize a massive change in the UI thanks to some alterations by the aforementioned company. Black borders around the menu screen regardless of resolution, the Barbarian is tossed into the Fighter sub-class category, the original new portraits are replaced with some new-new portraits, and a slew of bugs and incompatability problems that make the game bug out more than it ever has before.

An entertaining game hampered by poor connectivity issues and host migration.
Gear Up has a lot to offer in terms of experimenting with different parts to make interesting tank builds. There are many different parts to choose from, although there are a select few weapons and cookie-cutter builds that are more efficient than others.
Although you'll get your rear handed to you when you first start out, you can earn a profit by amassing coins through winning rounds, so long as the rest of your team is up to snuff. If you can bear with getting OHK'ed by snipers and other high-damage combos, you can start bulking up and getting your hands on some better gear for yourself. Or, you can try to stick to lobbies with lower average ranks, to minimize the chance of getting ganked by veterans. You can probably expect to earn 3-4 coins on average by winning a team-based game mode. Considering a lot of parts are around 6 coins and the most expensive stuff clocks around 12, it doesn't take too long to get out of your rookie gear. You can be less than five hours into the game and have everything you need to play at higher levels.
When you've broken the beginner's barrier of mediocrity, then the game starts to get better. With each level you gain, another part slot is avaliable to you. I wouldn't say premium or even basic are worth the investment unless you want cosmetic items, because you can replicate the few truly effective builds even before you hit level five if you buy the right gear.
Once you're this far in, you can start enjoying the gameplay for what it is and experiment a little with adjustments to your tank. The action is moderate to fast-paced and keeps you on your toes, ready to zoom in on an objective or blast an unsuspecting foe. However, by now you've probably already noticed a few issues with the game's connectivity.
Gear Up has a poor method of migrating hosts after the original disconnects. Ususally the lobby will suddenly drop everyone from the game and you'll zoom around for a minute, wondering where everyone went before being booted yourself. It also suffers from keeping you connected period; the red warning icon at the top left of the screen is literally the devil and you'll meet him more often than you'd like. If it pops, up, expect to be redirected to the lobby in due time. Sometimes you'll notice that you or other tanks won't take damage on your screen - because they're not actually there, despite what you see. The game is hosted client-side, so someone with a terrible connection can wonk everything up for the whole lobby. Ghost damage, late deaths and high-ping kicks are too frequent.
That said, sometimes you'll get lucky and fight through an evening without a problem, and sometimes you'll get dropped 9/10 rounds and earn nothing to show for the time spent playing.  Gear Up's connectivity issues really ought to be solved before I can recommend anyone actually buy premium at $20 when you can go buy something else. Also, there's no option to play with friends. If you've got a buddy or group of friends, you won't be able to ensure you'll be on the same team. Even if you do happen to be placed on the same team one round, there's no guarantee you won't be shifted around in subsequent rounds. For free, Gear Up's not a bad timesink and it certianly is capable of providing a few hours of fun, in-between the issues it does have.
Hopefully the problems affecting playability will be addressed and fixed in the near future. if you think you can stomach some lost time here and there, then go for it and enjoy the brawlfest. Or, you can follow along and hop aboard when things get smoother. Until then, I can't honestly click the recommend button, as much as I want to.

A very much worthy game for Japanese T-RPG enthusiasts. Definitely not NIS's best game (Soul Nomads? Makai Kingdom? It's been a while but I enjoyed their fighting mechanics more), it's not even as good as the Disgaea games. It is, though, their most endearing, with a clichéd but sad & cute story centered around a 13yo who thinks she can get away with her weirdness by being nice to people. It doesn't work in real life but it's good to perservere I guess.
I could discuss the game for hours, but I found it more enjoyable once I enabled a mod to multiply game speed by 2 (the game is really too slow-paced otherwise), and even better, after I made my way to LV100 through cheating the game (there are various methods documented in FAQs, or you can just install a 1-hit kill trainer if you don't want to bother). This helped me complete the fights faster and just focus on the story. (Yes, the game is really challenging and requires a lot of grinding, and exploiting leveling tricks that aren't explicited in the game like ranked titles, random RPGs, etc.)
It's too bad that the later post-game EX maps have high requirements (finishing a 1000-floor dungeon, really?!), because they have stories tied to them. Well, I guess I'll just watch those on YouTube. While I did spend hundreds of hours on other NIS games, I'm too old for that now (and I have too many games on Steam).
Also, a few minor hindrances: while everything is remastered well, the zoomed 2D sprites are really distracting in story sequences. And why do they call scenes 'demos' anyway? And the last scene after the final boss? It's like, "eh?". Did they remove something for that release? If you're going to add a last-minute emotional twist to your story, maybe don't act like it never happened just a few seconds later..? Oh, and the soundtrack isn't Tenpei Satô's best I'm afraid. Not a single great song here, just generic happy-RPG stuff. Not my favorite composer overall, but at least his Disgaea themes are funny and recognizable.
The worst thing in the game would have to be the combat UI. I couldn't find a shortcut to end a turn. Given that you'll be selecting that option once per turn, that is up to hundreds of times per fight, and you'll have dozens of fights to go through, I'm not sure that went through their head.
Yes, I probably won't play it again because some other games will have priority over it, but I really liked the universe depicted in-game, the interesting characters, some game mechanics, the humor and the dungeon-RPG aspects.

I was formerly familiar only with NIS' Disgaeas and ZHP, so this was a small gamble that
paid off. It's a wonderful game and I thoroughly enjoyed it.
+ Great story, though mileage with
Maronakins may vary for the first chapter or two.
+ No grid combat, instead using free-form movement with various aoe shapes. Not only refreshing, but I found myself liking it more than the way Disgaea does it.
+More post game content than the Disgaeas I've played: the Hermuda isle and a whopping 12 EX missions.
+ 2 story modes, similar to how Disgaea2 DHD does it. One for the main game, and one with greater difficulty added in the remakes.
+ So many skills. So many cool skills.
= Main character Marona is your only normal character. She "confines" her phantom allies into items strewn around the field, and those phantoms have turn limits before being removed. I didn't mind it, but it means pouring all your efforts into a single character can cause you trouble if she gets removed.
= Item World is again, the end-all for leveling. This time for leveling items and titles. Different items have different aptitude%s for both equipping and confining into, and these can be incrementally increased by fusing items. Getting over 100% equip% for any stat takes
. Titles stack with this, and can provide various skills. Stats too of course. I found grinding these less taxing than grinding innocents, and felt more accomplishment for doing so.
= (post game) Character stats mean little compared to those granted by equipment (and this in a series where it already doesn't count for much). I found leveling characters just didn't matter, except for stealing.
= Speed stat God stat. Lacking attack power doesn't matter if your character gets 10 turns before your enemies' first.
– Magic skills look disappointing when compared to their Disgaea equivalent. (except Omega Thunder)
Play it, enjoy it. The main game does not require grinding if you play smart. So if you don't enjoy grinding, you can still get your worth.

*First I want to apologize because my English is not good, it is not my first language*
I do not usually write game analysis, but Animallica has something that leads me to write.
I love the concept of the game, the idea of ​​mixing the open world in the first person with a management of an animal sanctuary; Is the game that for many years I searched, tirelessly looked for mods for zoo tycoon 2 to transform it into something like that, but they do not exist.
Years later I find this surprise that comes to fill that gap left in me the fact that more games of animals of good level did not come to the market.
I feel that this project has a huge potential, I love that the game is not the "typical" classic multiplayer survival shooter such as ArK, Rust, etc etc etc that NEVER come out of early access. That animalistic touch and to preserve the fauna and flora, that altruistic mission entrusted to us is one of the aspects that I loved Animallica.
Another thing that for me is excellent, is the fact that they focus on the singleplayer experience, I'm fed up and really tired of seeing Early Access ark clones, rust, where they launch a product without any clear objective, with a multiplayer being Falls to pieces and without background.
Now I will talk a little about the fears or anguish that this game produces; Like many people here, I have tried MANY Early Access, I have seen projects that dazzle at the beginning, they shine a lot (I will not give names, because the list would be eternal), but that after a few months, this flame slowly begins to extinguish, The development becomes slower, the reviews change to varied, and finally to mostly negative; Then some developers slowly abandon projects and leave them unfinished.
My biggest fear with Animallica is to have discovered a game that in its essence I loved, that I would love to play it finished someday with all its mechanics implemented; But that over time is abandoned as it happens with many Early Access.
Please developers, do not let this flame go out like many others I have seen ascend to glory and then plunge into oblivion (DayZ), or even completely abandon its development and cancel the project (Stomping Land).
In the current state I recommend it ONLY if you are aware that it is an Early Access which contains bugs, incomplete aspects and is devoid of concrete objectives; But if you like animals, walk through fields, forests and beautiful landscapes, then buy it.
Suggestions:
- Improve interactions with animals, it is necessary to be able to feed them, take care of them, bars of happiness or well-being, creation of links with the player, differences between the character or "personality" of different animals, better AI of these same ones.
-To improve the combat system, which at the moment is really bad.
-The voice of the protagonist sometimes looks very feigned and is annoying the sound she makes every time you jump, could be every number of jumps, not always.
- You can change the object in hand of the bar by means of the scroll of the mouse.
-Interface improvements
-Abilities
-Menus to view animal statistics, such as states of health, mood, etc.

No suelo realizar análisis de juegos, pero algo tiene Animallica que me lleva a escribir este análisis.
Yo amo el concepto del juego, la idea de mezclar el mundo abierto en primera persona con una gestión de un santuario animal; es el juego que por muchos años busqué, incansablemente busqué mods para zoo tycoon 2 para transformarlo en algo asi, pero no hay.
Luego años mas tarde me encuentro con esta sorpresa que llega a llenar ese vacío que dejó en mi el hecho que no salieran al mercado mas juegos de animales de buen nivel.
Siento que este proyecto tiene un enorme potencial, me encanta que el juego no sea el “típico” shooter multiplayer survival de construcción clásico, como ArK, Rust, etc, etc, etc que no salen NUNCA del early access. Ese toque animalista y de preservar la fauna y flora, esa misión altruista que se nos encomienda es uno de los aspectos que me encantaron de Animallica.
Otra cosa que para mi es excelente, es el hecho de que se enfoquen en la experiencia singleplayer, estoy harto y de verdad cansado de ver Early Access clones de ark, rust, donde lanzan un producto sin ningún objetivo claro, con un multiplayer que se cae a pedazos y sin argumento de fondo.
Ahora hablaré un poco sobre los temores o angustias que me produce este juego, al igual que muchas personas aquí, he probado MUCHOS Early Access, he visto proyectos que deslumbran al inicio, que brillan mucho (no daré nombres, porque la lista sería eterna), pero que pasados unos meses, esta llama se comienza lentamente a apagar, el desarrollo se hace mas lento, las reviews pasan a variadas, y finalmente a mayormente negativas; luego algunos desarrolladores abandonan lentamente los proyectos y los dejan inacabados.
Mi mayor temor con Animallica es haber descubierto un juego que en su esencia me encantó, que me encantaría poder jugarlo terminado algún día con todas sus mecánicas implementadas; pero que pasado el tiempo se abandone como pasa con muchos Early Access.
Por favor desarrolladores, no dejen que esta llama se apague como muchas otras que he visto ascender a la gloria y luego sumirse en el olvido (DayZ), o incluso abandonar totalmente su desarrollo y cancelar el proyecto (Stomping Land).
En el estado actual lo recomiendo SOLO si tienes presente que es un Early Access el cual contiene bugs, aspectos incompletos y está carente de objetivos concretos; pero si te gustan los animales, recorrer descampados, bosques y paisajes bonitos, entonces cómpralo.
Sugerencias:
-Mejorar las interacciones con los animales, hace falta poder alimentarlos, cuidar de ellos, barras de felicidad o bienestar, creación de vínculos con el jugador, diferencias entre el carácter o “personalidad” de los diferentes animales, mejores AI de estos mismos.
-Mejorar el sistema de combate, que en estos momentos es realmente  malo.
-La voz de la protagonista aveces parece muy fingida y es molesto el sonido que ella hace cada vez que saltas, podría ser cada cierto número de saltos, no siempre.
-Poder cambiar el objeto en mano de la barra mediante el scroll del ratón.
-Mejoras en la interfaz
-Habilidades para el jugador
-Menús para ver estadísticas de los animales, como los estados de salud, ánimo, etc.
-Poder contratar NPC para que cuiden del santuario o que te ayuden a alimentar a los animales, porque imagino que al tener muchos animales mas adelante y si se implementa un sistema de cuidado de estos mismos, sería muy complejo cuidar uno solo de todos los animales.
Si se me ocurren mas sugerencias las pondré aquí con el tiempo o si hay actualizaciones que cambian algo de mi análisis.
A los desarrolladores les deseo lo mejor con este proyecto y que nunca se acaben los ánimos ni el entusiasmo (además de los fondos, porque no solo de entusiasmo se vive jajaja) para que este juego pueda llegar a buen termino y sea recordado como EL GRAN juego de supervivencia y cuidados de santuarios de animales.
Gracias por permitirnos ayudar y participar en esto.

I first played this game back when I was 13. This was the first Elder Scrolls game that I was subject to (I was slightly too young to be interested in Morrowind at the timeit was released).  I had never played a game that allowed for such open-ended exploration and freedom.  This blew my mind when I first played and it seemed like there was always something new to find out in the world.  As a kid obsessed with this new experience, much of the flaws never really surfaced.
Fast forward 10 years.  For nostalgia's sake, I take another trip down memory lane.  It isn't as fantastic as I remember it (but nothing is as good as the first time).  The exploration is still the best part of this game (as it is with all Bethesda games), but the problem is, once you've seen everything, a game can get old quick when it relies heavily on exploration.  This is the problem with all future Bethesda games (but that's a conversation for another time).  The quests are what elevate Oblivion.  There are still some fetch quests, but I think those are few and far between in this game.  If there are fetch quests, they dress them up and throw in plenty of twists to make it interesting.  The best part is there are tons of quests in this game.  Reliving those, or trying out new ways to complete them made this second playthrough incredibly enjoyable. Oh, and do yourself a favor and play through the best DLC/expansion Bethesda has ever made.  Shivering Isles was so diverse and included so much content that I feel like I still haven't done everything to do there.
Downsides: Bugs, no real controller support, potato faces.

This game was a lot of fun at first, and I really liked the concept.  With Robocraft finishing its course with me, I thought this game would be a nice change, while still being similar.  I was sorta right.  This game does have some good stuff going on, but there is just too much wrong with this game for me to give it a positive review.
Pros:
-Not a P2W model, shelling out a few bucks helps you get things faster, but the in game currency makes things easily unlockable
-A lot of robot customization
-Fun fast-paced gameplay
Cons:
-Weapons are extremely unbalanced, only half of them are usable.  Snipers and machine guns will pretty much win nearly ever situation and are very easy to use.  Flamethrowers rip everything in range apart in less than 2 seconds.  Explosive weapons aren't TOO bad, though I rarely use them.  Tesla weapons are slow projectiles and are very awkward to use, and have low ammo.  Laser weapons are slow projectiles that will lose to solid shell counterparts every time, despite the TINY damage boost.  Laser autocannon has garbage ammunition for an automatic weapon.  The firing arc on cannons after the basic noob cannon makes them very difficult to use beyond short range, save for the dragon cannon.  Plasma is a very slow projectile - when you get in range to where it is actually usable, the large impact radius hurts not only your enemy, but you too.
-Constant crashes throughout the game (customizing in-game, loading new maps, random CTDs without warning at any point)
-Optimization issues - while running with a framerate over 60 the entire time, my game still performed very sluggishly, and it was NOT due to ping
-Random few-second freezes during matches
-Nothing that shows exact ping when entering matches, every match I entered had a ping of 100+ even though my connection was great in the match menu before entering
-Wheel propulsions excluding the 6-wheel have HORRID turning radiuses, making them fast but very hard to maneuver
While I do like the gameplay, there are too few builds that work and too many problems with the client that ruin the game for me.

Baldur's Gate 2 is an old classic, updated with a fresh coat of paint, and some community mods incorporated as well, along with a bit of extra content. It's a lot longer than most modern RPG's, and offers a ludicrous amount of replayability for its price tag, however, it's still, at heart, a really old game that has not aged well in a lot of aspects, while other components are still stellar to this day.
Baldur's Gate is based off of the antiquated 2.0e D&D ruleset, offering counterintuitive game mechanics, poor balance, limited flexibility, and poor character creation, with minimalistic control over appearance, stats, and no 'feats' like exist in most D&D based games. Its gameplay itself is incredibly wonky and variable, classes like Fighter having at best, a single self-buff skill until epic levels, and otherwise entirely being left click and watch, while classes like Wizard have ridiculously high, and unforgiving skill ceilings. In terms of gameplay, character creation, class balance, and art design, I'd have to say that Baldur's Gate is far inferior to its spiritual successors such as Dragon Age, or Pillars of Eternity. It's aged poorly, and doesn't hold up well, even for its low price tag in these regards.
However, there's aspects in which, it still holds up, and I would recommend it. While casters, rather infuriatingly, have their spells interrupted when taking damage, resulting in a lot of unforgiving requirements for positioning, the Wizard, Sorcerer, and Cleric classes are ludicrously powerful in ways that a lot of RPG's usually tone down for balance reasons. In Baldur's Gate, a high level caster will play like a demi-god, summoning pit fiends, controlling minds, calling down angels, raining meteors from the heavens, killing with a single touch, create hordes of undead, extend phantasms of yourself capable of casting spells and fighting for you, etc. The level of power given to casters in this game is phenominal and satisfying when mastered, and a Cleric/Wizard multiclass has such a ludicrous amount and variety of potent spells that it'll take you longer to scroll through them all than it will to handle the encounter itself.
But let's say casters aren't your thing, there's still a couple aspects in which Baldur's Gate 2 is worth a look. The first, is writing. There's a lot of it, and it's all stellar, and a lot of the time, easy to miss, as the vast majority of content in Baldur's Gate is optional sidequests, but regardless of how you slice it, Baldur's Gate offers a large amount of quality content, with interesting writing, characters, different tones, and those decision making mechanics that people love so much.
The second, is the main reason that, years later, I still find myself coming back to Baldur's Gate 2, and that is the game's pacing. The common RPG notions of "Oh, you're a normal person, then a thing happened, now there's a secret society, kill it, and save the entire planet", two act arc, is really quite overdone and forced. A lot of RPG's will quickly rush to topics of killing gods, or saving the world, sprinting headlong into the notion of the highest degree of escalation at a breakneck speed.  Baldur's Gate 2 escalates to the same level, but it paces it out, and gives the player time to adapt to each new level of capability before moving onto the next. When you hit epic levels, be prepared to
have to hold your own against entire armies. However, unlike a long RPG like say, Final Fantasy, do not expect to need to 'grind'. Doing quests is more than enough to fully cap out an entire adventuring party, with a fair amount of content left afterwards. I think the pacing of the game's content in terms of gameplay escalation of difficulty, and the pacing of the content in terms of plot development, is well balanced in a way that most games these days really miss out on.
As well, the game has built in multiplayer support, with Beamdog hosted servers, along with being able to run your own--usually for modded content--allowing you to bring along friends with split control over the party, which offers even more replayability to an already fairly lengthy game.

This will probably be a game you get addicted to (as you can no doubt see from my playing time). A few notes for a first-timer:
- Even if you've bought the DLC packs, I nevertheless recommend starting as a Christian. They tend to get a few more of the features to work with, such as extensive variations on the inheritance laws and CAROUSING. Also, it can be far more interesting to have only one wife - and many mistresses (or if your character is so inclined, male lovers).
- I also recommend starting at duke-level. You can then get in some experience of both lording it over a fun number of underlings whilst still having the challenge of (eventually) seizing the throne ahead of you.
- Keep one game going for at least a century. You might be tempted to suddenly flick your game as a Catholic French duke over to a Sunni Persian Satrap but the best games are the ones where you can see the full fruits of your labours.
- Don't be tempted to cheat. Believe me, losing wars, running out of money and ending up with an idiot drunkard son can sometimes be much more fun than having everything coming up roses.
I would recommend getting the DLCs just to add a tad more complexity to the game and some more variables in those occasional periods of eventless calm you get (and can fast forward through) between assassinating your nephew, appointing your new drinking buddy chancellor and recovering the Necronomicon from a desert hermit. I particularly recommend The Sword of Islam (letting you play as a Muslim ruler), The Old Gods (pagans and VIKING RAIDERS), Sons of Abraham (for those Poperific features and excellent events) and the Customisation Pack (yes, you CAN name that city Candyland and make your dynasty shield into a badass rainbow). Rajas of India and The Republic are perhaps best for later-game players who would enjoy the new variety an Indian Raja or Venetian Doge brings to the game. The portraits packs are also quite good, with the Turkish, Persian, African and Mediterranean faces being practically mandatory in my view.
Paradox is still continually fiddling with things and adding new features in both DLC and free patches - from the looks of it the DLC arriving tomorrow, 'Conclave', will be a must-have for any serious overlord - so there's plenty of new growth in this baby yet.
There are also a great and ever-increasing number of mods, from the mandatory Game of Thrones mod to ones enhancing the core game (CK2+ and Crusader Kings Expanded) or adding new features (the ever-popular Personal Castle mod and the Zun Invictus expansion of Zunist paganism).
Now, if you'll excuse me I have to go defend Sultan Hussayn II 'The Mad' of Filastin from a Byzantine attack (hopefully whilst getting one of my decadent and greedy younger sons killed in the process), secure a dynastic alliance with the Shah of Persia, arrange a trade mission to far-off barbarian lands and assassinate the Pope. All in a day's work...

So, I really like this game but I'll try to approach this from a reasonably neutral point of view.
Awesomenauts is a crazy 2D MOBA where you must push the enemy back and destroy their base (Guarded by turrets).
Pros:
-There are a lot of characters to choose from, all varying in abilities.
-Characters each have cute or funny little backstories, varying, strange, and quirky personalities Ex:       A gangster breakdancer frog who grew up in the ghetto.
-Almost all the abilities are all extremely different and interact together in so many different ways.
-Very well done balancing, and although you may think things are unbalanced when you start playing nauts, there is so much strategy involved in the game.
-There are a bunch of unlockable sidegrades that may fit your playstyle perfectly.
-There is a prestige system, once you get max level you have the option to reset your level and get a shiny medal beside your name. You'll keep all the characters you unlocked but all the sidegrades for them get relocked.
-The music in this game is amazing and fits the theme perfectly. Theres special music for each character.
Cons:
-Although earlier I said balancing seems awesome the more you play, its absolutely crazy when you start out! Things'll be doing what seems like an insane amount of damage! You'll be screaming for nerfs (Probably)!
-The community. There are some AMAZING people in the Awesomenauts community but thats like 3/10 people. Then maybe 5/10 people are batshit crazy and get angry super easily, troll, and basically take a dump on the sanctity of the game. 2/10 people though, are pretty apathetic to the whole thing. Silent mutes, the lot of them.
-No dedicated servers. The servers use steam, so if steam crashes you wont be able to play. They're working on it.
-Lag. A whole lot. You can minimize the lag by setting the matchmaking search to NOT worldwide, and then it becomes not too bad. Its usually not crazy rubberbanding or melee attacks hitting from across the map, just things like "I was behind that turret!" or "No way she has that much range!" or "THIS GAME IS ♥♥♥♥ING ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T!!!!11!11!".
-Requires teamwork. Some games (If you soloQ) you will get absolutely demolished by the enemy premade team, OR your team will just blow.
-You have to put around 10-30 minutes per game, depending on whether its a total stomp or both teams are evenly matched.
Awesomenauts is an awesome take on the MOBA genre (IMO) and should be enjoyed by everyone. If you think you might maybe enjoy Awesomenauts a tiny little bit, you should probably buy it. Its only $10.99 Candian, so if you have the money to buy this, you should. Remember to never rage, its just a game.
NOTE: Its amazing fun to play solo, but a team makes this much more fun.

Crusader Kings II (CKII) is the most tactical strategy game of all time. From the producers at Paradox, it incorporates a number of features missing from most strategy games, and provides a robust modding experience allowing players to rewrite history on their own terms. As a person who detested Paradox games, I went into CKII expecting to be turned away, but instead, I was sucked in to an intricately unique character development system.
Unlike most strategy games focusing on war and city-management, CKII's character development system sets the bar for future grand strategy games. Literally every character in the game has traits. These traits culminate into a character's statistics, and their behavioural A.I. For example, characters with the ambitious trait are aggressive in pursuing actions to further their own personal agenda; however, characters with the content trait tend to be passive. Characters who are lustful pursue multiple relationships, deceitful characters are more driven to betray others.
As your nation's leader, you must juggle between these behaviour types, and more, to create a peaceful and large country amongst threats from various warring fronts. You have rebels, political strife, assassinations, the Mongols, the Pope, and simply ill-fated events, such as the plague. Age is also a factor, and as you and your council grow older, your favorite characters are more suspectible to illness, and negative traits, such as being infirm. One day, my talented leader died because his heart wasn't healthy enough for sex. The game is profoundly deep, and you'll feel like it accounts for everything.
Speaking of sex, the game dives into very controversial taboos that would make some developers squeamish. There is imprisonment, torture, concubines, bi-sexual relationships, pagan religions, cruelty to children, making someone eunich, and that's just the original CKII content! Intrepid modders have already added slavery, assassinating your own children, and fantasy content, such as Succubi, werewolves, and vampires. The game is what you make of it!
CKII also has an ambitious Game of Thrones mod. It includes a customized map, and all the characters from the show with their corresponding behavioural traits, events, and more.
CKII is a ground-breaking ambitious title setting the bar for future strategy games. It's character-driven concept is fresh and innovative, and I hope Sega's Total War series embraces some of its ideas.

I've decided I should update my review with my feelings as time has progressed.
Maybe it is unfair to compare this to DotA, but the competitive moba nature lends to it well.  While the game is a lot more casual in nature, such that I feel like I can quit in the middle of the game if I need to, and that I do not need to invest as much energy or time to be competent in it, I find myself enjoying the game less.  In fact, as time has progressed, I feel I get much more frustrated with my games in Awesomenauts.  This is often due to matchmaking, or what I perceived as questionable balance.
The matchmaking of the game is quit frustrating.  I don't know if there' s anything that can be done to improve this, as the player base is relatively small.  But as it is, when you get matched up against a premade team of excellent players, it can often feel like there's nothing you can do to combat the opposition.  And due to the small player base, this can happen often, and multiple times in a row, especially once you start getting to around tier 3.
I question the balance and design decisions of some characters.  The only character I feel with certainty is unbalanced is Lonestar, for his ability to take out towers singlehandedly, and with relatively little farm.  His bull gives him ridiculous pushing power, and his dynamite and high dps means he can pick at a tower more efficiently than most.  I feel like if my team is not completely dominating or the opposing Lonestar is not incompetent, then we'll stand to lose simply due to his pushing and anti-pushing power.  Even with a kill advantage this can be a problem.  That being said, a lot of other characters can be very frustrating to deal with, even if they are balanced.  Gnaws plants have a lot of hit points and regenerate health.  Skolldir can get an almost guaranteed kill if he manages to get within throwing range on some maps.  Froggy G can deal crap loads of damage, has quick mobility, escape mechanisms, and an ability that can make him deadly to attack.
All in all, I want the community to grow, and I hope the developers consider revisiting the skills heroes and the mechanics of the game.  They do make balancing changes, so I do hope the game improves, especially with the Starstorm expansion in development.

Loved this game ever since the original PS2 release.

The overall game formula is a fairly standard isometric turn-based SRPG, with a few twists:
No gridlines. Movement range is a circular radius, most attack ranges/AoEs are spheres or cylinders.
Having a "Movement Radius Remaining" meter has some fun use cases on slippery terrain, you can "skate" to move further than you'd normally be able to.
The "OB" mechanic! Some generic monster causing you problems? Pick it up and throw it off the edge of the map!
Careful, though. Chucking enemies off the edge causes their buddies to gain levels.
(Oh, and they can throw YOUR guys off the map too!)
The story and voice acting are about "generic anime"-tier, but Marona as a character is really endearing.
It's more about Marona growing up as a person, and being able to make it on her own.
The "save the world" part feels a little ancillary, and that's okay!

TL;DR: It's a decent little game, but everything just kinda plays too slowly.
Good points:
* short levels that generally don't overstay their welcome.
* collectable items aren't irritatingly difficult to find.
* fully rebindable controls.  (They start off as WASD + something on the right side of the letters, but I rebound them to arrow keys + ZXCASD very easily.)
* level design on boss stages: bosses themselves are easily accessible, so you can practice on them, without going through the rest of the stage.  Basically, you can separately practice getting the kimonos and beating the bosses.  This is good stage design.
Not-so-good points:
* Basically everything in the game moves too slowly:
* * Left/right movement momentum effects, making it so that you can't turn or stop quickly.
* * Akane grabs the wall if she runs into it while moving downward, and doesn't ungrab it even when you let go of the direction facing the wall, so you can either slide down slowly or slide down somewhat more quickly (if you press down), but you can't just drop down.  (Strangely, boosting off of a wall causes Akane to move much more quickly.)
* * Level complete screen animation and music just takes too long to play out.
* * Game over sequence also takes too long to play out, considering how easy it is to fail a stage.
...So in general, it doesn't feel like you're playing a ninja.  You don't get to enjoy the agility of a ninja...though it's not like the enemy ninjas do either.
* Edges of platforms should be drawn so that they don't stick out beyond their hitbox (or don't stick out that much).  This applies mainly to the forest area.
* Bug: If you are in a corner and there is water flowing against you, you can't simply move left/right out of it.  You can only jump out of it.  (Please post a comment if this is fixed; then I will remove this item.)
* Soundtrack doesn't loop properly -- it fades out then restarts.  (You might notice this if you take too long to figure out the second boss's pattern.)
(Disclosure: I acquired this game as part of the Groupees Doujin Bundle 3.)

Atmosphere. Something that is so important in many games and something that Stalker completely nails right from the start. You begin the game on a lonely hillside and (if your PC is up to the challenge) the whole bleak and scary Pripyat region opens up around you. An urgency sets in that makes you desperate to reach the dim point of light in the distance that marks one of the few safe havens in the Zone. I've played through the game a few times since its release and even now I can't quite put my finger on how they managed to make even the open daylit areas so scary - and then you reach a point were the games narrative demands you go under ground and the fear just seeps out of the game in a wonderful adrenaline fueled way. You'll jump at every noise and wave your torch about in panic. For a game to make you feel insignificant and unprotected even when you are packing an automatic machine gun and plenty of ammo is a triumph in game design. Is it a FPS? Yes, and I for one enjoyed the rather clunky combat as it added to the realism. Is it an RPG? Yes, and the search for better gear and better anomoly upgrades to help combat the Zone will force you to brave the most dangerous areas. Above all, for me, this game is an adventure survival game. From the moment I stepped into the Zone I felt that I was simply trying to survive in a way that many other 'survival games' fail to achieve. The Zone is the enemy here - and it is trying to kill you
If you like your games atmospheric then I wholly recommend Stalker - it is absolutely dripping in it

My favoite game of all time, and I think it will always be my favoite game. Elder Scrolls Oblivion IV is set within the province of Cyrodiil, the heartland and Imperial capital of Tamriel. Emperor Uriel Septim VII is assassinated in flight from his own palace, but just before he dies he passes on to you—the foreordained of his dreams—the mystic Amulet of Kings. The adventure proper begins with the quest to find Uriel's lost and illegitimate son—the only heir to the throne. In a world where the forces of darkness seek their ultimate dominion over the ranks of man and mer alike, you alone stand between the future of Tamriel and the gates of Oblivion.
The game has a large collection of mods you may install to increase your game play if you would like, also I recommed getting all of the DLC's which are all included in the Game of the Year Edition. List of DLC's:
-Battlehorn Castle: Rescue Battlehorn Castle from marauders, and claim it as your own.
-Horse Armor Pack: Protect your horse from danger with this beautiful handcrafted armor.
-Knights of the Nine: A fallen King has been unchained from the darkness of Oblivion to seek vengeance upon the Gods who banished him. Only a champion pure of heart can vanquish the evil that has been released upon the land. You must heed the call, reclaim the lost relics of the Divine Crusader, and return the Nine to glory. New dungeons, characters, quests, and mysteries await.
-Unearthing Mehrunes Razor: Conquer one of the deepest and most challenging dungeons in all of Cyrodiil to claim this fearsome weapon.
-Repairing the Orrery: Harness the power of the stars. Rebuild the defiled Orrery and unlock the secrets of this Mages Guild Inner Sanctum.
-Spell Tomes: Add "Spell Tomes" to the world's random treasure which grant you new and powerful magic spells, just by reading them.
-Dunbarrow Cove: Uncover a famous pirate's lost ship and claim it as your own.
-Deepscorn Hollow: Deepscorn Hollow is an asylum for the wicked, a refuge from the persecution of the virtuous.
-Frostcrag Spire: In the frozen mountains of Cyrodiil stands Frostcrag Spire, a tower of wonders for your magic-oriented character to call home.
-Shivering Isles is the first and only major expansion for Oblivion. It takes place in Sheogorath's plane of Oblivion. Sheogorath seeks a mortal as his champion. Many mysteries await your investigations in this twisted, split reality that the Prince of Madness calls the Shivering Isles.
With such a large amount of DLC's, the Game of the Year Edition is worth the money by far. For $20 you can get normal Oblivion, or you can get the Game of the Year Edition for $25. The better deal is up to you though. You may be asking "What if I already have the normal Oblivion and I want the DLC's?". I belive that you can buy them separately... but don't take my word for that. I could be wrong.
There are many ways to create the game around you at the very start of the game. The factors that you must decide upon are:
-Your Race and Gender
Determines Attributes, skill bonuses, and special abilities (greater powers, lesser powers, constant effect characteristics)
Your Birthsign
Provides special abilities (typically attribute bonuses or greater powers)
-Your Class - the single most complex decision you need to make.
One option is to use one of the game's built-in standard classes.
The other option is to create a custom class, in which case you need to make decisions about specialization, attributes, and major skills.
-Your Appearance - While largely governed by your choices of gender and race, you can also fine-tune most aspects of your character's physical appearance. These choices have no effect upon gameplay.
There are also a few races you can choose from to determain your character that much more which include:
Altmer (high elf)

Argonian
Bosmer (wood elf)

Breton

Dunmer (dark elf)

Imperial

Khajiit

Nord
Orc
Redguard
with a decent selection, you can choose your race and his/her apperence. There are also mods to add more races if you would like. This is another way to increase the gameplay to your liking.
The game also has a great feel and the music makes it that much better. The music varies from slow, "exploration" themes to faster, "battle" themes. It is often easy to tell when an enemy sees the player character because the music will change sharply.
Quests are sorted by where they are assigned or by which faction assigns them. There are 231 distinct quests in the original game. The Official Plug-ins added 9 new quests total. The Shivering Isles expansion pack adds 40. This makes the game that much more interesting since you never know what quest there might be and makes you explore the land that much more. Most, if not all, of the quests have a good feel. They all are very entertaining and I encourage you to complete them all.
In conclusion, I believe this is one of the best game that you can buy for such a great price. Very expansive and will leave you playing for hours between the main quest and side quests. With thousends of mods to expand your game play, you can make the game fit you that much more. The game really never gets old, and the fun never ends. Rated 10/10

While Fallen Earth is an enjoyable MMO set in a Fallout universe, there are some glaring issues that impact the experience of the game.  The biggest problem I have had is to connect to the game.  As soon as you choose / create your character the game gets stuck on a loading screen.  No indication as to what the problem was, I looked online, and a huge amount of people had the same issue.  Eventually I narrowed this down to a connection issue between the game client and the servers.  The Devs refuse to be transparent about this, which says a lot, especially in a MMO.  This failure of the devs to be transparent and the 6 months of them failing to fix the issue since I became aware of and reported it, does not inspire any confidence in them being able to tend to a MMO.
So for all the game's successes, it is sad that there is one failure that no amount of successes can smooth over, which is the deplorable behaviour of the development / moderation team in a MMO.

Won best PvP of E3 2011. That's when it was still growing here. This game due to verious reasons , one being it's art style , is what makes this game subjective to your taste. Some people played for a bit and wrote it off as unbalanced or child-like. Clearly not giving it much of a chance.
First off it is in no way a pay-to-win.
Second I've never seen too many games where your level is NOT the main thing that matters , but skill. An example when i first started I had a guild carry me to level 24 . I then faced a level 10 in pvp and lost. He knew what he was doing unlike me.
With such a large variety or armour , sub-classes , and side-quest. It allows you to create and mold a unique powerful character to your liking. The story various character to character giving you more in-depth gameplay.
Movement is fluid , fighting smooth. The game and the players never ceases to challenge you . You wont get bored unless you spoil it for your self. I mean that in a lot of ways. The fun in this game comes with the story, not knowing what new move you'll get next level, discovering new places, ccreating amazing weapons and armour, defining your character, and playing with the community. Ignore these things and trying to hard can ruin the experience of any mmo for you. Dont outcast yourself and just try and enjoy it.
The only con i can actually think of is , gender lock. A lot of people just left huh? Well if gender choice is a must have , still give it a shot. If you are not having fun by level 25 (if you followed the quest the right way and paced your self) then go ahead and drop it. However you will be missing out.
Lastly have fun. Some characters might not be for you, try something else. Try talking to people. Figure out how to fight. What moves work. Learn how to do and use things from certain quest. This game keeps you on your toes. Everything seems over whelming at first , but it is much simpler then you realize, and a lot more fun too.
Personal opinon. Your first class just go for it. learn from your mistakes. you can always make a second class and trust me , eatch class is different enough where it wont be tedious in anway to start over. Assassin has my favorite story. Warrior my favorite moves. Cleric is fun for parties. Archer is good in PvP . I could go on forever , I already kind of did lol

Senet is a board game for two players against AI or hotseat, like an easier version of backgammon. It was created by Egyptians in a tech park ("smart village") outside of Cairo, Egypt.
The second video on the store page shows some of the gameplay. The game is quite similar to backgammon, except you're playing in the same direction, and a blockade (sort of) is formed by two or more pawns in sequence - there's never more than one pawn on any space of the board. The game provides little backstory. It is a single player against AI (3 levels of difficulty) or hot-seat two-player gameplay. The game runs fine even on older computers.
The pieces move across the board in a Z-shapes path, i.e. right on the top row, left on the center row, then right on the bottom row; your aim is to move all of your pieces off the board before your opponent does. Since there can never be more than one piece on any square, you can generally only move to unoccupied squares; you can also swap position with an opponent's pawn if it has no other pawn adjacent to protect it. Your "dice" are 4 sticks colored red and white; the number of whites is your roll, but if you have all red, that counts as 5. You get to roll again on any 1,4 or 5, as often as they keep occurring; play switches to your opponent as soon as you roll a 2 or 3 and make your move. To reduce swapping in the endgame, every pawn needs to reach the 5th to last square (with the paddles), from there, a 5 moves it off the board, 4,3 and 2 move it to end squares where it needs to stay until moved off the board with a throw of 1, 2 or 3 respectively; and a 1 (which must be taken if no other pawn is movable) moves it to the water square, which moves it up a row to the rebirth ankh, or if that's occupied, to the first unoccupied square before it; the same thing happens to pawns that get swapped out on the end squares. Strategy is generally to keep your stones grouped (any group of two or more is safe from swapping), preventing the opponent from forming groups and setting your own stones back, while trying to swap his own stones back.
I'd say that games are faster than backgammon because pawns that get "hit" don't move back as much; and the strategy is slightly easier, for the same reason. The rules are easy to pick up because the game marks all of your pieces that have legal moves.
If you plan to play against a friend, I'd recommend the tablet version (iOS or Android) since that's more comfortable than hotseat on a PC (the board is probably too small for a smartphone screen though); but there's nothing wrong with the Steam version. You're getting a simple board game, no bells and whistles; while you could easily make your own board or use a free flash version (or
for online multiplayer), this'll provide an AI to play against on your own and helps you learn the rules.

Alright, I was pleasently surprised with this game so here's teh simple breakdown:
Pros:
-Fun, fast paced style of gameplay. Death results in a few short seconds and you drop back onto the field.
-Style/Attitude works well, its heavilty stylized to not look too realistic nor too cartoony. Its a little whimsical and I personally like that. It doesnt take itself too seriously and therefore is an easy pick up and learn to play sort of game.
-Decent variety of parts, game types, etc.  You can build just about anything you'd like and play in a usual range of PvP game types, Deathmatch, with or without teams, capture the point. There may be a couple others I'd forgotten about but its all very standard.
-The tank controls are difficult but not too stupidly hard. They require some getting used to, but they make kills feel earned and skilled. One of a short list of PC titles I chose to play using keyboard and mouse rather than my xbox controller.
Cons:
-Pay to win; If you dont shell out the $20 price tag you have to earn your tank parts and customizations like in a normal game. Thats fine with me, but if you DO spend the money, every part in the game is instantly unlocked. There do not appear to be any game breaking destructive weapons that allow you to dominated if you have them, however the spirit of the game ruined by the random matches full of folks who spent the cash and have the best tank they could design.
-This means you better play with friends to have fun. Now I'm not saying you cant pick this game up and play against randoms and not have a good time. However logging in with a group of pals and building machines of war and playfully blowing eachother up is way better.
-The Host system is a little bit... not good. Its the usual idea, when you are in the lobby you can click a button to invite your list of friends. The problem is that it checks them off so you cannot resend the invite if there is an issue. And there were issues. A couple instances where players did not recieve the invite and the only fix was to back out and start a new room. There also is no 'ready up' system where the host can launch the game for everyone. Everyone in the lobby has to hit their respective 'start game' button before anything happens. Not game breaking, but clunky.
Final thoughts:
Yes. Download the free version, skype with some friends, and start building your tanks. It was absolutly worth the time and effort put in and was a lot of fun. I may even pay for the basic package that grants you extra colors to paint your tank in and unlimited storage so I can collect more than 9 parts at a time. The game looks good, feels good, and has some degree of depth to it that I enjoy (Like using a spider tank to clamber clumsily up the wall to avoid my enemies).

The original Baldur's Gate II is one of my favourite games of all time. A huge world with plenty of engaging characters, tough challenges, great dialogue, and tonnes of replayability. It's a game I've played once or twice a year since I first bought it ten years ago. This Enhanced Edition is a mostly improved version of that game, so of course I recommend it to anyone looking for a great game. The game has been improved graphically, multiplayer has been modernized, and extra content has been added. The additional content mostly matches the feel of the original Baldur's Gate, and anything that you don't like is easily ignored.  Generally speaking, bugs have been fixed, though there are still some minor ones present. Bugs are going to be present in any version of Baldur's Gate due to all of the complexity and variables. Fortunately, Beamdog is still releasing patches to fix what they can. Most of the mods for Baldur's Gate have been updated to work with the Enhanced Edition as well, so there's very little reason to play the original over the Enhanced Editions.
Basically, get this game. And Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition, obviously, because why would you want to start with 2?

Right away I have to get out there that in my top 20 list of all-time favorite games, Final Fantasy Tactics (War of the Lions) and Advance Wars (Dual Strike), and this, Phantom Brave (on the PSP) will most likely always have a spot.
Yes, the port was released lacking and it put a lot of otherwise dedicaed fans of Nippon Ichi off.  I'm crossing my fingers for some reworked sprites, but I have to say right now that the game on my 27" monitor doesn't look NEARLY as bad as Square's Android to Steam ports that have your characters taking up more than a third of the screen.  The menus are sized perfectly, and the controls allow you to navigate exactly like you needed to on the PSP.  If I remember correctly, they removed a vital stat from the Wii version in which this port is based, but a recent update remedied that.  Even if they drop the effort and don't at least fix some of the ugly sprite scaling (and some 3D artifacts that appear when rotating the camera) I still intend to play this game as I have many times in the past.
Overall, as a unique entry in a landscape of very diverse turn based strategy games, Phantom Brave, to me, is special.  Story progression is entirely at your own pace, and offers a nice middle-ground difficulty between FFT 1.3 (Insane) and Disgaea 1.  The character class roster is huge and the random battlefield/dungeon generation is quirky and simply FUN.
I never would have thought a SRPG that centered around a single character who served as, essentially, your main menu, but was also required in every single major battle to fight alongside you could work- the concept itself is baffling at first- but Marona functions marvelously and switches things up a bit when similar titles rely on more standard planning and execution.
I mean, this kid who can see ghosts can "confine" them to just about any inanimate object to have them fight for her is awesome and absurd; the fact that the game offers so much content for even basic stuff like
, huh?  The best thing is that it works, somehow.
Not for everyone, Phantom Brave has a decent hardcore underbelly but never once takes itself seriously- and there's bound to be a ton of fans complaining about the unfortunate scaling with the sprites and that's NIS's fault, because it most assuredly deserves the polish of a redraw and texture update.  This is one of those games that you either love or hate and there really isn't any way to sway you otherwise.  For the amount of time I played it on PSP, the price is more than fair.  If you've never played it but you enjoyed Disgaea or FFT, give it a shot, because this game offers up MASSIVE content and countless hours of enjoyment.

Please read my review on Baldur's Gate I: Enhanced Edition first as that details the general stuff about the Baldur's Gate series. This review features two specific parts: Shadows of Amn and the expansion, Throne of Bhaal. Additionally I'll give my overall experience having played both of these.
You start off captured as a prisoner* in a dungeon underground by an unknown individual whom you have never seen before and he is basically torturing you in your cell for some unknown reason which will ultimately become apparent as you progress through this game. Only thing that will be apparent at the start is that he seems to be trying to bring out some unknown power you have. All of a sudden the dungeon itself is attacked by an unknown group, forcing your capturer/the torturer to teleport out of the dungeon allowing another prisoner who somehow escaped from her cell (gee I wonder how she did that?) and she reveals to you her name: Imoen. After a discussion about what the torturer did to you and her, she springs you free from your cell, and from there, your immediate objective at that point, is to not only escape the dungeon, but to find anyone that is currently in the dungeon to join your party to make the escape a little easier, but you can attempt to escape on your own if you wish, having others with you just makes it easier. Once you finally escaped from the dungeon (you'll end up in Waukeens Promenade which is essentially a place within the City of Amn or rather "Athkatla"), your torturer, sounding particularly happy (and evil) commends you for escaping the dungeon, the exit of which collapses behind you after escaping. Imoen who had also been tortured by that guy demands to be released and launches a magic attack against him, he retaliates with a magic attack of his own, causing half-a-dozen hooded figures to teleport in to stop it and attempt to arrest him, and after the torturer resists both the hooded figure attacks and Imoen's own attacks, they ultimately arrest both the torturer and Imoen on grounds of using magic in a place (which is later revealed to be Amn) which is prohibited. From that point you'll have two primary objectives, find and rescue Imoen who was captured and settle the score with that torturer.
Additionally in this game, among the outstanding number of quests you can undertake, you'll have class-specific quests to take on too, so for example, if your protagonist is primarily a fighter, you'll be tasked by a kind-hearted noble, with clearing monsters infesting a huge Keep and killing their leader and if you succeed you'll get a chance to become head of the Keep which you can use as your own home to manage as you see fit.
Also for example, if your protagonist is primarily a Mage, you'll be tasked by a ranger to help him defeat his ancestor Lavok in what is known as a "Planar Sphere" located in Amn. That sphere will be yours if you defeat Lavok inside of it.
Those types of quests depend upon what your protagonist's class is. Something worth keeping in mind.
After you have successfully completed your final objective in Shadows of Amn, it is revealed that a certain prophecy describes children (including yourself by the way) of a tainted godly blood, that will cause a wave of massive destruction destroying all in existance including each other. in order to fulfil a certain purpose. You are urged by an Elven Queen to visit a sacred grove to discover some answers as to why this prophecy is even relevant to you and what part you will likely play in it. After you have visited the grove and listened to the prophecy spoken (which also states that there is a person you may encounter at some point on your journey, who has "the face of an ally", but has "the mask of a foe"), you are ambushed by what is revealed to be a "Bhaalspawn" (that's right a Child of the dead God of Murder, Bhaal) and her troupe, whose main objective is to kill you as a Bhaalspawn yourself. Once you have disposed of her and her troupe you get teleported into what is called a "Pocket Plane" which is essentially your sanctuary for you to rest and take up challenges and even upgrade certain weapons you have into powerful items via the imp Cespanar. At that point, you are visited by a familiar individual whom you had killed in the past, after vowing to never betray you if you let him join you, he gives you intel about the Pocket Plane you are in and states that it doesn't take you to where you want to go, it takes you to where you need to be: Saradush. Once you teleport to Saradush, which is under heavy enemy attack from outside its walls you meet up with a nice woman who is trying to save the people of Saradush, which ultimately becomes your objective as well, however it doesn't just end there as there are many quests to undertake after that, which may involve you ultimately battling other Bhaalspawn that will also seek your death among others etc.
Both of these games provide a super thrilling challenge the likes of which no other rpg strategy game is likely to provide, because among other familiar enemies, you'll even encounter monsters/creatures you have never fought before. In my particular case, I always enjoy the thrill of battle, so doesn't matter how hard an enemy may be, I'll always rise up to the challenge. Some will be easy, others will be hard to kill depending on how you have built your protagonist, let alone your own party members.
Nothing as yet, about either of these games has frustrated me personally, but that isn't to say these two games do not have faults of some sort. If nothing else though, I would've appreciated Beamdog implementing more fleshing out of the SoD story ending, to better transition into Shadows of Amn or even towards Throne Bhaal if it needed to be so late, namely regarding a quest of some sort about getting the "Soultaker Dagger" that the "Hooded Man" had on him and bringing it back to baldur's gate to prove the protagonist's innocence, even if it meant still being declared "exiled" due to being a "spawn of bhaal".
*Please be advised, that if you have imported your character from a BG1:EE game or from having played this previously, unless you have figured out the trick to keep your items, you'll lose them all at the start, so just a heads-up about that.

I like this game, just as I liked the first one. A lot.
It's a cool rulesystem, it has some depth, the enviroments are gourgeous ... but it has flaws. Big ones...
First off, it's a themepark kind of game. Follow the red line, from A to B to C. Don't bother doing anything other than the devs intended you to do, because you won't be leveled high enough to do so. And this game won't ever spawn random mobs for you so you can level up. Every single foe is put into the game for a reason. So you'll have to find your foes one by one in a predefined order to continue.
Second, well based on the first it's about foes and XP. That's pretty much the way to improve your character. Sure, you can roleplay your way out of some situations, but the game promotes slaughtering everything. You see, in Divinity, not only do you get stronger by fighting and killing, you also get smarter, more charming and persuative. Killing everything is the best way to go. Forget trying to be a good guy, asshattery is the divine path.
Third, balance. It's been a mess from the start. The first game favored mages and their CC abilities. They got smacked on their fingers about this, so this one favores physical fighters, melee and rangers. Mages have no use besides being aggromagnets with little ability to defend themselves. They simply can't get this balanced, magery versus fighting.
Fourth, Multiplayer. The announced "Drop in drop out" coop wasn't what I was expecting. It's still just as in the first game, the host has all the power, you simply join the a host and take over one of his characters. If you join from the beginning you have the power to designt that character. Just as in the first game. No evolution here at all.
But besides those issues, it's actually still a pretty good game. It's repetative with very little replayability, and you learn that red lined path quite fast, but still, it's fun. Combat is turn-based and pretty much the only reason to replay the game (to try different builds) and as earlier mentioned the game looks and sounds awesome. And that's why I have to give this one my thumbs up.  It has this unique feature to be played in split screen in combination with online, so you can do a 4 man team with two computers. That's friggin' awesome.
It's also quite immersive even with it's shortcomings around RP and how you wan't to play. You can still feel a world that is alive.
If you're into computerbased RP's and like turn-based combat, pick this one up. It won't dissapoint. But it's pretty much a one way trip like a Tripple A shooter. Go through it, and be done.
It's still fun, for now... =)
Edit: Unfortunally, the game is a downhill ride. It turns more and more annoying, frustrating and actually boring the longer I play it and the further the adventures take me. Every fight is a ambush against overwhelming enemies that are perfectly designed to support eachother. You need to mix max perfectly to go through it and that takes a huge toll on the RP. You even have to use the cheesiest exploative tactics on the border to cheating to win some fights. *sigh* Not good.

I would have to write several pages to review why this game is good. But I'll try to keep it very short:
+ Full voiced over
+ Entertaining NPC talks with a lot of laughs you get from it
+ Interesting and often suprising story, that will change in the details, when you play another character build.

+ A pretty intelligent and challenging AI that makes combat really hard and strategic if you like.

+ Beautiful music / soundtrack
