I really try to balance this review and tell you good and bad things about this game. But I have hard times to find any bad. This game is just so bloody good. But here aare things, I would like to see improved. They are highlevel critic on an almost perfect game:
- The quests in this game are recorded in some kind of diary. I like that kind of questlog, but it needs more information added to it: It doesn't tell you what level that quest is for, which is kind of a problem, as you have quests ranging over 6 and more levels in a region. I started to explore a region but didn't do every quest I got right away. So when I started to solve quests later on, I ran into a lot of enemies that were 2 or 3 levels higher than my group. In this game such a difference in level often means you don't stand a chance, especially on higher difficulty. So I would like to see a level written to each quest in the diary. At the moment you pretty much have to finish quests as you get them, which makes it a bit of a linear experience. I would like to be more flexible.
- Also the log doesn't tell you where you got a quest and not all of them get pinned on your map. So it's really hard to remember all the locations, which could also be improved.

Atmosphere. Something that is so important in many games and something that Stalker completely nails right from the start. You begin the game on a lonely hillside and (if your PC is up to the challenge) the whole bleak and scary Pripyat region opens up around you. An urgency sets in that makes you desperate to reach the dim point of light in the distance that marks one of the few safe havens in the Zone. I've played through the game a few times since its release and even now I can't quite put my finger on how they managed to make even the open daylit areas so scary - and then you reach a point were the games narrative demands you go under ground and the fear just seeps out of the game in a wonderful adrenaline fueled way. You'll jump at every noise and wave your torch about in panic. For a game to make you feel insignificant and unprotected even when you are packing an automatic machine gun and plenty of ammo is a triumph in game design. Is it a FPS? Yes, and I for one enjoyed the rather clunky combat as it added to the realism. Is it an RPG? Yes, and the search for better gear and better anomoly upgrades to help combat the Zone will force you to brave the most dangerous areas. Above all, for me, this game is an adventure survival game. From the moment I stepped into the Zone I felt that I was simply trying to survive in a way that many other 'survival games' fail to achieve. The Zone is the enemy here - and it is trying to kill you
If you like your games atmospheric then I wholly recommend Stalker - it is absolutely dripping in it

Chances are, unless you pour endless hours into this game, you will die over... and over... and the cycle will endlessly continue. It takes forever to respawn, and even then it takes way too long to get back into the battle, only to deal instantly. Want to be archer instead? Go ahead, just don't expect to kill a lot of people. An enemy will seem out of reach from you, so you prepare, but surprise, they registered their hit from far enough away, and you are now dead.

Despite being a startingly accurate recreation of my own days at high-school, right down to the possessed teachers trying to cut me up for failing assignments, I honestly can't recommend
The game starts off strong, with hapless everystudent Youngho being sucked into a twisted reflection of Sehwa High School, forced to explore the dark and eerie corridors with naught but a flickering flashlight at his side. The art design is fantastic in my opinion, and reminds me of
: classrooms appear distinctively "wrong" and get worse as the game progresses, while make-shift barricades keep you thinking "Wait, what was that I glimpsed....". I fully applaude the artists for their efforts, particularly their understanding that not everything has to be drenched in blood and gore right from the get-go, and combined with the superb ambient sounds -
- you have the recipe for a great horror game.
Tragically, it all falls apart when you realize there is very little to
threaten you.
The possessed teacher who shrieks for your blood? She can't keep pace with you at full sprint, she doesn't understand door handles, and she can't figure out where you went when you hide, even if she's literally just chased you into a room possessing one closet, which is labelled "I'M IN HERE DON'T MURDER ME." After the first hour or so, and you learn the audio cues that herald her appearances, all tension drains out of the game; I died just once in my entire playthrough, largely because I was testing if I could just run past the axe-murderer. Matters are not helped by a health and stamina system that are - in a word - broken. You have health enough to tank multiple hits, even in the endgame where the possessed teacher has been ubered up, and you lose so little stamina from running that the 10,000 recovery items you'll pick up in an hour's exploration are pointless. I of course exaggerate for comic effect, but seriously the game will fill your backpack with assorted goodies before you even realize and you'll just never need them.
Without the threat of death, there's no reason to be scared of anything, and without fear....well, something billed as a horror game loses its appeal doesn't it?

Awesomenauts is awesome. Who would've thought?
You play as one of many Awesomenauts, who are basically Dota heroes IN SPACE. Each and every 'naut is different. They are however similar in that every one of them has a basic attack (M1 auto-attack), 2 skills and a jumping or flying ability.
The game itself is a mix of MOBA and sidescrolling platformer where movement is a huge deal. If you know what you're doing, you can bodyblock enemies from escaping and abuse platforms so you don't take AoE damage from otherwise devastating skills. This might seem really complex, but it honestly isn't. All the movement related tricks are things you'll learn as you play the game.
In my experience, the 'nauts themselves are very well-balanced with each of them having a niche of some sort. Before a battle, you get to select which items will appear in the store. This is how you customize your Awesomenaut - if you want him to be meatier, give him some health upgrades. Want a more powerful basic attack? There's an item for that. Any aspect of your character can be customized, except their jump.
The maps are well-made. They are simple and easy to learn and all of them have a little gimmick. There's one with a jump pad for quick getaways, and one with a sandworm you can feed your enemies to! In addition to being well-made, the maps are also rather nice looking with some of them featuring water effects and the like. It's a joy walking through them and looking for enemies to destroy.
The game itself is gorgeous. The droids you have to accompany look funky, the 'nauts are all different but somehow share a unified theme and the music is simply great. Every 'naut has a theme that you hear when you select them at the beginning of the game and this theme actually replaces the battle music if you happen to get a nice killing spree going.
Something I really, really love about this title is that practice mode actually has decent bots and allows you to level your account up too. The bots are highly customizable, so you can make them really easy, or hard as nails. One thing that I personally really appreciate is the fact that playing against bots still allows you to progress and unlock further content for your game. For once, I don't actually feel penalized for playing against bots in a game!
I only have two complaints about this game: matchmaking and offline play. I had some terrible experiences in my first hour due to the online matchmaking putting me up against people who actually knew how to play. Getting stomped on was just no fun, especially when I was completely new to the game. Thankfully, I was able to practice against bots and still unlock items for the in-game store, so this isn't much of an issue unless you prefer online play. The greater problem is offline play. If you're not connected to Steam, the game won't even let you into the main menu. For a title with splitscreen multiplayer and great bots, this is just odd. This requirement could be an issue if your internet connection is unstable or if you were planning on playing this game on a plane for example.
Even with these two complaints, I still think this game deserves your attention. If you ever found yourself interested in Dota 2, League of Legends or Heroes of Newerth but were quickly scared off by the serious-pants nature of those games, this title is definitely for you. It's a more fun and casual take on the genre and it does what it sets out to do perfectly.
It really is fun to start the game and shoot some aliens.

BUT if you do like historical grand strategy games with varied factions, religions, countries and cultures that each have an huge impact on the game itself (even if you don't notice it until further down the road) then I absolutely recommend this game. It is simply awesome.

Well, while NIS did some great work cleaning up the backgrounds and menu graphics, they left the original sprites alone. Seriously, it's not that bad, but it's not exactly great either.
Further, rather than port the PS2 version or even the PSP version, the team at NIS chose to port the WiiU version (again, as they did this for Disgaea, but at least Phantom Brave didn't have the launch issues Disgaea did).  Here, rather than being glitchy and almost unplayable for a month or two, the menus leave out some important information that was included in the PS2 and PSP versions, which wasn't included in the WiiU.
One such glaring omission occurs when trying to fuse two items together using the Fusioner's mechanics.  Fusion is already an obtuse and obfuscated mechanic already, so to hide your weapon's base equip percents is ridiculous (look to the discussion boards to see that a majority of players are flummoxed and befuddled by this omission).
Fortunately, the base stats are shown, and the altered stats due to the equip percents, so if you're good with math, you'll be able to make the calculations necessary to determine your raw equip percents.
But again, why choose to port the worst version?  Likely because it's the most recent, I suppose, and the one the devs are most familiar with, so I understand the choice.  But really, don't just port and run, D-bags; there are always issues with old games getting ported, which might need more care than a simple "port-and-done" schema.
I hope the devs don't pull this same BS with their other NIS titles they plan to "bring to PC."  But I'm sure they will.  And I, the fool, will probably still buy it and recommend it.  Why?  Well, when you've got the only game in the house I'm interested in, this player's gotta play...  So, I'll cautiously recommend this game to previous owners of the title, and those who enjoy NIS or SRPGs.
Editor's note:  So, my main gripe about not seeing item equips in fusions was updated recently.  Apparently the staff at NISA agreed with my and other gamers' opinions and redid that particular part of the game to be like the PS2 version, showing the item equip % values.  So, the game is improved (though Marona still looks like Ash!).  Yay, dood!

The first time I hear about the original Alien Shooter, I was not even in Junior High. Back then, it could ran on Windows 2000 (just to show how far back the game goes!) and I tried the trial version, downloading it from the school's computer since a friend was playing it as well. 2 levels was all it took for me to scour the electronic center, looking for the bootleg version. (Hey, I barely have any cash back then! >_<)
Somehow, a guy from school found one, and that game was installed in every computer in the IT class. Of course, as time goes on and my preference changes, I start to play other games, forgetting that after 4 years, SIGMA made a sequel out of it. I on the other hand was busy with highschool, so I didn't pay much attention to games at that time. A year back, I received the game from a friend, and while I have installed it, I never have the intention to play it. I didn't think that finally, after all these years, it gave me the nostalgia feeling all over again. :)
So, the game itself, is pretty much similar to the original 2003 version with some additions to the characters and perks. Weapon wise, they have added new choices and classes, from the generic weapons like Colt .45; Rocket Propelled Grenade (RPG); AK47 to prototype guns e.g. M̶o̶r̶e̶ ̶e̶x̶p̶e̶n̶s̶i̶v̶e̶ ̶t̶h̶a̶n̶ ̶T̶r̶u̶m̶p̶'̶s̶ ̶W̶a̶l̶l̶ ̶b̶u̶t̶ ̶j̶u̶s̶t̶ ̶p̶o̶i̶n̶t̶ ̶a̶n̶d̶ ̶f̶o̶r̶g̶e̶t̶ ̶w̶h̶i̶l̶e̶ ̶i̶t̶ ̶t̶u̶r̶n̶s̶ ̶e̶v̶e̶r̶y̶t̶h̶i̶n̶g̶ ̶i̶n̶t̶o̶ ̶g̶i̶b̶l̶e̶t̶s̶ G5000 Ion Cannon. The aliens are also have more variety, a step up from the original, from generic spidery aliens and some notable ones from the original to mecha-Transformer suit wearing aliens with ion cannons. There are also traps abound, from thorn-like plants to green-containers that spew green goo which acts like acid and cause damage if you step on it.
However, the main thing that hooks people in (including me back then) is the action. Non-stop action, gun-blazing with almost endless aliens in the screen running towards you with 1 goal in sight. I can say that this was part of the positive traits that why I loved the original, and somewhat enjoyed this sequel. At one point in a level late in the game, there were so much alien teleporters, spawning aliens with rocket launchers, spitting acid, and firing ions shooting at me that I just blindly use my trusty M̶o̶r̶e̶ ̶e̶x̶p̶e̶n̶s̶i̶v̶e̶ ̶t̶h̶a̶n̶ ̶T̶r̶u̶m̶p̶'̶s̶ ̶W̶a̶l̶l̶ ̶b̶u̶t̶ ̶j̶u̶s̶t̶ ̶p̶o̶i̶n̶t̶ ̶a̶n̶d̶ ̶f̶o̶r̶g̶e̶t̶ ̶w̶h̶i̶l̶e̶ ̶i̶t̶ ̶t̶u̶r̶n̶s̶ ̶e̶v̶e̶r̶y̶t̶h̶i̶n̶g̶ ̶i̶n̶t̶o̶ ̶g̶i̶b̶l̶e̶t̶s̶ G5000 Ion Cannon. After ten minutes (which seems like an eternity), the battleground is quiet, and I faced the last boss. Of course, going down at 1/2 health is just a gimmick. Surprise! More aliens! D:
After a few more minutes, teleporters destroyed, 80,000+ aliens harmed-most of them turned into giblets-and the final boss falls! Oh, oh, almost forgot, before the last level, there is a juncture where you have to make a decision, which will lead to different outcome, and a great addition. :D Nonetheless, one thing that they haven't fully fixed from the original is the alien pathing, as they will get stuck by trees and corners allowing players to reduce the numbers slightly using explosive weapons, for example.
Still, while this game is 10 years old (gasp!) and can still run on Windows 2000 (!) it provides lots of action and entertainment for anyone who enjoys playing top-down shooting games. It also have other features like survival mode for those who liked more challenges.
P.s. I wonder, how long would the Viscera Cleanup team take to clean the last level in this game? :P

TL;DR: Awesomenauts is a game that's tons of fun to lay, with an original art style and unique gameplay, but the lack of varied battlegrounds may limit some peoples fun they have with the game.
Awesomenauts is a 2D Platformer-MOBA mix with cartoony graphics and fast and exciting gameplay.
The game is, (at leat in my opinion), an absolute blast to play.  Games are short, around 20-30 minutes, so you never have to dedicate too much time to play it.
The Art style is absolutely wonderful.  Almost every character looks and sounds amazing.  It's clear that Ronimo really spent a lot of time working on the aesthetics of the game.
Along with that, each arena in the game has a very distinct style, along with also have different layouts, and other aspects (a stealth orb, giant worm that eats you) which can be used to give a team the advantage if used well.  Because of this, games on different battlegrounds can be played differently, with teams securing areas to give tactical advantages, and certain characters can play in a completely different style on different arenas.
Some might argue that the amount of Arenas seems sparse, and this is partly true.  The 4 arenas (and growing) seem like hardly of an achievement at first, but the amount of polish and individuality that each arena has is something you won't see in many other games.
I do have some bones to pick with it though.  First of all, unlike other more competetive MOBAS, the various characters (AKA Awesomenauts) and upgrades (stuff you buy in the shop when in a match), have to be unlocked by gaining "Levels" each time you play.  This could be considered a little fun Metagame, but in certain ways it can be argued that it can give people a certain competetive edge.
Finally, there isn't an extremely large player base.  This may be just me, but I find it difficult to join games with a full group of players.  There could be 4/6, or 3/6, and sometimes 6/6.  This can be good in some cases, because often you could be in 2 or 3 games with the same people, or may find people you were playing with 2 games ago joining a current game.
All in all, Awesomenauts is a great game, and can be played competetively or casually.  Some people may argue that it doesn't have absolute 'fairness', and isn't very content-heavy, but everything in the game is very polished, and the amount of content is growing.

I'm tired of all these DLCs and their inflated prices. The content added often brings new depth to the game, but frequently has features that we shouldn't have to pay for. I'm looking at you Ruler designer! Also you dirty portrait, unit and music packs should be ashamed of yourselves for existing! If you look at other game companies, they often give comparable content for free as an update. At the very base of it, I'm sick of all this piece meal DLC. I can understand expansions increasing the longevity of the game, but seriously Horse Lord's cost is 37.5% of the price of the base game. And don't you lie to me and say that any of these expansions add enough content to justify their price. Most of these are just paid unlocks, not anything "expansive". Also don't talk to me about steam sales, the most recent releases only get 35% off. For Horse Lords, that's roughly 5 dollars, whoopee do. By the time, we get a substantial "deal" on any DLC, it's often way down the line and Paradox has already churned out another one. All of this means two plainly disappointing facts. You'll pay considerably to have a complete and current content version of any Paradox game and that when a new game releases it's evident you're only getting a bare bones version of the eventual game. However, I know that nothing will change as long as people keep apathetically buying the product. And so this 'just another ranting guy on the internet' is going to reach into his wallet, pull out his credit card and buy the next "grand" expansion for CK2 because oh well, right?
I'd prefer that more game developers learn from CD Projekt. Witcher 3, as an example, has become incredibly successful and it doesn't require a smattering of DLC to be enjoyable. I have no problem with additional content coming out after the base game's release, but it shouldn't take away the enjoyment from the base game. At some point just make a new game and quit selling us content piece by piece. Ck2 is an incredible game, but suffers from the DLC making the base game unappealing by itself. I didn't want to buy this game for the longest time because of the now classic DLC approach. I can understand that, after 4+ Years, having at most 6 expansions costing $5 to $10 could be reasonable especially if the base game was more fleshed out to start. However, the existing cluster pile of DLC acts as a major turn off for players. It creates the feeling of having to pay for the basic structure of the game and to flesh it out. At this point, we're not judging whether Paradox will make a good game, but how much it will cost us to enjoy every bit of it. I honestly enjoy Paradox games and I hope to enjoy more in the future. Just as usual if you purchase any of their games remember to be patient, wait for sales and slowly navigate the DLC barrier without letting it kill your wallet.

- The main character is just adorable
- I love the pixel art
- Tons of crazy items you can use as weapons, and each one has a ton of unique special attacks
But unfortunately the game disappointed me at what's most important in it: The combat system. Having turn-based combat not bound to tiles was a bold experiment, but in my opinion it failed.
- It is sometimes very difficult to select the object you want to target, especially when they stack
- Finding the right spot for your character to use an AoE attack effectively is a chore
- You have hardly any way to block enemy movement, so you can't properly protect your more fragile characters
- The mob AI has some serious problems. Far too often you have enemies which don't do anything on their turn even though they would have plenty of viable options.
I really would have liked to keep playing this game for the stories and character progression, but I just don't enjoy the combat system.

Overgrowth is a bunny platformer action game... that's been developed since World War II. Probably as a way to kill Stalin.
So... the combat's fast paced and great. It's robust. Two thumbs up for it.
The platforming's slightly wonky, but some fixes could help it out and have it become truly great. One thumb up for it.
The graphics also look very good while still demanding relatively little from your computer. But there are also issues with it. Some effects seem to slow down your game quite a lot. For example looking at a spot could suddenly make your game run at 10fps while it had been running at a speed of 55-60fps. No thumbs up but no thumbs down either.
Bodies have proper skeletons and the damage engine is great as well. Take this as an example: You run, jump high and... you fall on your head. You break your neck and die. That's it, you're done. Dead. Two thumbs up for that as well.
And here come the problematic things:
The campaign in the game is bare-bones at best. At worst it's a bunch of levels stringed together with minimal dialogue. One thumb down for that.
And the main, real issue about this whole game.
The amount of content compared to the amount of money being asked of you. It's just an awful deal. For $5, this game would be perfect. Even for $10 it'd be a good deal. But $30?? That's just outrageous. Not to mention that the sale prices are nothing to write home about either ($18 was the lowest in Feb 18th 2014). I did everything in the game in 2 hours. And also looking at the pace of the updates, I doubt that you'll get much more content soon.
Don't buy this at full price.
It was recently in the Humble Freedom Bundle, so maybe you can get a hold of a copy that's from that bundle, making the price relatively cheap.
Overall:
As a game - 6/10
As a product - 3/10
(All games start at a 5/10 and move up and down based on pros and cons in the game)

Finally out of early access so to update my reveiw; Since the alpha they added some mechanics and added polish as well as a few more modes to play.
To preface the long wait for devolpment and the existance of bugs i still expirence on the first "final" release are definantly their. Iv'e broken the map, had npc's ignore me, and had to kill myself. Some of the things the game does right even, still don't feel entirly flushed out. That being said a lot can be forgiven with them being a small indie company- they still made a fun game that is generally good looking and while not the best optimized game it's not bad and the game is worth a try.
Starting with what the game does best the fighting mechanics are new and refreshing, using a skelton structure damage system instead of a heath pool leads to a rewarding combat system that contrary to inital play goes deeper than jumping head kicks; overpowered as they may be. An important mechanic to the combat is to evade and counter attacks and like traditional fighting games even though, full discloser more rng is in play than most fighters, reading the opponent can lead to having quite an edge, be it a dodging into a punch, kick, throw, catching a wepon, or rolling from a jump kick to a leg sweep to snap a neck.
The platforming still feels new and not too sticky but I honestly perfered the beta platforming, I find myself falling off a lot more edges and missing more jumps, but this may in all honesty may just be me used to the old platforming. You can mario jump off walls, and mirror edge run across them all in all a pretty nice system, not quite perfect- not to me but close enough.
The story modes have a charm, the story is at least kind of intresting but in all honesty the writing needs improvment. Turner is just kind of a bad♥♥♥♥♥wich is fine but he knows it and every other line of dialoge is someone saying something like its 50v1 it not fair and turner will say some stupid thing like i know im sorry. They didn't really make an attempt to make him likable and the characters are all kind of 2-d, the dialoge in general just falls flat. The fights are cool and the platforming is pretty fun but it felt like (in the overgrowth story mode) a checkpoint was set at every jump making the system feeling perhaps a bit too lenient. As far as the bosses it would be nice to have a harder boss at least in the overgrowth campain at least in lugru the final boss is sort of challanging on harder difficulties without cheese. For playtime and replayabilty theirs not too much want to go back and the campains are both short, lugurus a bit shorter i belive. In summery the campain is decent but I wouldn't buy the game for it.
The other modes are arena and multiplayer. To keep the reveiw shorter than an essay arena is a gladitor type combat were the more challengers you beat the harder they become, and they mix up between teams, 1v1v1v1, and 1v1's with and without wepons. Their is a cap though and once you reach it theirs not much more to the mode, im sure they will add more. As far as the multiplayer I haven't played with anyone who did'nt enjoy the combat at least a little, the reaction combat mixed with the rng makes it so anyone can take a round.
FINALLY the modding community back in beta made good quality mods for sure but the community itself wasn't that large hopefully the addition of the steam workshop will make it more accesable for people looking into modding the game becaue it was kind of a pain to get the sumlauncher. Im optimistic about future modding.
Tldr: Overgrowth is a good game with good and refreshing mechanics, a decent modding community, and it makes for a good little party game just dont buy it for the campain. $30 maybe if you are really intrested in the game or have the money just laying around otherwise wait.

Honestly I do not see the reason behind some of the negative reviews. Yes, the game is clunky for today's standards and in more ways than one it doesn't age well. Yes there is a learning curve that can be frustrating to those who are unfamiliar to this game, but this game provided a certain aesthetic that no other game could emulate. From the graphics, to the music, even the story and the world in which you skate and tag in, are all unique. This game is more than a game. It is a culture.
For starters, a lot of people compare this to Jet Set Radio Future, which is really unfair for both games, as both games are way too different from each other to draw comparisons. That's like trying to compare Jax & Daxter to Jax 2, two VERY different games from each other, even though one is the sequel to the other.
A controller is definitely needed for this game and this goes without saying. With a keyboard it's near unplayable. But with a controller, I was able to play the game just as well as I would had on the original Dreamcast. In fact, I still say it's a very faithful port to the Dreamcast port, with upscaled graphics in widescreen. Considering how many times this game is on sale and the fact that it was even free at one point, if you hadn't played the game yet, I would highly recommend it.
Just be mindful that this is a game from the late 90's, a relic of an era where tricky platform jumps, cameras that are against you rather than for you (which the port GREATLY alleviates by using the secondary analog stick to move the camera, an option that WASN'T in the original game), and trial and error gameplay which forces you to follow a path and stick to it to complete a level.
This was, and still is, one of my all time favorite games so I'm definitely going to sound biased in reviewing this, but I do not care. I want to defend this game for those who wish to steer those interested away.

So... 0.2 hours. Not enough time for a review, right?
Well...
Lugaru... errr... Overgrowth has a lot to offer. It's got some excellent animation, a impact mechanic that is, AFAIK, unique, and some interesting parkour. Instead of a health bar, your character displays actual wounds, which is really neat. The combat is deep, I suppose, and I could probably come up with a few other positive things to say bout it.
But seriously...
There's no HUD - fine, I can live with that. No voice acting? Meh - many of my favorite games don't have that; who cares? But the text floats around in an ugly font like this is  Baby's First Unity Game, and that's just unacceptable.  The written dialogue isn't exactly prize-winning, but whatever. It looks terrible, and it looks unprofessional. That was okay for Lugaru - it was basically free. This one is $30 frakkin' dollars.
The worst problem, though, is that this is indicative of the quality of most of the game. This doesn't look like 10 or so years of development, guys. This looks like a tech demo. You've got something really interesting on your hands here- potentially a unique experience with facinating mechanics and fast-action gameplay...
But right now? You've gotta do better. You need to iron out the looks of the game, and bring it into focus. It's just not worth what you're charging in this state, and if this is what you call Beta, then I can assume the final product won't be a huge improvement. Not good.

This review hurts me to write, because I really wanted to like The Coma.  I really liked the Clock Tower games, and this game draws massive inspiration from those, so I had high hopes going in, but sadly, it fails to deliver on several points, both large and small.
As for the small problems, I'd mostly attribute them to the ui and controls.  Everything is real time, but all of the buttons are spread out over the keyboard.  ESC closes nothing, so you'll have to find the designated close button to get out of a backpack or something in order to interact with something else and the controls don't feel as responsive as they should be.  This causes a lot of cheap injuries that I felt I should've been able to get out of.   The biggest problem with the ui is the map, mainly in the later areas.  Once you get to the third building, several paths that look like they should be open are blocked off, requiring you to find alternate routes or teleporters.  The routes that are blocked off are not marked on your map, even after you encounter them, and this becomes a massive hassle when trying to navigate the later, maze-like, levels (as well as something else which I'll mention next paragraph).  These issues could be fixed with a simple patch, potentially, but the major issue I'll be mentioning, I'm not so sure of.
The big problem is the antagonist who follows you around.  The Clock Tower games had their Scissorman and this game has an analogue, but there are major differences between the two that hold this game back from its full potential.  In Clock Tower, encountering Scissorman was a relative rarity which served to add a bit of tension to the game.  You had more than one option on how to deal with the encounter, and the game also had several ways that Scissorman could show up (walk around, jump out from a closet, leap out from a pool, etc...), all of which added up to an antagonist who added spice and fear to an otherwise standard point and click adventure game.  In the Coma, the antagonist only shows up one way (walking around), there is generally only one way to avoid the antagonist, which is hiding.  You can flee, but you have to flee quite a ways away, which leads to my next issue.  The antagonist shows up far too often and kills all pacing.  If you touch the villian at all, you lose about 1/3rd of your health, so you have to run.  That means that while you are trying to solve the puzzles and navigate the maze, you'll randomly have to run in the opposite direction for a little bit, then find one of the many common hiding spaces, and then wait for about 10 seconds.  That may not sound too bad, but on your tenth time in a row in a short while. it becomes incredibly tedious.  I went from saying "Oh Crap!", to "God Damnit!  Not again!" fairly early on, and this only gets magified when navigating the mazes in the latter half of the game.  The one thing I'd recommend is perhaps cut the encounter rate in half and give some kind of way to fight off the hunter without damage, or at least reduced damage, because I really cannot overstate how much having to constantly run away kills all pacing.  Imagine a maze where you have to draw over what you've been drawing at random, frequent intervals, or Resident Evil 1 (mentioned Clock Tower enough in this review) where, every time you saw a zombie, you had to run back three rooms and wait, then hope the zombie wasn't there when you got back.
It's a shame, because there is a bunch about this game I like, primarily in terms of characters, story, and art style.  I would like to see this game get more refined, but as of right now, I just can't recommend it to anyone who values tension over tedium.

*Fanboy Alert*
Reviewing a game as old as myself is like reviewing your parentage. Funnily enough, this was one game that had missed my stash till now (I'd played Wolf 3D first about a decade and half back). So I decided that now  that Steam makes it so easy to head down nostalgia lane,  why not finish what I started so long ago ?
Plot - I don't care two finks about this  game's plot, never did. Wolf was all about gameplay, period. Even  the game doesn't bother to tell you much, throwing you directly into the game. So if you're looking for a story, you know nothing about how FPS  games were born.
Rating - 0/0 (= infinity, I know, but still).
Gameplay - Back when I first played Wolf, people used to be far more familiar in the forest of keys than gamers are today. Mouse usage was next to nil and where it was, it was painfully choppy. The current avatar of the game seems to have pretty good mouse support actually, but I decided to play with the arrow keys for old times'  sake. Once you have gotten the hang of the arrows+right Ctrl+Space (my fav config), the game is really all about anticipating where enemies are and killing them before they shoot at you. The game presents you with what today would be called mazes but back then felt like the insides of a real evil castle.
If point and shoot seems to be boring, you have no idea what Wolf can throw at you. And SoD simply pushes the envelope. Each turn seems to be a death trap, and you desperately try to round corners without developing that uneasy feeling that the next step would be your last. Rinse and repeat as much as you like, but it will still give you more jump scares than the average Resident Evil.
As for bosses, this game tries to make them harder by putting them in levels along with a large number of other enemies (Wolf had bosses secluded in their own level). This perhaps anticipates the boss and minion routine of modern  games, but I felt that somehow it pulled away from the "alone with the boss" (no innuendos please) feeling of the original Wolf. Also, the bosses seem easier to kill. Matured brain I guess ?
Rating - 6/5
Characters - None exist. There are four classes of enemies and a bunch of bosses. You have no allies to speak of.
Rating - 0/0 (except those Nazi  soldiers, they do look so innocent. I'll write a coming of age story on them someday).
Graphics - Top of the range graphics for when I was still in the cradle. Today, my eyes hurt as the pixelated artefacts scroll by. If you're looking for a better graphic experience, try out the later Wolf games (or the Mac Family ports of these games).
Rating - Err/Ummm
Conclusion - The sequel to the granddaddy of FPS games is still a great game in itself. If you haven't played Wolf, I'd  suggest going for it before taking on SoD. If you did though, this review is redundant for you. Either way, once you've feasted your eyes on the game (and vice versa, arghhh), you'll admit that this was one of the best games ever made.

Get Psyched! Released just four short months after Wolfenstein 3D, Spear of Destiny is the prequel follow-up release to the highly acclaimed grandfather of the first-person shooter genre. This is just the beginning of where the series' chronology becomes scattered, as Spear of Destiny is the fourth release in the franchise, but first in the original timeline; after that, comes the Nocturnal Missions from Wolfenstein 3D, then Wolfenstein 3D itself. Of course, the two releases that gave birth to the entire project, Castle Wolfenstein (1981) and Beyond Castle Wolfenstein (1984), are in a league of their own; but I digress.
So, Adolf Hitler has captured the legendary Spear of Destiny from Versailles, due to his utmost desire to master arcane powers. He has sent the religious artifact to Castle Nuremberg, but our hero B.J. Blazkowicz has something to say about that. Making his first chronological mission appearance in the original series, Blazkowicz enters the castle to blast all the Nazi scum to the depths of Hades, and in doing so he encounters the evil Dr. Schabb's genetic soldier mutants for the first time, which leads to his ultimate assassination in Wolfenstein 3D. Can Blazkowicz save the world by getting the Spear of Destiny back? Of course he can, because he's one unstoppable bad ace mofo!
Spear of Destiny also comes with the two mission packs that were released in 1994; Return to Destiny and Ultimate Challenge. Return to Destiny takes place six weeks after the base game, after Blazkowicz secures the spear, though the Axis forces managed to mount a successful raid attack to recover it. After a bloody battle and narrow escape, the Nazi forces take the spear to their secret Scandinavian base, which was carved from the solid rock of a fjord, where it must be recovered once more. As for Ultimate Challenge, Hitler has expanded his subterranean command bunker that lies beneath the chancellery in Berlin, so that he can keep the spear well-guarded. After harnessing the powers of the occult, he calls upon dark forces to help him see into the future so that he can build his mighty weapon systems.
If you enjoyed Wolfenstein 3D, then there's no doubt that you will also love Spear of Destiny. It's built on the same engine, and the gameplay is virtually the same; explore a vast maze of corridors and chambers, looking for keys to proceed to the level's exit, all the while picking up treasure for points, ammo, and health items. The base game, consisting of 21 levels, looks exactly like its predecessor, and offers little in the way of diversity other than new bosses and a very minimal amount of new textures. It's not really in the vanilla title that Spear of Destiny succeeds, but rather in its two mission packs, Return to Danger and Ultimate Challenge.
These mission packs feature all new textures, recolored enemies, and reskinned treasures, ammo, weapons, and health pick ups. The atmosphere and overall look of the game shifts dramatically, what were once brightly colored areas turn to dark, foreboding structures filled with even more skeletons, new pools of chemical waste, and biohazard symbols. There are also new music tracks, which are superior to those present in the base game. Return to Danger, and, to an even higher extent, Ultimate Challenge, house longer levels and feature more complex Nazi labyrinths to explore; the maps are absolutely gargantuan for games that came out in the early 1990's.
If you're looking for the tried-and-true experience from Wolfenstein 3D, then you're going to really enjoy Spear of Destiny. As previously mentioned, the vanilla game has very little to offer in the way of diversity with the exception of 21 new levels, and their hidden secrets. Return to Danger and Ultimate Challenge are really where it's at, and each of those mission packs also have 21 levels of Nazi killing goodness. It's a fun time, especially if you're in to oldschool retro games and shooters, though the two mission packs offer the same ending that's seen in the original game; but who plays these old things for the sake of story-line anyway?

Note: This is a follow-up review to Wolfenstein 3D and thus will only cover what's new to the game.
Wolfenstein 3D: Spear of Destiny is the prequel (often mistaken as a sequel) to Wolfenstein 3D and was released the same year as the original game as the 'retail version' of Wolf3D, as the aforementioned title was purchasable via mail order only. Using the same engine and features as Wolf3D, it acts more like a standalone expansion pack than a full fledged sequel, but there are a few key differences.
The story is once again set during World War II, with B.J. Blazkowicz, the famous allied spy and the Allies' most valuable agent, is tasked with capturing the Spear that legend has pierced the side of Christ from the clutches of an already unbalanced Hitler. Stolen from Versailles by the Nazis and secured in the impregnable Castle Nuremberg (not Castle Wolfenstein despite what the back of the box said). With the Spear heavily guarded, this Nazi stronghold is far too risky to attack directly, therefore B.J. must infiltrate from the bottom up. It's said that no man can be defeated when he has the Spear in his possession, and Hitler believes himself to be invincible as his brutal army sweeps across a battered Europe. But is the legend true? And if so what other secrets does the Spear hide?
Unlike the episodic progression of Wolf3D, Spear of Destiny (or SoD as it'll be referred as) is a continuous set of 21 levels, two of which are secret (accessible from floors 4 and 12), that make up as one large episode of sorts, split into five distinct 'units', each with their own theme and boss encounter towards the end of each. The first five levels consist of the 'Tunnels', the next five the 'Dungeons', then the 'Castle' which makes up the main portion of the game, followed by the 'Ramparts' and finally concluding with the mysterious 'Death Dimension'. There is a variety of new tiles in addition to the old ones to convey the new themes, so that each unit is distinctive from one another.
While there are no new enemies (in the normal sense anyhow) there are five new bosses, and though there are no new weapons a box of ammo pickup was added that grants 25 rounds. These are fairly common due to the increased amount of enemies on average per level (especially on the hardest difficulty), where using rows of the original ammo pickup would look somewhat comical, but it's also just more convenient. There are also a few new music tracks, which all sound great in that Adlib fashion, albeit strangely enough you'll only hear them very early on and towards the end as most of Wolf3D's music was recycled.
As far as SoD is concerned it is essentially more of the same but what's on offer is a must play for the diehard Wolf3D fans as most levels are well designed, very challenging at times, and often more creative than those found in the original game. Unfortunately the same cannot be said for FormGen's 'lost' Spear episodes known as Return to Danger and Ultimate Challenge. While the new graphics are very spiffy, if more cartoony than the originals, and the sound design notably improved, the mapping is completely abysmal and boring to look at. Uninspired, ugly, truly maze-like, with little to no thought put into placement of enemies or logical progression throughout. Both even recycle the same bosses, and no changes were made to the source code, so ceiling colors and intermission screens remain the same as the base SoD game.
I recommend and rate SoD on par with Wolf3D, but I would give a 1.0 to both FormGen SoD games, even though they come included with SoD free of charge. If you want a proper sequel to Spear of Destiny, play AReyeP's excellent Spear Resurrection and Spear - End of Destiny instead. They're also free!

Woodle Tree Adventures is a pretty basic 3D platformer. You jump around and collect three "fairy tears" per level and then reach the exit. You can collect berries on the way to unlock better versions of the leaf you use to attack, and avoid or kill enemies that mostly don't seem to care about much more than just standing there. The controls feel a little loose and impercise, so some jumps are a bit harder than they look like they should be.
The whole game just kinda seems unfinished. Except for a few that go on patrols or the rare one that will actually walk towards you, most enemies are just sort of out of the way and not doing anything. There are no camera controls; everything shown with pre-determined camera angles, and some of them are in bad positions. Some of them also won't trigger properly, leaving you with even worse views sometimes. The checkpoints seem broken too; SOMETIMES you'll respawn at a checkpoint close to where you died, but most of the time it sends you back to the very start of the level. Once,
. Since you can't fix that, I had to play the first part of the level basically backwards until I hit a point where the camera decided to change to something more reasonable.
The level select are just globes that show up in your house without any sort of labels and aren't presented in a linear order, so it could be easy to forget what level is the latest one you unlocked if you step away from the game and come back. On the other hand, since the game only lasts about 40 minutes, you'll probably beat it in one sitting anyway. I kinda considered going back to collect the rest of the berries to get the last weapon, but the game doesn't tell you how many berries you've collected in each level, so god knows where those are [edit: It turns out that doesn't matter, because you can go back to a level and just get as many berries as you want to get the next item. It's not counting your completion rate, so you don't HAVE to get everything].
This game could get better! It seems like the devs are patching it with new levels and features, like multiplayer and the ability to zoom the camera in and out (but really, full camera control is more important). I feel like they do care about the game, but it's just not all there yet. I will keep an eye on it as they continue to add to the game, and I hope those problems I addressed get fixed. Keep an eye on this game and its development, and hopefully I'll be able to change this review to a thumbs up someday.

Phantom Brave is my favorite Nippon Ichi game, and one of my favorite games of all time.
**GOOD**
You will love Marona
One of the biggest positives Phantom Brave holds is character development.  Now keep in mind, like many Nippon Ichi games, most of your roster is made up of generics.  In Phantom Brave, the only non-generics are Ash and Marona (until post game).  It is the development of other characters throughout the story that make it so good.  And of course, because of Marona.  It's quite depressing for the first few chapters.  Then things start going better for her and you love her even more.
You won't spend a week resetting to perfect items
Like Nippon Ichi's Disgaea series, Phantom Brave's items are able to level up and become stronger.  If I compared this to Disgaea 2, this system is 100% better.  Disgaea 2 requires extensive knowledge of how it works and hundreds if not thousands of resets to "perfect" your equipment.  It's quite a headache.  Phantom Brave is MUCH simpler.
A Blacksmith levels up items and opens skills, a Fusionist combines items together.  That's it.  You can level up items to increase their stats, open a variety of skills and transfer them to other items or characters, combine the raw stats of items together and gain the difference, or increase the efficiency% and confine%.
A huge variety of useful skills
Really.  You could spend days just tinkering around with skills, Find hidden gems on absurd items like Rolling Wood on some Driftwood.  Putting together a list of useful skills that work with a particular character's aptitude and stats can make a big difference.  Or you could just have fun with silly stuff.  If you've played Disgaea you will appreciate Phantom Brave's non-grid system, skills have a lot more freedom and are much less restricting and easy to pull off.
**BAD**
Low resolution sprites
Although the story scenes have gorgeous high definition backdrops, character sprites are as pixelated as they were on the PS2.  I understand that it would require a lot of work to make the sprites look better, but I wish they could have at least improved on them during cut scenes.  Try to use 4:3 resolution and if you have a huge monitor, play in windowed mode.  That'll lessen how bad it is.
***EDIT: These percentages have been added!***
It's too easy to become overpowered
Phantom Brave's systems make over-leveling VERY easy.  You have to limit yourself and make rules for yourself if you want to avoid feeling like you're cheating.  Some of my own rules include no mana farming, no combining with failure titles or higher level items, no confining characters to items you brought with you that are higher level than natural items on the map...really, it is WAY too easy to take advantage of things and become ridiculously powerful.  I also avoid random dungeons when I want to play story mode, instead doing dungeon-only games. (I do this with Disgaea's item world too)
Like I said in the first sentence, this is one of my favorite games of all time.  I absolutely recommend this game to anyone, especially fans of other Nippon ichi works.

Basically the definitive edition of Phantom Brave.  You've got arbitrary resolution support, instant switching of controller prompts/keyboard input, stability (not one crash or frame rate issue in the 40 hours I've played) and dual audio.
Nippon Ichi SRPG's are mainly about finding enjoyment in making the numbers go up, and Phantom Brave probably scratches that itch best for me among their various SRPG's.  Unlike most SRPG's, you have a circular movement radius instead of grid-based movement.  This does cause issues with path-finding and targeting at times, but I like the feel of it and the freedom of movement it gives you.  It's somewhat similar to Valkyria Chronicles to give a point of reference.
Another aspect of PB that's a bit different is that you only have one "permanent" party member.  Marona is always on the field, but you summon your allies by confining them into various objects that increase/decrease certain stats and/or provide various types of protection/debuffs to your allies and enemies.  Summoned allies also have turn limits before being removed for the rest of fight, so you have to use some actual strategy at times when it comes to deploying your characters.  There's a real sense of asset management here if you play the game as a straight SRPG instead of the usual Nippon Ichi "power level your character/item until you're unstoppable" type of gameplay.  That said, you're free to power level to your heart's content if that's what you want to do, just making a point that PB has more strategic gameplay than you might expect.
The fusion system is your primary method of making the numbers go up and basically consists of mashing together two weapons and making the stats go up, along with the choice of adding new attacks to the weapon.  Fusion also works between characters and items and serves to provide very useful passive and active skills along with level cap increases.  There's more stuff to crazy stat increases like titles, failure fusions, etc, so your numbers go up hankering should be sated.  There's just something about the fusion system that appeals to me more than Disgaea's Item World stuff.
Phantom Brave leaves a lot to the player to figure out on their own, which might be a plus or negative depending on how you like your games.  There's an extended tutorial, but there's just too much to the gameplay to make it all digestible to a new player without overwhelming them.  This probably isn't the worst game to look up a beginner's guide to get some tips as you figure out how to play, especially if you aren't familiar with Nippon Ichi games.
In short, if you've played Phantom Brave in the past and are wondering if this is worth picking up again, then the answer is yes.  If you've never played a Nippon Ichi game before, be warned that all the systems and numbers might be a bit overwhelming at first, but if it clicks for you, you'll probably find yourself abandoning the main storyline to level your characters and weapons to the point where the AI can't even make a turn before you kill all of them.  If that doesn't appeal to you, it can also be played as more a "normal" SRPG, more so than Disgaea.  Recommend if you have any interest in SPRG's.

Most games will crumble under their mechanics when the difficulty begins to ramp up. Sometimes a game just isn't precise enough for punishing level design. Akane the Kunoichi is, sadly, one of those games. It's a humble little title, that's for sure, but it does not do well in the final few acts.
The premise is simply Mega Man. To call it anything else would be silly. There are no cool transformations or extra weapons, but this game is heavily inspired by the classic Capcom series. You jump and shoot kunai, simple as that. There are a few different enemies with differing attacks and boss fights. Rinse and repeat.
The game feels completely cheap, though that would have to do with it originating from Xbox Live Indies. The game was priced at $1 on that service, so you should already know where the lack of production values come from. A game doesn't need flash to be solid, just competent controls and decent level design.
Akane the Kunoichi has neither. The levels don't pose any threat until Act 4 and the controls are incredibly sloppy. You can smash attack all you want, but you'll sometimes rapid fire or sometimes throw only one kunai. There is no rhyme or reason to your attempts.
Jumping is also really imprecise. Some of the levels demand pixel perfect precision, but you just will not be able to achieve that with regularity. None of the levels are long, but it hurts to be near the end and fall down a cliff only to restart the damn thing.
The bosses are also a missed opportunity. They are nice and big and look intimidating, but apart from the very first boss, none of them feel like anything new. You simply hit them in clearly defined weakpoints and dodge their simple attacks. The final boss is also a complete push-over, especially after how brutally stupid the level is.
Maybe this game functions better on iPad. I know there is a version available on that format. Honestly, though, I wouldn't recommend this to anyone. Unless you really just want another ninja themed game, take a pass.

The fun and beauty of Awesomenauts lies in it delivering the MOBA experience found in games such as DOTA, but at a far more casual and beginner-friendly level.
Just as with DOTA, the idea of the game is to destory turrets across numerous "lanes" to get to the opponent team's boss structure. Autonomous creeps are spawned from each team that attack the other team's structures, with the player commanding a hero that grows more powerful as the game progresses. Unlike most traditional MOBAs which are in 3D, Awesomenauts takes on a simpler 2D form reminiscent of platformer games. Games typically span 20 minutes and pit teams of 3 Nauts against each other.
Instead of over 80 heroes in DOTA, there is only a small pool of 10+ Nauts to choose from. There is also no need to delve into the nitty-gritty of what items to buy or what stats/skills to train - the skill tree of the Nauts is far more simple. Other elements such as warding, lasthitting, denying, creep pulling etc. are also left out.
That is not to say there is zero depth to the game. Individual player skill and teamwork remain of prime importance to ensure victory just as with any other MOBA. Some Nauts have a fairly high skill cap and various synergies which help add to the strategic element of the game - all this under a deceptively simple facade where each Naut only has two skills.
The artwork is crisp and colorful, with no disorienting clutter during teamfights. Other notable upsides to the game are its fairly large and active community (with at least 1000 players ingame at any moment, finding a game is easy) and a ranking system. There is no pay-to-win, with all heroes being unlockable and any additional purchases being cosmetic only.
Downsides to this game would be that associated with almost any MOBA - balance issues. This is especially pertinent when the hero pool is small - overpowered Nauts make the game less fun for everyone else.
Another major problem is that the game automatically fills empty slots with bots, which typically do little other than feed the enemy gold. Furthermore, there is little disincentive for a player to leave a game if they are losing, which perpetuates the problem of *most* games being one-sided stomps against a full party of bots at the end.
Despite this, Awesomenauts remains a fun game at heart, especially if you play it with friends.

So, here's the premise. A bunch of girls are stalking this guy Goro as they all adore him - even Akane, our heroine secretly loves him but stays in the back. He gets kidnapped however, and it is up to Akane to save him.
The gameplay is responsive and fluent, but being a ninja; Akane can cling to walls and slowly slide down on them and perform wall jumps if walls are close enough. She attacks primarily by throwing kunais and can use secret ninja scrolls, having a selection of 3 ninja arts; wether it be kunais shooting at all directions, death from above or devastate anything left or right.
The music fits the mood and overall it's pretty fun; although you best have patience - the wall-cling takes some time getting used to and there is no true game over, but dying means starting the whole level over. No checkpoints, but I feel that's fair given the short length. Each chapter consists of three acts where in the third a boss awaits.
I recommend the game - the difficulty ramps up as the game progresses as the final levels made me die a lot in comparison to the first act which was a cakewalk and it's an enjoyable experience.
The last thing to mention are the kimonos. These make you take longer and risky routes to get, but they make a notable difference: The ending.
As most people can expect; defeating the final boss has Akane kneel infront of her master Goro - the mission is complete.
However...
...if Akane can assemble all of the kimono outfits; she will have these jump in after defeating the final boss and dress her up; winning the love of Goro.
Now that, was pretty cute and felt worth my time.

It's not really a bad game for the price, but there are so many platformers out there that this isn't really special. Controls are pretty basic for a platformer but it took a while to learn the timing for wall jumps- you need to make sure to stick to the wall long enough before jumping. It makes it feel clunky compared to some other platformers, but it allows you to set up kunai throws. However, it also means it's clunkier to detach yourself from walls which is a pain when enemies are approaching. The bigger problem is that you can't control yourself well after wall jumping, so you can't really shorten your jump to avoid enemies or jump a little higher to make it up to the top of the wall. I don't know if it was me but sometimes it felt like it was strict about jump commands from ledges, there were a couple times I could have sworn I'd jumped in time yet ended up running off the cliff.
Pretty much no story, music is decent, animations and sfx are mediocre. There are 15 levels with 3 kimonos to collect. Since health pickups are very rare to come and enemies don't drop health, you should avoid as many enemies as possible. Later levels can be especially unforgiving and if you don't have the reactions/coordination necessary, will have a frustrating experience. In the longer levels, if you take 1-2 hits early on, it's probably best to reset. In the last level, collecting kimonos before facing the boss was infinitely harder than the actual final boss. Bosses have simple patterns that are pretty obvious and it's really just up to your execution.
Some other points:
* Obnoxious, wavy text appears after completing levels that wouldn't be so bad if you could skip them (they last about 10-15s)
* Controller support (used x360) seems bad because after a while it randomly pauses the game intermittently. Was forced to use keyboard.
* I would've liked more settings, especially volume controls to turn sound levels lower
* I played in windowed mode, and when it's out of focus the game just shows a purple screen
* The sprite of Akane doesn't match the game art
* I would've liked to be able to reset the level from the pause menu (can only resume/quit)
* Hurtbox on dogs are annoying: you need to crouch to hit them. Nothing wrong about that except that normally kunais go right through their head, you arbitrarily have to aim for their feet.
If you enjoy platformers and have already played through other more polished ones, you could give this a go. Otherwise there are better platformers out there.

As this game enters Beta, it becomes officially playable.
The combat was never lackluster, but the introduction of a campaign, however bare-bones, breathes real life into this game.
The combat is quite varied and versatile: There's effective stealth, where to keep from being seen you have to track your enemy's movements and keep them in your sight at all times. Sneaking up behind someone allows you to deal lethal damage, and the deadliest attacks (rabbit kick) are the most difficult (and satisfying) to perform.
Since there's a screen-share PvP feature, a map creation kit, and an endless Arena mode, I can't really complain for replayability.
On higher-end devices, or on lower settings, the game performs well enough for me to recommend it.
Solid 7/10, an anticipated 9/10 once it's been polished and leaves Beta.

The American version of one of my favorite simulators! What's there to not love?
This game is basically a reskinned Euro Truck Simulator 2, with the same interface, options, and physics in it, with updates being released to add the same gameplay changes as its sister version, but with American laws relevant to the state you visit and with American trucks.
For $20, it's a great game on its own, and the states of California, Nevada, and Arizona are all beautifully designed with more coming in the future. Out of the box, ETS2 has more cities and content to enjoy than ATS before you add in all the DLC that they've spent years developing, but when you think about the distance between cities and how much work you'll have to do to visit them all or set up a trucking empire, you've still got hundreds of hours put into the game and any game that can get in that much play time for that price point can't be a bad thing, right?
The business aspect of owning a trucking business and doing jobs, just like with its sister game, is a bit lacking, but the actual driving, hauling, and truck designs are better and better with each update.
If I could have one criticism it's that there are only a couple of Peterbilts and a couple of Kenworths to pick from, with no other SCS-provided variety for vehicles compared to ETS2, which had many different brands and models out of the box. Third-party mods are fine and good, but they can break with updates and the authors and stop developing them entirely making them useless in the future. As the map of the country is expanded, I would like to see more truck brands and dealerships added into the game to provide more options to the player for supported vehicles.

Horror games live and die on the world they create, and in this above all else, The Coma succeeds. The devs clearly put a lot of thought into how to organize their school to make it seem like a real place, and then how to turn it into shadowy ruins full of debris and spattered blood. Loads of text descriptions and interactions make up for the limitations of the graphics, and the more horrific elements are just detailed enough to have an impact. Scattered notes provide just enough information to make you want to search for more, even if that means venturing into dangerous territory. It's a shame that the process of making your way through the school isn't more enjoyable . . .
Opening up new areas and progressing the plot in The Coma tends to take the form of "go to this place and interact with this object," or else "go to one of these places, but we won't tell you which one, so search the entire school until it turns up." At best, this often feels padded, passing through the same areas with the same threats just to do one thing you couldn't do before. At worst, you'll circle around the school over and over, trying to find an unblocked path that isn't haunted by the killer. Which brings me to the worst part of it all . . .
Alien: Isolation succeeded in creating a terrifying enemy who stalks you throughout the game, because that game gave you all manner of tools with which to distract, avoid, and even fend off the creature. The Coma only lets you hide in a locker until she eventually goes away. The only way to change her patrol route is to deliberately bait her into following you in a circle, and if she's blocking the only available path, all you can do is wait and wait and wait and hope you can trust the audio cues when you stop hearing her. Perhaps this is an issue on my part, but I couldn't even consistently tell which direction her footsteps were coming from! I often felt like I had no power to actively progress the story until the game decided I'd wasted enough time and waved me onwards. It wasn't even scary anymore, just tedious.
I really wanted to like this game, but it felt like it had no respect for my time. I'm looking forward to seeing what the devs do next, and hoping they learn from their mistakes next time around.

It's always a good sign when I find myself repeatedly muttering the words "Hmmm, I actually really like this game" to myself when I'm playing something.  Well, a good sign that it's a good game.  Perhaps also the "first sign of madness", as they say.  But we won't go there...
Since an eccentric little foray into 2D, Silent Hill-inspired "survival horror" entitled Lone Survivor came out in 2012, a number of other indie devs have attempted to capture a similar charm.  While a couple have come reasonably close - last year's Claire comes to mind - The Coma may finally be a game which equals the inspiration of Jasper Byrne's little "neo-classic" (while also owing a tremendous amount to the "stealth horror" classic Clock Tower, as well as high school horror game Obscure and maybe, just maybe, the more recent DreadOut).  While The Coma does very little which could be considered terribly "new", what it does it does very well.

It looks great, sounds great, and plays just fine too.  It's scary enough - though it shouldn't stress any of you lightweights TOO much - and it also isn't that difficult really, until perhaps the very end, and might thereby be a rather good introduction to horror gaming for all of you thus far afraid to take the plunge.  It's a fantastic little game which manages to find a balance between "cute" and "creepy" without compromising either, and is perfectly good value given the moderate length and substantial entertainment which it provides.

Sure, I could make a few minor complaints.  The maps, for example, could take more cues from the likes of Silent Hill by showing you: a. where you've been, and b. where you can't enter (due to a barricade in a corridor, say, or something blocking a door "from the other side").  But on the whole, this still emerges as one of the more solid horror titles of recent years, and while that's not necessarily saying THAT much - it's been a quagmire of♥♥♥♥♥♥of late, let's face it - it'll still stand up pretty well in years to come, methinks, not least of all due to the frankly "ageless" art style it's chosen.

Nice job, Korea!  You're certainly putting the vast majority of Europe to shame at this particular point in time...keep up the good work!

It's a shame this game isn't as good as it could be.
Woodle Tree Adventures is a pretty basic 3D platformer. You jump around and collect three "fairy tears" per level and then reach the exit. You can collect berries on the way to unlock better versions of the leaf you use to attack, and avoid or kill enemies that mostly don't seem to care about much more than just standing there. The controls feel a little loose and impercise, so some jumps are a bit harder than they look like they should be.
The whole game just kinda seems unfinished. Except for a few that go on patrols or the rare one that will actually walk towards you, most enemies are just sort of out of the way and not doing anything. There are no camera controls; everything shown with pre-determined camera angles, and some of them are in bad positions. Some of them also won't trigger properly, leaving you with even worse views sometimes. The checkpoints seem broken too; SOMETIMES you'll respawn at a checkpoint close to where you died, but most of the time it sends you back to the very start of the level. Once,
. Since you can't fix that, I had to play the first part of the level basically backwards until I hit a point where the camera decided to change to something more reasonable.
The level select are just globes that show up in your house without any sort of labels and aren't presented in a linear order, so it could be easy to forget what level is the latest one you unlocked if you step away from the game and come back. On the other hand, since the game only lasts about 40 minutes, you'll probably beat it in one sitting anyway. I kinda considered going back to collect the rest of the berries to get the last weapon, but the game doesn't tell you how many berries you've collected in each level, so god knows where those are [edit: It turns out that doesn't matter, because you can go back to a level and just get as many berries as you want to get the next item. It's not counting your completion rate, so you don't HAVE to get everything].
This game could get better! It seems like the devs are patching it with new levels and features, like multiplayer and the ability to zoom the camera in and out (but really, full camera control is more important). Crusader Kings II is a masterpiece in its own right. Let me just get that off my chest.
TLDR: Complex Strategy game with a decent learning curve. Don't buy if you just want to kill things and take over the world in a few hours. This is a game for the patient detremined manipulator. If you are willing to sit back and do a bit of reading on the basics, this game will bring you hundreds of hours of enjoyment destroying middle ages Europe (without the loads of DLC)
If you had asked me that when I first bought the game, I would have laughed. At the back of my mind I knew it was, I just wasn't determined enough to learn how to actually play it coherently due to its imposing learning curve. I had played some games like it before, but nothing that actually tried to be more than every other game out there.
CK2 unlike games such as Total War, Civ, or any other strategy game. It is a game about people. You don't just declare war on the country next to you and send in the troops. At least in the base game and culture/goverment type. The game accuratly potrays how you as a Count/Duke/King would need to have a valid claim on the land you want, as otherwise you would be open target to every single other lord in the land. This is just scraping the ice of the complex political dynamics that I myself am still learning to manipulate. This game will take a bit of dedication as a newcomer to the genre to really fully grasp and play efficently. It isn't INSANElY difficult, you just need to be able to sit and go through the basics one by one. With a bit of time things will become easy, and that is when the real fun of the game begins.
Politcal manipulation is the name of the game. Weaving the fabics of history with a single smothering of an infant who has YOUR rightful claim to the crown. You want to become the Irish king of Brittania? You can do it with a few well placed marriages and claims. Want to pull a Trump and wipe out the Muslim Heretics? DEUS VULT ♥♥♥♥ FACE, you can do it. Any way you wish history went from the Early to High Middle Ages can become possible if you want it bad enough. I myself have destroyed Britain enough times to make my Irish wet dreams a reality.
So YES I reccomend this game.

I have bought this game 4 times throughout its life and beaten the story multiple times. I don't need to play through the game again to prove that I love this game. But I can at least vouch for the port.
Phantom Brave isn't a perfect game or a masterpiece. It's not too hard to make the game easy, and the battle system, while different, isn't the deepest out there. That all said, the game is great and I highly recommend getting it if you're interested in a more serious SRPG compared to Disgaea.
The story centers around Marona and her guardian phantom: Ash. Much of the themes of the game revolve around prejudice and hope. Marona constantly gets burned by the people she helps, as their hate for what they see her as makes them treat her like dirt. Despite constant absue, Marona sticks to her parents' ideals they taught her in the hopes that she will one day be rewarded for her efforts. While it may be a bit irksome for some to have her be so optimistic, I do find it at least grounded by the fact that she's not inherently that pure. It is because of the support of Ash that she is able to hold on to these ideals; not because she's some pure person who can take all of this on her own. The secondary story, titled Another Marona, isn't quite as good as the main one. It does shed a bit of light on all the characters that one couldn't see in the main storyline, so it does offer something to those that enjoyed the characters and wanted to see more of them.
The meat and bones of the game is the gameplay. The battles play out in a turn based format on a girdless field. Characters have a set limit to their movement represented in DMs, but can move as many times as they want until the number of DMs is fully depleted. You can summon phantoms by confining them to various objects on the field, which grant certain bonuses. Phantoms have a set number of turns they can stay in battle, and when that depletes they leave the battle. Marona is the only character that stays on the field permanently, though there are ways to make some phantoms stick around as long. Attacks themselves have various ranges and AOE "shapes" in which they can effect the field. If you find the going to get rough, then you can pick up and throw allies to better position them, or even toss enemies out of bounds at the cost of slightly empowering the other enemies(though the last enemy standing is immune, if I recall). Any items that a phantom has been confined into has a chance of being "stolen", as well.
There also a number of sub systems within the game. Titles can be bestowed upon any phantom or weapons you have, and each title has various stat bonuses. Some titles even contain special attack skills. You also enter random dungeons, fuse items and titles, and migrate any non-unique skills. There's a lot of customization available to players in this game. You can also "reincarnate" characters, which resets them to level one, but allows you to increase their base stat points in order to increase their overall strength.
The visual design is one of the few things that doesn't quite hold up. Sprites are somewhat simple, but not particularly ugly(unless you don't disable the filter they use in the options). That character design is pleasant, and there's a lot of variety in overall character design. The background art scales up well, and looks quite lovely. The game performs well, too, with easy 60 fps in most situations.
The audio design in the game is quite good. The English voice actors for the main story perform quite well, and the voices fit their characters. There's also a Japanese voice option for those who do not like dubs. The Music in the game is pleasant, varied, and is arguably some of the best that composer Tenpei Sato has put out in quite some time.
In terms of replayability, Phantom Brave has a lot to offer. There are a lot of items to collect through confining, characters to unlock, titles to find, and even a New Game Plus option. Delving through dungeons to power up can take a lot, or a little(if you know what to do), time.
In summation: The game is a great value at $20. The story, gameplay, and audio are great, with only some bits of the visuals not holding up quite as well. The port is functional, runs well, and contains all the content from every iteration of Phantom Brave. This is the definite experience, and is well worth your consideration.
