Phantom Brave was ahead of its time.
In the PS2 era, it seemed like every RPG (or maybe all genres, actually) needed to go BIGGER. More dramatic, more epic, more serious. Nippon Ichi carved a niche for itself with Disgaea, a silly RPG that tried to be as un-serious as possible. It was more of an episodic anime, full of comedy and parodies. It was in the right place at the right time, and got a lot of attention.
However, Phantom Brave took a riskier path. It was a "serious" story, yet instead of a fantasy epic, it aimed to be a gentle slice-of-life. You're not the center of the universe, but just a person in a tropical archipelago filled with strange and diverse characters. The story is about the orphan girl Marona, innocent and naive, watched over by her jaded phantom bodyguard, Ash. She tries to make her own way through the world, but her optimism clashes when it comes up against reality's cynicism and prejudices. This kind of character-driven story was very rare in games at the time, but is something that's become much more accepted in the past few years.
The gameplay system is also far ahead its time, though it may be still too advanced for us in 2016. There's a lot more freedom in this compared to the usual tactical RPG map battle. For one thing, you can free-roam instead of moving within a square grid. I like it better this way, but I have to admit it's a little clunkier just trying to move where you want. And there's more.... Confining phantoms to objects such as trees and rocks, which give different stat bonuses, yet they only last a limited number of turns in battle, so you have to pace yourself depending on the map. There's so much to keep track of. Yet there's no short-term pleasures like the team-attacks in Disgaea, it's all about the long-term strategy in each battle.
Same for outside of battle, you're given incredible freedom to customize and build your characters; even your ITEMS gain their own levels and new skills. You can even fuse characters/items together to break past the old limits of their potential.  It's not a regular RPG where you grind for a linear increase in power, but you use your brain and tinker with multiple systems to gain *exponential* boosts in power. The max level is 9999 for a good reason, not just to extend playtime. Yet this can be very overwhelming to a new player, as unlike Disgaea there's very little indication of what's effective RIGHT NOW, just hints of how godlike you can become later after you've "cracked the code." I don't recommend this at all for people who want a comfortable casual time, and to be honest it's too much even for me sometimes. I enjoy this kind of abstract stat manipulation stuff, yet this game was aimed at someone *even more hardcore* than me.
It's strange how such an accessible heartwarming story was fused with an inaccessible challenging game. It's definitely not for everyone (if you don't like complicated RPGs you might want to watch a LetsPlay instead). But it's bold and unique, and I love it anyway.

I'm not one to gush over a MOBA, but this one is great! The big problem I have with most of them is that there are so many characters to choose from and so many items to buy that a new player can easily be intimidated. League of Legends and DotA both suffer from that flaw. Awesomenauts is simple, easy to learn, and just plain fun.
Instead of 40-something characters to choose from, there are six or seven to start, and you unlock more as you play. Items are vastly simplified as well. Befor the match, you choose your character. He has three attacks, one for each button on your mouse. You choose three items for each attack, and those are the things you'll be able to buy during the match. You also choose three "utility" items that boost your health, your movement speed, etc.
Oh. And this isn't a top-down, RTS-style MOBA. This is a side-view shooty game that just happens to be a MOBA.
I highly recommend this game. The characters are all different enough that (a) there's one that fits your playstyle and (b) you'll never get bored. There's even one that has no basic attack and is just a support character. He heals and drop power-ups.
And this game is part of the Humble Indie Bundle 8, which is still available for another week or two. So get it cheap, play the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it, and never feel like you wasted your money.

As is, it feels more like a demo than a full game. It's early access game so the lack of content isn't unexpected, but it's been like this for a very long time now and $30 feels like a steep price for what you get.

The parkour system is where the game really shines.  Your character is extremely mobile and has almost complete freedom in the game envrionment. It's typically just a small enemy camp, or group of enemies surrounded by a vast, empty plain/desert/etc.  It offers some nice variety for stealth missions though. Port quality--
Its the original with basic PC options. It's not a remake with a ton of added features, but everything works great and the PC developers deserve a lot of credit considering what some ports end up like.
Music--
First off, the music is just excellent in this game. Buy the game if you like VGM in any way, shape or form. Who knows what Tenpei Sato was on when he did the music for PB, but I love this♥♥♥♥♥♥and its much more fun than his other works. Often extremely catchy and/or powerful, whenever battles start, the music exists to get the player in the mood for battle with great effect. Outside of battle its all over the place in terms of style and intensity but is often beautiful and creative.
Gameplay--
PB is a game with a slightly "different" take on the SRPG. From character building, development and battle. In some ways, akwardly branching out where it doesn't really make any headway, in ways where it feels like there's nothing more going on than backpeddling an already perfectly functional form of standardized SRPG gameplay.
The movement in battle is where the game falls flatter than Marona's...attack stat, its completely different than almost all other titles in its genre for seemingly no reason other than to be unique. The unique form of movement can be akward and even frustrating at times. This isn't a constant problem by any means and it definitely isn't a GAME BREAKER, but it does abrupt the flow of battle, sometimes causing numerous attempts at getting a character to attack or to be in a proper position. Whats frustrating is that other games like this one would play just perfectly in these scenarios, and really, this has to be by far PB's biggest flaw.
The core gameplay is mostly solid and theres a ton of fun in building a team together, though. Its somewhat barebones compared to a modern sandbox SRPG you would find today, but is also a lot less overwhelming. The distinct style and gameplay is largley refreshing to those familiar with the genre.
Story/Closure--
While not something I personally care deeply about with these types of games, the characters often grabbed me in different ways and are easy to love/hate. Unlike with most anime and japanese games, I found the characters to be very relatable in different ways. PB's story is touching and enjoyable overall.
PB has a fanastic charm of its own that feels much more down-to-earth than its bigger and much more popular brother Disgaea. As a game it definitely holds its own and some ways excels over its brother. Overall its a very creative take on the genre with a superbly catchy soundtrack.

After being let down by Clear Sky's unfinished gameplay, I was wary of Call of Pripyat, and although the game is beginning to seem a bit dated, it is still tons of fun.
Graphics-
The game looks both technically artistically brilliant. While the engine is beginning to show its age outdoors at long distances, the lighting effects, foliage, clouds, and especially the decaying urban environments all look fantastic. I have only played the game maxed with DX10, so I can't attest to how great the DX11 features look. However, even so, the game looks and plays phenomenally.
Sound-
The music and atmospheric noises are as good as ever, and the voice acting is decent, which is good for a game from Ukraine.
Gameplay-
They've really integrated features that worked from Clear Sky with features from Shadow of Chernobyl. You can upgrade weapons and repair them, using special calibration tools (which are a bit too difficult to find), but ballistics feels much more like it did in the first, and the focus is much less on combat with humans and much more on exploring and finding mutants. Factions are in place, but no one will attack you on sight unless you've made an enemy of them. Even bandits. This makes for some interesting interactions out in the wild. There are now blowouts which require you to hide indoors or you will die. Gone is the wonky factional combat from clear sky, and perhaps most importantly, gone are the bugs, glitches, crashes, and other instability issues. That stability is what makes Call of Pripyat so refined.
The story is weaker compared to the first, but it is still quite good, and the atmosphere of the game itself is great. If you liked STALKER, you won't be disappointed by Call of Pripyat. That being said, I'm expecting big things from STALKER 2. They've had plenty of time to refine their formula and train their skills. Now it's time to shine.

Basically, if you've only played Skyrim or invested the most amount of time into that over the other TES games, you might not appreciate the differences in Oblivion. Skyrim is a much more streamlined game, as well as having certain mechanics being completely different (i.e. having to go to an alchemy table in Skyrim to make potions). If you can tolerate the slow combat, dumb AI and hilarious voice acting, you'll find an amazing adventure RPG hidden below. In true TES fashion, explore dungeons and fight monsters for loot, explore huge cities filled with all sorts of interesting characters, and become the true hero of Cyrodiil. It may be partly due to my nostalgic attachment to this game, but this is my favorite TES game that I've played. This game does not try to take itself too seriously or make it somewhat realistic like Skyrim often does, instead it boasts it's high-fantasy setting and open-ended gameplay.
Only major cons would be the UI which can be fixed with DarNified UI (basically SkyUI for Oblivion). I'd also recommend using the unofficial patch as well as some other subtle mods that help improve gameplay, nothing major. With that said, this game does have an amazingly huge mod community that is still very much active to this day. Definately check out the Nexus.

Oblivion addresses many of the gameplay issues which plagued its predecessor, Morrowind, making it more accessible to a wider number of players and a less frustrating experience overall. It's considerably more friendly to modders as well, if its massive library of player-made content is anything to go by. Unfortunately, these improvements don't come without a price. The setting and 'flavour' of the game is comparitively rather bland.
Pros:
- Massive, sprawling world to explore with hundreds of locations to visit and loot.
- Interesting and well-written faction quests with epic finales
- Unusually bright and cheery as far as RPGs go, which is a refreshing change
- Fascinating background lore built up from a well-loved franchise
- A fantastic score composed by Jeremy Soule
- Mod support means you can fix pretty much any little thing that bothers you
Cons:
- Levelling system can be clunky and counter-intuitive
- NPCs that are frightening to behold, affectionately known as 'potato faces'
- Dialogue can be patchy and everyone is voiced by a small handful of people
- Dull combat
TL;DR: If you like immersive games with a lot of interesting background story and exploration, give this (and the other Elder Scrolls games) a try. If you're an action junkie, it's probably not for you.

This game had a metric ♥♥♥♥ton of potential, but wasted every ounce of it.
It used to be a fun, sand-box style fighting game with amazing combat mechanics and interesting ideas, but through the development hell it's been through, since the past 7 years - everything about it is completely soulless.
There's challenge - and there's having mechanics so broken you can't even do anything. I love challenge in a game, I like overcoming actual difficulty in order to achieve a goal. It's a great feeling when you overcome genuine challenge, to finally pass through levels that make you pull your hair out with anger. Overcoming obstacles in a game make it just that.
But there's one defining feature that seperates Overgrowth from being a fair, yet challenging experience - there's a line that's been crossed when Fun becomes Tedious.
There's having real challenge, and then you have mechanically handicapping the player until they can barely do anything at all. The AI will simply just spam generic attacks until you fall over, regardless of position, weaponry, or otherwise.
All those innovative combat physics are real neat until everything you're up against will do the equivilent of button-mashing with pitch-perfect accuracy (as AI are virtually unable to miss), and those great tactical ideas become completely meaningless.
What's the point in having Armor, or advanced strategy when the AI will simply do 1 attack over and over and instantly kill you?
When you fight in this game, you have to do special moves to catch your opponent off guard, swivel around him, confuse him, get the drop on the unsuspecting chap. The AI doesn't do any of this! They'll do the same exact attack over, and over, and over, and over - and
against the strategy the Devs put into the game. You get more out of spamming the Jump Attack than you do genuinely fighting your enemy through stealth and tactics.
Weapons are a joke. Nice Sword, but unfortunately, blade combat is extremely clunky, and the AI will actually break the physics engine to block your attacks. Which they'll do. Every. Single. Hit.
I've thrown knives at unsuspecting enemies, with their backs turned, and they manage to catch it, or block it
AI will constantly clip through their own hitboxes (when said hitboxes decide to show up at all), to block attacks of which they're not even aware of.
That's not the end of it, whenever given a weapon, the AI will almost change in behavior. They'll go from defensive and somewhat aware, to running forward and swinging madly.
But, because they're AI - Using tactics such as maneuvering or blocking is completely ineffective, so their braindead logic will win every time, regardless.
I feel like the game has hardly anything to do with the mechanics they introduced into combat and much rather have it centered around the idea of "we'll get to that later".
So many good ideas are wasted because they're either patched incorrectly, or overshadowed by the old, broken AI.
This has been in development for most of my actual life. It's still apparently "In Development". Needless to say, it's in development purgatory, and
.
I say that the development isn't really development, it's a process of regression. Or, for a lack of better word, complete stillness. The game is almost backtracking in terms of updates and "fixes".
I don't know how the developers managed it - but the good alpha mechanics that were interesting and innovative and have been turned into garbage.
With every update that is released, 1 thing is fixed and 2 things are broken. Or, better yet - nothing is fixed and the game remains completely stagnant.

While the only new item added to the game by Spear is a 25-ammo pickup, it makes up for this by providing 3 20-level campaigns that will give you an even bigger challenge than the original Wolf 3D campaign.
The first campaign, which was the vanilla Spear release back in the day, unfortunately suffers from level design that goes past "hard" and into "you need to know the map in advance to not die" territory. The Mutant, a special enemy with nigh-instant reaction time that originally only appeared in Episode 2 of Wolf 3D as that Ep's prime special feature ends up grossly overused throughout the campaign, often in cheap positions or in excessive numbers that pretty much guarantee you'll take hits if not get killed outright unless you magically know about their placement ahead of time, leading to a whole mess of deaths as you gradually try to learn the later maps in the campaign.
Thankfully, the other two campaigns don't suffer from this problem at all, you actually seldom see the mutant outside of the secret levels and the last three or so levels of each campaign. To top it off, these two bonus campaigns have a built in full-retexture mod to help keep things fresh.
Downloading the ECWolf sourceport to run the game is highly recommended (it even automatically looks for steam installs of the game!) for improved graphic and control options, as well as to remedy any issues you may run into running DOSBox.

Spear of Destiny is a prequel to
released months after Wolf came out. The Steam release also contains two third-party mission packs released in 1994.
If you're one of those folks looking for more classic Wolfenstein, the Spear of Destiny campaign is what you want: a challenging - if occasionally unfair - distillation of everything that made the original great in one single contiguous 'episode'. The only notable additions as far as I'm aware are new bosses, new music (the title track is my favorite), ammo boxes with 25 bullets each, and a couple of new textures.
The mission packs...aren't great. They were cash-ins by a company called FormGen, and are nothing more than janky reskins of the main Spear of Destiny campaign wrapped around amateur level design. I had to spurn my purism and turn on ECWolf's automap because I just did not want to put up with stumbling around maze after maze, not to mention level progression and even bosses hidden behind secrets.
Par times, boss names and a couple other things aren't changed from the original campaign, because it was only possible for FormGen to do sound and graphics swaps. Expect to be able to complete levels in as little as 30 seconds merely by stumbling across the exit, giving you stupidly high par bonuses.
Most of the new assets are actually pretty good, although some are just weird. They give the missions a different feel at least, but I wouldn't consider them essential playing even if you're the type of person who would buy Spear of Destiny.

So for modding, I didn’t do anything fancy or complicated. Here’s a step by step guide:
1). Download the ECWolf source port, it’s what I used, and it’s all I needed for this game. It’s based off the ZDoom mod for the

2). You need to navigate to a certain folder in your Wolfenstein directory. Since you downloaded it off Steam, by default that’ll be:
C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\SteamApps\common\Spear of Destiny\base
Copy paste that into Windows Explorer/File Explorer and it should take you there. If not, copy paste the following:
%PROGRAMFILES(X86)%\Steam\SteamApps\common\Spear of Destiny\base
If neither of those work, you’ll have to find where you saved it since you’re not using the default location.
3). That ECWolf  you downloaded in step 1? Copy/paste the zip folder it gave you into the location from step 1. Then unzip/extract all the contents of that folder into the folder from step 1. (the Spear of Destiny\base folder).
4). In the same folder, look for something named “dosbox.exe” and rename it to “Steamdosbox.exe”.
5). Still in the same folder, look for “ecwolf.exe” and rename it to “dosbox.exe”.
Congrats! You’ve now modded your game to feature more modern controls, better key bindings, unlimited saves, and you can use the Steam overlay while in game now. The game is still launched through Steam normally, and it’ll still track your playtime.

So, I am basically just going to assume that you have read the store page and have an idea of what this game is about. You should if you are here.
So I had watched some videos on Youtube earlier today and knew nothing about this game until today
. I bought the game without any expectations and off I went. Right of the bat I felt intrigued to search about the starting area and get to grips with everything. All the usual things are there like the crafting, scavaging, slots on your character for clothing. You know the drill. The crafting menus need love as you can really only scroll from the top to the bottom at present. You also have your typical hunger, thirst, health and stamina management.
Upon further investigation, I found what is like an underground science lab. Hmmm so? So this is the area where you can cure and tame animals. I am not going to waffle on about how you do all the different things, but this is the main feature (or so I believe) and how you go about building your reserve with different animals. The starting area contains your empty reserve with various different enclosures for you to start building up your collection. So far I rescued a dog and a Deer. From doing a liitle researching online, it seems there are different grade animals from common through to rare. Could be a lot of fun finding these?
So, I went out and had a good roam around the starting area and collecting resources lying about as well as hacking trees and rocks etc. I managed to make some tools and also a construction bench which opens up the next tier of items you can build as well as crafting stations like a tannery and all that good stuff. The crafting menu grew massively from laying down that initial crafting station. I can only imagine the crafting options being insane once you get all the core stations in place. And there were lots! Maybe slightly overwhelming for some. From food, to clothing, to structures, to tools, weapons, furniture.....there's loads!
I decided I wanted to just explore at this point. I had fun looking through all the structures in the starting area and gathering up all the materials I could find on the way. I even went for a look in the sea (seems almost empty other than weeds you can collect). I stumbled upon a ship on the shoreline and this is how you navigate from biome to biome. You click the portal and you are presented with a menu. Each box represents an area. Sorry about the pics. Taken on 3 screens.
There are quite a few places to go explore already, but based on those pics, this looks to be huge. My hope here is this becomes seamless rather than porting. I tried only one other area and the biome was completely different. This biome was more akin to the lands where Conan makes his stand (Conan the Barbarian - Battle of the Mounds) and the enemies were also very similar, though none on a horse back.
That said, I felt like the identity of the game was confusing. We go from the lush starting area and into the next biome where the portal area has a helicopter to indicate the protal area rather than the previously mentioned boat, which sort fits the biome. It's worth mentioning there were different animal types in the second biome. Want some camels? that's the place to go. I think this will be the case per biome, and searching each biome is gona be a lot of fun for me.
Speaking of animals. Once you capture, cure and tame your animals, you can have 5 of them as companions at a time. I have not tried this yet, but they can follow you around and attack or standby on your command. They also come labelled with their gender and rarity and so on.
And it shows it....
That said, It ran very well on ultra settings on my rig 50-60fps (GTX980Ti/4790/16g/Win10) and it also ran decent in Nvidia Surround at 5760x1080 at around 30-40 fps.
To sum it up, If you like exploring, lots of crafting, and building an animal sanctuary....this should be right up your street. But remember it has a ways to go. The potential is there and I'd honestly say there is plenty of content to play with right now. I will add to this as i go.

Crusader Kings II is a masterpiece in its own right. Let me just get that off my chest.
TLDR: Complex Strategy game with a decent learning curve. Don't buy if you just want to kill things and take over the world in a few hours. This is a game for the patient detremined manipulator. If you are willing to sit back and do a bit of reading on the basics, this game will bring you hundreds of hours of enjoyment destroying middle ages Europe (without the loads of DLC)
If you had asked me that when I first bought the game, I would have laughed. At the back of my mind I knew it was, I just wasn't determined enough to learn how to actually play it coherently due to its imposing learning curve. I had played some games like it before, but nothing that actually tried to be more than every other game out there.
CK2 unlike games such as Total War, Civ, or any other strategy game. It is a game about people. You don't just declare war on the country next to you and send in the troops. At least in the base game and culture/goverment type. The game accuratly potrays how you as a Count/Duke/King would need to have a valid claim on the land you want, as otherwise you would be open target to every single other lord in the land. This is just scraping the ice of the complex political dynamics that I myself am still learning to manipulate. This game will take a bit of dedication as a newcomer to the genre to really fully grasp and play efficently. It isn't INSANElY difficult, you just need to be able to sit and go through the basics one by one. With a bit of time things will become easy, and that is when the real fun of the game begins.
Politcal manipulation is the name of the game. Weaving the fabics of history with a single smothering of an infant who has YOUR rightful claim to the crown. You want to become the Irish king of Brittania? You can do it with a few well placed marriages and claims. Want to pull a Trump and wipe out the Muslim Heretics? DEUS VULT ♥♥♥♥ FACE, you can do it. Any way you wish history went from the Early to High Middle Ages can become possible if you want it bad enough. I myself have destroyed Britain enough times to make my Irish wet dreams a reality.
So YES I reccomend this game.

It's so refreshing to find a game like Animallica. The thought that YOU are the only person on earth that can save the 'planet', so to speak, is quite a responsibility.
The graphics are great, the crafting system is vast with the amount of items available for you to create. I personally will spend hours crafting everything I can. The game will appeal to people who play city builders, survival games and even interior designers, yes, interior designers will love setting up their first house and placing furniture all over the place!
If I understand correctly, the devs are still working on an opening to the game, right now you start in some kind of conservation center with a small knife and various items in your inventory. The gameplay is fairly smooth, I did encounter the odd lag here and there on high settings but not a game breaker. Remember this is ALPHA 1.0, so you will encounter bugs.
The devs have done things right. Too many early access games come out with little or no content, but this one does!
The amount of content is not so important in the early stages, what does matter is, is the game playable? and Animallica is more than playable. So far I've only explored the enclosure, picking up various items that will craft new items. The inventory system is easy to use and if you press F1, there is a small tutorial that you can read.
Having played for about 90 minutes, the game is very impressive, I'm excited to see how this game progresses. I give Animallica a big thumbs up and suggest you try the game for yourself. Boy, I played this game for 14 minutes. Here are my first impressions:
-The excuse plot makes the female lead look pathetic. All I know is that she is in love with some monk (indicated by her shooting more hearts from her face than an entire group of women), and can be taken out by a single kunai.

You're better off visiting a Flash Game website and playing something there for free.

This game is alive. Very alive. By alive, I mean it has many things happening all at once that seem like things people would be doing. Stalkers hunting animals for food, talking by campfires, hunting for artifacts, or making last stands against tougher foes. Even the animals, they too hunt, travel in packs, and attack others for food. The story may not be the best, but it has some amazing elements that seem what should be considered "survival horror". Choosing between sacrificing food for ammo, requiring sleep and meals, proper weapon maintenance, inventory organization, choosing between armor that'll let you take extra hits or sneak past enemies while considering the carry weight of both, the feeling of being hunted by enemies that are stronger than you, and finally coming across the grave of an unlucky stalker that could mean finding valuable resources. I love Fallout for its slightly comical take on nuclear holocaust, and Metro for its serious approach. But, this'll always be my go-to for the feeling of dread that one should expect from survival horror.

The "real" sequel to SoC. Sacrifices a little bit of the heavy, suffocating atmosphere and enthralling storyline of the first game for a massive improvement in virtually every other field. Surprisingly stable for something made by GSC, more balanced, devoid of the nerve-wracking loading times, dull random quests and broken mechanics. While the main storyline is noticeably more bland than in SoC, the side stories in all three of the main locations and the related quests more than make up for it. Increasing the size and decreasing the number of the main locations has been a wise decision, and while maybe a bit less varied in features, they are still rich enough. The re-worked survival, combat, anomaly, artifact and weapon customization systems all contribute to a much smoother and rewarding gameplay while the quests that involve going "off the grid" and often underground still ensure the teeth-rattling, creepy experience you all loved in SoC.

As someone's who has purchased this game over 5 times( 2x PS2, 1x PSP, 1x Wii, 1x PSP Digital for Vita) and for my 6th time, receiving it as a free gift as a Beta tester. This is a game that will not disappoint in the long-run. I have played Phantom Brave for over ten years(first time in 2005) and everytime I dive into it with a fresh start, I always learn something new.
Just to get this out of the way, this game comes as basically TWO games. The default story of Marona, then "Another Marona" playthrough which is basically an entirely new story mode, in which it can carry-over all your phantoms' strength AFTER you've beaten the default story.
As a strategy RPG it serves as both a dungeon crawler(optional, but used more for power leveling to obtain insane power levels and weapons for end-game, just like in Disgaea) and an extremely compelling story of a orphaned girl. Marona, seemingly hated by the world because of her unusual powers to communicate and summon Phantoms to aid her in battle, earning her the nickname "The Possessed". Her one true ally and guardian, Ash, a phantom, watches over Marona everyday as she deals with the struggles of being despised. As you progress through the story it'll tug at your heart-strings up until the final battle. You'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll get angry, you'll cry more, then you'll keep on playing.
This is easily my favorite NIS title to ever have dropped even more than Soul Nomad and the Disgaea series in its incredible entirety. A time-less RPG that will never disappoint with hundreds of attacks, dozens of character classes, hilarious/elaborate/highly detailed/unique particle effects/combination /over-the-top overkill type attacks. When I say hundreds of attacks, I'm not exaggerating, the game literally has hundreds of attacks, maybe even thousands of unique animations if you involve a fusionist into the mix.
It's incredibly difficult to find anything bad to say about the game, as someone who's played it for consistantly on and off for 10 years,
It's easy to say I have over several thousand hours logged on this game outside of steam, and it never gets boring seeing what kind of badass your heroes turn into. Time for me to log another few hundred on PC now.

Basically, if you've only played Skyrim or invested the most amount of time into that over the other TES games, you might not appreciate the differences in Oblivion. Skyrim is a much more streamlined game, as well as having certain mechanics being completely different (i.e. having to go to an alchemy table in Skyrim to make potions). If you can tolerate the slow combat, dumb AI and hilarious voice acting, you'll find an amazing adventure RPG hidden below. In true TES fashion, explore dungeons and fight monsters for loot, explore huge cities filled with all sorts of interesting characters, and become the true hero of Cyrodiil. It may be partly due to my nostalgic attachment to this game, but this is my favorite TES game that I've played. This game does not try to take itself too seriously or make it somewhat realistic like Skyrim often does, instead it boasts it's high-fantasy setting and open-ended gameplay.
Only major cons would be the UI which can be fixed with DarNified UI (basically SkyUI for Oblivion). I'd also recommend using the unofficial patch as well as some other subtle mods that help improve gameplay, nothing major. With that said, this game does have an amazingly huge mod community that is still very much active to this day. Definately check out the Nexus.
I'd give this game a 9/10

Stalker: COP is the latest installment of the series and does a fine job. The Stalker series is a very atmospheric open world FPS with Sci-fi and horror elements placed in a post radiated world. In Call of Pripyat there are factions, mutants, and naturally occuring anomalies that the player may have to deal with. The best part about this game is that everything is a MAY, i.e. you may encounter this or you may have to do that. The game is totally open world and there is usually multiple ways to acomplish anything. Not only this game, but this SERIES is a must have for anyone who is into atmospheric gameplay that allows you to control the character in a way that you feel is realistic to your own way of thinking. You feel the character is you and not you just controlling a stranger with your keyboard and mouse.
An important fact about the Stalker series is that none of the games have a working V-Sync even with the option turned on in-game. Also, turning on V-Sync in the Nvidia control panel did not work for me either. This is not a problem for COP because maxed out the game ran between 50-70 fps, but the older titles may have screen tearing if your pc runs them at 90+ fps.
There is a mod called Stalker Complete, which is available for all three Stalker titles that enhances the all around experience. I also recommend the mod immediately after purchase for the mod does not change the nature of the game in any way, but only makes improvements/additions to the game, such as improved graphics, audio, bug elimination, and a fast travel option. This mod doesn't fix the V-Sync issue.

Oblivion addresses many of the gameplay issues which plagued its predecessor, Morrowind, making it more accessible to a wider number of players and a less frustrating experience overall. It's considerably more friendly to modders as well, if its massive library of player-made content is anything to go by. Unfortunately, these improvements don't come without a price. The setting and 'flavour' of the game is comparitively rather bland.
Pros:
- Massive, sprawling world to explore with hundreds of locations to visit and loot.
- Interesting and well-written faction quests with epic finales
- Unusually bright and cheery as far as RPGs go, which is a refreshing change
- Fascinating background lore built up from a well-loved franchise
- A fantastic score composed by Jeremy Soule
- Mod support means you can fix pretty much any little thing that bothers you
Cons:
- Levelling system can be clunky and counter-intuitive
- NPCs that are frightening to behold, affectionately known as 'potato faces'
- Dialogue can be patchy and everyone is voiced by a small handful of people
- Dull combat
TL;DR: If you like immersive games with a lot of interesting background story and exploration, give this (and the other Elder Scrolls games) a try. If you're an action junkie, it's probably not for you.

The mechanics of the game are very fun. Every hit is satisfying, there is an intense thrill as you duel someone with only a sliver of health left, completing a seige feels like a monumental achievement, this game was clearly built by people who knew what they wanted to make and they made it very well.
Unfourtunatly, as there is no single player mode (you can play an offline match against bots but they aren't programmed well, in objectives they will completly ignore the targets) much of the fun has to come from the community. And unfortunatly this is one of the most caustic gaming communities I've encountered. Even on the low level servers expect to get screamed at if you accidentaly kill a single team member which can be easy to do when weapons can puncture through one target and into another, seige weapons have odd hit boxes, and the dropoff on ranged weapons is often more than you expect. In every game I played with only one or two exceptions (and those were on dedicated dueling servers) there was at least one (usually more) kick votes for team killing. This often wasn't even for anything intentional it just seems to be that this game attracted people with increadibly short tempers and they now have set the tone for the entire game.
I tried to ignore how abnoxious everyone was for as long as I could but when half of a server started yelling at one guy for triggering an enviornmental hazzard and killing a team mate I realized that while I was playing for fun from good gameplay everyone else was out to win and viewed anyone who wasn't as just a terrible person. This event also was on a low level server and so it's entierly possible that the guy didn't even know what he had hit until it was too late but I never found out, he left before the kick vote could start. Really the only mode that I was having fun with for the last couple hours was free for all and that was becase there're no teams so the whining about team killing went away (though there were still kick votes for no apparent reason).
It is very disheartening that I can't recomend this game. I love the gameplay and if there were even a token single player campaign then I would tell everyone to get it but when there isn't and the community is this bad I just simply can't.

I'm currently around 3 hours into the game so base this review as of how far I've gotten in.
First of all, the game has me hooked. Pulling back from memories of Clock Tower on the SNES, and running for my dear life has never been more fun in a 2D style horror. The art style oozes of anime, but it does not at all deter from the scares. In fact, the visual novel style aspect, along with how much dialogue and interactions are available make me look forward to the next time I can speak to a character, or find a new hidden note.
Right now, the only minor complaint I have is the frequency of being chased. Sometimes I just step outside a class room and have to hide only to find that I cannot proceed unless I wait awhile. I guess one can argue this adds to the suspense, but I felt it sometimes pulled me away. I love the background ambiance and sounds you can hear throughout the halls, and just the slight sound of footsteps was enough to make my hairs stand on end.
If you guys want a fun scary game to play this Halloween, I highly highly recommend this title!

Date: 2/10/16
Review Number: 14
Game: Wolfenstein: Spear of Destiny
From (Creator Publisher): id Software
Played On:Laptop
Steam Price as of Review: $4.99
Total Time played: 40 minutes
Review:
Ah, the classic Wolfenstein.  The games that can easily be called the grandfather of all first person shooters.  Within this game lies the seeds that have given us DOOM, DOOM 2, and every other FPS that followed (all of which were horrible).  Apparently the wheel of unintended consequences has decided that in homage to all of the games that followed in its wake, it was time to sit down and play a bit of where that all began (technically the sequel to that, though Wolfenstein 3D and Spear of Destiny were essentially the exact same game with slightly different map packs).  In the early 90s, consoles were well into their formative years, while PC gaming had just begun to crawl really, when a smaller software company known as id released a quasi-3d Nazi killing game that was essentially a bunch of flat textures in a structure that offered the illusion of 3D.  The game itself is fairly simple, playing a typical strong-man armed only with a knife and pistol, you sneak into a Nazi stronghold and proceed to do some significantly expensive interior redecorating, much to the chagrin of the current inhabitants,as they clearly did not expect  your arrival.  The gameplay is a barebones breakdown of everything current shooters are -- you walk around an environment looking for things to shoot, you shoot them before they shoot back, you find the way to the next area.  All in all, the game is surprisingly simple in comparison to games available today, the difference between the three guns primarily being the rate at which they spit out bullets, and the lack of auto aiming and realistic bullet physics means shooting a nazi in the elbow from half a post code away is as effective as a point blank center mass shot, but the game is still exceedingly fun.  the repetitive wall and floor textures hearken back to my childhood gaming years, and the sound of yelling nazis as they are shot never really gets old.  Though the game itself is comparatively short and simple in comparison to newer games, that's really okay, as this is better played in shorter stints, enjoyed as a brief trip down nostalgia lane.  Not entirely sure if it's worth five dollars of nostalgia, but it’s certainly worth something.
Game’s Fate: Its 13 megs, and a fun little time waster.  Kept
Buy/No Buy: I wouldn’t necessarily buy it at full price, but it goes on sale occasionally.  Definitely get it then.

When I played this game as a kid, I was awful at it. I learned how to cheat, but even that could hardly cover just how little I understood how the game functions. I'm in college now, and I still think about those first times I played Baldur's Gate 2: Shadows of Amn. Instead of focusing on the story, which I liked, or the awesome stuff I would find, or cheat for, I thought I should focus on what made me play the game again and again:
Minsc.
My introduction to Minsc was in Irenicus' dungeon. As we explored said dungeon, I enjoyed his quirky, funny style of thought and speech. Throughout the game, I grew to love his style. I absolutely enjoyed having him in my party, because he was quite a character. I reached the end of Shadows of Amn, eventually. Since Throne of Baal was not even a thing at that point, I started a new game. This time, I wanted to play as  an evil character. My intention was to horde and dish out vengence on whoever I jolly well pleased to. What I failed to realize at the start was that that would involve losing Minsc.
Instead of getting to listen to his hilarious speaches about goodness, buttkicking, and hamsters, I was instead subjected to stern, angry lectures about my actions. Eventually, Minsc left my party. I found others who could fill the role of meat shield, but no one could fill the role of "Minsc." No one had the same level of energy and enthusiasm for ANYTHING. A couple of the evil choices I would have to make as an evil character  also rubbed me wrong. Remember, I was a child at the time. So I abandoned that character.
I played as a good character mostly so I could keep Minsc. Having been the subject of his scorn, I started to seek his praise. I played as different classes again and again, and I continued to zealously court Minsc's favor. Looking back, I can see how much of an impact Minsc had on my development, and how I treat morality in video games. At some point, I internalized a number of Minsc's battlecries and sayings, and started playing as the good guy no matter the game. I played as the good guy because in the back of my mind was "this will allow me to keep Minsc."
I've since developed other reasons for nearly always doing good, but Minsc is still there, somewhere, in the back of my mind. The sting of his disapproval, and the happiness at seeing this strong character devote himself to goodness and justice. Did I idolize that about him? Absolutely. Do I still recall him fondly? Fondly enough to by a digital copy of the game so I can be with my idol and mentor again.
Baldur's Gate 2 didn't have much of an impact on me as an impressionable child. Minsc did.
Game contains Minsc. (11/10)

This is a dynastic simulation which comes well recommended.  It will eat up much of your life, I started one game and lost 70 hours to it.  I don't know what will happen if I start another.  It is filled with DLC and purchasing a complete version of the game will cost about 150 USD.  However, these DLC's drastically expand and change the gameplay into something much different from what it was on release and will continue to do so in the future.
To describe Crusader Kings, you are a dynastic lord, a count, duke, king, or emperor.  There is no real win or lose situation other than to keep playing.  Your assumed goal is to proliferate your dynasty into other families, marry into wealthy dynasties, and set things up so your successor will be in the best position to inherit the kingdom.  Your real goal is to screw around and mess things up in whatever way your hubris takes you, sleep with your lord's wife, sell your daughter to a polish lord, cage one of the great houses of Venice and sell them to the Egyptians, whatever your fancy takes you.  Everyone in the game, right down to the courtiers and peasant rebels, are individuals with their own stats, aspirations, goals, and families.  Manipulating their desires and maneuvering to get into power will make you personify each of these people, especially when they betray you.  You will scream "You ♥♥♥♥♥!  Did you forget who put your♥♥♥♥♥on that throne!?" at your computer over some plot.
The interface is bare and the map figures are not much to look at, this suits the type of game this is just fine.  There is a lot of depth, economy, trade, alliances, holdings, relationships between all the NPC's.  It will take time to figure out the many gameplay nuances, what holdings are valuable, who makes a desirable courtier, how to fill out your desmene, and other gameplay nuances.  None of these are easy to figure out and usually come over the course of repeated failure and checking guides and faqs.  This level of complicated combined with the directionless character of the game will turn people away and I don't blame them too much for doing so.
The largest issue I find with the game is the sheer amount of DLC this game has.  It has been released gradually over the years since this game has been released and update several gameplay functions and expand several parts of the map.  On release, Crusader Kings II only covered Catholic Christian feudal kingdoms in Western Europe starting from the Middle Ages.  Now, it includes Central Africa, India, Asia, their religions, and timelines going as far back as the beginning of Charlemagne along with the different type of governments - nomadic, tribal, Indian, Islamic, and city-state.  The down side is that gathering all the things which do this will require you to sink 150 USD or so on a purchase of the game.  It's no small matter and were it not for the thousands of hours you can sink into the game and the replayability each of the DLC's add, I wouldn't recommend it.  Even without DLC, the core game remains a solid game which will leave you with many, many hours of your life gone.  If you find you enjoy what you play, you can add a DLC for a different civilization and replay from there.
This is a solid grand strategy game with a lot of attention to detail and a lot of care put into its mechanics and personality.  The detail will be off putting to some and desirable to others.  If you are a fan of grand strategy this is definitely one to pick up.

Baldur's Gate II: Enhanced Edition is a visually rather simplistic, relatively old RPG.
Now why should it be critically acclaimed as one of the best RPGs of all time, and already is?
--It gives flexibility. You don't have to grind the main plot right away, there are sidequests, especially in SoA.
--Character development. During my run, I felt a strong connection to all the characters, especially your romance options.
--New characters. They may not exactly fit (per se) in the plot development, they add a bit of a flare to the story.
--Amazing music. Yeah, this isn't a "Great Soundtrack" game. I know. However, the soundtracks to this game is SO DARN AMAZING! My favorite music (personally) is the music that comes up when you fight Irenicus.

Phantom Brave is an amazing game and I can not recommend it highly enough. This game means a lot to me, so here I go trying to put it into words.
This game follows a young girl named Marona, whose only companions are the phantoms that she has the power to communicate with. Notable among these is Ash, who was allowed to live on as a phantom as a result of Marona's parents' dying wish. Marona remains optimistic and cheerful because of Ash's guidance, and the advice of her late parents, despite that the rest of the world seems opposed to her.
The dialogue is beautifully written, and is excellently voice acted by Sandy Fox and Lex Lang among others. Watching Marona slowly win over the people of the world of Ivoire, and seeing the effects of her efforts, not to prove everyone wrong, but just to be nice to everyone, is one of the most touching things I have ever experienced. The joy of Marona making her first friend, and the tragedy of the mysterious Walnut, are very heartfelt and earnest moments of storytelling.
The battle and leveling systems are wonderfully designed and mechanically complex, as you can expect from NIS. This is a game where you can use any item, including other characters, as a weapon. You go around the map, attaching phantoms to trees, rocks, etc. as Marona yells "confine!" and they can use regular weapons like normal, but you can also just pick up a brick that's just laying there and use that. This is the kind of game where you can really just do whatever you want and I love that. It is a SRPG, but there is no grid, which gives the feel of even more freedom. If you like watching numbers go up, you'll be right at home here, there's a lot of that and it's great.
As far as this PC port specifically goes, I couldn't ask for more. It includes all of the additional content from both the Wii and PSP remakes. The backgrounds and character portraits are high res, though the battle and cutscene sprites are the same as the original, which is a good thing because those look good. There is zero slowdown, at least on my setup, which was an issue on the PSP version, and I've played all the way up to EX-10 and it hasn't crashed once. Mouse support is okay and makes it easy if you want to browse the internet while playing, but I prefer to play it how I did originally, with a Dualshock 2.
Phantom Brave may not have the same kind of humor that you expect from a Disgaea game, but it has so much else to offer that makes it something special. This game had a huge impact on me when I first played it, and continues to, whether I'm replaying it or just thinking about it. Marona is my greatest role model, and I strive to live by her example.
And remember:
"People will judge you because they can't understand your gift, but don't hate them... You were blessed with that power so you could help people. Grow up compassionate and kind; help even those who hurt you. Then, one day, everyone will come to like you."
(Full disclosure: In order to be honest I checked the box that says I got this game for free. I did, but I also paid full price for the physical edition because I love the game so much)

I wish I could give the game a Maybe or Mixed rating. It's not a bad game per se, there's a lot to be enjoyed here: deep RPG mechanics, lots of roleplay, decent story and characters...
But the fun stops with the combat, while the core elements of it are very fun with all the tactics and elemetal madness going on, most of the time it just feels cheap, unfair, unbalaced and so on and on and on. Enemies always come in overwhelming numbers, with too much health and armor, they also happen to be omniscient and know all your weak spots, have more Action Points and sometimes they even ignore initiative/round order among others.
The difficulty is all over the place, in Classic mode (Normal difficulty) a single enemy a level above you can cause very serious damage to your party if you're not careful, if they're a single level below, it's a cakewalk. But if you do lower the difficulty to Explorer mode (Easy difficulty), then there's no challenge, it's so patronizingly easy that there's no fun. There's a real problem with stats bloat here.
The armor system is just stupid, all it does is add a second health bar that completely negates damage and status effects until depleted, afterwards it's useless, you can restore it, but it'll go down again soon enough. I really don't understand why they decided to make it this way.
And somehow I always felt underleveled to most situations even after completing all the quests I could get and trying not to stray away from the path too much, it just felt very unbalaced by the end of it all. And while I'm completely against it, you can't even grind levels in this game.
I can see people enjoying the combat, but to me it just didn't felt right, I didn't felt the diffilculty was because of my (lack of) skill, but because of bad design. I've played lots of CRPGs, including Original Sin 1, but this is the first time I ran into something like this. It's a shame, because I'm really enjoying my time with the game, just not the combat, the polar opposite of the first game, where I really loved the combat but not much the rest.
There's other little quirks with the game, but I don't think it's worth mentioning since the worst aspects are already here.
I would recommend the game if you have the patience to deal with the crazy difficulty or if you just don't care at all and don't mind playing a very, very stupidly easy RPG while on Explorer mode. But if you're like me, and don't like the concept of tying the difficulty to levels and stats or just didn't like the idea of anything written here, then there's better CRPGs out there for the likes of us.
I guess they were going for old school stlye platformer mechanics, but it just ended up being annoying.

Phantom Brave follows the story of a young girl named Marona whose family and friend were killed by a monster several years ago. The friend however managed to survive with the help of her father's miracle, but wasn't fully revived, turning him into a Phantom, who are beings not exactly alive or dead. Because of his presence, Marona is shunned by the outside world, thinking that she is possessed. Despite this, she still tries to help the very people who shunned her, believing in her motto that someday, people will like her. Unlike its predecessor (in Steam anyway) Disgaea, the story is much more serious. It is a story of the young girl (Marona) striving to become more liked, at first being treated badly, and then eventually finding people who believe that she does actually do good in her jobs and then finally treating her well. In my opinion, this is one of the main selling points of the game (the story, I mean).
The gameplay of the game might be surprising to newcomers as they it doesn't make use of the grid system. Instead, you can freely move across the map, having a set distance you can move per turn. Of course, objects can obstruct your movement, so the circle shown during gameplay is not accurate at all. Another mechanic this game has is the "Turn" system. It's a mechanic wherein all phantoms will "go home" after a set number of turns of being summoned by Marona, with the exception of this being Marona (obviously), who is not a Phantom (
). After this the phantom cannot be deployed again. As a result of this mechanic, the player must think in whether or not deploying the Phantom immediately or waiting for another time. Each phantom can be summoned by Marona from an item (
), in a big circle around her, unobstructed by height or objects. Bare in mind that there are limits in summoning phantoms, as there can only be a certain amount of Phantoms in the map at any time (items also count as Phantoms). As soon as one Phantom goes home, you can summon another Phantom to take its place.
In battle, much like Disgaea where you can pick up each other; you can pick up items, players or dead bodies (to equip them) and throw them. This allows for strategic summoning (an example) where Marona throws the item she is equipping and then immediately summons a Phantom there, for long distance action.
Each item/character gives stats to the player equipping it/him/her. Only items however can be used in fusion to increase their stats, their level caps and add new skills (characters can be used in fusion, but cannot gain stats this way, only increase their level cap and add new skills). This allows for some really lame looking weapons to be really overpowered. Generally, unless you are looking for a no-weapon playthrough of the game, this will be the main way of strengthening your characters (leveling up is another way of course, but it's much easier to use fusion instead of grinding levels).
In replacement of the item world we all know and love from Disgaea, the game has a random dungeon system, where dungeons are generated randomly by a DungeonMonk (yeah... no spaces). These can vary in level (linked to the DungeonMonk's level), in title name, floor number, size of the map, the number of enemies in the map, the type of enemies in the map, the ground type, the items that are spawned in the map and item restrictions.
The game also has titles, which are leveled up through going through dungeons with them. Each title can hold up to four skills and has a cap of 100% across the board of stats (the left side of the board anyway). Although you can do this, it isn't really needed, as grinding to get this kind of title is long and tedious. You don't even have to do this to finish all the extra maps.
Despite all these differences, I still think that it has that Disgaea feel to it. I also really feel that it's very strategic in the sense that you have to know when to summon Phantoms and the fact you can throw items around and then summon Phantoms there. For gameplay, I'd say this game is very solid and unique.

At last my favourite game has made it to Steam! I've played well over 200 hours on this game on both PS2 and PSP. This game has everything you could want of a super rpg. If you are a fan of Disgaea, this game will appeal to you. They have found ways to add twists to a number of common RPG tropes such as:
Turn based tactic battles with free movement (No grid!)
Over 400 skills which can be given to any character/item in the game for full class customization.
Stat bonuses change drastically from battle to battle.
Stats other than ATK and INT are used to calculate damage.
Healers reign supreme!
Ultimately this game is all about customizing an army and gives you enormous freedom in how you choose to do that. My primary complaint would be that the enemy AI can be sad sometimes. Surviving a battle simply because the enemy didn't do anything isn't very satisfying. Fully exploring this game will take well over 100 hours. Many of those hours will probably involve you wandering around your island aimlessly because you forget what you were just doing :)

Having played & loved Jet Set Radio Future, I was keen to try this out, but honestly, it's utter garbage compared to Future.
This is one of those rare occasions where the sequel VASTLY improves on the original.
It moves at a snail's pace, and the controls are so awkward & frustrating it takes away from any element of fun this tries to go for.
Characters interpret your control input as more of a vague optional suggestion than a command, throwing themselves at walls & off ledges and only landing on rails if they feel like it (but never the rail that actually has the items you need) and tags, when you can actually find them, take so long and so many cans to complete that you spend more time crawling around the level looking for health & spray cans than actually taking care of the objectives, while being bombarded & swarmed by enemies that never leave you alone and almost never miss, to the point I cannot finish a single level because they then have the nerve to put you on a TIMER through all this, so when I don't die from constant health loss from cycling around the level attempting the same failed grind over & over, I die from timing out because it takes too long to do anything.
This is honestly one of the worst games I have ever played, and this is a real shame, because I LOVE Jet Set Radio Future.
Future improves on almost every aspect of this god-awful game, and I can't possibly understand what went through Sega's heads when they thought THIS was the version they should port.
If you can, try to get your hands on Future, or help the fanbase convince Sega to port Future to Steam. Save yourself a headache, and more importantly, save your money.
If you have a 360, it's backwards compatible with minimal issues, so no worries there.

Not much I can say without spoiling anything but you play a young duder named Youngho.
He pulls an all-nighter to study (bad idea) before important tests.
Without saying to much, let us just keep it short but pretty much everything goes to hell.
It's a 2D korean horror game, run away like a sissy and hide like a crybaby.
Plain and simply, just book it!
When it comes to story and gameplay it seems it has the intention to mess with your head, make you feel lost, confused and it does it well.
Especially for me with no sense of direction.
Your best friend is a flashlight (ofcourse it doesnt talk...) when its turned off you're harder to spot and better at sneaking.
But that also means an easier time for the thing chasing you to sneak up on you just to give you a lil smooch.
It does give the feel of a visual novel during coversations, a very very bad (as in spooky) bedtime story if you want to punish
yourself and not letting you sleep.
I enjoyed that and I got to read ALOT out loud for viewers.
The run and hide mechanics reminds me very much of games such as Outlast and it clearly works.
The game is a big reminder of Corpse Party, with that said I have never played it myself but I know that I am not alone thinking this.
Would be surprised if some influence didnt come from that game and no shame in it as it got quite popular.
But in saying that The Coma is a game in its own right.
It has the classic exploration where you can aaaalmost go anywhere you want and try to find some goodies whilst listening to heavy panting
and feeling breathing down your neck.
The Art in the game is absolutely fantastic, it feels just how its supposed to. It clearly has that anime/asian visual novel look.
It never failed to deliver the atmosphere, you would feel the creepy areas. Female and Male characters looked really well the only character that I felt a bit off about was Yungho.
Yungho that just looked a bit off, he looked like a deer in the headlights throughout the whole game and it wasnt because of being scared.
Almost looked like constipation was his biggest worry (which is funny because I spent so much time in the bathrooms in game).
One of my viewers also pointed out that when out and moving about, Youngho seemed to be lacking a nose.
But in saying that all of this made Youngho stand out and even tho I find this model a bit less appealing its nothing I would bash the game overall for.
Its just my personal preference.
Music and sound effects also  helped building the atmosphere.
I like it as far as scary music and sound goes. It fitted really well and that is what is important here.
Even though its a horror, I managed to play the game (and as said I don't do horror games normally)  without much issues.
I'd say it gives you the horror of being chased, stressed and real sense of urgency to just get the hell out.
You just wanted to finish it to make it stop (In a good way).
Clearly as I played from start to finish in one sitting without a single break and it took 7 hours 30 minutes with chat interaction and reading everything.
There was no way I was not going to finish this game before sleep so it held my interest.
Even though I was quite exhausted close to the end there was just NO WAY I was going to give up.
As you can all see I truly enjoyed this game but it is in no means in a flawless state.
During my stream people bombarded me with "this game is so buggy" "this game crashes".
Yes, there are bugs and at very few occasions my game bugged out so hardcore I had restart my game and/or load a save.
Now I might have been pretty lucky but in my book especially coming from indie developers I really cannot complain to much.
So I feel that some people in my chat were a bit unfair.
The bugs I encountered were infact pretty minimal and hardly impacted my gameplay.
When I had to restart my game there was a patch waiting for me with bug fixes to download so they are working on the game.
Now my biggest "complaints" about this game.
Is probably that even though you can run however you want there are a few objectives that makes you run in a kinda repetative pattern backwards and forwards.
Now this could be because to cause confusion but at the same time it seemed like an attempt to make the game last longer.
One bug I encountered was when I used the stairs and I just felt through the ground and that was when I had to load a save.
The things chasing you seem to sometimes (on very few occasions) have a pathing issue where they are pretty stupid and get stuck behind blocks and just continuously
run straight into it. Atleast it gave me some time to look at said idiot monster and laugh at them.
Don't know why this happened, maybe because the distance between me and the thing was to long if it had to run out doors and corridors to get to me.
Even then I feel like the monster should give up after awhile.
Later on in game there are alot of damage you will take. Pretty unfair damage from poison, bleed etc.
This is pretty much right at the end of the game.
Reason to why I call this unfair knowing that I can dodge them is that there are times when you just get through a door and as soon as you entered.
BAAAM hit by poison. Its unavoidable unless you 100% learn which door to enter and not enter and if this is intended I feel like the difficulty curve is WAY to steep.
I wish I could say exactly where this happens but I was kinda stressed with a psychotic thing chasing me.
But overall I feel like the poison/bleed locations may need to be looked at.
Also I noticed that one time I got hit twice by a falling corpse (I admit I was stupidly standing there reading a note). So same corpse hit me twice at the same time.
At the end the save points are pretty darn hard to spot.
At one point I went into the menu the game bugged out and I couldn't leave it (after the patch). When I tried to turn character in hopes of leaving the menu  with menu up it basically just flipped my screen.
Now, it is fixable yourself by just clicking something in your bottom menu.
One bug where my character just stopped didnt want to move anymore. It happend right after going though a door.
I am really thankful I got the chance to play this game. I truly enjoyed it and I would infact recommend it.
So big thanks and congrats to Devespresso Games, you guys have made a great game in my book and I wish you all the luck with patches/fixes.

High school was rough, not being the most fast, smart, or tough, meant I fell into a small crew of outsiders. Despite this, things could've been worse. No one was trying to brutally murder me and freaky monsters were not hiding in shadows waiting to pounce. Now for our hero Youngho all of the above stands true. His only hope is hiding and gathering as much snacks from vending machines as possible. You will guide our young Korean hero as he seeks the answers to the dark and mysterious universe that is The Coma. Along the way, you will meet other strange inhabitants of this realm. Some who want to help you and others, not so much. What The Coma does well is mix narrative and horror survival in a unique fashion. The scenes and cinematic are presented in a visual style format and suddenly you're running for your life in a dark, well designed, high school. Inevitably you're going to die at some point and this can lead to some frustration if you do not take advantage of the many save spots the game presents you. Save often and save yourself the headache. Other minor gripes like scavenging for goods, can feel more like a chore then fun. More often leading to a quick death and having you repeat the process. Despite these gripes, The Coma is designed very well, it's an intriguing story and the universe seems rich with mystery and murder. The game feels very inspired from anime and the tone matches suit. Our hero bumbles his way through things and somehow just manages to survive. To sum, mechanically the game is very simple, but it makes up for this with atmosphere and drawing you into the universe. Just remember one thing as you play The Coma. SAVE OFTEN!

I got this game for free, and I sincerely think you should only get this game if you have the same opportunity.
If you really, really like platformers, you MAY like this game, however, there are countless other platformers for you to enjoy instead of this. I try really hard not to give a thumbs down review, but I just can't avoid it with this game.
The aesthetics are good - very simple, colorful environments. The music is nothing fancy, but appropriate for the simple gameplay.
The controls are very simple and easy to learn, the learning curve is pretty minimal if non-existent. The only real difficulty comes from the camera being fixed, you can only zoom in and out at a weird angle, however, you do this by moving the mouse back and forth (even though, intuitively it would be more ergonomic to use the mouse wheel for this function). I tried experimenting with the keyboard and mouse to turn/pan the camera, but it is indeed fixed for the game. The worst part, is that there are areas in the game where the camera will orient a different way, and if you die it will remain fixed in the new orientation, potentially making it even more difficult to navigate through the map. There also does not seem to be a checkpoint system, so everytime you die by touching an enemy or falling off the stage you have to restart from the very beginning of the area.
You play as a little tree stump and have to collect fairy water drops(?) and these floating orbs that you store in your pouch. The purple pouch gets bigger as you collect more orbs, and I thought this was a nice touch.
The game plays super casually and is not very challenging - you hit enemies with a leaf to destory them.
As a platformer, the game is kind of boring, and the story is not very engaging - a master tree created you to give water to the land (and that's about it).
I usually don't mention the game price if I think the gameplay (and everything else about it) outshines its price tag. That being said, this game currently costs $2.99, and I don't think you should bother getting it even if it was free (except maybe for the cards).
Do not recommend.

Cruel pure action RPG, one of the harderst games I played.
Combat is simple in nature but carefully balanced, never unfair, exremely fast and fun. You start with a simple sword combo and jump, but subsequently aquire other abilities, like dash and double jump, as well as elemental spells, that not only do damage, but change the way you move and behave in battle. Wind spell lets you glide in air, useful for making long jumps and avoiding some boss attacks; Earth spell can break some walls to reveal hidden paths and provides you with invincibility frames; Fire spell... just shoots fireballs, that's all.
Main gameplay basically consists of two sections.
First, you have to traverse the level and reach the next boss. Enemies in level may start as challenging and drive you back to town to heal and upgrade your equipment, but little by little you will be pushing forward, gaining levels and eventually will overcome any obstacle. Exploring levels rewards you with some very useful items as well.
Then, when you get to the boss, real fun starts. Game rewards you with an achievement for dying ten times in a single boss fight and I almost got it with the very first boss encountered - reached 9/10. Needless to say, I "succeeded" unlocking this achievment with the second boss. Boss attack patterns are varied and tend to change mid-fight, when you think you're adapted to it. The last boss in particular will mercilessly test everything you learned in the game - you have to have lightning reflexes and full control over your character movements to beat it, but when you'll do it you will feel like total badass.
Final word about music. It's often praised in reviewes, but I was afraid that it will not fit the fantasy setting. I was wrong - music is very fitting to non-stop hack and slash action and creates epic rock opera feel.
