Alien Shooter 2: Reloaded is a masterfully crafted horde-style action game with RPG elements (what a mouthful) that's all about running backwards and shooting. Shooting what, you totally didn't ask because it's in the title? Eeeeeveeeerythiiiiiiiing.
Horde games usually struggle with enemy balance and keeping those enemies interesting. And RPG games usually struggle with balancing an effort-to-reward ratio that makes players feel accomplished and powerful without stressing them out too much or taking too much time.
But Running Backwards and Shooting: The Game nails everything.
The enemy design is stellar. Enemies are slow-moving, come in droves, can attack the player from multiple directions, and are NEVER bullet sponges! The more powerful enemies are even slower, and many of them have ranged attacks that are telegraphed nicely. The game follows (and never breaks) the golden rule of enemy design: The faster the enemy, the weaker it is; the stronger the enemy, the slower it is.
The enemies are varied enough that the player must learn to prioritize and adapt on the fly. There are times when caution is the better part of valor, and other times when the player must be aggressive or they risk being overrun.
The progression system is also just right. Money is limited, and that can make the game stressful at first. The player is never sure if they should buy that shotgun, or that implant, or upgrade their armor, or save it all for that one powerful rocket launcher. But that's what makes it satisfying. Players must plan ahead and be smart about their choices, not just with their money, but also with their stats.
In a perfectly reasonable amount of time, the player is rewarded for their smart build choices and purchases, and a true sense of progression and accomplishment sets in. That's usually right around the time the player discovers that they have enough money to pay for that new assault rifle AND that RPG they've been eyeing, and then they enter the next mission and give the entire map a bloody makeover.
But make no mistake: The game is always ready to throw new enemies -- and tougher combinations of old enemies -- at the player. This game is challenging! But it's never too challenging, and that sort of game balance should be applauded.
Stylistically, the game is cheesy (in a charming sort of way) with a dark atmosphere. Surprisingly, these two things, combined with the overall challenge of the game, come together to create something that's easy to take seriously, but that doesn't take itself seriously, making for a truly fun game that never feels like it's being self-gratifying.
THANK YOU, Sigma Team, for showing us all how it's done!

I've never played the original but their official site makes a comparison between this and the original in terms of graphics.
Keyboard support is near non-existent as changing the controller settings also change the keyboard controls. Playing with either is left up to preference and it's just a bit faster to learn how to play with a controller.
There's no tutorial or instructions of any kind in-game so you'll have to figure out on your own how to make use of your 3 weapons on your own. The game's simplistic enough to be figured out in a short time, or at least have you know enough to play it.
The game's a SHMUP as well as a light bullet-hell. The gameplay is somewhat fast and can get hectic from the oncoming attacks, which is the reason why it's pretty much a light bullet-hell game.
You're equipped with 3 kinds of attacks; you've got a spread attack for when a large number of enemies are spread out on screen, a high damage straight shot for lined-up mobs or bosses, and a lock-on shot for any enemy you can't get a good shot with with the 2 other attacks. Because of a lack of tutorial or some kind of info about the attacks even in-game, you won't know that there are more than just the basic functions of these weapons unless you play around with the controls.
It's a 3D game with mostly 2D gameplay. The camera will switch back and forth from horizontal to vertical from time to time  as you progress through a playthrough, as well as some weird angles, but those ones are very few in number. The horizontal/vertical switching is really just for theatrics and a change of scenery so to speak, but the weird angles mentioned don't usually have actual enemies and merely just test your depth perception a bit when trying to avoid oncoming obstacles.
There are some occassions where the background & foreground become part of the gameplay; for example, enemies may be in the background shooting missiles at you and so you'll have to move around to dodge 'em.
Before starting a playthrough, you get a choice between "Original" and "Remaster" before starting the first Scene of the game. Original includes story-driven cutscenes with voice-less dialogue. Remaster just makes the cutscenes shorter as there won't be any story at all in this mode; you can't skip them, even though if you do so in Original, the game goes by much faster. Overall, there's no real difference between the two and the plot, while a bit interesting, feels like it's just there to be a placeholder.
A full playthrough takes 30 minutes, 40 if you don't skip the cutscenes. There's a "Scene Select" option but each scene can only be unlocked if you clear them from a new playthrough, thus encouraging practice of invidividual Scenes to unlock more if you fail a playthrough the first few times.
In the game, you get shields, which is pretty much your health. For every certain amount of points you get, you get an extra shield. The more you play the game—whether you die or win—the more shields you can start with until you hit the max. The same goes for earning continues: the more you play, the more you earn, although there's not much point to earning more continues if you keep getting better at the game.
If you want a challenge, or at least increased tension, you can set it so you don't start the game with shields and even have it so points don't give you any.
Special effects in the game are more flashy than anything. They have the potential to hide oncoming bullets, making them more of a hindrance than eye-appealing even when the graphics are set to the lowest setting. This especially goes for the "blur effect", but that can at least be turned off.
After you beat the game for the first time, you unlock an upgraded version of the original ship. If you beat the game with the upgraded ship, you unlock a ship with somewhat different attacks.
Like many arcade-y SHMUPs, it's a short game. The special effects are probably more flashier than they ought to be, the music's alright, the graphics aren't bad, and the gameplay is pretty nice for a doujin game originally made back in 2006.

In conclusion, Baldur's Gate II is an amazing game, filling the requirements of what all RPGs should and goes beyond.

The game runs at a stable 60 FPS for me, and it looks/plays just as good as it did in its past three iterations. I waited roughly 10 years for a PC release, and here it is now, not disappointing me in the slightest. I could not be any happier right now.
The story takes place in the world of Ivoire, and revolves around Marona, a 13-year-old Chroma (a mercenary that takes on odd jobs for payment) who can summon Phantoms to battle for her. She lost her parents eight years before the story kicks in, and lives in a blissful version of hell called "I love to help everyone but no one else likes me," thanks to her ability "Chartreuse Gale," which allows her to summon and talk to Phantoms. She commonly gets underpaid for this reason (despite working hard to complete the job), and basically everyone who knows of her refers to her as "The Possessed One" instead of using her actual name. She travels with her Phantom, Ash, who "died" along with her parents in the prologue, but was saved from
death when Marona's father turned him into a Phantom before they all got killed. Ash now watches over and protects Marona as she takes on her Chroma jobs and tries to win everyone who hates her over with kindness.
The game plays like a "turn-based" RPG in battles. Characters appear in a queue, with faster characters being able to attack first. You move your character around in a defined space, perform an action (attack, heal, etc.), move again if you have not already depleted your movement range, and then end the turn. Enemies follow this process, as well. Back on the home island, you can recruit new Phantoms, get healed, buy new items and weapons, and so forth. And on the world map, you can choose what (unlocked) locations you want to visit and play in.
Oh, and since this is a Nippon Ichi Software game, you can grind your characters all the way up to
. So, if you like being the physical manifestation of overpowered super death, that is something to work up to. I personally have never managed to accomplish this feat before, but goddammit, I will this time.
Also, this version includes 100% of the content created for this game. Everything from the base PS2 version and from the versions that were later made for the PSP and Wii are present here. If you want the "complete" game, then you will want to buy this one.
All in all, this is a game that will absolutely rob you of countless hours of your life. But in a good way, so it is very much worth it in the end.

Phantom Brave is a fantastic if very unique SRPG.
Based on the Wii version of Phantom Brave, but having all of the extra content of the PSP version, Phantom Brave PC is about a girl named Marona whose family was killed by a monster several years ago, with the exception of her brother, whose magical abilities allowed him to live in a state between life and death as a phantom. Now living alone with her brother, she is shunned by the outside world. Because of her brother, many assume she is posessed and want nothing to do with her. So she sets out to do work as a chroma helping people, hoping that someday people may appreciate her. Its a really heartwarming video game; the relationship between Chroma and her brother is endearing, and you can really tell he cares about her and will do whatever he can to keep her safe. The isolation that Marona feels is constantly heartbreaking, and you can feel the pain and struggle she goes through to be viewed and treated properly. In this lies one of Phantom Brave's strengths; unlike its Disgaea predecessor, the game is much more serious and down-to-earth. The characters are realistic and believable, so the game can really scratch at your heart.
Gameplay wise, unlike traditional SRPGs, this game is not grid-based. Instead, you can freely move across the map, having only a set amount of distance you can travel per turn as your limit for movement. Added to this, with the exception of the main character, Marona, you can only have your units on the battlefield for a few turns before they can no longer be used again. As a result, the player must struggle to best determine when and where to summon a unit, for it may be a waste to try and move a unit all the way across the battlefield to strike at an enemy. In this, I find that the game is a bit more strategic than other SRPGs; you can't rely on every unit at once, as doing so would waste your characters. You can't summon characters just anywhere on the battlefield. Every character summoned must be somewhere near Marona. Because of this, you also need to carefully protect Marona, because if she dies, the number of turns you have is limited to how long the remaining units on the battlefield have before they vanish for the rest of the battle. The game is challenging and rewarding. That's not to say that the gameplay is perfect though. The mouse and keyboard controls are a tad clunky. They're servicable to be sure, but ideally I would recommend playing this game with a controller. The game is also somewhat grindy. Its not TOO bad about this, especially if you know how to properly utilize the fusionist character, a unit you can create on the main hub world before going to a new level. With the fusionist you can combine weapons and characters to make better weapons and characters, but if you don't properly utilize this you'll be stuck replaying a few levels a few times over. The fusionist is a bit confusing to get the hang of, and replaying missions you already beat can get dull after a while. But its important to have a strong and sizable team, so you must do these things. Without a sizable party, you may run out of characters to summon too early, thus leaving you stuck with Marona to fight, which may not be ideal depending on how you've strengthened her.
Disregarding all that, the music of this game is really beautiful and relaxing, utilizing a violin as the main instrument.  The main menu theme, Angel Breath, is relaxing and comforting, befitting the more down-to-earth tone of this game. Then boss battle tracks like Game Breaker and Strange Wind offer a much faster pace for fights to make things a bit more exciting, however they continue to utilize an instrumentation that sounds almost like something you'd expect to hear out of classical music, though with a few more modern instruments. Game Breaker in particular makes good use of the acoustic guitar for its main melody. All in all, the music is really great, and a huge step up from Disgaea 1 in my opinion.
All in all, the game is great and I definitely recommend giving it a try!
Also, if you're worried about the game port: Don't be! Unlike Disgaea PC, this port is much cleaner and almost entirely devoid of bugs, complete with more menu options than its predecessor. The backgrounds are straight up HD even!

Phantom Brave is Nippon Ichi's most unique and innovative SRPG, and my personal favourite of theirs. It's also pobably their most serious in terms of story, even though there are still many comedic moments in that more dramatic overall framework.
However, what makes the game unique are really its gameplay systems, and most directly 3 of its features:
There's more to it of course, including the N1 staple character and item leveling, as well as a random dungeon generation system, and so on and so forth. But the 3 points above are what make it very unique even in the space of N1 SRPGs.
The PC version of the game is marketed as DEFINITIVE, and as far as I can tell that is absolutely the case. It includes all the content from all previous releases (including dual audio tracks), supports
, and includes recreated HD UI graphics as well high-res 2D art. Both mouse/keyboard and gamepad controls are supported and work well. Outside of recreating all the sprites - which is understandably out of scope for a port such as this - it's about as great a version of Phantom Brave as we are ever likely to get.
In addition to the unique gamplay, the game also features a fantastic soundtrack, probably one of the best in any N1 game.
(Oh, and I did play its previous versions, so this review is based on the entirety of the game, regardless of what the hour count says)

I previously gave this game a negative review but after the Beta 6 update, I feel inclined that I must rewrite my review.
As of the Beta 6 update, this game is not perfect. There are glitches that do occure once in a while and crashes that can occure once every great while along with some poor optomization. Sometimes I can get 150 fps and then drops to 25 in others while it is usually in the 60s area
A new Story mode has been added along side the Lugaru campaign which adds a lot of play time and some prettier scenery; however, the story is still very forgetable (as in I almost completely forgot it 1 day after completing it)
Although the story isn't one of the highlights by any means, it's the gameplay that really makes this game great.
Each level is completely open for the player to explore, I haven't encounter any invisible walls. When faced against enemies, you always have choices of how you want to make your approach ranging from sneaking up behind them and choking them out to facing them head on. Usually you are able to find weapons from the environment or picking them up from enemies as the level progresses allowing you to change your opproach as you go on.
What really makes the gameplay different from others on the market is the parkour. It takes some getting used to at first while learning the mechanics, but once you get the hang of it, you really feel "free". Unlike in Assassins Creed, the parkour feels much faster and far less annoying in the sence that you won't be running up walls when you just went to get up close to one.
Some other highlights of the game that weren't mentioned includes
Satisfying and brutal enemy deaths
Ragdolls can be good fun to watch
Added difficulty settings (the game is no longer impossibly difficult for beginners)
Community Workshop and level editor(There is currently 1 other player made campaign in the Workshop which adds over 2 hours to the game)
More music was recently added
Different types of enemies which forces players to change their opproach
As an end note I want to reiterate that this game is not perfect. The game has been incomplete for what seems a decade (if you include the other Lugaru game). However it is still being worked on to make improvments. If you are looking for a complete game any time soon I would say this purchase is definetly a gamble but the fun you will have in this game is well worth the $30.
If you are on the border wall of buying this game, I say just buy it, I doubt there is any other game that comes very close to this type of free feeling combat.

The Coma tells the tale of Youngho, an average high school student with normal worries such as controlling his raging hormones and stressful cramming for exams because of procrastination. His seemingly tame life takes a turn for the worse after discovering a strange pendant that belongs to his favorite teacher, Ms. Song. Unbeknownst to him, dark forces are at play, and soon during mid-exam, Youngho faints.
As soon as he wakes up, he finds himself in a twisted alternate version of his school with grotesque figures of his classmates and teacher roaming around its halls. Puzzled by the sudden transformation of his school, he wanders around until he meets up with Yaesol, an aloof young woman with a penchant for secrets. She knows something but isn’t straightforward with Youngho. Yaesol advices him to keep a cool head and that he should begin retracing his steps. It is the only way he will escape “The Coma.” With nothing else to do, he follows her guidance and realizes the cause of all this is closer than he thinks.
---
All Youngho can do is run and hide. If he brings attention to himself, all he must do is run around long enough until Psycho Ms. Song (The Coma’s demonic version of his teacher) stops chasing you. You can actually get her to chase you for an indefinite amount of time if you keep circling around the two exits of a classroom (it’s funny watching her go!) I found it easier to maneuver around the school when she’s right behind you because most of the time, she’s camping around the spot you need to go to (As long as you keep track of her whereabouts, you can let her chase you, otherwise, you might accidently bump into her.) It can be challenging at times, especially when Song doesn’t leave her spot. At this point, it’s just the waiting game. Listening for her footsteps and growling are her audio cues and wearing headphones will let you know which direction she is coming from. Her chasing segments become repetitive and can disrupt the tension of the game.
There is an inventory system and thankfully there is a separate slot for key items and consumables. Unfortunately (or maybe fortunately for you), Youngho has a limit to how much he can carry and I swear, I don’t know how many times I’ve picked up water (it recovers stamina), but it’s too many to count. I never needed to drink water because the stamina bar runs out very slowly and recovers as soon as you stop running. By the time Song stops her furious chase after Youngho, the stamina bar has already replenished.
Debilitating conditions like bleeding and poison is present but I found myself unconcerned by them. Bandages and antidotes are found in the world enough that you may never need to buy them at the store (there is a vending machine to buy all your curative needs). Really, they don’t do much damage and in fact, I played the entire final round of the game poisoned and nothing really happened. The only times I become overwhelmed by my worry is when I run out of healing foods because they’re rare. Unless I just have terrible luck, I almost always bolt towards the cafeteria (the safe zone) and buy a hamburger or chips to keep Youngho all fattened up.

There is also manual saving, in the form of writing your name on a chalkboard. No auto-saving. NOPE!
---
The scare factor of the game, on the scale of 1-10 (1 being, “me looking for something to scare me but couldn’t find it, no matter how hard I tried” and 10 being, “I ♥♥♥♥ my pants, I should’ve worn a diaper”), I rate The Coma a 4, “the game tries.”
I have to admit, it is unsettling during the beginning when Song is first introduced but after numerous chase scenes of her aggressively swinging her knife at you, you become desensitized of her. It becomes tedious and this is my main gripe about the game. It’s easy enough to avoid her since she always loses interest in Youngho when he hides in a closet or bathroom stall.
Although the enemy itself isn’t frightening, the sights and sounds immerses you into this dark, brooding world filled with hostile apparitions waiting to swat at you, hanging corpses waiting to crush you and soft moans and groans waiting to deceive you. I enjoyed the setting of the game and it is small reminder of games like “White Day.”
---
The graphics of the game is pleasant. It has an anime-style look to it. There isn’t much in terms of graphic options (it’s on the Unity Engine, by the way) and the game seems to be locked at 50 fps. I don’t know why. I’ve just accepted it. I’ve seen it drop to 40 at times but the drops are hardly noticeable (I have a fps counter at all times). For perspective, my specs are specs are GTX 970, i7-4790S, 12 GB of ram…so on and so forth.
I had several crashes. Additionally, I discovered some bugs like the screen turning black but I can still hear the in-game sounds and see the HUD. I had a glitch where Youngho would go to a room, exit and then when he tries to exit/enter other rooms, he teleports back to original room he came out of. For the most part, restarting the game solved these problems. I’m not saying it’s a glitchy game but these are the ones that would conveniently manifest from time to time when I haven’t saved in awhile. Oh, my poor. poor mouse. How abused you must have felt.
---
I like the story. It is told through interactions with several characters and notes scattered in the world. It’s important to read the notes to understand the minds of the staff and students of Sehwa High School. It ties to the plot of the story. The characters are quirky, especially Youngho himself, with his smooth talking (/sarcasm) and his amusing side comments (/notsarcasm).
It’s a shame that running away and hiding from Song got tedious in the long run. I had to soldier through the game and at one point, I had to stop because it got very aggravating.
I believe the game might have two endings (?). I will have to play it a second time. I think I left something undone, so you can miss certain events if you’re not careful. I will update as soon as I finish my second run.
Lastly, game time isn’t too long. I completed the game at around 6 hours and that’s only because most of the time, I’m hiding and avoiding that stupid hobag Song…yes…hobag! Go ahead Steam! Bleep me out!
---
Even though I enjoyed the story, some of the game mechanics and bugs that were mentioned really hold me back from fully recommending it at full price. I like it enough to thumb it up but wait for a discount.
Thanks for reading!

FULL DISCLOSURE: I was given a press copy of this game by the developers, but it will not affect, and has no affected, the way in which I conduct my reviews.
The Coma: Cutting Class; a 2D horror from, South-Korean-based, Devespresso Games. Interesting name for a studio.
While viewing screenshots for “The Coma”, as well as when I began playing the game, I was reminded of two other games. To a lesser extent, a game I haven’t played, but that I’ve heard a lot about, called Clock Tower which released on the SNES and, later, the original playstation. The only reason it popped into my head was because The Coma is 2D, and relies on “run and hide” mechanics where you are given no option to fight back, and, from what I understand, Clock Tower is the grandfather of the run and hide genre.
That’s a pretty loose connection, but the other game was Corpse Party. I’d be really surprised if Devspresso didn’t take inspiration from Corpse Party for this game. The atmosphere is *almost* carbon copied, and I don’t really mean that as an insult to the developers of the Coma, because Corpse Party is a great game. The Coma, like Corpse Party, is set in a school within a terrifying other dimension. And that’s about as far as the the similarities go.
But this review is for The Coma, not Corpse Party.
For the most part, I liked the way The Coma is presented. It’s got that Eastern-Asia style to it (or just anime-style). I will say, that it has carried over some negative anime tropes in the animation. A lot of of the female characters are ridiculously busty, and many of them are dressed pretty sexually. I mean, that’s not to say those design choices are objectively bad, but, to me, it came across as kind of juvenile and lazy in terms of writing. Though, it might not bother you that much, it bothers me a little, but Corpse Party was far worse in the fan-service department for sure, and I still love that game. Other than that, I think the design of the characters is good and varied, the monsters can be pretty freaky, and I particularly like the enviroment design -- it often remained fresh, for me, despite being exclusively set within a school. Plus the performance was perfect, which was really the icing on the cake; I always love it when a game runs buttery smooth.
At the beginning of the game I think the mechanics worked well. It’s kind of an open-world, in that all areas that you access can be re-visited at any time. You even have side-quests which I’ll explain in a little bit. Basically the entire game consists of you wandering around this, pretty much, empty school. You just have to complete objectives, find items, etc. in order to progress. At the same time you are trying to avoid a monster that is stalking the hallways. This is fine when you’re in a relatively small area, and where navigation is pretty easy. I found that the way the monster runs at you in this game was genuinely scary, and I did feel anxious walking around the hallway as I tried to listen for footsteps and breathing to let me know it was near. For this reason, headphones are recommended for this game.
But this kind of fell apart the later the game went on. Part of the reason for this is the fact the monster doesn’t change all that much. It changed once about 2/3rds of the way through the game, but it’s pretty much the same enemy with a slight re-skin and buffed to do a bit more damage. However most of the reason for the decline in quality, was that as the environments got bigger, they also got more complicated and tedious to navigate. By the end of the game avoiding the monster was a complete chore, and it didn’t help that many of your objectives were structured in the same way: go to point A, go to point B, and then return to point A. There’s a direct negative correlation with my enjoyment and the length of time I played this game. It’s only about 4-6 hours, and I feel that was enough for me.
I think I could’ve looked past the mechanical shortcomings, but the story just wasn’t there. The plot felt really basic; it didn’t go anywhere compelling past “Trying to escape this nightmare”. The only character who received any kind of real development was the main character, and even then nothing really that interesting goes on with him. It just feels like the story is a straight shoot to the end and, most of the time, doesn’t diverge in any meaningful way.
Now, I’m going to give this game the benefit of the doubt; I think the ending I got was not the “true” ending. Or, at least, I really hope it wasn’t. There’s side-quests in the game, and I did all of them bar, I think, one, so I didn’t get the “good” ending. Maybe do some research before you buy, and see if there are multiple endings, because if there isn’t the story is abhorrently bad. The ending I got was so awful that I can only assume it was a bad ending.
Otherwise, there are some pretty funny little references in the writing, even if a lot of the jokes fell flat for me. If you’re a fan of typical anime-style humour, then you may very well enjoy the jokes. There’s a lot of jokes that are based on the main character’s attraction to different women in the game -- it’s that kind of humour.
I have to say, that for $10 it’s a pretty ok experience. I think that’s a reasonable price for the, roughly, 4 - 6 hours you’ll get out of this game. Though, I think for the majority of people, it may be a “wait for a sale” situation. It’s not a terrible game, and there is certainly some value with the genuine creepiness, but it’s not really mind blowing either. If you’re dying to play it, it’s not a bad deal, but if you’re only “kinda” interested you should definitely wait.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, is a game full of life and color, that stands the test of time easily. It has one of the most charismatic, and charming worlds in gaming history to date, with plenty of things to do. I'm only twenty-two hours into the game, but I can already tell you that when I finish, I'll be coming back. There's easily hours upon hours of content here for people to enjoy, but is all that content worthwhile? Well, first of all, it's a game, second, if we're speaking in terms of fun and enjoyment to be had, then the answer is a definite yes.
Still, Oblivion has it's issues, ones that are visible and create tiny blemishes on the otherwise perfect game.
One problem with the game has to do with some of the detail of the world. Yes, I know that Oblivion had great graphics when it was made, ones that could even stand up to some newer games, but just hear me out. When you're speaking to some in Oblivion, the background freezes. Sure, this is a minor problem, but it still bugs me. This can lead to some very awkward conversation with people, and it's very noticable when there's something like a torch behind the person your talking to. I'm just saying that it gets a little on my nerves.
Another issue, is the character models. Not only do they look clunky, even for 2006, but some of the lip sinking while talking to people is off by a long shot. It's not nearly as bad as something like, "Dragon's Dogma," per say, but sometimes it's just not good.
If I were to have anything bad to say about the gameplay, it would have to be the lockpicking system, and how unoriginal the combat is, even for it's time. When it comes to combat, everything feels enhanced since Morrowind, but it's still the same basics. Slash hime with a sword, cast a spell, block, slash, spell, block, spell, block, slash. You get the point, it's all still the same. I crave something new to come out of the combat system, not the same stuff.
The there's the rediculous lockpicking system. Basically, you move the mouse up, and when you think it's time to cvlick, then you click. There's no obvious clicking sound that the game makes when you're supposed to use the LMB or anything like that, you're just supposed do it when you think the times is right, and hope for the best. Do this five times, and you can open up whatever you want to open up. You're better off just to buy a bunch of cheap lockpicks and keep clicking auto attempt.
Then there's the glitches, oh the glitches. There are so many glitches in Oblivion that I've encountered in the twenty-two hours I've played in it, and a lot of them are minor, but some of them can be quite large. There's a bug that crashes the game when you leave a menu sometimes, something that's happened to me multiple times, something that can be very annoying when you haven't saved recently. There are also minor ones, like being able to skip through certain parts in the story, being able to kill enemies that you shouldn't be able to by exposing the games other glitches, etc.
Still, even with it's downsides, Oblivion is a game I suggest you all check out. Every single charcter has great voice acting as far as I've seen, along with interesting personalities, and quests that they want you to go on. The freedom the game gives you is massive, even by today's standards. You are the one that crafts your adeventure in this game, and that's what makes it so great. Oblivion also has a great main story thus far, and doesn't seem to forget about side quests, which are also great.
Creating your own character feels great in the beginning, even if a little dated. You don't have such a massive choice of what your character is going to look like physically, but choosing attributes and creating your own class can be a blast. I'll probably go back after one playthrough, just to experiment with everything I can choose while making my character, to see what kind of things could happen if I decided to be a Mage instead of a Warrior, or an Assassin instead of a Mage. My point is, however dated the system is, it's still great, and a lot of new games are missing the key features.
Now, I would talk about the DLC, but I haven't gotten to play that yet, sorry.
Anyways, for all of Oblivion's flaws, it still stands as a great game.

When getting this game for free from the IndieGala giveaway, I expected a calming experience of being a treestump, running around exploring the world. Now, the idea itself sounded quite decent and the videos were also fun to watch, but after a short while the good idea behind it turned into a rather troublesome outcome.
Where to start... You get pressed out of the surface of earth to then suddenly be the child of a big tree sitting in the center of a place that never was explained. He tells you to go save the world by gathering tears that spend life and water to all creatures and plants. Having said such, you then live on a floating island with the stages sitting inside your house, taking away all you space you need to live... It's not like you'll ever make use of the furniture you have in there anyway.
Having selected a stage you are greeted by music which I found okay at the start, but it turned out to be quite irritating, especially in a stage where you spawn on some beach. The music there turned into a madness of keys being pushed without an end to it, the song ends, you sigh in relief, and there, the song starts all over again.
The graphics look fun and are childfriendly, the same goes to the gameplay. Dealing with the camera though forced me to actually get a bit upset playing this game, as I had a hard time of non-resetting, locked viewpoints after dying. There even was a moment, where I saw a huge stretched out texture all across the screen due to my character being reset without the camera. That incident made the game be unplayable and I had to reboot. You can zoom the camera out, which is a start, but not being able to rotate it and it not resetting to it's original position make it challenging to enjoy this game. To add up to it, checkpoints seem to be placed in a weird fashion, as dying sometimes resulted with me being all the way at the beginning of the stage, which can be a bit frustrating after a while. If there was a checkpoint and you messed up, it would throw you back by another one which could be waaaay back from where you came from. This made things a bit sad sometimes aswell.
The gameplay itself was just okay I'd say. The controls are kept simple, which is nice, but the movement can be a bit weird to deal with at times. Enemies don't feel challenging and you usually just spam the attack button to get rid of them. Some foes also seem to be randomly placed, and I saw no reason for them being there. There were spiked enemies in a big field and I never saw a way of accidently dying by them. They were just standing there, in the open space. Now, who would jump ontop of them without an obstacle making you jump in the first place? I just feel like they were placed there to fill a gap.
And then there you are, running around from one stage to another, gathering the berries and tears you find to save the world from... drying out? He never has gone into detail, and he also never re-appears as you progress in the game, so there basically is close to no story to this game. After 69 minutes, I saw him again, sitting in his old spot telling me two lines of text, then booting me into the credits where I was stuck, even after them finishing, until I closed the game, lovely.
There is a bit more content to it afterwards, a stage that unlocks when you have 600 berries, and items that unlock as you progress with gathering named berries during the stages. Now... I never got to experience what the unlocked stage is about, as it seemed only responded with a white screen, then freezing, waiting for me to kill the .exe.
All in all, I'd say that the game was okay for the fact that I didn't have to pay for it. Same goes to the frame, I like the idea of having a peaceful platformer without any punishment or time-limits in addition with cute and simple graphics. But I was punished by the lack of camera movement, the weird checkpoints that threw me back a lot all the time, and the fact of the camera just locking into weird places afterwards.
Too bad...

EDIT
I guess i should be a little more precise.
PROS:
Combat System: COMPLETELY INCREDIBLE. This is a 4/5 year old game, and that fact there are no target locks, and no other game that i can think of with a combat system that also DOES NOT USE target locks, makes this game stand out way above the others. If you miss, its just bad aiming, or the inevitable lag.
Story Line: Ive only played one class completely to the current level cap storyline (80 atm), and i absolutely love it. People say that MMO storylines arent the greatest, and i understand that having played few other MMOs as well, but i have to say DN has a amazing storyline (For Kali class anyways, havent branched out into other classes as much.)
Leveling: This is not a grind-cringing spending months to hit level cap. In fact, just recently they LOWERED the needed exp needed to level up per level. If you no-lifed 4 days, im pretty sure you could be level cap, or really close.
Content: The amount of content in game is enourmous, albeit alot of it are lower cap level nests and such. But the game doesnt totatlly abandon, having weekly nests to have a chance of getting level cap equipment to gear up. But the thing that kept me playing for 6000+ hours was the raids. Finding a dedicated group of 7 other people, to learn, and defeat the dragons every level cap, and finally doing it for the first time. That'll never get old.
Communtiy: Ive met alot of nice, friendly, funny people in this game. There are alot of people in here that are willing to help you, whether through tips or finding someone to leech out of (dont leech please), to make youre experience be a good one, and helping you learn about your class. I spent so much time in game, in chat systems talking to these people, theyre family to me. More so than my real life friends.
CONS:
Communtiy: The saltiest people are in this game. I swear they eat a bag of salt before they start playing everyday, thats how salty there are. But ofcourse, every community has those right? Dont be suprised to meet one. Want some help running level cap nest? If you join a party and you dont have decent gear, -permakicked from party-. But they did add diffilcutly levels to nest, so i guess it balances out..... to a point...
Latency: THIS IS THE SINGLE THING KILLING THIS GAME (Well nexon in general). DDOS on MapleStory AFFECTS DRAGON NEST BECAUSE WE RUN ON THE SAME SERVER. Why? Cant they afford dedicated servers for Dragon Nest? Im pretty sure they can from the $$$$ people spend in this game for cash shop items. Lag is so bad, it affects pvp, character skills going off when youre juggling them, getting hit by stomp mechs WHILE IN THE AIR, and just bad lag in general. I know there will always be lag, but when people start mass dcing from the world, then yea, im pretty sure its not our bad comps. Also PVP is a terrible mess. A beautiful, stunnin, bright, and at times, VERY VERY LAGGY MESS. But i digress...
Randon Number Generator(Cash Shop, Enhancing, Etc): Alot of beautiful costumes, pets, wings etc. Too bad the Random Number Generator is terrible. Want the newest wings? Buy a 30 egg pack, worth $29.90, and hope that RNGods are with you. Ive seen people spend THOUSANDS trying to get things in those eggs, myself included, and to be dissapointed in my bad luck. Want to enhance a Legendary Grade weapon to +12? Good luck grinding for the gold, to just see it gone in 1 try, that probably wont succeed anyways. With so much people spending money on this game, they should atleast compensate those who spend past a certain limit. i mean, to spend a months paycheck in one go... and to get nothing in return... yea thats definetly not worth it.
CONCLUSION
Would i recommend this game? Hell yeah, this is a awesome game, with not that bad graphics, and a incredible story line and combat system. Find the right people in game, find the right group to do stuff with, and to find a right guild to be a part of, then this game will be very enjoyable. Dont try to be a leecher, cause many people WILL ignore you, or avoid replying to you. Plan on spending on this game? Your choice, i gave you my outlook of the cash shop, but i guess if youre lucky, it wont be so bad. But ive seen so many unlucky people. Akane might be the clumsiest ninja to ever find her way into a video game.
She moves like a stone statue that has suddenly been given the ability to walk, sliding around as if every surface she touches is ice and often forgetting how to properly jump. Though I suppose I'd find it pretty hard to move effectively if I had two watermelons bouncing around on my chest, making the simple act of walking across a room an involved procedure as you desperately attempt to deal with the sheer uncontrollable force of your own momentum. Making matters worse are dozens of the worlds second dumbest ninjas, who patrol around in obnoxiously difficult to reach places while starring at you like you're a harmless circus animal jumping through hoops.
And that would be somewhat accurate, though there are rather a lot less giant flaming rings and many more exceedingly dull platform layouts and cheep traps. Checkpoints apparently missed the cut and to seal the deal an agonizingly long death screen makes retrying levels far more tedious than they had to be. Not that you ought to bother starting over, mind you. Akane never gets better through its five worlds, instead becoming so outrageously cheap and difficult that I confess to having abandoned ship on the second to last level.
What I'm getting at here if it wasn't incredibly obvious, is Akane the Kunoichi is rather outrageously incompetent. It feels like someone ripped a platformer template out of their rear, painted some very ugly textures all over it, and then spent the rest of their time carefully animating the lead characters breasts. Because that's what really matters in a platformer: boob physics.
Too many dancing ballerinas spinning around and hitting you from crazy angles.

Did you like Life Force on the NES? Do you like StarFox? if so then this game is just for you! Like Life Force, Ether Vapor is a fast-paced shmup that changes perspectives throughout. Blast enemies in stages that change from horizontal to vertical between each stage; the stages will even do a 3D over-the-shoulder view that either sends you in a lock-on assault minigame or starfox-like railshooting segments seemlessly. The game does the transitions smoothly, and gives the game a cinematic feel (particularly during stage 4's airship raid.)
Instead of powerups, you have three weapons with two of them having alternate functions. In order to master this game, you will have to learn to know which weapons to use when. Of course we have the standard forward shot, but make sure to use the wide shot to attack enemies from the side, and get ready to put up the forcefield when things get too hot. are enemies attacking from behind, or are they assaulting you in the background? lock on to them and attack with powerful homing lasers!
If you worry about the game being to hard, it's actually one of the more forgiving shmups, and even when you get a game over the game will unlock the option to use more lives and credits, so you can keep going on until you're able to beat it, and even then after you beat the game you can customise the options to give yourself a challenge or make thing easier. There's also plenty of unlockables  such as extra playable ships as well
Also, keep in mind that Remaster mode lacks cutscenes and text for those who would perfer a more arcade-like experience free of abundant text, while Original mode contains all the story and character dialog for those who would like more exposition in their shooters.
Overall, I can say I reccomend this game.

This is a dynastic simulation which comes well recommended.  It will eat up much of your life, I started one game and lost 70 hours to it.  I don't know what will happen if I start another.  It is filled with DLC and purchasing a complete version of the game will cost about 150 USD.  However, these DLC's drastically expand and change the gameplay into something much different from what it was on release and will continue to do so in the future.
To describe Crusader Kings, you are a dynastic lord, a count, duke, king, or emperor.  There is no real win or lose situation other than to keep playing.  Your assumed goal is to proliferate your dynasty into other families, marry into wealthy dynasties, and set things up so your successor will be in the best position to inherit the kingdom.  Your real goal is to screw around and mess things up in whatever way your hubris takes you, sleep with your lord's wife, sell your daughter to a polish lord, cage one of the great houses of Venice and sell them to the Egyptians, whatever your fancy takes you.  Everyone in the game, right down to the courtiers and peasant rebels, are individuals with their own stats, aspirations, goals, and families.  Manipulating their desires and maneuvering to get into power will make you personify each of these people, especially when they betray you.  You will scream "You ♥♥♥♥♥!  Did you forget who put your♥♥♥♥♥on that throne!?" at your computer over some plot.
The interface is bare and the map figures are not much to look at, this suits the type of game this is just fine.  There is a lot of depth, economy, trade, alliances, holdings, relationships between all the NPC's.  It will take time to figure out the many gameplay nuances, what holdings are valuable, who makes a desirable courtier, how to fill out your desmene, and other gameplay nuances.  None of these are easy to figure out and usually come over the course of repeated failure and checking guides and faqs.  This level of complicated combined with the directionless character of the game will turn people away and I don't blame them too much for doing so.
The largest issue I find with the game is the sheer amount of DLC this game has.  It has been released gradually over the years since this game has been released and update several gameplay functions and expand several parts of the map.  On release, Crusader Kings II only covered Catholic Christian feudal kingdoms in Western Europe starting from the Middle Ages.  Now, it includes Central Africa, India, Asia, their religions, and timelines going as far back as the beginning of Charlemagne along with the different type of governments - nomadic, tribal, Indian, Islamic, and city-state.  The down side is that gathering all the things which do this will require you to sink 150 USD or so on a purchase of the game.  It's no small matter and were it not for the thousands of hours you can sink into the game and the replayability each of the DLC's add, I wouldn't recommend it.  Even without DLC, the core game remains a solid game which will leave you with many, many hours of your life gone.  If you find you enjoy what you play, you can add a DLC for a different civilization and replay from there.
This is a solid grand strategy game with a lot of attention to detail and a lot of care put into its mechanics and personality.  The detail will be off putting to some and desirable to others.  If you are a fan of grand strategy this is definitely one to pick up.

Baldur's Gate series brought the computer fantasy RPG genre back to life after the golden era of C64 and Amiga games. The second part of the series was in many ways the paramount game that every other computer RPG was compared to and rare were the ones that managed to nail it as well as this.
It is epic, massive, interesting, it has well written NPC characters, romance options and battles. It manages to find good balance between story and battles. Time has taken it's toll on the mechanics a bit, but not too much. It is still very enjoyable game to play although a bit clunky at times. In my opinion the battle mechanics and stats are more enjoyable than in the modern Pillars of Eternity for example, which felt a bit too "fuzzy" for me. Here +1 is +1, period :)
But in my books, the very best computer RPG of all times is still the masterpiece Planescape: Torment. BG2 is close second.

The voice acting is so bad I genuinely can't tell if they're the worst VA's doing a terrible job, or the best VA's doing an amazing job of sounding like they're some sort of hammy B-movie terrible. The graphics are low res, and not in a charming, deliberate Terraria way, but a 'this engine sucks and we're a team of carefree chancers' kind of way.
But dear God the gameplay, it just works. There's lots of delicious little details that conspire together to make this game just a pleasure to play even though it's generally the kind of janky product Jim Sterling concerns himself with on Greenlight. The graphics may be generally humdrum at best, but then you start mowing down vast hordes of aliens and the visceral way they come apart is.....glorious. It's just so satisfying. And the sound, it's mostly pretty threadbare, but it proves that all you really need to feel good in life are decent, gutsy weapons sounds you'll never tire of as you march through every level with an increasingly overpowered arsenal of automatic shotguns, miniguns, and energy cannons.
You're not going to sink your life into this game, you can complete a whole campaign for yourself in an afternoon once you know what you're doing, but this shoddy, thrown together mess of a game actually manages to have some serious lessons to teach about how you make it fun to massacre thousands of enemies again and again and again.
Tough it through the surprisingly unforgiving at times initial stages of the campaign, and you too can discover the simple joy of sweeping your mouse lazily over a few hundred enemies and watching your minigun tear them to pieces in seconds.....you know, like better single player games never seem to give us, because they don't understand that sometimes balance should play second fiddle to fun.

CK2 - without additional DLC or mods to add depth to it - has a long learning curve. It is never going to be a game for everyone.
If games like Dwarf Fortress or Nethack don't appeal to you because of a slow to learn interface, or you don't find appeal in recognising warning signs of abstract threats, hard to spot opportunities, and slowly earning hardwon experience of mechanics that makes the game easier, then a game like CK2 won't appeal to you either. And neither additional DLC, nor mods nor picking it up at a lower price point will change that fact.
There's no faster or more effective way to learn than a genuine desire to play what is (to a beginner) an unforgiving, ruthless, sphinx of a game that can feel like simultaneously learning a foreign tongue and juggle; watching a Lets Play or reading the ckiiwiki might make a mechanic or two more understandable but it may equally be specific to an outdated version; nor does either make the game more enjoyable when it's simply a poor fit for many kinds of players.
Regarding multiplayer, it's neither an excellent or terrible experience. Playing with pubbies is basically unheard of and you can expect nearly every session online to be password protected. Join a community and you'll find games, but the matches aren't drop-in-drop-out flexible and CK2 doesn't have Hotjoin. MP isn't a faster way to learn the game. Anyone hosting an MP match essentially gives all players a free loan of the DLC for that match too, so you may find a surprise or two.
I'd advise any new player to CK2 to delay buying, well, any of the DLC. Knowing what's a basegame mechanic and playing it enough to have a clear comparison and opinions on what's good and bad about it teaches you the game at a pace you're in more control of. Throwing more on the pile is just counterproductive.
That said, since this is a review, I'll go through what I own, what I think of them, and whether they're good or not. In *all* cases I advise
- prioritise getting the DLC you really want over kinda want
- adding the DLC to an Is There Any Deal waitlist at a pricepoint you're happy to pay
- buy them over time rather than several at once
You both learn the game faster, spend less, and appreciate what you bought more.
--Music DLCS:
-See also -
and youtube
So far, the overwhelming majority of these I think are excellent. I'll say I dislike hearing Orchestral House Lords, Viking Metal and Full Plate Metal as in game music; they're too different from the rest of the music, but I listen to them outside of gameplay happily. I don't own yet Songs of Revelation. What I said about buying over time I still believe applies here.
--Gameplay DLCs:
Note: I don't exhaustively cover all features from these DLCs or the patches that came to the game with them. Just a short, what to expect from your first impression, who I think it's aimed for, and whether I like it enough to recommend.
- Sword of Islam
Play as the Muslims, and a whole other part of the map. These do play differently enough from Christendom that it adds enough new challenge to the game to be it's own DLC.
- Legacy of Rome
Adds depth to the Byzantine Empire realm, Greek culture, and retinue mechanics. Greek culture means blinding and castrating. It's about as big a power trip fun as you'd expect. This is maybe something that doesn't offer much value to a new player, as advancement in an empire and managing an economy to both buy and maintain a retinue aren't beginner level stuff, nor is new forms of torture since their incorrect use is self sabotage.
- Sunset Invasion
If there's one gameplay DLC most CK2 fans don't love, it's this. SI is swimming the deep end of alternate history: what if Europe was the new world and was discovered by the Aztecs, who invade in force? Not recommended unless you see it at a price point low enough that you'd be satisfied to use it for one playthrough for curiosity's sake and not again. The problems include the invasion appearing to attack likely newbie areas like Ireland, Britain, and Iberia, and their *wildly huge* numbers of troops that don't have upkeep or attrition like the players do.
- The Republic
Coast republics like Venice become playable, with new mechanics and inheritance. Not there's still some unplayable republics that are landlocked. Republics play very differently to feudal govs.
- The Old Gods
Adds one earlier start date (867); adds playable pagans and zoroastrians (aka that incest religion sub-reddits obsess over), and war threats from unlanded characters that have raised an army to pursue a claim - adventurers. This is excellent. Though vikings are so, so different and have their own weaknesses, they've a clear and very fun gameplay loop for raiding that new players can both learn a lot from quickly and have a lot of fun with in a kind of 9th century PAYDAY fashion.
- Sons of Abrahams
- Playable Jewish characters. Some pope manipulation. These mechanics are more of a nicety, not an essential. and what is here again demands a lot of preparation and attention from players that make it a poor choice for beginners.
- Rajas of India
- Playable India subcontinent. Several new religions. If the achievement for killing the tiger with your bare hands doesn't impress you, check out the one for crushing the pope with an elephant. A lot of value to be had, though what makes it good also makes it confusing for a beginner.
- Charlemagne
Adds one new start date - 769, older than the Old Gods. Whole new kingdom and empire creation options, Zuni religion stuff. Gives players clearer resons to despise the Karling dynasty. Playable tribal, with options to develop into feudal (or, with The Republic, into a republic) All good.
- Way of Life
Primary personal interests for rulers. Get religion, want to learn business better, seduce absolutely anything with a pulse, become a hard partying drunk. Makes peace time more fun and war time something you can be better prepared for.
- Horse Lords
This is easy for me to review. Is it good? I don't know, I don't own it. Playable hordes and horsy invasions. Maybe I just am slow to trust that big numbers of invaders are bringing FUN with them to after Sunset Invasion...
- Conclave
Way of Life for raising your kids. This I'm not too fond of, as relearning how to raise competent heir is like regressing back to an earlier level of player inexperience with little payoff. Combine that with the DLC adding a whole load of power to your supporting courtiers in how they feel you should run the realm and this is a DLC for making the game harder. This DLC maybe added more to confuse me than most others, and I'd be the most hesitant to recommend this above all others - even Sunset Invasion.
- The Reaper's Due
The contagious disease DLC. Beginners, avoid this. You've already at least 10 other things you need to be watching for warning signs for, you don't also need to try and discern what looks like a weather forecast for waves of sweeping pestilence and death with limited options for surviving them and difficult choices and sacrifices to make. Intermediate and advanced players will have masochistic glee learning how not to die. Also: new tortures and elaborate ways to execute.
- Monks and Mystics
Adds societies. Choose a celibate monk Or a pre scientist. Or a wannabe assassin. Or a power mad devilworshipper. A nice way to make peacetime more interesting.
-- EU4 convertor
If you don't already play enough EU4 to know you want this, don't get it. Plain and simple. My understanding is such saves often make EU4 a bit too easy too. This said, it is a backdoor to some interesting exclusives - SPQR, Euro Aztecs and ancient religons which maybe is the real appeal.
-- Cosmetic and Graphical DLCs
Non essentials. Maybe pick up ones around your local favourite region when they're on sale.
--Ruler Designer/Customization pack
Non essentials, but renaming is nicer than other cosmetics.

Lemma almost makes the cut for being a good game, but there are some key parts that let the entire thing down.
Lemma is a parkour game come walking simulator. The minimal story is told through textual snippets found throughout the game, rleaving much of the rest up to the player to explore. When it works, the running, jumping, and sliding on platforms is good fun.
The problems I see are in 3 key areas:
- The shift key is used for nearly every action you can take in the game. That makes it nigh on impossible to play when it unlocks the ability to spawn in platforms.
- The actual spawning in of platforms is poorly explained at the start, and there don't seem to be any clear rules about what makes a platform spawn and stay spawned or just ghost out of existence.
- The "climbing" ability is very jerky. Sometimes when you're very far from  grabbable surface, if you press shift the game bumps your chharacter forwards in a very unclean fashion, and pushed you up to the surface, often clipping through the world while doing so.
When the game is just about running, and sliding in simple terrain it works very well, but as the levels get more complex it becomes nightmarish to try and manage.

This is definitely, in my experience the smoothest parkour game on steam. The gameplay is fluid, exciting, and rewarding. The music and scenery are minimal but beautiful, and the story is solid, for a game that one wouldnt expect to have much of one.
The first portion of the game is fairly linear and simple, as you learn the mechanics and are allowed to test and play with them. Around the midpoint of the game, however, it opens up hugely, and exploration becomes a big component of the gameplay. This slower more open portion of the game also really allows the player to explore the limitations of the mechanics and have a great time wallrunning all up and down these expansive environments. On that note, the game is also much longer than i expected, which is welcome, because, again, it allows for a lot more exploration and experimentation.
That said, the game is not without its bugs. Collision detection is at times buggy, i was able to get out of bounds in a few places, and the ability to spawn new platforms was confusing, poorly explained and inconsistently responsive.
All in all, Lemma has a few hiccups, but when you get into the flow of it, its very satisfying and fun.

If I wasn't a filthy achievement rentboy, I would not be recommending this game.
Lemma is not one game. It is two.
One of these games is pretty good. Not bad at all. It's a first-person parkour game  that has a nice sense of momentum and a neat mechanic that can best be described as Shaun White Skateboarding meets Mirror's Edge - terrain generation by wallrunning or sliding off edges.
Now this game is alright. It's based around swiftly running through levels and attempting player made challenges, most of which are worthless templates thrown in for the achievement but occassionally something nice pops up (like my own, go check it out,
) using the game's excellent robust level editor that somehow lacks an undo button.
The first game isn't perfect, but it's fun. While the terrain generation is okay and doesn't do much to alter the game, the ancilliary mechanic of using a powerup to generate platforms midair is plain horrible to deal with. The platforms are generated randomly, enjoy your suicide runs.
All the enemy types range from annoying to annoying and horrible. This is a game where death just resets you to the nearest ledge, so to punish your immortality, two of the four enemies can cause massive terrain destruction, and easily just lock you into a cycle of despair or cut off paths completely. Not sure why these are even in the game.
The art direction is voxel based, apart from the character models, and with smart texture choice this works. The sound library for BGM and ambience kind of sucks, and you're probably better off just putting on your own music, but judging from the credits it was mostly put together from free resources, what can you do.
This the first game. This is the game I'm recommending Lemma for. Play this game.
The second game absolutely sucks.
Once you're out of the tutorial levels, Lemma throws you into the grinder. No real direction, a thoroughly unhelpful guide, you're left to just figure things out. Due to the real lack of asset variety within the bulk of the levels, with no map apart from a vague scribble on paper, Lemma's second game is a game of exploration and slowly understanding the world.
This translates to getting lost a bunch and reading some terrible lore that's either technobabble or just entire character arcs in a paragraph.
Don't play this game. Just get around it. Make your own map - you know what,
It's not fun at all. Look up a guide, watch a playthrough, resign yourself to 5 hours of misery out of a 6 hour initial playthrough, do what you gotta do, because Lemma - for all its focus on mystery - only actually starts getting fun once you figure out what you're doing.
Is it worth the investment? Yeah. I enjoyed messing with community levels and spent more time with the level editor than the actual game. I recommend that first game a whole bunch and would consider it a hidden gem. But that mysterious, worthless approach that wastes your time and leads you in circles, that would've ensured that if I wasn't a said rentboy who wastes time on achievements and reviewed this after a first playthrough, it would've been a solid "don't bother".
Like the platforming, approach Lemma with a running start. It'll reward you for it.

I am not so good at the whole review thing but here is my review on The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion® Game of the Year Edition!
I don't know what it is about Oblivion that makes me keep coming back for more. It was the third Elder Scrolls that I ever played, and personally my favorite. Everything in this game was perfect. Maybe it was the higher sense of exploration and less emphasis on slashing your way through enemies. Maybe it was the breathtaking soundtrack. Here is my pros and cons list of this game and my final verdict.
Pros: Masterful story, great combat although bow can be a pain sometimes, side quests that will keep you hooked for hundreds upon hundreds of hours, memorable characters, I could literally get so caught up in seeing what certain npc's would be doing and seeing how there everyday lives unfolded one time i remembered seeing Penniless Olvus dead next to the poor guy were a few guards my best guess of what happened to him is that since he begs he might not have been getting enough to live and tried his hand at pickpocketing someone and got caught because i saw a good amount of gold on his corpse.
Cons: Bow combat can be annoying if you did not mean to pull it back because there is no way to retract it, potato faces which you can easily overlook, and not many voice actors but can also be overlooked seeing as how the quests are great.
The point is, is that this game brings endless possibilities for you to experience and how you play the game is up to you. Will you be a great hero who fights off the mythic dawn and puts a stop to corruption, or will you be a crazy bloodthirsty serial killer who teases the guard egging them on to catch you, perhaps even becoming a adverage citizen earning money off of game, errands, and or investing in shops. The choice is yours, but i can what I can tell you is that you can not pass up on playing this game it is just such a well thought out game, I myself have put in over 1k hours on this game on console, steam, and pc disc combined. If you have not got this already go and get it now, trust me you will not regret it! Final result 5/5 WILL PLAY AGAIN!

This is definatly one of the most fullfilling games I have ever played. The S.T.A.L.K.E.R series in my opinion has very few flaws to begin with. Add the Modding community behind it and any percieveable flaws vanish and what is left is the near perfection that all games should aspire to achieve. Very much its own brand, the game has 4 shining stars that make it so great.
Frist and foremost is the atmosphere created right from the get go.  No other game has as believeable an astmosphere as the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series. Very engaging and at times frightening.  Getting ambushed by whatever whenever is an experience players shouldn't be left not having and stalker lets ya have it......alot..like seriously. Fire fights are quite amazing and requires  strategy to over come.
Another star atribute this game possesses and the open sand box aproach to FPS.  You can go anywhere you want on the three maps, which are giant. There are some "dungeons" to be explored to but most gameplay takes place in the open areas. Now i say open areas I really mean on one of the three main maps that are mainly countryside or urbana areas.  Because it is sandbox you can choose whether or not to mess with the missions or if you want to just explore and shoot ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and monsters.  To open the other 2 map areas some missions are required but after that you are free to do as you please. At the end of the game you can also choose to end it or continue to explore and do as you please.
Looting. pretty much all I have to say. The inventory system in this is great. You can take ammo, armor, medkits, food, energy supplements, weapons, and artifacts from downed foes and add them to your collection. More shooters are starting to do such with looting and inventory and I positivly agree with it and the first fps i remember playing with such a system was the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series. I love the blend of FPS and RPG games.

Ballistics. Some don't even know what it means. But S.T.A.L.K.E.R sure does. believe it or not the game engine has a ballistics calculator.  When you fire a round in game it has bullet drop and starts loosing energy at a distance. They really couldnt do alot with it since true ballistics would need wind drift, atmosphereic pressure, temperature and other variables into account that would take alot of man power and computer power to put in a game, but modders have been playing with this and have done some pretty awesome stuff.
I would recommend this to any and all gamers if you got the balls to survive the Zone

This very much feels like the beta release that it is... And that's not a bad thing, the game lacks polish and it's only fair to note that Overgrowth is developing slowly, but it was a pleasant surprise to see that it is still developing.
Overgrowth is, at it's heart, quite a simple, very fluid parkour / kung fu game played at blistering speed and with an interesting damage system which left me wincing in more than one situation as a brutal kick sent me face first into a rock or a building for an instant KO. Landing face first, does matter. The locational damage system will leave you just hoping that maybe you survived that hit. But what's more rare is that the weapons actually feel weirdly realistic most of the time, to the point that in the storyline mode (which isn't great, but it's not the worst I've played) you will fear and respect when you meet an enemy with a knife... And learn the value of fighting only one enemy at a time.
Sure, the graphics are a little dated, sure, the combat seems simple (it's actually a little more nuanced than you might first give it credit for), but it's a rare case when ragdoll physics actually adds to the feel of a title, rather than take away. Oh, and the AI is unforgivingly hard, whilst not actually being unfairly so. Contrary to the feeling you're likely to get at the first fights, you CAN beat the story mode.
Well, the storymode is basically a port of the company's earlier title, Lugaru, to the new engine. If you haven't played Lugaru, it answers four questions and defines a word quite well.
Q) So, if a rabbit got into a fist fight with a pack of wolves... Who would win?
A) The wolves.
Q) How about if the rabbit knew kung fu?
A) The wolves
Q) Give the rabbit armor?
A) The wolves win
Q) And a sword?
A) The wolves still win.
Definition: Hubris - A rabbit thinking he can win in a fist fight with a pack of wolves.
And yes, I still giggle when a member of said pack of wolves punts you clean into the next valley. For all of the fluid feeling kung fu, powerful hits can get wonderfully silly.
Did I enjoy it? Yes.

Played this after Skyrim, which I guess is 'wrong' to do by some standards, so for anybody who was interested in Morrowind/Oblivion after playing Skyrim can maybe appreciate my insight here to at least compare the two (I've yet to play Morrowind, I'm so backwards).
Skyrim was a fantastic game, but the whole dragon prophecy approach you can only do so much with (and dragon combat was kind of pathetic), and Oblivion feels a lot more creatively driven-- the oblivion gates are really neat and good areas to get some combat experience. I like that you can kind of take a lot of approaches in this, stealth feels just as powerful as all-out warrior combat where I felt rogues were underpowered in Skyrim. (The whole, shoot-arrow-and-cower-in-the-shadows approach could get a little tedious and became more than necessary as a rogue after things scaled enough) In Oblivion as a more stealth-oriented class, my movement speed allows me to dodge and bait enemy attacks and then strike after dodging the blow, and illusion spells combo wonderfully.
Also, you can choose main specs that affect your level, so leveling non-combat things doesn't completely screw you over. I remember my lockpick had gotten me high in level in Skyrim and I was fighting things that completely outgeared and outdamaged me because my
levels were low, but in Oblivion their leveling system is more specific and you can avoid that problem easily. Though, the scaling is global and REAL, so expect to run into bandits with daedric weapons at some point. You'll probably be strong enough by then though, so it's just good gold if you can carry their stuff.
Overall, an awesome game in my opinion, lots of hours of gameplay and playing it lets you appreciate the plot of Skyrim a little bit more, personally experiencing the history that you were told about in Skyrim.

I've been playing this game for a while now, and, though I haven't finished it, I feel I've been playing long enough to speak my mind, because this game has a lot of things I think will be of interest to the potential buyer.
First off- unless you're a masochist, get yourself a controller for this. I rarely, if ever, play any game ever with anything less than a mouse and keyboard, but for this one it's absolutely essential.
This game has character. Ever watched a strange anime on adult swim or online at two AM, half asleep? This is the best way I can describe it. The characters are nice, the world is interesting, the textures, while they show their age in the form of pixels on static, animated faces, do their job well enough.
The controls are on and off for me. I've seen gameplay of people handling their chosen character very well and acing levels, as for me I've been having a lot of trouble coming to grips with so much as maintaining a chain of grinds or getting my character to jump exactly where I want them to- something that in free play or graffiti missions doesn't make much of a difference, but in something like a race is crucial, and this game loves to make you race other characters to try and see who can tag a certain area first.
One missed jump or failed grind, and it's over, and unlike the trick competitions, this game doesn't have the courtesy of failing you outright- you've got to wait until your opponent sprays his tag, either by futiley trailing a country mile behind him, or having your character standby and do a little jig while you have a fit in the corner and try to compose yourself for the twentieth go at it- after you've skipped the cutscenes, which you can do unless you quit the game, return to the garage (which acts as a sort of hub for choosing your level and character, among other things) or otherwise have to leave in the middle of one of them.
When whichever is the real problem here- the game, or my thumbs- works, it works like a damn dream, and it's a fine little piece of entertainment here for eight bucks- it looks nice if a touch dated, it runs great (as well it should, given how old it is), and everything going on it keeps you guessing, for better or worse. Just when you think they've gotten predictable with riot police and parachute troops on your tail, they bring out missile firing helicopters and tanks to try and waste you, and grinding down the road, tagging the wall up and jumping onto a rail for an added boost, all this stuff combined makes this game great and a joy to play and replay despite it's age and my lack of mastery of it.
Now, from what I hear, they made a sequel a while back, and if it improved on all these things or at least kept in the spirit of the original game, I'd love to have a crack at it, or better yet, another sequel.
Until then, I hear there's a spiritual successor in the works by one of the people who used to work on the series named Hover: Revolt of Gamers. Might be worth a shot, who knows?
