I had a review for this game already posted, but after so many changes that have happened over the years (especially recently) I feel like this game is due for a fresh review. In the process, I'll try to be as honest as I can, having played this game pretty much since its release.
This game genuinely provides a unique experience that I've not had anywhere else.
It has strengths and it has flaws. The biggest cause of the negative reviews is just that veterans (including myself) are tired of the poor decisions that Ronimo has made (from a consumer standpoint) over the years. However, I feel like the game is in a solid state right now, and as it stands, I have few complaints.
Honestly, this is just a solid game overall. It's a 3v3 MOBA with the unique factor of it being designed as a 2D-platformer of sorts. Most fights involve very quick skirmishes that often end in no one dying due to how easy it is to get out of situations but some will involve entire team wipes or huge outplays like any MOBA.
From an aesthetic standpoint, which may or may not matter to you, the game is honestly perfect to me. Nothing feels out of place; the music tracks all do what they're trying to do well; the art style feels like it belongs with this kind of game.
The matches themselves are fairly short, so you don't have to commit to hour-long games which is something that makes the game easy to jump into.
Also, the "Zork" word filter is hilarious.
BY FAR, the thing that causes players the most frustration is Ronimo's poor decisions they've been making over the past few years. They frequently add aesthetic things you can purchase for money instead of, I don't know, actually fixing the matchmaking which took them
to finally do. Don't get me wrong, the purchasable skins and such are great, but most would agree that they'd rather see other things being worked on. I could make an endless list of the poor decisions they've made, but I think you get the idea. This is the single thing that has driven so many players away from this game over the years.
Another thing that consistenly bothers players including myself is that lag favors the player attacking, rather than the player being attacked. This tends to cause you to get hit when you clearly shouldn't be. A laggy player can completely ruin a game if it persists.
I also find that playing by yourself can be annoying at higher level games because most people are a full premade team and there isn't an easy way to communicate with your team in this game. This usually results in a fully premade team completely stomping a non-premade team because the latter can't communicate well enough to do anything.
People seem to have a lot of mixed feelings about Awesomenauts going Free-to-Play. I personally think that this game will benifit greatly from it overall, though I do have my worries about things like hackers, which as of now, you can only report via email.
A lot of players are saying things along the lines of "Do I get a refund then? I payed money for this thing and get very little out of it." I could say a lot about this, but overall, I personally have no regrets buying the game, many skins, and 2 DLC packs (one of which I payed even more for on kickstarter). I think I've gotten my money's worth already and will probably end up spending even more in the future.
Going F2P should bring in a lot more players which should overall increase the money that Ronimo makes, negating the need for DLC kickstarters and the like. However, this is assuming that it's executed well, but we'll just have to wait and see how it goes. If it goes absolutely horribly, then I will probably note that in this review.
This will pretty much be a repeat of the tl;dr at the top, but I think that after an
bumpy ride, this game is reaching a good state. I think this is a solid MOBA that provides an experience you will not get anywhere else. While many may disagree with me, I think that going F2P is the best thing that Ronimo could have done and will hopefully increase the playerbase which is something that the game currently lacks and desperately needs (having 500 players during peak hours on a weekend all divided into regions on top of that for the sake of ping, isn't really ideal).

Another classic Dreamcast game. Another classic SEGA game, for that matter.
If you expect this to be at all similar to Tony Hawk's Pro Skater... then you're sorely mistaken.
"Mr. Osaki asks, 'how do I get rid of these nasty roaches,' easy, just burn your house down!" -DJ Professor K, in-game soundtrack DJ and story narrator.
Being a release from well over a decade and a half ago (2000), you can't expect much in the graphics department, but even then, they're nothing to scoff at. The combination of bright, colorful artwork, cel shaded models, and heavily atmospheric level design makes it a quite remarkable display.
Whereas many games parade their flagship visual style as defining feature, Jet Set Radio goes one step further and banks heavily off of the amazing soundtrack, featuring incredible remixes, and Hideki Naganuma's excellent tracks.
The plot is perhaps too short to explain in a review without spoiling the game, but I'd recommend watching the trailers to get a sound idea of what the gameplay will be like.
Just a few things to point out before you buy,
-The game speed is tied to 30FPS. Any attempt to run the game at 60FPS will result in the game running at 200% speed.
-A controller is absolutely necessary. If you don't have a 360 controller, use a PS3 controller with Better DS3 Tool.
-The camera can be a bit wonky at times. Use the left trigger to straighten it out.
-Jet Set Radio Future, SEGA's 2002 XBox exclusive is worth buying an old XBox for. Seriously. Check that out if you enjoyed this game.

It's a really cheap game, but you get what you pay for. Wait for a sale and buy something better for the same price or less. The game is functional, but has a lot of mistakes that could be fixed with experience. I might be interested in another game by this developer in the future, but definitely pass on this one. Longer review below. Nitpicks below that.
This game is basically a difficult NES-style platformer, but the controls just aren't good enough to make it work. There's a slight delay after attacking that feels very inconsistent, sometimes letting you mash the button and sometimes ignoring your input. Most ledges have decorative borders that you can't walk on but look perfectly solid, leading to a lot of deaths and mistimed jumps. It doesn't help that enemies appear to walk on these ledges constantly, even though they're only technically on the platform by a pixel or two. Wall jumping feels very slow and sticky, as you don't grab on until you start to descend rather than when you hit the wall. You also grab on every time you touch a wall while descending, and there's no way to drop off. You either have to jump halfway across the screen or ride the wall all the way down. Level design is about on par with any given flash game. It's generally not memorable, and later levels have stage hazards that don't really add anything to the game. They're just kinda there. A lot of levels are vertically designed or have vertical sections, where one bad jump or unlucky hit will set you back about 30 seconds of platforming, assuming you don't drop into a bottomless pit. Bosses are awful all around and are a definite low point of the game. It all adds up to a pretty poor experience.
There's also a lot of small quality of life issues that shouldn't be there.
-Bosses have about twice as much health as they need, so each battle feels very slow and tedious. The ones I've encountered also only have one attack, which adds to the problem. They're not even complex attacks that are challenging to avoid, so you're just repeating the same five-second loop for two to three minutes.
-Bosses are also drawn art instead of pixel art, so they clash with the rest of the game. Some are poorly animated as well, making them stand out further.
-Trying to skip a cutscene causes a slow fade out. Dying causes a slow fade out. Winning a level causes a slow text fade in. Bosses have a slow introduction and defeat 'cutscene'. None of those can be skipped. The first couple times you won't notice it, but if you replay any levels or have trouble beating one, it becomes irritating.
-There's no restart option. You have to quit, die, or win if you make a mistake. Ties into the previous problem and makes it more noticeable.
-The timer continues to count down after you die or win, and doesn't stop for boss cutscenes. Cut about ten seconds off the timer of all levels, plus another ten on boss levels.
-Two of the three special powers aren't very useful. Most levels are enclosed, making the kunai rain power bounce off the roof in most situations where it could be useful. The forward attack special will kill anything in front of you, but there's not really any open stretches with a lot of enemies, and you're not allowed to have specials on boss levels. This leaves the omnidirectional special, which will generally kill everything on the screen. There's just no reason to use the other two.

Crusader Kings II is another of Paradox Studio's grand strategy games. It is an enjoyable experience all around. Though the learning curve might be a bit steep for some. When I got started a couple years back there were around 18 individual tutorials and even that needed to be teamed up with an hour youtube tutorial to learn to really play it properly. However, it seems like an easier/shorter tutorial has been added in the way of a short tutorial campaign.
The graphics and sound are simple, but get the job done. The sound track is earthshattering on the first opening of the game so be on the look out for that. The game also begins to lag after several hundred years of gameplay so people with weaker computers might want to prepare for that.
This game has a nice blend of character building RPG and kingdom building strategy. The RPG comes in the form of elements centred around raising your heirs, getting them specific traits, going on questlines, and interacting with other characters. The kingdom building comes in the form of raising armies, dealing with your vassal (or lords), and adding to your kingdom.
The game comes with a lot of DLC which can be pricey, but the good news is most of the features of the DLC are free with the only exception being you can't play as DLC kingdoms. An example is a DLC which added India. Without the DLC you can still interact, conquer, and play within India, however you can not start the game as an Indian.
The game has a massive timeframe going from 1066-1452, with DLC bumping that up to 769-1452. It is also highly replayable. Which is good because you will probably lose more games than you win. Speaking of which I have never actually made it beyond 1350 myself.
Pro: Deep medievel experience, well written event lines, nice family system, large world spanning from the Atlantic to Tibet.
Con: DLC can make this an expensive game, combat can feel arbitrary to new players, hard to learn.
Rating: 15 Sacked Constanipoles.

Looking for a more SRS BSNS game like Fallout NV? Well, you've come to the right place.
STALKER COP is an open world, sandbox style FPSRPG. Its more serious, and less people enjoy your company - but its more fun too. This game doesnt have much humor, no VATS-esque system, no level ups. Its all in the gear you acquire through missions, raids, and stash hunting. You can pretty much do whatever you want, whenever you want - though it is wise to have the proper gear for the job. You can play however you like, from stealth to full auto brawler to sniping and everything in between - or all of it.
The human enemy AI can be fairly cunning at times. You cannot simply hole up in a room and wait for them - they will lob grenades in, bait you out, even lay down suppressing fire while their buddies come around to flank you. I can complain slightly that they seen to 'forget' about the player at times - but their reaction is quick when you reappear as if 'reminded' of the previous battle. This has only happened when I have successfullly evaded them, never in any circumstance do they simply abandon a battle when you are detected. Enemies can detect you not only by sight and your flashlight, but sound as well!
The graphics in the game are great, should be able to max everything out on a GTX 460 or better; a 9800 1GB handles the game very well too. In fact, they are some of the best graphics to date IMHO. It also scales well when turning down the settings for less capable rigs.
The only thing I can possibly pick at in this game are some of the weapon sounds. They just arent crisp enough - but thats it. The ambient sounds and everything else audio-wise is wonderfully done.
I give this game a 10/10. Masterfully executed, lots of content and replay factor.

() Clunky controls with a wall grabbing manuever that will kill you more often than be useful.
() Poor collision detection. Particularly spikes; You actually abuse the poor collision detection to retrieve a collectible in 5-1. There are also major issues with your own character's sprite wherein parts of your head/hair are included in the hitbox and other parts are not.
() Limited number of enemy types with no variation.
() Blind jumps
() The randomness of enemies projectile attacks that make the final levels either trivial or impossible.
() Cookie cutter boss fights you've seen in hundreds of times in other games before.
There are many other minor issues with the game:
() Game over screen lingers on for too long. Simply pause and exit to get back into the game faster.
() Music isn't great.
() Sound effects are basic and trigger at odd times.
() Almost non existent story. To get the "good" ending (or additional lines of text on the ending screen) you need to collect 45 identical kimonos because....reasons.

Easily the worst platformer I have ever played.
The graphics are incosistent and bland. There is not a shred of artistic cohesion to be found. There is hardly a story to speak of either.
What passes for enemy AI in this game is basically that ranged enemies will begin randomly attacking the air whenever you're on the same screen as them. They will also occasionally shoot you through the floor. Other than that, they simply pace backwards and forwards. The bosses are uninspired, and some are simply built around wasting as much of the players time as possible.
The game's design is highly questionable at the best of times. On average, it's barely passable. Difficulty is primarily achieved through enemy-stacking. In other words, any hard section of this game is achieved through artificial means, by simply putting you, the player, in a situation that you can't effectively counter. This is especially true in the latter half of the game.
The gameplay is what really brings this title down. Akane, the main character, is the least ninja-like character I've ever played. She controls like a hot potato being rolled down a hill. She's floaty, the momentum makes any kind of precision nigh impossible to achieve, and once she's in the air it's like trying to control the descent of an oily brick. Even bosses ten times her side seem to move about with much more ease than our titular kunoichi.
All in all, this game reminded me of the free Flash-platformers I'd play on various websites before I had my own credit card.

A neat 2.5D doujin shmup that mostly plays in a vertical fashion, but will occassionally switch perspective to horizontal, and even through gameplay moments simlar to Starfox 64 and Rez, using it's 3D capabilities to it's advantage. You can get a better feel of bullet mechanics thanks to the hitbox option. It's great to let you know where you can be hit and where to hit enemies, but it's a bit wonky because the red, circular hitbox overlays are on the upper most layer, so it will be above damn near everything, including cutscene tech. It's worse when there are so many hitboxes on bots - anything with collison has hitboxes, including you and your own damn bullets, so you will see red circles all over the damn screen. Whats worse, a blue hitbox typically means it's a defeated enemy that is exploding into the background, but the hitboxes for actual enemies in the background are still red, so you can't quite tell if something is in the foreground or background until you shoot it. I think it's a better job than Sine Mora IMO, but all you have to go by is depth. Which brings me to the biggest issue of the game, and that is being able to tell what is in the background. You might find yourself dying a bit to enemies shifting to the foreground, and dodging bullets in the background that aren't actually going to hit you yet. Otherwise, the difficulty is is fair and mostly "your fault if you die". It's a pure shmup in a sense, so it isn't a bullet hell, but it can almost get there. You don't have powerups, but you rely on a forward gatling gun that can charge a penetrative blast , a laser missle lock on a la Zone of the Enders, and a wide shot that can be charged to release a bullet cancelling bomb, which is great for personal defense and doesn't damage you, but doesn't protect you from collision damage. Soundtrack is good, but nothing award winning. If you're big into shmups, I can recommend it, thought you may want to watch some videos to see if the 3d aspect will bother you.

I feel like I'm alone in saying the game excels more the acrobatics than it does in the combat. I've always had more fun jumping around and exploring than I did in the arena mode (although I did do that every once in a while and still had some fun.); but for some reason, anything over 1v1 combat in this new story mode feels cheap and unfair. You could argue "but it's only in beta!", but that argument goes out the window when it's been in development for 9 years. People say that the combat is extremely fluid, but I don't really see it. You get two buttons, one to attack, one to block. It makes it difficult to do any sort of combos that can get you out of a tough situation. oh, and before anyone says it, no I'm not complaining that it's too hard, I'm complaining that there's a lack of options for combat that I didn't really have a problem with during arena mode for whatever reason.
Also, not making a huge point of this because it could just be early dialogue, but man is it terrible. It feels like something ripped out of an edgelord's naruto fanfic. I honestly hope that gets better.
Anyway, before this gets too long, I'll just say don't pick this game up for anything over $15 and don't pick it up if you're expecting a super in depth exploration game. $30 is waaaaay too much for the amount of time it's taking to get out of development.
Also, if you disagree and you see something I don't, instead of hitting the "not helpful" button, comment and lemme know. I really want to like this game, but I just can't find any reason to.

In short: Solid game, exceptional combat, nice story.
Pros:
- Combat; it's just great. Combat in the first game was good, and here it's even better. Feels very smooth and polished, makes the player want to try different approaches, different skills. On normal difficulty fights are challenging enough to keep the entertainment up while encouraging min-maxing. I honestly believe this is the best aspect of the game.
- Story; engaging, pleasurable to play through, great companion stories. Companions and their stories through the game make the game way better and I'd suggest going through the first playthrough without the Lone Wolf talent, just to get as much story from them as possible.
- Graphics; game looks pretty. Nothing much to say, really.
Cons:
- Unpolished; many threads feel unfinished. It's small things, but leaves a "meh" feeling when encountered. Quests have various way of solving them but not all of them actually "close" the quest. Sometimes it feels like "real pen-and-paper experience" idea is forced, leaving the player annoyed and looking for a solution on the internet. Last act feels rushed.
- Quests; I covered a bit of it in "Unpolished" but I believe it deserves it's own place here. Companion quests interfere with each other forcing the player to either temporarily kick one person from party or miss out on part of the companion quest. Many quests don't give the player a hint of what to do, so you end up just wandering around not really knowing what to do and just stumbling upon a solution.
Netiher, my own preferences:
- 3D world; I'd prefer a game where I don't need to keep rotating the camera to find all the things on the map.
- Lack of container highlights; a specific key can be assigned to highlight an item, but never a container so you end up wanting to mouse-over everything.
- Quest reward in experience should be the same no matter the choice; since killing people gives a lot of experience I end up prefering to just kill people instead of using my presuasion skills to solve the conflict: finishing the quest gives the same amount of experience and the loot no matter what the player does, but combat results in killing people (bonus experience).

Now that I've actually beaten the game, I feel the need to write a new, more detailed recommendation. To go along with this game of many bullets, bullet points!

- Beautiful, crisp and refined polygons; 3D graphics for a 2D shmup is pretty uncommon
- Well-drawn character portraits and nice character design
- Cool looking ships
- Surprisingly good dialogue
- Good music and atmosphere
- Actually has a story worth your attention, but also allows for skipping and turning off outright
- You can turn on hitboxes being visible for the enemies and your shots
- Good progression
- There are parts that are on-rails with a lock-on cursor and parts where the angles change
- Boss rush mode and extras
- As to be expected of a bullet hell shmup, it is challenging
- 60 FPS, no load times and responsive menus

This is not a review. This is me after hours of playing this game and hoping for more. I like this game a lot, but there are things that I wish they could do differently. The overall idea of the game is great, but there are countless seemingly little game machanics that frustrate me, including:
-Overly stable Muslim and Nomadic (Horse Lords) states.
-Empires are too stable, largely because its too easy (even for the AI) to homogenize them. It should be harder to demand religous conversions and educate vassal children.
-Characters live for too long. Life expectancy back in the Middle Ages was 30, yet too many character reach their 60s easily and even their 80s with little issue.
-Their needs to be more coordination with factions. Vassals angry with their lords (including you) should be able to ask each other to join factions rather than just hope they randomly join.
-Elective Monarchy is OP. It should be balanced out by being able to ask voters for their support for a candidate and only grant that opnion boost to the voters.
-religious and cultural differences between rulers and provinces should make said provinces more willing to revolt.
-needs more random decision-making. the ones we have are predictable and its easy to tell which decision is the right one. Also, a character's traits should have more influence over what decisions are available to them and how they can react.
These are just a few of the main gripes I have with this game. If any modders are reading this and have some free time in the Steam Workshop maybe you can apply some of these ideas to mods.

Akane isn't perfect, but its pros and cons balance out thanks to some well crafted level designs and a short length that feels just right for the action it delivers.
Controls initially felt muddy, but after getting used to the rhythm of jumping and attacking, I had little trouble with them.  The slower pace of the gameplay actually benefits you as the map layouts are well designed into tricking those who attempt to speed through without caution.  Graphically the game looks quite good.  The color pallete and characters remind me favorably of some of Nippon Ichi's work, like Rhapsody and La Pucelle.  The music is a bit of a disappointment, however.  Songs are of good quality, but many do not fit the theme of the game nor the atmosphere of the level in which they are used.
The difficulty curve is well handled, and ramps up smoothly at the final set of levels.  They are certainly a good challenge and will test your patience and timing.  Overall I enjoyed my time with Akane the Kunoichi and feel it would be enjoyable to players of all skill levels.  This one's worth your money.

I would recommend all of the STALKER games, as they are all fantastic. But in truth, I can only recommend Pripyat to the gamers of this generation. It is primarily because Pripyat is the most complete version of all the games and it in general, is a fun game. Add in a mod known as "Misery" and you have yourself one of the hardest and most realistic post apocalyptic games out there.
Pripyat doesn't hold your hand. Once you press start, you spawn in the middle of seemingly nowhere, as you open your map, figure out where you are, fiddle with the controls and read your objectives. In short, there are five helicopter crashes and you've been sent to investigate what caused those crashes. Beyond that, the world is your oyster. It's free roam. You manage supplies, make people happy, shoot a few heads, deal with mutants, and pursue the odd side quest or two.
In the world of STALKER, everyone is indifferent to you. You aren't a super hero or some tank who can take dozens of shots without flinching. You get shot, you slow down, you bleed, your vision dims and you die. Assuming you didn't get medical attention, of course. Similarly, enemies die just as fast, and it's a blast (no pun intended) fighting against the AI in this game.
The mutants are probably some of the best well-done ones out there. They are believable, some more scary than others, and they all pose real threats. Even small packs of dogs can be a threat - easily disbanded if you kill a few, but you'd be wasting bullets on something so easily dealt with. Probably the highlight of mutants would be an encounter with blood suckers. You're in the middle of a pond, shooting at the small movements you think you see. The only way to tell where they are, is when they break invisibilty and are about to suck the life out of you - or you could play it smart and try  to watch the water ripples as they run by.
Beyond mutants and humanoid enemies, there is one other thing that plagues the world. Anomalies. They are some of the most devastating things known in the STALKER universe - it is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥trying to deal with them, avoiding them and having the right equipment to deal with anomalies. But at the same time, they are what makes the world of STALKER - You can find relics from heavily anomalated sites (is that even a word?) which you can use to your advantage, or sell for a hefty profit to purchase even an even greater arsenal of weapons - or even upgrade your current equipment with the various weapon gurus you can find throughout the game.
STALKER is a must play... If you've got the guts to play it. It does include some horror at times. I highly recommend modding it with at least the "STALKER pripyat complete" mod, so the bugs are taken out and some realism added (such as sleeping to avoid night time). Well worth the money.

Akane is agreat throwback to the classic 16bit gaming era. In fact, it actually feels like a "blast from the past" has been locked away in a time capsule in the early 1990s, sealed tight and only opened up recently.
The levels are short and sweet; no checkpoints and every hit you take from enemies drain one of your hearts. If you die, you restart from the beginning.
Enemies are attack pattern based as well as bosses.
Plattforming may feel unresponsive at first, but once you get the hang of it (Akane's plattforming is not speed-based precision plattforming) they get the job well done and provide you with enough precision to get all the collectables (especially in the last 3 levels).
Keeping that in mind, I highly recommend Akane to everybody who remembers or is interested in classic gaming era style games.

At first when I played speedrunners I got it for a fun party game as well as online play with my friends. It would be a lot of fun running, jumping, and grappling around the map as we laughed. I didn't play it much like that when I started playing Online Matchmaking. People started crushing me in speed and that's where the game took more of a competetive feel. It wasn't until I felt like I was good enough to go on Ranked, where the real fun begins. I would've never expected such a simple game to have so much depth to it. The great thing about this game is that it has a variety of aspects that all do well. It is a party game for if friends come over, it is a fun online chill-out game to have a laugh as well. Then it is more about winning in online. After online and into ranked you start in entry league and it is pretty basic. It is around when I am now expert league and I am facing bronze league's where the game really starts to show what it has to offer. Serious competition, but still about laughing and having a good time with random people you are facing. This game is for almost anyone except people who rage easily for no reason. Please don't get the game if you are that person. Nobody wants to play with that person. Actually nevermind, just don't get any game that I play. I never want to play with that person.
tl;dr  The more you play, the more you discover about the game, the more you have fun. If you don't want to pay full price that is ok because if you want to support the devs more you can buy trails for .99 cents each. It's an in-game store I actually enjoy having for many reasons. Whenever you are playing, always remember that there is room to get better so don't worry!

There isn't much about Woodle Tree Adventures that seems complete. The idea is simple, jump around some woodland and find some water or something.   The art design and concept are good, but everything else is riddled with problems.
It’s not really clear what you’re supposed to be doing at given moment and the levels are haphazard at best. Every enemy is the same amount of useless.  When you die you start over at the beginning of the level, unless you start over at some other arbitrary point. After playing the first level for a while it seemed like I was supposed to gather up 3 tears or water drops of some sort to move on the next level. I only found two water drops, restarted the game and suddenly the next level became available?
There is essentially no interface to be found in the game, no menu or settings once you start up the game. You can’t start a new game or do anything at all besides jump around and whack stuff with a leaf.
From the first splash screen you have some graphics settings and control configuration which are just as incomplete as everything else. If you set the resolution to low you probably won’t be able to read any of the text, which isn’t much of a problem because the dialogue and story are apparently contained entirely in three sentences when you first boot up the game. The control options are downright confusing.
I don’t want to disparage the developer too much because the game is very charming and I think there is some potential here, but Woodle Tree Adventures is far from complete. I couldn’t recommend anyone buy it if they’re expecting a finished product.

Alien Shooter 2: Reloaded is the follow up to Alien Shooter. Much like its predecessor, you spend the game shooting lots and lots of aliens. It improves on the original in many ways, and in the process becomes a game that can become worthy of some of your time.
The graphics have seen a marked improvement in AS2. Everything looks crisper, there's more details to the characters and environments, and the aliens are varied and unique. The shooting is also much improved, with aiming being much tighter. The movement controls are as crisp as the original. You will be spending a lot of time dancing around with WASD and holding the left mouse button, so get used to that.
AS2 has some RPG lite elements. You earn experience through your actions, and can level up in about 6 categories. I am not quite sure how a high intelligence would help you in this game, but it is one of the categories. You also spend your cash on weapon upgrades to help your hunting a little easier.
Alien Shooter 2 has voice acting that is serviceable, and the music adds a nice touch much like the original.
Alien Shooter 2: Reloaded can be recommended for the improvements that were made over its predecessor. All of the major flaws were addressed, with better controls, graphics and enemy variety. If you are looking for a mindless shooter than this game is worthy of a try.
Grade: C+



I think this game will appeal to you if you are a certain kind of person. Do you like Firefly or Mad Max? Does the post disaster/apocalyptic setting appeal? Do you like melancholy, moody music? Do you tend to like more serious  'grown up' games that allow true role playing? Are you happy to wander around on your own, sometimes for long stretches of time, without seeing a soul? Are you more of a loner (a strange question for an MMO perhaps)? Are you more of a calm person who takes gaming slowly rather than rushing to experience a game in the shortest possible time? If the answer is mostly yes this game could be for you...
For me, the atmosphere in this game is second to none. Fantastic music, incredible view distance that really hammers home the immense size of the game (around 1000 square kilometres I believe - to put that into perspective Skyrim is around 40 I think) and true freedom to go pretty much wherever you want right from the very start of the game. Note though that I play as a single player - I'm not a clan type of person - so I can't really tell you much about the social side of the game. It is fairly quiet of late - not too many players - but that suits me fine.
It's certainly not a polished experience but then, if you're anything like me, that won't matter in the slightest. There's plenty of minor bugs although hardly any will stop progress (a simple relog usually sorts out most things) and there are plenty of minor gameplay things to moan about but, overall, the game is very unique and well worth the download. A huge thing in its favour is that it's a true free to play game. You can play the entire game without spending any real world money. Real world money will get you cool items to wear, cool vehicles, nice buffs and such but almost all of it can also be purchased with in game earned currency if you are patient and keep an eye on the auction house for bargains. It's also worth noting that a lot of the coolest, unique weapons and clothing items can only be earned through questing.
I'm not going to go too heavily into the mechanics of the game - it's pretty standard MMO levelling and crafting (but a very deep and rewarding crafting system) and such but it is one of the very few MMO's with real time skill based combat - think first person shooter - and the whole experience of the game is very 'manual' - nothing's on auto pilot - it's all on you to use your skill to stay alive basically.
Right, I think I've talked enough now...

Ether Vapor: Remaster is an arcade shooter that focuses on being cinematic and challenging.  As shooters go, it's pretty difficult (your hitbox is quite large); although, some of this difficulty can be of the unnatural variety.  For example, a lot of the colors for projectiles run together.  It's extremely difficult to avoid a projectile if it is the same color as the weapons you fire, or is blocked out by your own laser beams.  To partially rectify this, the game allows you to turn on "hitboxes", which is nice in theory, but it adds hitboxes to *everything* in the game, including your weaponry and your enemies weaponry.  This helps to allow you to see what's shot at you for *some* projectiles; however, it also clutters up the screen and everything has a red border, so it blocks out other projectiles that weren't very hard to see before.  It's a rock and a hard place, and it's really a shame because it's a major strike against a shmup.  In trying to be cinematic and not make every projectile pink (the best color to use in shmup IMO) they've added an unfair difficulty spike to it.  But, the game is mostly good, hence the recommendation I'm offering for it.  There are two ships to select from (one is unlocked after the game) and you have three modes of firing - Frontal, Side, and Homing - nothing surprising there; however, you can also charge up the weapons for a massive piercing frontal attack, a shield that damages everything caught in it and blocks projectiles and lasers (extremely handy) and a massive AOE homing explosion attack.  Homing attacks are very important in this game.  A unique mechanic of Ether Vapor is that the game is semi-3d, I think it's officially classified as 2.75D.  The perspective changes from top-down, to left-to-right, to even behind the ship (think Star Fox).  It's really neat and is done well, flowing into and out of combat.  There are also really neat periods of time where you use the ships homing lasers to destroy missiles while autopilot is on and you rack up huge points - extremely fun!  That said, another strike against this game is that the Z axis is played with a lot, and it's nigh impossible to determine if enemies are able to be hit by conventional weaponry or if you need to use the homing lock on because they're off your Z-plane.  It can get annoying and the only way to know for sure is experience in the game.  Speaking of experience, this game teaches you how to play it pretty well.  It seems extremely unforgiving as you need to start over every time you play, but in reality you get better, learn the levels, and you unlock more continues and more "shields" (hits you take before you need to continue again) as you play.  So it eases you into the game and it makes what at first seems daunting and impossible easier as time goes on.  I felt it was paced really well and still kept its arcade roots, unlike other shmups like Sine Mora.  After beating the game, besides the new ship you also unlock Boss Rush mode that adds replayability.  You also unlock "extras", which is really just a link to a Japanese-only website, so that's kin of a bummer.  The switching of weapons and arcadey style is really reminiscent of Ikaruga, and if you enjoyed that game you'll probably like this one.
Pros:
Cinematic
Fun
Varied/Useful weaponry
Pacing
Challenging
Cons:
"Cluttery"
Z-Axis woes
Lack of leaderboards (and personal ones don't work quite to my satisfaction either)
All in all this is a difficult shooter that has a lot of fun and fast paced action.  Even a veteran will find himself challenged by this game and new players can get eased in and earn more continues but still feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥since there is only one difficulty level.  There's a story as well, but like most Japanese shooters it's not much of note.  I'd buy this if you like shooters, but note it's not the best one I've played.  B+

Lemma Review
It seems like it’s been ages since we were last gifted with a game featuring a female free-running hero at the helm, with Mirror’s Edge release occurring over five years ago and its sequel currently only existing as a tease. Luckily for us lone developer Evan Todd took it upon himself to craft a parkour adventure of impressive scale and quality to say the least. Enter Lemma, the 5 year development project taken on almost entirely single-handedly that was entirely worth the effort.

You awake to little explanation for your strange environment or what brought you there. Gradually a backstory is revealed while you’re busy scaling the floating monoliths that overwhelm your surroundings. Signal towers act as beacons that are used to communicate via SMS with a mysterious character named Mark, someone your character has an apparent history with. He informs you that your name is Joan and that you’ve been trapped in Lemma, a world built in a computer simulation for an unknown experiment. A group of your friends are in the outside world trying to rescue you, but in the meantime it’s up to you and your parkour abilities to attempt to find an escape. Though your companion on the other end of the phone is your only help through the void, it seems you’re not even sure who he really is, what his true intentions are, or even if he’s the one you’re consistently communicating with. Discovering hidden notes in hard to reach locations reveals some of the game’s philosophy on abnormal physical properties and provides a healthy narrative backbone. It all works on a cognitive level and it gels with the gameplay effectively; theories and ideas on the true nature of matter and observation fit well into game of hovering indiscernible matter in endless space. The level of mystery brought about by the way the story is presented to you is intriguing enough to motivate deep exploration, and players who do so are rewarded with a greater understanding for this narrative through the scattered pages.
The world of Lemma offers a great feel of segmented openness. Players are free to explore open-ended puzzles and terrain that’s connected by more linear sections. Challenges are presented uniquely and with no explanation, an aspect that promotes discovery and that great sense of enlightenment upon success. While some concepts might be more apparent than others, there’s a problem with it not always being clear what you just did in order to complete a puzzle. The game sometimes becomes a victim of one button performing too many actions and the unintended outcome happening more often than you’d expect. Despite this, the control still feels extremely smooth and natural. At first running may feel a bit janky with arms being thrust with force in front of you, but this feeling quickly vanishes, and it feels as though you’re actually free running amongst the impossible shapes. Eventually players gain the ability to create their own floors and walls to branch out past existing architecture with rolls and wall-runs, adding a fluid extension to the parkour that we’ve never seen before in a first-person platformer. At first this seems like an element that can be easily exploited, but thanks to thoughtful level design there’s never really a situation in which the player can cheat the game. Instead it’s confidently designed around your understanding of how to use it properly. New elements are introduced later on as well; just as you think you’ve seen everything in the way of puzzle mechanics the game brings about new player abilities and environmental pieces. Later in the story you earn a skill to visualise blocks to wall run on out of thin air, giving your free running a new level freedom. Those who master handling the controls will be able to pull of some of the craziest platforming moves imaginable. A decent amount of challenge is given by hostile blocks and textures that hunt you down. These situations can get tense and lead to fun chases and escapes, but unfortunately are watered down by the reality of unlimited retries and object permanence upon respawn.
For an independent development and the money asked of the consumer the visual and subtle audio presentation is fantastic. Textures are simple yet have a fine look upon closer inspection, and the intentional overuse of cubic shapes to construct the majority of the world really cooperates well with the gameplay. The use of music is sparse and tastefully added to extraordinary situations. It’s clear that a ton of care went into how you take in each new aspect as you encounter them from your first person perspective, and the inclusion of Oculus support goes even further to demonstrate that. Unfortunately we lacked the equipment to experiment with this addition, but we can only imagine the level of intensity it would add. Climbing obstacles that are only half obstructing your path can sometimes induce some obtuse animations, but otherwise the game is truly an immersive experience.
Without a doubt the release of this game is an achievement in indie creative skill and credibility. It’s unquestionably on par with the AAA competition that it took such wise inspiration from. Lemma is a certain type of limbo that we wouldn’t mind getting lost in.

==Pros==
+Pretty deep character customization at the start of the game.
+Amazing music that you never get tired of listening to.
+Though rather generic when compared to Skyrim and even Morrowind, the game world is beautifully designed and helps add to the immersion, while being decently sized.
+A level of player freedom that only an Elder Scrolls game can give you. After the tutorial mission, you can literally do whatever you want, from murdering and robbing random citizens, to roaming the lands as a nomad, never taking a single life unless needed.
+Great mod support can help keep the game fresh long after you've completed every quest and found every landmark.
+Lots of neat little activites to do, like join the Thieves Guild or Dark Brotherhood, to reading the many books scattered across the land, and much more.
+NPCs live out their lives (going to bed, talking to people in a bar, etc) even when the players isn't near them, giving the game this feeling of actual being a living, breathing world.
+Game difficulty can be adjusted at will, allowing you to turn it up if you want a more rewarding combat experience, and tone it down if you want to explore the land with little risk.
==Cons==
-While the game doesn't look too bad, the graphics are quickly becoming dated, even at max settings. There are plenty of mods to enhance the graphics though.
-Though the game runs fine on my crappy laptop and should run well on high settings on low end rigs, it tends to stutter alot, more so in third person. Not sure if it's just me, but even if it is, it's really annoying.
-The voice acting is a mixed bag. The actual voices are good and the acting is decent, but you'll quickly notice that several people have the same voice actors. Even worse, some characters will switch to a completely different voice actor if you talk about certain topics (such as Rumors). This can really break the immersion of the game.
-People's facial expressions sometimes don't match their tone of voice (for example, a character will look bored even though they're talking with a nervous tone), but for the most part it's usually fine.
-Bethesda Games are known for being buggy at release and onward, and though I haven't really encountered anything odd yet, be prepared for weird♥♥♥♥♥♥to happen.
-The item system is a bit weird, as one item may take up more space than 3 seperate items combined. If you aren't careful about this, you could get over-encumbered fast, requiring you to dump many of your items.
-Bounties are a bit of a pain, as they spread across the entire land. The bigger the bounty, the more people on your♥♥♥♥♥ and the more people on your♥♥♥♥♥means more people to kill, which results in a bigger bounty, and the cycle goes on and on until you talk to a guard and go to jail or pay a fine.
Overall, despite some annoying mechanics and slightly dated graphics, Oblivion is a great RPG, with an unprecedented level of freedom, and a great immersive world. Be prepared to spend hours exploring the land and completing the quests.

Three Pros, Three Cons
Cons:
-The only really big flaw in this game - It's veeerry easy to get lost.  You WILL lose track of where to go next several times.  There's a large open world but no system of objectives and little or no guidance whatsoever.  I got very frustrated even though I had already beaten the demo.
-The protagonist (you) act like a jerk sometimes.  There's a phone where you receive a bare minimum of guidance for the first couple of levels, with a simple dialogue system with between one and three choices.  Typically the choices are either "I need help" or "♥♥♥♥ off, I don't need your help".
-The parkour animations aren't very seamless.  Joan (you) can do things that shouldn't be possible and in the process often hauls herself up by empty air or shoves a hand into solid rock.  This happens so, so often.
Pros:
-It's beautiful.  Skies, landscapes, textures, sounds, all of it.  Soundtrack is amazing - not the sort of thing that I'd listen to a lot myself, but it fits the game very well.  Sometimes it reminds me of Mirror's Edge soundtrack, sometimes Dear Esther.  The enemies go through three stages - unsettling when watching from afar, for which I applaud, then terrifying as they chase you, then boring and frustrating later on when you have five of them chasing you while you  just try to accomplish a task.
-Puzzles are satisfying and puzzly.  Some of them are quite simple, but others are Myst-caliber.  The parkour is very fun.  I'm going to compare it to Mirror's Edge because it's a well known game that I've played extensively.  Lemma's parkour is technically inferior, I guess, but it's more fun because of the nonlinear nature of it, especially when you add on Joan's special abilites.  It's also more intuitive, less realistic (even discounting Joan's powers) and glitchier, although IMO not glitchy enough to be really frustrating.
-The story and lore... Wow.  The story is compelling and ties into the lore well, which is very fleshed out.  Also, you can look back and see clues to some of the big reveals in the game.  The lore ties Joans' powers quite solidly into a layman's knowledge of quantum mechanics, and the whole alternate universe thing makes sense as long as you accept the basic premise and don't think too hard.
Overall, 8/10 would recommend, would play again.

I would recommend all of the STALKER games, as they are all fantastic. But in truth, I can only recommend Pripyat to the gamers of this generation. It is primarily because Pripyat is the most complete version of all the games and it in general, is a fun game. Add in a mod known as "Misery" and you have yourself one of the hardest and most realistic post apocalyptic games out there.
Pripyat doesn't hold your hand. Once you press start, you spawn in the middle of seemingly nowhere, as you open your map, figure out where you are, fiddle with the controls and read your objectives. In short, there are five helicopter crashes and you've been sent to investigate what caused those crashes. Beyond that, the world is your oyster. It's free roam. You manage supplies, make people happy, shoot a few heads, deal with mutants, and pursue the odd side quest or two.
In the world of STALKER, everyone is indifferent to you. You aren't a super hero or some tank who can take dozens of shots without flinching. You get shot, you slow down, you bleed, your vision dims and you die. Assuming you didn't get medical attention, of course. Similarly, enemies die just as fast, and it's a blast (no pun intended) fighting against the AI in this game.
The mutants are probably some of the best well-done ones out there. They are believable, some more scary than others, and they all pose real threats. Even small packs of dogs can be a threat - easily disbanded if you kill a few, but you'd be wasting bullets on something so easily dealt with. Probably the highlight of mutants would be an encounter with blood suckers. You're in the middle of a pond, shooting at the small movements you think you see. The only way to tell where they are, is when they break invisibilty and are about to suck the life out of you - or you could play it smart and try  to watch the water ripples as they run by.
Beyond mutants and humanoid enemies, there is one other thing that plagues the world. Anomalies. They are some of the most devastating things known in the STALKER universe - it is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥trying to deal with them, avoiding them and having the right equipment to deal with anomalies. But at the same time, they are what makes the world of STALKER - You can find relics from heavily anomalated sites (is that even a word?) which you can use to your advantage, or sell for a hefty profit to purchase even an even greater arsenal of weapons - or even upgrade your current equipment with the various weapon gurus you can find throughout the game.
STALKER is a must play... If you've got the guts to play it. It does include some horror at times. I highly recommend modding it with at least the "STALKER pripyat complete" mod, so the bugs are taken out and some realism added (such as sleeping to avoid night time). Well worth the money.

Lemma is an incredible first-person parkour game without combat that somehow manages to beat the original Mirror's Edge by *bad pun alert* miles.
*cough cough*
Lemma’s first triumph is found in its relative simplicity. Anything you wish to do in the game can be accomplished by hitting a key or two and looking towards your goal (which is especially handy considering Lemma features Oculus Rift VR support). Want to climb an object, slide across a wall, or even create one? Just hold the Shift key on your keyboard. Want to slide, roll, or perform a jump kick? Just click the Left Mouse Button.
Players can look at almost any point in the world and reach it if they try. The fact that you’re not told to go there, or compelled by some external force (such as the promise of gold or XP), is exciting in a time where exploration in games is defined by its tedium. Go here, do that, get a small amount of compensation and a pat on the back…In Lemma, exploration is its own reward. You can go from running through humid bogs to clambering snowy pillars in moments by choosing YOUR route through the game’s humongous environments...

3. Building is fun. Sometimes placing things just wont work and the options for foundations and stuff are lacking. But I still enjoyed building.
4. The devolopers are active and fixing exploits (slowly) and adding more content (even slower) but they still appear to be working towards the goal of a finished product.
Cons-
1. Combat is uninspired. I just don't get that epic rush it should be. There is no strategy besides run up to you opponent and spam attack. He who has the most players online wins.
2. The servers are empty and the player base is really low.
3. Griefing is pretty easy with no protection. I understand EA games and Sandbox games. However, a clan or even a single player can essentially wall off a whole server in a few hours. Glitchers and Exploiters run rampant on official servers(There are no Admins) and it appears to be without bans.
4. The forums are moderated with heavy handed moderators. If you post anything negitive about the game the post is deleted. In my first review of Conan Exiles Jens Erik one of the Developers said they are softening up their Steam Forum Moderators. Which is a good thing but most of the damage is already done.
5. One of the biggest Con's for me is that: Yes, They are adding content to the game. It is just not meaningfull content. They add decorations, Dyes, Emotes etc. But, after 5 months what do we have that has some substance; A (20min) dungon, catapults, and traps. Funcom should be focused on not adding content untill they are happy with the balance and playability of what they currently have.
I can not recommend this game untill Funcom desides to fix all the hacking, exploits (to be fair they are working on them), and the feel of combat. Save the fluff for the end.

Higher XP rate, better resources, and less or no decay makes it less of a grind.
And I don't really want to spend hours/days building things to have someone exploit to pilfer and destroy my base.

Woodle Tree Adventures is a simple, colorful, and cute platforming game that will appeal primarily to younger players. More experienced gamers won't get as much out of this short adventure, but the game isn't bad.
Woodle Tree Adventures consists of six stages (plus one unlockable level), and the player - or players in two player local co-op - has to guide their cork-like avatar around the maps in search of three giant tears and then haul them to the level exit. Levels also contain collectible berries, which are used to unlock new leaf weapons for your character as well as the bonus level. Enemies dot the maps too, and they can be easily dispatched with the leaf weapon or avoided altogether.
Each level will take about 10 or 12 minutes to complete, and they can be replayed at any time. Since there are Steam achievements for collecting 800, one thousand, and three thousand berries, expect to play through Woodle Tree Adventures several times if you want to get all of the game's eight achievements.
For the most part, Woodle Tree Adventures is a pretty easy game, although the lack of a rotatable camera makes lining up some of trickier jumps a bit frustrating. Fortunately there are unlimited lives and the small map sizes ensure that players won't have to retread the same ground too much. Even so, expect to plummet to your doom more than once because you couldn't line up a jump properly.
Woodle Tree Adventures is bright, family-friendly, and a bit bland. You've definitely played better 3D platformers than this. But if you need something to keep your kid quiet for an hour and there's no booze on hand, Woodle Tree Adventures will do the job.

This is a really fun, well done shmup. Gorgeous 3D models with 2D gameplay that shifts from vertical to horizontal action and some chase cam sequences. The mechanics are solid and fair, the hitboxes feel good and the weapons systems are versatile and powerful with excellent situational mechanics. The gameplay is about optimal placement, there isn't any weaving through bullet mazes. Scoring is based on enemies destroyed and time to clear on bosses and mini-bosses. Finally you can opt completely out of all of the anime style dialogue scenes that occur at various points in the stages. If you ever enjoyed shmups this is something you should take a look at.

Gear Up's customization is very simple, not complex.
Tanks consist of 4 main parts: Propulsion, Hull, Turret, and Weapon and then there are decoration parts.
Some parts grant the ability to add Auxialry parts that are either weaponry or mobility related and you can mix and match AUX parts. There are also accessories and flags, of which some accessories allow for unique in-game taunts.
Gameplay is equally simple. You use WASD to move with the propulsion you equiped, mouse to rotate and aim your turret. You can rebind your functions to make certain functions easier to reach.
There are a few things I must make you aware of though:
- There are only 3 game modes; Conquest (capture markers and hold claim to them), Deathmatch, and Team Deathmatch
- All games are hosted by fellow players -no dedicated servers.
- There is no engine brake; Hovercraft/floating legs will creep backwards. Bug legs will do the same ontop of objects such as on domes, but do not creep backwards from standstill when on solid ground.
- There is no feature to switch teams, thus don't expect to make clans (I actually find this a positive thing)
- There is no auto balance of teams based on rank, team count, nor kill counts
- If ia game is 8 v 8 team and all but one of the other team suddenly disconnects the game is 1 v 8 (happy hunting) and on rare occasion the game glitches and puts all players on the same team.
- Snipers are trouble for new players, but so are harpoon+spear builds, builds that run say machinegun+minigun extensions, etc. You will eventually be able to get the same things (no need to pay money) provided you stick with the game long enough and amass G coins to get your upgrades.
- G coins can not be bought and can only be earned through in-game participation, victory, or every 10 enemies destroyed -thus the game is accurately classified as FTP.
EDIT FEB 21, 2015: The DEVs have been doing a good deal of considering suggestions and actively updating to resurrect issues (glitches, rendering problems) that were making the gameplay unbearable for a decent number of players.
NOTE: A lot of new players cry that this game is pay-2-win. This is not true. A lot of players who have powerful builds have not purchased BASIC nor PREMIUM. If you do not have the pateince to perservere as a new player and learn the ropes by being tossed about, you will never get to the point where you yourself have a more robust inventory of parts. Every game will net you at least 1 G just for being a participant in the match. You keep your spirit up for enough matches and you will find that after hours you suddenly have better parts, are doing better, and can actually be competitive. We all tend to suck at this game. Come join us in sucking at this game!

Looking through my Steam library, I noticed how much I enjoy puzzle games. With one caveat though: Most of the ones I enjoy are in first person and feature some form of exploration in them. I greatly enjoyed games like
,
,
,
and obviously the progenitors of this new wave of first person puzzlers, the
series. So it’s not surprising that Lemma immediately caught my eye.
Aside from this aspect,
obviously takes a lot of inspiration from other games as well.
popularized it many years ago, and parkour has firmly established itself as a core mechanic that many games nowadays employ. An obvious influence to the aesthetic aspect of
comes from
. Voxel graphics are showcased in plenty of titles, though
manages to set itself apart by using realistic stone textures instead of stylized materials. This manages to invoke a certain cognitive dissonance in the player, since we know rock formations don’t adhere to these geometric rules. It’s almost like the world tries to convince you that it’s a real place.
And that’s really the crux of the matter. Early on we get to know that we’re actually in an entirely different dimension. However it’s not immediately clear if it’s a real place or just a virtual construct. To solve the mysteries of this world, we can find a bunch of documents distributed across the levels. In addition to that, we also have a mobile phone through which our protagonists communicates with a friend of hers who is ostensibly responsible for bringing us here. This is where the game reveals that it dabbles in quantum physics.
Now I’m not smart enough to make qualified assessments about how accurately the game portrays its subject matter. But I do know that not many game designers willingly try to present their players with concepts that a large part of the audience is bound to not understand. And that’s where
earns my respect. We need more games that challenge us intellectually because only through this kind of experimentation are we able to broaden our horizons.
During our travels through the cubic dreamscapes we’re confronted with a series of problems. A lot of the time, the floating pieces of rock are too far apart to simply jump from one to the next. In other cases, tiles in floors and walls are missing, preventing power to get from a generator to a corresponding object that needs to be powered.
Since we’re in a different dimension, we’re granted a power that lets us overcome these obstacles. In
's case, we are able to create walls and floors by interacting with the world around us. Doing a roll or sliding along the ground will make a floor appear next to a piece of ground that we’re sliding off of. Running along a wall or a column will instantly create a wall for you to continue running on. It incorporates gameplay directly into level design in a way few games have before. And it truly tests the creativity of the player to get form one point to the next.
One thing that might surprise people is the fact that
’s world is inhabited by creatures that aren’t too happy about us wandering about the place. These enemies are all constructed out of cubes as well and if you happen to attract their attention – which you invariable will – they’ll relentlessly chase you through the levels.
The presence of these enemies is really the only negative aspect I could find here. Mostly because they’re constantly on the move and there don’t seem to be any patterns to predict their behavior and movements. This can often lead to a lot of frustration when you’re trying to come up with a way to traverse a particularly difficult section and also happen to be chased by exploding enemies who further destroy the level, making it even harder for you in your next attempt.
is the result of five years of hard work by a single person, which is somewhat noticeable. There is a certain lack of polish in some spots. The parkour mechanic for example includes very big tolerances that take away from the challenge a bit. Character movement also isn’t as fluid as you might have grown accustomed to from other first person games.
Nevertheless, I can wholeheartedly recommend
to fans of first person puzzlers. It’s rare to see a game that offers so much freedom to players with the ways they can solve the problems they’re presented with.

Pros:

Cons:

Alright, for whatever reason, there's a soft spot in my heart for this game, as I can't bring myself to refund it despite being perfectly eligible to do so (Or at least when I WAS eligible). However, I really don't reccommend buying this game because as I've said, there's just such little content, and the game has such little replay value, if any play value in the first place. There's just no way to guarantee you'll get your money's worth, and considering how painfully slow the development process for this game has been (if at all existent), there's little to no guarantee the game will ever even be 'completed', whatever that means in this case. Now, is that to say it's outright the worst garbage to ever disgrace steam with its presence? Oh hell no. On it's own, it honestly not so bad. However looking at it objectively and considering the sort of gameplay experience versus money spent ratio, and considering how long it took the game to even get to 'this' point, it's just such an awful deal, and really doesn't seem like the best investment one could make for a game. To put it into perspective, I currently have approximately 2.3 hours of gameplay on my account as of writing this review. I've literally experienced everything that this game has to offer in that time span, and admittedly I could have done it all in less time had I a better understanding of the full extent of the combat mechanics (My fault for not doing the tutorial which explains it all, not the games fault). That and I spent a considerable amount of time playing the Arena mode. Granted one might argue the 'endless' arena mode offers 'infinite' replayability, but that's just a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. I give a solid 6-7 rounds (Maybe 5 minutes max, for all 6-7 rounds, if you really draw out each fight) in arena and you'll see everything there is to see. The 'campaign' itself I would estimate would take maybe an hour, give or take, maybe even less if you actually do the tutorial and screw up a minimal number of times.
So, if all this rambling is to say anything, it's simply that I can't reccommend this game, but I can't condemn it either. It is what it is.
TL;DR - Little to no content, little to no gameplay value, little to no reason to buy the game. Don't buy it, but don't hate it.

Here is my 30Second Game review:
Mirror’s Edge mixed with a dash of Portal. You’re a scientist stuck in an unknow world and all you have is your parkour skills and some strange abilities. The flow is so immersive, you’ll find yourself getting up from the chair on difficult jumps.
The world evolves so adapt or die. You solve puzzles and talk to a friend who’s also in this universe. You choose what to answer, giving the plot different layers of revelation.
The choice of graphics isn’t new, but it is surpisingly well done, specially when the scenery grows in front of you. You can also create or play in levels made by other players.
7 jumps out of 10.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Call of Pripyat takes a different approach to the series. Where SoC and CS were made up out of different areas, or 'levels' that were attatched to another with individual missions and story development per area, CoP takes a different aproach: open field. This open field is divided in 3 parts: Zaton, Yanov and Pripyat.
This is also where the first problem starts: you are forced to pay a sum of money while travelling from major area to area. While this might seem not too big of a deal, it in fact is. To travel from one place to another, the player is forced to pay a guide that will lead them there. It's impossible for players to move themselves. The fee for this is often a hefty one. What this means, is that the player will need money. Loads of it. And to get this, he/she would have to go about side missions. Now, again this wouldn't be too big of a deal weren't it for the fact that the main storyline FORCES you to travel from one place to another quite often, basically forcing the player to play side missions, which should, IMO, always be optional.
Next up: enemies. This game has the most annoying enemies and scripting for the AI in any stalker game. The fact that 80% of them is made out of 'wildlife' makes this even worse. Inmagine a dog. Now, inmagine that same dog, but 12 of them. Inmagine a dog being capable of taking you out in 3 hits, and it has this scripting where it sprints around (half teleporting due to bad scripting), being effectively unhittable, and attacking in packs. That's right, woof woof ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Oh, there's bloodsuckers and snorks with the same problems.
So, whatever happened to the humans of all factions that made SoC so fun? Taking them out with sniper rifles from afar? Oh, those are all peaceful. Bandits? Hey bro :D. Freedom and duty? At peace. This leaves you with only one group to fight: monolith. And needless to say, you don't encounter those untill far into the game, meaning you'll spend the biggest part shooting dogs.
Since I've spewed out all this negativity I'm throwing in a good thing. Night time. This game's atmosphere is AMAZING at night. The entire open world turns into a dangerous, dark place. The music changes, the wildlife sounds change and the flashlight goes on. Around every corner potential death. The amount of mutant activity also increases greatly, resulting in epic fights with bloodsuckers emerging from the fog in a pitch black night. Really cool.
Now, back to bashing: the storyline. It basically comes down to this: something happened. You're supposed to find out why and when you nearly have it figured, the game is like: LOL PLOTHOLES! HERE'S A RE-OCCURING NPC TO TELL EVERYTHING SO YOUR QUEST WAS BASICALLY POINTLESS. Add a bunch of weird characters to that that make absolutely no sense, and cutscenes that take 20 seconds to load (no joke, it takes THAT long) and you're complete.
Alright, fun time, let's get to exploring! Most points of interest within a major area are empty or boring, and if you did a specific mission (yes, you require an active mission to explore most, there's no such thing as setting out on yourself) they will be cleared for the rest of the time. No random scattering of stashes either, everything has a set location. Laaaaame.
The one thing that *is* fun while 'exploring' (or what's left of that) is the emissions/psy storms. I had one great point in the game where I was in the middle of nowhere and an emission was about to start. I rushed over to a warehouse only to find out it was being held by bandits. As I didn't have a really good relation with bandits, they turned hostile on sight, forcing me a race against the clock to take them all out before the emission would hit. A truly awesome moment, one of few that were memorable.
Obligatory quests, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story mechanics, boring/annoying enemies and an insanely thin story. If it weren't for the fact that the atmosphere is so great, and how the audio transition works in the Yanov Power Plant (really, this is *awesome*) then I would've put this game down after 20 seconds.

At the beginning of the game, you have a "special trait" that you can choose,  which ranges from being able to recover some health x second to have some extra perception (for being able to find secrets), among others. Although you can clear the game with any, changing from one to another may affect how you progress in the game drastically according to your style of gameplay. Choose wisely.
You can use some vehicles. Not many, but its fun to squash aliens with a tank, not to mention that they would kill you in matter of secons if you are not inside.
Secret areas. To aditionally keep you busy, the game has many secret areas, most are just an extra room with some money/weapons, but you do feel rewarded, since its a decent extra loot for finding it. i found a lot, but way too far from finding every single one for every single level.
Playing time:
I finished this game a long time ago, i dont remember how many missions does it has (around 30), but the time to complete the game is around 7-8 hours since most missions are short, however, if you are looking every secret, killing most monsters, etc, ill be a lil bit longer. Also, the end missions are harder, and i mean it, sometimes takes longer to complete those ones (since you have only 3 lives) if going carefully.
Replay value: This game is very fun, but the amount of enemies is overwhelming, that i can become tedious at times (so basically, at the end of the game you should have slayed a couple of MILLIONS of enemies) so yeah, virtually the grey floor is red at the end of the mission. Each time you play it, you can go for different characters/stats/passive trait, but at the end, you will do about the same build, the replay value relays on killing the alien horde over and over and over again. (This is my first run with this game @Steam, but i have finished it lile 10 times or so)
Graphics. The game is not new, it has some 5~7 years under the belt, and still look nice. but seriously graphics is not really an issue,  my graphics card (ati radeon 3870 at the time.) was having some trouble at the final stage due to the amount of enemies at the same time. medium graphics are OK for this game.
Sound. Not a masterpiece for sure, but it does the job, sets the mood in the game, you forget about it.
Bad things
It has a co-op survival and probably a versus mode i think, Shame that no one is online ever, it might be fun to have a partner.
Survival is fun but alone feels like meh. Its quite challenging though.
Dumb AI. Although they will always try to get you, some will stuck in corners or any object that is in  between, some will stuck with other aliens. However, not a great deal, since there are many enemies, being stuck they will not overwhelm you from all sides every single time, you can create some bottlenecks.
Not my intention to write a wall of text, but just to give you a general idea for your money. (probably worth 15~ bucks )

So here I am recommending Stalker Call of Pripyat, probably the last Stalker game that will have been produced. Stalker Call of Pripyat is the third stalker game and features items and weapons not featured in the other Stalker games. Stalker Call of Pripyat is about a Ex-Stalker and now Military "Major Alexander Degtyarev". The major's mission is to follow the investigation of "Operation Fairway" and why it failed. The game does not feature many bugs as for maybe some crashes due to loading issues and graphical issue with mods. Mods! Oh yes, oh yes. In conclusion: Stalker Call of Pripyat is one of the best games I've personally played, it never ceases to amaze and keep me from being bored. It has an amazing modding community! The third and final game in the series of STALKER, which takes place in an entirely new area of the Zone.  The new areas are Zaton, Jupiter, and Eastern Pripyat, which are a swamp, general STALKER area, and a city, respecitvely.  The "story" follows and undercover USS operative that is tasked with finding 5 downed helicopters and the reasons why they crashed. The reason I say "story" is because there's no linearity to it. The game basically starts you out with freeplay, with the first "mission" being to find a useless artifact. In the other games, this would be a blessing, as there are potentially an unlimited number of quests. Here though, that's changed, and many of the quests you recieve are one-of-a-kind, creating a total count of somewhere around 20. I don't find much replay value in this game, and to me, it is my least favorite of the series. Now on to the mods:
The most popular mod for CoP is MISERY, which adds a ton of items, weapons, and other stuff. It also makes the game harder than Hugh Hefner's♥♥♥♥♥♥ which goes to say that a merc with a gasmask will shrug off a 7.62x54 round like a fly. This can all be fixed of course, with a simple edit of the actor immunties in the config files. Edit the enemies values by a factor of..oh...10 or so.
There are other mods that are available, such as MSO, SMRTER, SWARTZ and Redux that are worth checking out. Many of these make the game harder, but not to the extent of MISERY.  What you can find is usually the addition of weapons, items, and other stuff, but again, not to the same extent as MISERY.
And as always, play the game Vanilla or with Complete first, to fully appreciate the game.

Controls and level design are PUTRID.  This game is a platformer, so that's basically a kiss of death.
Some examples:
Many of the games jump sequences, which can be over 25 inputs long, are set up so that if you miss any one of them, you have to restart the level.
Fallaway platforms never reset, so if you spend 4 minutes on a level trying to get all the collectibles, then miss a jump / get touched, you have to restart.
Wall jumping requires that you WAIT for the character to grab the ledge which she ONLY will do on her descent from her jump.  So even in a thin tunnel, "chimney climb" situation, you have awkward delays.
Many floating platforms are solid when you stand on them, but you can jump up through them.  Then later the same sort of platofrm will be a fall away, or it won't allow you to jump up through it.  There's no rhyme or reason.
There's like 4 enemies in the entire game, minus the bosses.
The games timer doesn't stop during cutscenes, so if you kill a boss while time is running out, instead of winning, you lose.  It shows the victory animation... and then game over.
