I purchased this game due to the premise - an anime style ninja platformer (if that makes sense). However, it was a little bit underwhelming and disappointing.
Gameplay is pretty much how you would expect your normal platformer - it is nothing special. There are 3 levels in each stage, with the last being a boss battle. Each level gets more difficult as it goes along (as you'd expect). Whilst what you get here is nothing too bad, very few new gimmicks are introduced as you go along (certainly no new enemies (excluding bosses) in the second and third stages), making gameplay seem a little monotonous at times. The secret ninja technique mechanic is ok, but it is a shame that these cannot be used in the boss fights and that there aren't more to unlock or use (I seem to only ever use one).
Controls are unfortunetly clunky and still feel a little slow despite the update. There is no tutorial - and as far as I am aware the keyboard controls are a little odd. Despite using an xbox controller, controls in some areas are a bit tempermental; this is especially the case with the wallhang aspect, whereby getting a bit close to a wall sticks you to it, leaving you to either slide or jump umpteen steps in the opposite direction. These controls ultimately (and unfortunetly) affect gameplay, making it difficult to dodge in some situations and leaving some areas a little bit tedious to navigate.
In other areas, the game is adequate but not excellent. Graphics are standard, with some areas featuring tiling that is a touch too obvious. Sound works but is nothing special. Cutscenes are relatively uneventful and slow, and can be a little slow to skip.
All in all, it is and little things that let this game down - it just needs a bit more usability and polish. Every time you die or which to retry, you have to do so from the level menu; I'd be more inclined to continue playing if there was a restart button on the menu or game over screen. Likewise, there could be more options changing sound volumes in game. Again, bosses could be better - the first two bosses were both disappointingly repetitive affairs, especially as one critic outlined them as "impressive and fun".
Whilst nothing special was necessarily expected from this game, the controls and little usability things prevent it from being a decent game. That is not to say it is a bad game - some people will definitely find some charm within and with the game as cheap as chips it might be worth a look. However, I can't say I got a great deal of enjoyment from it - whilst the premise has potential, the overall controls and execution of the game could be a lot smoother.

Consider this a recommendation for the entire STALKER series so far (latest as of this being Call of Pripyat). The STALKER games are FPS/Survival Horror/RPG hybrids where the emphasis is on the FPS gunplay and the survival elements.
You can get thirsty or hungry or need sleep and have to manage those needs alongside that of the deteriorating conditions of your weapons and armors. Ammunition, food, and drink needed to survive are scarce, but can be traded for with almost anyone if you have the right amount of goods or money to sacrifice for it. The game has large maps you can travel between like a sandbox game, and the gunplay is some of the tightest I've seen with really good gun physics. The games also have a wildlife simulation system similar to the one in place in FarCry 3 in a way; animals and mutants will run around and do their own thing after they spawn and kill each other (and maybe you) for survival or food.
Despite the large amount of freedom these games afford you to carve your own path, they feel very focused and are best approached with a strategic mindset.

Growing up on JSRF brought my attention to this when the SEGA pack was released for free, I've played a few hours, enough to give a solid review of this anyway.
TL;DR I recommend it with a controller, basically impossible otherwise. OST is always killer, and I'm glad I could play the previous game in the Jet Set Series.
Pros:
+ OST: First and foremost probably the biggest mention and the top thing about this game, if you don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the game go and listen to this on Spotify anyway.
+ Artstyle: It looks dated, but this is a port from the SEGA Dreamcast. Setting is a cyberpunk Tokyo-esque vibe, graffiti, young punks on roller blades.
+ Story: Unique experience with a colorful cast, each character has their differences but they're not terribly noticable,
Cons:
- Controller basically a requirement, they're not terribly expensive but still an inconvenience.
- 30 FPS, I personally am not a stickler for these sorts of things but for those that are
- Dated, this game looks incredibly dated, boxy characters, clunky animations.
- Controls, even on a controller the controls feel funny, I often do things I don't intend to do, grinding is weird, sometimes you just grind the ground if theirs a rail on it, sometimes you don't.
- Difficulty, now I can't believe I ACTUALLY put this in but in addition to the controls some things have a ridiculous skillcap to them. To unlock some of the skaters you have follow their trick pattern, or beat them in a race. It can be extremely frustrating, especially since the races don't exactly give you the best idea of where to go, so you generally do it once, get so far behind the bot waits for you, catch up, try to follow their path, lose. Try again and find a shortcut (I believe every race has several shortcuts if you can find them) and then beat them to the objective.
Summary: All in all, you definitely feel the games date. It's controls are funny, it looks a little old, it definitely feels a little old. However if you are a fan of Jet Set Radio Future, like quirky, and almost silly looking characters, appreciate Electronic Dance OST's, or appreciate Future Tokyo Dystopian settings I feel like this is the game for you.

Combat feels like a mechanic of the game to simply reduce your health to a certain point before you move to the next passage, thereby managing the difficulty. The whole game is just a laggy, linear Assassin's Creed challenge area with a forgettable story. I know I don't have many hours on the game, to be honest it's not something you can play for hours. At least in my opinion, the game does get a bit frustrating at times and I'll explain why.
So essentially you own one airport. You buy the aircraft using money and XP (virtual, of course). You go through a process of clicking, allowing it to forward between taxiways to the gate. You have to do a sequence of unloading, choosing new destination, refueling, boarding and then more clicks to get it to the runway, it takes off and you don't see it until it returns to land in which you need to clear it and again start the process of guiding it to the gate.
Now, it's not too bad. Although the clicking process becomes tedious; when you have 3 aircraft on the ground you'll appreciate it better (you don't want aircraft crossing paths and crashing on the ground).
You build upon your airport by buying additional features, ie an extra gate, ways of increasing passenger numbers (you'll need to do this as I found out when you have a lot of aircraft frequently attending; you can't make an aircraft leave until it's full it seems).
It's an okay game for what it is and at £2.51 you can hardly grumble. Essentially this is a game you'll expect to play on an iPad (or of course, other tablet system on the market). The large buttons and clicking really gives it that impression it's ported from a tablet.
Pros
- Cheap, good for a bit of time wasting
- Easy to play once you get the general idea of it
- It is interestingly challenging when you have many aircraft to juggle all trying to land, take off at once
Cons
- Aircraft crash too much (i'll explain below)
- Not enough money made to make reasonable progression.
- Low resolution (yep, it's a tablet game for sure)
So to explain the cons..
Aircraft will crash. Some can be avoided, some can't. The obvious is making sure they're fueled up before they leave. Don't send the smaller aircraft on too much of a long haul as I found out. However, the frustrating part, essentially what has made me stop playing it, is the fact that your aircraft crashes and it's lost. All but one of my aircraft crashed within 5 flights and I went through about 8 or 9. This means they never make their money back and eventually you run out of money and have no planes to fly; game over. Likewise with lack of XP. There are events that can crash your aircraft. For example, an icey runway you have to deice before a plane lands on it. Also windy conditions will crash a plane everytime. The ice is easily avoidable hower the wind appears random to me and on the occasion the wind randomly kicks in as I've authroised a plane to land.. causing it to crash. Overall I think it's a massive overkill for the amount of times aircraft crash, you just cannot progress as this happens. As your plane is flying over the Alantic, you hear a crash terrain alarm and that's it; you're powerless to do anything and it's gone.
I was expecting a bit more control over what happens, everything is very linear. For example plane servicing. I thought maybe more plane servicing would prevent crashes, however you cannot service a plane until it's 'due' a service when the light flashes.
Bugs? Yeah there's a few. Only one I can really highlight as an issue however.. To progress an aircraft you have to click on it, which will pop up yellow buttons to guide the plane to taxiways, hangar etc. I noticed a few times you need to click the plane a few times before they appear. No biggie, however still contributes to the frustration.
If you have a few £ spare and want to waste a few hours, have a bit of patience and you might enjoy this.. until your last plane crashes then you can only really start again.

I really want to like this game.  Literally everything I want in a transport management game, but it really suffers from the technical aspect.  First off the game feels like it was designed to be played on a tablet, only offering windowed and full screen options, and that's it.  You're also constantly dealing with multiple currencies (Fuel, XP and Money), but seeing as how the game is only $4 I can forgive those minor issues.  Other issues however include that the game looks really rough, everything just feels unfinished, and lacks polish.  The UI also looks quite rough and in need of a coat of paint, and some tweeks in funcionality.  Navigating a plane from the gate to the runway takes a few too many clicks in different locations for my taste.  Same goes for navigating a plane from the runway to the gate.  Why do I have to load the plane with passengers prior to sending it to the hanger for repairs?  I doubt the passengers want to sit on the plane while it's being repaired.
The tutorials suck as explaining the game to you, you're better off just going with Trial and Error.  Danger symbols aren't explained until you figure out what they are, which probably means your plane will explode before you figure out why it exploded.  There is also very little incentive to fly anywhere other than Miami, as it gives you a bunch of XP and Money.
I really want to like this game since I have always wanted to have a good airport management sim, this game lays the foundation, but needs work technically and design wise.  If the developer is able to clean up the graphical issues, and smooth over the learning curve there might actually be an excellent game here.  However for now, it still needs a lot of work.

Forgotten Sands feels like the dying breath of a once-great series. Previously, the overall gameplay had the player explore their newfound time-changing abilities by not only solving pathway puzzles but also using them in combat to gain an advantage on a certain enemy type or boss. It was up to the player to find the solution to each little challenge. It was a, forgive the pun, sandbox to discover new uses for each ability. Forgotten Sands instead holds the player's hand throughout each room and hallway: as the camera pans away (in almost every room) to show the next path to take or where a button is located, it never allows the player a feeling of full control. The only time manipulation tricks here are the ability to rewind in case of a missed jump or death by sand zombies and pausing time to use water as a traversal tool. Its never as cohesive as the previous games. Combat is done through repetitive sword swinging or sometimes kicking away an enemy shield. Upgrades to create whirlwinds that knock enemies down or one that creates a trail of fire are attempts to add some variety but these don't replace the excitement of slowing time to take out three enemies in five seconds. Its a bare-minimum Prince of Persia experience and while it isn't cluttered with a lot of button memorization or a deeper story it wouldn't have hurt to inject a few things into the overall package. Is it worth playing? ONLY if you want to experience a PoP game without all the distractions. But for most: those distractions are what made the previous games good in the first place.
Without any real depth to the story, it means the ludonarrative dissonance is at an all-time high, never giving the player a connection between the gameplay and the story. What you're doing is never fully connected to why you're doing it. Who thought it was a good idea to line a hallway with a dozen spinning spike traps? Who was originally in control of the sand zombie soldiers? How did the Prince becomes so adept at wall-running and traversal? What's at stake if things get too far out of hand? It skips parts of what could be a juicy story and leaves a lean minimum of connectivity. Figure out a way around a room, fight some enemies, see a short bit of story. Repeat ad nauseam. The Sands of Time trilogy and even the 2008 relaunch offer more overall enjoyment than this, which should have been a budget release.
(I can't believe I'm saying this but if you ever get the chance, play the Wii version instead. The combat feels better, the exploration feels rewarding, the story isn't half-hearted, and the Prince doesn't feel like a cheap imitation. It really is a better game overall.)

This is my first outing into an RPG that isn't Final Fantasy, and... After going back after playing Skyrim... Meh. It's got it's merits, no doubt. Easiest way to review, would be a point system.
Pros:
1: Soooo much♥♥♥♥♥♥to do! I feel it's more than Skyrim, or maybe they're just more densely packed.
2: Hard to reach areas. Wanna reach that corner of the map? OK, here's... no path at all! You'll just have to go off road and find your way there, which is actually pretty cool, it gives a much more RPG-ish feel (I made a word!) to travelling. Altmer ruins are a MAZE to get to the bottom of, and you better stock up on supplies, because they are very long in time, and very big, and lots of enemies.
3: Travelling feels like an adventure. Unlike Skyrim, which is still good, I feel compelled to actually walk around and explore, despite the boring environment at times, because there is always some cave with your name on it, where as Skyrim just is a slog if you don't fast travel to the nearest location. Without mods in that, you'll get attacked by Dragons every 5 seconds. Where as here, you can stop to just chill for a bit, no enemies for miles.
4: Guilds. Aside from the Thieve's Guild, which is really the Robin Hood Fan Club, you actually feel you belong. Dark Brotherhood feels evil, Mage's Guild feels intelligent, Fighter's Guild is Pretty much Knight's Club, Arena feels like Gladiator Fighting, so something for everyone.
5: Add-ons. Shivering Isles, Knight's of the Nine, Mehrunes Razor, they're all good Add-ons. And when you've dried the game up, off to Nexusmods you go!
Cons:
1: Combat is a drag. Later on in the game, you'll be hacking away at an enemy for 10 minutes, and they still won't die, which is really, REALLY, annoying.
2: Can't play mage. Wanna be a mage? Wanna go burn everyone with Fire? WELL TOUGH♥♥♥♥♥♥ By the time you have the skills for those powerful spells, they won't be so powerful anymore, making sword and shield the only way to play, really.
3: Ridiculous Main Quest. Don't even bother with the Main Quest, go do everything else though. So I gotta go find an old guy who knows where this son is, and doesn't bother saving him? WHAT THE HELL!? Then you go back. So you didn't put the amulet somewhere safe, you dingus?
4: Limited NPC personality. "I saw a mudcrab the other day. Annoying creatures." Expect to hear that A LOT. From every NPC ever.
5: Lots of awesome but useless items. So you spent ages gathering money for that awesome sword? Too bad it doesn't actually serve much purpose after 5 uses. You're better off enchanting your own stuff.
So overall, if you're looking for a fun romp doing exploring, attacking, looting, or just being silly, I recommend this. If you're looking for an incredibly deep, interactive, and moving game, look elsewhere.

This one was so disappointing. I'd been keeping my eye on this game for years after falling in love with the art style and the concept of a 2.5D side-scroller set among the pages of an origami pop-up book. But now that I've finally gotten around to playing it, sadly I've found there's little here to really love beyond the shallow surface.
Inspired by Japanese culture, Tengami sees you control a little paper cut-out man as you flip and fold the paper scenery to move forward. It's a really great idea, and you could almost even call it "cute" with how aesthetically endearing it is to grab on a point at the side of a river then pull it open to reveal a bridge for you to cross, or pry apart some paper rocks to open up a cave entrance. But when it comes to the actual moment to moment gameplay, that's where it sorely falls flat.
The problem is, it feels like there's very little to really do. You'll spend most of your time walking slowly across the pages, only occasionally coming upon points of interest that you can actually interact with in any significant way. This will typically involve moving some paper around into the right place to either unlock the path ahead or gain a new item used to unlock the path ahead, and I hate to say it, but I just didn't find many of the puzzles to be all that interesting. Some are clever, some are tedious, all are incredibly pretty, but almost none of them were particularly satisfying. I didn't feel any great sense of joy or accomplishment upon completing them, but rather relief at getting them out of the way so I could finally move on - which is frequently hindered by the amount of backtracking you sometimes have to do as you slowly point and click your way over old scenery.
I've no problem with slow-paced games, and backtracking doesn't have to be a burden provided it's in small doses and with something interesting to pass the time on the way there, but when those two things are combined, it doesn't make for a fun time.
The aural side of things was a little disappointing, too. Maybe it's just my horribly uncultured Western knowledge rearing its ugly head; only being familiar with the hard clichés and stereotypes of other cultures rather than their subtlety and nuances, but I just wasn't getting a very strong Japanese tone to either the music or audio in general. I simply wasn't feeling as steeped and immersed in the sound anywhere near as much as I was the visuals.
I don't want to be down on the game too much; it was made by a very small team, and if I recall correctly, had a pretty drawn out development, but the love for the product does come through, even if it doesn't entirely pay off.
As loathe as I am so say this, I think this is a game that's far better enjoyed when viewed rather than played, as its beauty lies almost solely in its visuals and little else. I'd kill for a Neutral recommendation button right now, but I'm going to rate it positively, partially as it's a valiant and sincere effort far more worthy of praise for its attempted creativity rather than its failed ambitions, but also as a gesture of good faith of sorts, as I really hope the studio will carry on and produce even greater works in the future.

This is one of my favorite strategy games of all time--as my almost 450 hours at the time of writing show--because of its focus on human interactions rather than (necessarily) warfare, which is pretty unusual for a grand strategy game. I get attached to my characters in ways that I really don't with generals in the Total War games or nameless units in Civilization. This is all about building your dynasty and ensuring your legacy, which leads to a lot of different playstyles. You can try to be an independent count resisting assimilation. You can form a super empire that encompasses the entire world. You can be the dutiful vassal, etc., etc.
It's incredibly complicated (less so in a lot of ways from Europa Universalis) but it begins to feel intuitive after a while. Being able to play as small as one county at first helps with the learning curve quite a bit.
If you like historical strategy games, this is definitely for you.

First off I am very happy with the controller support in the game. I would not have expected it, but it is here and as good as it should be.
It is very easy to draw parallels between Mirror's Edge and Lemma, but they are very different games. Lemma is a giant maze with parkour and puzzles. There is no combat, the physics are less realistic but more fun. The game is extremely impressive for having been made by a single person. While I never got stuck too badly I would come in expecting to get lost a bit.
The world is built out of large connecting open areas. You have to figure out where to go and how to get there and that can be quite a challenge in the later areas. I sometimes felt a little directionless, but I followed my gut and felt out where the level was trying to lead me and that has carried me through so far. The game is very hands off on teaching concepts. It expects that you are smart enough to figure things out. This can be seen in both the lack of a map, and very little hand holding in puzzles. This is both bad and good. On one hand it is refreshing to have a game that challenges me to figure things out. On the other hand there are some things I am not sure if I am understand correctly.
For example : there are red blocks that chase you by changing block colors to red. I am not sure if there is any way to change the tiles back once they have turned red. If there is a way I have missed it and will continue to play the rest of the game this way. Not a bad thing, just a consequence of not holding my hand.
With so many games overcharging for what they are, it is nice to see that the game is priced correctly for what it is. It is fully functioning and polished, but it is not a triple A title. You will get hours of enjoyment out of it, and there seems to be a story to find if your willing to dig deep enough. Much like the rest of the game, the story does not hold your hand.
My take? If you liked Fez you may like this. It is more about digging for secrets and finding your way than playing with the core mechanic of the game.
Full disclosure I know the maker of this game. I am glad to see the first of hopefully many games coming out of Columbus Ohio.
I am glad it turned out well. It took 5 years to make and it would really suck if I had to say it was no good after all that effort.

Spawning into a strange world and being introduced to grad student Joan Emerson. You discover a colleague named Mark via breakthroughs in the field of physics has disappeared into this same world known as
. Now more curious then ever, Joan is ready to continue onward and unlock the secrets inside. Rest of the story slowly unfolding through text messages on your phone, occasional popups on-screen or mysterious notes left in levels.
Lemma is very impressive for a solo project. Does have similar art-style and gameplay to Mirrors Edge but a little rougher around the edges and far more focused on puzzles. With that said I really enjoyed the atmospheric soundtrack, intelligent level designs and fluid control system. The addition of being able to 'build your own path' using special moves like wall-slides and army-rolls was  wonderful but also added to the challenge of the previously mentioned puzzle design.
Minimalistic by nature and with plenty of video settings, it should scale and perform well on a range of systems. As someone who suffers from motion sickness was a little concerned initially. Thankfully options like field of view sliders were included and I have no problems playing longer sessions whatsoever. Worth mentioning Oculus Rift is also supported but unfortunately I don't have the hardware required to test.
If you enjoy puzzle platformers, jump-maps, parkour driven gameplay and surreal worlds, it's well worth taking a look at Lemma. With leaderboards and level editor included it should keep the community alive for some time.  Not sure why this game isn't being talked about more as it deserves to be and I'm still looking for the downsides. Cheers folks. :)

Let me start by saying that I LOVE the remake of this, Jet Set Radio Future. I grew up playing the copy of it that came with the original xbox, and I can honestly say that it's in my top 3 games ever. That being said, I had hoped that the original version was just as good, already figuring that it would probably have some problems due to its age.
Now, I won't say the game is awful, but it's definitely not the best. The controls are EXTREMELY clunky, without a controller it is very hard to spray paint, and you almost always feel like you are going slow. The missions are all timed, which would be managable if the AI's attacks weren't near impossible to escape from. Constantly getting shot and knocked over on a timed mission is a drag.
In general, its really not a game most people could really pick up and get into, most will just rage quit after the first few missions. The people I can see enjoying this would be the old SEGA veterans that are used to the clunky gameplay this presents, and maybe some JSRF fans, although I was quite disappointed.
Pros
- Good soundtrack
- Unique artstyle
- Memorable characters
Cons
- Clunky, slow controls
- Enemies are nearly impossible to deal with
- Need controller to play properly
- Frustrating gameplay

Well despite what other people write in their review we can build a few buildings, but the possitions of them are pre set, but you can expand as you go along with xp and money.

Once you get a fleet of aircrafts then the game start to become fun...  First of all you have to tell your planes where to go, and if they should land or do a go around. Also taxi on the ground are simulated and such things as refueling.

All in all for 3,59euro I think this game is great and for that kind of money you get what you pay for, and EVEN MORE than you pay for.. It is a nice little game.

People tend to like this entry in the series much less than the original Sands of Time trilogy, but having replayed it seven years after release (and with no new PoP titles available since) - I found it quite entertaining.
It has aged much better than the SoT trilogy and still looks good. Well, in fact it looks pretty amazing - it utilizes a similar material and texture approach as my favorite entry in the series - Prince of Persia "2008". The textures are crisp, extremely rich and detailed, but all fit together rather well. The art style is consistent, palettes - solid (if a bit too brown at times) and characters - well designed and recognizable.
The Forgotten Sands utilizes a strange combat system, similar to that of the Batman Arkham series (Freeflow Combat), though not qute as polished or refined.
The parkour / puzzles have a decent difficulty curve to them, with the final climb being quite a challenge - at least to my, not-so-nimble fingers.
Definitely worth a buy if on sale, should run on pretty much anything these days. Recommended with a game pad. Took me around 8 hours to complete, ignoring the challenges and focussing on the main story.

I'm in two minds about this game... Ok, I've not played it very long, but I thought I'd write this review to tell others before they buy it.  It needs A LOT more work.
Firstly, the blurb is quite misleading - It's not a tycoon/sim style game.
It feels like a port from a tablet game.  There is an element of planning when it comes to controlling where and when your aircrafts go, but a major downside is when you want to build a new building, the game has already told you where it's going to be built.
The tutorial is poorly done.  It gives no indication of how to play the game, no tutorial text, it just runs like the regular game with a hand now and then that pops up on screen.
Pros:
- The price is right (£2.50 in UK)
- The Jetway is a nice touch (also would have been nice if you'd mentioned it was manual)
- The maps and how you can see your plane's position over the US/EU
- Has potential
Cons:
- No real freedom, everything is pre-built
- Very bad tutorial
- Very repetative
- No real indication of how to play the game
- Passengers don't scream when a plane crashes
- The sound effects are horrible, and some are REALLY LOUD like the plane taking off and the emergency services
I would recommend this game IF - and ONLY IF - you are a fan of what I've written above, or you just need a new game to pass a couple of hours.

The Prince Of Persia The Forgotten Sands in my opinion is an enjoyable ride. With all games, good, bad, or just plain ok, I found things I enjoyed and things I did not. Overall, I enjoyed it. The story itself is simple, you are the Prince visiting his brother Malik in the middle of a battle. Trying to save his kingdom Malik accidentaly opens up a ancient sand army run by an evil Djinn. The prince meets a Djinn named Razia who helps the Prince in defeating the army and putting a end to the sand army. Simply story, it does offer inside into the Prince Of Persia verison of Djinns but overall it is a simply story to follow. Even for the time it came out, it looks great, a few hiccups of texture and sometimes the models look a little weird, but it looks great. Gameplay ways is where the game shines, the Prince's usually parkor is still present from the wall jump wall run swinging on polls etc. I found the Parkor system easy to follow. Puzzle solving was ok, some simply and some SO simple that I over thinking it. One of the Sands Of Time powers return to really help with the parkor when ever you make a little mistake or start to get a little impatient which I have done manytimes. Combat is simple with just one button for basic attacks, the same attack button for heavy attacks just by holding it, a kick button, and a dodge button plus an upgrade system to upgrade your health, and powers again simple. Again I found enjoyment out of it even with the simplistic story and combat system. I do recommend it if you are willing to give it a try.

Sigh. Where to start with this.
So, I got the game, downloaded it, Uplay got installed. Couldn't create an account. Downloaded the latest version and launched the game. Right here, all of this is an insult to the players. Pirates will still pirate, all of this is useless.
After that, I found out that there are "awards" for the game which unlocks additional content for you. Pretty sweet, eh? No. I made progress in game, earned Uplay points, went on the website and unlocked every single award, then I just needed to open Uplay from the game's main menu. But boom, the Uplay browser crashes. Every single time, and I haven't found a proper fix for it.
The game sucks in many ways. "But it's freaking Prince of Persia dude! It's a must-have for me, right?!" that's what I thought before buying this game as well. Trust me, you will be disappointed.
Ubisoft forgot how their game actually was. In the trilogy, the Prince was the serious type and in the 2008 reboot, he was humorous. This game was meant to be more like the trilogy, yet he's far away from the Prince we know.
The plot is pretty light and boring. Some dialogues make you cringe. The music is pretty forgettable, just like the game itself. Nothing like the mysterious OST of Sands of Time and the reboot or the epic Warrior Within. Gameplay is really, really repetitive. You mostly do the same thing you do in every other level. The combat is extremely easy compared to the trilogy, you can almost blow the sand creatures up. All of the boss fights require the same, simple technique except for the last one.  But graphics. Who cares about that? Yeah, it's fairly improved, but it won't cover the actual content up.
Overall, I'd say forget about it. Thanks for taking time and reading this.

I got this game back in 2012 from someone buying it as a gift for me. It was a grand ol' time until they added in the StarStorm Kickstarter characters. The store set-up has improved to some degree, but you still have to unlock everything for each individual character and a characters store will have something that another won't which unfortunately is where the balancing issue comes into play because one might have a life-steal while another won't. Another minor problem is jungle placement, due to either being on JUST the bottom of the map or JUST the top of the map AND it only gives 3 solar plus some health. Jungles should give temporary buffs from things such as the solar boss, but that also only gives health and +30 solar which honestly won't go that far.
Besides these issues that most people have with this game I really recommend this game. It's fun and easy to get someone into, especially because people don't have to pay for anything (besides skins if you care about that).

I understand the idea that the dev(s) had going in, but they have ultimately failed.  To be honest, wouldn't recommend spending even the $3 purchase price on this, I got it completely free and was still disappointed by it. I could easily write pages upon pages extolling the virtues of this game, but this is 2015 and we should be realistic, so I will simply and concisely explain why this is the greatest game of all time....but not the most fun.
1.) The Writing - Quite simply, above and beyond anything you find in most modern games.  A compelling story (IF YOU LIKE HIGH FANTASY), memorable characters, beautiful set-pieces, and the best flavor text in any game...well, maybe ever.  If you love fantasy epics, this one is a classic!
2.) The D&D - Let's face it: this is a Dungeons and Dragons game.  For people playing it for that reason, it delivers!  A perfectly (well...mostly) executed take on 2nd/3rd editions, with the best parts of both (THAC0 forever!) mixed together in a way that translates well.  To get the true D&D experience, show the dice rolls in terminal and and pause after every round.
3.) The Graphic Design - Yes, by today's standards, this looks like an indy game.  But what a game!  Beautiful static backgrounds...I mean, hang them on your wall gorgeous.  Excellent effects that made the spells and effects really pop off the screen.  Detailed, well animated sprites that gave the characters a sense of life that other, similar games still struggle to achieve.  The monsters were so varied and detailed, it's a wonder the game didn't win more awards than it did.
There are some downsides.  It's a big game, takes hundreds of hours to do everything.  The gameplay can be frustratingly hard for the uninitiated (PROTIP: drink all the potions!!!!), and the lack of quest markers and waypoints and glowing exclamation points means the casual gamer will be lost without a walk-through guide.
But if you're like me - and if you are reading this, you probably are - and you want an old-school, authentic experience, BG2 is IT!  It's a masterpiece that I will continue to play into my waning years.  GOAT

So I feel I have enough information to give a well-informed review now that I'm 36.2 hours in. I've been reading, however, that
Immediate kudos for a content-packed game.
Having played the original Divinity tile from 2002, I've seen this game develop from a Diablo-esque point-and-click action RPG to the turn-based strategy game that is now Divine Divinity: Original Sin 2. Although I've missed a game or two since then, I wasn't quite sure what the storyline was, but the game clearly helps you understand what's been going on in the world of Rivellon right from the start. The immediate immersion into the game has the amazing quality to have me asking questions and wanting to seek out the answers to those questions. I was compelled to keep playing as I see the story unfold and each decision leads to more tangled pieces of the web of mystery that I need to solve.
The combat was easy to figure out immediately and I have to give Larian Studios another amazing pat on the back for integrating
for a turn-based isometric RPG. One of my big turn-offs is that, although I've played for keyboard and mouse combo for many years, I like my gamepad much better and will not buy any titles that don't support it.
There's some dispute about the Tactician mode and whether or not it's too hard. Having played 8 hours in Tactician mode, I finally discovered that if I wanted to enjoy the game and be able to progress in it, that I would have to play in Classic mode. Even in Classic Mode, the fights are still difficult and I've had to play a few of those, get killed multiple times, go level up my characters and improve my gear, and then finally win. Sometimes winning just barely with half my party killed.
The character creation was a little strange from most RPGs I've played, since you aren't really locked into a particular class and you can be whatever you want, based on the allocation of your Talents and Skills. I chose to play as origin character Ifan ben-Mezd, since I wanted to find out more about the storyline and how people fit into it. The build-selection during character creation made it easy to figure out what Skills and Talents were appropriate for the style of play you wanted for your main character. I always choose a good combination of melee and magic, so Battlemage was perfect for me.
Character dialogues have an added flair to them that give you extra choices based on certain tags you have or aquire or choices specific to certain origin characters.
The voiceovers are amazing and abundant, even down to having your own personal narrator. Many RPGs don't put that level of artisitic detail into their games when it comes to audio choices.
The environment is beautifully rendered and I enjoy it in full 4K resolution on my 65in. television. Full camera control with zoom in and out makes the environment easy to navigate.
Overall notes about Divinity: Original Sin 2:
* Content-packed (packed like it could rival the amount of content in Skyrim)
* Mysterious and interesting storyline that makes you want to keep playing
* Combat system is easy to figure out, but beware of Tactician Mode (was too hard for me)
* Full Gamepad Support in a turn-based RPG (a rare find...I would play Tyranny if it had
Gamepad support)
* Detailed voiceovers and soothing soundtrack
* Great-looking environment that scales well to 4K resolutions
I hope this review helps someone!

A very fun parkour/puzzle game with an intriguing story.
Lemma is your basic parkour game. It follows much of the same aspects as games such as mirrors edge. It carries out this parkour mechanic very well and fluidly. You can find yourself running across walls, jumping over ledges and walling jumping  to get to higher places in lemma. It does very little differently to other games in this respect.
Later in the game however you do get access to an interesting new mechanic that changes up the gameplay slightly. As you slide across ledges or run across walls you create a blue area. This area can be used to carry the games electricity system, The mechanic is used to create thought provoking puzzles. You have to figure out exactly how to get to an area through parkour so you can continue the track of electric power. This aspect of the game created a rather fun way of combining puzzles and parkour together.
One thing about this game really suprised me. I wasn't expecting it to have a very good story, if even a story at all. However the game has a really interesting story. To put it simply it involves you talking to another person who is trapped in this world with you. My description doesn't do it much justice but there is much more to it than that. It involves a heavy amount of physics so if your into that then this is a good game for you.
The story is told through use of notes and a mobile phone system in which you chat via text to your friend. Usually I would hate the fact that the story is told via notes cause this usually means the developer has run out of interesting ideas to tell the story with. Although Lemma seems to somehow wipe this notion from me and tell the story incredibly well through notes. The telephone system also means you feel like your interacting with the other person.
Lemma contains plenty of stuff for the collectors out there. Each level contains multiple orbs and notes to find. They are hidden in increasingly difficult places making them a challenge to get to.
Personally I found one thing that really let the game down. The graphics aren't particularly great. Texture quality is not up to a very high standard throughout the majority of the game. The game also repeatedly uses the same textures throughout a level making it seem extremely repetitive and can get boring after a while. However the amazing lighting effects do counteract this issue greatly and can redeem the game of this very minor flaw.
The majority of the time I found the animations to be very fluent and look great. The grabbing, running and jumping animation of the arms looked great, when they worked. Although sometimes I did find myself grabbing onto nothing and kind of jumping about glitching a bit. This did kill the experience a little for me. But luckily this wasn't too common of an occurance. I was also very disappointed with the rolling and sliding animation. When doing these you completely use track of your character and your screen just spins without you knowing what is going on. This completely disorientates you and can make you end up falling off the world accidently.
The games options menu is about as complete as I would want it to be. It contains pretty much the full range of resolutions. There are seperate volume sliders for SFX volume and Music. There are a wide variety of graphics options available with options such as Ambient occlusion, Volumetric lighting, V-sync and a lot more all being present. The only thing it may be missing that it should probably have is anti-aliasing. There is also a full control menu with entirely rebindable keys present. The interface also is very uninspired presented in a see through black box but this is another minor flaw.
Overall I felt this game to be a fantastic experience that should be played by anyone looking for a game with great parkour mechanics as well as a fantastic story.

Lemma is a parkour exploration game which makes gamers immediately think of Mirror's Edge.  But is it any different or even possibly better?  Let's find out in the Lemma First Impression Review.
Let's identify what Lemma is and what it sets out to do.  It is a first person parkour game with mystery and exploration in a surreal world.  You start off in this strange floating platform world in the sky not knowing who your character is, where you are, or why you are there.  It's a total mystery and that's the best part.
The game is developed entirely by one person, Evan Todd, and he was kind enough to provide a review code for this game.  I had a chance to play it for a few hours, and I can definitely tell you about the gameplay and whether it's worth your time.
As you begin traversing you'll pickup notes which seem very esoteric, but gives clues to the world you're in.  You'll also pickup a phone and begin communicating with a mystery man that you have some sort of vague relationship with.  You jump with the right trigger, grab with the left trigger, and roll or slide with the left thumbstick clicking in.  The world seems daunting at first as platformers are slim and far apart, but you will quickly realize just how intuitive the game is.
The game teaches you without putting you through a tutorial specific mission.  Controls are actually very easy to pickup and have varying degrees within their techniques.  You quickly find yourself utilizing the moves you learn to reach new areas.  And you begin to make your own conclusions on how to solve puzzles.  It does a good job of introducing you to a new concept and then challenging you with a much harder to solve situation.  That's video game basics, and surprisingly this game excels  where a lot of games fail.
The game also has some innovation as you can spawn platforms and challenge elements exclusively with your steps.  You can wall run and extend a wall.  Slide and extend a floor.  Or solve puzzles by stepping on an illuminated surface.
The world design and art style of Lemma is also surprisingly good.  A lot of the world is built with Voxel graphics, those chunky 3D pixels and it adds to the game's mystique.  The world is truly huge as you can look out at platforms far away and even look into the vanishing point.  Everything from the ambient music to the large spaces conveys how the game is really an isolated and unknown world.
Everything about the game is very subtle.  The way you learn the moves, the puzzles presented to you, and the revelation of the story.  Even the graphic effects look nice, but there's no crazy eye candy.  The game has slow but very balanced pacing in every way possible.
Lemma is very polished for an indie game.  As I've stated many times, everything is intuitive and unfolds naturally.  The game looks very attractive and it feels very natural to move through this artificial world.  It even has oculus rift support which could be very immersive for those oculus early adopters.
My only complaint is that I wish there were voice acting for the sections where you read notes or text message on your phone.  Arguably this could be a game design choice to make the character feel even more isolated.  The game can also be a little slow, it's definitely not an action combat game.  It's exploration, mystery, and parkour movement.
I can highly recommend Lemma if you are interested in an exploration and mystery game with intuitive movement.  The game sets out to accomplish a unique design and it is successful. If you don't have patience for a slower game, you may want to look elsewhere.  Subscribe to the Skilled Channel for more game reviews.

As someone who loves the Sands of Time Trilogy, I absolutely cannot recommend buying this game. Reasons why are below.
Not much of a plot. The Prince visits his brother (huh, he has a brother?) in Azad and they have boring banter. Something something, the brother unleashes an ancient army, something something, sand monsters, something something,
Honestly, I took a three month hiatus from this game and when I came back wasn't overly compelled to restart, and I still don't feel like I missed much of the plot, as forgettable as it was. 1/10
The three characters who have any real dialogue in the game are probably some of the most bland and slowest talkers I've ever witnessed. Where's the snappy banter between the Prince and Farah in Sands of Time and Two Thrones? Why do the cutscenes take five minutes to go over details that should be said in five seconds, details that I already know? We don't get to know much of the Prince's brother Malik aside from the fact that he's a warrior leader and thinks he's hot stuff. All we learn of Razia is that she's a good djinn who opposes the evil djinn that killed all the other good djinn. The prince is neither the witty, snarky prince of SoT, the angrier, cynical prince of WW, or the wiser but stilll sarcastic prince of TT. Overall, characters get a 0/10.
The graphics were alright, but nothing superb. The villain was a generic demonic design, the sand monsters were bland (if high-res) sand monsters. The human characters looked pretty good, but the Prince doesn't look anything like the Prince from the original trilogy. 5/10
Slow and clunky. The Prince takes forever to wind up an attack (feels like he's waiting to see if you're charging up your attack before he swings, like in the old 2D games) and will often attack an enemy nowhere near the one you were trying to hit. That's because anytime you enter combat (about every two minutes or so) you have to face at least 10, if not 20 or 30 enemies at once. There's no block button, so you have to rely on dodge-rolls to avoid attacks, and it just doesn't work well with that many enemies all trying to get a piece of you. There aren't any secondary weapons like in WW or TT, the only variation is kicking enemies that have shields to lower their guard, and you can't do any acrobatic attacks aside from jumping onto an enemy and stabbing or kicking them. They tried to make it more cinematic (you occasionally get a special kill cam where he will kick an enemy off a cliff or stab them throught he head) and, unsurprisingly, I felt more like I was watching a movie than playing a game. The only time power you have is rewind, and your other powers, as far as I can tell are useless in a fight. Once you get the sword towards the end of the game, combat becomes more of a mindless button mash than anything else, because enemies die in one hit, or two if they have a shield. Overall, combat gets a 2/10
This is the heart and soul of a Prince of Persia title! Wall runs, jumps, rolls, using powers to get to new heights! This was the only place where the game shined at all, but unfortunately it was only a spark that died in the wind. You start the game with nothing, and once the sand army is unleashed, you get rewind. Alright, cool, you can undo mistakes. Then a bit later you get the Flow power that lets you stop water. That's pretty awesome, too! You use this to run up frozen sheets of water, swing on pillars and columns of it. They even throw in some fun tricky timing bits where you have to pause the flow of the water, jump onto it, jump off of it, unpause, then repause it to catch the next segment. Pretty cool!
Then you get a power that lets you home in on enemies after jumping off a ledge. Okay, that's alright I guess, why didn't you just give me this earlier though? And then, in the last hour of gameplay, you get the ability to rebuild crumbled pieces of the architecture one at a time and that's... pretty alright, but they sort of wasted any potential for it because you use it in exactly three areas of the game leading to the final area, then not at all going to the final boss.
So what gives? Why give us a new power every quarter of the game instead of introducing them in pretty quick succession? "Here's time powers. Get used to those. Alright, now here's the flow. Learn to use that with rewind and we'll give you the glide boost. Learn to use glide boost and then we'll give you reconstruction. Now, enjoy the whole game with all these." That makes a lot more sense than spreading them out over the course of the entire game.
The free running and pole swinging and all is a lot slower compared to SoT, WW, and TT. You jump, and the prince takes a second to leap. You hit a pole you have to swing on, and he fumbles his grab, so you have to wait for him to come to a complete stop, then tilt the analog stick in the proper direction for him to swing. That's right, the swing button is no longer mapped to the same button as wall runs.
While some of the mechanics are fun, the rest just sort of felt tacked on and not all that useful in the long run, and this whole game just feels really slow compared to previous games. 6/10 and I'm being generous.
So, all in all, the game isn't worth getting unless you have to complete your collection. Characters are bland and nowhere near as witty, the story is utterly forgettable, the combat is somehow slow and arbitrarily hard at the same time, and the exploration mechanics are so-so. Overall score: 2.8/10

I freakin' love it!
I dunno why there aren't more games like this all in all. Somethin' about a more tactical, turn-based combat just tickles me sideways, and all the effects and strategy and little abilities and terrain and all is delightful.
There are some definite flaws - it *feels* a little clunky at times, a few small things aren't terribly intuitive - some of the terrain is a little hard to say, it's not obvious at first what is 'impassable' without the square coordinates turned on, it's not clear if you can 'pass' a turn or have to take an action (hint, you do, but you seem to have several at-will abilities you can use every turn, so fair enough), it also seems like you must take your minor action before your major, which doesn't seem super intuitive, it'd be nice to have some higher resolution option..
With that said, I think the positive dramatically outweight the negative. They did a great job capturing a lot of the 'feel' of a table-top turn based type game. Options aren't always good or bad, it isn't always just 'fight or don't fight', there's neat little tidbits that give extra options later, equipment otherwise unavailable, and so forth. You can play entirely asyncrhonously so you need not worry about awkward scheduling - people can pop on, review turns up to theirs, do theirs, and move on. It'd be amazing for a group of folks who want to play but don't often have time to play together, but still want to play.
The classes are familiar but unique enough to be intriguing - I personally love the feel of a 'leader' type role, not a "tank" or a "holy-roller" healer, nor a back-row support buffer, but a character that sorta halfway fits all the roles. Equipment items seem to grant various passives and usable abilities as much as not, which adds that many more little fiddly fun options during combat to use and strategize with. It also seems to work well with fewer than four - my husband and I have tromped through the first handful of adventures, and had quite a bit of fun doing so.. A few were close calls, we even died once, but we used what we learned and stomped it next time..
Altogether, I would love to see more of what Conclave has to offer, no questions asked. I can see some of the criticism - the visuals could use a little tuning up most notably at a glance - but that always takes a back seat to the core game, and to me it's downright delightful. Solid recommend from me, no question about it.

The Prince of Persia series has a big nostalgia factor for me and I would have to say this one has been the worse one I've played.  This game commits just too many sins for me to ever be able to recommend it.
The game does not go to far away from the POP formula.  You have to platform through the room to get to the next room which I typically enjoy and did enjoy in this game.  Albeit they show the path most of the time when you enter a room which really destroyed the puzzle aspect for me.  The puzzles themselves were not difficult.  I would say I probably enjoyed the first half of the game but then it started to just feel uninspired for the last half and I didn't like the final boss fight at all just fight wrong.
My biggest problem with the game is it feels like ubisoft rushed it out to time it with the movie and there are multiple bugs and during my 6-7 hour playthrough (I left it on which is why my hours are inflated), it probably crashed 6 times and would become unresponsive if I opened the steam overlay whenever I wanted to chat with a friend.  It saved often enough that I didn't lose much progress but I feel that is far too frequent.  Some of the controls for the second half made it feel the prince was not listening to me.
The second biggest problem for me is I was playing on the harder difficulty and the enemies just gave no issues in fact the entire combat felt boring, luckily it did not require much brain power so I could just quickly plow through it.  But the final boss final was pretty much just combat, and he had an attack that knocked me down and for some reason if the prince gets knocked down he just stays on the ground for what feels like forever (Probably 3-8 seconds).   This caused the boss would follow up with another hit killing me.  So if my prince got knocked down he was dead in this battle.  I guess they felt that's how they would make the final boss hard, but it just felt like bad design.
I thought the story was servicable but entirely forgetable.  I don't expect good story from the POP series so I was not really disappointed.
Overall I would say not the worse game but the worse POP game I've played.  I feel if you just want a adventure/3D platformer and you've played through all the better ones then I would give this some consideration but I feel there are just better games on the market.

I see potential in Woodle Tree Adventures.
I see a lot of potential, but in it's current state it's pretty hard for me to recommend it:
Camera: The camera is fixed (to be fair, i read that you can zoom in or out but couldn't find a button in the Xbox 360 controller assigned to that function), a mayor letdown because precision platforming is all about that, precision. The game was not comfortable at all to play for me because of this.
Music. The music NEEDS A LOT of work. And i hope the developer hears me on this: Mario games are good not only because of their gameplay, they are also, because their music is awesome and adds to the experience.
The music in the game makes me want to sleep, it is not engaging, it doesn't motivate me to keep playing.
Gameplay:  It's interesting and a new take on a classic genre, a platformer in the same vein as Mario, Crash Bandicoot and Sonic the Hedgehog, which is not a bad thing at all! Found it very similar to Super Mario 3D World.
The control is responsive but this is counteracted by the camera which creates a constant struggle for the player, who is calculating distances without different perspectives, all the time.
The hit detection needs work, i found myself a lot of times attacking, killing the enemy and magically dying myself too.
Characters: They are cute and simple, but more charisma would be good, specially for the main character. I understand that the plot is simple, but a lot of the success of the old platforming games comes from the "mascot", a charismatic character that we (the players) want to see victorious because we feel identified with it.
Graphics: The graphics are pretty colorful and add to the experience, simple shapes made me remember the N64 and Playstation era.
All in all, WTA is not a bad game, and i really wanted to enjoy it because i have played platforming games all my life, but the game needs work, a lot of work. I'll be looking forward to updates of this game and change this review if i see progress.

See original review below, but as it stands I can't recommend it. It's an alright game, but at the price point and now charging $12 for one state that took 16-17 months(yes 16-17! I watched the Squirrel review of New Mexico and it looked like every other town in game other than Roswell and a couple new truck stops. Not paying $12 per state. That would make the final game cost me around $550 for the U.S. NOT including the DLC other than states or the fact that it would take 60 YEARS to put out the rest of them.
I bought this for $20 US after playing ETS2 for about 2 weeks and loving it. This game is ALMOST a clone other than there are less trucks to choose from(which is just silly, but American companies love getting cash for licensing rights), currently only Kenworth and Peterbilt, great trucks but not the only ones in America by FAR. I hear there are mods for Freightliner and International but honestly I hate installing mods.
The game has been out about a year or so and it looks like in 1 year they have added 1(Arizona) of 46 missing states(I'm guessing Alaska and Hawaii are out, although I wouldn't mind trucking to Alaska) to the existing 2 they started with(California and Nevada). That seems a bit slow paced. Anyone looking for a coast to coast driving experience need not look here. When I bought this, the first thing I thought was, "oh this will be so cool driving across the US!".....but alas, no.
Also another BIG difference from ETS2 to this is the speeding tickets. When I started ETS2 it took a little getting used to noticing where the speed cameras were, but I got it after a couple days. In ATS forget all you have learned... I went from Sacremento through Los Angeles and racked up probably about $4000 in fines, the majority of which were less than 5-10 mph over the limit. I used to drive a truck....no cop and I mean NO COP tickets a truck driver for going 71 mph in a 65mph zone on a highway at 5pm in the afternoon. Also most of my tickets came from police on the other side of the highway, I would get a fine THEN see lights across the median flashing....WTF.
Seriously the game is great, but the police need to have an option for aggressiveness or something and states need to be added a bit quicker. I hear New Mexico is coming, but as far as im concerned, you can call that Arizona part 2.
As it sits I will give it a thumbs up, but on a scale 6/10. If you are debating between this and ETS2, go for ETS2 first. If you have $20 to blow and already have ETS2, go ahead and try it, but try and wait for a sale. If you like modding I guess theres a lot more options for you.
TLDR; ETS2 with no ferries or trains and WAY more fines and WAY less trucks, and you always drive on the right side.

Time makes fools of us all. That is the perfect phrase to describe this game.
I'll be honest, the concept of a first-person PVP medieval warfare game is a pretty good one. I'd say it's a fairly fresh new idea that definitely feels like a better substitute for playing the majority of first-person shooters which all seem to be the same idea regurgitated countless times. However, this creative concept, and my love for medieval subject matter in general do not blind me from seeing a game that could be so much more.
This game is years old now, and it definitely shows. I picked this game up because of the 90% off sale, having had this on my wishlist for a while because I wanted to check it out. And now I'm fitting to ask for my money back.
But all things considered, Chivalry: Medieval Warfare does have some good qualities, such as:
+Interesting concept
+Some of the weapons are fun to mess around with (Heavy Crossbow and Smoke Pot)
+Customization
+Well-designed maps
Sadly for what was a promising game has since been left for dead. It seems as though the game was abandoned for years until the big discount roped more people in.
-Poor server performance (In any PVP game this is a massive problem because it messes up gameplay)
-Limited diversity in playstyle (4 Classes each with a very limited selection of weapons. Most function exactly the same way, with only a few standing out in my head (As mentioned in the Pros section).
-Bots are awful (It may not bother everyone, but sometimes I like to use offline mode to practise a class or just to blow off steam, but the bots in this game are abyssmal. Their AI is flawed in many different ways, including, but not limited to: Walking back and forth between trees and having no animations when firing a crossbow so you cannot gauge when to dodge of block)
The biggest problem that I see with this game is that, because of how limited the playstyle is, the game can and will grow stale after a short time. You'll end up getting annoyed with just how truly simple the game is. That said, if you want to try something new, and you like medieval history (particularly those that involve bloodshed), then you may as well try this game. You may enjoy it, but I personally don't.

So, the game. There is no story to speak of, which wouldn't be a problem if the game was actually fun to play, but it isn't. I did look at a walk through for one right at the end, not because it was hard but because I got tired of back tracking and was getting really bored. Which brings me to my next point: movement speed. Oh my god, the character walks slowly and as you spend the entire game walking to various points with brief breaks for puzzles (some of which involve back tracking to solve) this gets incredibly annoying. The game is already pretty short (my play time was 85min, but that included a break for a phone call so it was really closer to an hour) and most of it was spent clicking on a spot on the screen then looking at my phone while my character laboriously made their way there. If you are asking me to pay $10 for an hour long game don't have most of it be filler.
The only thing to really recommend this game is the art style, but I was disappointed there too. The backgrounds are very monotonous and never really make use of the origami gimmick . I can think of a dozen games that actually have really enjoyable gameplay and/or stories and look way better (Okami, Child of Light, Ori and the Blind Forest, Hyper Light Drifter, Bastion, Dust: An Elysian Tail, Gravity Ghost, Titan Souls, They Bleed Pixels, Limbo, Fez, Road Not Taken).
Overall, this game lacks depth in just about every way. Maybe I would recommend it if it was free on a mobile device, but $10 on a computer? No way. This game is not worth your time.

TL;DR: Great game, not for everyone, like grind? come play, don't? still come because it is amazing
Where do I start with this game? Firstly, it's a great game. Secondly, it's not for everyone.
Let me explain:
The game, depending on your playstyle, can be very grindy, because this game is what you make it. I for one, don't make the game grindy, I enjoy going slower. I have been playing for 1 year now in Warframe since October 2016. (It's November 2017 as of the time of writing this review).
The great part about this game is you can take your time with it, or you can rush through it.
While the game definitely isn't for everyone, and I can see why some people might not like it, I still highly recommend this game for anybody that wants an amazing story. If you don't see what I mean by the story, just wait until you get to the Second Dream quest. That quest is single-handedly the best quest in the game. The story of the game and the lore hidden away in the maps is just plain amazing.
The lore and the story is not mouthfed into the player and you have to work it out for yourself, now if that's not your cup of coffee, there's the other part of the game, grind.
As a "veteran" so to speak, I don't personally consider myself a veteran, but some people with older accounts than mine, called me veteran so, I guess that works, it is hard to describe the game, because I genuinely care for it and I could list a host of problems that do not affect newbie gameplay in the slightest and only really affect high-level content which most people don't even do.
By high-level, I mean 1.5-2 hour long Survival runs. I think you can see why people don't do those. There just isn't a point to doing them for so long, unless you want a real challenge. The new player experience in Warframe is getting better, by the day and it's harder and harder to say no to the game.
This is the end of the review, in case you are interested in a few tips, which may or may not save you a bit of your sanity and a bit of your hair (if you know what I mean), read on.
Some tips for starting out:
-Only use the starting platinum for slots. Warframe slots, weapon slots, pet slots and the like. The early limit on how many weapons and warframes you can have is abysmally low, intentionally so, but the starting platinum helps cope with that.
-Do not use your platinum in the market for warframes, weapons, mod packs, relic packs, skins (unless you are already later into the game that you really don't need platinum that much anymore, or have bought platinum through the website)
-On the note of platinum, you can get platinum cost discounts on the daily login, they recently introduced more percentages, which for better or for worse. You can get 10/20/30/50/60/75% off of platinum price. You can guess that the 75% off is a huge♥♥♥♥♥deal. Use those if you plan on spending money on the game.
-Use the wiki of warframe, but carefully if you wish to avoid spoilers. There are spoilers on the wiki(duh), but it is rather easy to skip them and rather hard to find unintentionally. The reason I am saying to use the wiki, is because the game does an excellent job of not explaining ♥♥♥♥-all to you, and letting you figure it out yourself. If you love figuring out games for yourself, Warframe is for you. It explains absolutely ♥♥♥♥-all past the tutorial.
-If you wish to up your fashion on anything, the first thing I recommend is a color pack, after which come skins. The main color packs I'd recommend are Basic, to unlock the rest of the panel, Basic Saturated, Fire, Smoke, Ki'Teer when Baro Ki'Teer comes around which is every two weeks on Fridays until Sunday the same time he appears. (You will learn of Baro Ki'Teer through the game when he comes around since he sends you a message that he appeared at a relay, and that message will burst into your face the first time you start up warframe on friday when he already arrived.)
-Do note, that Baro Ki'Teer brings new things every time he comes so he might not have the color palette that I mentioned.
These would be my tips to any starting player, if you want to add me, I'm "Eurobenzin" ingame. Gladly willing to help newbies whenever I'm online.

I'm usually pretty decent at games, and can figure out how to play pretty quickly. I mean, I've been playing video games since I was 5. This game, though, is overly complicated to the point of insanity. You have to micromanage everything, and sometimes the game just throws a curveball at you you'll never expect. Like why is my left click suddenly attack instead of walk, or vice versa? I don't know and it doesn't explain it. An Assassin comes up looking for the Red Prince and wipes your party in two turns? Cool, why not. Party member decides not to move and you get in a fight with one party member 200 yards away? Yeah, that's a thing. It just doesn't make sense.
There are positives. The combat, when it works, is pretty good. It's solid turn based combat. It is kinda infuriating when you try to shoot an enemy and your character, for no real reason, decides to walk towards them through fire and poison, but apparently you have to deal with that. Loot make sense, even if it isn't explained very well. The crafting is cool and doesn't seem to have any negatives. The trading is pretty cool. Instead of saying "Item X costs 40g" it's "Item X is worth 40g". You can offer your own items and gold to buy it. If you want to buy boots worth 5g, you can offer up a 3g book and  2g to buy it. If you offer, say, a 10g book for it, the merchant will like you more. Pretty cool.
Overall, I can't recommend the game. It's just way too complicated. Not for the sake of fun, it seems, but just for the sake of making the game harder. I'm all for hard games, but this one doesn't make any sense. Dark Souls, for instance, doesn't just change on you in the middle of a fight. This does, and I can not stand that. In the two hours I played, I did not get a single moment of enjoyment out of it

This is the game I always come back to. While other games might give me a few days of enjoyment, when they're "new game shine" wears off, this is the game I return to. This is the game that has been holding my interest for years.
Nothing else has the same combination of things to do. It has the war and development of a grand strategy game, but also the personal development and relationships of an RPG.
What's more, there is always something new to experience. A game as a French duke clawing for power in Western Europe has a very different feel from that of a Viking raiding across the North Sea or that of a Armenian king struggling to survive a Muslim onslaught. Depending on my mood, I can set up a slow game of carefully constructing marriage ties and improving my demense or I can set off on a whirlwind game of conquering and plundering.
I came into this as a veteran of other Paradox strategy games, such as Europa Universalis (my previous favorite game, before discovering this one), but if you've never played such a game before, CKII can certainly be a bit overwhelming. However, this is also not a game you need to become an expert in all at once. Picking a minor Irish count, for example, can allow for learning how the game works, while picking a more precarious position can increase the challenge later.
I have played this game for years and I have never finished a game, because "finishing" is not what CKII is about. It's about enjoying the experience. The people and families in the game truly make this game more engaging than any other strategy game I play.

After 1800+ hours playing Crusader Kings II, the most recent DLC and free content expansion, Conclave, has forced me to withdraw my formerly enthusiastic approval.  CKII used to be one of the premiere Grand Strategy titles available.  Sadly, over the course of several expansion/DLC releases the game has lost its way, becoming increasingly tedious and straying far from the original wonderful gameplay.
The Conclave DLC and the accompanying free content patch was released completely unbalanced and apparently largely untested.  It caused a widespread negative reaction which forced Paradox to immediately begin work on a fix patch.  That patch, now in open beta testing, goes a long way toward fixing the worst of the problems.  Unfortunately, it doesn't go far enough.
The root of the problem is that the entire concept of Conclave makes councils far too powerful.  The intent of Paradox seems to be to make the game more difficult and thus hinder the ability of players to "paint" the map all in the color of their empire.  The intended result was achieved.  And now the game is a mess of micromanaging council votes and council favor which detracts from the initial design concept of a fun game focused on dynasties and war in the medieval period.  Paradox might as well change the name of the game to Crusader Kings II: The Council -Hindered, Blocked and Trolled.  The game is no longer focused on dynasty and conquest and religious fervor in the medieval milieu.  Now it is just a grumpy, greedy pseudo-democracy council simulator set in a medieval era with the player forced into spending inordinate amounts of time dealing with fractious, constant council problems almost to the exclusion of everything that once made this a great game.
Congratulations, Paradox.  The greed pushing a need to continually release more DLC to line corporate pockets has finally sent the core game into oblivion. You succeeded in satisfying a vocal minority who wanted the game to be more difficult (with no proof that many of those who complained had even played the game beyond the Easy setting).  In return, you've so drastically altered the basic gameplay that Crusader Kings II is no longer really about Crusader Kings.  You've turned a fine Grand Strategy game set in the medieval period into something entirely different. Short of removing the Conclave DLC and the free content expansion entirely, there is no fix for this.  The game has moved too far from its original design concept, which attracted many of us to the game in the first place.  There are other better democracy simulators available.  They aren't Grand Strategy games; but neither is Crusader Kings II since the changes of the last expansion.

An interesting blend of new and old.
GFX: Beautiful, and remarkably well performing; 130-180fps average, never saw it dip below 120.
SFX: Good music and sound effects.
STRY: Set between The Sands of Time and The Warrior Within a fair story involving his brother, but unless I missed something major there appears to be no tie-in to the other games. Would've been nice to leave this one off knowing how the Dahaka came about since it was never explained in the WW. It felt more like TSoT storytelling vs either of the others, and I actually enjoyed the D'jinn character and her banter.
GMPLY - Depressingly short...
The good: They took all the best parts of TSoT and TWW and combined them here. The water based puzzles were an amazing addition. The obnoxious balancing act on beams was removed, hazah!
The bad: Combat was downgraded from needing a of skill to a button mashy and far less of a challengeing affair than any of the other games. The classic traps: spike-pillars, darts, floor-spikes, etc; were no challenge at all, unlike the old games. A little bit of assistance on jump direction is one thing, this game takes it to the extreme, at least in the first half of the game; over-assisted-hand-holding-platformer-mode engaged.
4.5/5
tl;dr: Worth a playthrough, just slog through the first half (basically a tutorial) to get to the fun water puzzles.
