I just finished this game after beating every single PoP Game in a row on the hardest difficulty and I must say: This game really gives me hope for the PoP Franchise.
After the 2008 PoP Reboot I was really worried about PoP as a whole. I beat it, was really dissapointed and moved on to the last entry of the franchise: PoP The Forgotten Sands. Now don't get me wrong, this game is by far not perfect. I would not even go as far as to say it is particularly good. Moreover it is so short that I can really understand if people who bought this game at full price or even half the full price feel betrayed. But it adresses alot of issues the well known sands of time trilogy had with fresh ideas that could lead to some really awesome PoP Games in the future. Heres a list of my personal views on this game:
Story:
The story is nothing special but it is serviceable. The Djinn focused setting is a really fresh and cool idea. I would love to see future PoPs delve into persian mythology instead of coming up with a generic "we need a tie-in to the sands of time universe"-story.
Presentation:
The graphics are alright for my standards but people who demand flashy graphics will not be impressed. Enemy design is kind of cool but nothing extraordinary. The voice acting is surprisingly good and does not feel out of place. The animation quality is a bit of a setback since the prince does not feel as fluid in his movements as he did in the sands of time trilogy. The princes sword looks freaking badass.
Fighting:
The fighting is very bland. You basically only need one button and constantly hit hordes of enemies in a very slow fashion. Flashy acrobatic combos are also missing - something that upsets a lot of people. Let me say, I am not one of them. As I mentioned above I beat all PoPs that let me choose difficulty at the highest possible setting. It may be an issue with those difficulties but to me the combat system in the SoT trilogy was pretty boring. Combos were very often just blocked by enemies after the second hit and you could easily be interrupted. The most efficient way of dealing with enemies was to either dash from a wall, grab hit them until they die or jump over them and hit them until they die. So even though there were various really cool looking combos I personally did not feel rewarded for using them. At some point in Warrior Within I got so upset with the fighting system and how boring and tedious I felt it was, that I started just throwing enemies off of cliffs to dispose of them quickly. In two thrones I rather died on purpose and retried to stealth kill the enemies instead of taking the fight because those enemies had like a quadrillion health on the hardest difficulty. The fact that they added experience and a slight RPG-Style customization for the Prince in Forgotten Sands gave the fighting some purpose. I hope they can keep this formula and just replace the bland fighting system with something better.
Platforming:
The platforming in this game is pretty awesome for a PoP title. It is not the most difficult platforming ever. But the added water manipulation and the ability to recall structures from the past just made me feel really good when platforming. Alternating between solid and liquid water to pass waterfalls while still grabing the stream coming from the wall that I just recalled from the past in midair was just a really awesome feeling.
Biggest Issues:
The worst thing about this game is how short it is. You can finish it in 5 to 8 hours if you are an experienced PoP player. And even if this is your first PoP title it will probably not take you longer than 12 hours at max. Also the more european looking prince is a real bummer. But I honestly think that was just changed in order to make him resemble the movie actor.
Verdict:
Do I recommend this game ? Probably not to everyone. But if you are a PoP fan or just like a nice game that keeps you entertained for a few hours and you can grab it for 2 to 5 bucks then it can be a really nice game to take a little break from super engaging AAA titles and enjoy some really cool platforming. If you LOVED SoT and hope to find more SoT in this game: Stay away. This game is very unlike SoT and will dissapoint you.

Deliberately slow-paced (but, crucially, not slow enough that you'll lose patience or grow bored), "Conclave" does a pretty good job at recreating the tabletop roleplaying experience. The quests - or at least the early ones I've played so far - are interesting enough, although their branching paths often seem to boil down to you choosing (or, on quests with other players, voting) whether to run away, fight or use a specific character skill to even the odds.
The main meat of the game is the combat system, as that's what you'll spend 90% of your quests doing, and that's where "Conclave" shines. It's not groundbreaking but it doesn't really need to be. You get a minor and a major action each turn, during which you can move your character around the battlefield or perform actions such as healing, casting spells or focusing your bow on a specific target. You'll be surprised at how engrossing such a simple thing can be, especially when played with others.
And that's all there is to it, at the moment at least. Let's be under no illusion here: the game has its share of flaws (the number of pictures you can use for your character's avatar is extremely limited for example) and I've seen a few people say it can be buggy in places. But, if you want a cheap but fairly solid game that lets you explore dungeons and save princesses without having to use your kitchen table as a board whilst keeping track of dice-rolls and minitures, "Conclave" is probably for you.

Adult themed Minecraft/ARK style gameplay with King of Monsters/Rampage/Black or White thrown in, ala deity avatars. Will re-evaluate my review once game leaves early access.
Pros:
Full frontal nudity option for both genders.
NSFW jiggle physics.
Lots of mods via steam workshop.
Snap-to construction.
Enslavement system ala thralls.
Pretty UE4 graphics engine.
Decent themed music.
Cons:
Now loads extremely slow on current hardware, especially when modded.
Extreme creative license taken by adding many mobs/creatures not found in Conan/REH lore
Cannot zoom out beyond shoulder, without loading mods - many other mods should be incorporated options by this point in development
No way to tell which mods are conflicting with others, or even compatible with the current game version
Only one static map, no random gen (size of a single large zone in most MMOs).
Glitchy mobs that become invulnerable or are damage-sponges (headshots should be 1-2 power hits with a weapon, depending on armored or not).
Stats overly-weighted towards combat and not stealth or social options.
Very clunky, marginal variety of combat and movement physics (no riposte, parry, shield bash, charge, figure 8, dodge roll, slide, sweep, etc.).
Lack of quests or storyline - cannot track down and take vengeance upon ones that crucified you initially.
Mob difficulty does not scale with number of players working together (CRITICAL BUG).
Mobs will chase you for an exceedingly long time and do not interact with each other appropriately (predator/prey often seen just hanging out together).
Still uses a level-based system (skill-based without any sort of level up or HP increase would best emulate the REH atmosphere).
TLDR; Robert E. Howard probably rolling over in his grave. Recommend saving your $$ for a finished and polished product. Cannot recommend in current state.
Closing thought: Valve really needs to crack down on early access scamming (no intent to ever fix/finish, selling DLC or expansions before release) by many studios currently leveraging the survival game trend.

I bought this for $20 US after playing ETS2 for about 2 weeks and loving it. This game is ALMOST a clone other than there are less trucks to choose from(which is just silly, but American companies love getting cash for licensing rights), currently only Kenworth and Peterbilt, great trucks but not the only ones in America by FAR. I hear there are mods for Freightliner and International but honestly I hate installing mods.
The game has been out about a year or so and it looks like in 1 year they have added 1(Arizona) of 46 missing states(I'm guessing Alaska and Hawaii are out, although I wouldn't mind trucking to Alaska) to the existing 2 they started with(California and Nevada). That seems a bit slow paced. Anyone looking for a coast to coast driving experience need not look here. When I bought this, the first thing I thought was, "oh this will be so cool driving across the US!".....but alas, no.
Also another BIG difference from ETS2 to this is the speeding tickets. When I started ETS2 it took a little getting used to noticing where the speed cameras were, but I got it after a couple days. In ATS forget all you have learned... I went from Sacremento through Los Angeles and racked up probably about $4000 in fines, the majority of which were less than 5-10 mph over the limit. I used to drive a truck....no cop and I mean NO COP tickets a truck driver for going 71 mph in a 65mph zone on a highway at 5pm in the afternoon. Also most of my tickets came from police on the other side of the highway, I would get a fine THEN see lights across the median flashing....WTF.
Seriously the game is great, but the police need to have an option for aggressiveness or something and states need to be added a bit quicker. I hear New Mexico is coming, but as far as im concerned, you can call that Arizona part 2.
As it sits I will give it a thumbs up, but on a scale 6/10. If you are debating between this and ETS2, go for ETS2 first. If you have $20 to blow and already have ETS2, go ahead and try it, but try and wait for a sale. If you like modding I guess theres a lot more options for you.
TLDR; ETS2 with no ferries or trains and WAY more fines and WAY less trucks, and you always drive on the right side.

Well, after getting into the game, I saw that I could use my controller to play this game. And surprisingly, this is one of the rare games where my controller works (Speedlink XEOX gamepad, Xbox 360 edition). And I gotta say, the controls were pretty basic, yet enjoyable.
The goal in this game is pretty easy. In each levels, you have 3 tears, you need to collect to finish the level. Also, you can collect these "apples" that are scattered around the world, to upgrade your leaf (weapon). Levels in this game are pretty amazing. Simple, yet difficult. I was enjoying my time platforming through the levels, finding all of those apples.
the Soundtrack was just brilliant. I loved it. It was bright, happy and theme-fitting soundtrack for every level. I would even say that the soundtrack on this game is one of my favourite ones.
One bad thing about this game right now, is that it is simply too short. I finished the game in 1 hour, and it has currently only 6 levels. I heard that the developer is planning new levels and bosses, but as right now, it's just too short and easy. Also most of the enemies are simply too easy to dodge. These rushing types of enemies are most likely the best enemy right now in this game, since the ranged ones just stand there, waiting for 20 seconds before throwing something at you. I only accidentally found this feature in the snow level.
In short, excellent platformer with great soundtrack, but tends to be too short and easy. But for that small price, it is definitely worth a try.

I grew up with this game. It's one of my favorites of all time. The story is quite good, and there are so many different party/class configurations that will keep you coming back for more. There are a huge number of quests, a great deal of them with hours worth of content and multiple outcomes. Every class has their own unique quest chain, and there are numerous others for each side of the alignment spectrum. The game is hugely improved over Baldur's Gate 1, and there are even a few small improvements here over BG: EE.
I like the additions that Beamdog made, but it's worth noting that this game is still very, very buggy - especially in online multiplayer. Unfortunately, it seems like they've created more problems than they've fixed. It can be tolerated or worked around, but people who have the original and are thinking of upgrading to this should perhaps weigh their options. If you're looking to play multiplayer, expect to see good old Biff the Understudy fairly often.
My personal favorite additions are the hugely reduced load times, auto-loot, and the conveniently organized/bulleted journal. I haven't played around a lot with the new NPCs, but I like them a lot so far. Their romance options, however, seem incredibly superficial at present. There is now a same-sex option for both males and females respectively, so that's nice, though both of these NPCs are unfortunately evil.
This version is compatible with a lot (although not all) of the countless mods created for this game over the last fifteen years, allowing you to configure your gameplay experience if the hundreds of hours of vanilla content aren't enough for you.
I cannot recommend this game enough, and that extends also to the first game. They're just fantastic.

This is a 230 Hours review on Tactician.
TLDR: This game is 10/10 and deserves a spot in the RPG Hall of Fame. IT is a must buy hands down.
Pros:
- Story: Amazing Introduction that ramps up to a very good confusing mid game meltdown and ends in emotional chaos.
- Gameplay: Top Notch, skills, spells, interactions, AI, everything feels smooth and fights never get boring.
- Length: You dont know when the game is finally over it is soooo long and thats a good thing
- Difficulty: On Tactician the game starts absolutely brutal, towards the end it unfortunately becomes easier except a few exceptions who are crazy hard again.
Cons:
- Merchants: 1 Hour waiting to get a chance of new piece of gear, no gear leveling with you, lots of unique armors or weapons capped at level 18. You can fix this though by using mods but then you get no achievements. It's not noticeable until the very end but then you notice it very hardly, to the point you go afk for 1 hour to get some new gear.
- Skills: Some skills felt lacking, especially the source skills resolve into 2-3 being better then all the others which makes you feel pidgeon holed since the enemies on harder diffs are going to spam you with the good stuff. Some skills npc's use cant be learned... also you cant make true new classes in the SDK currently which is a big downer
- Story: I understand that with so many choices it gets more complex to keep track of everything, sometimes the game does not explain or give you a chance on understanding why a character in the story would do something. One example would be Gareth if you chose to destroy everyone but side with him always, he still will be opposing you at the end while not explaining why so yeah thats unfortunately not the only story let downs.
- Thievery: only 1 pickpocket per NPC per character this is ridiculous by the astronomical prices you have to pay and the minimal gold you get for selling stuff.

So for a review i'll give you a little glimpse of my experience with the game. You draw your own conclusions.
(Just as a fore warning cos there's always "that" guy who says "eww weird almost top down camera angles and graphics are meh" the game is almost 20 years old now, suck it up and focus on the story its what it's known for)
I decided I was going to be a Paladin, I was going to be good! Travelling the lands, righting wrongs....
I Lost my Paladin status within the first hour of playing...god dammit! Instead of restarting I decided to roll with it, (the game was letting me so might as well right?) I mean now I was just a crappy warrior with low weapon skills and no fancy healing abilities and buffs to make me useful in any way but surely something will turn up...it got progressively worse over the next few hours of play. (Solely my fault not the game I should point out.)
The solution to losing all my abilities I decided, was to make my character almost constantly drunk for approximately 4 in-game (thankfully) months (i dunno like 3 days worth of play real time? It was strong mead...real strong.) This did little but lower my all ready pitiful weapon skills to nothing and cost me all my gold but I did hear a few interesting rumours. (basically hints on where to find quests) Then through more bad choices or drunken stupor, I ended up having to flee the city with a drow cleric (evil) and a deranged gnome (basically evil too) in tow. Don't cast magic without a license friends! I tried to redeem myself by helping out a local lord with a dragon problem, ended up killing some paladins, you know, reeeaaallly "good" guys.
However it gets better from here (no, seriously) I end up killing a dragon after solving some puzzles and finding some awesome dragon slayers gear (very handy obviously) and fighting some other nasty monsters, I saved a girl, reunited her with her father, the Head Paladins decided I had atoned and everything was all good, paladin status given back (sweet sweet abilities) I go back to the city do more quests help more people, earn a good reputation, earn TONS of gold, pay for my magical license (fear my mad gnomes level 8 magic missile!) Then remember I'm supposed to be saving my friend. So head off on my merry way, band of probably 85% evil party members in tow. (Kept 'em cos I assumed I could try and convert them to good being a paladin and all, I could not, however, the inter-party banter was pretty hilarious bloody jan jansen and Viconia.)
Without spoiling the storyline, s*** goes south real quick. My guy ends up going full rage mode mid way through some maze, PERMANENTLY killing (as in hit them so hard they explode into chunks kinda dead) all my party members barring the drow cleric and the friend I came to rescue, who I managed to get outside the room my main guy was in till he regained control. So at this point i'm down 3 party members heading into what ends up being the more difficult part of the game. Does this dishearten me? pfft, no! I'm loving every minute of this!
So I end up through good luck and several reloads (god dam acid breathing dragons man...yeesh!) beating "Shadows of Amn" I then rolled my character and what few party members that still survived into "throne of bhaal" and came out the other end (several days and reloads later) with hither-to unheard of attributes for a mere human paladin. I had some sweet armor, some super paladin only 2-handed, Holy Avenger, demon smiting, sword of awesomeness, became a God, (cos why the hell not right?) and then sat and read through the "what happened next" for my few surviving party members. Wrapping up my play through very nicely. I actually felt quite sad at this point as I had to lay my Paladin to rest. (No carrying on questing for you when you ascend to Godhood, but I guess theres more important things to do at that point...like maybe killing Gaelan Bayle, god I hate that "Coo!" noise he makes...)
In short, in my opinion of course, best rpg hands down, possibly that good that nothing else will ever come close in terms of storyline.
Totally worth the money, i've played what...70+ hours...i'm defintitely gonna be replaying this and exploring all the places i skipped, finding the party members I missed etc there is sooo much I still have to do. What more can you ask for...maybe a Baldur's Gate 3? oh whats that? Its possibly in the works right now!? Take my money...Just...take it...

This is an esoteric/walking simulator from France.   Games in this genre are often very hit or miss and the good ones marry a deep experience with high quality graphics and art direction and a solid technical implementation.   Bad ones don't.   Bientôt l'été is unfortunately in the latter category.
At face value the game has you walking around on an empty beach (not a new experience for walking simulators).  The twist is that eventually you'll collect a few "romantic" thought concepts and share them in a cafe with another avatar played by another player.
The gimmick falls very flat and overall it's not very interesting.  Esoteric games are very much a personal experience to discover the game which the developer in their quest for "Art" eschews for the 2 player gimmick.   Technical issues also detract from the experience.
Graphics:  Thumbs down here because they actually try to charge more for high res textures.   Otherwise okay but few options in fine tuning and shoddy "film grain" makes everything look like mud.
Gameplay: Practically none - the 2 player gimmick is weird and doesn't make up for the lack of single player story.  You're walking around on a beach.
Technical:  The game works okay in 4K but the graphics engine is fairly weak and lacks fine tuning options like getting rid of the film grain.   Worst of all is the game somehow assumes you have a flight sim HOTAS and maps all the buttons that way - and if you do have one, it binds the axes in bizarre and ridiculous ways - and there's no way to disable them, so you end up staggering around the beach like you're drunk.  The shoddy "film grain" effect does enhance the drunken experience.
Overall this game misses the mark by quite a way.   If developers want to do "art" instead of making an actual game, they need to exceed other games technical implementations.   Falling behind on gameplay and delivery is a quick way to get a thumbs down.

This may be the most complete and well rounded historical simulator available, and its mechanics are unique without being gimmicky. You see CK2 is about forging a dynasty, which is a fancy way of saying a rules heavy family. It's technically sandbox and you can have quite a bit of fun with it. You can roleplay as the traits that you have, or just try to make every character into Julius Caesar, or just keep assasinating popes, forever and ever. When your character dies, whether it be at 4 or 88, the play goes to the direct heir, whether he or she be 4 or 88, and you are given control over their decision making process.
As long as your dynasty has not died out in terms of inheritance laws, and someone in your dynasty has a sufficient title the game will continue until it stops after maybe dozens or a hundred hours of game play. You manage titles under your realm. Count is the lowest, than Duchy, than King, than Emperor, with some variety on the names depending on your culture. The key here is feudalism, that is vassalage. The standard is to pledge fealty to someone of the next higher title, who then pledges fealty to the title above them. This standard is never reached unless you conquer the world and make it be reached. In general, there will be sovereign Dukes, Counts pledged directly to Kings, and Emperors often forgo vassal kings.
You have advisers which are assigned from your court,  which is a pool of loyal or disloyal followers whom you can consider for various roles, and to accomplish various tasks. These advisers assist you in running the operations of your feifdom, and allow religious, educational, espionage, stewardship, and martial decisions. Each character has an RPG style stat for each of these, and these along with a portion of your wife's stats and your advisers stats creates the stats used in game for you.
Key decisions in this game are marriage, and war. Marriage is the influence you have over your dynasty, and you can get good traits, titles, claims on titles, or political alliances in exchange for the matrimony. Wars allow you to cement alliances and shape the geopolitical landscape. There is much more to the game, as it has surprising complexity, but this is not to be a guide.
The game is visually very appealing, despite largely being a giant map. The music is nice, and even after several hours you may not be bored. There is also a ton of DLC for this, for better or worse. These are largely all expansive on the game, and most will be on for most games. Some like the Sunset Invasion are cheesy alternative history which you likely will not want on at all times. There are an absurd number of starting rulers at any of a number of initial scenarios, and a bit of imagination makes all interactions fun as you write your own story of world history amongst the players who have interesting personalities derived from their traits. This game remains an absolute treasure, and is still updated from time to time.

The setting is mildly interesting, but the stories ultimately come down to 'Option A, Option B or Option C due to a bonus skill' and don't seem to offer much more than generic fantasy drivel that's about on par with your average homebrew setting dossier.
There's a 'demo' available in the form of a F2P mode not mentioned on the Steam page, which allows players to try out the first couple dozen or so missions and get to grips with what the game offers... I urge you to try that before buying the game on Steam... In fact, due to the numerous bugs in the game's UI, playing via the browser is in fact EASIER, since you can just F5 to get around what would otherwise require you to restart the client from scratch.
TL;DR: It's a buggy browser game that takes the worst aspects of modern MMOs (Pre-determined builds, overreliance on random players) and tabletop games (Decidedly average homebrew settings, achingly slow character progression and glacial box-text-based pacing) and combines it into one messy experience. Better to stick to Roll20 for now.

This is a weird one. It tries to be too many things at once, but despite that it succeeds.
Some of the time.
Conclave's meant to simulate the simple fun of tabletop DnD. Its interface is uncomplicated. Its character choices and build options are flavorful. Its maps are clunky grids and its story is full of unpronouncable names.
It moves pretty slowly, but if you and some friends want to do something different for an evening and still fondly remember 3.5 ed, this might not be a bad pick.
Unfortunately, if you're not in exactly that circumstance, Conclave is a little harder to play. Playing with randos over the internet is ponderous. Often it'll move at a rate of one turn a day, if that, assuming that the party leader or some other dude doesn't just give up on playing midway through the first quest.
This would be fine, if you could build and run a full party on your own. However, you're restricted to just controlling one character. It is possible to solo quests, but the game doesn't feel quite balanced for it, and I'm expecting an eventual difficulty spike to come along mid-game and make solo questing no longer an option.
On top of that, skill lists are very limited, so if you want your party to be able to use both Lore and Persuasion, you need to do multiplayer.
Still, Conclave does get some things absolutely right. Important choices during quests are handled with a voting mechanic that's simple, but works. Gear is bought from a pool of Renown, rather than with expendable gold, and your character can be completely respec'd at any time. There are no existing micro-transactions, and there is a pretty solid swath of content.
If you don't have the option of sitting down to play a game of DnD with friends, or you just want something that's less hassle than filling out all those character sheets and deciding on a game master, Conclave can scratch that itch. Otherwise, I'd urge caution with this one, as it's a very specific sort of game and likely not to everyone's taste.

Usagi Yojimbo: Way of the Ronin is a side-scrolling beat-'em-up along the lines of classic arcade games like Renegade. As with all such games, there are some light platforming elements (jumping over pits), but most of the gameplay is avoiding the attacks of a variety of enemies that swarm you, while simultaneously clobbering them with melee attacks.
The levels are framed by a story taken from/inspired by the Stan Sakai "Usagi Yojimbo" comic book series, in which Jei is tasked by the "gods" to destroy a particular mirror, the only thing that can stop these "gods" from escaping from their imprisonment. Once the game begins, the story is told via in-game cut scenes between each level.
This game was originally developed for cellphone touch screens, and then ported to this PC version. The controls using the keyboard are solid, though they can be re-mapped to other keys or you can use a video game controller if you like. But there are some artifacts that are instantly recognizable from mobile games: each level is awarded 1 - 3 stars (and a numeric tally of points) upon completion, with 3 stars being awarded only for a perfect score (killing all opponents but taking no damage). The levels end as soon as you've defeated the last enemy, which is annoying, because it means that you will usually not get all the items/coins from the level. It's single-player only and there aren't multiple save slots, so you can't easily play and compare saved games with friends or family on the same system.
Despite all those drawbacks, I've enjoyed what I've played of Way of the Ronin so far, and will likely continue to play it to the end.

CONAN EXILES is a janky, awkward, mess of a game with core mechanical issues, propped up by its atmosphere, a great IP, and a surprisingly strong modding scene.
To say EXILES is a diamond in the rough would be an understatement. Instead, I want you to imagine a diamond caked in manure, questionable fluids, and flecked with radioactive isotopes. Something great may eventually come of all this, but you have to wonder if it's worth digging through the muck.
To express how frustrating this game can be, I'd like to tell you about my epic quest to create a blacksmithing bench.
A blacksmithing bench requires 50 bricks (made with 100 stone) and 100 iron bars (made with 200 ironstone). Ironstone has a chance of dropping whenever you gather regular stone and has a greater chance of dropping if you find rocks with a dark coloration. After traveling the land for the specific type of rock, I managed to gather five ironstone for every 1,000 stone I gathered over the course of 45 minutes.
This is not fun.
You could argue that high-level equipment should be unattainable for newer characters, that you should work up to it by building up your infrastructure and finding tools that let you gather resources more effectively. The problem is that you need a blacksmithing bench to create any tool that doesn't break within eight minutes. If the game doesn't expect me to create a blacksmithing bench until the late game, then it should make the lower level items more powerful, or create some mid level items for me to try in the meantime.
Granted, all of this can be made easier with the use of thralls: enemies that you literally knock out, drag to your base, and brainwash into your servants. They can take your resources and build things while you're out gathering more, drastically reducing the time and effort required to create new equipment. To craft the tool necessary to create thralls...you need 800 ironstone.
This is the part where I start throwing things.
Even as an early access game, CONAN EXILES is a hard sell at 29.99. If you're a hardcore fan of the IP and simply want to exist within the world of Hyboria, this may have something to offer you. If you plan on setting up your own server with your own friends, then you're more likely to get some mileage out of this.
If you're a modder who plans on improving the game yourself, then you'll definitely have some fun toys to play around with. Otherwise, you may want to wait until the full release. I'm hopeful that EXILES will eventually become a solid title, but hope alone can't make a good game.

Dragon Nest:
Much like the latest Folger's commercial, Dragon Nest doesn't seek to surpass the typical MMO, it looks to land right where every single other one has already innovated, and in most cases, the others have done so in much more engaging and profound ways.  In fact, Dragon Nest doesn't tread any new ground what-so-ever.
Prepare for another... Umm... Adventure?  Dragon Nest features a tired storyline that never engages the player, character classes and progressions you've seen for the last decade (or two), an uninspired crafting and upgrade system that's been done to death by every j/k-RPG on the market, and an overpriced cash shop that attempts to lure you in with functions that remove many of the, simply put, intentional annoyances of trying to play the game, such as pitifully limited inventory space and automatic loot pickups.
Gameplay is nearly completely combat-based, with drawn-out town segments featuring quest gathering and loot selling.  Combat fails to innovate; expect keyboard gymnastics and mouse-flinging typical of this genre, often interrupted by loading screens every few minutes.  Seriously... The loading screens destroy any immersion to be had here.
I would dare to say that the game features some unique artwork and a handful of beautifully modelled monsters and characters, but most of the game centers around scantily-clad female characters (because that's what appeals to the typical gamer, right guys?) which you are introduced to immediately during the game's first loading screen, and 'emo' androgenous males that have left their "provocative" stink on every RPG from the east since Square-Enix.
Music and sound effects are nothing worth mentioning; I was mostly annoyed by the droning music clips that are featured and muted it within an hour of my playtime.  Sound effects are cartoonish and repetitive, and their lack of variety becomes painfully apparent during combat.  It should be no surprise that the voice acting featured in the game is top-notch, cream-of the-crop, steaming garbage-on-a-hot-summer-day that always sounds completely out of context; how these voice actors are cast or maintain careers is completely lost on me.
The story begins with you being some ho-hum walking randomly through the wilderness, and two little girls are attacked by orcs, one being some oracle that you're desperately trying to save for eons, yet every single time you get close, you feel like you should see "Sorry Mario, but the princess is being held in another castle!"  Oh, and there are evil dragons, apparently.  Most NPC dialogue seems to assume you know what's going on in this world, but the game doesn't ever make an earnest attempt at introducing any of the lore to you so that you know what the hell is going on.
Overall, Dragon Nest is a mediocre game; it doesn't innovate in any area, and it's formula is tried and true.  It may be free-to-play, but it makes every possible attempt to make you open your wallet to essentially unbreak itself.  Being a Nexon game, expect their lovely gem 'HackShield' to break and crash your game on a near-hourly basis, often throwing false-positives or simply having some kind of failure that will cause you to lose your progress mid-dungeon.

For those who think this plays like Tony Hawk: IT DOES NOT.
That, and I used exclusively a controller for this game (it was designed with one in mind back when it was released on the dreamcast, ergo that is the best way to play)
Now that we have that covered:
GRAPHICS: The graphics are incredibly dated, but with a certain charm to them. This game was one of the first to use a cell shaded style, which helps this game in this department. If you are looking for cutting edge, look elsewhere. If you don't mind old-school graphics, or just have a rig that can't handle a who lot, this is for you.
GAMEPLAY: As mentioned before, this game does not play like what has become the tradition for skating games. Instead, there are only a small handful of moves that can be performed: Movement (Handled by the left stick, if you are playing with a contoller), jumping, grinding (which happens automatically when you land on a rail), speeding up, and tagging. Once you start tagging, you have to follow on screen prompts with the analog stick in order to finish the pattern and tag a section. There are several areas around each map where you must tag your gangs designs whilst avoiding an over-zealous police force. Before you can paint, however, you must collect cans to fill your paint supply. Sometimes, in between levels, you will be challenged by rivals. If you complete all the challenges, that rival will join your gang and will become playable, each with a unique stat-set.
TLDR; skate around collecting paint cans, then spray-paint stuff while avoiding the cops through various areas.
STORY: In the city of Tokyo-to, gangs called rudies skate around the streets expressing themselves through graffiti. There are various gangs in Tokyo-to, each with a unique visual flair (Noise-Tanks being techno, Love-Shockers being valentines-ish, etc.) Although the gangs differ in style, they all listen to the titular Jet Set Radio, a pirate radio station run by DJ professor K. Not all is well for the Rudies, however, as they must avoid the clutches of an overzealous police force, hell-bent of putting every single one of them in jail through any means necissary
TLDR; Tokyo-esque gangs spray paint to tell the world how unique they are whilst listening to rad music and avoiding crazy police.
Sound: Some of the greatest ever made. Seriously. Search this games soundtrack on youtube and give it a listen.
REPLAYABILITY: The game is arcade-ish in feel and execution, and at the end of each stage you are graded for how well you did. The gameplay is fun in it's own right, and working out the best flow is reason enough to re-play stages
This game is a gem, truly it is. The control scheme may take a while to get used to, but soon you will be skating around tokyo-to like a pro. Biggest piece of advice? Work on flow and use the environment to your advantage.
EXTREMELY RECOMMENDED

Ideal for *Certain* Players
This game has already given me four hours of solid play and I have enjoyed it greatly.
It wont be for everyone. It's a very slow-paced game in comparison to many, because it is turn-based and you are relying on other players if you are in a party. If you are doing something else at the same time and are able to play this as well, that's when I think you will get maximum enjoyment out of it. If you sit there staring at the screen, waiting for all players to finish a round, it could get annoying for you.
I have some fast-paced games (on console, not on this profile, hehe) but I like the pacing of this game. It's very easy-going in that respect, very zen-like...and there sre not many games with this kind of pacing that work in multiplayer RPG's I think - but I might be wrong, just not that I have experianced.
You can create individual characters and then play solo or join a party - or you can flag yourself for people to join you. It has a seamless drop-in/out feature, so if there are gaps in your party, people can come in at any time. You can also leave a party at any time. Up to four players can be in any one party.
This can lead to problems if people drop out during a quest. Quest difficulty ramps up the more players you have, so you could have a situation where you have enough enemies for four players and one drops out, you're in trouble! Or you could wait until someone joins...
The nice thing is that you can stay in the party but put everything on hold...then get emailed when things have started up again. This is ideal for keeping characters with friends, but games could be slow going.
You have to create a profile on the dev's websit, and this will allow you to add party members as friends and invite them to fuuture games.
Peopl have been asking on the forum for the ability to play a party solo (you can only ever control one character) but I do feel this would take a lot away from the game. The idea is that you play as a team and rely on your party to do the right thing, and to help them when they need it. This game comes alive when four people are playing, and the option to party-solo would reduce online availability.
So you have a selection of character classes, races and portraits. The portraits are nice but there are only three for each race. An option to import would be good.
There is a decent selection of skills when you level up, and you can respect at any time (between quests) to try out different abilities. The skills can really make-or-break a battle, so it helps to try out different ones.
The selection of weapons and armour are very limited. There are some random drops from boss fights. I do hope that in the future a greater selections of weapons, armor and trinkets are added because I feel they are missing a big part of what people like about these games. Armor/weapon sets and random added abilities would be great, but I realise that is asking a lot.
The fights themselves are pretty good. Tactical use of movement and abilities comes into play when you are outnumbered and/or faced with powerful foes. There *is* friendly fire, adding another tactical layer: do you run to meet them and activate an AoE ability that affects many of them but also makes you the main target?
Maps are varied and can be effected by fire. Each square between you and them can matter.
I would recommend watching a playthrough to get an idea of the speed of the game. If you are happy with how it plays out time-wise, you will enoy this. I have already got my money's worth from this  - it is a very social game, and has a kind of magic in it that you don't see very often. 10/10 for me.

Quick verdict - AWESOME
Criteria - Early Access with full launch in March 2018 and major feature roadmap clearly laid out
Who Says - Old-time REH/Conan fan and P&P RPer, *not* a console or habitual FPS or MMO (or Steam) player, in The Secret World (also by Funcom) since beta, has looked over the shoulders of players of Ark
Specifics
- sound, music, and visuals are authentic and mature for Conan the Barbarian (no fluorescent cartoony MMO graphics or sounds or floating numbers)
- blood, gore, and non-sexual nudity is authentic and mature (again, for Conan the Barbarian)
- combat is realistic and intuitive (maneuvering for advantage or to find weak areas works)
- still early days (and nerfing to placate whiners may already be happening), but the challenges from the start are hard enough to give real satisfaction when overcome
- skills and progression likewise are a moving target, but so far stay nicely out of the way for those uninterested in builds and stats and suchlike
- crafting is mostly clear and commonsensical
- building is smooth and forgiving, and an enormous amount of fun
- introduction of new features and filling in of content proceeds visibly and regularly consistent with the roadmap
- server performance, loading lag, and so forth are variable as patches come in, but this is to be expected in Early Access and does not prevent enjoyment if that is kept in mind
Compared to? - So far, CE can be characterized as "Ark plus Conan setting"; if that appeals from either angle, try it.
What about? - Having heard and read a massive number of denunciations and gripes, I have yet to see any that hold water; FC has stated up front that this is Early Access, that it's a survival game, that the full game will launch in March 2018, and that various named major features are coming in specified time frames.  Nobody ought to buy or play it until launch if any of that is going to cause them upset.
Am I a shill? - Nope, plenty of gripes and denunciations of Funcom can be had on request, and I am well aware that things could go south at any time in any number of ways (can you say server region lock?) so that I would not be able to play any more except single-player, in which case I'll be posting another review with different conclusions.  ;)

They just added the campaign (a million years later!), so I feel it's finally time to give it a review. Let's get straight to business.
PROS:
+ Fantastic combat. I never really like fighting games because it's all memorizing move sets and weird terminology (I'm talking stuff like SB:Melee fanboys who gush about Wave Flipping Grab Dash Jumpity-Skidoo Slam: Electric Boogaloo moves). This game has no combos to remember, it's all dynamicly done. It's super hard to explain how the combat works, I suppose just watching any video will explain it better than I can. It's faster and reflexes are the most important thing. Defeating your opponent without taking a single scratch is the most satisfying thing ever.
+ As a continuation of above, the health is also fantastic. Instead of health bars, it's all based on a blood and bone structure. You can literally snap your own neck by rolling before you hit the ground. Hit an enemy in the head and you'll probably kill them (and also launch them against a wall in the process). Blood drips off your character. When you slash someone, there's an actual slash mark where you hit them. Enemies clutch their wounds when they are low on health. It's brutal.
+ Parkour. You run fast, jump far, and can climb and wall jump. It's certainly not Mirror's Edge -- I mean, it's not meant to be, this is a fighting game -- but it's still great fun to bound across the landscape and then leap into a kick that smashes someone's face.
+Speaking of landscapes, with the exceptions of the arena maps (for obvious reasons), the maps are expansive and look great. Even if the story missions take place in possible one tenth of the map area, it gives you not only a great vista to look at, but also a wide area to sneak about and scout out the area. The maps you can use for the editor are varied fairly nicely. They're not going to knock your socks off, but they're still interesting and have lots of verticality for running and jumping.
+ The graphics are good. Even on lowest settings, it's not hideous. On high it looks pretty damn good.
+ The arena mode is a good time waster. I feel like that's the wrong word for it (sounds too negative), but what I mean is that it's fun to boot up the game every so often and whack some rabbit butt for an hour or two. There are a couple of arenas to choose from, plus a local versus mode. It's a good time waster in the sense that it takes a while for you to get bored, and even when you do get bored, you don't feel disappointed.
+ You can literally kick someone in midair and launch yourself into the air (and launch your opponent's floppy and now unconscious body into the dirt). Hard to pull off but god are they satisfying... until you launch yourself into a wall and break your neck.
+ Comes with a free copy of Reciever and Low Light Combat. I haven't played the latter, but I can tell you now that the former is a wonderful freebie to get. It definitely alleviates the high price tag of this game, especially if you like shooters with the difficulty of Dark Souls. No, I'm not exaggerating.
EH
~ I can't really talk about FPS stuff with much authority because my computer is getting on in years -- though I might be getting new parts for my PC soon. If I do, I'll definitely boot the game up again and put it on highest settings to see how it fares (and edit my review). I will say that the FPS takes a hit the more NPCs (in combat mode) there are on a screen. One mission has around 6 enemies walking about, and I had 60 FPS. Once I aggro'd them all, it dipped to about 50. The Arena and Story don't throw tons of enemies at you, but if you're planning on using the editor to plonk down more than, say, 15 enemies, be prepared for an FPS hit once combat starts.
~ The story is a port of Lugaru (the game that this studio made before this). If you've played Lugaru and liked it, you'll definitely get some nostalgia feels. Seeing the story in new graphics is great. However, it comes with many of the downsides as well. There's many loading screens -- some levels are literally just 2 minutes long with some dialogue, and then it loads the next level. The story is still just as barely passable as it was 10-ish years ago. Basically, you're gonna play the story just for the challenge rather than anything else. I finished the campaign in about 2 1/2 hours.
~ The story ends on a cliffhanger now (unlike Lugaru), which makes me think there's a "part 2" of the campaign in the works. It took a damn long time for them to make the campaign, which makes me wonder how long it'll take to continue it. Granted, it'll probably be faster since the devs have their footing now, but still.
~ Combat with weapons doesn't feel right. It's not terrible, but it needs work. Unlike hand-to-hand combat, which feels tactical and tense, weapon combat just feels like you're wailing away at an enemy until they fall over, which generally takes about 5 seconds since every weapon except the dagger is essentially an instant kill.
~ There is stealth, but it's not the best. What makes it unfortunate is that some story missions essentially require it so that you don't take on 5 enemies at once, but it can be trial-and-error. Better than nothing I guess.
~ It's early access, so there are still bugs and grahpical glitches. None of them so far were game- or immersion-breaking, but they're still a bit annoying to see.
~ The editor is hit-and-miss. It doesn't explain much, and while it's not that difficult to use once you look up a tutorial or two, it's still a bit slow and you'll have to put a lot of effort into your map in order for it to be anything more than just a silly little battle you slapped together.
~ Wolves can only be damaged by weapons and jump kicks. I can sorta see why, but still. Eh.
CONS
- No online multiplayer. Hopefully it will come. I doubt it, because this game requires split-second reactions, which are hampered by internet.
- Speaking of "latency", there are MANY frustrating times where blocking wouldn't work, especially during the campaign. This new update did change the combat in a lot of ways, and I'm hoping it didn't affect the reaction time of your character. Sometimes I'd be blocking perfectly and he'd still stand there like a bucket of jell-o. Before, I could fight my way through two-on-one battles easily; now a one-on-one can be a hit-or-miss. Strangely enough, it only seems to rear its ugly head once weapons are in the mix. Hand-to-hand combt is (largely) still the same.
- Quarterstaves. Oh my god. Oh. My. GOD. At the risk of sounding like "volvo plz nerf", they really need to be taken down a notch. When I'm fighting an enemy with a staff, I literally cannot block them. At all. All I can do is try to do the jump-kick. Strangely enough, once I have the staff, it sucks. I think the combat AI for staff attacks is too powerful. Avoid at all costs.
- It's been in development for like.... 8 years or something. There are times where an update comes out that's just "new lighting" and once every so often there's a massive content drop (such as now). Still, it's arduously slow. I don't have a huge problem with it, but for those of you who want something substantial, this can be a turn off.
- The price is high. If it were half the price I'd 1000% reccomend this game even with all the bugs and stuff. As it stands, the price means you'll really have to want this game. If you like fighting games, try it.
SUMMARY
A fantastic fighting game featuring rabbits, wolves, cats and dogs, and even weird mice, finally with a rudimentary campaign, several great arena maps, and a level editor. While it looks great and runs quite well, it's a slow-to-update game that might not have enough content for most folks out there to warrant a 30-buck purchase. It's not the best game I have, but it's one of the most ambitious and interesting for sure. I recommend it.

Gear Up is a relatively new addition to the growing "tank pilot" games, and has many of the features you find in similar games. You build a tank from a selection of various parts that you can buy with in-game currency. There is a VAST selection of different turrets, different builds, wheels, and weapons to choose from, allowing for almost complete customization of your own tank.
The game modes vary from Conquest (drive near towers and capture them all to win) to Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, and sandbox-style lobbies. The maps are where the game shines, many of them featuring enough ramps to rival a Tony Hawk game. They are very small maps, allowing for very quick games regardless of mode. However, the game falls apart when it comes to controls.
Those used to tank games will be pleased to find that the turret moves independant of the actual tank itself, and while I might be biased (because I hate this movement style), I find it very clunky at best. This may have been due to server lag, but even with my settings all the way down, the framerate drops made the tank very difficult to control. Aiming is another problem, with many shots falling shy, even when point-blank.
As for building tanks, all I can attest to is that the "demo" version (although it's advertised as an FTP full game) doesn't allow for much building outside of what is provided. You're often prompted to buy the full game in order to get more spaces to save parts, but the price just simply isn't right. All in all, if you like tank games, you might very well enjoy this TF2 styled tank game, and the FTP version is extensive enough to allow for full play with minor limitations. Otherwise, steer clear of this in favor of better tank games (ie. World of Tanks).

I'm usually pretty decent at games, and can figure out how to play pretty quickly. I mean, I've been playing video games since I was 5. This game, though, is overly complicated to the point of insanity. You have to micromanage everything, and sometimes the game just throws a curveball at you you'll never expect. Like why is my left click suddenly attack instead of walk, or vice versa? I don't know and it doesn't explain it. An Assassin comes up looking for the Red Prince and wipes your party in two turns? Cool, why not. Party member decides not to move and you get in a fight with one party member 200 yards away? Yeah, that's a thing. It just doesn't make sense.
There are positives. The combat, when it works, is pretty good. It's solid turn based combat. It is kinda infuriating when you try to shoot an enemy and your character, for no real reason, decides to walk towards them through fire and poison, but apparently you have to deal with that. Loot make sense, even if it isn't explained very well. The crafting is cool and doesn't seem to have any negatives. The trading is pretty cool. Instead of saying "Item X costs 40g" it's "Item X is worth 40g". You can offer your own items and gold to buy it. If you want to buy boots worth 5g, you can offer up a 3g book and  2g to buy it. If you offer, say, a 10g book for it, the merchant will like you more. Pretty cool.
Overall, I can't recommend the game. It's just way too complicated. Not for the sake of fun, it seems, but just for the sake of making the game harder. I'm all for hard games, but this one doesn't make any sense. Dark Souls, for instance, doesn't just change on you in the middle of a fight. This does, and I can not stand that. In the two hours I played, I did not get a single moment of enjoyment out of it

I waited years to get this game. I watched every video iDubbbz made about this game and I fell in love. I read the comics, I followed the lore, and I was a fanatic. After a few years of wanting to buy it, I finally caved in and coughed over the $30 that the devs simply refuse to lower.
There's barely anything to it. A few flat environments with random rocks everywhere, a couple enemies here and there, and that's all. Also an editing mode that crashes every time you try to use it. If it was free (as it should be) I wouldn't have any complaints. But this game has been in development since 2008. Every single update they've made is just "bug fixes" but I've seen more bugs in my few hours of playing than any other game I have ever played. It crashed every single time I played it. I don't think I ever legitimately exited the game. I fell through the ground, walls, you name it. The game simply does not work. It's a buggy, lackluster, empty, forgotten mess.
One of the two things this game had going for it was the combat, which is a nightmare to work with a keyboard. Sometimes you die in a single punch, other times you can fall off a cliff and get stabbed without dying. It's a interesting system when it works, but it's an ungodly amount of hard when the computer blocks everything you do and sees your movements before you can even make them. When it worked, I definitely had fun. But navigation with an active, fast-paced combat system on a keyboard just doesn't work.
The other thing this game had going for it was the modding community, which has been dead for a year. I can barely get any of the mods to function correctly. When they do, it's only a matter of time before the game crashes.
I really wanted to like this game, but the fact that the developers can charge $30 for an unfinished, neglected mess of a "game" is an insult. If they want this to work, make it a free demo, support the modding community, and add a story mode. Or they could add an adventure mode with missions on the (empty) maps. Or they could add anything that offers real value.
I hate this game so much I left a review a few hours after buying it. I *really* wanted to like it, but the negatives far outweighed the positives. Don't buy this. Especially not for $30. At this point, it's not worth any price tag. It's a joke, and the developers just don't care.

Computer game designer Chris Crawford, founder of The Journal of Computer Game Design, has attempted to define the term game using a series of dichotomies:
1 Creative expression is art if made for its own beauty, and entertainment if made for money.
2 A piece of entertainment is a plaything if it is interactive. Movies and books are cited as examples of non-interactive entertainment.
3 If no goals are associated with a plaything, it is a toy. (Crawford notes that by his definition, (a) a toy can become a game element if the player makes up rules, and (b) The Sims and SimCity are toys, not games.) If it has goals, a plaything is a challenge.
4 If a challenge has no "active agent against whom you compete," it is a puzzle; if there is one, it is a conflict. (Crawford admits that this is a subjective test. Video games with noticeably algorithmic artificial intelligence can be played as puzzles; these include the patterns used to evade ghosts in Pac-Man.)
5 Finally, if the player can only outperform the opponent, but not attack them to interfere with their performance, the conflict is a competition. (Competitions include racing and figure skating.) However, if attacks are allowed, then the conflict qualifies as a game.
Crawford's definition may thus be rendered as[original research?]: an interactive, goal-oriented activity made for money, with active agents to play against, in which players (including active agents) can interfere with each other.

Tengami is a light adventure/puzzle game set inside a pop up book with a Japanese aesthetic.  The puzzles mostly involve flipping pages, which changes the terrain. The game is only an hour and a half, so it's a nice game to play in one sitting.  I wish it had one more area, but the game is satisfying without overstaying it's welcome.  I say check it out if you just want to play something a bit relaxing.

As the sequel to BG1, BG2 picks up on new adventures with old and new characters alike. Quests will take you through the huge world of DnD as you uncover more of the story left off from BG1.
My personal favorite feature is the ability to import a character from BG1 to use right from BG2. This is not required, but it adds more sentiment to your character in my opinion, as well as adds some flow to the game and story.
The graphics and gameplay are roughly the same, but the gameplay is expanded on a bit more simply due to the fact that all characters are higher level and; therefore, have better rewards for completing tasks.
BG2 is so well done that it feels like all of the Baldur's Gate games are one big adventure waiting to be played and finished in any way you choose. Would definitely recommend.

• Was it just me, or can you not refill empty water bottles? I was dehydrating fast and staring longingly at the numerous puddles/lakes I kept passing, spamming every button I had in a desperate attempt to fill my bottles. On a small map, I quickly ran out of things to quench my thirst and could not, for the life of me, find any sort of drink from looting.
• While inside of a house, sometimes I was affected by the dust storm and sometimes I wasn't.

Other than those few things, I'm definitely going to put some real hours into this game. Just playing for a few minutes sparked my creativity. I'd love a purely sandbox mode if more building options are added, since I can already see wood and stone becoming a problem. Currently, trees don't seem to be a renewable resource.

Pros: undoes the excessive streamlining of controls that mars the series up to this point. You can actually fight dozens of enemies in a single fight, and for discount Arkham combat, it's not bad. Slightly more actual enemy variety. Decent mechanics for combat, acrobatics, puzzles, traps, and great balance between how much they appear in this, albeit few to no real changes or additions. Saving Checkpoints are very well-placed. Great design all the way... everything looks and sounds great. Pretty much every good element from the series is in this, and they almost all work.
Cons: as is typical for midquels: irrelevant and, yeah, forgettable, through and through: story, location, conflict, enemies, characters(other than the Prince), etc. Watered down traps. Plays it too safe. Lazy, half-hearted attempt at recapturing the, well, magic, of the Sands of Time trilogy: it especially wants to be the first of those three, with an opening way too similar. Why does control of the four elements essentially amount to a handful of parlor tricks? Bland magic powers, and they replace, rather than being added to, the use of Time manipulation during combat: all that's left is Rewinding(which in this doesn't comes from the Sands of Time. How many different magic sources in ancient Persia let you rewind time?). Stiff control of the Prince, especially with the Rewind, which feels like you have to rewind a certain amount, rather than you pinpointing the second you want to proceed from. Being knocked down half the time glitches to where it's difficult to get back up for a few seconds. Enemy AI kind of just... stops if enemies aren't in a group, and a few meters away from you. Ah, Oblivion.
A grand journey. Granted, it is not Morrowind. It is Skyrim neither. All the Elder Scroll's series games receive lot of talk on the internet. Usually its fighting about which one is the best one. Oldschool / hardcore gamers like to point out Arena or Morrowind, casual gamers love Skyrim. It is Oblivion though, which I am going to review now.
Oblivion had astonishing graphics when it came originally in 2006. Nowadays its very outdated, but the graphics mod still make it look good to this day! And this is for most of the Bethesda's games, thanks to their understading to the importance of good modding support. Modding can make a good game to great one.
Oblivion has pretty generic and cliche main storyline, but the side quests are where it is at it's best. Very interesting characters, lore and missions. Brotherhood of Dark, Glarthir's paranoia, mage stuck on dream world, man missing in a painting... Amazing guests and mods add even more of them. And not only quests, but bunch of weapons, redone (better and sharper) textures, better sound world etc.
Speaking of sound... Music is very, very good in the game, as it is in The Elder Scrolls games in general. Oblivion however has been stuck in my head as a best one. I love how easily you can add your own choice of music too and even for the right spots (battle music, wilderness music, dungeon music,...). It is such a wonderful feeling coming back to Oblivion once again, walking down the roads and finally coming in to Anvil or perhaps to Skingrad, listening relaxing soundtrack and just wondering around, talking to townsfolk. It is a fantastic feeling, especially if you hold that special place in your heart for Oblivion.
Scenery and cities are way better than in Skyrim, cities like Anvil, Imperial City and Cheydinhal actually are interesting and beautiful.
Books (if you like to read) are very interesting as well and can give you plenty of new information about quests or just lore in general.
Factions are mostly great, Dark Brotherhood especially. Thieves guild is pretty interesting too. Mage's guild was disappointing, as it was in Skyrim too.  Fighters Guild was decent. There are other (minor) factions too, some joinable, some not.
Arena is a wonderful place to bet (and lose) some money or just fighting yourself. Imperial City - what a place.
Sure, animation can be pretty bad, technology outdated and it has plenty of bugs and crashes (as does every Bethesda game) - but if you can play with these flaws you might have a great time ahead. I know I've had.
Overall, its a great experience with flaws. It is not the most hardcore RPG, but not as casual as some of the others we have nowadays. There is a chance that you may or may not like the game. Give it a chance though.

Don't want to read the entire review?  Just read this: Yes.
American Truck Simulator is an amazing, challenging game designed for a relaxing experience.
Now, I know what you're thinking.  "Nate, why the heck would a game about work be fun?  I work enough already!"  It's great.  There's just something about commanding a huge tractor pulling 50k pounds of freight at 90mph that's exciting.
Don't want the grind?  I didn't either.  I downloaded a free profile with about 60 million dollars.  "Nate, that defeats the purpose!" No, I paid for a fun, relaxing driving sim.  I didn't want to worry about money issues, I just wanted to make deliveries and run my company.  I have now brought that profile from 60mil to 138mil as of this moment from my work and having my company at the largest possible at this point in the game.  I can afford repairs if I have an accidental crash or if the AI (Artificial UNintelligence) cars ram me.  I can afford any truck with any upgrades I want.  It's great.
Pros:
-Semi-Realistic driving sim (as long as you don't ram the invisible walls)
-Easy-to-use, straight forward interface
-Extremely ‘replayable’ (I mean, just look at my hours)
-Great customization of truck exteriors with many options (and, according to SCS, many more to come)
Cons:
-The AI cars need a bit more common sense.  It gets annoying when you lose $3,000 on a job just because a car rammed your trailer when you pull out of a gas station or something.
-The game needs more development.  I will give credit to SCS.  They have a small team working on a BIG game.  But, compared to ETS2 (Euro Truck Sim 2), ATS is under-developed.
-Interior customization could be expanded.  As a professional truck driver, you are going to be spending lots of time in the cab.  After about 50 hours straight in the exact same cabin, it's going to get a bit boring.
Conclusion:
ATS is a great, laid-back pass-time game.  With a large map in a great setting with thick forests, large deserts, and a beautiful coastline, the game has many different environments that make it hard to get tired of.  While the game is somewhat under-developed, SCS Software is quite obviously working hard to update it frequently.  I find this game worth every penny and more.

Now, on to the review! If you want action-oriented MMORPG with flashy / cool-looking moves then Dragon Nest is the game for you. You have your basic rpg classes in the form of Warrior, Archer, Cleric and Sorcerer. The other available classes are Tinkerer (a sort of engineer) and Dancer. Upcoming classes are Assassin and Lancer.
The world is instance type wherein areas (including towns) are separated like dungeons. Although, the towns are very big themselves. The dungeons get bigger and bigger as you progress into the game. Lastly, the environment details are well made and numerous.
You gain exp in the game by killing mobs in dungeons, clearing the dungeons themselves and completing NPC quests. When you gain a level you get skill points which you can use to unlock your skills. Core stats are pre-set by the game. Pretty much a standard level and skill system. There's a nifty feature wherein you can see a demo of a skill first before you get it. That way, you can see if you'll like the skill or not.
Exp is very fast from Level 1 to 50. 50 to 70 is when the grind starts but still doable and not boring because of the awesome combat system. If you're a hardcore player that can sit a whole day in front of a computer then you can get to the level cap in a week or so. If you're a casual player like me, at level 50 onwards you can gain 2 levels a day or 4 while still being able to stand up and do other stuff. That's pretty fast by today's MMORPG standards.
I won't go into the other details of the game because to be honest, it's very big even though it's instanced type. I just provided feedback on the basic features that players tend to look forward to.
So again, if you're into action and flashy moves, this is the game for you. You're not really missing anything by not dowloading the Steam version so go the Nexon website I provided on this review and get their client instead. Trust me, it'll be less hassle in the long run.

The berries appear to have no point, except to be hoarded at your little Woodle house so nobody else can have any. Also, be careful going up the stairs. When I was at that 'hub' between worlds, I managed to trip (read: drag woodle face first) up the stairs. It's those adorable, low-quality legs.
I didn't want to judge a book by it's cover, and when I saw it on Greenlight, I thought I'd give it a chance.
Is it worth it? Probably not. Did I get some amusement out of it? Sure. I'm always up for bright and shiny collectathons. As long as they are marginally functional, which Woodle is, I'm in. (Don't get too inspired to jump while in the left-right moving platform on level 1.. you'll go through the floor! And the camera angles? OH LAWD!)
My recommendation? Pick it up uber-cheap and farm it for cards, or if you've got a kid in the house, stick them on the controller for a bit. After all, it's always better to beat on unsuspecting ladybugs, sheep, turtles and other adorable creatures in a videogame than in real life, right?
Edited to add after completion of game: The inability to move the camera is my main pet peeve. And holy crap the game is so EASY. Don't like where you're at? Walk off the edge, there's no penalty. Just collected a faerie tear and don't want to jump back through the puzzle you did to get there? let something hit you, you'll start over with the tear and no penalty. At least it's relaxing. The greatest game ever made.
I was going to preface the review with the greatest WCRPG ever made, or perhaps the greatest RPG ever made but neither of those really describe the scope of this game's promise.  Sure, you'll probably end up having more hours in other games.  If you play a multiplayer game and you're playing for the people, you aren't really going to credit the game for those relationships but as I stare at my original BG II: SoA case sitting on my shelf, I'm supremely happy that I bought the Steam Enhanced Edition.  BG II quite simply has everything you can want out of a video game.
Unlike so many RPGs, BG II has the perfect balance of linear story, and branching exploration.  In fact, it's one of the few RPGs I've ever played that has successfully achieved that goal.  In BG II, you pursue a tense and captivating story, but the game allows you to explore Amn and the surrounding countryside at your leisure.  The result is an experience that doesn't feel like a plot train, nor like a meandering sandbox devoid of purpose.  Every main quest and its satellite components fit neatly in the plot mythos, creating a truly organic and wonderful experience.
Thematically, the location of Faerun is as rich and varied as high traditional high fantasy can be, rivaling even that of Tolkien's creations.  The game features a large, exotic sister city to Baldur's Gate (Amn), rife with political intrigue and a myriad of hidden secrets.  Walk past a bar a dozen times, and yet on the thirteenth a new adventure allows you to find an underground cellar with new, untold dangers.  The cavernous Underdark, hidden druidic groves, pirate ships, desolate islands, dark forests, castles of every imagination, ruins and even planar travel await you in this game.
The variety is staggering but theme alone doesn't propel this game's story.  A plot full of surprises, twists, moments of worry, panic and dread make this game something that you experience, not play.  The game organically develops, unfurling the finale like petals in a flower, instead of so many other, formulaic RPG plots.  Perhaps the characterization however, is the game's strongest storytelling element.  A diverse array of characters exist, both comically memorable and fearsomely grim and they not only interact with the protagonist but also with each other, with staggering consequences.
After playing through BG II and its expansion ToB, and logging over 240 hours with the original release, I am now happy to introduce other gamers to this forgotten classic.  With rich and deep tacitcal gameplay, endless customizeability and properly functioning multiplayer, everyone can now enjoy this gem of a game.  And because the game has such low system requirements, no one is left out.
I played this game 15 years ago, as an adult but even as a grownup, I was still transformed by the depth and breadth of this amazing gaming experience.  Fifteen years later, middle aged as I am, I still appreciate what a special title this really is.  From art design, to music, to gameplay this title will give you exactly what you put in.
Buy it, sit down, steep yourself in the lore.  Go slow and luxuriate in the rich tale that will unfold.  As a gamer, I can think of no better gift to my peers than to recommend this game.
Must buy.

It's a pretty fun game but there are three main flaws that can ruin the entire experience. The first two flaws have basically been confirmed by the devs as game features so they probably won't be removed. You'll most likely enjoy the game if you can ignore these flaws. If you can't, it's going to suck.
Flaw number 1: the combat gets really counter intuitive. At the lower levels, you see a lot of people fighting how you'd expect two medieval dudes to fight. Both face each other exchanging blows while attempting to parry and aiming for weak spots. Slightly up the ladder of skill, you see people doing what is called dragging. A swing will follow the camera of the swinger so people will drag their mouse into their attack to speed it up or away from their attack to slow it down. This often causes the opponant to parry at the wrong time so it's used quite a bit. The speed is capped so there aren't any beyblade fighters. Just thought I'd be clear about that. This is all pretty intuitive and makes sense for the most part. It's stops being intuitive once you run into the ballerinas. Ballerinas are players who abuse the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of dragging with slow weapons. They'll start the attack looking away from you and flail around in order to hit you. They often spin around in circles which gave them the name. This would be fine if the animation looked decent. it instead just looks like they are glitching out which leads a lot of players to believe they are hacking. You can counter it but it takes some time. It's annoying and it drives a ton of players out of the game. There is no use complaining about it on the steam forums. The mods there will just call you bad and say this garbage tactic is a legit strategy despite it looking like a laggy glitchfest. The only good news I can provide is that not everyone uses it so just throw all of your hatchets/knives at those who do.
Flaw number 2: Archers are pretty OP. In a game of melee combat, you have high damage archers who can one hit kill you from the safety of their spawn. The archer class can also be deadly in duels if you actually manage to get close enough. They have a slight disadvantage as they are slow and don't have much/any armor but they can still fight just fine. Most archers that you will run into will be complete garbage. Most don't bother trying to melee fight and can't hit the broad side of a barn. Issue is, they are balanced for these people. They deal a ton of damage because they aren't balanced for people who can aim. Once you find someone who can aim and duel, the only solution is to hide behind a shield or leave.
Flaw 3: Hit reg is pretty terrible. A lot of times, you'll see an enemy blade go straight through you but you take no damage. You will have several moments where you are pretty certain that you cut straight through some other guy. You will find youself saying "Well that should have been a block" several times. The hit detection is just bad at times.
Update: More flaws? Why not! The kick key just doesn't work at times. I'll have enough stamina and I'm using a keyboard that works but the game goes "nah, you didn't kick". Rebound it. Still doesn't want to work when it's supposed to. Suicide key doesn't want to work half the time. Not sure why. Just have to spam it until I eventually die or suicide rush the enemy with fists. Pretty disapointed with this game.
